 ix

1 INTRODUCTION
Argonne National Laboratory (ANL) operated four split-table critical experiment facilities, ZPR-
3, ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR, between 1955 and 1990. ZPR is the abbreviation for Zero Power
Reactor, and ZPPR was the abbreviation for Zero Power Plutonium Reactor which was changed
to Zero Power Physics Reactor in the 1980s due to negative views on Plutonium breeding and
proliferation concerns. ZPR-3, ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR were four reactors in a series of zero
power (or lower power reactors) designed at Argonne in the 1950s and 1960s.
The first ANL split-table critical experiment facility, ZPR-3 or ZPR-III, was constructed at
Argonne’s facilities in southeast Idaho. These facilities were frequently referred to as Argonne
National Laboratory-West or ANL-W until they became part of Idaho National Laboratory in
October 2005. The first ZPR-3 assembly program began in 1955, and the last ZPR-3 critical
assembly program ended in 1970.
ZPR-6 or ZPR-VI, the second Argonne split-table facility, was constructed in the early 1960s in
Building 315 at the Argonne National Laboratory site in Illinois. ZPR-6 operated from 1963 until
1982. Until the formation of Idaho National Laboratory, the Argonne site in Illinois was often
referred to as Argonne National Laboratory-East or ANL-E. After the formation of Idaho National
Laboratory, the ANL-E designation became meaningless.
The third Argonne critical experiment facility, ZPR-9 or ZPR-IX, was constructed in Building 315
at ANL-E in parallel with or shortly after completion of ZPR-6. ZPR-9 operated from 1964 until
1981. The reactor cells, or rooms, housing the ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 machines were located on
opposite sides of a common workroom and vault, and the same staff operated both facilities. ZPR-
6 and ZPR-9 used the same inventory of materials for critical experiments.
ZPPR, the fourth and largest of Argonne’s critical experiment facilities, was constructed at ANL-
W in the late 1960s. The first ZPPR critical experiment program began in 1969. The last ZPPR
critical experiment program ended in 1990.
The word “assembly” is used in two contexts in this document. When “Assembly” appears with
an uppercase “A” and is followed by a number, it refers to a specific extended experimental
program consisting of a series of related experiments or measurements performed on the same
basic configuration or on minor variations of the same basic configuration. The words “assembly
program” refer to a related series of measurements performed on the same basic configuration or
on minor variations of the same basic configuration in general. The duration of an assembly
program could range from several weeks in early ZPR-3 programs to many months or even a few
years, depending on the extent and complexity of the measurements to be performed. Examples
of assembly programs are ZPR-3 Assembly 12 and ZPPR Assembly 19.
Note that the ZPPR convention for identifying assembly programs differed from the convention
use at ANL’s other three facilities. An assembly program at ZPR-3, ZPR-6 or ZPR-9 was
identified as either ZPR-M Assembly N or ZPR-M/N where M was 3, 6, or 9 and N was the
assembly program number. Assembly program N at ZPPR was identified as ZPPR Assembly N
or ZPPR-N. For example, the 10th assembly program at ZPR-6 was identified as ZPR-6 Assembly
10 or ZPR-6/10, and the 10th assembly program at ZPPR was identified as ZPPR Assembly 10 or
ZPPR-10.

 1

When “assembly” appears with a lowercase “a” and is not followed by the word “program” or by
a number, it is a general term referring to a reactor configuration, e.g., critical assembly. In general,
the distinction between “Assembly” and “assembly” will be clear from the context.
The term “ZPR/ZPPR” in this report means that the material in a paragraph or section applies
broadly to all four machines.
Critical experiment facilities are operated for various purposes. Some critical experiments are
designed to provide basic nuclear data in a particular energy range or for particular materials.
Some critical experiment facilities were intended primarily to provide data to support the criticality
safety of production operations at the site where the critical experiment facility was located. The
critical experiment facilities at Oak Ridge National Laboratory and Rocky Flats, for example,
primarily supported operations with fissionable material at those sites.
Argonne’s four critical experiment facilities were originally designed to support the development
of sodium cooled fast reactors (LMFRs, LMFBRs or LMRs). The experiments conducted at
Argonne’s ZPR/ZPPR facilities ranged from basic fast reactor physics measurements to very
detailed simulations of specific reactor designs and various configuration possibilities. The
ZPR/ZPPR measurements provided data to support the designs of EBR-II, Fast Flux Test Facility
(FFTF), Southwest Experimental Fast Oxide Reactor (SEFOR) and the Clinch River Breeder
Reactor (CRBR) among others. Because all of the machines were flexible, there are several
instances where the ZPR/ZPPR machines were used to model fast reactors not considering sodium
coolant (gas cooled, nuclear rockets, etc…).
Because there are no operating critical experiment facilities that can support present day fast
reactor design, some of the accumulated ZPR/ZPPR data is deemed vital to support present day
reactor design efforts. One goal of this document is to provide information regarding creation of
detailed high-fidelity models of ZPR/ZPPR experimental measurements and analysis of those

Section 2 provides an overview of the four ZPR/ZPPR facilities. Sections 3 – 6 discuss the four
categories of records that are needed to construct a model of a ZPR/ZPPR configuration and how
the records in each category are used. Section 7 discusses various types of measurements that
were performed at the ZPR/ZPPR facilities. Note that the set of experiments discussed in Section
7 is not a complete set of all experiments performed at the ZPR/ZPPR facilities between 1955 and
1990. In some cases, the experiments that were performed are no longer relevant to fast reactor
design. In other cases, either the available information is not sufficient to construct models of the
experiments or the measured data are not available.

 2

2 GENERAL CHARACTERISTICS OF THE ZPR AND ZPPR FACILITIES
The general characteristics and operating principles of ZPR-3, ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR were very
similar. Each reactor consisted of a split-table machine in a large room or reactor cell. Each table
of the split-table machine supported an array or matrix of nominally square stainless steel tubes
referred to as matrix tubes. To simulate a fast reactor, the matrix tubes were filled with drawers
containing plates of various materials to represent the average composition in each reactor zone
(core, radial blanket, axial blanket, radial reflector, axial reflector).
The most obvious differences were the sizes of the four machines and the increasing detail and
sophistication of the experiments and reactor simulations conducted over the operating history of
the ZPR/ZPPR facilities. Table 2.1provides a comparison of the sizes of the four split-table
machines. The expansion of the ZPR-6 array from 45 x 45 to 65 x 65 began after the end of the
ZPR-6/7 program. This expansion was intended to support installation of a large heated zone in
the center of the matrix, but the heated zone was never installed due to changing program priorities.
 Table 2.1. Comparison of Matrices and Matrix Tubes.

 Machine Array Matrix Tube External Matrix Tube
 Dimensions, in Thickness, in
                         ZPR-3             31 x 31 2.1835 x 2.1755 x 33.5         0.040
                  ZPR-6 (original)         45 x 45        2.175 x 2.175 x 48      0.040
                 ZPR-6 (expanded) 65 x 65                 2.175 x 2.175 x 48      0.040
                         ZPR-9             45 x 45        2.175 x 2.175 x 48      0.040
                   ZPPR (original)         53 x 55        2.177 x 2.277 x 48      0.040
                  ZPPR (expanded)          77 x 77        2.175 x 2.175 x 60      0.040
Three principal types of assemblies were built on the ZPR/ZPPR machines. Clean physics
benchmarks were designed to test the fast reactor physics data and analytical or computational
methods of the time. Consequently, the geometry and composition were intentional keep as simple
as possible to simplify analysis. There were no (or few) internal structures present in the core,
blanket or reflector of a clean physics benchmark.
An engineering benchmark included more reactor details than a clean physics benchmark, but an
engineering benchmark was less detailed than an engineering mockup.
An engineering mockup was a highly detailed simulation of a realistic reactor design. Engineering
mockups include details such as zoned cores, internal blankets (radial and axial), radial and axial
external blankets, radial and axial reflectors, simulated control rods (inserted and withdrawn) and
other structures. Engineering mockups were sometimes used to provide data to support the designs
of actual reactors such as EBR-II and FFTF.
The desired average composition in each region of the simulated reactor was achieved by loading
the matrix tubes with drawers containing small rectangular plates of different materials such as
plutonium, highly enriched uranium (HEU), depleted uranium (DU), stainless steel, graphite,

 3

sodium, etc. Most non-reactive plates such as stainless steel and tungsten were bare material.
Reactive materials such as sodium and hazardous materials such as plutonium were clad in
stainless steel. Uranium metal plates had a protective coating to prevent corrosion and material
loss during handling. Some other plate types also had a protective coating.
The fuel plates used at the ZPR/ZPPR facilities were HEU metal, DU metal, clad Pu-Al alloy metal
and clad Pu-U-Mo alloy metal. Most of the assembly programs performed were based upon oxide-
fueled or carbide-fueled reactor designs. Carbide fuel was simulated by mixing columns of fuel
plates with columns of graphite plates in the core drawers. The graphite plates provided the carbon
required to simulate UC or PuC fuel. Oxide fuel was simulated by mixing columns of fuel plates
with columns of iron oxide (Fe2O3) plates and/or columns of depleted U3O8 plates in the core and
blanket drawers. The oxygen in the Fe2O3 plates and U3O8 plates provided the oxygen required to
simulate UO2 or PuO2. Columns of stainless steel plates plus the stainless steel in the drawers and
matrix tubes provided the stainless steel to simulate fuel cladding and the structural material in
fuel assemblies and other reactor components. Columns of stainless steel-clad sodium plates
simulated the sodium coolant.
By carefully mixing columns of fuel plates, depleted uranium plates, stainless steel plates, sodium
plates and plates of other materials, the ZPR/ZPPR staff could simulate the average composition
in the core, radial blanket, axial blanket, radial reflector and axial reflector of the fast reactor
concepts and designs of interest when the ZPR/ZPPR machines operated.
2.1 ZPR-3 Fast Critical Facility
Loading of ZPR-3 Assembly 1 (ZPR-3/1) began in the autumn of 1955. The final ZPR-3 program,
ZPR-3 Assembly 63 (ZPR-3/63) ended in December 1970, and the ZPR-3 facility was then shut
down. Note that for any assembly program N, ZPR-3/N is the conventional shorthand for ZPR-3
Assembly N. ZPR-3 assembly programs ranged in length from several weeks to approximately 12
months. The longer programs were generally engineering benchmarks or engineering mockups.
After ZPR-3 was shut down, the fuel plates and some of the more valuable non-fuel plates were
transferred to the other ZPR/ZPPR facilities, but most of the non-fuel plates in the ZPR-3 inventory
were discarded. Some of the experimental equipment may have been transferred to the other
ZPR/ZPPR facilities. It is likely that the ZPR-3 drawers were discarded. The matrix tubes, tables
and much of the other ZPR-3 hardware were discarded.
The initial ZPR-3 material inventory was limited. There were no plutonium plates or sodium plates
in the initial inventory. The fuel for all early ZPR-3 assembly programs was a combination of
highly enriched uranium plates and depleted uranium plates. ZPR-3/37 was the first assembly
program to use Pu-Al plates (clad plates of Pu-Al alloy). Pu-U-Mo plates (clad plates containing
Pu-U-Mo alloy) were first used for the SEFOR program. The initial ZPR-3 plate inventory did
not include sodium plates, so sodium was simulated by aluminum plates that were drilled or
perforated to approximate the density of sodium in early ZPR-3 programs. The atomic mass of
aluminum is close to the atomic mass of sodium, and the holes drilled in the aluminum plates
allowed the average density of those plates to match the density of sodium reasonably well. Given
the limitations on modeling and analysis at that time, this substitution was probably not a major
source of error in the analysis of the experiments.

 4

Early ZPR-3 assembly programs studied basic physics parameters such as critical mass as a
function of effective 235U enrichment for mixtures of HEU and DU plates with various diluent
materials such as plates of steel, graphite and/or aluminum. Later ZPR-3 assembly programs were
intended to support the design and/or operation of specific reactors including EBR-I, Fermi-A,
Fermi-B, PARET, SEFOR, FTR/FFTF and EBR-II. During the design phase, Fast Test Reactor
(FTR) was the name of FFTF.
Modeling and computing capabilities were very limited in the late 1950s and early 1960s, so
models of early ZPR-3 assemblies were focused on providing one-dimensional sphere, cylinder
and slab models usable with the modeling capabilites at the time. The concept of buckling was
used to account for leakage in the cases of cylinders and slabs. Obviously, many simplifications
and corrections were required to convert the three-dimensional reactor configuration that was built
and measured to a one- or two-dimensional model that could be analyzed with the tools available
at that time. To test the effects of required approximations, the experimenters built a simulated
slab, simulated cylinder and simulated sphere in ZPR-3/6. Measurements of the simulated slab,
cylinder and sphere in ZPR-3/6 provided data to assess the effects of the modeling approximations
required in more realistic reactor configurations. The pseudo-sphere configuration in ZPR-3/6 was
rebuilt with different materials and different effective uranium enrichment in at least one later
ZPR-3 assembly program.
As computer hardware, computer software and analytical techniques improved, it became feasible
to construct two dimensional models, so later ZPR-3 models tended to be either R-Z or X-Y
models. The limitation to one- or two-dimensional models for analysis is a principal reason why a
cross section of a ZPR-3 assembly generally shows an approximately cylindrical core with an
approximately annular radial blanket and/or radial reflector.
2.1.1 Physical Characteristics of ZPR-3
The ZPR-3 fast critical facility was a horizontal split-table type machine consisting of a large, cast-
steel bed supporting two tables or carriages, one stationary and the other movable. Details of the
ZPR-3 facility are given in the hazard evaluation report for the facility [1]. A pictorial view of the
ZPR-3 facility is shown in Figure 2.1. Each table was 100 in (2.54 m) wide and 67 in (1.70 m)
long. Stainless steel square tubes, nominally 2 in (51 mm) on a side (inside dimension), 0.040 in
(1 mm) thick, and 33.5 in (851 mm) long, were stacked horizontally on each table to form a 31-
row by 31-column square “honeycomb” matrix. Each 31 x 31 array of matrix tubes was pressed
tightly together and clamped in place on its table by steel structural members.
Many details regarding the design and operation of ZPR-3 were provided by J. M. Gasidlo, a
former staff member at ZPR-3 and ZPPR. Other details were obtained from ANL reports related
to ZPR-3 design and experiments.
During reactor startup, a neutron source had to be present in each half of any ZPR-3 loading that
did not contain an inherent source in the core (e.g., 240Pu). Figure 2.1 provides a partial view of
the movable half’s spherical source pig (shielded container) and the source transport tube
connecting the pig to matrix row P, the middle row in the matrix. The source pig is the light sphere
at the lower center of Figure 2.1 circled in red. It is between the movable half and the wall and is
partially hidden by the movable half. There was a corresponding source pig and tube for the
stationary half which is not visible in the provided picture. The ZPR-3 safety documents, which

 5

were based on uranium fuel, required the presence of drawers that could accommodate a source
tube in uranium-fueled assemblies.

 Figure 2.1. View of the ZPR-3 Facility.
The matrix tubes in ZPR-3, ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR were horizontal, and the control rods moved
horizontally in the matrix tubes at selected core locations in all four machines. In ZPR-3, a steel
back plate, roughly 18 inches (457 mm) behind the matrix tubes on each table, supported the
control rod drives. The drives were mounted on the outboard side of the plate and were connected
to control rods by steel shafts that projected through holes in the plate. The back plates and control
rod drives in ZPR-3 are visible behind the stationary and movable tables in Figure 2.1 and are
circled in blue.
Figure 2.2 shows ZPR-3 technicians loading drawers into matrix tubes. All matrix tubes were
loaded and unloaded manually. The physical size of the machine is clear in this photograph.

 6

 Figure 2.2. ZPR-3 Technicians Loading Drawers into Matrix Tubes.

The original fuel used in ZPR-3 critical assemblies consisted of highly enriched uranium (HEU)
and depleted uranium (DU) metal plates. The decay heat load in the uranium-fueled cores was
small, and the original ZPR-3 design had no active core cooling system.
Plutonium fuel was first used in ZPR-3 in the early 1960s. The initial plutonium plates used at
ZPR-3 were clad Pu-Al plates, i.e., plates consisting of Pu-Al alloy in stainless steel cans. Pu-U-
Mo plates were subsequently manufactured for the SEFOR program. A Pu-U-Mo plate consisted
of a plate of Pu-U-Mo alloy in a stainless steel can.
When plutonium fuel was introduced into ZPR-3, a rudimentary forced-air cooling system was
added to address the decay heat load issue in plutonium-fueled cores. This cooling system
consisted of a blower with filtered exhaust, hoses (similar to a clothes dryer exhaust hose) and two
plenums. The face of each plenum matched the stepwise-cylindrical outline of a matrix loading
of core plus approximately one row of radial blanket. Except when back drawers were being
loaded, one plenum covered the central portion of the back end of the movable half. A hose
connected the plenum to the blower, which sucked air through the small air gaps between the
outside edges and top of each core drawer and the interior surfaces of its matrix tube. When the
matrix halves were closed, air was sucked from the back of the stationary half, through the core

 7

matrix tubes in both halves. When the halves were separated, the second plenum was attached
temporarily to the interface side of the stationary-half matrix, and this plenum was connected by a
second hose to the single blower. It is not clear how the plenum behind the matrix tubes
accommodated the presence of the back plate and control rod drives behind the matrix tubes as
shown in Figure 2.1.
A small number of thermocouples were distributed in the ZPR-3 matrix to monitor the core
temperature. Before plutonium fuel was used at ZPR-3, there was only one thermocouple per half.
Five more thermocouples per half were added when plutonium fuel came into use. Each
thermocouple, and its electrical lead, was installed in the small, axial interstitial gap that existed
where the rounded corners of four matrix tubes met. No record of the axial and radial locations of
these thermocouples has been found.
The logbook entries for critical configurations usually include measured temperatures. The
rudimentary cooling system devised for the advent of plutonium fuel kept core temperatures
reasonable, but they were not uniform. Inspection of the ZPR-3 logbooks for plutonium-fueled
cores generally shows thermocouple readings in the 30°C – 40°C range with one outlier in the
19°C – 23°C range for a critical configuration. That outlier was clearly an inlet temperature. After
any outliers were discarded, the remaining thermocouple readings were averaged to obtain a
representative core temperature. Although this average temperature was representative of the core
as a whole, it was not necessarily the true mean core temperature.
Figure 2.3 shows a later photograph of ZPR-3. The hose and blower for the cooling system are
just barely visible in Figure 2.3behind the movable table and are circled in red. The two red
structures on the right side of Figure 2.3 that are suspended from horizontal beams and highlighted
with blue circles were movable biological shields. Each of these shields could be moved in front
of one of the tables to reduce the dose received by ZPR-3 staff working on loading or unloading
matrix tubes from the other half. These shields were a later facility modification because they are
not present in Figure 2.1 and Figure 2.2. It is likely that these shields were added to address the
higher radiation source for plutonium fuel compared to the original uranium fuel used in ZPR-3.
The ZPR-3 matrix machine was near (approximately 2 m from) a corner of a large cell (room),
approximately 45 feet by 42 feet and 30 feet tall (14  13  9 m).
The matrix tube pitch was measured in November 1959. The reported pitch values were 2.1835
in (55.461 mm) in the horizontal direction and 2.1755 in (55.258 mm) in the vertical direction.
Except during reactor operation, the tables were separated by 5 feet (1.5 m). For reactor operation,
the movable table was driven against the stationary table with a nut and lead screw mechanism,
forming a cubical 31 x 31 matrix array, 67 inches (1.7 m) on a side.
A matrix position in the ZPR-3 matrix array is specified by three parameters: matrix half, row
letter, and column number. The stationary table or matrix half was designated by S or 1, and the
movable table or matrix half was designated by M or 2. The horizontal rows in the 31 x 31 matrix
were designated by the letters A – Z and AA – EE starting with A at the top and ending with EE
on the bottom in both matrix halves. The vertical columns in the stationary half were numbered 1
– 31 from the left to the right while looking at the stationary half and standing in between the two
halves. The vertical columns in the movable half were also numbered 1-31 but they are numbered

 8

from right to left while looking at the movable half and standing in between the two halves. This
approach means that the columns numbers are aligned for both matrix halves. Note that the
technicians in Figure 2.2 are loading a drawer into the movable half at approximately column 9.
One standard designation for the matrix position located on the stationary table at row F, column
12 is S-F/12. Likewise, the standard designation for the matrix position located on the movable
table at row F, column 12 would be M-F/12. This convention for identifying matrix locations
applies to all rows and columns of the matrix. Some ZPR-3 documents will show 1-F-12 in place
of S-F/12 and 2-F-12 in place of M-F/12. In general, for any row N and column nn in the ZPR-3
matrix, S-N/nn is identical to 1-N-nn, and M-N/nn is identical to 2-N-nn.

 Figure 2.3. Later View of ZPR-3 (circa 1968).
Reversing the numbering for the columns in the movable half, i.e., numbering the columns with
31 on the left and 1 on the right for an observer standing between halves and facing the movable
half, allowed the rows and columns to align when the two matrix halves were brought together.
For example, matrix tube S-F/12 was directly aligned with matrix tube M-F/12 when the movable
table touched the stationary table at the full closure position.
The coordinate system for ZPR-3, ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR was unconventional. The ZPR-3
convention for numbering rows and columns was used in ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR except that
numbers replaced letters in the row designations for ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR. The rationale for
this should be obvious as using letters to represent 65 and 77 rows is impractical. The Z-axis was
horizontal and parallel to the long axis of the matrix tubes. The axial origin (Z = 0.0) was at the

 9

interface between matrix halves with positive values of Z (Z > 0.0) in the stationary table for all
four machines. This convention for the Z-axis and the conventions for numbering rows and
columns of the matrix resulted in a standard right-handed coordinate system for analysis purposes.
In general, the Y-axis of a ZPR/ZPPR assembly was the center column of the matrix, and the X-
axis of a ZPR/ZPPR assembly was the center row of the matrix. In ZPR-3, for example, the center
column is column 16, and the center row is row P (the 16 th row). For the 45 x 45 ZPR-9 matrix,
the center column is 23, and the center row is 23. The same principle applies to ZPR-6 and ZPPR.
The preceding paragraph applies if the assembly was centered in the matrix and was symmetric
about the center row and center column. There were exceptions to this general rule regarding the
X-axis and Y-axis for some assemblies. For example, in some assemblies, the Y-axis was the line
between two adjacent columns and/or the X-axis was the line between two adjacent rows.
Another possibility is that the center of the assembly was offset from the center of the matrix to
allow space particular experimental configurations. In ZPPR-15, for example, the X-axis was the
line between rows 58 and 59, and the Y-axis was the line between columns 48 and 49.
2.1.2 Operational Measurements and Corrections
Much of the following discussion of ZPR-3 operations applies to ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR as well
because all four ZPR/ZPPR machines had similar operating characteristics. Measurements in a
ZPR/ZPPR assembly fall into two categories: programmatic and operational.
Programmatic measurements were the measurements that provided the desired data for the
assembly program. Sodium void worths, the worths of simulated control rods, reaction rate
distributions measured by irradiating small foils, small sample worths, the Doppler reactivity
worth of samples and the reference critical configuration are examples of programmatic
measurements. The programmatic measurements were the desired end product of the assembly
program, i.e., the work product, that would be used by reactor analysts and designers.
Operational measurements were measurements such as control rod worth curves and the reactor
temperature coefficient that were made after the reference critical configuration was established
and that were used to support reactor operations. The operational measurements were used by the
ZPR/ZPPR staff to support daily operations but they were not part of the programmatic
measurements and were not generally used by anyone other than the ZPR/ZPPR staff.
ZPR-3 had an inventory of stainless steel drawers and aluminum drawers. Small rectangular plates
of fuel and diluent materials were loaded into these drawers to create approximate homogeneous
compositions of the core, axial blanket, axial reflector, radial blanket and/or radial reflector of the
reactor configuration of interest. If the radial reflector and/or radial blanket consisted of large
blocks, such as 2 x 2 x 5 inch DU blocks or 2 x 2 x 6 inch stainless steel blocks, those blocks would
sometimes be loaded directly into the matrix tubes without drawers.
The radial blanket and/or radial reflector drawers were loaded into the empty matrix tubes first.
Then core drawers were loaded in the standard approach-to-critical. This means that core drawers
were loaded in batches or steps. After each loading step, the two matrix halves were brought
together, the control rods were moved, the degree of subcriticality was measured, and the number

 10

of core drawers required for the next step was determined. This process was repeated carefully
until a critical configuration was achieved.
Drawers were loaded into the matrix tubes with the stationary and movable tables in their separated
position. After the required sets of drawers were loaded, the staff vacated the reactor cell, and the
reactor operator drove the movable table toward the stationary table slowly while monitoring the
detectors. During this process, the control rods were fully withdrawn in their least reactive
positions.
Unlike conventional control rods containing a poison such as boron carbide, the ZPR-3 control
rods were special drawers connected to the control rod drives behind the tables. Each of these
drawers, referred to as a dual purpose drawer or DP drawer, contained a normal loading of fuel
and diluent plates. Moving a DP drawer toward the axial core center inserted positive reactivity;
moving a DP drawer away from the axial core center inserted negative reactivity. In this regard,
operation of the DP drawers or DP control rods was the opposite of standard poison control rods.
When the DP control rods were in their fully withdrawn positions, the core reactivity was
minimized. DP drawer motion toward the core center was slow for safety reasons. In a scram
situation, all DP drawers were rapidly withdrawn from the core to remove fuel from the core and
to insert negative reactivity.
When the position sensors indicated that the movable table had reached the limit of its motion, i.e.,
when the movable table touched the stationary table, the reactor was still subcritical. At that point,
the DP control drawers would be slowly inserted into the core sequentially. If the reactor was still
subcritical with all DP drawers fully inserted, the movable table would be moved back to its
separated position, and the next core loading step would begin.
In most assemblies, there were five DP drawers in each half. In general, one DP drawer per half
functioned as a control/shim rod, and the remaining DP drawers functioned as safety rods. When
the critical configuration was achieved, one or possibly two of the DP drawers, i.e., the shim rods,
were not fully inserted. Sometimes one DP drawer in each reactor half was only partially inserted.
Sometimes only one drawer in one reactor half was only partially inserted. Typically, the gap
between the core axial centerline (interface between matrix halves) and the front of the partially
inserted DP drawer(s) in the critical configuration was in the 2 – 8 inch range. The safety rod
drawers were fully inserted during during normal operations, i.e., during measurements, and were
fully withdrawn during shutdown.
After the initial critical configuration was achieved, some core/blanket/reflector drawers were
rearranged or exchanged to create the approximately cylindrical zone boundaries discussed above.
This final configuration became the reference critical configuration. Subsequent configurations
for other measurements in the assembly program were variations of the reference critical
configuration.
After the reference critical configuration was established, measurements were made for important
operational parameters. Note that the following discussion is general and that not all of these
operational measurements would necessarily be made for any given assembly program. The most
obvious operational measurement was the Dual Purpose (DP) control rod worths. This was an
important safety measurement and would be performed for every assembly program. The control
rod worth measurements included the axial worth profiles or rod worth curves for the control rods.

 11

The modeling limitations discussed above resulted in core configurations that were approximately
cylindrical. In reality, zone boundaries were necessarily jagged because the matrix tubes
containing the drawers were square and the plates in the drawers were rectangular parallelepipeds.
One approach to cylindricizing the core boundary involved the use of partial drawers (or partials).
A normal core drawer consisted entirely of core materials, and a normal radial blanket drawer
consisted entirely of blanket materials. A partial drawer contained a mix of core and blanket
materials. The part of the partial drawer nearest to the radial core center contained plates of core
materials, and the part of the partial drawer nearest to the radial blanket contained plates of blanket
materials. The fraction of the partial drawer containing core material was 25%, 50% or 75%,
depending on requirements and on the availability of smaller plates to make a 25%, 50% or 75%
partial drawer. Partial drawers did not eliminate the jagged boundary issue entirely, but they did
reduce the influence of the jagged boundary. It was also possible but less common to make a
partial drawer of radial blanket and radial reflector materials.
The second approach to cylindricizing the core boundary involved measuring the worth of a core
drawer (or drawers) at the core-radial blanket interface by replacing a core drawer with a blanket
drawer or vice versa at the core boundary and measuring the resulting change in reactivity. This
was generally referred to as an edge worth measurement (or some similar term). The edge worth
measurement resulted in a measured reactivity worth per unit mass of uranium or plutonium fuel
at the core boundary. A cylindrical core boundary could then be obtained by drawing a circle on
the core map with a circular core area that was approximately equal to the area of the true core
with jagged boundaries. The circular boundary included parts of some blanket drawers in the real
reactor and cut off parts of core drawers that were not entirely within the circular boundary. The
difference between the area of the blanket drawers included within the circle and the area of core
drawers excluded from the circle could be computed and converted to an equivalent amount of
fuel gained or lost by cylindricizing the core boundary. The amount of fuel gained or lost could
be multiplied by the measured reactivity worth per unit mass of fuel at the core boundary, i.e., edge
worth, and used to adjust the measured core reactivity to correct for the effect of cylindricizing the
core. In early assembly programs, it was common to adjust the critical mass and/or core boundary
rather than adjusting the measured core reactivity.
It is important to understand that such adjustments were the standard practice, especially in earlier
assemblies, so published reactivities, critical masses and core dimensions of reference critical
configurations are likely to have been adjusted and do not exactly reflect the true as-built reactor
configuration. In order determine the unadjusted reactivity of a configuration of interest, there are
three possibilities. First, it may be possible to determine what the original measured reactivity of
the reactor was prior to adjustment from the published information. Second, it may be possible to
determine the reactivity worths of the various adjustments and then to determine the original
measured reactivity by reversing the adjustments. Third, if the reactor logbook lists the control
rod positions for the reference critical configuration, it is possible to estimate the measured excess
reactivity by computing one as-built model with all DP control rods fully inserted and one as-built
model with all DP control rods at the axial positions shown in the logbook entry. The difference
between those two calculations is an estimate of the measured excess reactivity.
Core reactivity had to be increased or decreased for some experiments. For example, neutron
spectrum measurements with proton recoil spectrometers required a slightly subcritical reactor to
avoid saturating counters and dead time corrections. Core and radial blanket drawers were

 12

interchanged to adjust reactivity. Full and partial core drawers were interchanged for the same
reason. A third option for adjusting reactivity was addition to or removal of a second column of
fuel plates in selected drawers at symmetric positions in the outer core.
One minor complication regarding the partially inserted DP drawer is determining which drawer
was partially inserted. The reactor loading records and published reports show where the DP
drawers were located in the matrix. The reactor logbook shows the DP control rod drawer number
and the axial position of that DP control rod drawer for each DP control rod drawer in the reactor.
However, to date, no document has been identified that connects the DP drawer numbers in the
logbook with the DP drawer positions in the matrix. After discussion with J. A. Morman [2], a
former experimenter at ZPR-6 and ZPR-9, it was concluded that the DP drawer that was partially
inserted was probably the DP drawer that was farthest from the radial center of the core. The
rationale for this conclusion is that most experimental measurements were performed at the center
of the core. In order to minimize the effect of the partially inserted DP drawer on the measured
value in an experiment, it would be desirable to maximize the distance between the experiment
and the partially inserted DP drawer.
The point of any experiment in any ZPR/ZPPR facility was to produce a measurement that could
be analyzed with the methods and computational tools available when the measurement was made.
It will be difficult for any current reader of this document to grasp fully the modeling limitations
imposed by the software and computers available before 1990 and how that impacted the
experimental operations, especially for ZPR-3. Producing measurements and configurations that
could be analyzed with available computational methods and tools resulted in several adjustments
to the measured excess reactivity in addition to any reactivity adjustment related to replacing the
jagged core boundary in the actual reactor with an equivalent cylindrical boundary. Note that
excess reactivity will be used in this document to refer to positive and negative reactivity values,
so excess reactivity may refer to a configuration that is slightly supercritical or to a configuration
that is slightly subcritical.
Excess reactivity is the reactivity of the reactor with all control rods in their most reactive
configurations. For the DP rods used in ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9, the most reactive configuration
is the configuration with all DP drawers fully inserted. In order to facilitate analysis, the measured
excess reactivity of the reference critical configuration was commonly adjusted to a standard set
of reporting conditions.
First, it was not possible to model accurately a partially inserted DP drawer when ZPR-3, ZPR-6
and ZPR-9 operated. The control rod worth curves measured during the operational measurements
were used to adjust the measured excess reactivity to a condition with all DP rods fully inserted to
simplify analysis. This adjustment increased reactivity.
Second, excess reactivity was adjusted to a common reporting temperature such as 25°C in most
ZPR/ZPPR assembly programs. The temperature in the reactor cell varied slightly from day to
day and from season to season, and this variation could have a small effect on the core temperature.
A uranium-fueled core had a very small decay heat load. It is not clear what adjustments were
made for temperature in a ZPR-3 uranium-fueled core or how those adjustments were made.
A plutonium-fueled core had a large decay heat load. Measured thermocouple temperatures for a
plutonium-fueled core in ZPR-3 were generally in the 30°C – 40°C range although legitimate, i.e.,

 13

non-outlier, thermocouple measurements outside this range occurred in some cases. One
legitimate temperature significantly below this range appears to be an inlet temperature. Note that
the 30°C – 40°C range was the actual range in thermocouple readings for any given ZPR-3
assembly configuration with plutonium fuel and that the thermocouple readings for any given
assembly configuration were not necessarily clustered closely around some mean value.
For a plutonium-fueled core in a ZPR/ZPPR assembly, the measured excess reactivity was adjusted
to the standard reporting temperature. The temperature adjustment was based on the average of
the legitimate thermocouple readings after any outliers were discarded and on a measured
temperature coefficient for the assembly in the reactor. The cooling system was turned off, and
the reactor temperature was allowed to rise due to decay heating. The change in excess reactivity
as a function of average reactor temperature was measured as the reactor temperature increased.
The measured data were converted to a temperature coefficient. The product of the measured
temperature coefficient and the difference between the average thermocouple reading for the
measured assembly configuration and the standard reporting temperature was the reactivity
adjustment to the standard reporting temperature.
The temperature adjustment was made for many types of reactivity measurements to provide a
standard basis for analysis. In addition to the reference critical configuration, this adjustment was
made for a connected series of measurements such as a series of sodium void worth measurements
based on the same reference configuration.
Third, reported excess reactivity was adjusted to a zero interface gap. The two halves of the ZPR-
3 matrix were neither perfectly flat nor perfectly parallel due to normal manufacturing and
construction tolerances. This is equally true for ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR. A slight misalignment
of the bundles of matrix tubes on the two tables was unavoidable. In addition, the weight of a
heavy load in the matrix tubes could cause a slight deflection of the support plate. Because the
matrix halves were not perfectly aligned, some parts of the two halves were not in physical contact
at full closure. In other words, there was a small, non-uniform gap between the two matrix halves
at the nominal full closure position. There could also be a small gap because of uncertainty in the
actual position of the movable half at full closure relative to the position indicated by the
instruments. This gap was referred to as the interface gap. The interface gap was small, non-
uniform and imprecisely known because it was impractical to measure the interface gap accurately
at all points on the interface between the stationary and movable tables. As stated, it was not
possible to include the interface gap in models during analysis of ZPR-3 experiments, so the ZPR-
3 staff corrected reported reactivity measurements for the presence of this gap, i.e., they adjusted
the measured reactivity to a condition with no interface gap.
An interface gap (reactivity) coefficient was measured in the following manner. Starting from a
critical configuration at the full closure position, the movable table was driven slowly away from
the stationary table with no change in control rod positions, and the resulting decrease in reactivity
was measured as a function of the separation between matrix halves. The resulting measured data
were converted to an interface gap coefficient. Multiplying the interface gap coefficient by the
average interface gap provided a reactivity correction for omission of the interface gap in analytical
models. The same procedure was used at ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR to account for the interface
gap because models of assemblies at those facilities also omitted the interface gap. The interface
gap correction in a ZPR/ZPPR assembly was small, but the size of the correction for any specific

 14

assembly depended on various factors including the assembly size and the weight of the assembly.
For example, a heavy assembly could cause a slight deflection of the support plate below the
assembly, and that deflection would affect the interface gap.
Fourth, a reactivity correction applies when the plutonium plates were used in a loading as decay
of 241Pu is non-trivial from the date of manufacture to the time they were used in the experiment
and can be non-trivial over a measurement series. To explain, the excess reactivity for the reference
critical configuration was measured at a specific time on a specific day, so there was no need to
correct the measured excess reactivity of the reference critical configuration for radioactive decay
during the elapsed time of the measurement, but defining the model itself does require the
composition to be defined correctly. In contrast, a connected series of measurements, such as
measurements of sodium void or simulated control rod worth, could span many days. The standard
practice to account for decay was to correct the measured reactivities in those connected
measurements to a common decay date to eliminate any bias or uncertainty related to decay of
241
 Pu. The long half-lives of uranium isotopes make any correction for radioactive decay during
a series of related measurements unimportant for a uranium-fueled core. The short half-life of
241
 Pu makes decay corrections relevant for a related series of measurements in a plutonium-fueled
core.
The differences in measurement dates for a connected series of measurements were known from
the reactor logbook. A 241Pu decay coefficient could be calculated from the known 241Pu inventory
in the core and the known 241Pu half-life. A 241Pu decay coefficient could also be measured by
observing the measured reactivity change for a reactor configuration at different time points. In
some cases the 241Pu decay coefficient may have been calculated. The product of the 241Pu decay
coefficient and known differences in measurement dates provided the 241Pu decay corrections for
a series of related measurements in a plutonium-fueled core. A connected series of measurements
only spanned a limited time period, e.g., a few days to a few weeks, so the 241Pu decay correction
was very small.
The adjustment of excess reactivity to standard reporting conditions, i.e., all control rods in their
most reactive positions, standard temperature, zero interface gap and common 241Pu decay date (if
applicable), apply to all four ZPR/ZPPR machines. Other operational measurements were made
as required for each specific assembly program.
2.1.3 Reactor Compositions in ZPR-3
The four ZPR/ZPPR machines were used primarily to simulate fast reactors although basic fast
reactor physics measurements were performed in simplified configurations designed to emphasize
the measurements or parameters of interest.
The desired average composition in each region of the simulated reactor in a ZPR/ZPPR assembly
was achieved by loading the matrix tubes with drawers containing small rectangular plates of
different materials such as plutonium, HEU, DU, stainless steel, graphite, sodium, etc. Figure 2.4
shows a ZPR-3 matrix tube, drawer and related hardware.
The drawer shown in Figure 2.4 was heavily perforated to reduce the steel content. Drawers and
plates were perforated to facilitate creating the desired average composition in each region of the
simulated reactor. For example, the initial ZPR-3 plate inventory did not include sodium plates,

 15

so aluminum plates were used as a substitute for sodium. Holes were drilled in the aluminum
plates such that the average density of the perforated aluminum plates approximately matched the
density of sodium. Sodium plates were eventually acquired for the ZPR-3 plate inventory. The
filler plate shown in Figure 2.4 was probably placed in the bottom of the drawer to adjust the
effective steel volume fraction in the drawer or to raise the plates in the drawer slightly. The
drawer spring shown in Figure 2.4 was placed at the back of the drawer behind the plates to push
the plates to the front of the drawer. Plate shifting, i.e., unintentional movement of plates within
a drawer during drawer loading and handling, introduced an undesirable uncertainty into reactivity
measurements. Placing a drawer spring behind the plates in the drawer reduced the effect of plate
shifting.
The combination of fuel plates and diluent plates (steel, sodium, iron oxide, depleted uranium,
etc.) plus the steel in the drawers and matrix tubes was intended to match the average homogeneous
composition of fuel, cladding, coolant and structural material in each core region. The same
principle applies to matching the average homogeneous compositions of blanket and reflector
regions.

 Figure 2.4. Typical ZPR-3 Drawer and Hardware.
Not all of the drawers used in ZPR-3, ZPR-6, ZPR-9 or ZPPR were as heavily perforated as the
drawer shown in Figure 2.4. In some cases, only the sides and/or front of the drawer were
perforated. In other cases, there were no perforations in the drawers.
Figure 2.5 shows a typical loaded ZPR drawer. Note that the plates are elevated above the bottom
of the drawer in Figure 2.5 to make them more visible for the picture.

 16

 Figure 2.5. Typical Loaded ZPR Drawer.
A specific plate-loading pattern in a ZPR/ZPPR drawer was called a drawer master. Physically, a
drawer master was a drawing or blueprint showing the location or position of each type of plate
in a drawer. The drawer masters were guides or templates used by the technicians to load the
drawers. A drawer master figure specified exactly where each plate of each plate type should be
placed in a drawer. The specification of which drawer master was in each matrix position in each
half of the split-table machine is known as a matrix loading map, matrix map or interface map.
Another term that is occasionally used in place of matrix map is all master map (AMM). Drawer
master is used in this document to refer both to the physical drawing or blueprint used by the
technicians and to the specific plate-loading pattern in a drawer. Which of these two meanings
applies in a specific case will be obvious from the context.
There were usually many plate sizes available for a given material and a limited number of plates
of any one size. Consequently, there were often several drawer masters that described the same
unit cell and had essentially the same composition. However, those drawer masters differed in the
specific set of plate sizes used and possibly in the locations of those plates in the drawer. The
number of unique drawer masters was increased by the fact that matrix locations in the stationary
and movable halves sometimes had different (opposite, mirror image) drawer masters, particularly
for asymmetric drawer masters. An asymmetric drawer master is a drawer master in which the
plate loading is not symmetric about the long axis of the drawer.

 17

It was frequently the case that a given matrix tube or position in a ZPR/ZPPR assembly contained
two drawers, a front drawer and a back drawer. In that case, there would be two matrix loading
maps for each half, a front map and a back map. If a matrix tube contained front and back drawers,
the front drawer in each matrix half was the drawer adjacent to the interface between the stationary
half and the movable half, and the back drawer in each matrix half was the drawer farthest from
this interface. A back drawer might be required if the front drawer was not long enough to contain
the core, axial blanket and axial reflector for the desired simulation or if the front drawer was not
long enough to contain the radial blanket or radial reflector. That situation arose if most of the
long drawers were used for the core and radial blanket, and only shorter drawers were available to
load the remainder of the radial blanket and radial reflector. Note that the preceding discussion on
drawer masters, front drawers and back drawers applies equally to ZPR-3, ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and
ZPPR.
For some configurations, there was an alternative to the use of a back drawer. In addition to small
plates of various sizes, the inventories of the ZPR/ZPPR facilities contained larger blocks of steel,
depleted uranium, graphite and possibly a few other materials. These blocks were 2 x 2 x L inches
where L ranged from 1 inch to 12 inches. If appropriate lengths were available, these blocks were
sometimes loaded directly into matrix tubes without drawers to complete the axial blanket and/or
axial reflector. These blocks also were loaded directly into matrix tubes to make the radial blanket
and/or radial reflector surrounding the reactor core in some cases. This practice applies to all four
ZPR/ZPPR facilities.
The back plate of a front drawer and the front plate of a back drawer were smooth and flat. If the
procedures for handling drawers and loading matrix tubes were followed, the back plate of the
front drawer contacted the front plate of the back drawer, and there was no gap between the front
and back drawers. The same consideration applies to blocks of the various materials that were
loaded directly into matrix tubes to make the radial blanket and/or radial reflector.
The ZPR-3 drawers themselves can be categorized as either normal drawers or control drawers.
Each normal drawer had 2 inch-tall front, back, and side walls, and a nominal 2 inch-wide bottom
wall. The actual interior width of a normal drawer was slightly larger than 2.00 inches to
accommodate a plate loading with a nominal width of 2 inches. The plates were expensive,
particularly HEU plates, plutonium plates, and sodium canned plates. Damaging those plates by
forcing them into a drawer was not acceptable both from the economic standpoint and from the
safety standpoint, so the interior width of the drawer had to be sufficient to allow plate loading and
removal without damaging plates. At the same time, the interior drawer width had to be small
enough to minimize any lateral plate shifting during drawer handling.
Most normal drawers in the ZPR-3 inventory consisted of ~0.03-inch thick, highly perforated Type
304 stainless steel wall material. The rest of the normal drawers in the inventory had a ~0.04-inch
thick unperforated aluminum walls. Each normal front drawer had a tab at the front edge of each
side wall. There were corresponding notches in the side walls of the matrix tubes. The tabs fit in
the notches to provide positive seating of the drawer in the tube, with the front of the drawer flush
with the front of the matrix tube. Each normal back drawer had a handle extending from its back
wall, which allowed the drawer to be extracted from the back of the matrix tube.
The only type of operational control rod used in ZPR-3 was the dual-purpose (DP) control rod
discussed earlier. Each control rod drive shown in Figure 2.1 through Figure 2.3 was connected

 18

to a shaft that was connected to the back of a DP control rod drawer. Typically, there were five
DP rods in each matrix half in ZPR-3. The number of DP control rods was constrained by the
number of available DP control rod drives, the number of DP control rod drawers, the space
required for each DP control rod drive and the positions of the holes in the back plate in each half.
In some cases, one or more of the DP control rods in the movable half was not directly aligned
with a corresponding DP control rod in the stationary half. The reasons for that slight asymmetry
are not known.
The DP control drawer itself was similar to a normal drawer, but the control drawer had some
special features. Because the DP control drawer had to be strong enough to undergo rapid
acceleration and deceleration, it was made of unperforated Type 304 stainless steel with twice the
wall thickness (0.063 inch) of the walls of normal drawers. To minimize the possibility of a DP
drawer binding in the matrix tube through which it moved, the DP drawer width was made 0.063
inch less than that of a normal drawer. A consequence of these two design features was that the
width of the plate loading had to be 0.125 inch less than the normal 2-inch wide plate loading.
Only fifteen 0.125 inch plate columns could be loaded into a DP drawer instead of sixteen in the
normal drawer. To act as a single rigid body, a DP drawer had to be thick-walled, and it had to be
at least as long as the combination of a normal front drawer and back drawer. The DP drawer’s
nominal length was 32 inches which is nearly as long as the 33.5 inch matrix tube. Finally, the
design included a wall at 15.25 inches dividing the drawer into front and back compartments. This
helped stiffen the drawer, but, more importantly, it allowed the drawer’s plate loading to be locked
in place more effectively with springs inserted at the back of each compartment. It was important
to lock the plates firmly in place to avoid damaging the plates during the rapid acceleration and
deceleration in a reactor scram. In some cases, multiple springs were inserted in the back of each
compartment to accomplish this.
Some of the matrix tubes in row P contained a small hole in the side walls through which a source
tube could pass. In cases where the source tube was required, the plate loadings in the source tube
locations were adjusted to make space for the source tube. Safety documents required the presence
of the source tube drawers, which had side wall holes aligning with the matrix tube side wall holes,
even if an external neutron source was not needed.
2.2 ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 Fast Critical Facilities
ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were constructed at the same time in Building 315 at ANL-E (now Argonne
National Laboratory or ANL). Construction of both machines began in the early 1960s and was
completed in 1963. For practical purposes, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were essentially identical until ZPR-
6 operations were halted for facility modifications during the ZPR-6/6 program. After completion
of the ZPR-6/7 program, ZPR-6 operations were suspended for major modifications including
expansion of the matrix from 45 x 45 to 65 x 65 and installation of a large test zone in the center
of the matrix. This test zone was called the Variable Temperature Rodded Zone (VTRZ). The
VTRZ was designed as a heated central test zone containing rod-type fuel. ZPR-6/8 would have
been the first program to use the VTRZ. However, changing program priorities resulted in
cancellation of ZPR-6/8. The VTRZ was never used, but the modifications allowed ZPR-6 to
accommodate a 65 x 65 array of standard matrix tubes for later assembly programs. Figure 2.6
shows the VTRZ being installed in ZPR-6.

 19

 Figure 2.6. Installation of the VTRZ in ZPR-6.
ZPR-6 Assembly 1 (ZPR-6/1), the first ZPR-6 assembly program, began in July 1963. ZPR-6 was
shut down in 1982 after ZPR-6 Assembly 10 (ZPR-6/10) completed. ZPR-9 Assembly 1 (ZPR-
9/1), the first ZPR-9 assembly program, began in February 1964. ZPR-9 was shut down in
February 1981 after ZPR-9 Assembly 36 (ZPR-9/36) completed.
The ZPR-6 and ZPR9 reactor cells were located on opposite sides of a common workroom and
vault. ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 shared a common materials inventory, a common staff and common
experimental equipment. Drawers for both machines were loaded and unloaded in the workroom.
The HEU and plutonium fuel plates for ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were stored in the vault behind the
workroom. DU plates, other non-fuel plates, drawers and other equipment were stored in another
area.
The initial fuel plate inventory for ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 contained HEU plates and DU plates. Mixing
HEU plates and DU plates in drawers produced effective average enrichments in the desired range
for the fast reactor simulations of interest at that time. After ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were shut down,
the HEU plates at ANL-E were shipped to ANL-W for use in ZPPR assemblies.

 20

The ANL-E plate inventory did not contain any plutonium plates until approximately 1969. In
preparation for the startup of ZPPR, Pu-U-Mo alloy plates were fabricated by Dow and NUMEC.
The majority of those plates were delivered to ZPPR; the remainder were delivered to ANL-E for
use at ZPR-6 and ZPR-9.
ANL-E had an inventory of sodium plates prior to construction of ZPPR. However, when sodium
plates were fabricated for ZPPR, some additional sodium plates were made for use at ANL-E.
ANL-E and ANL-W maintained separate plate inventories. With the exceptions of the Pu-U-Mo
plates and some sodium plates mentioned above, plates used at ANL-E and ANL-W were typically
purchased from different vendors at different times. In general, the mass and composition of a
plate in the ANL-E inventory differed slightly from the mass and composition of a plate of the
same material and the same dimensions in the ANL-W inventory.
Plutonium plates and possibly HEU plates were shared between the facilities at ANL-E and the
facilities at ANL-W if an assembly program at one site required more fuel plates than were
available in the facility inventory. In general, diluent plates, i.e., non-fuel plates such as stainless
steel plates, were not shared between ANL-E and ANL-W, but there were occasional exceptions.
For example, graphite plates were sent from ANL-E to ZPR-3 to meet the needs of one ZPR-3
assembly program. More expensive plates such as sodium plates may also have been shared
occasionally.
