2.2.1 Physical Characteristics of ZPR-6 and ZPR-9
Much of the preceding discussion of ZPR-3 in Section 2.1 applies to ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 as well.
ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were horizontal split-table type machines. Each consisted of a large, cast-steel
bed supporting a stationary table and a movable table. Figure 2.7 shows the ZPR-6 machine with
major reactor features labeled. ZPR-9 would have looked very similar. Figure 2.8 shows the ZPR-
9 machine and its supporting structures. Figure 2.9 shows the ZPR-6 machine and its supporting
structures.
Comparison of Figure 2.8 and Figure 2.9 shows that ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were essentially identical
prior to the ZPR-6 facility modifications. Comparison of Figure 2.7 through Figure 2.9 for ZPR-
6 and ZPR-9 with Figure 2.1 through Figure 2.3 for ZPR-3 in Section 2.1 shows many similarities
and some significant differences. Aside from the difference in physical size, the principal
differences are a) ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were designed with a core cooling system rather than
retrofitted with one and b) the matrix supporting structures on the sides of ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were
much larger and thicker than the matrix supporting structure on the sides of ZPR-3. The ZPR staff
referred to the tables supporting the matrix tubes and the supporting structure restraining the matrix
tubes in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 as the bed and knees.
Each table was 12 feet wide and 8 feet long. During loading operations, the tables were separated
by 5 feet. In operation, the movable table was driven toward the stationary table with a nut and
lead screw mechanism. Square metal tubes, 0.040 inches thick, 2.175 inches on a side (outside
dimension) and 4 feet long, were welded into 5-tube by 5-tube bundles and stacked horizontally
on both tables to form a 45-row by 45-column square “honeycomb” matrix in the initial ZPR-6
and ZPR-9 configurations. As stated earlier, the ZPR-6 matrix was expanded to 65 x 65 during the
facility modifications for ZPR-6/8.
The 2.175 inch pitch of the matrix tubes is the nominal value used by the staff of ZPR-6 and ZPR-
9. No documents have been found to support another value, but it is possible that the actual pitch
could have differed slightly (~0.001 inch).
The matrix tubes in ZPR-6 were stainless steel tubes, and the drawers used in ZPR-6 assemblies
were stainless steel drawers. The matrix tubes initially installed in ZPR-9 were aluminum, and the
drawers used for ZPR-9/1 through ZPR-9/9 were aluminum. The first nine ZPR-9 assemblies
studied nuclear reactors for rocket propulsion. The fuel was uranium-tungsten, which was
simulated with uranium plates and tungsten plates. The loaded drawers were very heavy, and it is
possible that the weight of the fully-loaded core produced undesirable deformation of the
aluminum matrix. In any case, the aluminum matrix tubes and aluminum drawers used for the
first nine ZPR-9 assemblies were replaced by stainless steel matrix tubes and stainless steel
drawers after completion of the ZPR-9/9 assembly program.

 24

 Figure 2.7. View of the ZPR-6 Facility.

 25

 Figure 2.8. ZPR-9 Machine and Supporting Structure.
Row numbers in ZPR-9 started with 1 at the top of the 45 x 45 matrix and increased downward
with row 45 at the bottom of the matrix. For an observer standing between the matrix halves and
facing the stationary table of ZPR-9, column numbers start with 1 on the observer’s left and
increase to column 45 on the observer’s right. Facing the movable table, columns start with 1 on
the observer’s right and increase to column 45 on the observer’s left. This numbering scheme is
identical to the ZPR-3 numbering convention except for the difference in matrix size and
replacement of letters in the ZPR-3 row designations by numbers in the ZPR-9 row designations.
As was the case for ZPR-3, the intention of the column numbering is that the positions are aligned
when the matrix halves come together. ZPR-6 numbering of rows and columns was identical to
ZPR-9 numbering of rows and columns except for the fact that the ZPR-6 matrix was later
expanded to 65 x 65.
A matrix position in ZPR-6 or ZPR-9 is specified by three parameters: matrix half (S or M), row
number and column number. The central positions in the stationary and movable halves of ZPR-
9 and the pre-expansion ZPR-6 are S-23/23 and M-23/23, respectively. After the ZPR-6
expansion, the central positions in the stationary and movable tables of ZPR-6 are S-33/33 and M-
33/33, respectively. This is the standard convention for identifying matrix positions in ZPR-6 and
ZPR-9. In this naming convention, S-7/15 refers to stationary table, row 7, column 15 and M-7/15
refers to movable table, row 7, column 15. Because the column numbers for both halves start from

 26

the same side of the machine, the row and column numbers in the stationary and movable tables
of the machine align when the tables are brought together. For example, the matrix positions
designated as row 7, column 15 in the stationary and movable halves (S-7/15 and M-7/15) are
directly aligned when the movable table touches the stationary table.

 Figure 2.9. ZPR-6 Machine and Supporting Structure.
The matrix tubes were supported by massive cast-iron, L-shaped structures known as the bed and
knees. These structures are seen clearly in Figure 2.8 and Figure 2.9. A plenum region, which
included control-rod drives and experimental apparatus, existed beyond the matrix at the outer end
of each half. The plenum provided a flow path for cooling air into and out of the assembly matrix.
The (horizontal) control rods projected through holes in a steel back plate, and the drive
mechanisms were positioned on the outside of this back plate. The matrix machine was near the
center of a large cell (room), approximately 40 feet by 30 feet and 30 feet tall (12  9  9 m).
Figure 2.10 shows a view of the stationary half of ZPR-9. The row numbers and column numbers
are clearly visible in this figure. The projection in row 23 of this figure probably facilitated
installation of the radial tube oscillator used for small sample worth measurements (discussed in a
later section).

 27

 Figure 2.10. Stationary Half of ZPR-9.

 28

Kato, Fischer and Dates [3] and Dates [4] provide additional information regarding the design and
planned operation of ZPR-6. In general, that information also applies to ZPR-9. These two
references also contain photos, drawings and descriptions of the equipment, matrix tubes, drawers
and plates used at ZPR-6.
The desired average compositions in the regions of the reactor to be simulated were achieved by
loading the matrix with drawers containing rectangular plates (or, in small regions of some
assemblies, with cylindrical rods) of different materials such as DU, HEU, natural uranium,
stainless steel, sodium, graphite, etc.
The fuel plates used in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were HEU metal, DU metal, natural uranium metal, Pu-
U-Mo metal alloy and Pu-Al metal alloy. The uranium metal plates were coated with Kel-F to
prevent corrosion and material loss during handling. The Pu-Al and Pu-U-Mo fuel were sealed in
thin stainless steel cans.
The reactors simulated in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were predominantly oxide-fueled or carbide-fueled.
The plate inventory did not contain any UC, PuC, UO2 or PuO2 plates. A carbide-fueled reactor
was simulated by mixing columns of metal fuel plates with columns of graphite plates in the
drawers to achieve the desired U:C and Pu:C ratios in the core and blanket (if any). To simulate
an oxide-fueled reactor, columns of metal fuel plates were mixed with columns of depleted U 3O8
plates and iron oxide (Fe2O3) plates to achieve the desired U:O and Pu:O ratios. As one might
expect, finding the right mix of fuel plates, diluent plates, stainless steel in the drawers and stainless
steel in the matrix tubes to achieve the right average compositions for fuel, clad, coolant and
structural material that matched the core, blanket and reflector of the reactor to be simulated was
a difficult process.
In the early ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 assemblies, dual-purpose (DP) control rod drawers were the only
control rods used for reactor control. The DP control rod drawers used in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were
very similar to the DP control rod drawers used in ZPR-3 except for the length of the DP drawer.
In all three cases, a DP drawer containing a normal core loading was connected by a drive shaft to
a control rod drive behind the reactor. The rod drive moved the DP drawer inward toward the core
center (the interface between matrix halves) to increase reactivity. The rod drive moved the DP
drawer outward and away from the core center to reduce reactivity. The DP control rods were
capable of scramming, i.e., rapid withdrawal to reduce reactivity. DP control rods were not used
for “rod drop” experiments to avoid plate damage resulting from rapid acceleration and
deceleration.
Typically, there were five DP control rod drawers in each half of ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 although there
were assemblies with fewer DP rod drawers. One DP drawer in each half served as a shim/control
rod; the other DP drawers served as safety rods. In general, at least one DP rod in the stationary
half was not directly aligned with the corresponding DP rod in the movable half when the
stationary and movable tables were in the full closure position.
Available documents do not indicate which DP rod in each half served as the shim/control rod. As
in the ZPR-3 case, it seems likely that the shim/control rod was the DP drawer farthest from the
core center because that location would minimize the influence of the partially inserted DP
drawer(s) on experimental measurements performed at the core center.

 29

In the late 1960s or early 1970s, a second type of control rod was introduced into ZPR-6 and ZPR-
9. This second type was the poison shim rod or poison safety rod (PSR in both cases), which
contained a blade of boron powder or B4C clad with stainless steel. The PSR blade moved in a
narrow stainless steel guide tube on one side of a matrix tube. The external width of this guide
tube was 0.5 inches. A PSR functioned like a conventional poison control rod. Moving a PSR
toward the core center reduced reactivity by inserting poison, and moving a PSR away from the
core center increased reactivity by removing poison.
The distinction between poison safety rods and poison shim rods was largely a matter of function
and core location. Poison safety rods were the PSRs located in the inner core positions closest to
the core center to maximize their worth. Poison shim rods were the PSRs in the outer positions
farther from the core center to minimize their effect on experimental measurements at the center
of the core. Poison safety rods were normally parked at their fully withdrawn positions during
normal operations. This position was ~30 inches from the interface between matrix halves, so the
poison safety rods generally had no significant effect on experimental measurements. Poison shim
rods at symmetric locations were partially inserted during normal operations to maintain a critical
configuration.
The number of PSRs in each half varied according to the size of the core, the number of DP rods
in the core and possibly other factors. One obvious constraint was available space for control rod
drives. Figure 2.8 and Figure 2.9 show the control rod drives behind each matrix half. The space
required for each control rod drive limited the number of control rod drives that could be mounted
on the back plate, especially for small cores. Another constraint was the number and locations of
the holes in the back plate. Typically, there were about six PSRs in each half of an assembly, but
the actual number of PSRs present could vary, depending on core size and control requirements.
When DP control rods were the only control rods available in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9, their method of
operation in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 was similar to their method of operation in ZPR-3. The two tables
were fully separated during matrix tube loading or unloading operations. After a loading operation
was complete, all staff members left the reactor cell. The reactor operator slowly moved the
movable table to the stationary table until the position sensors indicated that the full closure
position had been reached. The reactor was still subcritical at the full closure position. The DP
control rods were then moved inward slowly to establish a critical configuration. When the critical
configuration was achieved, at least one of the DP shim/control rods was only partially inserted.
The introduction of PSRs provided some experimental freedom. Since plate damage was not an
issue for PSRs, the PSRs could be used for “rod drop” experiments. In addition, the PSRs could
be used to eliminate the asymmetry introduced by the partially inserted DP shim/control drawer(s).
All DP drawers could be fully inserted in the critical configuration because the critical state could
be maintained by the partially inserted poison shim rods. The poison shim rods were generally
located at symmetric positions far from the core center, so their effect on experiments at the core
center was minimized, and the asymmetry introduced by one or two partially inserted DP
shim/control drawers could be eliminated.
The drawers used in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 typically were made of 0.03-inch thick stainless steel, and
their front, back, and sidewalls were 2 inches tall. Drawers were purchased or fabricated to meet
the needs of various ZPR/ZPPR assembly programs, so the drawer inventory contained drawers of
various lengths. A new set of drawers was added to the inventory occasionally to met the needs

 30

of a specific assembly program. The interior width of a standard drawer was slightly greater than
2.000 inches to allow loading of the nominal 2 inch plate loading. The width of drawers in matrix
tubes containing PSRs were 0.5 inches smaller than standard drawers because the external width
of the PSR guide tube in a matrix tube was 0.5 inches.
The drawers used in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 can also be divided into front drawers and back drawers.
The drawer inventory for ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 contained drawers of various lengths as drawers were
acquired for different assembly programs, but it was not practical to acquire a new set of drawers
for every program. As a result, it was frequently necessary to construct an assembly with the
available inventory of drawers.
The lengths of the core, axial blanket and axial reflector varied in different ZPR/ZPPR assembly
programs, depending on the details of the reactor to be simulated. In some cases, a single drawer
was long enough to contain the core, axial blanket and axial reflector plates to be loaded into a
matrix tube. This drawer was the front drawer in such cases. In cases where the total length of
the core, axial blanket and axial reflector exceeded the length of the front drawer, the part of the
axial blanket and/or axial reflector that could not fit in the front drawer was loaded into a back
drawer. Front drawers and back drawers were also used to load the radial blanket and/or radial
reflector in a ZPR/ZPPR assembly. In fact, it was probably more likely that back drawers would
be used for the radial blanket and radial reflector than for the core. If it was possible to load the
core, axial blanket and axial reflector into a single front drawer, the longer front drawers were
likely used for the core region. Combinations of front drawers and back drawers would then be
used to load the radial blanket and/or radial reflector as needed.
The front drawer occupied the front of the matrix tube and was adjacent to the interface between
matrix halves, i.e., adjacent to the interface between the stationary table and the movable table.
The back drawer was loaded behind the front drawer and occupied space in the back of the matrix
tube closer to the back plate and control rod drives behind the matrix tubes.
In general, back drawers were shorter than front drawers, but the key difference between front
drawers and back drawers relates to the fronts and backs of the drawers. A drawer consisted of a
front plate at the front of the drawer, a back plate at the rear of the drawer, and the drawer bottom
and sidewalls between the front plate and back plate. Most front drawers had small tabs on the
sides of the front plates of the drawers. These tabs mated with small notches in the fronts of the
matrix tubes to assure consistent positioning of the front drawers in the matrix tubes. The back
plate of a front drawer was flat and smooth.
The front plate of a back drawer was flat and smooth in order to eliminate any unnecessary
separation between the back of the front drawer and the front of the back drawer. In at least some
cases, a small handle was welded to the back plate of a back drawer to allow the staff to remove
back drawers from the backs of the matrix tubes. That ability facilitated unloading of the matrix
tubes. If it was possible to remove back drawers from the backs of the matrix tubes, it was also
possible to load back drawers into the matrix tubes from the back, which would have facilitated
loading of the matrix tubes.
If back drawers were used in a ZPR/ZPPR assembly program, then there were actually two matrix
maps for any configuration in that assembly program. One matrix map described the drawer

 31

masters in the front drawers, and a second matrix map described the drawer masters in the back
drawers.
The plate inventory of ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 contained 2 x 2 x L inch blocks or 1 x 2 x L inch blocks
of various materials where L ranged from 1 inch to 12 inches. The primary materials in this
category were DU, steel and graphite, but there may have been others. In some cases, these blocks
were loaded directly into the matrix tubes without drawers to form part or all of the radial blanket,
radial reflector, axial blanket and/or axial reflector. Such direct loadings might be treated as
drawer masters for recording purposes, but no actual drawers were used.
DP control rod drawers used in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were slightly different from the DP drawers
used in ZPR-3. A ZPR-3 DP drawer had an interior wall at 15.25 inches to stiffen the drawer and
to allow the plates in the front and back compartments to be locked into place more firmly. Based
on available documents, this interior wall was not present in the DP control rod drawers used in
ZPR-6 and ZPR-9. The DP drawers used in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 had a single long compartment.
The nominal length of a ZPR-3 DP drawer was 32 inches because the ZPR-3 matrix tube length
was 33.5 inches. The nominal length of the DP drawers used in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 was 40.75
inches because the matrix tube length in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 was 48 inches.
The walls of the DP drawers were thicker than the walls of standard drawers to accommodate the
stresses of rapid motion, and the width of a DP drawer was slightly smaller than a standard drawer
to minimize the possibility that the DP drawer would bind in its matrix tube during DP drawer
motion. Consequently, the interior width of a DP drawer was slightly smaller than the interior
width of a standard drawer. The wall thickness of DP drawers used in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 was
~0.060 inches. Because the DP drawers used in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were slightly narrower than
standard drawers and had thicker walls than standard drawers, the usable interior width of the DP
drawers used in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 was 0.125 inches less than the usable interior width of a standard
drawer.
In addition to the PSRs and dual-purpose control rods, some core loadings in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9
contained a device called a fine autorod, which was used to measure very small reactivity worths
such as small sample worths. The autorod system consisted of a tapered polyethylene blade
extending through both halves of the assembly, a servo-drive mechanism, and an analog rod-
position indicator system. The system was controlled to hold the assembly power level at a preset
value automatically. The polyethylene blade was designed such that the value of Δρ/Δz was nearly
constant with z, where ρ is reactivity and z is the axial position of the blade. No additional
description of the fine autorod has been found to date. When the fine autorod was used, it was
generally located somewhere in the middle of the radial blanket or radial reflector where it would
have minimal effect at the core center.
Temperature monitoring of the core in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 was done using thermocouple drawers.
In this type of drawer master, small thermocouples were attached to fuel plates in several places
along a fuel column. The adjacent plate column had to be less than full height to allow room for
the thermocouples and wires. Several thermocouple (TC) drawers typically were present in each
matrix half in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9.
A neutron source had to be present in each matrix half during the startup of any ZPR assembly not
containing an inherent source in the core (e.g., 240Pu). The neutron source and associated hardware

 32

were not required in cores containing Pu-U-Mo fuel plates because the plutonium in those plates
contained ~11% 240Pu.
The practices regarding operational measurements and corrections discussed in Section 2.1.2 for
ZPR-3 also applied to ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 although there were some changes in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9.
Advances in computer software and hardware allowed better modeling of ZPR-6 and ZPR-9
assemblies, so the need for some of the corrections required in ZPR-3 assemblies was reduced but
not necessarily eliminated. The corrections for excess reactivity, edge smoothing, the difference
between the average core temperature and the nominal reporting temperature, the interface gap,
and, in the case of an extended series of related measurements, 241Pu decay discussed earlier also
apply to ZPR-6 and ZPR-9. However, because ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were designed with cooling
systems rather than retrofitted with a cooling system as was the case in ZPR-3, the average core
temperature and the range of core temperatures were smaller for a plutonium-fueled assembly in
ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 than for a plutonium-fueled assembly in ZPR-3.
2.3 ZPPR Fast Critical Facility
Construction of ZPPR began in the late 1960s and was completed in late 1968 or early 1969. The
first experimental program, ZPPR Assembly 1 (ZPPR-1), began in March 1969 and ended in
November 1969. The last ZPPR program, ZPPR-21, began in January 1990 and ended in
September 1990. ZPPR was shut down after completion of the ZPPR-21 program. The last ZPR-
3 assembly program, ZPR-3/63, ended in December 1970, so ANL operated all four critical
experiment facilities simultaneously for approximately 21 months.
Pu-U-Mo plates were fabricated for the critical experiment program by Dow and NUMEC in the
late 1960s. The majority of these plates were shipped to ZPPR; the remainder were shipped to
ANL-E for use at ZPR-6 and ZPR-9. Likewise, when sodium plates were fabricated for ZPPR, an
additional set of these plates was fabricated for use at ZPR-6 and ZPR-9. Most of the diluent plates
in the ZPPR inventory were acquired specifically for use at ZPPR. New drawers and experimental
equipment were fabricated or acquired for use at ZPPR.
After ZPR-3 was shut down, the Pu-Al plates, Pu-U-Mo (SEFOR) plates and HEU plates in the
ZPR-3 inventory were sent to the other three ANL facilities. It is likely that sodium plates in the
ZPR-3 inventory were sent to ZPPR or ANL-E, but most of the non-fuel plates in the ZPR-3
inventory were discarded. Likewise, most or all of the drawers and experimental equipment used
at ZPR-3 were discarded.
As stated above, sharing of plates between ANL-E and ANL-W was largely limited to fuel plates
and possibly sodium plates although there were infrequent exceptions for other types of plates.
Table 2.4 shows a list of the assembly programs performed on the ZPPR machine. ZPPR-17,
ZPPR-18 and ZPPR-19 were the largest ZPPR cores ever built and may have been the largest cores
ever built anywhere. They used the entire ZPPR plutonium fuel inventory plus HEU plates. For
example, the critical mass in ZPPR-18 was approximately 3500 kg of 239Pu and 241Pu (combined).

2.3.1 Physical Characteristics of ZPPR
The ZPPR fast critical facility also was a horizontal split-table type machine consisting of a large,
cast-steel bed supporting two tables, one stationary and the other movable. ZPPR documents
generally referred to the stationary half or table as half 1 and to the movable half or table as half
2. An artist’s rendering of the ZPPR facility which labels the components of the machine is shown

 34

in Figure 2.11. A photograph of the ZPPR matrix being loading is shown in Figure 2.12.
Comparison of Figure 2.2 and Figure 2.12 shows the difference in size between ZPR-3 and ZPPR.
Each ZPPR table was 14 feet wide and 5 feet long. During loading operations, the tables were
separated by 5 feet. In the original ZPPR machine built in the late 1960s, stainless steel square
tubes, nominally 0.040 inches thick, 2.175 inches x 2.277 inches (outside dimension), and 48
inches long, were stacked horizontally on both tables to form a 53-row by 55-column square
“honeycomb” matrix. The matrix tubes were supported by massive cast-iron table and L-shaped
structures known as the bed and knees. In some documents, these L-shaped support structures on
the sides of the matrix are referred to as the clamp.
A plenum region, which included control-rod drives and experimental apparatus, existed beyond
the matrix at the outer end of each half. The plenum provided a flow path for cooling air into and
out of the assembly matrix. The (horizontal) control rods projected through holes in a steel back
plate, and the drive mechanisms were positioned on the outside of this back plate. The matrix
machine was near the center of a large cylindrical cell (room) with a diameter of 50 feet (15 m)
and height of 30 feet (9 m).
ZPPR was expanded in the mid-1970s, and the number of matrix tubes on each table approximately
doubled as a result of that expansion. Figure 2.12 shows the final expanded machine. In the
expanded ZPPR configuration, the matrix tubes were square stainless steel tubes, nominally
0.040 inches thick, 2.175 inches x 2.175 inches (outside dimension) and 60 inches long. Those
tubes were stacked horizontally on both tables to form a 77-row by 77-column square
“honeycomb” matrix. The reader should be aware that the matrix tubes in the pre-expansion ZPPR
had slightly different dimensions from the matrix tubes in the post-expansion ZPPR and that the
expansion increased the matrix size from 53 x 55 to 77 x 77 (see Table 2.1).
A matrix position in ZPPR was specified by the matrix half (1 for stationary half and 2 for movable
half), row number and column number. ZPPR differed from its predecessors in how row and
column numbers were assigned and in how they were designated. In the ZPPR matrix numbering
convention, each matrix position is identified by two numbers separated by a hyphen. The row
number was appended to the half number, so all rows in the stationary half begin with 1 and all
rows in the movable half begin with 2. In the original ZPPR matrix, the range of row numbers
was 111 to 163 in half 1 and 211 to 263 in half 2. The range of column numbers in both halves of
the original ZPPR matrix was 10 to 64. For an observer standing between matrix halves and facing
the stationary table, column numbers start with the lowest column number on the observer’s left
and increase to the highest number on the right. Facing the movable half, the column numbers start
with the lowest numbers on the observer’s right and continue to the highest number on the
observer’s left.
For example, consider matrix position 133-27. This designation corresponds to half 1, row 33,
column 27. Matrix position 233-27 corresponds to half 2, row 33, column 27. The column
numbers for both halves start at the same position such that 133-27 and 233-27 are directly aligned
at the full table closure position. The center positions in the original ZPPR matrix were 137-37
and 237-37.
The ZPPR convention for numbering rows and columns changed only slightly when the ZPPR
matrix was expanded from 53 x 55 to 77 x 77. The range of row numbers was 111 – 187 in half 1

 35

and 211 – 287 in half 2. The range of column numbers was 11 – 87 in both halves. The convention
for designating positions did not change, so 133-27 still meant half 1, row 33, column 27 and 233-
27 still meant half 2, row 33, column 27. The center positions in the expanded matrix were 149-
49 and 249-49.
To date it is not clear why the ZPPR staff chose to start the row numbers with 11 and the column
numbers with 10 in the original matrix or why the row numbers and column numbers in the
expanded matrix started with 11.

 Figure 2.11. Artist’s Rendering of the ZPPR Facility.
Like its predecessors, ZPPR achieved the desired average compositions of the regions of the
reactor to be simulated by loading the matrix with stainless steel drawers containing rectangular
plates (or, in some experiments, with cylindrical rods) of different materials such as plutonium,
depleted uranium, enriched uranium, stainless steel, sodium, etc.
The fuel plates used in ZPPR were HEU metal, DU metal, natural uranium metal, Pu-U-Mo metal
alloy and Pu-Al metal alloy. The reactors simulated in ZPPR were predominantly oxide-fueled.
To simulate an oxide-fueled reactor, columns of metal fuel plates were mixed with columns of
depleted U3O8 plates and iron oxide (Fe2O3) plates to achieve the desired U:O and Pu:O ratios.
Columns of clad sodium plates, clad fuel plates, stainless steel plates, and the stainless steel in the
drawers and matrix tubes provided the sodium coolant content, cladding and assembly structural
components for the reactor of interest. Careful planning and assembly design were required to
determine the mix of fuel and diluent plates combined with the steel in the drawers and matrix
tubes to achieve the fuel, coolant, and structural material content of the targeted core, blanket and
reflector regions in the reactor.

 36

The earliest ZPPR assembly programs used DP control rod drawers and PSRs for reactor control.
The designs and operating principles of the DP control rod drawers and PSRs used at ZPPR were
similar to the designs and operating principles of the DP control rod drawers and PSRs used at
ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 (see Section 2.2). ZPPR-2 had both types of control rods in the core. The DP
control rod drawers were phased out sometime after ZPPR-2 ended. The later ZPPR assemblies
only used PSRs for reactor control.
The stainless steel drawers used at ZPPR were similar to the stainless steel drawers used at ZPR-
6 and ZPR-9 in terms of dimensions and function. Back drawers were used if the core, axial
blanket and axial reflector exceeded the length of the front drawer or if the length of the radial
blanket or radial reflector exceeded the length of the front drawer. If back drawers were used for
an assembly, then there was a front matrix map and a back matrix map for each half of the

A neutron source had to be present in each matrix half during the startup of any ZPPR assembly
not containing an inherent source in the core such as 240Pu. Most ZPPR assemblies used the Pu-
U-Mo fuel plates. The plutonium component of a Pu-U-Mo plate contained ~11 wt.% 240Pu, so a
neutron source was not needed in most ZPPR assemblies.
Two shields could be moved between the matrix halves when they were separated to reduce
radiation exposure for staff members loading or unloading drawers. Figure 2.11 shows a shield
inserted between the matrix halves. In Figure 2.12, the shields are circled in blue. As seen, behind
the person loading the drawer is one shield in its withdrawn position. The other shield is just
visible to the left of the right half of the matrix and is in the inserted position.

3 DRAWER MASTER RECORDS
It is worthwhile to address a few obvious comments the user of the ZPR/ZPPR records may have.
The first comment is that many of these records are difficult to read. The second comment is that
many of these records are difficult to interpret. The unfortunate answer to these comments is that
the ZPR/ZPPR records were never intended for use by people many decades after the critical
assemblies were built and the experiments were run. These records were intended for use by the
staff of ZPR-3, ZPR-6, ZPR-9 or ZPPR. The loading records, drawer master records, reactor
logbooks and other records supported daily operations in the facilities. If some information was
missing or unclear, someone in a nearby office could answer any questions. It is likely that no one
who produced or used those records when the ZPR/ZPPR facilities operated anticipated the
possibility that someone would try to construct detailed models of the experiments many decades
after the experiments were run.
In the 1950s, 1960s and early 1970s, it was reasonable to expect that the fast reactors for which
the ZPR/ZPPR assemblies provided design data would be built and operating. Further, it was even
more reasonable to assume that the experimental facilities like ZPR/ZPPR would continue and
potentially grow in complexity. Finally, it is unrealistic to assume that the staff of ZPR-3, ZPR-6
or ZPR-9 would have considered it feasible to construct geometrically accurate models of these
experiments and obtain numerical results. In the mid-1980s, the ZPPR staff developed a code to
construct such models but obtaining highly accurate continuous energy Monte Carlo solutions or
mult-group deterministic solutions for high fidelity as-built models was not feasible with the
computing technology available at that time.
When ZPR-3 was shut down, the ZPR-3 records were stored at ANL-W. When ZPR-6 and ZPR-
9 were shut down, their records were placed in boxes and shipped to ZPPR for storage. Likewise,
the ZPPR records were placed in boxes and stored after ZPPR was shut down. All of those boxes
were probably stored in the basement at the ZPPR facility in Idaho.
In the late 1990s or early 2000s, the Department of Energy Nuclear Criticality Safety Program
started a historical records preservation program. ANL-W received money to scan the stored paper
records and convert them to electronic files. The actual scanning was performed by a retired ZPPR
technician and supervised by R. W. Schaefer, a former analyst at ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR.
It is likely that all available ZPR-3 records were scanned. The first ZPR-3 assembly was ZPR-3/1,
and the last ZPR-3 assembly was ZPR-3/63. The scanned ZPR-3 records include almost all of
those assemblies. There are one or two missing ZPR-3 assemblies in the scanned records, but
those assemblies may never have been built. Occasionally an assembly program was planned but
never built due to shifting program priorities at a higher level. ZPR-6/8, for example, falls into
that category.
The records for all ZPPR assemblies except ZPPR-1 were scanned. According to R. W. Schaefer,
the ZPPR-1 records were stored on some unconventional medium that was not amenable to
scanning.
A significant number of records for ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were not scanned. The missing records for
ZPR-6 are ZPR-6 Assemblies 1, 2, 3 and 4 although that loss may not be important (see Table 2.1).
ZPR-6/1 was just of test of the ZPR-6 facility, experimental equipment and techniques. ZPR-6/2

 39

and ZPR-6/3 were clean physics benchmarks for a sodium-cooled uranium carbide-fueled reactor,
and ZPR-6/4Z was a zoned uranium carbide core with sodium cooling. ZPR-6/5 was similar to
ZPR-6/4Z.
The missing records for ZPR-9 are ZPR-9 Assemblies 11 through 27; ZPR-9/10 was never built.
The most important missing records for ZPR-9 are ZPR-9/26 and ZPR-9/27 because these were
design and engineering mockups of the Fast Test Reactor (the initial name for FFTF). The
prevailing story regarding these omissions is that some group at ANL-W wanted the space where
the boxes were stored by a fixed date that determined the termination of the scanning.
It seems likely that some boxes that were not scanned were discarded along with various ZPPR
records. However, there may be some records that still exist. After the formation of INL, an INL
staff member (J. B. Briggs) was able to locate and scan the ZPR-3 reactor logbooks to allow the
creation of an ICSBEP benchmark in 2009. In addition, the LLNL staff located and scanned some
records related to the ZPPR plate inventory for use at the National Critical Experiment Research
Center (NCERC) in Nevada. Consequently, there may be existing boxes of records stored at INL
that have not been scanned. However, it would be necessary to spend time at INL examining each
box to determine whether there were additional useful records that could be scanned. At present
that is a funding question which demands significant interest to be placed on oxide fueled, sodium
cooled fast reactor technology.
3.1 Drawer Master Characteristics
As stated previously, the ZPR/ZPPR staff attempted to match the desired average composition in
each region of the reactor to be simulated by loading small plates of various materials into drawers.
Those drawers were loaded into the matrix tubes in a specified pattern to simulate the core, axial
blanket, axial reflector, radial blanket, radial reflector and any special regions of the reactor design
of interest.
The term drawer master is used in two related contexts in this document. Physically, a drawer
master was an actual drawing or blueprint showing the plate loading pattern in a drawer. The
drawer master figures served as guides or templates for the technicians loading the drawers. A
drawer master figure showed the plate type, plate size and location for each plate to be loaded into
a drawer. The drawer master figure specified exactly where each plate of each plate type and size
should be placed in a drawer.
Plate type refers to the composition of the plate. In some cases, a composition might be sufficient
to identify the plate type, especially if all plates of a material were obtained from the same source
at the same time. In other cases, plates of similar sizes and of the same basic material may have
been purchased at different times from different vendors. Stainless steel plates provide one
example. Groups of stainless steel plates were purchased from different vendors at various times
to meet the requirements of experimental programs. The average mass and composition of one lot
of stainless steel plates may differ slightly from the average mass and composition of another lot
of nominally the same stainless steel plates purchased from another vendor and/or at a different
time. Sodium plates provide a second example. Sodium plates were purchased or fabricated at
various times for ZPR/ZPPR programs, and the different sets are not necessarily identical. It was
important to be specific about the plate type and size at each location in a drawer to minimize
experimental uncertainty.

 40

In addition to specifying the plate type and size at each location in a drawer, the drawer master
figure also included any special instructions for loading the plates into the drawers or notes related
to the drawer master. For example, occasionally plates were rotated to produce the required
orientation when the plates were loaded into drawers. Partial drawers were discussed above. It
was sometimes necessary to rotate plates 90° about the Z-axis of the drawer (or matrix tube) to
achieve the necessary plate positioning in partial drawers. Loading of detectors or special
experimental equipment into drawers might also require special instructions.
The term drawer master is also used in the context of physically loading and unloading the matrix
tubes. The loading records for each assembly program specify the drawer master (plate loading
pattern) to be placed in each matrix tube during a core loading operation. In some cases, the
loading records also specify the drawer master to be removed from each matrix tube during a core
loading operation and the disposition of that drawer master. Loading records and core loading
operations are discussed in more detail later.
The specification of which drawer master was in each matrix position in each half of the split-table
machine is known as a matrix loading map, matrix map or interface map. Another term that is
occasionally used in place of matrix map is all master map (AMM). Drawer master is used in this
document to refer both to the physical drawing or blueprint used by the technicians to load drawers
and to the specific plate-loading pattern in a drawer or matrix tube.
In general, multiple different drawer masters were required to create the core of the desired
configuration. Multiple different drawer masters might also be required to create the radial blanket
and/or radial reflector.
The most common reason for using multiple drawer masters to describe essentially the same unit
cell is the finite size of the plate inventory in the facility. There were usually several plate sizes
available for a given plate type (material), but the number of plates of any one size was limited.
As a result, several different drawer masters might be required to describe the same unit cell.
Those different drawer masters had approximately the same average composition, but they differed
with respect to the specific set of plate sizes used and possibly with respect to the locations of the
plates in the drawer.
If the plate loadings in the drawers were asymmetric about the axial centerlines of the drawers, the
number of distinct drawer masters required to define the reactor increased significantly. The axial
centerline of the drawer is the centerline of the long axis of the drawer. Asymmetry in the drawer
plate loadings might require opposite or mirror image drawer masters between matrix positions on
the left side of the Y-axis of the assembly and the corresponding matrix positions on the right side
of the Y-axis and/or between matrix positions on the stationary table and the corresponding matrix
positions on the movable table. In this context, the Y-axis of the assembly is the center column of
the assembly or, in some assemblies, the line between the two center columns of the assembly.
Likewise, the X-axis of the assembly is the center row of the assembly or the line between the two
center rows of the assembly. Note that in some assemblies the center of the assembly is offset
from the center of the matrix tube array to provide space for special measurements.
A third factor that might increase the number of drawer masters required to define the reactor
relates to the unit cell for the reactor to be simulated. Generally, the width of the unit cell for the
core to be simulated corresponded to the width of one drawer, so a drawer master defined one unit

 41

cell of the reactor core. However, there were exceptions where the width of the core unit cell did
not match the width of a drawer. ZPR-9/29, the second gas-cooled fast reactor (GCFR) assembly
program at ZPR-9, provides an example. In ZPR-9/29, the basic unit cell was only 75% of the
drawer width, so three adjacent ZPR-9/29 drawers were required to define four GCFR unit cells.
In the present context, this means that the repeating pattern of plate columns occupied 75% of one
drawer. Consequently, the repeating drawer unit cell in ZPR-9/29 consisted of three adjacent
drawers containing four repeating cells of plate materials. There were other assembly programs
at ZPR-3, ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR in which the repeating unit cell in the assembly consisted of
two or more adjacent drawers.
If back drawers were required to create the configuration of interest, then there were drawer master
figures for the back drawers as well. In addition, there were drawer masters for drawers containing
special equipment such as detectors, proton recoil spectrometers and other experimental
equipment. In principle, there was a separate drawer master for every unique front drawer, back
drawer and special experimental drawer loaded into the matrix tubes. In practice, there were some
exceptions to this general principle.
One exception relates to plates loaded directly into matrix tubes without drawers. In some cases,
a drawer master figure was created for the situation where plates were loaded directly into the
matrix tubes. The drawer master figure in such cases typically included a note or some other
indication that the plates were loaded directly into the matrix tubes with no drawer. In other cases,
no drawer master figure was created for the case where plates were loaded directly into matrix
tubes. In those cases, the fact that plates were loaded directly into matrix tubes was indicated by
a note in the loading records, reactor logbook, an associated report or some other document.
A second exception relates to a drawer master containing special equipment that was used in one
matrix tube in only one loading in an assembly program. It has occasionally been discovered that
the the loading records (discussed below) for an assembly program refer to drawer masters that
were not included in the scanned drawer masters for that assembly program. There may have been
an omission during the scanning process, or the drawer master figure may not have been preserved
for some reason. It is also possible that no actual drawer master figure was created for a
configuration that would be used only once and in only one location.
3.2 Evolution of Drawer Master Figures
Drawer loading remained a manual process from the first drawer loaded for ZPR-3/1 in 1955 until
the last drawer was loaded for ZPPR-21 in 1990, and the technicians at all four Argonne critical
experiment facilities used the drawer master figures as guides for drawer loading. Although the
process of loading drawers did not change, the drawer master figures did evolve significantly over
the years. This document shows some representative examples, but other forms were developed.
It is not practical to show every variation of a drawer master figure used at ZPR-3, ZPR-6, ZPR-9
and ZPPR.
All drawer master figures used at ZPR-3 were drawn by hand on printed forms. Figure 3.1 and
Figure 3.2 show two drawer master pictures for ZPR-3/1 from 1955. Figure 3.3 shows a drawer
master drawn for ZPR-3/63, the last ZPR-3 assembly, in 1970.

 42

The numbers across the tops of Figure 3.1 through Figure 3.3 are axial positions within the drawer
in inches. The sixteen letters A through P on the left sides of Figure 3.1 through Figure 3.3
designate columns. The ZPR-3 staff divided the two-inch interior width of the drawer into sixteen
0.125 inch columns that were identified by the letters A through P. This provided a convenient
way to identify positions within a drawer.
In some cases, the ZPR-3 staff wrote the nominal masses of the different types of plates in the
figures, but this was not a completely consistent practice.
As these figures show, different plate types were designated by different colors and/or different
patterns on the figures. Note that “25” and “28” in Figure 3.1 were standard designations for 235U
and 238U, respectively, during the early years of ZPR-3 operations. Likewise, “49” was a standard
designation for 239Pu during that era. This may have been a holdover from the Manhattan Project
and the early years of the Cold War, but it was a common practice in any event.

 Figure 3.1. ZPR-3/1 Core Drawer Master.
One problem that arises in interpreting the drawer master figures is determining the lengths of the
plates in the drawers. In some cases such as Figure 3.1, the drawer master figures show clear lines
across the plates that indicate the boundaries between plates and, consequently, the lengths of the
plates. In other cases such as Figure 3.3, the drawer master figures show small gaps between
adjacent plates in a column to indicate the lengths of the plates in the column.

 43

In other cases, such as Figure 3.2, it is not entirely clear from the drawer master figure what the
correct plate lengths are because the figure just shows continuous lines such as the lines for
depleted uranium (black) and aluminum (green) in Figure 3.2. In those cases, it is necessary to
examine the plate inventory records to determine what plate sizes were available when the
assembly was built. Plate inventory records are discussed later. It may also be useful to examine
other drawer master figures for the assembly of interest because it is possible that other drawer
master figures for the assembly of interest may provide more detailed information regarding the
plates used in the assembly.
Other drawer master forms were developed. In some of those forms, the types and sizes of the
plates to be loaded were written on the form.

 Figure 3.2. ZPR-3/1 Core Drawer Master with Rotated Plates.

 44

 Figure 3.3. ZPR-3/63 Core Drawer Master.
ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 initially used drawer master figures that were hand-drawn on standard printed
forms. Both facilities later transitioned to drawer master figures that were machine-generated as
standard blueprints. Figure 3.4 shows a manually colored drawer master for ZPR-6/6A.
Comparison of Figure 3.4 with Figure 3.1 through Figure 3.3 shows that the standard printed form
had changed between ZPR-3 and ZPR-6. In fact, the standard printed form probably changed
multiple times at each facility during the years when the facility operated. ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were
more consistent than ZPR-3 with respect to indicating plate lengths. In cases where a plate column
contains plates of different lengths, the drawer masters used at ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 generally showed
the plate lengths clearly.
After the end of the ZPR-6/7 program, ZPR-6 transitioned from hand-drawn drawer masters to
machine-generated standard blueprints. The blueprints were easier to read and use. Figure 3.5
shows a blueprint drawer master for ZPR-6/10.
Figure 3.6 shows a hand-drawn drawer master for ZPR-9/1, and Figure 3.7 shows a blueprint
drawer master for ZPR-9/31. Figure 3.8 shows a blueprint drawer master for ZPPR-18. All ZPPR
drawer masters for all assemblies were blueprints like that shown. Figure 3.6 again shows the
potential difficulty in determining plate lengths for the hand-drawn figures if there are no clear
delineations on the figures.

 45

It seems likely that the transition from hand-drawn drawer master figures to machine-generated
blueprints occurred around the same time at ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR because all three facilities
were part of the same division at Argonne.
The numbers on the top or bottom of Figure 3.4 through Figure 3.8 are axial positions in the drawer
in inch units. ZPPR, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 also divided the two-inch interior width of a standard
drawer into sixteen 1/8th inch columns. The columns were identified by numbers 1 – 16 in ZPR-
6 and ZPR-9 rather than by letters A – P that were used in ZPR-3 assemblies.

identifier consisted of 1 – 4 letters that provided unique identification for the plate type. For
example, PUMN is the identifier for Pu-U-Mo plates manufactured by NUMEC, and PUMD is the
identifier for Pu-U-Mo plates manufactured by Dow. Plates of similar sizes and materials
purchased from different vendors at different times had different identifiers. For example, SST,
SS75 and SSET denoted different lots of stainless steel plates acquired at different times from
different vendors. These identifiers are discussed in more detail later.

3.3 Drawer Master Labeling or Identification Conventions
The conventions for assigning identification numbers or labels to drawer masters developed
differently at ANL-W and ANL-E. The initial scheme used at ZPR-3 for assigning drawer master
identification numbers or labels consisted of one or more letters and one or more numbers. In
some early ZPR-3 assemblies, the drawer master figure also showed the matrix position in which
the drawer master would be placed. There was no way to determine the ZPR-3 assembly in which
the drawer master would be used from the drawer master label.
The ZPR-3 staff developed a better approach beginning with ZPR-3/21. In the new scheme, a
drawer master label consisted of the assembly number, a hyphen, and a combination of numbers
and letters. For example, one drawer master label in ZPR-3/21 was 21-C-103B. This approach
provided a positive link between the drawer master and the assembly number, but the combination
of letters and numbers that uniquely identified each drawer master in an assembly program varied
between assembly programs and lacked consistency.
The final ZPR-3 labeling scheme was developed for ZPR-3/53. In this scheme, each label
consisted of three parts and had the form aa-b-ccc where “aa” was the assembly number such as
53, and “b” was 0, 1 or 2. In general, 0 indicated that the drawer master was used in both halves

 50

of the machine, 1 indicated that the drawer master was used in the stationary half (half 1), and 2
indicated that the drawer master was used in the movable half (half 2). The “ccc” was the unique
two- or three-digit identifier for the drawer master. One example is 053-1-101. This is interpreted
as Assembly 53, half 1 (stationary half), type 101. Some ZPR-3 drawer master figures have labels
such as 053-1,2-205. This is a shorthand for 053-1-205 and 053-2-205 and indicates that the
drawer master is used in both halves. This labeling scheme was used for all subsequent ZPR-3
assemblies although the 0 before the assembly number was eventually dropped.
ZPPR adopted the final ZPR-3 labeling scheme and used it for all ZPPR assemblies. All ZPPR
drawer master labels are of the form aa-b-ccc where “aa” is a two-digit assembly number, even for
the first ZPPR assemblies, and “b” is 0, 1 or 2. The 0 indicates that the drawer master is used in
both halves of the machine, 1 indicates that the drawer master is used in half 1 (the stationary half),
and 2 indicates that the drawer master is used in half 2 (the movable half). The “ccc” is the unique
two- or three-digit drawer master identifier. An example from ZPPR-2 is 02-1-402, which is
interpreted as Assembly 2, used in half 1, type 402. An example from ZPPR-21 is 21-0-100, which
is interpreted as Assembly 21, used in both halves, type 100.
ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 developed various labeling schemes before settling on a final version in the
early 1970s. The available drawer master figures for early ZPR-6 assemblies (through Assembly
6A) and early ZPR-9 assemblies (Assemblies 1 – 9) show three- or four-digit identification
numbers. A separate part of these drawer master figures shows the drawer type. The drawer type
is generally listed as S (stationary half) or M (movable half) although there were other qualifiers
in the drawer type in some cases.
A unique labeling scheme was developed for ZPR-6/7. This scheme was based on a prefix
followed by several numbers and letters. The prefix was 7 for ZPR-6/7. The numbers and letters
following the prefix identified the specific drawer master type. The letters identified the specific
types and sizes of plates used in the drawer master.
In the early 1970s, the staff of ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 developed the labeling convention that was used
for all subsequent ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 assemblies. The final scheme used at ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 was
based on a drawer master name or label of the form abcd-ef-ghi. The “ab” identified the assembly.
The “cd” was part of the identifier for a particular drawer master or a particular class of drawer
masters such as core, radial blanket or radial reflector. Typical values for “cd” were 00, 01, 02
and 10. The “e” was either F (front drawer) or B (back drawer), and “f” was either S (stationary
half) or M (movable half). The “ghi” consisted of one or more characters that identified the unique
configuration in the drawer master. For example, 2901-FS-1 and 2901-FS-2 were two front (F)
drawer masters in the stationary (S) half of the core of ZPR-9/29, and 2910-FS-1 was a front radial
blanket drawer master in the stationary half of ZPR-9/29.
3.4 Use of the Drawer Master Records
When ZPR-3, ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR operated, available analytical methods, computer
hardware and computer software limited the complexity of the models that could be created.
Initially, models of assemblies were one-dimensional spheres, cylinders or slabs. As methods,
computer software and computer hardware capabilities evolved, the standard models of assemblies
became two-dimensional R-Z or X-Y models. Eventually, methods and computer capabilities
advanced to the point where X-Y-Z models were possible.

 51

All of those models were based on homogeneous compositions in regions of the core, axial blanket,
axial reflector, radial blanket and radial reflector. At ZPR-6 and ZPR-9, the staff developed a
computer program that could automatically calculate the homogeneous composition in each region
based on the region volume, the number of plates of each type in each region, the mass of drawer
steel and matrix tube steel in each region, and the recorded nominal compositions of the plates,
drawers and matrix tubes. ZPPR developed a similar capability. Later versions of these programs
may have been able to create the homogeneous composition for each individual drawer master.
In the mid-1980s, the ZPPR staff began to write the BLDVIM program. BLDVIM used the drawer
master descriptions and loading records to create a high fidelity as-built model of an assembly for
VIM, the continuous energy Monte Carlo code developed at Argonne primarily to analyze the
critical experiments performed at ZPR-3, ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR.
Using available drawer master records and loading records to create as-built models of ZPR/ZPPR
assemblies requires converting those records to digital files that can be read and interpreted by the
software used to create the model. This was true when the ZPR/ZPPR facilities operated, and it is
equally true when this document was written.
All available drawer master figures are scanned PDF copies of the original paper versions. It has
been suggested that optical character recognition (OCR) software could be used to convert the
drawer master records and loading records to the digital files required by the software the creates
the as-built model. That approach has never been tested, but inspection of Figure 3.1 through
Figure 3.8 shows that the task would be non-trivial, particularly for the drawer master figures that
predate adoption of standardized blueprint figures.
The ages of the drawer master figures at the date of scanning ranged from ~10 years to ~48 years.
Many of those records are faded, discolored or stained. For the hand-drawn drawer masters, there
are wide variations in how individual drawer masters were drawn, the standard printed forms used,
and the notes and other written text added to the individual figures.
The clarity of the scanned blueprint drawer masters depends in part on age and in part on how
clear the originals were. Some of the scanned blueprints are difficult to read due to the fact that
printing on the originals was very light. As is the case today, the age and condition of a toner
cartridge affects the quality and legibility of pages printed on a laser printer and that same issue
affected the machines that printed the blueprints at the time.
It is not obvious that OCR will save much effort over manually converting the drawer master
figures to a text file or other digital record. It may be necessary to tailor the OCR application to
the drawer master records for the assembly of interest, and it would certainly be necessary to check
the resulting digital file carefully against the original PDF version of the drawer master records.
This is true whether the drawer master figures are converted to a text file or other digital record
manually or by OCR.
It is certainly possible that some combination of OCR and artificial intelligence could facilitate
conversion of the blueprint drawer masters to the required digital form for processing. It is less
clear how successful that approach would be for the hand-drawn figures, especially the earlier
ZPR-3 figures.

 52

The drawer master figure shows the plates in a drawer, but it does not show the drawer itself, and
the figure generally does not show the small spring inserted at the back of the drawer to push the
plates forward.
The spring is small and is located at the back of the drawer in a region of low importance, so an
accurate representation of the spring is not important. Figure 2.4 shows an example of the drawer
spring used in ZPR-3. Traditionally, the spring has been modeled as a 2 x 2 x 0.0625 inch steel
plate at the back of the drawer for standard drawers and as a 1.5 x 2 x 0.0625 inch steel plate for
narrow PSR drawers. There are very few DP control rod drawers in an assembly, so neglecting
any spring at the back of a DP drawer has a negligible effect on reactivity or other measured
parameters.
It is necessary to represent the drawer accurately because the drawer mass is much larger than the
spring mass and because at least the front part of the drawer is located in a region of high
importance compared to the location of the spring. The entries for a drawer in the material records
(discussed in a later section) consists of the front plate, back plate, bottom and sides. The mass of
the front plate of a front drawer includes any tabs on the side of the drawer that mate with notches
in the matrix tubes to ensure consistent drawer positioning. The mass of a back plate of a back
drawer includes any handle or fold used by the technicians to remove the back drawer from the
back of the matrix tube. The mass listed for the drawer bottom and sides in the material records
is the mass per inch. The mass value listed for the bottom and sides of a drawer is the combined
mass of the bottom and sides. A separate record in the material records partitions this mass into
the mass of the bottom and the mass of the sides. The masses listed for the drawer components
(front plate, back plate, bottom and sides) include any perforations (see Figure 2.4 and Figure 2.5).
Because the masses of the drawer components include perforations, tabs on front plates of front
drawers and handles on back plates of back drawers, the computed densities of the drawer
components based on the nominal listed physical dimensions of those components may be greater
than or less than the actual density of stainless steel (or aluminum in the case of aluminum
drawers).
3.5 Limitations of Drawer Master Records
In principle, the drawer master records for an assembly program describe every drawer master
used during that program. In practice, there are gaps in the available drawer master records for
several reasons.
 1. For special experimental drawers, the drawer master figures frequently do not show the
 experimental equipment. For example, the neutron spectrum was measured with a proton
 recoil spectrometer in a drawer. The drawer master figure for that drawer shows the plates
 in the drawer, but spaces occupied by the spectrometer and pre-amplifier are just empty
 rectangles. In general, the spaces occupied by anything other than plates or calandria
 (described in later section), appear as empty rectangles in the relevant drawer master figure.
 2. It is possible that a drawer master figure was inadvertently skipped during the scanning
 process.
 3. The ZPR/ZPPR staff did not necessarily archive every drawer master figure used in an
 assembly program. If a drawer master was used only once in a single core loading, that
 figure was not necessarily saved. For that matter, it is possible that a drawer master figure
 was never created if the new drawer master was a minor modification of an existing drawer

 53

 master that was only going to be loaded once in a single matrix location.
In the case of experimental equipment such as the proton recoil spectrometer, it is necessary to
consult other documents to model the spectrometer or other experimental equipment.
In the case of a missing drawer master, the importance of the missing drawer master depends on
the purpose of the model and the specific situation. Clearly, if the missing drawer master defined
the experimental measurement of interest, it will be difficult to proceed without at least an
approximate model of the missing drawer master.
On the other hand, if the missing drawer master is loaded in a small number of matrix positions
and is not strongly related to the measurement of interest, using a reasonable approximation of the
missing drawer may have very little effect. Consider a criticality measurement with a missing
drawer master that is only loaded in two matrix positions. Replacing the missing drawer master
with a reasonable approximation of it is unlikely to have a significant effect on the measured
reactivity because the substitutions are only in two locations out of thousands of occupied matrix
positions. The experimenters attempted to maintain symmetry whenever possible to simplify
analysis. Consequently, the best substitute for a missing drawer master is likely to be the drawer
master at a symmetric location on the other side of the X-axis or Y-axis. Note that there are a few
exceptions to the statement in the preceding paragraph about attempting to maintain symmetry
across the X-axis and Y-axis of the assembly and between matrix halves:
 1. If special experimental equipment was located in only one drawer at one location, the
 drawer master in that location would differ from the drawer masters in symmetric locations.
 2. The thermocouple drawer masters in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 would be slightly different from
 the drawer masters at symmetry positions.
 3. The detector drawers used in some measurements in ZPPR were intentionally placed in
 asymmetric locations and widely dispersed to sample as much of the core, radial blanket
 and radial reflector as possible.
3.6 Modeling Drawer Masters
To construct a model of any ZPR/ZPPR experimental configuration, it is necessary to model the
contents of each matrix tube accurately. In other words, it is necessary to model each drawer
master as accurately as possible.
The length of the smallest as-built Monte Carlo model, a ZPR-3 assembly, to date is ~2,000 lines,
and the length of the largest as-built Monte Carlo model of a ZPPR assembly was ~50,000 lines.
Constructing accurate as-built models of ZPR/ZPPR assemblies, i.e., models without
typographical or other errors, requires computer software and digital processing, so it necessary to
convert the drawer master figures to a text file or other form of digital record that can be processed
by the software developed for that purpose.
As discussed earlier, it would probably be difficult to use OCR software to convert the drawer
master figures to usable, reliable digital files that could be processed to create an accurate as-built
model of a ZPR/ZPPR assembly. However, digital technology is advancing rapidly on many
fronts, so a future reader of this document may successfully use OCR software and/or artificial
intelligence (AI) to create the required digital drawer master file without the tedium of manual

 54

processing. Nevertheless, it would be necessary to verify that the final digital form of the drawer
master figures is an accurate conversion of the original drawer master figures.
To model a drawer master correctly, it is important to understand certain conventions and general
principles. Figure 3.9 is an asymmetric core drawer master used in ZPPR-13. It illustrates several
important features that are relevant for modeling purposes:
 1. In Figure 3.9, the X-axis of the drawer master is on the left side, and the positive X-axis
 points toward the bottom of the page from .00 to 2.00. This is true for all ZPR/ZPPR
 drawer masters regardless of symmetry or asymmetry of the plate columns in the drawer.
 2. The positive Y-axis of any drawer master is normal to the page and points toward the
 reader.
 3. The positive Z-axis of any drawer master is the long axis of the drawer master. For
 example, in Figure 3.9, the positive Z-axis extends from left to right, i.e., from 0.0 to 36
 inches. The axial centerline of any drawer master extends from left to right. In Figure 3.9,
 the axial centerline is at X = 1.00. For a drawer master with columns labelled A – P, the
 axial centerline is the line between columns H and I. For a drawer master with columns
 labelled 1 – 16, the axial centerline is the line between columns 8 and 9.
 4. The standard plate orientation in a drawer is the orientation shown in Figure 3.9. For a ¼
 x 2 x 8 inch Pu-U-Mo plate (ZPPR PU in Figure 3.9), the ¼ inch side is in the X-direction,
 the 2 inch side is in the Y-direction, and the 8 inch side is in the Z-direction. This is the
 standard orientation for all plates of all sizes.
 5. Plate columns should align across the interface between matrix halves, i.e., across the
 interface between the stationary half and the movable half or, equivalently, between half 1
 and half 2. Alignment in the present context means that the drawer in half 2 is a mirror
 image of the drawer in half 1. For a drawer master such as ZPPR-18 drawer master 18-0-
 206 shown in Figure 3.8 that is symmetric about the axial centerline of the drawer, this
 alignment will happen automatically.
 6. For asymmetric drawer master NL in the left half of either table (or matrix half), drawer
 master NR at the corresponding location in the right half of that table (or matrix half) will
 be the mirror image of drawer master NL. More generally, the drawer masters at
 corresponding locations on either side of the Y-axis of the assembly will be mirror images
 in almost all cases. The main exceptions are cases where limitations in the inventory of
 available plates make it impossible to match plate sizes exactly. Another exception is the
 case where detector drawers are placed asymmetrically in the matrix as they were for some
 ZPPR measurements.
 7. A drawer master figure shows the positions of plates in drawer, but any special equipment
 in the drawer, e.g., a proton recoil spectrometer, is generally represented as a blank
 rectangle. If the user wants to model the experimental equipment, it is necessary to consult
 other documents.

 55

 Figure 3.9. ZPPR-13 Core Drawer Master.
Note that a column or plate column is a row of plates in the Z-direction. For example, in Figure
3.9, the horizontal row from X = 1.75 to X = 2.00 labelled “ZPPR PU” is a plate column. If the
plate columns are labelled A – P as is the case in ZPR-3 drawer masters as shown in Figure 3.3,
the positive X-direction is from column A to column P. Likewise, if the plate columns are labelled
1 – 16 as is the case in Figure 3.7, the positive X-axis is from column 1 to column 16.
With regard to plate orientation, it was sometimes necessary to rotate some plates about one or
even two axes to load them into the a drawer in the correct position and orientation. This rotation
may be required to make one of the partial drawers discussed above. In addition, sometimes plates
were rotated 90° in alternating drawers in a checkerboard pattern in one or more loadings to
measure the effect of neutron streaming in the Y-direction. In some cases the finite size of the plate
inventory also required plates to be rotated to fit into some spaces of a drawer. In other cases, such
as Figure 3.2, the drawer master figure or an accompanying note will clearly indicate any required
rotation. The available plate sizes in the material library (or plate inventory) and the indicated
space in the drawer master figure will determine the rotation that allows the plate to fit into the
available space.
With regard to plate alignment across the matrix halves, for an asymmetric drawer master such as
ZPPR-13 drawer master 13-0-260 shown in Figure 3.9, alignment of the plate columns means that
materials must be continuous across the interface. The ZPPR PU column from 1.75 in to 2.00 in
in half 1 must line up with the corresponding ZPPR-PU column in half 2, the Fe 2O3 column from
.00 to .125 in half 1 must line up with the corresponding Fe 2O3 column in half 2, each NA column
must line up with the corresponding NA column of the same size in half 2, etc. For an asymmetric
drawer master, if the plate columns in half 1 do not line up with plate columns of the same type

 56

(material) and size in half 2, there is an error either in the definition of one of the drawer masters
or in the software that processes the digital drawer master file to produce the model.

 57

4 REACTOR LOGBOOKS
The reactor logbooks provide details of reactor operations and operating conditions, but they are
not experimental notebooks. The logbooks contain information that can be useful for constructing
models in some cases, but the logbooks only include information about reactor operations.
Measurement data were recorded by the data acquisition system and in laboratory notebooks. The
reactor logbooks did not function as laboratory notebooks, and generally there are no measurement
data values recorded in reactor logbook entries except data directly related to reactor operation.
The format of the logbook changed over the years. The available information and the usefulness
of that information varied according to the logbook and the facility. ZPR-3, ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and
ZPPR recorded somewhat different information in their reactor logbooks.
The following discussion presents the key features of the logbooks used at the four facilities, but
it not practical to show every possible example of the logbooks used at these facilities between
1955 and 1990.
4.1 ZPR-3 Logbooks
It is difficult to find useful information in the ZPR-3 logbooks for several reasons. First, it is likely
that the set of scanned logbooks does not encompass all of the ZPR-3 logbooks compiled between
1955 and 1970. The first pages of some ZPR-3 logbooks indicate that they are continuations of
other logbooks that do not seem to be included in the available set of scanned logbooks.
Second, ZPR-6, ZPR-9, and ZPPR used a separate logbook (or logbooks) for each assembly
program. ZPR-3 did not use a separate logbook for each assembly program. After one ZPR-3
assembly program ended, logbook entries for another ZPR-3 program generally began on the next
blank page of the existing logbook. As a result, a single ZPR-3 logbook frequently contains entries
for several different assembly programs. The motivation for this practice may have been the fact
that many early ZPR-3 assembly programs were very short and lasted for only a few weeks.
Third, the entries in the logbooks do not appear to be in sequence in some cases. There are gaps
between the assembly programs included in one logbook, i.e., the programs included in one
logbook are not necessarily sequential. For any given assembly program of interest, it may be
necessary to look through several logbooks to find entries for that program. In addition, it may be
necessary to look through several logbooks to verify that all entries for that assembly program
have been located.
Fourth, the logbooks generally do not have separate entries for the assembly number and the
loading number. Instead, those two numbers are combined in the entry for the loading number.
For example, the logbook entry for loading 22 in ZPR-3 Assembly 18 (ZPR-3/18 loading 22) is
18-22. It is necessary to examine each logbook entry carefully to determine the correct assembly
number and loading number.
ZPR-3 logbooks were just blank notebooks. The date and the spaces for entries were rubber
stamped, and the relevant information was written in the appropriate blank spaces. The amount
and nature of the information included in a logbook entry varied from one assembly program to
another assembly program, from one loading to another loading, and possibly according to which
staff member was making the entry.

 58

Figure 4.1 shows a logbook entry for ZPR-3/25 loading 22. There are several relevant pieces of
information in this entry. The date is important because it is necessary to correct for radioactive
decay. The isotope masses in the ADEN library (materials library discussed below) are normalized
to January 1, 1977, so it is necessary to correct for decay between the date of the experiment and
the normalization date of the ADEN library. This correction is mostly relevant for 241Pu because
its half-life is ~14.29 years.
Each experimental measurement in an assembly program corresponds to a particular reactor
configuration. The loading number (LOADING #) entry in Figure 4.1, 25/22, corresponds to
Assembly 25 loading 22. This identifies the specific assembly and loading number and,
consequently, establishes the correspondence between the measurement configuration and the
reactor operating conditions.
The critical rod positions in Figure 4.1 may or may not be important, depending on whether the
measured excess reactivity was reported. At the critical condition, the four DP drawers in each
half that functioned as safety rods were fully inserted. At least one of the two DP drawers that
functioned as shim/control rods was only partially inserted at the critical condition.
The experimenters adjusted the measured excess reactivity to a set of standard conditions that
corresponded to all DP control rods fully inserted, a zero interface gap, and a standard temperature
to simplify analysis. The control rod adjustment was based on a calibrated control rod, the
interface gap adjustment was based on a measured interface gap coefficient, and any temperature
adjustment was based on a measured temperature coefficient. The reported or published excess
reactivity was the measured value adjusted to standard conditions unless the source document
states otherwise.
If an excess reactivity was reported, then it is sufficient to construct an as-built model with all DP
drawers fully inserted. Available documents do not list the excess reactivity in some cases. If no
reported excess reactivity is available, it is necessary to compute the worth of the partially inserted
DP drawer(s). This is accomplished by constructing one as-built model with all DP drawers fully
inserted and one as-built model with the DP shim/control rods at the positions indicated in the
loading records. The difference in reactivity between these two models is the adjustment for the
partially inserted DP drawer(s).

 59

 Figure 4.1. ZPR-3/25 Loading 22 Logbook Entry.

For purposes of clarification, the critical rod position listed in the ZPR-3 logbook is the distance
between the front of the DP drawer and the front of the matrix tube, i.e., the distance between the
front of the DP drawer and the interface between the stationary and movable tables at the full
closure position. For DP rod #10 in Figure 4.1, the front of the DP drawer is 6.362 inches from
the interface between the stationary and movable tables.
It is not clear what is meant by carriage alignment in Figure 4.1 or how it relates to the interface
gap. In some cases the logbook entry and other documents may list the interface gap coefficient
and the interface gap. The interface gap and interface gap coefficient are discussed in more detail
in Section 7.1.1 in the context of uncertainty analysis for criticality measurements.

 60

Figure 4.1 also shows the temperatures measured by the thermocouples in ZPR-3. For a uranium-
fueled core, these temperatures were relatively uniform and did not deviate very much from room
temperature. For a plutonium-fueled core, there were ~12 thermocouples in the core. Aside from
the thermocouple that measured the inlet temperature, the measured temperatures were typically
in the 30°C – 45°C range. After discarding the inlet temperature reading and any outliers, the
average temperature for a plutonium-fueled core is likely to be in the 35°C – 40°C range or 308 K
– 313 K range.
When the ZPR-3 staff adjusted excess reactivity to standard reporting conditions, they used a
