standard temperature. The documents that report the experimental results for an assembly program
may list that temperature. A common adjustment temperature for uranium-fueled cores was 25°C
(298 K) or 27°C (300 K). The adjustment temperature for a plutonium-fueled core may have been
significantly higher than 298 K because the average core temperature for a plutonium-fueled core
was significantly higher than the average core temperature for a uranium-fueled core.
If the reader wants to adjust reactivity to some other standard temperature such as 294 K, there are
at least two options for making that adjustment. The first option is to generate a set of cross
sections at the average core temperature for the as-built Monte Carlo model. The difference
between the reactivity of the as-built model at the average core temperature and the reactivity of
the as-built model at the nominal room temperature, e.g., 294 K, is the temperature adjustment.
The temperature adjustment is generally small, so the two Monte Carlo calculations may require
large numbers of histories to obtain a statistically meaningful reactivity difference.
The second option is to create a deterministic model and then to generate a set of cross sections at
the average core temperature and a set of cross sections at the nominal or standard reporting
temperature. The difference between the reactivity of the deterministic model at the standard
reporting temperature and the reactivity of the deterministic model at the average core temperature
is the temperature adjustment. Using a deterministic model will reduce the computational effort
required to obtain a meaningful reactivity difference. This latter approach was used for several
ZPR-3 assemblies.
The key entries for ZPR-3 logbooks are the assembly number, loading number, date, control rod
positions, reactor temperatures and the experiment or objective of the loading. The description of
the experiment or objective of the loading on any ZPR/ZPPR logbook or loading record (discussed
below) can be used to determine whether that loading is of interest for modeling purposes.
4.2 Logbooks for ZPR-6 and ZPR-9
ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 maintained a separate logbook for each assembly program, so it is much easier
to locate relevant information for a ZPR-6 assembly or ZPR-9 assembly. The logbooks used at
ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 also were just blank notebooks. The date and the spaces for entries were rubber
stamped, and the relevant information was entered in the appropriate blank spaces provided by the
rubber stamps.
Figure 4.2 shows a logbook entry for ZPR-6/7 loading 57 while Figure 4.3 shows a logbook entry
for ZPR-9/28 loading 45. Because each assembly program had a separate logbook, it was not
necessary to include the assembly number in the logbook entry.

 61

 Figure 4.2. ZPR-6/7 Loading 57 Logbook Entry.
Figure 4.2 contains several relevant entries. The loading number establishes the correspondence
between the measurement configuration and reactor operating conditions during the measurement.
The loading defines a particular core configuration with a specific set of drawer masters in the
matrix tubes, i.e., a specific matrix map. In addition to the loading number, logbooks for ZPR-6
and ZPR-9 include the startup number.
In the shutdown state, the stationary and movable tables were separated, any DP rods were fully
withdrawn, and any PSRs were fully inserted. Bringing the tables together, adjusting the DP rods
and any PSRs to obtain the desired critical or subcritical configuration, and making any desired
measurement was a startup. For some loadings, there was a single startup. For other loadings,
there were multiple startups to make different measurements. For example, making the necessary
operational measurements (control rod worths, interface gap coefficient, temperature coefficient,
etc.) to support reactor operations for an assembly program typically required multiple startups
from the reference critical configuration.
Measuring the neutron spectrum provides another example where two startups were required. Two
proton recoil spectrometers were required to measure neutron spectra because they measured
different but overlapping energy ranges. One spectrometer contained hydrogen gas, and the other
spectrometer contained methane. It was necessary to make the measurement with the hydrogen-
filled instrument in one startup and then to replace that spectrometer with the methane-filled
spectrometer in a second startup.

 62

The startup number matters occasionally because a specific measurement was made under the
conditions listed in the logbook for the startup in which that measurement was made.
The date is important because it is necessary to account for radioactive decay between the date of
the measurement and January 1, 1977, the date to which the material library is normalized.
The temperature listed in the logbook entry is not important because that is just the temperature of
the reactor cell (room containing the split table machine). ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were designed with
cooling systems, so the large temperature ranges in the core that prevailed in plutonium-fueled
ZPR-3 cores did not exist in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9. Temperatures in the core were measured with
thermocouples attached to fuel plates. Those temperatures were used to adjust the measured excess
reactivity to the standard reporting temperature, but the measured core temperatures were generally
not included in logbook entries. A typical value for the standard reporting temperature was 25°C
or 298 K although that value may be different for some assemblies. The cell temperature is not
very relevant today.
“Fuel Rod” in Figure 4.2 and Figure 4.3 refers to the DP control rods, and “Boron Rod” in these
figures refers to the PSRs. The DP rod positions in Figure 4.2 and Figure 4.3 are in centimeter
units rather than inch units.
The critical rod positions in Figure 4.2 may or may not be important, depending on whether the
measured excess reactivity was reported and on whether PSRs were present in the reactor. Early
ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 assemblies only used DP control drawers for reactor control. PSRs were
probably used in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 around or shortly after the time when ZPPR began using PSRs.
If only DP control rods were present in the reactor, the four DP drawers in each half that functioned
as safety rods were fully inserted at the critical condition. At least one of the two DP drawers that
functioned as shim/control rods was only partially inserted at the critical condition. For standard
reporting conditions with only DP rods present, all DP drawers were fully inserted, and the control
rod worths measured during the operational measurements were used to adjust the measured excess
reactivity to the excess reactivity corresponding to the configuration with all DP drawers fully
inserted.
If both DP control rods and PSRs were present, there were two options for establishing the critical
configuration. First, all PSRs could be fully withdrawn to their parked positions, the four DP
safety rods in each half could be fully inserted, and criticality could be maintained by partial
insertion of one or both DP shim/control rods. This is the case in Figure 4.2.
Second, all DP drawers could be fully inserted, most PSRs could be fully withdrawn, and one or
more PSRs could be partially inserted to maintain the critical state. This is the case in Figure 4.3.
For standard reporting conditions with both DP drawers and PSRs present, all DP drawers were
fully inserted, and all PSRs were fully withdrawn to their parked positions at ~30 inches from the
front of the matrix tubes (~30 inches from the interface between the stationary table and the
movable table).
If there is a published excess reactivity, that excess reactivity corresponds to standard reporting
conditions with all DP drawers fully inserted and all PSRs fully withdrawn to their parked
positions. The control rod positions listed in the logbook will not matter if there is a published
excess reactivity. If there is no published excess reactivity, the adjustment for partially inserted

 63

control rods can be calculated by determining the reactivity difference between an as-built model
with all control rods in the positions listed in the logbook and a model in which all DP drawers are
fully inserted and all PSRs are fully withdrawn.
There is one other circumstance in which the control rod positions may have a small effect. The
presence of any partially inserted control rods affects the flux distribution, so some measurements
of parameters other than reactivity can be affected, at least in principle. For example, foil
measurements near a partially inserted control rod may be affected by that control rod. In practice,
the effect of partially inserted control rods on a measurement other than criticality is likely to be
much smaller than other uncertainties related to that measurement.
The “Operations Parameters” box in Figure 4.2 and Figure 4.3 provides information about the
interface gap. The table separation entry indicates the full closure position. The corner separation
entry shows the measured separations at the four corners at the nominal full closure position. It is
likely that TW means top west corner, TE means top east corner, BW means bottom west corner
and BE means bottom east corner. In any event, the four numbers shown are the separations
measured at the four corners of the matrix half interface. The staff of ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 averaged
those four values and used the result as a measure of the interface gap.

 Figure 4.3. ZPR-9/28 Loading 45 Logbook Entry.
The units for the table separation values in the logbooks for ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 are not clear. The
staff stated that the interface gap varied from 0 mils to 30 mils (0.0 – 0.8 mm) and that measured
gap worths were of the order of 0.8 – 1.5 Ih/mil (~30 – 60 Ih/mm). The uncertainty in the measured

 64

gap worths or interface gap coefficients was 10 – 20%. The smaller gap worth values were typical
for the larger assemblies such as LMFBR simulations. If it is necessary to assume an average
interface gap and interface gap coefficient for a ZPR-6 or ZPR-9 assembly, a conservative
assumption of the associated uncertainty would be 100%.
If a published excess reactivity is available, that published value has been adjusted to a condition
with a zero interface gap. If no published excess reactivity is available, the worth of the interface
gap can be computed as the difference between the reactivity of a model with an interface gap and
the reactivity of a model with zero interface gap. The worth of any adjustment for the interface
gap is likely to be small compared to the worth of the adjustment for control rod positions.
The average interface gap also serves a purpose in uncertainty analysis for the reference critical
configuration. The interface gap exists because the fronts of the stationary and movable tables
were neither perfectly flat nor perfectly parallel in any of the ZPR/ZPPR machines due to normal
tolerances associated with manufacturing and assembling the equipment, i.e., the matrix tubes,
tables, supports, etc. At the nominal full closure position, the two tables touched at some locations,
but small gaps existed at other locations. The gaps were not uniform, and there is an uncertainty
in the average size of the interface gap. That uncertainty is included in the uncertainty analysis for
the reference critical condition (Section 7.1.1).
In most cases, the reactor logbook entry lists the purpose of the reactor startup or the measurement
to be performed during the reactor startup. That information can be useful in determining which
loading corresponds to the reference critical configuration because available documents may not
indicate exactly which loading corresponds to the reference critical condition. The logbook entry
may indicate that the reference critical condition was being established or that operational
measurements were being made. Operational measurements were normally made just after the
reference critical condition was established and normally used the reference critical configuration
as the base case. Consequently, an entry stating that operational measurements were being made
indicates that the reference critical configuration had been established. Likewise, the purpose of
the reactor startup can also be used to identify other configurations of interest for modeling
purposes.
In some cases, there is no logbook entry for a loading. Since the logbook records information
about reactor operations, there might not be any logbook entry for a loading if there was no actual
reactor startup for that loading. For example, a new assembly program generally began with all
matrix tubes empty on both tables. The radial reflector and radial blanket drawers were then
loaded, leaving empty matrix tubes in the matrix center in a volume corresponding to the estimated
size of the core.
In later ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 assemblies, pre-loaded drawers were placed in the empty matrix tubes
in the core region. A pre-loaded drawer was identical to a normal core drawer except for the fact
that a pre-loaded drawer contained non-fuel plates where the fuel plates would be located in an
actual core drawer. For example, a pre-loaded drawer might contain a column of aluminum plates
in place of fuel plates. In each step of the approach-to-critical, the aluminum plates were replaced
by fuel plates in a group of pre-loaded drawers. Eventually, a critical configuration was achieved.
Any remaining pre-loaded drawers were replaced by core drawers or radial blanket drawers. Core
drawers were replaced by blanket drawers or vice versa at the core-radial blanket boundary to
achieve the desired core shape and excess reactivity.

 65

There was no point in a reactor startup if there was no fuel in the core, so reactor startups with
corresponding logbook entries did not happen until the beginning of actual fuel loading and the
approach-to-critical. The assignment of loading numbers was not entirely consistent over the
lifetimes of the facilities. In some cases, a separate loading number was assigned to every step of
loading the radial blanket, radial reflector and pre-loaded drawers. Suppose the first loading of
real fuel plates occurred in loading 11 and that loadings 1 through 10 just consisted of loading
blanket drawers, reflector drawers and pre-loaded drawers. In this case, the first startup and the
first logbook entry would be for loading 11.
In other cases, all blanket, reflector and pre-loaded drawers were loaded into the matrix tubes as a
preliminary step, and loading number 1 was assigned to the first step in which real fuel plates were
loaded. In that case, the first startup and the first logbook entry would be for loading 1. The point
is that there would not necessarily be a logbook entry if there was no reactor startup, and there
might not be a reactor startup for various reasons. The absence of logbook entries for some
loadings does not necessarily mean that there are missing logbook entries.
The two pictures at the top of the left side of Figure 4.3 are photographs of the core loading in
ZPR-9/28 loading 45. These are not photographs of the stationary and movable tables of the actual
reactor. There were two boards upon which the staff affixed small colored squares representing
the different types of drawer masters in the matrix tubes on the two tables for each loading. As
part of each startup, the two boards were photographed, and the photographs were attached to the
logbook entries. The boards were probably used for planning purposes, and it seems likely that
there were separate boards for ZPR-6 and ZPR-9. The purpose of the photographs is not clear
although the photographs or the boards may have been used to create the core layout figures used
in reports. With rare exceptions, those photographs are not useful today.
The key entries for ZPR-6 logbooks and ZPR-9 logbooks are the assembly number, loading
number, startup number, date, control rod positions, the experiment or objective of the loading,
and the corner separation entries in the “Operations Parameters” box or equivalent entries.
4.3 ZPPR Logbook
A ZPPR logbook consisted of pre-printed forms bound in a notebook. There was a separate
logbook for each assembly program. Figure 4.4 shows the logbook entry for ZPPR-3 loading 212,
reactor run 356.

 66

 Figure 4.4. ZPPR-3 Loading 212, Reactor Run 356 – Logbook Entry.
Figure 4.5 shows the first page of the logbook entry for ZPPR-15A loading 38, reactor run 61. A
reactor run for ZPPR is identical to a startup for ZPR-6 and ZPR-9. Comparison of Figure 4.4 to
Figure 4.5 shows that there were some changes in the standard form and in the information
recorded on the standard form between the early 1970s when the ZPPR-3 experiments were done
and ~1986 when the ZPPR-15 experiments were done. The ZPPR-15 logbook entry provides more
complete information, so the discussion of the ZPPR logbooks will focus on Figure 4.5.
In ZPR-3, ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR, all loading numbers in an assembly were sequential. The
number of actual loadings in an assembly program could be as low as 20 (or less) for a short ZPR-
3 program or greater than 300 for the longer assembly programs in ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR.
ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 did not subdivide an assembly program, regardless of the length of the program,
the number of loadings in the program, or the changes in the configuration of the simulated reactor

 67

during the program. In some ZPR-3 and ZPPR assembly programs, the staff divided an assembly
program into phases and assigned a different letter to each phase. For example, ZPPR-15 was
divided into phases A, B, C and D, which were designated as ZPPR-15A, ZPPR-15B, ZPPR-15C
and ZPPR-15D. Phases A – D of ZPPR-15 were four significantly different configurations of the
simulated reactor. Likewise, ZPR-3/6 was divided into phases A, B, C, D, E and F.
For practical purposes, Figure 4.5 can be divided into an upper section, a middle section and a
lower section.
4.3.1 Upper Section of a ZPPR Logbook Entry
The first line of this section shows four entries. The date is the date of reactor operation (reactor
run), June 27, 1985. This is relevant because all masses in the ADEN library (materials library)
are normalized to January 1, 1977. It is necessary to correct plate compositions in models for
radioactive decay between the date of reactor operation and the normalization date for the ADEN
library.
The cover of the first ZPPR-15 logbook lists the logbook volume number (32), the assembly (15A
and 15B), the reactor runs covered by the logbook (1 – 201 for volume 32) and the dates covered
by the logbook (April 1985 – January 1986 for volume 32). The assembly number for this
configuration, 15A, is listed in the second entry on the first line of Figure 4.5.
The third entry on line 1 is the loading number, loading 38, for this reactor configuration. Loading
records are discussed later. Each loading corresponds to a particular configuration of drawers and
experimental equipment in the ZPR/ZPPR matrix, and each loading corresponds to a particular
experimental measurement or to a step in establishing the required configuration for that
experimental measurement. Experimental measurements were sometimes reported with the
loading number and/or reactor run in which the measurements were obtained. Any reactor model
must correspond to the loading number in which the measurements of interest were made to
represent the configuration of interest accurately.
The fourth entry on line 1 of Figure 4.5 is the reactor run number. The reactor run number is
distinct from the loading number. The loading number designates a particular configuration of
drawers and experimental equipment in the matrix. The reactor run number is the sequence
number for reactor startups or related operations for an assembly program. There is generally not
a one-to-one correspondence between loadings and reactor runs. For some experimental
measurements, multiple reactor runs were required with the same loading and reactor configuration
to obtain the necessary data. In this case, reactor run 61 for the ZPPR-15 assembly program
occurred on June 27, 1985 for ZPPR-15A loading 38. The reactor run number matters because
sometimes experimental measurements were reported with just the reactor run number rather than
the loading number and reactor run number. In those cases, it is necessary to determine the
correspondence between the reactor run number and the loading number from the logbook to
model the correct core configuration and the correct operating conditions.

 68

 Figure 4.5. ZPPR-15A Loading 38, Reactor Run 61 – Logbook Entry, Page 1.

 69

Line 2 (Total Fissile Material, etc.) and line 3 (Total Safety Rod Worth, etc.) in the upper section
are of limited value with respect to constructing models although the number of core drawers can
be a worthwhile check on the accuracy of a model.
Line 4 lists the experiment to be performed in this loading and reactor run. This entry in the
logbook and the corresponding entry in the loading change summary form in the loading records
indicate which measurement was performed in each loading. That information is useful in
deciding which experiments to model and in determining the correct loading configuration to
model for published results that do not include information regarding the core loading or reactor
run in which an experiment was performed.
Lines 5 – 9 (“Reactor power trip settings” – “Daily checkout completed”) in the upper section are
not of any value with respect to constructing models or analyzing experiments.
4.3.2 Middle Section of a ZPPR Logbook Entry
The five lines in the middle section of page 1 of the ZPPR logbook entry (“THIS SECTION TO
BE COMPLETED BY THE REACTOR SUPERVISOR”) are not of any value with respect to
constructing models or analyzing experiments.
4.3.3 Lower Section of a ZPPR Logbook Entry
The startup time, reactor operators and reactor supervisors listed in the beginning of the lower
section are not of any value with respect to constructing models or analyzing experiments.
In the lower section, the line labeled “Table Closure Indication” provides details on the interface
gap between the two halves of the matrix, i.e., the stationary table and the movable table or half 1
and half 2. The two halves of the matrix were neither perfectly flat nor perfectly parallel as
discussed earlier. In addition, the weight of the drawers in the matrix could cause a slight
deflection of the support plate. As a result, there was a small, non-uniform gap between matrix
halves in some places even at nominal full closure of the tables.
There were position indicators at the four corners of the two halves of the matrix. The four
numbers listed on the “Table Closure Indication” line are the measured separations at the corners
of the tables at the nominal full closure position for the tables. The numbers are in units of “gap
separation units” or mils, so the corner separations ranged from 29.2 mils (0.0292 inches) to 54.1
mils (0.0541 inches) in Figure 4.5. In principle, the two tables touched at some points, but the four
corners were separated by distances from 0.0292 inches to 0.0541 inches.
The average of the four corner values is an estimate of the interface gap. The two tables touched
at some points, so half of the average of the corner readings might be regarded as a better estimate
of the interface gap. On the other hand, there could also be gaps at some matrix locations that
were larger than the average of the corner readings. Valid arguments can be made for assuming
the interface gap is the average of the corner readings or half of the average of the corner readings.
The standard practice at ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 was to use the average of the four corner indicators as
the interface gap. The true value is unknown and unknowable, so assuming the interface gap is
the average of the four corner readings at least provides a defensible and consistent estimate.
Measurements were made after the reference critical configuration was established to determine
parameter values required for normal reactor operations. For one operational measurement, the

 70

reactor halves were driven apart with no change in control rod positions from the critical positions,
and the reactivity change as a function of table separation was measured. This measurement was
converted to a gap coefficient. Multiplying the gap coefficient by the fully closed measured and
then estimated interface gap yields the reactivity worth of the interface gap. The reactor
temperature coefficient was measured from the reference critical configuration by turning off the
cooling system and measuring the reactivity change as a result of the change in the average core
temperature due to radioactive decay in the fuel as determined from the thermocouple readings.
Other measurements were made as required to support daily operations.
The ZPPR staff used the operational measurements to correct measured values for the interface
gap, temperature effects, 241Pu decay, etc. However, operational measurements were sometimes
omitted from published reports. If the gap coefficient was published, determining the worth of the
interface gap is straightforward. If the gap coefficient was not published, the worth of the interface
gap can be calculated by modifying the computer model to introduce the interface gap between
half 1 and half 2 and then computing the reactivity difference between the model with the gap and
the reference model with no gap. Correcting for the gap is only necessary if there is no published
excess reactivity because standard conditions for adjusted excess reactivity are based on a zero
interface gap.
The chart below the “Table Closure Indication” line in the lower section of Figure 4.5 shows the
parked positions of the poison control rods (PSRs). Specifically the columns labeled SR-1 through
PSR-31 for ZPPR-15A, loading 38, reactor run 61. As stated earlier, the poison control rods (PSRs)
in a ZPPR assembly were divided into two rod banks. The control rods in the inner portion of the
core, i.e., in the positions of highest worth, were designated as safety rods. The safety rods were
fully withdrawn during normal operations to minimize their effect on measurements. The parked
positions for the safety rods during normal operations were approximately 30 inches from the
interface between matrix halves. In addition to the safety rods, there were operational or shim rods
in each half. The values shown are the distances of the rod tips from the axial centerline of the
reactor, i.e., the interface between half 1 and half 2. For example, the tip of SR-1 was 13.703
inches from the interface between half 1 and half 2.
The available records do not show exactly which operational or shim rod was in which matrix
location in most cases. For example, the loading records for ZPPR-15 show the eight locations
that were occupied by operational or shim rods, but the records do not indicate which location was
SR-1, SR-2, etc. This is not important in this example because the positions of these eight rods
were nearly identical. In general, the operators maintained the shim rods at nearly identical axial
positions to minimize flux and power tilting.
The first few ZPPR assembly programs included both PSRs and DP control rods. After the first
few assembly programs were completed, the DP rods were eliminated, and only PSRs were used
in ZPPR. In cases where both DP rods and PSRs were present in a ZPPR assembly, the discussion
above regarding DP rods and PSRs in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 also applies to ZPPR.
In some cases there were multiple entries in the chart of control rod positions if the control rod
positions, reactor power or the instrument values in columns 3 and 12 changed over time during
the reactor run.

 71

The remainder of the lower section of Figure 4.5 does not contain any useful information for
modeling purposes.
There was a second page for each logbook entry for later assemblies. Figure 4.6 shows the second
page of the entry for ZPPR-15A, loading 38, reactor run 61. The “Anomalies or Comments”
section allowed the staff to note any anomalies such as equipment malfunctions and to note any
comments or other relevant information for the reactor run. The chart in the bottom portion of
Figure 4.6 allowed additional space to record control rod positions and other relevant operational
parameters.
The form used for the ZPPR logbook entries changed over the years, but comparison of Figure 4.4
and Figure 4.5 shows that both entries contain the essential information required for modeling
purposes. In this context, the essential information consists of the assembly number (and phase if
relevant), loading number, reactor run number, date, purpose of loading or experiment, table
closure indicator readings and control rod positions.
4.4 Use of the Logbook Information for Modeling Purposes
The reactor logbook entry describes the reactor operating conditions for a reactor startup or run
and may describe the purpose of the reactor startup or run. The purpose of the startup or run can
be used to identify particular configurations of interest. The reactor operating conditions such as
control rod positions, reactor temperature and table closure indicator positions (interface gap) can
be useful in the analysis of the experiment, particularly with respect to uncertainty analysis for
criticality and other reactivity measurements.
4.4.1 General Run Information
The information in line 1 in the upper section of Figure 4.5 or the corresponding information in
logbooks from ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 is always needed for modeling purposes. The date is
needed to correct compositions for radioactive decay between the date of the measurement and
January 1, 1977, the normalization date for the ADEN (materials) library. The loading number
and the reactor run number or startup identify the correct configuration and reactor operating
conditions to model for the measurement of interest. Note that ZPR-3 logbooks do not necessarily
include the reactor run or startup number.
The description of the experiment to be performed on line 4 of Section 1 of Figure 4.5 or the
equivalent description in the logbooks for the other facilities relates the experimental measurement
configuration to the published measurement data in cases where the published experimental results
do not show the loading number or reactor run number.

 72

 Figure 4.6. ZPPR-15A Loading 38, Reactor Run 61 – Logbook Entry, Page 2.

 73

4.4.2 Reactor Operational Data
The information for the table closure indicators and control rod positions is only needed under
certain conditions that depend on the measurement of interest and on the available reports or other
documents. The operational measurements performed after the reference critical configuration
was established included the reactor temperature coefficient, 241Pu decay coefficient, interface gap
coefficient and rod worth curves.
The operational measurements were always performed because they were required to support daily
reactor operations, but the operational measurements were not published consistently in reports
and other publicly available documents.
Computer capabilities in the 1960s, 1970s and 1980s limited use of Monte Carlo for analysis
purposes, so most ZPR/ZPPR models were deterministic. It was difficult to model features such
as control rods accurately with the deterministic codes available at that time, and producing
accurate cross section libraries for use with those deterministic codes was equally difficult. The
measured operational parameters were used by the ZPR/ZPPR staff to adjust or correct measured
reactivity data to standard conditions for reporting and analysis purposes.
When ZPR-3, ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR operated, it was not practical for analysts to model the
interface gap. The measured interface gap coefficient was used with the measured corner
separations to adjust measured reactivity values to a zero gap condition to simplify analysis.
Although the reported measured reactivity may have been adjusted to standard reporting
conditions, the interface gap data (interface gap coefficient and table closure indicator values) are
still useful for uncertainty analysis of the reference critical configuration (discussed in Section
7.1.1 below). From the earlier discussion, the actual size of the average interface gap is uncertain,
and there is uncertainty in the measured interface gap coefficient. These uncertainties are
components of the total uncertainty for the reference critical configuration.
The time of year (midsummer versus midwinter), the amount of plutonium in the core (decay
heating), the core configuration and other factors affected the temperature distribution and the
average core temperature during a reactor run. Thermocouples located at various positions in the
ZPR/ZPPR matrix provided an estimate of the reactor temperature. The measured temperature
coefficient for the assembly was used with the thermocouple data to adjust measured reactivities
to a common reference temperature such as 294 K, 298 K or 300 K for reporting and analysis
purposes. Uncertainties in the measured reactor temperature coefficient, thermocouple calibration
and average core temperature associated with the temperature correction are discussed below.
For a plutonium-fueled core, the core reactivity decreased by a very small amount every day due
to 241Pu decay. For a single measurement such as the reference critical configuration, the reported
value and the model correspond to the actual date of the reactor run in which the measurement was
obtained. For a series of connected reactivity measurements, e.g., a series of sodium void worth
measurements or simulated control rod worth measurements, that extended over several or many
days, the 241Pu decay coefficient was used to adjust measured reactivities to a common reference
configuration and date to eliminate the effect of 241Pu decay on measured reactivities.
Reported excess reactivities were adjusted to standard reporting conditions. Those conditions
corresponded to full insertion of all DP control drawers and full withdrawal of all PSRs. The

 74

control rod positions listed in the logbook are important if no excess reactivity is listed in available
documents. In that case, constructing one model with all control rods at the positions listed in the
logbook and a second model with all DP rods fully inserted and all PSRs fully withdrawn allows
calculation of the reactivity worth of partially inserted control rods.
Parked control rods cause local flux perturbations, so modeling parked control rods at the correct
axial positions may have a small effect in calculations where the local flux perturbations may affect
measured values, e.g., irradiation foil measurements of reaction rate distributions near control rods.
However, the effect of parked control rods is likely to be smaller than other uncertainties related
to the measurements.

 75

5 LOADING RECORDS
A loading record is a record of each drawer master inserted into or removed from a matrix tube on
the stationary table (half 1) and/or the movable table (half 2) during a loading along with the matrix
location where that drawer master was inserted or removed. The loading records provided the
instructions for the technicians loading or unloading the matrix tubes and provided the historical
record of loading/unloading operations during that loading. The loading record might also include
any special notes added by the technicians or experimenters.
In most cases, a new assembly program began with an empty matrix, but there were exceptions.
A new assembly program might not begin with an empty matrix if either a) there were many
similarities between the new assembly program and the previous assembly program or b) the new
program was essentially a continuation of the previous program. For example, assembly program
N might be a continuation of or very similar to assembly program M. In that case, loadings for
program N might start with the last configuration in program M, and the matrix would not be
empty at the start of loadings for program N.
The radial blanket drawers and radial reflector drawers in program N might be identical to the
radial blanket drawers and radial reflector drawers in program M. Likewise, the general size and
shape of the radial blanket and radial reflector in the new program might be very similar to the size
and shape of the radial blanket and radial reflector in the previous program. If the new assembly
program was a continuation of or at least very similar to the previous program, the ZPR/ZPPR
staff might begin with the last configuration in the previous program and just make the changes
required to transition to the new program.
The transition from one phase of a ZPR/ZPPR program to the next phase of the same assembly
program also began with the last configuration in the previous phase. For example, the transition
from Phase B (ZPPR-15B) to Phase C (ZPPR-15C) of the ZPPR-15 program began with the last
configuration in ZPPR-15B.
In general, however, there was enough difference between successive assembly programs that the
matrix tubes were emptied prior to commencement of loading for the next assembly program. In
that case, drawers were first loaded into the matrix to create the radial reflector and radial blanket
for the new program. Pre-loaded drawers with non-fuel plates in place of fuel plates were loaded
into matrix tubes defining the anticipated core region in some assemblies. Fuel was then added to
the core zone by either a) replacing unfueled pre-loaded drawers in the core zone with fueled
drawers or b) replacing the column(s) of non-fuel plates with column(s) of fuel plates in the pre-
loaded drawers.
Note that the discussion in the preceding paragraph regarding pre-loaded drawers applies to ZPR-
6 and ZPR-9. It is not clear whether ZPR-3 or ZPPR used pre-loaded drawers. Regardless, if
loading began with empty matrix tubes, the standard procedure was that no fuel was loaded into
the matrix until loading of radial reflector and blanket drawers was finished.
After loading of radial reflector and blanket drawers was completed, fueled drawers were added
gradually in steps in the standard approach-to-critical. After each loading step, the degree of
subcriticality was measured, and an extrapolation was made to estimate the amount of fuel required
for criticality. The amount of fuel added in each loading step was some fraction of the amount

 76

estimated to be needed for criticality until a configuration was reach that was close to critical and
that the ZPR/ZPPR staff understood well enough to make the final loading that would achieve a
critical configuration.
Note that the reactor was still far subcritical after this final loading step because at the end of the
loading step, the two matrix halves were separated by five feet (150 cm), the PSR blades (if
present) were fully inserted, and the DP control drawers (if present) were fully withdrawn. After
the staff vacated the reactor cell, the movable table was slowly moved toward the stationary table
until full closure was achieved, and then the control rods were moved to create the critical
configuration. The number of fuel loading steps required to achieve a critical configuration ranged
from five to approximately twenty, depending on the assembly and on how closely the assembly
being loaded resembled previous assembly programs for which operational experience existed.
When the assembly was close to the critical state or possibly after the initial critical configuration
had been established, drawers were changed at the core-blanket boundary or blanket-reflector
boundary to achieve the desired layout for the reactor simulation. After the reference critical
configuration was established, drawers and equipment were inserted, modified or removed as
needed to meet the requirements of the experimental program.
Loadings in any ZPR/ZPPR assembly were cumulative. Each configuration in a ZPR/ZPPR
program was based upon all previous configurations constructed during that program. Loading 2
began with the configuration at the end of loading 1, loading 3 began with the configuration at end
of loading 2, and so on. In general, loading N began with the configuration at the end of loading
N – 1 until the end of the program was reached. For example, loading 185, the reference critical
configuration for ZPPR-15D, was based upon the previous 184 loadings in the ZPPR-15 program.
It is not possible to construct the matrix configuration for ZPPR-15 loading 185 without processing
the loading records for loadings 1 – 184 first. Likewise, it is not possible to construct the matrix
configuration for loading N in any ZPR/ZPPR assembly program without processing all of the
loading records for loadings 1 through N – 1 first for that program.
The only exception to the last sentence in the preceding paragraph is the case where there is an
existing benchmark for the assembly of interest in the ICSBEP/IRPhEP Handbooks [5,6]. If there
is an existing benchmark in those Handbooks, that benchmark may provide the matrix maps for
one or more loadings, i.e., core configurations. If that is the case, then it is possible to use those
existing matrix maps as the starting point and to just process the additional loading records between
the published matrix maps and the loading of interest.
The paper loading records stored at ZPPR were either handwritten or computer printouts. These
records were scanned and converted to PDF files as described above. All ZPR-3 loading records
are handwritten on standard forms.
The ZPR/ZPPR staff began to computerize loading records at some point in the 1970s. For early
assembly programs at ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR, all loading records are handwritten. For later
assembly programs at ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR, available loading records are a mix of handwritten
records and computer printouts, and that applies to the loading records for a single assembly
program in a single facility as well as to successive assemblies in the same facility.

 77

As one might expect, the legibility of the handwritten records varies for several reasons: 1) the
poor quality or legibility of the handwriting of the person who filled out the form, 2) the age and
degree of fading of the record, and 3) the choice of writing implement.
Although the computer printouts eliminate the handwriting legibility issue, they do not eliminate
the age and degree of fading issue. Legibility of the computer printouts is also dependent on the
printer available. The older printouts were printed on the old impact printers that used a printer
ribbon, and the newer printouts were printed on a laser printer that Argonne obtained in the 1980s.
The age and condition of the ribbon affected the legibility of older printouts, and the condition of
the equivalent of a toner cartridge in a current laser printer affected the legibility of the newer
printouts.
Some loading records included additional pages of notes or drawings. Those notes or drawings
may be useful in determining the changes that occurred during the loading. It is not possible to
make any general statements about any such material because the form and content of material
will be specific to the facility, assembly, loading, objective of the loading and probably the
personnel involved.
5.1 Matrix Tube Numbering
Matrix tube numbering was discussed above, but some of that discussion will be repeated here for
convenience. ZPR-3, ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR used similar conventions for numbering rows and
columns of the matrix tubes on the stationary (half 1) and movable (half 2) tables. For an observer
standing between the two tables and facing the stationary table, the lowest row number is at the
top of the matrix, and the highest row number is at the bottom of the matrix in both halves. For
example, ZPR-9 had a 45 x 45 matrix. Row 1 was at the top of the matrix, and row 45 was at the
bottom of the matrix.
For the same observer standing between the tables and facing the stationary table, the lowest
column number in both halves is on the observer’s left, and the highest column number in both
halves is on the observer’s right. For the 45x 45 ZPR-9 matrix, column 1 in both halves is on the
observer’s left. The observer would see column 1 of the stationary half on the left and column 45
of the stationary half on the right. If the observer turns 180° and faces the movable half, the
observer would see column 45 on the left and column 1 on the right. This convention for
numbering columns applies to all four ZPR/ZPPR machines. This convention for numbering
columns allowed the row numbers and column numbers in the two halves or tables to align when
the tables were brought together.
5.2 ZPR-3 Loading Records
The horizontal rows in the 31 x 31 ZPR-3 matrix were designated by the letters A – Z and AA –
EE starting with A at the top and EE at the bottom. The vertical columns in the array were
numbered 1 – 31 starting from the left looking from the movable half towards the stationary half.
Figure 5.1 shows a loading record from ZPR-3/6, and Figure 5.2 shows a loading record from
ZPR-3/60.

 78

 Figure 5.1. ZPR-3/6 Loading Record.

ZPR-3 used standard forms for the loading records, but the standard loading record form itself and
the information recorded on the standard form changed multiple times over the operational lifetime
of the facility as a comparison of Figure 5.1 and Figure 5.2 shows.

 79

 Figure 5.2. ZPR-3/60 Loading Record.
The stationary table was designated by 1 or S in the loading records, and the movable table was
designated as 2 or M in the loading records. The most common designation for a matrix position
in the loading records is of the form m-N-nn where m is 1 or 2, N is one of the row letters A – Z
or AA – EE, and nn is a column number in the range 1 – 31. Examples are 1-F-12 (stationary half,
row F, column 12) and 2-F-12 (movable half, row F, column 12). This convention applies to both
tables and to all rows and columns of the matrix. The hyphen (-) between m, N and mm was
omitted by some ZPR-3 staff members, so m-N-nn and mNmm are equivalent designations.
An alternative designation for a matrix location in the loading records is m-N/nn where m is S or
M, N is one of the row letters, and nn is the column number. S-F/12 is identical to 1-F-12, and

 80

M-F/12 is identical to 2-F-12. In general, for any row N and column nn in the ZPR-3 matrix, S-
N/nn is identical to 1-N-nn, and M-N/nn is identical to 2-N-nn.
The most important pieces of information on any ZPR-3 loading record are a) the assembly
number, b) the loading number, c) the location (matrix position) where the drawer master will be
inserted or loaded and d) the drawer master to be loaded at that location. In Figure 5.1, the
assembly number and loading number are listed at the top of the form. In this example, the
assembly is 6B (ZPR-3/6B), and the loading number is 1. The date of the loading on the loading
records is not important if the reactor logbook entry includes the date of the reactor run or startup.
In Figure 5.1, the location where the drawer master will be loaded is listed in column 1, and the
drawer master to be loaded in that location is listed in column 3. The checker and approver in
columns 5 and 6 of Figure 5.1 were important during reactor loading and are relevant to
demonstrate the level of quality assurance in the record itself. Likewise, columns 2 and 4 (Ck) in
Figure 5.1 provide a similar detail on quality assurance of the record.
ZPR-3 used front drawers and back drawers, so there were loading records for both sets of drawers
unless the front drawer was long enough to include all of the core, axial blanket and axial reflector.
Back drawers were generally loaded in the early loadings of a program, and the front drawers were
loaded in subsequent loadings. Most of the loading records will pertain to front drawers because
back drawers were rarely moved after they were loaded. The loading may explicitly state that back
drawers are being loaded, or that fact may be obvious from the drawer masters being loaded.
Another indication of the distinction is the presence of F (front) or B (back) in the drawer master
column.
For a small loading involving a relatively small number of locations, the loading record may
consist of a single page. For a large loading involving many locations, the loading record may
consist of many pages. If the loading record consists of multiple pages, they will generally be
numbered. The page number in Figure 5.1 is the 5 in the upper right corner.
In some cases, the page numbers and the order of the pages in a loading did matter. The page
number and order did not matter if all drawers to be inserted in the loading were loaded in the
workroom, transferred into the reactor cell and loaded into the matrix tubes because each drawer
was loaded into a separate, distinct, empty matrix tube.
However, there were loadings where some drawers in the matrix were moved to other locations in
the matrix, and new drawers were loaded into the vacated matrix tubes. In those cases, the order
of the pages mattered because the loading record pages told the technicians where to find the
drawers to be relocated within the matrix. If the order of the pages was wrong, some matrix tubes
might contain the wrong drawers.
The ZPR-3 staff entered the information they needed for daily operations and to maintain a record,
but they did not necessarily fill out every entry on every page of a loading record. Again, no one
at ZPR-3 anticipated the possibility that people would make use of these records many decades
after the experiments were run; those records supported facility operations at that time.
The vertical arrows in column 3 of Figure 5.1 represented a shorthand way to indicate that the
drawer master just about the start of the arrow repeated in the locations encompassed by the arrow.

 81

For example, drawer master C-610 was loaded in 2-P-17 and the following 14 locations (2-P-18
through 2-R-13).
A more confusing situation arises if the vertical arrow stops, there is an entry for a drawer master
in one location, and then the vertical arrow resumes. For example, drawer master A is loaded in
one location, there is a vertical line for 10 rows of the loading form indicating that drawer master
A was loaded in those 10 locations, drawer master B is loaded in one location, and then the vertical
arrow resumes. Does the second vertical arrow mean that drawer master B was loaded into the
following locations? Or does the second vertical arrow mean that drawer master B was loaded in
only one location and that drawer master A was loaded in the locations covered by the second
arrow? Examples of both loading results occur in the ZPR/ZPPR loading records. It is necessary
to make a judgement based on context in such cases. For example, are A and B both standard
types of core drawer masters? Or is there something special or unique about drawer master B
compared to other drawer masters?
In one situation the decision about whether the vertical arrow below drawer master B applies to A
or B is easy. If drawer master B is a DP control rod drawer, then B is only loaded in one location,
and the arrow below B applies to A. There were only five DP drawers in each half of the assembly,
so any loading instruction for a DP drawer applies only to that drawer and location. The same
consideration applies to a special experimental drawer, e.g., a drawer containing a proton recoil
spectrometer, that was loaded in only one matrix position.
Figure 5.2 shows a loading record from ZPR-3/60, an assembly built about 11 months before the
last assembly program in ZPR-3 ended. The assembly number, loading number, page number and
purpose/experiment for the loading are shown at the top of Figure 5.2. Column 7 of Figure 5.2
shows the position where the drawer master was to be inserted, and column 9 shows the drawer
master to be inserted at that location. Column 1, the comments column, sometimes contains useful
information about the drawers to be loaded. If a drawer was to be moved from one location in the
matrix to another location in the matrix, column 4 shows the original location of the drawer to be
moved. Columns 2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, 11 and 12 are generally not useful today.
The birdcage number in columns 2 and 5 refers to the location of the birdcage where a loaded
drawer could be stored temporarily. A birdcage was a framework that provided fixed spacing
between adjacent loaded drawers in the birdcage to prevent a criticality accident. If a drawer
removed from a matrix tube was not likely to be reloaded into the matrix in the near future, that
drawer was taken to the workroom where the plates in the drawer were removed and returned to
inventory. If a drawer removed from a matrix tube would be reloaded into the matrix in the near
future, that drawer might be stored temporarily in a birdcage until the drawer was needed again.
Storing a loaded drawer temporarily in a birdcage saved the cost of unloading the drawer and later
reloading it in the same configuration. In addition, use of the birdcages minimized worker
radiation doses associated with drawer loading and unloading and minimized the time required for
drawer loading, drawer unloading and loading the matrix tubes.
Figure 5.1 and Figure 5.2 show loading records from near the beginning of ZPR-3 operations and
near the end of ZPR-3 operations, respectively. There were other versions of the ZPR-3 loading
record form, but it is neither practical nor useful to show every version here. The essential features
of any loading record are a) the assembly number, b) the loading number, c) the location where
the drawer master will be inserted, d) the drawer master to be loaded in that location e) the sheet

 82

number or page number of each page of the loading record and f) any information about a drawer
master that is being moved from one matrix location to another matrix location (if applicable).
Any comments or notes added to the loading record may provide useful information for
determining the correct drawer master in each matrix tube. Some engineering judgement based
on context is required to resolve ambiguities such as the use of vertical arrows to indicate that the
same drawer master was loaded in successive locations.
5.3 Loading Records for ZPR-6 and ZPR-9
The horizontal rows in the 45 x 45 ZPR-9 matrix were numbered 1 – 45 with 1 at the top and 45
at the bottom. The vertical columns in both halves in the ZPR-9 array were numbered 1 – 45
starting from the left for an observer looking from the movable half towards the stationary half.
Prior to expansion, the row numbering and column numbering in the 45 x 45 ZPR-6 matrix were
identical to the row and column numbering in ZPR-9. After the ZPR-6 expansion, the ZPR-6
matrix was 65 x 65. The horizontal rows in the expanded ZPR-6 matrix were numbered 1 – 65
with 1 at the top and 65 at the bottom. The vertical columns in both halves of the expanded ZPR-
6 array were numbered 1 – 65 starting from the left looking from the movable half towards the
stationary half.

ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 used a standard form for the loading records, but the standard loading record

operational lifetimes of the facilities.

The text in Section 5.3 regarding the interpretation of the vertical arrows and of the occasional
ambiguity in interpreting the meaning of those arrows apply to ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR as well.
Note that this ambiguity only applies to the drawer master loaded (or possibly removed). There is
no ambiguity if the arrow is applied to rows or columns. For example, in Figure 5.3, the same
drawer masters are being loaded in successive rows in columns 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 and 14. Likewise,
there is no ambiguity if the same drawer master is being loaded in successive columns of the same
row.
There were only five DP drawers and a small number of narrow PSR drawers in each half of a
ZPR-6 or ZPR-9 assembly, so any vertical arrow below a DP drawer master or PSR drawer master
generally does not apply to the DP drawer master or PSR drawer master. There may be rare
exceptions, but in general the loading instruction for a DP drawer master or PSR drawer master
applies only to that drawer master and does not copy or propagate.
The vertical arrow shorthand is only used to designate successive matrix locations in handwritten
records. Every matrix location and every drawer master are listed in the computer printouts. The
only use of vertical arrows on the computer printouts occurred as a shorthand when the same
person checked or approved a series of loading instructions in a loading record as done in Figure
5.4.
ZPR-3, ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR used front drawers and back drawers, so there were loading
records for both sets of drawers for all four machines if back drawers were used in an assembly.
Back drawers were generally loaded in the early loadings in a program, and the front drawers were
loaded in subsequent loadings. Most of the loading records will pertain to front drawers because
back drawers were rarely moved after they were loaded. The loading may explicitly state that back
drawers are being loaded, or that fact may be obvious from the drawer masters being loaded.
Another indication of the distinction in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 is the presence of F (front) or B (back)
in the drawer master column.

Figure 5.4 is an example of a computerized loading record from ZPR-9/29. Column 1 is just the
step number in the loading and has no relevance today. Columns 2, 3 and 4 show the matrix half
(S or M), row number and column number, respectively, of the matrix location where the loading
or unloading operation will occur. Column 5 indicates whether the drawer is a front drawer (F) or
back drawer (B).
Column 6 of Figure 5.4 lists the reactor loading instruction. The standard abbreviations for the
loading instructions are listed in Table 5.1. LM just means load the drawer into the matrix. UM
means unload or remove the drawer from the matrix and return to drawer to the workroom where
the plates will be removed from the drawer and returned to inventory.
Loading and unloading drawers were manual processes, and the technicians who loaded drawers,
unloaded drawers, loaded matrix tubes and unloaded marix tubes received some radiation dose
during those processes. In order to minimize labor costs, schedule delays and radiation exposure,
the staff of the ZPR/ZPPR facilities avoided unnecessary drawer loading and unloading operations
and unnecessary drawer handling. Consider an experiment in which it is necessary to replace a set
of drawers in the matrix temporarily with another set of drawers that matches the desired
experimental configuration. At the end of the experiment, the experimental drawers will be
removed from the matrix, and the original drawers will be reloaded into the matrix. Taking the
original drawers to the workroom, unloading them and then later reloading them is expensive,
time-consuming and counter to ALARA principles. It is more efficient to store the original loaded
drawers temporarily until they are needed again than to unload and reload them.
ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 had storage boxes and storage racks for temporary storage of loaded drawers
that were removed from the matrix. A storage box was used to store radial blanket drawers and
radial reflector drawers for which criticality safety was not a relevant consideration. A storage
rack was used to store core drawers in a criticality-safe configuration. The storage racks used at
ANL-E were the equivalent of the birdcages used at ZPR-3 for criticality-safe drawer storage.
UMLR means remove (unload) a drawer from the matrix and place (load) the drawer in a storage
rack. URLM means remove a drawer from a storage rack and load that drawer into the matrix.
UMLM means remove a drawer from the matrix, transfer the drawer to the workroom for
inspection or adjustment, transfer that drawer back into the reactor cell and load it back into the
matrix. UMLB means remove a drawer from the matrix and place the drawer in a storage box.
UBLM means remove a drawer from a storage box and load that drawer into the matrix.
It is important to pay attention to the reactor loading instruction in column 6. The computerized
records included every individual loading and unloading operation or step that occurred during the
loading. If the user does not pay attention to the reactor loading instructions, unloading steps can
be misinterpreted as loading steps and vice versa. To complicate the issue further, the computerized
records typically list all loading steps first and all unloading steps after the loading steps.
Logically, unloading steps should be listed before loading steps because it is necessary to remove
the old drawers from the matrix tubes before the new drawers can be loaded into those matrix
tubes. Nevertheless, the computerized loading records list the loading steps before the unloading
steps that must precede loading.

 cell and load back into matrix

 UBLM Unload from storage box, load into matrix

Column 7 of Figure 5.4 is the drawer master number or identification label. Drawer master naming
or numbering conventions were discussed above.
Columns 8, 9 and 10 of Figure 5.4 are the 235U mass, 239Pu mass and 241Pu mass, respectively, in
the drawer master to be loaded or unloaded. The drawers being loaded in Figure 5.4 contained
Pu-U-Mo alloy fuel plates. The nominal composition of the Pu-U-Mo alloy consisted of 28 wt.%
Pu, 69.5 wt.% U and 2.5 wt.% Mo. The uranium in those plates was depleted uranium, which
accounts for the small amount of 235U shown in column 8 for each drawer.
The 235U, 239Pu and 241Pu masses shown in columns 8 – 10 are average values for the fuel plates
in the drawer masters. In reality, normal manufacturing tolerances would result in small mass
differences for fuel plates of the same type and size and, consequently, in small fissile mass
differences for nominally identical drawers.
The fissile masses per drawer in columns 8 – 10 of Figure 5.4 were important for inventory control
and general reactor operations when ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 operated, but the fissile mass information
in columns 8 – 10 is not important today.
Columns 11 and 12 of Figure 5.4 relate to checking the drawers and the assembly. These columns
were important during reactor operation, but they are not relevant for modeling purposes except
as a demonstration of the degree to which loadings were checked and verified.
In a computerized record such as Figure 5.4, the fissile masses per drawer master (columns 8 – 10)
are not generally relevant today. The step number in column 1 is not important except to keep
track of the individual loading steps.
The computerized records frequently include a few pages before the actual list of loading steps.
The first page lists the loading number, the purpose of the loading and some general information.
The second page is a summary of the changes in the numbers of plates and drawer masters of
different types resulting from the loading changes. These two pages are only useful for general

 88

information purposes in most cases although there are exceptions where they contain relevant
notes.
The computerized records may also include two pages after the list of loading steps. One page is
a summary of the masses of 235U, 239Pu and 241Pu in the core and in the storage rack. The second
page is an inventory of the fuel plates and diluent (non-fuel) plates in the core. These pages also
are only useful for general information in most cases unless they contain relevant notes.
Figure 5.5 shows a handwritten loading record for ZPR-9/29. Figure 5.3 and Figure 5.5 show two
of the various standard loading forms used at ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 in the 1963 – 1982 period. The
important entries in Figure 5.5 are the assembly number and loading number at the top, the page
number at the bottom, the matrix location (columns 1 – 3), indicator for front drawer (F) or back
drawer (B) in column 4, reactor loading instruction in column 5 and drawer master number in
column 7. The information in the other columns is not relevant for modeling purposes.
The important parts of any handwritten or computerized record are the matrix location, any
indication regarding whether the drawer master is a front drawer or back drawer, any specific
reactor loading instruction, the drawer master number (or other identification) and possibly the
source of the drawer if the drawer is being moved from one matrix location to another matrix
location.
Figure 5.6 shows a summary loading sheet. The summary loading sheet appears as the first sheet
of the handwritten records for loadings in the later assemblies in ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR. The
summary sheet is occasionally useful because it lists the objective or purpose of the loading, a
summary statement of the loading change and any comments or special instructions. This
information can be used to determine the reference critical configuration or the loading in which a
particular experiment was conducted.
