 Figure 5.5. ZPR-9/29 Alternate Loading Record.

 90

 Figure 5.6. ZPR-9/29 Summary Loading Sheet.
5.4 ZPPR Loading Records
The original ZPPR matrix was 53 x 55. The horizontal rows of the original matrix were numbered
11 – 63 with 11 at the top and 63 at the bottom. The vertical columns of the original matrix were
numbered 10 – 64 starting from the left for an observer looking from the movable half towards the
stationary half.
After expansion, the ZPPR matrix was 77 x 77. The horizontal rows of the expanded matrix were
numbered 11 – 87 with 11 at the top and 87 at the bottom. The vertical columns of the expanded
matrix were numbered 11 – 87 starting from the left for an observer looking from the movable half
towards the stationary half. It is not clear why the ZPPR convention for numbering rows and
columns started with 10 or 11 rather than 1.

 91

The stationary half was designated by 1, and the movable half was designated by 2. In the ZPPR
matrix numbering convention, each matrix position is identified by two numbers separated by a
hyphen. The row number was appended to the half number, so all rows in the stationary half begin
with 1 and all rows in the movable half begin with 2. In the original ZPPR matrix, the range of
row numbers was 111 – 163 in half 1 and 211 – 263 in half 2. The range of column numbers in
both halves of the original ZPPR matrix was 10 – 64 with 10 on the observer’s left and 64 on the
observer’s right for an observer standing between matrix halves and facing the stationary half (half
1).
In the expanded ZPPR matrix, the range of row numbers is 111 – 187 in half 1 and 211 – 287 in
half 2. The range of column numbers in both halves of the expanded ZPPR matrix was 11 – 87
with 11 on the left and 87 on the right for an observer standing between the matrix halves and
facing the stationary half (half 1).
For example, in the ZPPR numbering convention, 133-27 is half 1, row 33, column 27. Likewise,
233-27 is half 2, row 33, column 27. Matrix tube 133-27 and matrix tube 233-27 are aligned at
full table closure.
Figure 2.12 displays a small section in the lower left corner of the matrix half that the technician
is facing that does not have any matrix tubes. A similar section can be seen on the lower right
corner of the matrix just behind the technician’s leg. Similar sections are present on the other
matrix half. Those spaces in each lower corner of half 1 and half 2 were likely used for
instrumentation. The bed and knees (the support structures for the matrix tubes) may also have
taken some of this space.
Unlike ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9, ZPPR maintained a consistent drawer master identification
convention throughout its operational life. The ZPPR drawer master identification convention was
based on the final approach used at ZPR-3.
For ZPPR, each drawer master identification consists of three fields, xx-y-zzz. The first field, xx,
is a two-digit identification for the assembly program such as 13, 14, 15, 16, etc. The second field,
y, determines whether the drawer master applies to half 1, half 2 or both halves of the matrix. The
possible values for y are 0 if the drawer master applies to both halves, 1 if the drawer master only
applies to half 1 and 2 if the drawer master only applies to half 2. The third field, zzz, is a three-
digit identifier for that specific drawer master or loading pattern. For example, for drawer master
15-0-101, the “15” in the first field designates assembly program 15, i.e., ZPPR-15, the “0” in the
second field indicates that this drawer master is used in both halves of the matrix, and the “101”
in the third field designates the unique plate loading pattern for drawer master 15-0-101.
The available loading records for early ZPPR assemblies consisted entirely of handwritten sheets.
For later ZPPR assemblies, the handwritten records were entered into the minicomputer used at
ZPPR and were either stored on that computer or archived on magnetic tapes. ZPPR was shut
down in 1990. The ZPPR computer and the magnetic tapes were discarded years ago. In any case,
it seems unlikely that any computer records from the ZPPR computer or magnetic tapes could be
accessed and read reliably today due to equipment obsolescence and physical degradation of the
storage media. The same consideration applies to the hardware and magnetic tapes used to store
computerized records for ZPR-6 and ZPR-9.

 92

The scanned loading records for early ZPPR loadings are the original handwritten forms. The
scanned loading records for later ZPPR assemblies are a mixture of handwritten records and
printouts from the ZPPR computer. It is not clear why the loading records are a mixture of
handwritten and computer-generated forms.
Figure 5.7 is the first page of the loading record for ZPPR-4 loading 28 from January 1974. The
top of Figure 5.7 shows the assembly number, loading number, page number and description of
the experiment or loading change. The upper part of this figure is the equivalent of the separate
loading summary sheets used in the loading records for later ZPPR assemblies.
The lower part of Figure 5.7 shows the individual steps or loading changes. If there were
subsequent pages for loading 28, those pages would only show loading changes. Column 1 of this
figure shows the matrix location, column 2 shows the drawer master removed from that location,
column 3 shows the drawer master loaded in that location, and column 4 shows the disposition of
the drawer master removed. In some cases, the drawer removed from one location was moved to
another location during the same loading. Column 5 is not relevant for modeling purposes.
ZPPR also had the capability to store drawers removed from the matrix for later reuse to avoid
unloading and then reloading drawers that were removed from the matrix temporarily. Lines 1
and 6 of the loading changes in Figure 5.7 indicate that the drawers removed from the matrix were
transferred to a temporary storage location.
In later ZPPR assemblies, a loading record consisted of three parts. The first page is the “Loading
Change Summary Form” or loading summary page which generally lists the assembly and phase,
the loading number, a date, the objective of the experiment or loading change, and a summary of
the loading change. This form also has spaces to list any relevant references and any special
comments or instructions and space for approvals. Figure 5.8 is the loading summary page for
ZPPR-13A loading 30.

 93

 Figure 5.7. ZPPR-04 Loading 28 – Loading Record.

 94

 Figure 5.8. ZPPR-13A Loading 30 – Summary Loading Sheet.
The second part of the loading record for later ZPPR assemblies was a listing of the specific
loading changes in that loading. This listing included the matrix location where changes were to
be made, the identification of the drawer master to be removed from that location, the identification
of the drawer master to be inserted in that location, and the disposition of the drawer removed.
Figure 5.9 is the first page of the second part of the loading record for ZPPR-13A loading 30. This
page shows the actual loading changes for ZPPR-13A loading 30. Figure 5.9 shows that there had
been at least one minor change in the standard loading record form between 1974 and 1982. In
Figure 5.9, the disposition column shows that the drawers removed from the matrix tubes were
actually being moved to other locations in the matrix in this loading change.

 95

 Figure 5.9. ZPPR-13A Loading 30 – Loading Record.
The third part of a ZPPR loading record consisted of one or two diagrams showing the locations
in the matrix where changes are to be made or have been made.
Figure 5.10 shows a sample Loading Change Summary Form or loading summary page from
ZPPR-15A. This form is typical of the loading summary pages used in later ZPPR assemblies.
The top of Figure 5.10 shows the assembly number (ZPPR-15A), the loading number (67), date
and page number.
The Objective of Experiment (or loading change) for loading 67 was to establish a subcritical
reference configuration. In this particular case, the purpose of establishing a subcritical reference
was to begin the transition from ZPPR-15A to ZPPR-15B.

 96

The Summary Statement of Loading Change explains the intended changes. The proton recoil
counter and split fuel plate drawers will be removed. “Despike” means replacing drawers with
two fuel columns (double column fuel or DCF) with drawers containing one fuel column (single
column fuel or SCF). The purpose of despiking was to remove fuel and lower reactivity. “Spike”
means replacing SCF drawers with DCF drawers to add fuel and increase reactivity. The despiking
was planned for eight drawers at symmetric positions in half 1 and half 2. The designation “1,253-
34” was a ZPPR shorthand for the matrix locations 153-34 and 253-34.
Spiking and despiking involved drawers at symmetric locations across the interface between
matrix halves, across the center row(s) in each half and across the center column(s) in each matrix
half. Depending on the size of the assembly (number of occupied rows and columns), the
horizontal centerline of the assembly might bisect a row of drawers or fall between two rows of
drawers. The vertical centerline of the assembly might bisect the center column of drawers or fall
between two columns of drawers for the same reason. In addition, the center of an assembly might
be intentionally offset from the actual center of the matrix to leave space for a special experiment.
Spiking and despiking were common ways to make small adjustments in reactivity.
There is a reference to the Assembly Document. For some loadings, there were references to other
documents. There are also special comments or instructions for the disposition of materials in the
some drawers.

 97

 Figure 5.10. ZPPR-15A Loading 67 – Loading Change Summary Form.

 98

Figure 5.11 and Figure 5.12 show samples of the handwritten loading records from ZPPR-15A
loading 65. These figures show another version of the standard loading form used at ZPPR.
Consider Figure 5.11 first. The “Matrix” (first) column of Figure 5.11 shows the matrix location.
The “Action” columns are blank. That is common. People frequently left those columns blank.
The ZPPR loading records printed by the ZPPR computer generally showed the full drawer master
identification for a drawer removed from or inserted into the matrix. For example, the first row of
data in Figure 5.13 shows that drawer master 15-0-102 was removed from matrix location 155-43,
modified, and inserted into matrix location 155-43 as drawer master 15-0-126. Any change in the
configuration of plates in a drawer such as rearrangement or replacement of one plate type with
another plate type changes the drawer master number because each unique plate configuration is
identified by a unique drawer master number. Consequently, the modification of the drawer
converted that drawer from drawer master 15-0-102 to drawer master 15-0-126. The relevant point
for modeling purposes is that drawer master 15-0-102 was removed from location 155-43 and
drawer master 15-0-126 was inserted in location 155-43.
Handwritten ZPPR records may show only the last part of the identifier, i.e., the last three digits,
if that was sufficient to uniquely identify the drawer master. The full identifier was abbreviated
for convenience by the person filling out the handwritten form because the meaning and intent
were clear to the ZPPR staff members who used the form for reactor loading and unloading.
This abbreviation only works if the same drawer master can be used in half 1 and half 2. Recall
that ZPPR drawer master labels were of the form xx-y-zzz where “xx” identified the assembly
number and “zzz” identified a unique drawer loading pattern. The values of “y” were 0 if the
drawer master was used in both halves, 1 if the drawer master was used only in half 1, or 2 if the
drawer master was used only in half 2. Most ZPPR-15 drawer masters were used in both halves,
so “y” was 0 for all regular ZPPR-15 drawer masters. The exceptions were special experimental
drawers that were only used at specific locations in the matrix. Because “y” was 0 for all regular
ZPPR-15 drawer masters, the last three digits (“zzz”) sufficed to uniquely identify the drawer
masters. For assemblies where drawer masters could only be used in half 1 or half 2, it might be
necessary to indicate the matrix half in addition to the last three digits of the drawer master
identifier.
In any case, the full identifier could frequently be determined from context. Drawer masters for
ZPPR-10A were not symmetric, so drawer master 10-1-110 would be inserted in half 1, and drawer
master 10-2-110 would be inserted in the corresponding location in half 2. The matrix location
identifier is sufficient to identify half 1 of half 2. For example, 158-32 designates half 1, row 58,
column 32 while 258-32 designates half 2, row 58, column 32. For an assembly with asymmetric
drawer masters such as ZPPR-10A, the matrix half determined which drawer master would be
loaded. The correct drawer master to load in each matrix location was clear to the ZPPR staff
performing the loading and unloading operations. For example, drawer master 10-1-110 might be
loaded into location 158-32, and drawer master 10-2-110 might be loaded into location 258-32.
The location identifier (158-32 or 258-32) and “110” provided sufficient information to load the
correct drawer master in that location.
The “Master Drawer Out” column shows the drawer master that is being removed from a matrix
location. For Figure 5.11, drawer master 105 (15-0-105) is being removed from matrix location

 99

158-32 in this loading change. The downward arrow indicates that the same drawer master is
being removed from the following three locations. Likewise, drawer master 15-0-201 is being
removed from matrix location 158-33 and the following three locations. Drawer master 15-0-105
is being removed from 258-32 and the following three locations and so on.
The “Disposition of Drawer Out” column shows what is being done with the drawer that is being
removed from a matrix location. For the first entry in Figure 5.11, drawer master 15-0-105 is
being removed from location 158-32. According to the “Disposition” column, that drawer is being
moved to matrix location 158-33. For the last eight entries in Figure 5.11, the drawer master that
is being removed from a matrix location is being stored on one of the carts used to transport loaded
drawers between the workroom where drawers are loaded or unloaded and the cell where the ZPPR
split table machine is located. It is useful to note that later in the same loading information, the
158-33 drawer is marked as being removed and placed in 158-32.
The “Master Drawer In” column shows the drawer master that is being inserted into the matrix
tube at the location in the first column. For the first entry in Figure 5.11, drawer master 15-0-201
is being inserted into the matrix tube at location 158-32. Figure 5.11 shows a downward arrow
through row 159-65 indicating that 201 was loaded in 159-65 and also shows 817 as being loaded
into 159-65 with the initials “SBB” in that row. The same ambiguity appears for row 259-65. In
this case, the 817 is a correction and “SBB,” the initials of the assembly coordinator, shows that
the assembly coordinator approved the correction. It is not obvious just from this particular page
whether 201 or 817 was loaded in rows 159-65 and 259-65. However, the loading records for
loading 67 show that 817 was removed from 159-65 and 259-65, which confirms that 817 was
loaded into 159-65 and 259-65 in loading 65. Resolution of ambiguities and discrepancies in the
loading records is discussed later in this section.
The “Source of Drawer In” column shows the original location of the drawer that is being inserted
into the matrix tube. For the first entry in Figure 5.11, the drawer master 15-0-201 that is being
inserted into matrix location 158-32 came from matrix location 158-33. For many entries in Figure
5.11, the actual loading change consists of just swapping the drawers between matrix locations.
For the last eight entries in Figure 5.11, the drawers to be loaded came from a transport cart which
means they may have been stored on the cart during a previous loading change or they may have
been loaded in the workroom.
The source of the drawer master to be inserted and the disposition of the drawer master removed
were important during reactor operations. The source and disposition of drawer masters are also
important for modeling purposes if a drawer master was being moved from one matrix location to
another matrix location.
If the source or disposition was the transfer cart, workroom, vault or other storage area away from
the matrix, the source and disposition are not necessarily important for modeling purposes. One
circumstance in which the source of the drawer master to be inserted and the disposition of the
drawer are important for modeling purposes is in resolution of ambiguities and discrepancies in
the loading records. The loading records are not perfect. They do contain occasional ambiguities,
discrepancies, omissions and errors. During reactor operations, questions could be resolved by
discussion with other staff members or by physically inspecting the drawers present in the matrix
tubes. Neither of those options is available today. If a current user of the loading record data finds

 100

a discrepancy or ambiguity for a loading, inspection of drawer masters loaded or removed in earlier
or later loadings provides information that can be used to resolve any discrepancy or ambiguity.

 101

 Figure 5.11. ZPPR-15A Loading 65 – Loading Record, Page 2.

 102

 Figure 5.12. ZPPR-15A Loading 65 – Loading Record, Page 3.

 103

In Figure 5.12, drawer master 15-0-203 is being removed from the matrix tubes listed in the
“Matrix” (first) column. The drawers that are removed are being stored in the ZPPR vault. Drawer
master 15-0-105 is being loaded into the matrix tubes in the “Matrix” column. The drawer master
15-0-105 drawers that are being loaded are being retrieved from the ZPPR vault where they were
stored.
Fuel plates (Pu-U-Mo, Pu-Al, HEU) were stored in the ZPPR vault. Empty drawers and non-fuel
plates such as sodium plates, stainless steel plates and depleted uranium plates were stored
elsewhere in the ZPPR facility. Drawers were loaded in the ZPPR workroom adjacent to the ZPPR
vault. Carts were used to move loaded drawers between the workroom and the matrix tubes in the
reactor cell.
Figure 5.13 is an example of a ZPPR printed loading record. The columns have the same
interpretation as the columns in the handwritten records. The “Modify” in the “Disposition”
column means that drawer master 15-0-102 was removed from a matrix location and modified by
changing some of the plates in the drawer. For this change, some plate columns were rearranged
and each 0.125 inch-thick depleted uranium plate column was replaced by a 0.0625 inch-thick
depleted uranium column and a 0.0625 inch-thick zirconium column as part of the transition from
ZPPR-15A to ZPPR-15B. Any change in the plates in a drawer or rearrangement of the plate
columns in a drawer produces a new drawer master. In this case, the modification converted
drawer master 15-0-102 to drawer master 15-0-126. Modifying an existing loaded drawer to match
the desired configuration was more efficient than unloading the existing drawer and loading
another drawer to match that configuration. The essential point is that drawer master 15-0-102
was replaced by drawer master 15-0-126 in the listed matrix locations in Figure 5.13.
In general, the “Matrix” column and the “Master Drawer In” column determine which drawer
master is being loaded into the indicated matrix locations in a loading change. The “Master Drawer
Out” and “Disposition of Drawer Out” columns indicate what is being done with the drawer
masters removed from matrix locations. In particular, the “Disposition” column may indicate that
the drawer master removed from one matrix position is being moved to another matrix position.
The other columns are useful occasionally to resolve discrepancies or ambiguities in the loading
records.

 Figure 5.13. ZPPR-15B Loading 72 – Loading Record, Page 2.
Figure 5.14 and Figure 5.15 shows the loading change diagrams for half 1 and half 2, respectively,
in ZPPR-15A loading 65. These diagrams show where loading changes were made in the matrix

 105

in half 1 and half 2. The original purpose of the loading change diagrams is uncertain. They may
have been aids for the technicians or the experimenters. For converting the loading records into a
matrix map for a configuration of interest, these diagrams are of limited value. However, they are
useful on occasion to resolve uncertainties when the loading records are ambiguous or difficult to
read. In addition, for some assemblies, the loading records omit loading of the radial reflector and
just start with loading of the radial blanket and core. In those cases, these diagrams can be used to
determine the boundaries of the radial reflector and radial blanket.
Figure 5.14 and Figure 5.15 are examples of the matrix numbering scheme discussed above. The
row numbers on the left and right sides of Figure 5.14 for half 1 are numbered from 111 at the top
to 187 at the bottom. The row numbers from 111 to 187 indicate rows in half 1. The column
numbers at the top of Figure 5.14 for half 1 are numbered from 11 on the left to 87 on the right.
This is the view that an observer standing between the matrix halves and facing half 1 would see.
The row numbers on the left and right sides of Figure 5.15 Figure 5.15for half 2 are numbered
from 211 at the top to 287 at the bottom. The row numbers from 211 to 287 indicate rows in half
2. The column numbers at the top of Figure 5.15 for half 2 are numbered from 87 on the left to 11
on the right. This is the view that an observer standing between the matrix halves and facing half
2 would see because column numbering is reversed in half 2. Reversing the column numbering in
half 2 ensures that column numbers in half 2 line up with column numbers in half 1. When the
two halves are brought together, column 11 in half 2 is in a direct line with column 11 in half 1,
and column 87 in half 2 is in a direct line with column 87 in half 1.

5.5 Resolving Ambiguities and Discrepancies in Loading Records
5.5.1 Order of Loading Records
When ZPR-3 was shut down, the ZPR-3 records were placed in boxes and stored either at ZPPR
or elsewhere on the ANL-W site. When ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were shut down, their records were
placed in boxes and sent to ZPPR. Likewise, when ZPPR was shut down, the ZPPR records were
placed in boxes and stored. In some cases, the records were carefully placed in the boxes in an

 108

order that matched the sequence of loadings in each assembly program. In other cases, records
were loaded into boxes without any consideration of the actual sequence of loadings in an assembly
program.
When the retired ZPPR technician scanned the paper loading records, it appears that he just
removed the papers from the boxes and scanned them without examining them to determine
whether the records were in order or complete. In addition, the scanned records for most assembly
programs were divided into many separate PDF files to keep the file sizes manageable.
ZPPR-15 provides an example of the out-of-sequence problem for some loading records. The
records for any given ZPPR-15 loading were scanned sequentially, but the records for different
loadings were not scanned in the standard order (loading 1, loading 2, loading 3, etc.). The likely
reason is that the people who loaded the boxes did not pay attention when loading the boxes. The
technician scanned the loading records in groups and created fourteen PDF files. The order of the
loadings was reversed when the records were scanned. For example, files 40-99a.pdf, 40-99b.pdf
and 40-99c.pdf include loadings 40 – 99. The first record in 40-99a.pdf is loading 99. The last
record in 40-99c.pdf is loading 40.
Some loading records were scanned completely out of order. This is common for the records for
loadings in the 100 – 150 range. The scanned records include all loadings in the ZPPR-15 program,
but the records for some loadings were scanned out of sequence. Consequently, it may be
necessary to search all of the PDF files for an assembly program to locate the loading records for
a specific loading. In addition, some pages were scanned upside down which probably reflects
how they were placed in the boxes.
The format of the standard forms changed occasionally, so there were handwritten or computer-
generated ZPPR-15 records on different standard forms.
It may also be necessary to inspect all PDF files for an assembly program to verify that loading
records for all loadings are present because there is at least one case in which there are missing
loading records. The last available loading record for ZPR-9/29 is loading 53, but the ZPR-9/29
logbook shows that the last ZPR-9/29 loading was loading 136.
5.5.2 Ambiguities and Discrepancies in Loading Records
The loading records for ZPR/ZPPR assemblies are not perfect. There are apparent errors,
discrepancies, ambiguities and corrections in those records as discussed in Section 5.4 and shown
in Figure 5.11 above. There are some basic principles that can be applied to resolve apparent
ambiguities and discrepancies in the loading records.
 1. In some cases, the correction and any added notes on the loading record indicate the correct
 interpretation.
 2. The loading change summary form or equivalent shown in Figure 5.8 and Figure 5.10 lists
 the objective of the experiment or loading change, a summary statement of the loading
 change, and any special comments or instructions for the loading change. Similar forms
 for ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 such as Figure 5.2 and Figure 5.6 provide at least the
 objective of the experiment and possibly additional information. The logbook entry for the
 loading also lists the objective of the loading. Any drawer master inserted or removed in
 a loading change should be consistent with the loading change summary form and logbook

 109

 entries.
 3. In general, the experimenters tried to maintain symmetry in core loadings across the central
 column or columns (left – right), across the central row or rows (top – bottom) and across
 matrix halves (half 1 – half 2). Maintaining symmetry reduced experimental uncertainty
 and produced cleaner configurations that were easier to model and analyze. If the drawer
 masters were symmetric, the experimenters attempted to maintain symmetry at the four
 symmetric positions in each half. If the drawer masters were asymmetric, the
 experimenters generally tried to maintain mirror image symmetry at the four symmetric
 positions in each half.
 4. In general, plate columns lined up across the matrix halves. A fuel column in half 1 lined
 up with a fuel column in half 2, a sodium column in half 1 lined up with a sodium column
 in half 2, a depleted uranium column in half 1 lined up with a depleted uranium column in
 half 2, and so on. Maintaining alignment of like columns across the interface between half
 1 and half 2 simplified modeling and reduced experimental uncertainty.
 5. If a particular loading record is ambiguous, it is important to look at the loading records
 for prior loadings and subsequent loadings. The records for prior loadings will indicate the
 drawer master that was in each matrix location during previous loadings, and the records
 for subsequent loadings will indicate the drawer master that is being loaded in each matrix
 location. Some versions of the handwritten and computerized loading record forms show
 the drawer master removed from each matrix location, the disposition of each drawer
 master removed, and/or the source of each drawer master loaded. This information can be
 very valuable. Records for previous loadings may show where drawer masters were
 moved, whether drawer masters were moved to the locations in question, and when such
 movements occurred. Records for subsequent loadings may show which drawer masters
 were removed from the locations in question and when such movements occurred.
 6. There were 961 matrix locations in each half of the 31 x 31 ZPR-3 matrix, 2025 matrix
 locations in each half of the 45 x 45 ZPR-9 matrix, 2025 matrix locations in the each of the
 original 45 x 45 ZPR-6 matrix, 4225 matrix locations in each half of the expanded 65 x 65
 ZPR-6 matrix, 2915 matrix locations in each half of the original 53 x 55 ZPPR matrix and
 5929 matrix locations in each half of the expanded 77 x 77 ZPPR matrix. For most types
 of measurements, any reasonable assumption about the drawer masters in one or a few
 matrix locations that are uncertain is not likely to have a significant effect.
 7. There is an additional method to check for errors, omissions or discrepancies in the loading
 records or for errors when the loading records are converted to a digital form that can be
 used to construct an as-built model of an experimental configuration. After the loading
 records have been converted to a digital matrix map for the configuration of interest, the
 user can create a graphical version of that matrix map. Figure 5.16 and Figure 5.17 show
 the two halves of ZPPR-12 loading 9. The digital matrix map for ZPPR-12 loading 9 was
 reformatted as a text file, imported into an Excel spreadsheet and manipulated to produce
 Figure 5.16 and Figure 5.17. There are various other ways to create similar figures.
 Inspection of those figures can reveal errors or omissions in the matrix map and,
 consequently, errors and omissions either in the original loading records or in the
 processing of those loading records.

 110

Overall, experimenters attempted to maintain symmetry to the maximum extent possible within
the constraints of the plate inventory and the assembly design. In particular, PSR control drawers
were placed at symmetric locations whenever that was possible. In some assemblies, such as
ZPPR-10, the drawer masters were not symmetric. To maintain symmetry, different drawer
masters were used on the left and right sides of the central column(s) to maintain left – right or
mirror image symmetry about the centerline which increases the effort for creating the assembly.
There are many reasons why symmetry cannot always be preserved where Figure 5.16 and Figure
5.17 serve as examples of an asymmetric loading. In some cases, experimental equipment or
drawers were placed in asymmetric locations because the experimenters wanted to measure a
parameter at those specific locations. Similarly, when ZPPR began using the modified source
multiplication method for reactivity measurements, it was necessary to place detectors in drawers
in the core, radial blanket and radial reflector. Initially, the ZPPR staff use 16 detectors, then 32
detectors, and finally 64 detectors. The detector drawers were intentionally not placed at
symmetric locations because the experimenters wanted to sample as much of the core, radial
blanket and radial reflector in half 1 and half 2 as possible to obtain a representative detector
response for the whole assembly. The asymmetric distribution of the detector drawers in the matrix
introduced minor asymmetries in the matrix maps for half 1 and half 2. Finally, when DP control
rod drawers were present, typically there were five DP drawers in each half, and a DP drawer in
half 1 was not always directly aligned with a DP drawer in half 2. If DP drawers and PSRs were
both present, there might be an odd number of DP drawers in each half and an odd number of PSRs
in each half.

One suggested approach is to create a program (or script) that performs various tests on the matrix
map which was done for the ZPR and ZPPR analysis work performed to date. The key parts to
check include:

 1. Examine the matrix map for gaps and holes such as empty cells in the core, radial blanket
 and radial reflector. The presence of empty cells within the core, radial blanket and radial
 reflector is suspicious because generally there would not be any empty matrix tubes in
 those regions unless the experimenters were specifically measuring the worth of a drawer.
 The statement of the objective of the experiment or loading in the loading records or

 113

 logbook should indicate such a measurement, and the loading records should indicate that
 a drawer master was removed from the location where the empty cell appears.
 2. Test for unexpected asymmetry across the vertical centerline of each half. The vertical
 centerline of each half is either the center column or the vertical line between the two center
 columns of the the assembly. If the drawer masters are symmetric about the center of the
 long axis of the drawer, there will generally be symmetry about the vertical center of each
 half, i.e., between the left side and right side of each table. The drawer masters at
 symmetric locations on opposite sides of the vertical centerline will generally be identical.
 If the drawer masters are asymmetric about the center of the long axis of the drawer, e.g.,
 ZPPR-10A, there will generally be mirror image symmetry about the vertical center of each
 half. Any program or script can be adjusted to account for mirror image symmetry when
 comparing drawer masters at symmetric locations across the vertical centerline of each
 half.
 3. Test for unexpected asymmetry across the horizontal centerline of each half. The
 horizontal centerline of each half is either the center row or the horizontal line between the
 two center rows of the assembly. Symmetry or asymmetry within the drawer masters is
 not an issue for the test for symmetry across the horizontal centerline. Typically, there will
 be symmetry about the horizontal centerline in each half, so drawer masters at symmetric
 locations on opposite sides of the horizontal centerline will generally be identical.
 4. Test for unexpected asymmetry between matrix halves, i.e., between half 1 and half 2 or
 between the stationary and movable halves. If the drawer masters are symmetric about the
 centers of the long axes of the drawers, it is likely that there will be symmetry between half
 1 and half 2. In the case of asymmetric drawers, columns of like plates such as fuel or
 sodium were aligned across the interface between half 1 and half 2. If the drawer masters
 are asymmetric, it is likely that either there is direct symmetry across the interface or there
 is a mirror image symmetry that would require a minor adjustment to the program or script
 to account for the mirror image symmetry.

For the program developed for past work, the program flagged all matrix locations within the core,
radial blanket and radial reflector of the matrix map that were empty. It also flagged all matrix
locations within the core, radial blanket and radial reflector that did not display symmetry across
the vertical centerline of the assembly, the horizontal centerline of the assembly and the interface
between half 1 and half 2. The user could then investigate the reasons why those locations failed
the test criteria.
There are a limited number of valid reasons why a matrix location might be empty. The principal
valid reason for an empty matrix tube is that a drawer was removed from that location to measure
the worth of that drawer type at that location. The experimenters might remove a core drawer at
the core center to measure its worth. Likewise, the experimenters might remove a core drawer or
radial blanket drawer at the core-radial blanket boundary to measure its worth at the core edge
(edge worth) to provide data for adjustment of the core boundary from the actual jagged boundary
to a smooth cylindrical boundary. In general, however, an empty matrix location likely reflects
either an omission in the loading records or an error in transcribing or converting the loading
records to a digital form.

 114

There are several reasons why matrix locations might fail symmetry tests. In most assemblies,
there was axial symmetry about the interface between matrix halves. That interface was the axial
center of the core, and there were equal amounts of core, axial blanket and axial reflector in half 1
and half 2. However, there were exceptions in which the axial center of the core was offset from
the interface between matrix halves. In ZPPR-12 for example, drawers in half 1 contained 24
inches of core material while drawers in half 2 only contained 12 inches of core material. That
asymmetry was necessary to accommodate some of the intended measurements. One set of
measurements included the use of calandria (discussed below). The calandria had a fixed 12 inch
length, so it was necessary to offset the axial center of the core by 6 inches from the interface
between matrix halves. There may have been a few other assemblies in ZPR-3, ZPR-6, ZPR-9
and/or ZPPR that were not axially symmetric about the interface between matrix halves.
Locations of special experimental equipment might fail symmetry tests. In some cases, such
equipment was located at an off-center location to obtain a measurement at that point such as the
core-radial blanket boundary. Alternatively, the equipment might only be present in one drawer
in one half. For example, in neutron spectrum measurements, the proton recoil spectrometer used
for the measurements was located in one drawer in one half. When irradiation foils were used to
measure reaction rate distributions, the foils were placed in drawers in one half. Likewise, when
thermoluminescent dosimeters (TLDs) were used to measure gamma doses, the TLDs were only
placed in one half.
Drawers containing thermocouples are likely to fail symmetry tests because thermocouples would
be placed at asymmetric locations to obtain representative core temperatures.
When ZPPR began using the modified source multiplication technique, many drawers containing
detectors (16, 32 or 64 detector drawers) were placed in the core, radial blanket and radial reflector.
The detector drawers were intentionally placed at widely dispersed and asymmetric matrix
locations to sample as much of the core, radial blanket and radial reflector in both halves as
possible. Consequently, detector drawers and drawers at symmetric locations in ZPPR are likely
to fail some symmetry tests. It is likely that the same considerations apply to detector drawers in
the other facilities as well.
In general, at least one DP drawer per half will fail some symmetry tests because a) there usually
were an odd number of DP drawers in the core and b) DP drawers in half 1 did not necessarily
align directly with the corresponding DP drawers in half 2.
In most cases, the PSR drawers in each half are in symmetric locations, and the PSRs align across
the interface between halves. However, there are occasional exceptions where there were an odd
number of PSRs present or where the PSRs were not in symmetric locations. These cases are most
likely to occur when both DP control drawers and PSRs are present in relatively small assemblies.
5.6 Use of the Loading Records for Modeling Purposes
Constructing a high fidelity model of any ZPR/ZPPR assembly requires the user to model the
contents of each drawer in each matrix tube accurately. Modeling the individual drawer masters
was discussed in Section 3. The loading records are used to place the correct drawer master in
each matrix tube for the configuration of interest.

 115

The discussion in Section 3.6 regarding the use of OCR software and/or AI to convert the drawer
master figures to a usable, reliable digital file that could be processed to create an accurate as-built
model of a ZPR/ZPPR assembly applies equally to processing the loading records, and the same
caveat applies. It would be necessary to verify that the final digital form of the loading records is
an accurate transcription or conversion of the original loading records.
Loadings in any ZPR/ZPPR assembly were cumulative. Each configuration in a ZPR/ZPPR
program was based upon all previous configurations constructed during that program. Loading 2
began with the configuration at the end of loading 1, loading 3 began with the configuration at end
of loading 2, and so on. In general, loading N began with the configuration at the end of loading
N – 1 until the end of the program was reached. It is generally not possible to construct the matrix
map, i.e., the specification of the drawer master in each matrix tube, for loading N without
processing all loading records for loadings 1 – N plus any loading records for radial reflector
drawers, radial blanket drawers and any pre-loaded core drawers that may have been loaded into
the matrix tubes before the records for loading 1 start.
The issue of drawers that were loaded into the matrix tubes before the loading records for loading
1 start is occasionally a relevant consideration. Recordkeeping for loading of radial blanket
drawers and radial reflector drawers is not consistent, particularly for the early assemblies, so there
are several possibilities.
 1. In some cases, loading 1 starts with loading of the radial blanket drawers and radial
 reflector drawers. Thus the loading records for loadings 1 – N are a complete record of all
 radial reflector drawers, radial blanket drawers, pre-loaded core drawers (if any) and
 regular core drawers loaded into the matrix tubes.
 2. In some cases, particularly for early assemblies, the loading records include all radial
 reflector drawers and radial blanket drawers, but loading 1 starts with loading core drawers.
 The loading records for the blanket and reflector drawers precede loading 1 and do not
 have an assigned loading number.
 3. The available loading records just do not include loading of radial blanket drawers and/or
 radial reflector drawers. This has been encountered a few times for early assemblies in
 which available loading records omit radial blanket and reflector drawers. In those cases,
 it was necessary to reconstruct the radial blanket and radial reflector from the core maps
 provided in reports and other documents.

The ZPR/ZPPR staff members were very careful regarding the outlines of core zones, the radial
blanket and the radial reflector published in reports and other documents, so it is reasonable to
assume that the core map outlines in published documents are accurate. A related source of
information is the core maps for half 1 and half 2 that are included at the back of each loading
record for some ZPR/ZPPR assemblies. Those core maps show the outlines of the various zones
and also can be assumed to be accurate.
By working backwards from the core maps, one can reconstruct the shapes of the radial blanket
and radial reflector and, consequently, can reconstruct a set of loading records for the radial blanket
and radial reflector. Those reconstructed loading records for the radial blanket and radial reflector
will not show the drawer master in each matrix tube, but they are sufficiently accurate for most

 116

purposes. Differences between different radial blanket drawer masters of the same general type
or of reflector drawer masters of the same general type are a reflection of the limited number of
plates of any specific type and size. The radial blanket is in a region of low importance, so it is
unlikely that substituting one blanket drawer master for another very similar blanket drawer master
that differs only in the lengths of some plates will have a discernible effect on measured quantities
that can be calculated today. The previous sentence applies equally to substitution of one radial
reflector drawer master for another very similar radial reflector drawer master.
The core maps in published documents and the core maps in the loading records for some
assemblies can serve another purpose with respect to the location of the PSRs. The core maps
show whether the PSR guide tube was on the left side or right side of the narrow PSR drawer at
each location where a PSR drawer was present. In some assemblies, the drawer master figures
make a clear distinction regarding the position of the PSR guide tube (left side or right side) relative
to the PSR drawer in the matrix tube. In other cases, particularly for some of the early assemblies
that had PSRs, the drawer master figures do not make the left side/right side distinction. In those
cases, the core maps can be used to position the PSR guide tubes more accurately with respect to
the PSR drawers.

 117

6 MATERIAL LIBRARY
The procurement acceptance process for materials used in the ZPR-3, ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR
facilities required thorough documentation regarding dimensions, masses, compositions and other
relevant properties. The ZPR/ZPPR staff extracted important information required for normal
operations from the procurement documents and compiled that information in working documents
referred to as hot constants memos and in the ADEN library, i.e., the materials library.
The ADEN library is a compendium of dimension and composition information for plates, drawers
and matrix tubes used at ANL-E and ANL-W. The ADEN library contained the composition
information for the plates used in the facilities. This library also contained composition
information for the drawers into which the plates were loaded and the matrix tubes into which the
drawers were loaded. ADEN is an acronym for atom density. The information in the ADEN
library was used by the staff for experiment planning and for construction of models of
experimental configurations.
The hot constants memos were used for daily operations and experiment planning. Most of the
original documents related to plate acquisition and measurements have been lost, but the ADEN
library and hot constants memos are still available. The available paper copies of the hot constants
memos were scanned and converted to PDF files. The available hot constants memos include three
versions for operations at ZPR-3, the last version of the hot constants memo used at ZPR-6 and
ZPR-9 at ANL-E, and the last hot constants memo used at ZPPR.
6.1 Plate Inventories
ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR operated simultaneously from 1969 until the early 1980s when ZPR-6
and ZPR-9 were shut down. ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 operated simultaneously from 1963 until
ZPR-3 was shut down in 1970. ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were located in Building 315 at ANL-E. They
shared the plate inventory at ANL-E. ZPR-3 and ZPPR at ANL-W maintained a separate plate
inventory from the ANL-E inventory.
ANL-E and ANL-W shared fuel plates such as HEU plates, Pu-Al plates and Pu-U-Mo plates when
necessary, but ANL-E and ANL-W rarely shared non-fuel plates until ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were shut
down. At that point, all fuel plates and the more valuable non-fuel plates in the ANL-E inventory
were shipped to ZPPR.
In addition, when some plate types were purchased, a fraction of those plates were delivered to
ANL-E for use in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 while the remainder of the plates were delivered to ANL-W
for use in ZPPR. The Pu-U-Mo plates manufactured by Dow and NUMEC fall into this category.
The sodium plates designated NA in the ADEN library also fall into this category.
The ADEN library and the hot constants memos make a distinction between ANL-E plates and
ANL-W plates in some cases. If there are ANL-E and ANL-W entries for the same plate type
(material and size), the plates with the ANL-E designation would have been used for ZPR-6 and
ZPR-9 assemblies, and the plates with the ANL-W designation would have been used at ANL-W.
After ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were shut down, some non-fuel plates in the ANL-E inventory were sent
to ANL-W, so some of those plates may have been used in later ZPPR assemblies.

 118

6.2 Addition of Materials to the ADEN Library
For present purposes, the hot constants memos are a supplement to the ADEN library. The
standard ADEN library was developed for use at ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR after ZPR-3 shut down.
After ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were shut down, the ZPPR staff maintained the ADEN library and made
any additions required to support ZPPR operations.
The standard ADEN library is not a complete compilation of all plates in the inventories of ZPR-
3, ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR. Because the ADEN library was developed to support current
operations in ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR, the materials added to the ADEN library were the materials
used for current operations in those facilities. Plates and other materials used only for assembly
programs that were completed prior to development of the ADEN library were not necessarily
added to the library. Likewise, the ADEN library may not include some plates that were only used
for one assembly or a single experiment in one assembly at ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR.
For example, the standard ADEN library does not include most of the plates used at ZPR-3 because
most of the ZPR-3 inventory was discarded when ZPR-3 shut down. In addition, it is likely that
analysis of ZPR-3 assemblies more or less ceased after ZPR-3 was shut down, so there would not
have been any motivation to include ZPR-3 plates in the ADEN library with the exception of ZPR-
3 plates such as fuel plates that were transferred to one of the other facilities.
It is occasionally necessary to add plate descriptions to the ADEN library to model experiments.
This is most likely to be true for ZPR-3 assemblies. ZPR-3 was shut down shortly after ZPPR
began operations. After ZPR-3 was shut down, there probably was little further effort to model
ZPR-3 assemblies until the late 1990s when benchmarks of a few ZPR-3 assemblies were prepared
for the International Criticality Safety Benchmark Evaluation Project (ICSBEP) [5]. In any event,
it is occasionally necessary to consult the hot constants memos for information about materials
that are not included in the standard ADEN library and to add materials to the ADEN library to
model specific experiments. It should be no surprise that special versions of the ADEN library
were created and used for these situations when building models.
In addition to the hot constants memos, old ANL reports sometimes contain relevant information
about plates, drawers or matrix tubes that are not included in the ADEN library.
Documentation of ZPR and ZPPR critical assemblies is inconsistent. In some cases, formal ANL
reports were published. There may also be relevant information in monthly, quarterly or annual
reports published when or after the critical assembly of interest was constructed. However, in
some cases there is little documentation available. It is not clear why this disparity exists. Work
on a new program may have been viewed as a higher priority than thoroughly documenting a
completed program if the ANL analysts and sponsoring agency had all of the information they
needed. In some cases, programmatic priorities changed at the sponsor level, so there was less
need to document a completed program of low priority. There also was a gradual transition from
issuing formal ANL reports to issuing informal reports or monthly reports in the ZPR-TM series.
In addition to providing information for plates that are not included in the standard ADEN library,
the hot constants memos and ANL reports are useful to improve modeling of some plates in the
ADEN library. The uranium plates (HEU, natural uranium and depleted uranium) used at ZPR-3,
ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were not clad. Instead, they were coated with Kel-F, a coating similar to paint,

 119

to inhibit corrosion and material loss during handling. The components of Kel-F are carbon,
hydrogen, fluorine and chlorine. After ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were shut down in the early 1980s, the
HEU plates at those facilities were shipped to Idaho for use in ZPPR. The ZPPR staff put those
HEU plates into cans to create clad HEU plates. All natural uranium plates and depleted uranium
plates used at ZPPR were coated with Kel-F but were not clad.
ZPR/ZPPR analysts typically ignored the Kel-F for modeling purposes. This was due in part to
the assumption that the effects of the Kel-F coating were negligible in the hard ZPR/ZPPR
spectrum compared to other approximations and in part to the limitations of computers at that time.
As a result, the standard ADEN library entries for HEU plates may include Kel-F in some cases,
but the standard ADEN library entries for natural or depleted uranium plates typically do not
include the Kel-F coating. If the ADEN library entry for a coated plate includes non-zero entries
for F, Cl, C and H (the four constituents of Kel-F), then the ADEN material includes the Kel-F
coating. If the ADEN library entry for a coated plate does not include non-zero entries for F, Cl,
C and H, the ADEN material entry does not include the Kel-F coating.
Note that some other plates, e.g., some iron plates and some graphite plates, also were coated with
Kel-F, titanium oxide or other materials to inhibit corrosion and material loss during handling.
The hot constants memos indicate whether plates were coated, the nature of the coating and the
average mass of the coating on each plate of a given material and size.
Many times during the past ZPR/ZPPR analysis activities, special versions of the ADEN library
were made which added the coating to the relevant ADEN library entries for coated plates to
improve the fidelity of as-built models. The added coating masses were based on the average
coating mass per plate listed in the hot constants memos and were mixed uniformly with the plate
material.
It was suggested at one ICSBEP meeting that the coatings should be represented explicitly in as-
built models. This seems unrealistic. The coatings are functionally equivalent to paint, and the
coating thickness on a plate would be similar to the thickness of paint. However, the actual
thickness of the coating on a plate is unknown, and any assumed thickness would be arbitrary. In
the hard ZPR/ZPPR spectrum, the effect of representing the coating explicitly versus mixing the
coating uniformly with the plate material should be very small compared to other uncertainties and
biases related to calculated values of measured experimental parameters. In addition, because the
coating is so thin, there is a realistic prospect that roundoff and other numerical effects would cause
problems in calculations as well as considerable increase in difficulty in building and running the
models.
Some plate types were clad in stainless steel for a) safety reasons, b) to prevent corrosion and
material loss, c) to prevent damage to the meat material or d) because it was not practical for
technicians to handle the unclad materials. A partial list of the clad plates includes Pu-U-Mo alloy,
Pu-Al alloy, sodium, sodium carbonate, lithium, boron carbide and HEU metal plates although the
HEU metal plates were only clad at ZPPR. The standard cladding material was stainless steel.
The cladding library (discussed below) contains dimension and composition information for the
cladding components for the clad plates. The cladding library also contains information regarding
the drawers and matrix tubes. The cladding library is used in conjunction with the ADEN library
to construct models of experimental configurations.

 120

The ADEN library and cladding library were compiled over many years. The versions available
are the final versions compiled by the ZPPR staff before ZPPR was shut down in 1990 with some
later additions required to prepare benchmarks for the ICSBEP Handbook [5] and the International
Handbook of Evaluated Reactor Physics Benchmark Experiments (IRPhEP Handbook) [6]. For
convenience, ZPR is used below to refer to ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9, and ZPR/ZPPR is used to
refer to all four ANL critical experiment facilities.
6.3 ADEN Library
The original version of the ADEN library was a text file created at ZPPR, an excerpt of which is
provided in Figure 6.1. This version contained entries for 599 materials. Approximately 555
entries (ADEN numbers 1 – 555) were added by the ZPR/ZPPR staff while ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and
ZPPR operated. Entries 556 – 599 were added for use in preparing ICSBEP benchmarks of
ZPR/ZPPR assemblies in the late 1990s. Additional entries have been added for follow-on
ICSBEP and IRPhEP benchmarks of ZPR/ZPPR assemblies.
In 2018 the ADEN library text file was converted to a spreadsheet because the spreadsheet is more
convenient to use for some purposes. A screen grab of the spreadsheet is shown in Figure 6.2.
The following discussion of the ADEN library is based on the spreadsheet version of the ADEN
library. Comparing Figure 6.1 to Figure 6.2, one should understand that the text file version of the
ADEN library provides the same information as the spreadsheet version, but the organization of
the text file version differs from the organization of the spreadsheet version.

 121

 Figure 6.1. ADEN Library Text File Excerpt.

 122

 Figure 6.2. ADEN Library Spreadsheet Excerpt.
The ADEN_Library worksheet in Figure 6.2 is a complete listing of the most recent version of
ADEN library. There were many different plate types (plates with different materials and/or
dimensions) in the ZPR/ZPPR inventory to allow the flexibility to simulate many different reactor
designs and configurations. Generally, there were two or more different sizes for any plate
material. Different sizes of the same plate material were needed to provide adequate flexibility to
construct reactor cores of different sizes. Focusing on the easier to read spreadsheet version of the
ADEN library, the following details are needed to understand the ADEN library.
6.3.1 ADEN Number
Looking at Figure 6.2, column 1 (A) lists the ADEN number for each plate type in the library. The
ADEN number is an identification number assigned to each plate type by the ZPR/ZPPR staff.
Some of the software used at ZPR/ZPPR used the ADEN number as an identifier for various
purposes including calculation of material compositions for deterministic models. When the ZPR
and ZPPR facilities were operating, it generally was not practical to construct and run detailed as-
built Monte Carlo models of ZPR/ZPPR assemblies due to computer limitations in that era.
Analysts had software programs that could use the ADEN numbers, the number of plates of each
different plate type, the number of drawers of each drawer master type and other information to
construct deterministic R-Z, X-Y or X-Y-Z models of ZPR/ZPPR assemblies for analysis
purposes.
The order in which ADEN numbers were assigned to plate types is not important. It seems likely
that the initial library entries were made for the plates that were used most frequently in experiment
planning and analysis and that later entries were added sequentially as the need arose for those
particular plate types in experiment planning and analysis.

 123

6.3.2 ADEN Identifier
Column 2 (B) in Figure 6.2 lists the ADEN identifier for each plate type in the library. This
identifier consists of 1 – 4 characters and designates a group of plates that are very similar or
identical except for dimensions. The ADEN identifier designates the class of plates, and the
ADEN number designates a particular group of plates within that class based on nominal plate
dimensions. For example, consider ADEN numbers 1 – 5 for which the identifier is PUMD. The
PUMD identifier refers to Pu-U-Mo plates manufactured by Dow for ZPPR and ANL-E. Each of
these plates has nominal dimensions of 0.25 x 2.0 x L inches where L can be 4, 5, 6, 7 or 8 inches.
As will be evident in Figure 6.2, ADEN number 1 is a 0.25 x 2.0 x 4.0 inch PUMD plate, ADEN
number 2 is a 0.25 x 2.0 x 5.0 inch PUMD plate, ADEN number 3 is a 0.25 x 2.0 x 6.0 inch PUMD
plate, etc. PUMN refers to similar Pu-U-Mo plates manufactured by NUMEC (ADEN numbers
91 – 95) for ZPPR and ANL-E.
Likewise, NA refers to a particular set of sodium plates. The cans were made by D. K. Aerospace.
The empty cans were filled with sodium and sealed by Central Shops at Argonne. NAHY and
NALT refer to other sets of sodium plates manufactured at different times.
For practical purposes, the ADEN identifier identifies the material type or composition, and the
ADEN number identifies a particular plate size for that material.
In some cases, the ADEN identifier refers to groups of plates obtained from the same supplier at
the same time. For example, there are several different ADEN identifiers for stainless steel plates
because these plates were obtained from different suppliers at different times.
6.3.3 Nominal Plate Dimensions
Columns 3 – 5 (C, D, E) in Figure 6.2 list the nominal exterior dimensions of each plate in inches.
To clarify the interpretation of dimensions, consider ADEN 1, a 0.25 x 2.0 x 4.0 inch PUMD plate.
The X-dimension corresponds to the width of this plate, 0.25 inch. The Y-dimension corresponds
to the height of this plate, 2.0 inch. The Z-dimension corresponds to length of this plate, 4.0 inch.
To begin, there were many thousands of small plates in each experimental ZPR/ZPPR assembly,
and each assembly was very large relative to the dimensions of a plate. Thus the effects of
uncertainties in the exact dimensions of individual plates were always assumed to be negligible
compared to other uncertainties, particularly uncertainties in composition and mass. With that
stated, there are several important qualifications to the term “nominal exterior dimensions” to
discuss:
 1. For an unclad plate, the listed dimensions are the nominal external dimensions of the plate.
 For a clad plate, the listed dimensions are the nominal external dimensions of the clad. The
 dimensions of the meat (Pu-U-Mo, sodium, etc.) inside the cladding are slightly smaller
 than the external dimensions of the clad.
 2. The listed dimensions are nominal dimensions. The true dimensions of each individual
 plate of each plate group (ADEN identifier and number) could differ from the average
 dimensions of the plate group because normal manufacturing tolerances and uncertainties
 in calibration standards introduce small variations between individual plates of the same
 type and same nominal size.
 3. The listed nominal dimensions were convenient values for constructing models and

 124

 analysis. In reality, plate designs and purchase specifications may have intentionally
 specified dimensions that were slightly smaller than the listed nominal dimensions. The
 nominal width of a plate loading in a standard drawer was two inches. The actual interior
 width of a standard drawer was slightly greater than two inches to facilitate drawer
 loading/unloading operations and to minimize the potential for plate damage during those
 operations. Oversize plates would make drawer loading difficult and might make it
 impossible to load the nominal two-inch plate loading in the drawers. Specifying plate
 dimensions slightly smaller than nominal dimensions in purchase orders would facilitate
 plate loading/unloading operations. At the same time, it would be undesirable for the plates
 to be very much smaller than the nominal values because too much free space in a drawer
 allows plates to change positions when the drawer is moved or loaded into a matrix tube.
 This plate shifting introduces an additional uncertainty into reactivity measurements. In
 most cases, the true average dimensions of a plate group are unknown, and only the
 nominal dimensions are available today. The exceptions to this statement for some clad
 plates are discussed below.
 4. The listed nominal X-, Y- and Z-dimensions for the clad uranium plates with ADEN
       identifiers U93A, U93B, U93C, U93D, U93E, U93F, U93G, U93H and U93I (ADEN
 numbers 280 – 288) are only approximate because they are the nominal dimensions of the
 HEU meat. The original HEU plates used at ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were metal plates
 coated with Kel-F. After ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were shut down, the coated HEU plates were
 shipped to ZPPR. The ZPPR staff put the HEU plates into stainless steel cans to make clad
 HEU plates. The nominal lengths of the original HEU metal plates were 1 , 2 and 3 inches,
 the nominal thicknesses of the HEU metal plates were 0.0625 inch and 0.125 inch, and the
 nominal height of the HEU metal plates was 2.0 inch. Two or more HEU metal plates were
 placed in a steel can to make one clad HEU plate. The steel can increased the external
 dimensions from the base HEU plate. Table 6.1 shows the nominal dimensions of the HEU
 metal and the external dimensions of the can for the clad HEU plates.

6.3.4 Total Weight
Column 6 (F) in Figure 6.2 shows the nominal average total weight for each plate type. The
software used by the ZPPR staff did not use this entry, so it is not necessarily accurate for all
materials in the ADEN library. A more accurate total weight for a plate type (ADEN number) can
be obtained by summing the entries for the masses of the individual elements or isotopes in the
following 63 columns (columns G – BQ) some of which are partially viewable in Figure 6.2. All
masses in the ADEN library are in gram units.
6.3.5 Individual Plate Component Masses
Columns 7 – 69 (G – BQ) in Figure 6.2 show the masses of the individual components of the plate.
The masses of the individual components listed in the ADEN_Library worksheet are the best
estimates of those masses that are available today.
Columns 7 – 69 (G – BQ) in row 7 of the ADEN_Library worksheet show the element or isotope
identifiers for the individual columns. The ZPR/ZPPR software used two character identifiers for
all isotopes and elements. The entries in columns 7 – 69 (G – BQ) of row 7 are ordered by atomic
mass.
For elements in which the chemical symbol consists of a single character such as H, C, F, P or S,
the ZPPR software used a hyphen as the second character. For example, H is listed as H-, C is
listed as C-, F is listed as F-, etc. L6 is Li-6, L7 is Li-7, B0 is B-10, B1 is B-11, E1 is Eu-151 and
E3 is Eu-153.

 126

Actinides were designated by the first letter of the chemical symbol and the last digit of the atomic
weight. U is uranium, T is thorium, P is plutonium, and A is americium. For example, U5 is U-
235 and P0 is Pu-240.
Column S, not shown, lists the component as LIP, and column AI lists the component as HIP.
Note that the original identifiers were LI and HI. LI and HI were changed to LIP and HIP,
respectively, for clarity. LIP stands for light impurities, and HIP stands for heavy impurities. The
light and heavy impurity entries are non-zero only for a limited number of plate types, and those
entries only list the impurity masses without specifying the impurity elements.
There is no further information regarding the light and heavy impurities. The ZPR/ZPPR staff
ignored these impurities because it was believed that the impurities would have no significant
effect in the hard spectrum of ZPR/ZPPR assemblies.
There is no direct impurity information available for most plate types in the ADEN library. In
some cases, it may be possible to obtain at least an estimate of the reactivity worth of the impurities
in a plate type. A reasonable approach is to assume that the impurities in the materials used in the
ZPR/ZPPR facilities are approximately the same as the impurities in materials that are available
commercially today. If there is a reactor grade product and a standard product, it seems likely that
the reactor grade product would be closer to the material used in the ZPR/ZPPR facilities.
The masses in the ADEN library are listed with five decimal places. Many entries in the ADEN
library end in 99, 999, 01 or 001. In most cases, these are probably artifacts of rounding that
occurred when the format of the ADEN library was converted to the present form by the ZPPR
staff in the 1990s.
For an unclad plate, the masses in the ADEN_Library worksheet are the masses of individual
components of the plate. For a clad plate, the masses shown on the worksheet are the combined
masses for the meat and clad. For example, for a sodium plate, The C entry (carbon) includes the
C impurity in the sodium and the C from the stainless steel clad. The cladding library discussed
later provides the information required to separate the ADEN library entries for clad plates into
the masses of meat components and the masses of clad components.
The masses for the matrix tube (MTU/ADEN 226, 227 and MTUA/ADEN 583, 584) are masses
per inch of length. Likewise, the masses for the bottom and sides of any drawer are masses per
inch of length (ADEN identifiers DAB, DAF, DSB and DSF with a length of Z = 1.0 inch). The
masses for a PSR control rod guide tube (GTS/ADEN 102) also are masses per inch of length.
6.3.6 Text Version of ADEN Library
As stated, the text version of the ADEN library, an excerpt of which is shown in Figure 6.1,
contains the same material as the spreadsheet version, but the organization or arrangement differs.
The entry for each material consists of 13 lines. These lines are:
 1. Line 1:
 a. Columns 1 – 6 list the ADEN number for the material (Column A of spreadsheet).
 b. Columns 7 – 10 list the ADEN identifier (PUMN, NA, UOD8, etc.) (Column B of
 spreadsheet).
 c. Columns 11 – 80 describe the plate dimensions, material/type, characteristics, etc.

 2. Line 2:
 a. Lists the nominal external X-, Y- and Z-dimensions of the plate, respectively
 (Columns C, D and E of the spreadsheet).
      3. Lines 3 – 12:

 through line 11 list the individual component masses for all elements or isotopes
 between hydrogen and Am-242 (Columns F – BP of the spreadsheet). The first
 entry on line 12 is the Am-243 component mass and the last six entries on line 12
 are all zeroes and are not used.
 4. Line 13:

 6.1) is the number of plates of that type in the ZPPR inventory. The purpose of the
 first entry and third entry on line 13 is not known. They may have been used for
 some purpose in the software used at ZPPR, but at present they can be ignored.
6.4 Cladding Library
The Pu-U-Mo plates, Pu-Al plates, clad HEU plates, sodium plates, sodium carbonate plates,
lithium plates, some boron carbide plates and various other plates were clad in stainless steel. The
cladding library provides the information needed to define the cladding on clad plates and to
separate the masses of cladding components from the masses of meat components for elements
that are present in the cladding and the meat. Cladding and can will be used interchangeably in
the remainder of Section 6.4 because the cladding was a can that isolated the contents, i.e., the
meat, from the outside environment, prevented corrosion or oxidation of the meat, and protected
the outside environment from contamination by the meat. The front end cap of a clad plate could
be clearly distinguished from the back end cap of that plate.
In most cases, a clad plate is modeled as seven rectangular parallelepipeds (RPPs). Separate RPPs
model the front end cap, back end cap, top of the can, bottom of the can, left sidewall of the can,
right sidewall of the can and meat in the can. The top and bottom of the can have the same
dimensions, and the left sidewall and right sidewall of the can have the same dimensions. The
front end cap and back end cap do not always have the same dimensions because different types
of plates had different designs. Two examples of plates in which the front and back end caps have
different dimensions are the NA (sodium) plates and the VDC (void can) plates.
There are a few plate types that do not consist of seven RPPs. The VDC can (void can or sodium
void can) is an empty can used to simulate sodium voiding. The VDC can consists of seven RPPs.
The VDCG can is a sodium void can with open ends, so there are no end caps. A VDFS can is a
frame with open sides, so there are no sidewalls.
The cladding library includes three other types of components that do not consist of seven RPPs.
First, a matrix tube (MTU/ADEN 226, 227 and MTUA/ADEN 583, 584) for ZPR or ZPPR consists
of an open-ended, empty rectangular stainless steel tube into which drawers containing plates were
loaded. The first inch of a matrix tube had notches to accommodate tabs on the sides of the drawer
fronts. The notch/tab system provided consistent, uniform positioning for drawers in matrix tubes.
Consequently, the ADEN library and cladding library have separate entries for the first inch of a
matrix tube and the remainder of the matrix tube.

 128

Second, the cladding library contains an entry for the bottom and sides of each drawer type (ADEN
identifiers DAB, DAF, DSB and DSF with a length of Z = 1.0 inch). A drawer consists of a front
plate, back plate, bottom, left side and right side. The front plate and back plate have entries in
the ADEN library and are represented as standard RPPs. The bottom and sides have a single,
combined entry in the ADEN library that lists the combined mass for the bottom and sides of the
drawer per inch of length. The cladding library entry for the bottom and sides of the drawer
provided the information required to partition the ADEN library masses into the separate masses
of the drawer bottom and drawer sides.
Third, a PSR control rod guide tube (GTS/ADEN 102) also consists of an open-ended rectangular
stainless steel tube that served as a guide tube for the PSR control blade.
Representing a clad plate by seven RPPs is an approximation and simplification. The ends and/or
edges of the real can were rounded in some cases. In some cases, the edges of the real meat also
were rounded. For Pu-U-Mo plates, Pu-Al plates and probably clad HEU plates, there was a small
gap between the meat and the interior of the can to allow for thermal expansion of the meat in
accident scenarios. End cap designs were more complex structures than simple RPPs in some
cases. The historical records preservation program that supported scanning of the ZPR/ZPPR
records stored at ZPPR terminated before all available materials could be scanned, and the scanned
records do not include any drawings of plate designs. There may be boxes at INL containing those
drawings. However, many records were discarded or lost after ZPPR shut down, so it is possible
that those drawings no longer exist.
If those drawings still exist and could be located, it might be possible to incorporate the design
information into more accurate representations of the plates. That effort might not be worthwhile
for several reasons. First, the effort required to make improved clad plate models would not be
insignificant. Second, there are many clad plates (Pu-U-Mo, HEU, sodium, sodium carbonate,
etc.) in ZPPR assemblies. The additional tracking and cross-section lookup in small, complex
geometries in the clad plates would significantly increase the computer time required to compute
the resulting as-built models. Third, compared to the fundamental uncertainties in material
compositions such as 235U enrichment in depleted uranium plates and the geometry uncertainties
(interface gap, matrix pitch, etc.), any small improvements in the modeling of clad plates is likely
to be a second or third order effect.
The ZPPR staff compiled the cladding library based on plate design drawings and other available
information. The geometries of the cladding components and the meat have been simplified as
discussed above, but the actual constituent masses associated with the end caps, top of the can,
bottom of the can, sidewalls of the can and meat are preserved in the ADEN library and cladding
library.
6.4.1 Clad Dimensions
The Clad_Dimensions worksheet, an excerpt of which is shown in Figure 6.3, contains the
information required to create the RPPs defining the clad and meat.

Column B lists the ADEN identifier (see Section 6.3.2) for each entry in the cladding library.
Column C lists the length (Z-direction) of the front end cap of the can in inches. Column D lists

6.4.1.1 Standard Cans
Most entries in the cladding library are for standard cans. The following is an example for
determining the dimensions of plate components of a standard can. Consider row 14 of the
Clad_Dimensions worksheet. The ADEN number is 15, and the ADEN identifier is NA. Looking
at Figure 6.3, this corresponds to a 0.5 x 2.0 x 8.0 inch canned sodium plate.
From Figure 6.3, the length of the front end cap is 0.032 inch. The dimensions of the RPP defining
the front end cap are 0.5 x 2.0 x 0.032 inch.
The length of the back end cap is 0.100 inch.The dimensions of the RPP defining the back end cap
are 0.5 x 2.0 x 0.100 inch.
The length of each sidewall and of the top and bottom is 7.868 inch (8.0 – 0.032 – 0.100). The
thickness of each sidewall is 0.019 inch; the thicknesses of the top and bottom are each 0.0175
inch.

6.4.1.2
The dimensions the RPP defining a sidewall of the can are 0.019 x 1.965 x 7.868 inch (2.0 – 0.0175

The dimensions of the RPP defining the top or bottom is 0.5 x 0.0175 x 7.868 inch.
