6.4.1.3 Non-Standard Cans
As stated, a can with ADEN identifier VDCG has a top, bottom and sidewalls, but it does not have
a front end cap or back end cap. A can with ADEN identifier VDFS has a front, back, top and
bottom, but it does not have sidewalls. A matrix tube (MTU or MTUA) or a PSR guide tube (GTS)
has a top, bottom and sides, but it does not have a front or back.
The front plate and back plate of a drawer have listings in the ADEN library and are treated as
standard plates. The drawer entry in the cladding library only applies to the bottom and sides of
the drawer. Figure 2.5 shows a typical ZPR or ZPPR drawer. The plates are elevated above the
bottom of the drawer in Figure 2.5.
Different assembly programs simulated cores of different sizes and designs, so different core
simulations could require different steel volume fractions to simulate cladding, duct walls and
other steel structural materials in a fast reactor fuel assembly, radial blanket assembly or radial
reflector. The steel required for a core simulation was supplied by the matrix tubes, drawers, plate
cladding and steel plates. In addition, new drawers were occasionally obtained for new programs.
Consequently, ZPR/ZPPR maintained inventories of drawers of different lengths and slightly
different designs. In some cases, the front plates, back plates or sides of drawers were perforated
as shown in Figure 2.4 and Figure 2.5.
In addition to ordinary drawers with nominal interior widths of 2.0 inches, there were two special
types of drawers used for reactor control purposes. A dual-purpose (DP) control rod drawer was
a drawer attached to a rod drive that could drive the dual purpose drawer into or out of the core.
A dual purpose drawer was loaded with standard core materials, so motion of the dual purpose
drawer moved its contents toward or away from the core center to increase or decrease reactivity.
A poison safety rod (PSR) drawer was a drawer with a nominal width of 1.5 inches. The other 0.5
inches in the matrix tube was occupied by a stainless steel guide tube (ADEN number 102). This
guide tube housed a stainless steel-clad boron carbide blade (ADEN number 221) attached to a rod
drive that moved the boron carbide blade into or out of the core in the conventional manner for
control rods.
The entries highlighted in yellow in Figure 6.3 with a value of 0.00000 on the Clad_Dimensions
worksheet indicate the components that are not present for a plate type or ADEN number/ADEN
identifier. For example, a void frame (ADEN identifier VDFS) had a front, back, top and bottom,
but it did not have any sidewalls.

 131

6.4.2 Clad Mass
The Clad_Mass worksheet, an excerpt of which is provided in Figure 6.4, contains the details on
how to calculate the compositions of the front end cap, back end cap, top, bottom and sidewalls of
each canned or clad item.

 Figure 6.4. Clad Mass Spreadsheet.

 132

Column A lists the ADEN number (see Section 6.3.1) for each entry in the cladding library.
Column B lists the ADEN identifier (see Section 6.3.2) for each entry in the cladding library.
Column C lists the elements in the clad/can. There are multiple entries for each plate type because
there are multiple elements in the clad/can. Column D is the fraction of the element mass in the
ADEN_Library entry in the top and bottom (combined) of the clad/can. Column E is the fraction
of the element mass in the ADEN_Library entry in the left and right sidewalls (combined) of the
clad/can. Column F is the fraction of the element mass in the ADEN_Library entry in the front
end cap of the clad/can. Column G is the fraction of the element mass in the ADEN_Library entry
in the back end cap of the clad/can.
The sum of the four entries in columns D – G will be 1.0 for most elements because the element
is only present in the can. Note that the actual sum may be in the range 0.99999 – 1.00001 due to
roundoff.
For an element that appears in both the can and the meat, the sum of the four entries will be less
than 1.0 because the four entries do not account for the mass of the element in the meat. The NA
sodium plates provide an example. Carbon is an impurity in the sodium and a trace element in the
stainless steel can, so the sum of the four entries for carbon is significantly smaller than 1.0 for
NA sodium plates which is observable in Figure 6.4 on row 12.
For example, the ADEN_Library worksheet shows (not shown in Figure 6.2) that the can for
ADEN 6 (NA) contains 24.94099 g of Fe. Based on the FE entries (row 4 in Figure 6.4) for ADEN
6 (NA) in the Clad_Mass worksheet, the Fe content of the clad components for this NA plate are:
    a) 24.94099 x 0.09718 = 2.42377 g for the top and bottom,
    b) 24.94099 x 0.78909 = 19.68069 g for the sidewalls,
    c) 24.94099 x 0.05346 = 1.33335 g for the front end cap, and
    d) 24.94099 x 0.06026 = 1.50294 g for the back end cap.

The dimensions and volume of the meat are preserved, and the external dimensions of the can are
preserved. The interior dimensions of the RPPs defining the front end cap, back end cap, sidewalls,
top and bottom are increased slightly in some plate types to eliminate any free space inside the
plate.
This issue is more important for clad fuel plates than for clad non-fuel plates. The clad fuel plates
are Pu-Al plates, Pu-U-Mo plates and clad HEU plates. The clad HEU plates consist of existing
HEU metal plates that were placed in cans at ZPPR. For the Pu-Al and Pu-U-Mo plates, the fuel
meat was cast and machined to dimensions slightly smaller than the interior dimensions of the
cans. The free space surrounding the fuel meat allowed for thermal expansion of the fuel meat
under accident conditions. In the case of the Pu-Al and Pu-U-Mo plates, the free space also
allowed for normal thermal expansion of the meat due to decay heating of the Pu-Al or Pu-U-Mo
alloy. For the sodium plates, it seems likely that molten sodium was poured into the empty cans.
There are several important points to note about the various types of canned plates.
 1. The dimensions, masses and mass fractions listed in the ADEN library and cladding library
 for each plate type are average values. There were slight differences between individual

 133

 plates due to normal manufacturing processes. However, many hundreds or, more likely,
 thousands of each plate type were used in any ZPR/ZPPR assembly, so the small variations
 between individual plates are negligible for practical purposes.
 2. The nominal external dimensions of the clad fuel plates and clad non-fuel plates are
 preserved subject to the qualification discussed in Section 6.3 and Table 6.1 for the canned
 HEU plates.
 3. The nominal dimensions of the materials inside of the cans are preserved.
 4. The average masses of the materials inside of the cans and the average masses of the front
 end cap, back end cap, sidewalls, top and bottom in each plate type are preserved.
 5. Representing the front end cap, back end cap, left sidewall, right sidewall, top and bottom
 of a clad plate as six RPPs is an approximation of a more complex structure. Designs of
 end caps were more complex than simple RPPs in many cases, and actual surfaces were
 rounded in some cases. The interior dimensions of the RPPs representing the clad structure
 in the cladding library eliminate any free space surrounding the meat in the plates. As a
 result of these approximations, the mass of the meat and the mass of each clad component
 are preserved, but the effective densities of the clad components will not necessarily match
 the physical density of stainless steel.
 6. The effective densities of drawer components will not necessarily match the physical
 density of stainless steel due to perforations and other design features of the drawers. The
 mass of the drawer front plate includes the mass of any attached tabs although the tabs are
 not explicitly modeled. The back plate of a drawer may also incorporate the mass of special
 design features such as a small handle that allow back drawers to be removed from the
 back of a matrix tube. The masses of the bottom and sides of a drawer include the effects
 of any perforations in the bottom or sides of the drawer.
6.4.3 Text Version of Cladding Library
The text version of the cladding library, an excerpt of which is shown in Figure 6.5, contains the
same material as the spreadsheet version, but the organization or arrangement differs. The entry
for each material consists of 18 lines. These lines are:

 Figure 6.5. Excerpt of the Cladding Library File.
Line 1 lists the ADEN number for the clad plate or other item.
The five entries on line 2 list a) the length of the front end cap (Z-direction), b) length of the back
end cap (Z-direction), c) thickness of each sidewall (X-direction), d) thickness of the top (Y-

Line 3 lists the chemical symbols for the elements that are present in the cladding for the plate
corresponding to the ADEN number in line 1. Each element is represented by two characters. For
an element whose chemical symbol consists of one character such as hydrogen or carbon, the
second character is a hyphen, e.g., H- or C-. For an element whose chemical symbol consists of
two characters such as iron or chromium, the entry would be the standard chemical symbol, e.g.,
FE or CR. LP and HP designate light impurities and heavy impurities, respectively.
Lines 4 through 18 list the fraction of the mass of each element identified in Line 3 in the can. The
four entries on each line are the fraction in the top and bottom (combined), the fraction in the left
and right sidewalls (combined), the fraction in the front end cap, and the fraction in the back end
cap, respectively. This is identical to the information provided in Figure 6.4. There is one line for
each element in line 3 ordered according to the order of the elements in line 3. There are up to 15
lines for each clad plate or other item. If there are less than 15 elements listed in Line 3, a few
rows in Lines 4 – 18 will contain all zeroes. In Figure 6.5, there are 13 elements in Line 3 for
ADEN number 6, so lines 17 and 18 all contain zeroes. Lines 35 and 36 are similarly all zero for
ADEN 7 as there are only 13 elements listed.

6.5 ADEN Library and Drawer Master Definition
Section 3 discussed drawer masters. Figure 6.6 shows drawer master 15-0-101 which was a
standard drawer master in ZPPR-15A. Note that the plate identifiers are similar to the previous
ADEN names. Figure 6.6 and all other drawer master figures show the contents of a drawer with
two exceptions:
First, a small spring was placed at the back of each drawer to push all of the plates toward the front
of the drawer. This spring is not typically shown in drawer master figures, but it was present at
the back of each drawer. The ADEN identifier for a spring is SPR. The ADEN number for the
spring placed behind the plates in a standard 2.0-inch wide drawer is 108. The ADEN number for
the spring placed behind the plates in a narrow 1.5-inch wide PSR drawer is 555. The ADEN
number for the PSR guide tube placed next to a narrow PSR drawer in a matrix tube is 102, and
the ADEN number for the stainless steel-clad boron carbide blade in the PSR guide tube is 221.
The second exception is experimental equipment. Drawer master figures leave blank space where
experimental equipment is located and do not attempt to define or describe the experimental
equipment.

                             Figure 6.6. ZPPR-15 Drawer Master 15-0-101.
In addition to the spring, the drawer master figures do not show the actual drawer. The length of
the drawer is determined by the length of the drawer contents and by the inventory of available
drawers in the ADEN library. Figure 6.6 shows that the total length of the drawer contents is 36
inches, so the correct drawer is the 36.252 inch drawer in the ADEN library.

 136

The ADEN library and cladding library contain descriptions of most of the drawers used in the
four facilities. However, a few special drawers were not included in these libraries because they
were rarely used or were only used for special equipment. The standard practice is to assume these
special drawers were similar to a normal drawer except for length. The ADEN library entry for
the bottom and sides of a drawer is mass per inch of length, so that value can be applied to longer
or shorter special drawers. If there were only a few special drawers in the core, the effect of this
approximation will be negligible in most cases.
The following relates the ADEN library to the drawer master figures by interpreting Figure 6.6.
The horizontal axes at the top and bottom of the plate loading in Figure 6.6 are marked in half-
inch units and show that the total length of the loading in the drawer is 36.0 inches. The plate
arrangement shows three distinct regions which include the active core (0.0 to 18.0 inches), an
axial blanket region (18.0 to 31 inches), and an axial reflector region (31 to 36 inches). Thus the
active core length is 18.0 inches, the axial blanket length is 13.0 inches, and the axial reflector
within the drawer occupied the last 5.0 inches at the back of the drawer with a small spring behind
the axial reflector section. In addition, the comment at the bottom of the drawer master 15-0-101
states that there was a 2 x 2 x 6 inch stainless steel block loaded into the matrix tube behind the
drawer to complete the axial reflector.
The matrix tubes in the ZPR and ZPPR machines were horizontal. In the ZPR/ZPPR coordinate
system, the Z-axis (the axial direction) is parallel to the axis of the matrix tube or drawer and
extends from left to right, i.e., from 0.0 to 36.0 inches, in Figure 6.6. The origin of coordinates for
this matrix tube is at the interface between the two matrix halves. The positive Z-axis extends
along the matrix tube in half 1, the stationary half of the machine. The Y-axis is normal to the
page, and the positive Y-axis points toward the reader. The positive X-axis extends from 0.0 to
2.0 inches in Figure 6.6 with coordinates increasing from the top of Figure 6.6 to the bottom.
Consider the 0.25 x 2.0 x 8.0 inch NA plate in the top left corner of Figure 6.6. For the normal
plate orientation in a drawer, the 0.25 inch width of the plate is in the X-direction, the 2.0 inch
height is normal to the page in the Y-direction, and the 8.0 inch length is in the Z-direction (the
horizontal direction in Figure 6.6). By convention, a horizontal row of plates parallel to the Z-axis
in Figure 6.6 is referred to as a plate column, and columns are numbered from X = 0.0 at the top
of Figure 6.6.
The vertical axes on the left and right sides of the plate loading are marked in 0.125 inch units and
cover the range 0.0 – 2.0 inches, the nominal width of the plate loading inside the drawer. The
following is an interpretation or explanation of the plate loading information for drawer master 15-
0-101 in Figure 6.6. The height of each plate in Figure 6.6 is 2.0 inches unless otherwise indicated.
An important consideration for loading drawers is that columns of like plates should line up across
the interface between half 1 and half 2. For example, a column of NA (sodium) plates in the
drawer in matrix position 147-58 lines up with a column of NA (sodium) plates in the drawer in
matrix position 247-58. Likewise, columns of fuel plates line up in these drawers, columns of
steel plates line up in these drawers, etc. Columns of the same material or plate type should line
up across the matrix interface. If drawer masters are symmetric, e.g., drawer master 15-0-101
shown in Figure 6.6, this alignment is achieved by default. If drawer masters are not symmetric,
extra care is required when defining drawers for half 2 to achieve this alignment.

 137

6.5.1 Interpretation of Drawer Master 15-0-101
Drawer master 15-0-101 shown in Figure 6.6 defines a normal core drawer in ZPPR-15. Each
plate in the drawer is a rectangle. That rectangle contains the 1 – 4 character ADEN identifier and
a number. The number is the nominal length of the plate. For example, the rectangle in the upper
left corner of Figure 6.6 shows “NA” and “8.” The “NA” is the ADEN identifier and the “8”
indicates that the nominal length of the plate was 8 inches. This plate is a 0.25 x 2.0 x 8.0 inch
NA plate. From Figure 6.2, the ADEN number for this plate can be identified as 10.
If several contiguous plates in a column are identical, the drawer master figure may only show the
ADEN identifier for the first plate, but the figure will show the length for each of the identical
plates. For example, in the axial blanket region (18 to 30 inches in Z) in Figure 6.6, there are 6
identical UD (Uranium Depleted) plates from Z = 18.0 to Z = 30.0 at the top of the figure. The
first plate shows “UD 2” which designates a 0.125 x 2.0 x 2.0 inch UD plate. The following five
plates also are 0.125 x 2.0 x 2.0 inch UD plates, but the figure only shows the “2” indicating the
plate length.

6.5.1.3 Axial Reflector Region of Drawer Master 15-0-101
The axial reflector region consists of columns of plates in the 31.0 – 36.0 inch axial range in the

In some drawer masters, particularly drawer masters for detector drawers, the axial reflector region
consists of multiple columns of plates. In drawer master 15-0-101, the axial reflector region in the

Although it is not shown in the drawer master figure, there is a small retainer spring (SPR, ADEN
108) behind the axial reflector. This spring is modeled as a 2.0 x 2.0 x 0.0625 inch steel plate.
This is an approximation for a more complex structure.
The comment at the bottom of the drawer master figure indicates that there was a 2.0 x 2.0 x 6.0
inch stainless steel block behind the drawer. This block was loaded directly into the matrix tube
without any drawer.
6.5.2 Interpretation of Drawer Master 15-0-701
Approximately 64 drawers in ZPPR-15 contained detectors because these detectors were required
for the modified source multiplication technique that ZPPR experimenters used to measure
reactivity worth for sodium voiding and control rod worth experiments. Figure 6.7 shows a typical
detector drawer used in ZPPR-15. Detector drawers were more complex than ordinary core
drawers because a detector drawer had to accommodate the detector and cables that extended
through the drawer and through the empty matrix tube behind the drawer.
The interpretation of drawer master 15-0-701 is generally similar to the interpretation of drawer
master 15-0-101, but there are a few special features in a detector drawer.
Note the plates in Figure 6.7 that are marked with asterisks and the asterisk at the end of the
comments at the bottom of the drawer master shown in Figure 6.7. Cables connected to the back
of the detector extend through the detector drawer on top of the plates labeled with asterisks. The
cables continue from the back of the detector drawer through the end of the empty matrix tube. It
was necessary to leave space for these cables in the drawer. Placing standard two inch-high plates
behind the detector would interfere with the detector cables. To accommodate the detector cables,
a column of plates behind the detector had a height of one inch. The plates designated “SST 2”
in Figure 6.7 have ADEN number 110. The ADEN 110 SST plates had nominal dimensions of
0.25 x 2.0 x 1.0 inches. The ADEN 110 SST plates behind the detector were rotated 90° such that
their effective dimensions were 0.25 x 1.0 x 2.0 inch. The plates designated “SSTX 8” have
ADEN number 242. The ADEN 242 SSTX plates had nominal dimensions of 0.125 x 1.0 x 8.0
inches. The point is that plates for the cable run behind the detector were chosen because they
have a height of 1.0 inch or were rotated 90° such that they allowed a pathway for the detector
cables. In any detector drawer, it is necessary to allow space behind the detector for the detector
cables.
The drawer master figures do not shown the cables. The cables are not modeled because 1) there
is no information available to model them, 2) they constitute a relatively insignificant amount of

 140

mass in the assembly, and 3) their composition and density would not lead to a significant effect
in the modeling calculations of interest.
Detector drawers were not necessarily placed in symmetric positions in half 1 and half 2 of ZPPR,
so the alignment of columns of plates in half 1 and half 2 that was discussed above may not apply
to the columns of a detector drawer that contain an actual detector.

                             Figure 6.7. ZPPR-15 Drawer Master 15-0-701.

6.5.3 Interpretation of Drawer Master 15-0-801
Figure 6.8 shows drawer master 15-0-801, a typical PSR control drawer used in ZPPR-15.

 144

                             Figure 6.8. ZPPR-15 Drawer Master 15-0-801.
The interpretation of the drawer master for a PSR control drawer such as drawer master 15-0-801
is almost identical to the interpretation of a standard core drawer (see Section 6.5.1). The following
are the special features of a PSR control drawer:

 1. A normal drawer has a nominal interior width of 2.0 inches. A PSR control drawer has a
 nominal interior width of 1.5 inches. For this reason, a PSR control drawer is sometimes
 referred to as a narrow drawer.
 2. The retainer spring at the back of a PSR drawer is smaller than a standard retainer spring.
 The PSR drawer retainer spring (SPR, ADEN 555) has nominal dimensions of 1.5 x 2.0 x
       0.0625 inches.
 3. A PSR drawer leaves approximately 0.5 inches of free space in a matrix tube. This free
 space is occupied by a PSR guide tube (GTS, ADEN 102).
 4. The control rod blade in a PSR guide tube has the ADEN identifier BCPR and ADEN
 number 221. The control blade was a long, thin stainless steel can filled with boron carbide.
 The control blade has entries in the cladding library (Clad_Dimensions worksheet and
 Clad_Mass worksheet). There are entries for the front end cap, sides, top and bottom of
 the control blade can. There is no entry for the back end cap of the control blade can
 because the PSR blade was rarely modeled and because models that included the PSR blade
 terminated before the end of the blade.
 5. The PSR guide tube (GTS, ADEN 102) does not extend to the front end of the matrix tube,

 145

 i.e., the interface between halves. The front of the guide tube is 0.402 inch from the front
 of the matrix tube.

 146

7 EXPERIMENTS AND MEASUREMENTS
Many types of measurements and experiments were conducted at ZPR-3, ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and
ZPPR. Criticality was measured in every assembly program on every machine. The range of other
measurements performed varied over time, between machines and between assembly programs.
It is not practical to cover every type of measurement performed in a ZPR/ZPPR assembly between
ZPR-3/1 in 1955 and ZPPR-21 in 1990. Some of the early measurements and early configurations
are no longer of interest for reactor design or modeling purposes. For example, the configurations
in ZPR-3/6 that simulated slabs, cylinders and spheres did so because modeling software in the
1950s was more or less limited to slabs, cylinders and spheres. Those limitations are no longer
relevant. Likewise, better equipment, better experimental techniques, and a broader, more
complete, plate inventory make some of the early approximations (such as using perforated
aluminum plates to represent sodium) obsolete for reactor design purposes.
In some cases, available documents do not provide sufficient detail for a meaningful discussion of
the experiments covered in those documents. In other cases, an experiment was a one-of-kind
measurement to address a very specific question that may no longer be relevant to fast reactor
design.
The classes of experiments discussed here are the classes of experiments that were performed on
a regular basis to support fast reactor development and for which sufficient detail is available in
existing documents.
For discussion of reactivity measurements below, “worth” generally refers to “reactivity worth.”
Any exceptions will be noted when they occur.
In order to assess the agreement between an experimental measurement and the calculated value
obtained from a high fidelity model of the experiment, it is necessary to perform an uncertainty
analysis for the experimental measurement. Much of the discussion in Section 7 is related to
uncertainty analysis for the various types of measurements performed in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies.
It is important to recognize that the uncertainties reported with published experimental values are
not necessarily the total uncertainties associated with the measurements. Uncertainties reported
with published ZPR/ZPPR experimental values are frequently just the statistical uncertainties
associated with the measurements, e.g., statistics related to detector count rates. There may be
other sources of uncertainty that contribute more to the total uncertainty for a measurement than
the statistical uncertainty in the measured value.
There is a set of uncertainties related to the actual measurement. Measurement uncertainties
include parameters such as temperature, control rod position, measurement equipment calibration
and statistical uncertainty in detector count rates. Even if the experimental configuration can be
modeled to an arbitrary degree of accuracy, uncertainties related to the measured value(s) would
remain.
There is a separate set of uncertainties related to the configuration in which the measurement was
performed. This set of uncertainties relates to how accurately the experimental configuration is
known and can be modeled for analysis purposes. For example, there are uncertainties associated
with the dimensions, masses and compositions of the plates, drawers and matix tubes. There may

 147

be similar uncertainties associated with some types of equipment used in the experiment. These
uncertainties reflect the limitations in the knowledge of the precise configuration that was
measured in the experiment.
The total uncertainty associated with a measured value is the combination of the uncertainty in the
measured value and the uncertainty in the exact configuration that was measured. For some types
of measurements, e.g., criticality, uncertainties related to the exact configuration that was
measured are the dominant components of the total uncertainty.
High fidelity as-built Monte Carlo and deterministic models of ZPR/ZPPR assemblies can be
created. Both Monte Carlo models and deterministic models are useful in uncertainty analysis,
but there are uncertainties for which a Monte Carlo model is better than a deterministic model and
vice versa.
The current state of the art for deterministic modeling assumes a “drawer homogenized”
methodology where the contents of a matrix tube (lattice part) and the drawer loaded into it over a
given axial range are homogenized together [34]. Doing detailed geometry representations has
been attempted, but the cross section generation procedure proved to be unreliable and grossly
inaccurate compared with the “drawer homogenized” methodology. To facilitate the analysis
work, a program name BuildZPRmodel [34] was built to convert the as-built Monte Carlo models
of ZPR/ZPPR assemblies into a drawer homogenized deterministic model. Input to that program
is the composition specification for each part of the model (e.g. matrix tube, drawer front, plate
cladding, plate meat, etc… derived from the ADEN library) along with the location and geometry
of the part. That input is generated by processing the Monte Carlo model. The output from
BuildZPRmodel is the set of input needed to generate a multi-group library [14] and the
deterministic model itself [15].
Given the BuildZPRmodel program to generate a deterministic model, the process of generating
perturbed deterministic models for uncertainties can be automated. The following is a general
description of the deterministic modeling process used for recent uncertainty analyses at Argonne.
For compositional uncertainties, the compositional input to the BuildZPRmodel program is
modified by another program [34] to include perturbed compositions associated with the known
or estimated uncertainties for each plate or other component (e.g. drawer front, matrix tube, etc…)
used in the loading of interest. Running BuildZPRmodel on each perturbed composition file will
generate a deterministic model different from the base model. Obtaining the base k eff value and the
perturbed state keff value for all perturbations of interest using the steady state neutronics code [15]
will give the associated worth of each perturbation. Regenerating the cross section library was
found to be impactful for some perturbations, but not for most. An assessment of space-angle-
energy impacts of the deterministic methodology was performed, and the best estimate possible
(the highest space-angle-energy result attempted) of the true uncertainty was determined for each
perturbation of interest. Only a few perturbations were impacted by the energy discretization of
the library and none were found to have any strong dependence on the space-angle approximation.
In the uncertainty analysis discussion in follow-on sections, the source of the uncertainty
calculation is based upon the deterministic model described above when the values being reported
are less than ~1 pcm (e.g. 1.35 pcm). In many cases it is preferred to use Monte Carlo, but the
computational expense and general inability to obtain answers for near zero reactivity worths
necessitates a deterministic pathway for some uncertainties. For the purposes of uncertainty

 148

analysis, there is a difference between a Monte Carlo model and a deterministic model with respect
to correlation in the calculation of the reactivity worth associated with an uncertainty.
Suppose there is a reference model, R0, and N perturbed models (P1, P2, . . ., PN) and that the
analyst computes the reactivity difference between the reference model and each perturbed model.
Each perturbed model, Pi, will have a separate Monte Carlo keff, ki, and statistical uncertainty, σi.
Model R0 will have a keff, k0, and statistical uncertainty, σ0. If the same values of k0 and σ0 are
used to compute all of the reactivity differences and associated uncertainties for the N perturbed
cases, that will introduce a correlation between all of the reactivity differences and a correlation
between all of the associated uncertainties. The correlation may be small, but it will be present.
To eliminate the correlation between keff and σ for model R0 and the corresponding quantities for
each perturbed case, it is necessary to recompute the reference case, R 0, with a different seed
random number for each perturbed case such that the reference case for each perturbed case uses
a different random number chain or sequence. Consequently, there will be N calculations of the
reference case with different seed random numbers, N values of the reference k eff, k0i, and N values
of the statistical uncertainty, σ0i. The reactivity worth for each perturbed case will be based on a
separate calculation of the reference case, R, with a different seed random number, and,
consequently, independent estimates of keff and σ for the reference case. In other words, the
reactivity worth of each perturbed case P i will be based on separate values of k0i, σ0i, ki and σi.
This correlation issue is avoided in deterministic calculations of reactivity worths. If it is possible
to construct a high fidelity as-built deterministic model and an accurate cross section library, a
deterministic model is likely to be better for calculation of composition uncertainties, particularly
in cases where there are many composition uncertainties and/or composition uncertainties of low
reactivity worth. On the other hand, it may be difficult or impossible to compute some of the
uncertainties and biases related to the geometrical configuration with a deterministic model.
7.1 Criticality Measurements
Many ZPR/ZPPR assemblies simulated an operating reactor, an upset condition in an operating
reactor or, occasionally, an accident configuration. Examples in the upset condition and accident
categories are the sodium void worth measurements that were performed in many ZPR/ZPPR
assemblies, the severe hypothetical fast reactor accident scenarios simulated in ZPR-9/32, and the
space reactor launch accident simulations in ZPPR-20D and ZPPR-20E. Other ZPR/ZPPR
assemblies such as ZPR-6/9, ZPR-6/10 and ZPR-9/36 were built to obtain basic physics data for
fast reactors in general rather than to simulate a fast reactor design.
L. G. LeSage [7] provides an overview and summary of all assembly programs performed in ZPR-
6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR. Reference 7 does not include any details for ZPR-3 assemblies.
In all ZPR/ZPPR assemblies, criticality or the degree of subcriticality was a fundamental
measurement. In addition, the reference critical configuration was the starting point for many
other types of measurements. Note that ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 always reported measured
excess reactivities in inhours (Ih); ZPPR reported measured excess reactivities in cents. For
reactivity measurements reported in Ih, the experimenters also reported the conversion factor
between Ih and Δk/k. For reactivity measurements reported in cents, the experimenters reported
βeff, which is required to convert between cents and Δk/k or pcm. For the purposes of comparison

 149

in the remainder of this section between measurements and calculations, either the measured
reactivities were converted to the calculational units (Δk/k or pcm), or the calculated reactivities
were converted to to the measurement units.
7.1.1 Criticality Measurement Experimental Technique
The first step in any assembly program was experiment planning. The ZPR/ZPPR staff developed
a planned sequence of experimental measurements and then reconciled that plan with available
resources (budget, schedule, manpower, equipment, materials inventory, etc.).
The next step was to plan the core configuration based on the facility plate inventory, available
analytical tools such as methods, codes and nuclear data libraries, and the accumulated data and
experience from previous assemblies. Obviously, this phase of planning became much more
detailed as operating experience accumulated and available methods, codes and nuclear data
libraries evolved between ZPR-3/1 in 1955 and ZPPR-21, the last ZPPR assembly, in 1990.
Drawers were loaded in the reactor workroom, transported to the reactor cell, and placed in the
designated matrix tubes. The criticality measurement experimental technique consisted of a
standard approach-to-critical followed by establishment of the reference critical configuration.
The first physical step in the approach-to-critical was to load the radial blanket drawers and/or
radial reflector drawers in the matrix locations determined during planning of the core
configuration.
In some cases, the radial blanket and radial reflector were combined. For example, the radial
blanket in some assemblies consisted of solid depleted uranium blocks, e.g., 2 x 2 x 4 inch blocks.
There was no separate reflector in such cases because the thick depleted uranium blanket provided
adequate reflection and effectively isolated the core from outside influences such as room return
(reflection of neutrons back into the reactor from external structures such as the tables, supports
and reactor cell).
If the radial blanket and/or radial radial reflector consisted of large blocks of depleted uranium or
steel, these blocks were loaded directly into the matrix tubes without drawers in some assemblies.
In ZPR-6/7, for example, the radial reflector consisted of 42 inches of depleted uranium blocks
loaded directly into the matrix tubes without drawers. If blocks were loaded directly into matrix
tubes in an assembly, this fact will be noted in the drawer master figures, loading records, logbook
and/or reports for that assembly.
Note that loading records from different facilities and from different times are not consistent with
respect to including loading of radial blanket and radial reflector drawers in the loading records.
In later ZPPR assemblies, for example, the loading records for loading 1 begin with loading of
radial reflector drawers and list every radial blanket drawer and every radial reflector drawer as
it was loaded. On the other hand, in many early ZPR/ZPPR assemblies, all radial blanket and
radial reflector drawers were pre-loaded before the loading records begin. In such cases, the
loading records begin in loading 1 with loading of core drawers.
In cases where the loading records begin with loading of core drawers, it is necessary to consult
other sources to construct a model of the radial blanket and radial reflector. One source of
information regarding the core configuration is the final report documenting the measurements. It
was standard practice to include core maps for reference configurations such as the reference

 150

critical configuration in those reports. The core maps did not show the specific drawer master in
each matrix tube, but they did show the outlines of the core, radial blanket and radial reflector.
Another source of information regarding the core configuration is the loading records. In some
assemblies, particularly ZPPR assemblies, the loading record for a loading includes diagrams of
the core layout or diagrams of the configuration changes, e.g., locations of drawer changes, in that
loading. The diagrams in the loading records generally show the outlines of the core, radial blanket
and radial reflector although those diagrams do not identify the specific drawer master in each
matrix location.
The core maps allow the reader to construct a model of the radial blanket and radial reflector, but
it may be necessary to make some assumptions regarding the drawer master in each radial blanket
or radial reflector location. In cases where there is only one type of drawer master for the region
or where large blocks were loaded directly into the matrix tubes, constructing a model of the region
will be easy. If there are multiple drawer master types for the region, the analyst must make some
assumptions. One reasonable assumption is that the least complex drawer master would be the
most common version and would be the drawer master loaded into locations closest to the core.
Another reasonable assumption is that the drawer master for which the plate inventory contained
the most plates would be the most common version and would be the drawer master loaded into
locations closest to the core. Any reasonable assumption regarding radial blanket and radial
reflector drawers is unlikely to have a large effect on calculations of measured values or on total
uncertainties for the measured values. Interchanging a radial blanket drawer and a core drawer to
measure the edge worth of the fuel or blanket or to smooth the boundary of the core may have a
significant reactivity effect, but the effect of replacing one blanket drawer by another blanket
drawer that differs only in the lengths of the plates is not likely to be significant. This equally true
for reflector drawers.
After the radial blanket and radial reflector drawers were loaded, the next step was to load the pre-
loaded core drawers into the empty matrix tubes in the core locations. A pre-loaded core drawer
was identical to a real core drawer except for the fact that a pre-loaded core drawer contained
dummy fuel plates such as aluminum plates or stainless steel plates in place of real fuel plates.
In each step of the approach-to-critical, a group of pre-loaded drawers was removed from the
matrix, the dummy fuel plates in those drawers were replaced by real fuel plates, the real core
drawers were loaded back into the matrix, and the reactivity of the resulting configuration was
measured. This process proceeded in steps until a critical configuration was achieved.
The pre-loaded drawers were used at ANL-E, and they may have been used at ANL-W as well
because they make sense from an operational standpoint. Having a large number of completely
empty matrix tubes inside the radial blanket would complicate the approach-to-critical because the
resulting axial neutron streaming would make prediction of the next step in the approach more
difficult.
In any event, loading of core drawers in steps continued until a critical configuration was achieved.
Achievement of a critical configuration can be determined from the logbook and/or the loading
records. The first page of a loading record generally indicated the purpose or objective of the
loading change, and the stated objective provides an indication regarding whether criticality has
been achieved. Note that this may not be true for early ZPR-3 assemblies. In the early years of

 151

ZPR-3 operations, the staff were still developing and refining operating practices, so general
statements regarding practices at ANL-E and ZPPR do not always apply to ZPR-3 operations,
particularly early ZPR-3 operations. The reactor logbook also indicates whether a loading or
reactor run was critical.
The initial critical configuration in a ZPR/ZPPR assembly is not necessarily the reference critical
configuration for that assembly. In many cases, changes were made at the core-radial blanket
boundary and possibly even at the radial blanket-radial reflector boundary of the initial critical
configuration to adjust reactivity and to produce core/radial blanket/radial reflector boundaries that
were more amenable to analysis with the analytical tools that were available when the
configuration was built. The adjustments consisted of interchanging radial blanket drawers and
core drawers at the core-radial blanket interface and possibly of interchanging radial blanket
drawers and radial reflector drawers at the radial blanket-radial reflector interface. Drawers that
contained a partial loading of core material and a partial loading of blanket material also were used
to adjust the core/radial blanket boundary.
In general, the adjustments were intended to produce boundaries that were closer to cylindrical to
facilitate analysis with the one-dimensional cylindrical codes or R-Z codes that were available at
the time. Development of X-Y and X-Y-Z modeling capabilities reduced the reliance on
cylindrical or R-Z models, but adjustment of boundaries to be more symmetrical or cylindrical
remained a common practice.
After the reference critical configuration was established, the ZPR/ZPPR staff performed a series
of operational measurements. These measurements provided the data required for subsequent
reactor operations. Control rod worths, control rod worth curves and control rod calibrations were
measured. An interface gap coefficient and a reactor temperature coefficient were measured.
Delayed neutron fractions were frequently included in operational measurements. These were
common operational measurements, but other parameters were measured or determined by other
means if they were needed. One example is a 241Pu decay coefficient to account for the reactivity
change resulting from 241Pu decay between the dates of different measurements in the same
plutonium-fueled assembly. Measuring βeff was difficult, and the experimenters frequently
calculated βeff using available deterministic tools at the time for an assembly rather than measuring
it.
Some of the operational measurements such as the interface gap coefficient and temperature
coefficient are useful for performing uncertainty analysis of criticality measurements and other
reactivity measurements. Unfortunately, the ZPR/ZPPR staff were not consistent regarding
publication of operational measurements. Some reports do not include operational measurements,
and those reports that do include operational measurements may include only a subset. This again
relates to the fact that the ZPR/ZPPR staff published the information for which there was a need
or an anticipated need when the experiments were performed. No one at that time anticipated that
someone might have a use for that information many decades later.
Identifying the loading that corresponds to the reference critical configuration is not always
straightforward. In some cases, the report documenting the measurements lists the loadings in
which the measurements were taken, including the criticality measurement. In other cases, it is
necessary to consult the logbook and loading records. The logbook entry for a reactor run will
indicate whether the reactor was critical and will show the control rod positions if the reactor was

 152

critical. The logbook entry generally indicates the objective of a reactor run, and the first page of
a loading record generally indicates the objective of the loading change in that loading. If the
stated objective is to perform operational measurements, that loading is likely to be the reference
critical configuration.
Multiple reactor runs generally were needed to perform all required operational measurements for
an assembly. One reason for multiple reactor runs is that the clock time required for the
measurements exceeded an operating shift. A second reason is that some measurement techniques
used for operational measurements were incompatible, i.e., the techniques for some measurements
required different and incompatible reactor operating conditions.
If neither the logbook nor the loading records states that operational measurements are being
performed, another approach is to examine the loading records and logbook entries for loadings
after the initial critical configuration was achieved. Some drawer changes after establishment of
the initial critical configuration are likely to be interchanges of core and radial blanket drawers to
establish the desired configuration shape. There may be a few other minor adjustments as well.
Relatively minor adjustments, especially after any core-radial blanket interchanges have been
completed, indicates that the reference critical configuration has been established. A reactor run
or loading objective stating that an experimental measurement such as a foil irradiation or
reactivity worth measurement is being performed is another indication that the reference critical
configuration was achieved in a recent loading.
While it is desirable to determine the reference critical configuration based on a published report,
logbook entry or loading record, it is occasionally necessary to choose the reference critical
configuration based on engineering judgement. The number of matrix tubes in each matrix half
was 961 for ZPR-3, 2025 for the original 45 x 45 ZPR-6 matrix, 4225 for the expanded 65 x 65
ZPR-6 matrix, 2025 for the 45 x 45 ZPR-9 matrix, 2915 for the original 53 x 55 ZPPR matrix and
5929 for the expanded 77 x 77 ZPPR matrix (if one ignores a small number of matrix locations in
the lower corners that may have been occupied by instruments). As long as the choice for the
assumed reference critical configuration is reasonable, the effect on modeling and analysis of the
reference critical configuration of choosing loading N when loading N – 1 or loading N + 1 was
correct is likely to be small.
An experimental reference critical configuration is established at the reactor operating temperature
with the control rods at the positions required to establish and maintain the critical state. If only
DP rods are present in the reactor, all DP safety rods are fully inserted, but one or more DP shim
rods is only partially inserted at the critical state. If only PSR blades are present in the reactor, all
PSR safety rods are fully withdrawn to their parked positions outside the core, but one or more
PSR shim rods is partially inserted at the critical state. If both DP rods and PSRs are present in
the reactor, it is not clear whether criticality would be maintained with partially inserted DP shim
rods or partially inserted PSR shim rods. The analyst must consult the reactor logbook to
determine which rods are partially inserted at the critical state when both DP rods and PSRs are
present in the assembly.
At present, it is practical to construct an as-built Monte Carlo model with partially inserted control
rods and to compute keff for that configuration. When the ZPR/ZPPR machines operated, computer
hardware and software limitations precluded using detailed as-built Monte Carlo models for

 153

routine analysis in most ZPPR assemblies and completely precluded construction or use of as-built
Monte Carlo models for analysis of assemblies in ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9.
For practical purposes, most analytical models used for analysis of ZPR/ZPPR assemblies were
deterministic models. Modeling fully inserted control rods accurately in a two-dimensional
deterministic model was impossible or at least very difficult, depending upon whether the model
was cylindrical, R-Z or X-Y. Modeling partially inserted control rods was only possible in X-Y-
Z models. Generating accurate region-wise cross sections for the control rod is a noted difficulty
for deterministic modeling.
For these reasons, the experimenters used the measured control rod worths and control rod worth
curves to adjust the actual measured reactivity to a configuration with all DP control rods fully
inserted and all PSRs fully withdrawn.
The reactor operating temperature varied from day to day, depending on the season, the reactor
cell temperature and decay heating in the core. To facilitate analysis, the experimenters adjusted
the measured excess reactivity to a standard reporting temperature. This adjustment was based
upon a temperature coefficient determined during the operational measurements for the assembly
and upon the average core temperature determined from in-core thermocouple readings. The
standard reporting temperature varied between facilities.
ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 measured reactivity in inhours. ZPPR initially measured reactivity in
inhours, but ZPPR eventually switched to measuring and reporting reactivity in cents. An inhour
(Ih) is a unit of reactivity and is defined as the amount of positive reactivity corresponding to an
asymptotic power rise with a time constant or period of one hour. Reactivity is rarely (if ever)
measured or reported in inhours today, but the inhour was a common unit for measuring and
reporting reactivity when ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 operated. The ZPR/ZPPR staff determined
the factor required to convert reactivity from the natural measurement units, inhours or cents, to
the natural calculation units, %Δk/k or pcm.
7.1.2 Criticality Measurement Uncertainty Analysis
The experimenters sometimes published the adjusted experimental k eff for the reference critical
configuration. However, in many cases the experimenters just published the adjusted measured
excess reactivity for the reference critical configuration. In this context, “excess reactivity” means
the excess reactivity that would be present if all DP control rods were fully inserted, the PSR blades
were fully withdrawn, the autorod (if used) was withdrawn, the reactor temperature was adjusted
to a reference value, and a correction was made for the interface gap (discussed below).
The adjusted experimental keff or excess reactivity was not published for some ZPR-3 assemblies
and may not have been published for a few assemblies built on the other ZPR/ZPPR machines. If
no published keff or excess reactivity is available, the only recourse is to set up two as-built models.
In one model, all control rods are at the positions listed in the logbook (there will be one or more
partially inserted control rods). In the second model, all DP drawers (if present) are fully inserted,
and all PSRs (if present) are fully withdrawn to their parked positions approximately 30 inches
from the front of the matrix tube. The difference in k eff between these two models is an estimate
of the excess reactivity.

 154

Criticality was established with one or more DP rods partially inserted or with the shim PSRs
partially inserted. Modeling partially inserted control rods was difficult when the ZPR/ZPPR
machines operated. The analysts constructed models with all DP rods/drawers fully inserted and
all PSRs fully withdrawn. For computational purposes, it was necessary to know what the
measured reactivity would be under those conditions. Rod worth curves were measured as part of
the operational measurements performed following establishment of the reference critical
configuration. Those rod worth curves were used to determine the reactivity change from the
critical configuration to the configuration with all DP rods/drawers fully inserted and all PSRs
fully withdrawn. That reactivity change is the excess reactivity.
For partially inserted DP rods and PSR rods, the distance listed in the logbook is the distance
between the front end of the control rod and the front end of the matrix tube, i.e., the interface
between matrix halves at full table closure.
The loading records and some other documents such as loading diagrams show where the control
rods were located in the assembly, but those documents may not show the correspondence between
the control rod locations in the assembly and the control rod identification numbers or labels in the
logbook. Consequently, it may be necessary to make an assumption about the correspondence
between rod locations in the assembly and control rod numbers or labels in the logbook.
For DP rods or drawers, the safety rods are the DP drawers that are full inserted to maximize their
negative reactivity insertion in a reactor scram when the DP drawers are withdrawn from the core,
and the shim rods are the DP drawers that are partially inserted to maintain the critical
configuration. For the PSRs, the safety rods are the PSRs that are fully withdrawn to their parked
positions to maximize their negative reactivity insertion in a scram, and the shim rods are partially
inserted to maintain the critical configuration.
In the absence of any other information, safety rods are the rods that are radially closest to the
center of the core to maximize their worth, and shim rods are the rods that are farthest from the
center of the core to minimize their impact on experimental measurements at the center of the core.
When the ZPR/ZPPR machines operated, it was not the standard practice to perform a full
uncertainty analysis as one would do today for validation or benchmarking purposes [5,6]. The
uncertainty published with the adjusted experimental keff or measured excess reactivity for a
ZPR/ZPPR assembly was generally the statistical uncertainty in the reactivity measurement
combined with some small uncertainties related to the adjustment to standard reporting conditions
with all DP drawers (if present) fully inserted, all PSRs (if present) fully withdrawn , the average
reactor temperature adjusted to a standard value for reporting purposes, and no interface gap
between matrix halves.
This published uncertainty is not the total uncertainty for the criticality measurement. In fact, this
published uncertainty typically is only a small component of the total uncertainty for the criticality
measurement because the total uncertainty includes both uncertainty related to the reactivity
measurement and uncertainty related to defining the exact configuration that was measured.
Three types of uncertainties contribute to the total uncertainty in a ZPR/ZPPR criticality
measurement. The first category covers uncertainties related to the measurement. In addition to
the statistical uncertainty in the measurement, this category includes uncertainties related to the

 155

minor adjustments made to the actual measured uncertainty to produce the published adjusted
experimental keff or excess reactivity, uncertainty in conversion of the measurement units of
reactivity to the computational units of reactivity and a few other factors. In general, uncertainties
related to the measurement make the smallest contribution to the total uncertainty for criticality

The second uncertainty category for criticality measurements covers uncertainties related to the
assembly geometry. It is not possible to describe the assembly geometry to an arbitrary degree of
precision. There was a small, nonuniform gap between the matrix halves, even at the nominal full
closure position. The pitch of the matrix tubes has a small uncertainty. In addition, there was a
small uncertainty in the actual positions of the plates in a drawer.
The third and generally largest uncertainty category for criticality measurements relates to the
masses and compositions of the plates, drawers and matrix tubes in an assembly. Neither the
masses nor the compositions of the plates, drawers and matrix tubes in an assembly can be
measured to an arbitrary degree of precision or accuracy. The uncertainties in component masses
and compositions contributes to the uncertainty in the configuration being measured.
The combined contributions of measurement uncertainties, uncertainties related to geometry and
uncertainties related to the masses and compositions of the components of the assembly yield the
total uncertainty for the criticality measurement.
7.1.2.1 Measurement Uncertainties for Criticality Measurements
The published uncertainty for the criticality measurement includes the statistical uncertainty in the
measurement, i.e., counting statistics, and some small uncertainties related to the adjustment to
standard reporting conditions. Uncertainties for the adjustments probably included detector
calibration, control rod calibration, temperature adjustment and possibly a few other minor factors.
However, there are additional factors that determine the total measurement uncertainty.
7.1.2.1.1 Temperature Uncertainty
The reactor cells housing the ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR machines were maintained at
approximately uniform temperature (allowing for possible small seasonal variations), and these
three machines were designed with systems to force air through the matrix for cooling purposes.
Thermocouples were placed at various locations in the assembly to provide an estimate of the
average core temperature. In ZPR-6 and ZPR-9, thermocouples were attached to plates in drawers
at several locations in the core. The drawer master figures usually show the thermocouple drawers,
and the loading records show the locations of the thermocouple drawers in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9

More thermocouples were used for temperature measurements in ZPPR than for temperature
measurements in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9. In ZPPR-15, for example, at least 15 thermocouples were
used to measure core temperatures. Drawer masters examined to date have not shown
thermocouple drawers, so it is possible that ZPPR thermocouples were attached to matrix tubes.
The locations of thermocouples in ZPPR assemblies are not listed in any document consulted.
ICSBEP/IRPhEP benchmarks of ZPR/ZPPR assemblies assumed a 0.5 °C uncertainty in
thermocouple calibration and 1 °C as the uncertainty in the average core temperature for ZPR-6,

 156

ZPR-9 and ZPPR [5,6]. The designs of the ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR machines included active
cooling systems, so the 1 °C uncertainty in average core temperature seems reasonable. It is
possible that logbook entries for a particular assembly may provide the individual thermocouple
readings, which would allow a better estimate of the temperature uncertainty. However, inspection
of the logbook entries examined to date for ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR assemblies have not yielded
individual thermocouple readings. In the absence of individual thermocouple readings for an
assembly, it is unlikely that any data can be found to support a value different from the assumed 1
°C uncertainty in average core temperature for a ZPR-6, ZPR-9 or ZPPR assembly many decades
after the last of those facilities closed.
Early ZPR-3 assemblies contained only uranium fuel, so there was very little decay heat in those
assemblies. Because the decay heat load was small, ZPR-3 did not have an active cooling system
prior to the acquisition of plutonium fuel plates. After ZPR-3 began using plutonium fuel in
assemblies, the ZPR-3 staff devised a rudimentary forced cooling system (see Section 2.1 above).
Initially, there was only one thermocouple in each matrix half of ZPR-3 although logbook entries
for some early ZPR-3 assemblies such as ZPR-3/6 and ZPR-3/12 consistently show three
temperatures. The location of the third thermocouple is not known. Five additional thermocouples
were added in each matrix half after ZPR-3 acquired plutonium fuel. Logbook entries for ZPR-3
assemblies built after the acquisition of plutonium fuel show 12 temperatures.
The 0.5 °C uncertainty in thermocouple calibration discussed above is a reasonable estimate for
ZPR-3 assemblies. The uncertainty in the ZPR-3 average core temperature is less clear. In
ICSBEP benchmarks of early ZPR-3 assemblies with two or three thermocouples, the evaluator
assumed that the average core temperature was the mean of the temperatures recorded in the
logbook. The corresponding uncertainty was assumed to be one-half of the range of the
temperatures listed in the logbook. A reasonable assumption for the uncertainty in average core
temperature for an early ZPR-3 assembly, i.e., an assembly with only two or three temperatures
listed in the logbook, is the greater of one-half of the range of temperatures listed in the logbook
or 1 °C.
For a plutonium-fueled ZPR-3 assembly, the logbook entry generally lists 12 temperatures. The
analyst should check the logbook entries for the reference loading and for several succeeding
loadings to determine whether the temperatures are consistent over the range of loadings
examined. This will identify any outliers in the temperatures, i.e., thermocouple values that are
not consistent over the range of loadings. A few of the consistent temperatures may be
significantly lower than the others and significantly lower than the average temperature. The
lowest recorded temperature is an inlet temperature and should be discarded for that reason. In
analyses of plutonium-fueled ZPR-3 assemblies for ICSBEP/IRPhEP benchmarks, the inlet
thermocouple was assumed to be TC 1. One additional thermocouple reading was discarded
because it was assumed to be not representative of the true average core temperature, i.e., it was
significantly lower than the other ten readings. It is reasonable to discard the two lowest values if
they are significantly lower than the other ten thermocouple readings because they are not
representative of the true average core temperature.
The average core temperature for a ZPR-3 assembly with 12 in-core thermocouples is assumed to
be the mean of the remaining thermocouple readings. The uncertainty for this average core
temperature is treated as a Type B uncertainty characterized by the range of accepted thermocouple

 157

readings [8]. In this case, the uncertainty is the range of accepted thermocouple readings divided
by √12.
The ZPR-3 staff acknowledged that the thermocouple average temperature was not the true core
average temperature, but they asserted that the thermocouple average temperature was a reliable
parameter to measure changes in the true average core temperature. Given the larger sizes of
assemblies built in ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR and the limited number of thermocouples present in
these machines, the previous sentence probably applies to ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR as well.
There is one additional temperature uncertainty that may apply to some ZPR-3 assemblies. The
temperature distribution in the core changed when the matrix halves closed, and it took significant
time to establish a new asymptotic distribution in some assemblies. For a uranium-fueled assembly
with a very low decay heat source, it seems unlikely that changes in the core temperature
distribution over the duration of the measurement could be a significant issue. For a plutonium-
fueled assembly, the time required to reach an asymptotic temperature distribution was probably
around 90 minutes. In some early assemblies, sufficient time was not always allowed for
establishment of a new asymptotic temperature distribution. In practice, it is not possible to
quantify any uncertainty related to the asymptotic temperature distribution in an assembly decades
after the ZPR/ZPPR machines were shut down. In any case, the uncertainty related to the
asymptotic temperature distribution should be small compared to the uncertainties related to
geometry and materials, so further exploration of any uncertainty in the asymptotic temperature
distribution is not warranted.
The temperature coefficient for a ZPR/ZPPR assembly was measured in the following way. When
the reactor was at the critical state, the active cooling system was turned off. The experimenters
then observed the change in reactivity as the average reactor temperature increased due to
radioactive decay in the fuel without active cooling. The resulting reactivity change data and
temperature change data were fitted to determine a temperature coefficient and associated
uncertainty. The temperature change for the temperature coefficient measurement was not large
because a large temperature change increased the risk of damaging plates in the assembly.
In some cases, the available documents do not list the measured temperature coefficient for an
assembly. It is possible to compute an approximate temperature coefficient by computing the same
model with cross sections at two temperatures. For a deterministic model, it is necessary to
generate cross sections at room temperature and at a higher temperature. For an as-built Monte
Carlo model, it is likely that the room temperature cross sections already exist. However, it will
probably be necessary to generate cross sections at a higher temperature for the Monte Carlo model
or to interpolate between existing data sets.
For both deterministic models and Monte Carlo models, the temperature difference between room
temperature and the higher temperature should probably be in the 20 °C – 30 °C range because it
is unlikely that the temperature change in the physical measurement was much larger than this
range.
The reactivity difference between the model at room temperature and the same model at the higher
temperature can be combined with the temperature difference to compute an approximate
temperature coefficient for the assembly. The uncertainty for a measured temperature coefficient

 158

in a ZPR/ZPPR assembly is typically ~10%. For a computed temperature coefficient, an assumed
uncertainty of 25% seems reasonable.
Note that the computed temperature coefficient is an approximation because it neglects thermal
expansion of the materials in the assembly. Thermal expansion would have a small effect on the
temperature coefficient, but there is not enough information to compute the reactivity effect of
thermal expansion. In particular, there is not enough information to determine a realistic
temperature distribution in the reactor.
The total average core temperature uncertainty is combined with the measured or computed
temperature coefficient to determine the total reactivity worth of the uncertainty in average core
temperature, ρT1. However, the temperature coefficient is uncertain, so there is an additional
component, ρT2, that is the product of the uncertainty in the temperature coefficient and the total
average core temperature uncertainty.
The total average core temperature uncertainty, σ T, is the quadrature sum, i.e., square root of the
sum of the squares, of the uncertainty in the thermocouple calibration (σ tc), the uncertainty in the
measured average core temperature (σTavg) and any assumed uncertainty in the asymptotic
temperature distribution in the reactor (σTasy):
 σT = √(σtc2 + σTavg2 + σTasy2)
The measured or calculated temperature coefficient is C tc ± σtc
The reactivity worth of the uncertainties related to temperature consists of two parts:
 ρT1 = Ctc x σT

 ρT2 = σtc x σT
The total reactivity worth is the quadrature sum of the contribution from ρ T1 and ρT2:
                                                 ρT = √(ρT12 + ρT22)
The uncertainty in the asymptotic temperature distribution only applies to early ZPR-3 assemblies.
For ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR, the uncertainty in the asymptotic temperature distribution is likely
to be negligible.
For example, for ZPR-9/29, the estimated uncertainty in the thermocouple calibration is 0.5 °C,
and the estimated uncertainty in the average core temperature is 1.0 °C. When these two values
are added in quadrature, the combined uncertainty in the temperature is 1.12 °C. The measured
temperature coefficient was -2.19 ± 0.03 Ih/°C for ZPR-9/29 (Ih is the abbreviation for inhours,
an obsolete unit for reactivity measurement). Using the measured temperature coefficient, the
1.12°C temperature uncertainty translates to an uncertainty of ±2.45 Ih. The ± 0.03 Ih/°C
uncertainty in the measured temperature coefficient contributes an additional ±0.03 Ih uncertainty.
Adding in quadrature the 2.45 Ih and 0.03 Ih yields a total temperature uncertainty of 2.45 Ih.
For ZPR-9/29, the total temperature uncertainty was 2.51 pcm, the total uncertainty related to
measurement technique was 8.04 pcm, and the total uncertainty for the criticality measurement

 159

was 72.88 pcm. When the uncertainty components are added in quadrature, the temperature
uncertainty generally makes a very small contribution to the total uncertainty for a criticality

7.1.2.1.2 Reproducibility Uncertainty
In the general sense, non-reproducibility and reproducibility uncertainty refer to the inability to
reproduce an experimental configuration to an arbitrary degree of precision. The ZPR/ZPPR staff
used the term reproducibility uncertainty, but some other people use the term repeatability
uncertainty to refer to the same effect. The components of reproducibility uncertainty depend
upon the type of measurement. Reproducibility uncertainty is discussed in greater detail in Section
7.2 in the context of sodium void worth measurements.
For ZPR/ZPPR criticality measurements, reproducibility uncertainty refers to the following result.
The matrix halves are brought together, the control rods are moved to establish criticality, and the
excess reactivity is measured. The control rods are used to shut the reactor down, and the matrix
halves are separated. The matrix halves are brought together again with no change in the contents
of the matrix loading, the control rods are moved to establish criticality again, and the excess
reactivity is measured again. The second measured excess reactivity generally will not be identical
to the first measured excess reactivity. The small difference between the two measured excess
reactivities is an estimate of the reproducibility uncertainty or repeatability uncertainty.
The reproducibility uncertainty has several components. First, there can be a very small springing
or rebound when the movable table contacts the stationary table, and that rebound introduces a
small gap between the tables at the nominal full closure position. This gap is not constant over
repeated attempts to close and open the tables. Second, control rod positions were not absolutely
reproducible to an arbitrary degree of precision between successive reactor runs with the same
matrix loading. Third, there could be small differences in the reactor temperature distribution
between different reactor runs with the same matrix loading.
Reproducibility uncertainty applies to any criticality measurement in any ZPR/ZPPR assembly.
Reproducibility uncertainty is generally very small for criticality measurements in ZPR/ZPPR
assemblies. In some cases, the report documenting the criticality measurement will list the
reproducibility uncertainty. If there is no published reproducibility uncertainty, it is necessary to
make a reasonable assumption.
The reproducibility uncertainty in ZPPR assemblies is typically in the 0.5 pcm – 1 pcm range.
Assuming a reproducibility uncertainty of 1 pcm is reasonable for a ZPPR criticality measurement.
For ZPR-6 and ZPR-9, reported reproducibility uncertainties tended to be in the 0.5 – 2 inhours
(Ih) range. Assuming a reproducibility uncertainty of 1 Ih – 2 Ih is appropriate for a ZPR-6 or
ZPR-9 assembly if no published value is available.
The reproducibility uncertainty for ZPR-3/56B was 2.5 Ih (see ICSBEP benchmark MIX-COMP-
FAST-004 in Ref. 5). Other ICSBEP benchmarks of ZPR-3 assemblies also assumed a 2.5 Ih
reproducibility uncertainty because no reproducibility uncertainty was found in the reports for
those assemblies. In the absence of a published value, assuming a 2.5 Ih reproducibility
uncertainty for a ZPR-3 assembly seems reasonable.

 160

Compared to other uncertainties for criticality measurements, the reproducibility uncertainty is
small and has very little effect on the total uncertainty of a criticality measurement. Consequently,
detailed analysis of reproducibility uncertainty is not warranted.
7.1.2.1.3 Reactivity Conversion Uncertainty
The natural units for reactivity measurements are cents or inhours, but the natural units for
reactivity calculations are Δk/k1k2 or pcm. Conversion from the natural reactivity measurements
units to the calculation units or vice versa requires knowledge of the delayed neutron kinetics
parameters, particularly βeff. However, βeff is uncertain, and that uncertainty contributes to the total
measurement uncertainty expressed in Δk/k1k2 or pcm.
Measurement of βeff was difficult, and the experimenters typically calculated β eff. The calculation
or measurement of βeff is uncertain, and its assumed uncertainty is 5%. This is the uncertainty in
βeff assumed in all ICSBEP/IRPhEP benchmarks of ZPR/ZPPR assemblies [5,6]. A brief review
of some of the βeff measurements performed on ZPR/ZPPR assemblies displayed a spread in the
measured values when βeff for the same configuration was measured by different methods, in
addition to the uncertainty reported in the individual β eff measurements. Considering the
uncertainty in an individual βeff measurement and the spread in measured values when different
methods are used to measure βeff, the assumed 5% uncertainty is not unreasonable or excessively
conservative.
The excess reactivity, total temperature uncertainty, reproducibility uncertainty and any other
measurement uncertainty that is specific to a particular assembly are converted from the
measurement units (Ih or cents) to the calculation units (Δk/k 1k2 or pcm) and multiplied by the
assumed uncertainty in βeff. The quadrature sum of these products is the contribution of the
reactivity conversion uncertainty to the total measurement uncertainty.
7.1.2.1.4 Total Measurement Uncertainty
The total measurement uncertainty is the quadrature sum of a) excess reactivity uncertainty
(published uncertainty), b) total temperature uncertainty, c) reproducibility uncertainty, d)
reactivity conversion uncertainty and e) any additional measurement uncertainty that is specific to
a particular assembly.
From experience, the total measurement uncertainty in ZPR/ZPPR is the smallest component of
the total uncertainty for a criticality measurement.
7.1.2.2 Geometry Uncertainties for Criticality Measurements
Some uncertainties in configuration geometry arise from normal tolerances in manufacturing and
installing equipment such as the tables and matrix tubes. Other geometry uncertainties result from
drawer loading and handling practices. In all cases, the result is that the as-built model that can be
constructed is a high-fidelity model of the physical assembly, but the as-built model is still an
approximation of the true geometric configuration that was measured. In other words, the true
physical configuration that was measured is uncertain.

 161

7.1.2.2.1 Interface Gap Uncertainty
Section 7.1.2.1.2 discussed the fact that the position of the movable table at the nominal full closure
position relative to the stationary table was not perfectly reproducible. That component of the
reproducibility uncertainty could be described as the table closure uncertainty.
There were position indicators at the four corners of the matrix in each matrix half that measured
the corner separation, i.e., the separation between the corner of half 1 and the corresponding corner
of half 2 or the corner of the stationary table and the corresponding corner of the movable table, at
the nominal full closure position. The corner separations were recorded in the reactor logbook for
each reactor run in at least some ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR assemblies. The ZPR-3 logbooks that
have been examined to date do not include the corner separations. The table closure component
of the reproducibility uncertainty discussed above refers to the fact that position indicator readings
at the nominal full closure varied between successive reactor runs even if there was no change in
the contents of the matrix tubes during those reactor runs. The interface gap uncertainty discussed
here refers to a separate type of uncertainty.
The two halves of the matrix in any of the ZPR/ZPPR machines were neither perfectly flat nor
perfectly parallel due to normal manufacturing and machining tolerances plus tolerances related
to installation of the tables and matrix tubes. In addition, the weight of a large assembly could
cause a slight deflection of the support plate. Because the matrix halves were not perfectly aligned,
some parts of the two halves were not in physical contact at full table closure. There was a small,
non-uniform gap between the two matrix halves at the nominal full closure position. There could
also be a small gap because of uncertainty in the actual position of the movable half at full closure
relative to the position indicated by the instruments. As-built ZPR/ZPPR models do not include
an interface gap because of its small, non-uniform and imprecisely known size.
The ZPR/ZPPR staff adjusted the reported excess reactivity to a condition with zero interface gap
to facilitate analysis, but uncertainty related to the interface gap contributes to the total uncertainty.
Consequently, a gap worth is derived in conjunction with a gap uncertainty analysis as part of the
uncertainty analysis for the criticality measurement.
The worth of the interface gap was determined experimentally by measuring an interface gap
coefficient during the operational measurements that were performed after the reference critical
configuration was established. The gap coefficient was measured by establishing a critical
configuration and then driving the tables apart from the full closure position without any control
rod motion. The associated reactivity change as a function of table separation was recorded. The
gap coefficient was derived by dividing the reactivity change by the recorded table separation
change and was expressed in units of inhours or cents per gap separation unit. A gap separation
unit was one mil, i.e., 0.001 inch.
The size of the interface gap is estimated from the values indicated by the position indicators for
the corner separations. The interface gap is the average of the four corner separation values. Since
the matrix halves did touch at some points even though the position indicators showed small
separations at the corners, one could argue that one-half of the average of the four corner separation
values would be a better estimate of the interface gap. On the other hand, the gap was not uniform,
and there could be places in the matrix where the separation was larger than the average of the four
corner separations. With modern measuring equipment, it might be possible to measure and map

 162

the surfaces of the matrix halves and to use that mapping to determine the interface gap more
precisely. However, that was not an option when the ZPR/ZPPR facilities operated, and none of
