those machines exist today. J. A. Morman, an experimenter at ANL-E, stated that the interface
gap used in the correction was assumed to be the average of the four corner separations for ZPR-
6 and ZPR-9 [2]. In the absence of any additional information, it is assumed that the interface gap
was determined to be the average of the four corner separations at ZPR-3 and ZPPR as well.
Analysis of the interface gap in ZPPR-15A loading 15 (L015) is used as an example here. The
measured interface gap coefficient for ZPPR-15A was -0.13 ± 0.02 ¢/mil. The product of the
measured interface gap coefficient and the average gap determined from the position indicators is
the gap worth.
The excess reactivity of ZPPR-15A L015 was measured in reactor run 16. According to the ZPPR-
15 logbook, the measured table closure indicator values were -32.5, -54.2, -32.6 and -56.6 mils for
reactor run 16. The average of these four values is -43.975 gap separation units or -43.975 mils.
The average gap determined from the position indicators is 43.975 mils or 0.1117 cm for ZPPR-
15A L015 (reactor run 16) according to the logbook, so the worth of the interface gap was -5.72 ±
0.88¢ [43.975 mil x (-0.13 ± 0.02 ¢/mil)] or -19.19 ± 2.95 pcm.
The interface gap is not uniform. A reasonable estimate of the uncertainty associated with the
non-uniform gap is 25% or 4.80 pcm (0.25 x 19.19). When the 4.80 pcm uncertainty is added in
quadrature with the 2.95 pcm due to uncertainty in the measured interface gap coefficient, the final
value for the interface gap worth is -19.19 ± 5.63 pcm. Consequently, the uncertainty in the
interface gap worth is ± 5.63 pcm.
The key points here are:
 1. The interface gap is not uniform.
 2. The average interface gap is assumed to be the average of the four corner separation values
 in the reactor logbook.
 3. A reasonable estimate of the uncertainty associated with the non-uniform gap is ~25%.

Sometimes the interface gap coefficient was not published. If no interface gap coefficient was
published for an assembly, it may still be possible to compute the reactivity worth of the interface
gap if the average interface gap can be determined from the logbook or if a reasonable assumption
can be made regarding the size of the interface gap. The assumed average interface gap could be
based on logbook entries for other loadings in the same assembly program or on data for other
assembly programs in the same facility.
One way to get an estimate is to calculate the interface gap worth which requires constructing one
as-built model of the assembly with no interface gap and a second as-built model of the assembly
with the assumed interface gap. The reactivity difference between those two models is a
reasonable estimate of the interface gap worth.
From experience with ZPR/ZPPR models, one billion (10 9) histories in a Monte Carlo calculation
of an as-built model produces a one sigma statistical uncertainty of 1 – 2 pcm in k eff. Because the
interface gap is small and the full ZPR/ZPPR matrix is large, a direct deterministic transport

 163

calculation might not produce an accurate estimate of the interface gap worth. There is some
possibility that a perturbation theory based deterministic approach would work, but the stated
Monte Carlo approach works and would always be considered more precise.
If it is necessary to compute the worth of the interface gap, a reasonable estimate of the total
uncertainty in the gap worth is the quadrature sum (square root of the sum of the squares) of a)
25% of the gap worth for the uncertainty associated with the non-uniform gap and b) 25% of the
gap worth for uncertainty in the effective interface gap coefficient that would correspond to the
assumed average interface gap.
7.1.2.2.2 Drawer and Plate Position Uncertainty
Besides the interface gap, there are three issues regarding the exact location of materials in the
assembly. One is the possibility that the drawer fronts might not have been flush with the front
edges of the matrix tubes. In ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR drawers, the drawer fronts had tabs that
mated with notches in the fronts of the matrix tubes to ensure consistent positioning of drawers in
the matrix tubes. When drawers were loaded into matrix tubes, care was taken to make the drawers
flush with the matrix. It is not clear whether the ZPR-3 drawers had tabs or whether ZPR-3 matrix
tubes had notches, but the ZPR-3 staff would have been aware of the issue and it is reasonable to
assume they would have taken care when drawers were placed in matrix tubes.
Another issue is the possibility that the plate columns might not have been all the way forward
against the drawer fronts. This problem was minimized by taking care when loading the plates in
the drawers, by inserting springs at the backs of drawers to push the plates toward the drawer fronts
and by inserting the drawer tabs into the matrix tube notches slowly. However, small axial shifts
in plate positions could still occur during drawer handling. A third issue to consider regards
deviations from nominal dimensions for plates, drawers and matrix tubes. Deviations in the
dimensions that affect the precise X and Y positions of materials in the unit cell are too small to
impact keff significantly. The dimensions that determine the volumes over which the material
masses are distributed can have an effect. The plate lengths, drawer front thickness and the length
of the front drawers affect the axial positions of the materials, similar to the interface gap effect.
In early ICSBEP benchmarks of ZPR/ZPPR assemblies, it was assumed that the worth of any
uncertainty in the axial positions of the plates was covered by assigning 50% of the interface gap
worth to the plate position uncertainty [5].
A better approach is to construct an as-built model in which there is a small gap between the front
plates of the drawers and the front ends of the plate columns in the drawers. This gap accounts for
any plate shifting that may occur during drawer handling and for any uncertainty in the axial
dimensions of the plate materials or drawer fronts. The worth of the plate position uncertainty is
the difference in keff between a) the as-built model with the small gaps between the front plates of
the drawers and the fronts of the plate columns in the drawers and b) the reference as-built model
with no gap between the drawer front and the fronts of the plate columns. This will probably be a
slightly conservative estimate of the plate position uncertainty, but it will be more accurate than
assigning 50% of the interface gap worth as the plate position uncertainty.
For ZPPR-15A, a model was constructed with a 0.0075 inch gap between the front plates of the
drawers and the front ends of the plate columns in the drawers. The gap was uniform and was
present in every drawer in both matrix halves, so this was a conservative estimate of the plate

 164

position uncertainty. The computed worth of this gap was -10.02 ± 2.83 pcm for ZPPR-15A. For
comparison, the worth of the interface gap in ZPPR-15A was -19.19 ± 5.63 pcm.
7.1.2.2.3 Matrix Tube Pitch Uncertainty
A deviation from the nominal average spacing or pitch between matrix tubes would have a small
effect upon neutron leakage and, consequently, keff. Deviations from the nominal matrix tube pitch
arise from two sources:
 1. Manufacturing tolerances introduce a small uncertainty in the pitch due to uncertainties in
 the external dimensions of the matrix tubes, and the matrix tube installation process may
 have introduced an additional uncertainty.
 2. The weight of the loaded drawers could produce a small distortion in the matrix geometry
 although the size of any such distortion is limited by the clamping structure surrounding
 the matrix tubes (see Figure 2.1, Figure 2.7, Figure 2.9 and Figure 2.12).

The measured uncertainty in the matrix pitch for ZPR-3 was reported as 0.001 inches. It seems
likely that the matrix tube pitch was measured for each of the ZPR/ZPPR machines during or after
the installation process, but no documentation has been found to date that cites the measured pitch
uncertainty for ZPR-6, ZPR-9 or ZPPR. The matrix tubes in ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR were nearly
identical to the ZPR-3 matrix tubes, and the ZPR/ZPPR staff would have taken similar care care
in assembling the matrix tubes and tables in ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR. A 0.001 inch matrix tube
pitch uncertainty has been assumed for all ICSBEP/IRPhEP benchmarks of ZPR/ZPPR assemblies
[5,6]. This seems like a reasonable pitch uncertainty in the absence of any additional information.
If a reported measured pitch uncertainty for ZPR-6, ZPR-9 or ZPPR is ever identified, that
measured value should be used in place of the assumed 0.001 inch value for the relevant
ZPR/ZPPR machine.
The worth of the matrix tube pitch uncertainty is determined by creating two modified as-built
models of the the ZPR/ZPPR assembly reference critical configuration. In the first as-built model,
the matrix tube pitch in the X- and Y-directions is increased by the assumed pitch uncertainty. In
the second as-built model, the matrix tube pitch in the X- and Y-directions is decreased by the
assumed pitch uncertainty. The matrix tube density is changed in each model to conserve matrix
tube mass when the matrix tube pitch is changed. The assumed worth of the matrix tube pitch
uncertainty is taken as one-half of the reactivity difference between these two models.
7.1.2.2.4 Total Geometry Uncertainty
The total geometry uncertainty is the quadrature sum of a) interface gap uncertainty, b) drawer and
plate position uncertainty, c) matrix tube pitch uncertainty and d) any additional geometry
uncertainty that is specific to a particular assembly. In general, the total geometry uncertainty is
significantly larger than the total measurement uncertainty and significantly smaller than the total
mass/composition uncertainty.
7.1.3 Mass and Composition Uncertainties
A bit of history about the materials inventory records is needed to appreciate the extent and
limitations of the information available regarding the masses and compositions of materials used

 165

in the ZPR/ZPPR facilities. The material inventory for Argonne’s ZPR/ZPPR facilities was
accumulated over a period of more than thirty years, starting with ZPR-3 in the mid-1950s. The
procurement acceptance process required thorough documentation regarding compositions,
masses, dimensions, etc. Information needed for day-to-day operations was extracted and
compiled in working documents known informally as “hot constants memos.” These memos give
batch or lot average values of dimensions, masses and weight fractions of constituents, but they
do not include uncertainties. The original documentation on most of the inventory used in
ZPR/ZPPR assemblies has been lost, but the hot constants memos and the ADEN library created
by the ZPR/ZPPR staff are still available. Consequently, indirect evidence and estimates are used
to quantify many composition uncertainties. Compositions given in the hot constants memos and
ADEN library are used directly. That is, weight fractions are not adjusted or renormalized to sum
to 100%.
Composition uncertainty for a component is treated in two parts – the uncertainty in total mass and
the uncertainties in the weight fractions of the constituents. Since these two uncertainty sources
are independent, they are added in quadrature (square root of the sum of the squares). The
reactivity effects of composition uncertainties can be determined by computing the changes in k eff
using either an as-built Monte Carlo model or a deterministic methodology with sufficient spatial
resolution. A deterministic model has two advantages in most cases. First, a deterministic model
allows the analyst to compute small reactivities that would be difficult to resolve by Monte Carlo.
Second, using a deterministic model to compute the reactivity effects of composition uncertainties
requires less human effort, less calendar time and much less computer resources than using Monte
Carlo to compute these reactivity effects.
Details of the mass measurements for assembly components are unknown. For the plates and most
of the drawers, it is assumed that measurements of masses were within 0.01 g of the actual values
for plates with masses up to tens of grams and within 1 g for larger plates weighing kilograms (i.e.,
the uncertainty in weighing was 0.1%). This assumption is based upon the number of significant
figures listed in the hot constants memos and the ADEN library entries. There is one important
qualification regarding the entries in the ADEN library. The current version of the ADEN library
was developed from the last version in use at ZPPR when ZPPR was shut down. Too many entries
in the current ADEN library end in “01”, “001”, “99” or “999.” Clearly, some roundoff occurred
during the conversion process from the original ZPPR file to the current text file version of the
ADEN library.
The working standard used to calibrate the scale is assumed to have an uncertainty of 0.05%, which
is a systematic uncertainty. The 0.1% uncertainty in weighing could be statistical, but since no
details of the process are available, this uncertainty is assumed to be systematic. The total
uncertainty in mass is taken to be the sum of these two uncertainties, or 0.15%. This treatment of
mass uncertainties has been used to date for every ICSBEP and IRPhEP benchmark of ZPR-3,
ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR assemblies [5,6]. There is no evidence to support an alternative
assumption. With a few exceptions noted below, this 0.15% mass uncertainty applies to all
ZPR/ZPPR plates and drawers in the absence of better information.
One exception to the generic 0.15% mass uncertainty is that the mass uncertainty for the matrix
tubes is assumed to be 2%. The 2% mass uncertainty for the matrix tubes was developed by R.
W. Schaefer and R. D. McKnight, former ZPPR and ZPR staff analysts, to provide a reasonable

 166

upper limit for the uncertainty in the mass of the matrix tubes in ZPR-3, ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR.
The number of matrix tubes was 1922 for ZPR-3, ~4050 for ZPR-6, ~4050 for ZPR-9 and ~11858
for the expanded ZPPR matrix. The physical size and mass of a matrix tube were much larger than
the physical size and mass of a drawer, stainless steel plate or stainless steel can, so it seems
plausible that normal manufacturing variations could produce a mass uncertainty for the matrix
tubes that is larger than the 0.15% uncertainty for the masses of standard plates. The reactivity
effect of the matrix tube mass uncertainty is not a dominant uncertainty component in ZPR/ZPPR
assemblies, and there is no information available to justify a different value.
The second exception relates to the various types of plutonium plates. A database of data for the
plutonium plates still exists. This database contains detailed information regarding the masses and
isotopic compositions of the plutonium plates although the database does not contain any
information regarding impurities in the plutonium plates. This database can be used to determine
the mass uncertainties for the components of the meat in the plutonium plates. The meat in the
plutonium plates consisted of plutonium, depleted uranium and molybdenum for Pu-U-Mo plates
and of plutonium and aluminum for Pu-Al plates.
A limited range of materials was used in most ZPR/ZPPR assemblies. The discussion in Section
7.1.3 covers common plate types and materials, e.g., stainless steel, that were used frequently in
ZPR/ZPPR assemblies, but this discussion cannot cover every plate or material that was used in
an assembly over the 35 year period between the start of ZPR-3/1 and the end of ZPPR-21. The
hot contants memos list many types of plates and materials that are not in the ADEN library and
that have not been encountered in preparing as-built models of ZPR/ZPPR assemblies.
The composition uncertainties for plate types and other materials that are not discussed in Section
7.1.3 must be determined from other sources. The hot constants memos may provide information
regarding impurities and composition uncertainties. The ADEN library lists the masses of light
impurities and heavy impurities for some materials, but the ADEN library does not provide any
additional information regarding the elements in the light impurities or heavy impurities. In many
cases, it is necessary to consult other sources to determine the impurities in a material and the
uncertainty in the material composition. Possible sources of information regarding material
compositions are materials handbooks, commercial vendor documents and materials standards
such as ASTM standards.
The 0.15% mass uncertainty applies to all plate types, drawers and other components used in
ZPR/ZPPR assemblies except the matrix tubes and the plutonium fuel plates. The mass uncertainty
for the matrix tubes is assumed to be 2%. Mass and composition uncertainties for the meat in a
Pu-U-Mo plate or Pu-Al plate can be determined from an existing database.
7.1.3.1 Treatment of Impurities in Materials
All plates, drawers and matrix tubes in a ZPR/ZPPR assembly contained small amounts of
impurities, but the ADEN library entries and hot contants memos provide limited information
regarding those impurities. In some cases, the ADEN library entry includes impurities. In other
cases, the ADEN library only lists the main constituents of a material and ignores any impurities
that may have been present in the material. The hot contants memos, particularly the ZPPR hot
constants memo, provide a limited amount of additional information regarding impurities in
materials. The ZPPR hot constants memo may list specific impurity elements for some plate types.

 167

The hot constants memo used at ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 generally just lump all impurities together as
“other elements.”
ZPR/ZPPR analysts generally neglected impurity elements in analyses of ZPR/ZPPR assemblies.
It is not presently clear why impurities were usually neglected in analyses, but there are a few
general possibilities:
 1. In some cases, it was not possible to generate cross sections for elements or specific
 isotopes because the required nuclear data files did not exist or could not be processed with
 available software.
 2. Available computer software and hardware imposed significant limits on what could or
 could not be calculated when the various ZPR/ZPPR assemblies were built and analyzed.
 For example, early ZPR-3 assemblies were modeled as spheres or one-dimensional
 cylinders. Many assemblies were approximately cylindrical to facilitate cylindrical or R-
 Z diffusion calculations. Minor constituents of materials were neglected for similar
 reasons.
 3. Impurities can be important in a thermal neutron spectrum because some impurity elements
 such as boron and cadmium have very large capture cross sections at thermal energies. In
 the hard neutron spectrum characteristic of ZPR/ZPPR assemblies, neutron capture in
 impurities is small, and the reactivity worth of impurities is small.
 4. The ZPR/ZPPR staff may have regarded the effects of impurity elements as small
 compared to other approximations required for analysis purposes.
 5. The ZPR/ZPPR staff may have regarded the effects of impurity elements as small
 compared to the uncertainties in the basic nuclear data for the major elements and isotopes
 present in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies.
 6. Standards for acceptable accuracy and approximations change over time. These changes
 are in response to a) the evolution of computer software and hardware, b) improvements in
 the nuclear data and c) the need for reduced uncertainty in reactor design. For example,
 many ICSBEP benchmarks [5] that were accepted in the mid-1990s would be rejected
 today or would require major revisions to meet present standards for uncertainty analysis
 and specification of the benchmark model.
Because impurity elements in ZPR/ZPPR materials were present in the physical configuration that
was measured, it is necessary to account for them in some manner for modeling purposes, at least
in principle. In practice, the reactivity worth of impurities in most materials is small or negligible
in the hard neutron spectrum characteristic of a ZPR/ZPPR assembly.
There are two options for addressing impurities for analysis purposes. The first option is to include
the impurities in the reference as-built model. This can be done by a) modifying the ADEN library
to include the documented or assumed impurities in the reference as-built model or b) manually
adding the impurities to the reference as-built model afterwards. If the impurities are included in
the reference as-built model, it is only necessary to acknowledge any assumptions made about the
impurity elements present and about their concentrations or masses in the material(s) in the report
documenting the analysis.
The second option is to neglect the impurities that are not present in the existing reference ADEN
library. Those impurities were present in the physical configuration, so neglecting them in the as-
built Monte Carlo model and in any deterministic model derived from the as-built Monte Carlo

 168

model introduces a bias. The topic of bias and its treatment is discussed in more detail in Section
7.1.4.
If the impurities are neglected in the reference as-built model, it is necessary to adjust the
experimental or measured keff to account for the resulting bias in the as-built model. The
adjustment is made by calculating the reactivity worth of the impurities and subtracting that worth
(positive or negative) from the experimental keff. The reactivity worth of the impurities is
computed by adding the impurities to the relevant material compositions in the reference model
and calculating keff for the resulting model (see Section 7.1.4 for details).
The ADEN library entry for a material treats impurities in one of the following ways:
 1. The entry lists only the principal components of the material. No impurities are listed for
 the entry. For example, the entries for iron oxide plates list the masses for Fe and O, but
 those entries do not list any impurities. Likewise, the entries for depleted uranium plates
 list only 235U and 238U.
 2. The impurity masses in a material are listed as LIP (light impurities) and/or HIP (heavy
 impurities), but there is no way to identify specific elements in the light impurity and heavy
 impurity categories.
 3. The entry for a material includes the principal components and some or all of the known
 impurities. For example, the sodium composition in sodium plates corresponds to 99.93
       wt.% Na, 0.04 wt.% Ca, 0.005 wt.% O, 0.02 wt.% C and 0.005 wt.% Cl.
It is necessary in most cases to make some assumptions regarding the impurity elements present
and the amounts of those elements that were present in ZPR/ZPPR materials. With rare exceptions,
it is unlikely that additional information regarding the actual ZPR/ZPPR materials can be found
today. However, there are a few potential sources of information to justify assumptions regarding
material compositions and impurities:
 1. Standard materials handbooks may provide some information regarding the composition
 of a material and the associated impurities.
 2. There may be an ASTM standard for the material. If an ASTM standard exists, that
 standard may provide information regarding minor constituents and impurities in the
 material. In the ideal case, the ASTM standard would date from around the time when the
 material was purchased or the time when the ZPR/ZPPR assembly was built. In practice,
 it may not be possible to find an ASTM standard from that time.
 3. It may be possible to find compositions and specifications for identical or at least similar
 materials from commercial vendors.
 4. It may be possible to find chemical analyses of similar materials.
None of these sources will match the ZPR/ZPPR material exactly, but they provide the basis for
reasonable assumptions regarding impurities. In general, any reasonable assumption regarding the
impurities in a material should not have a significant effect on the total uncertainty. The known
exceptions for specific materials are discussed below.
Impurities in a material may be listed as a range of values, or a lab report may list an impurity
element as being less than the detection threshold for that element for the test used in the analysis.

 169

A reasonable approach under those circumstances is to assume a mid-range value or half of the
listed detection limit for the element.
The uncertainty assigned to an impurity element usually requires an assumption unless a lab test
lists an uncertainty in the measured value. An upper bound for the reactivity worth of the
uncertainty in the impurities could be determined by calculating a model with the impurity
concentration doubled and assuming a uniform probability distribution over that interval [8].
Unless the reactivity effect of doubling the assumed impurities is relatively large, i.e., large enough
to have a significant effect on the total uncertainty for the criticality measurement, further
refinement of the impurity treatment does not seem to be warranted.
In principle, if impurities are not included in the reference as-built model, omitting them should
be treated as a bias as discussed in Section 7.1.4. Uncertainties in the impurities should be included
in the total uncertainty for the criticality measurement for the same reason.
In practice, the reactivity worth of the uncertainty in the impurity content of almost all materials
is negligible in the hard ZPR/ZPPR spectrum, especially if the worth of the mass uncertainty of
the basic material is small. Because individual uncertainties are added in quadrature to determine
the total uncertainty, the total uncertainty for a criticality measurement is dominated by a few large
uncertainty components. The large composition uncertainty components are generally related to
the fuel and to a few other important materials such as graphite plates or stainless steel.
If the reactivity worth of an impurity is small, the reactivity worth of any uncertainty in the
impurity concentration will be negligible. Water vapor in graphite plates and impurities in HEU
are the principal exceptions in which the impurity or contaminant level and any related uncertainty
have been found to be important.
7.1.3.2 Coatings on Plates
Several types of ZPR/ZPPR plates were coated to prevent corrosion and to minimize material loss
during plate handling. The mass of coating per plate was small, and coating materials were chosen
to minimize hydrogen content.
In general, the coating on a plate is not included in the material composition for that plate in the
ADEN library. ZPR/ZPPR staff analysts typically ignored plate coatings when models of
experiments were constructed. There are a few possible reasons why plate coatings were neglected
in ZPPR/ZPPR models.
 1. It is possible that the staff analysts regarded the effects of the coatings as insignificant
 compared to other approximations required for modeling purposes.
 2. The available nuclear data, computer software and computer hardware of the period
 imposed a separate set of constraints on inclusion of coatings in models. The cross section
 processing codes used at Argonne during that period may not have been able to process all
 of the elements present in some coatings, and reliable nuclear data may not have been
 available for some of those elements.
 3. Computer storage and computer execution time were limited and expensive. Probably the
 major component of storage for VIM, the continuous energy Monte Carlo code used at
 Argonne when the ZPR/ZPPR machines operated, was storage of nuclear data for the
 isotopes or elements in the model. Likewise, a major component of the execution time for

 170

 any continuous energy Monte Carlo code is processing the nuclear data at each track
 through a material and/or collision within the material to determine the appropriate cross
 sections. Cost considerations dictated minimizing the number of isotopes/elements in
 models and excluding any isotopes/elements that were assumed to have an insignificant
 effect on the physics of the calculation. Readers whose experience with computer
 hardware and software is limited to current hardware and software do not really grasp how
 important the hardware/software limitations were in these types of decisions. In the mid-
 1970s, an input file for the VIM Monte Carlo code was limited to twenty isotopes and
 elements, and a large Monte Carlo calculation ran ~200,000 histories.
In any case, coatings were generally ignored in ZPR/ZPPR models, and the entries in the ADEN
library upon which those models were based generally do not include coatings.
Ignoring the coatings introduces a bias in the calculations. This bias may have been regarded as
unimportant during the period when the ZPR/ZPPR facilities operated. However, current
approaches to creating benchmarks and models used for validation include all known biases and
uncertainties [5,6].
Given the need to account for the coating, there are two basic options:
 1. Include the coatings on all coated plates in the reference as-built model and in any
 deterministic model derived from the as-built model. Since the coatings are explicitly
 included in the model(s), there is no bias and no need to adjust the experimental k eff to
 account for neglected coatings.
 2. Neglect the coatings in the reference as-built model and treat that omission as a bias (see
 Section 7.1.4). Neglecting the coatings requires development of two as-built models. In
 the reference as-built model, the coatings on coated plates are neglected. In a second as-
 built model, the coatings are included on all coated plates. The reactivity worth between
 these two models is an estimate of the worth of the coating. Note that the reactivity worth
 of the coating may be positive or negative, depending upon the coating material(s), the
 composition of the assembly and the spectrum of the assembly.
Both of these options are valid. In the first option, the coatings are included in the final reference
as-built Monte Carlo model and in any deterministic model derived from the reference as-built
Monte Carlo model, so no bias adjustment is needed. In the second option, the coatings are not
included in the final as-built reference model, and the experimental k eff should be adjusted to
account for this bias.
In either case, as is applicable, modified version of the ADEN library should be made to add the
coatings to the material entries for coated plates in that library if there is sufficient data available
to do so The principal coating material was Kel-F although titanium oxide and Teflon were also
used at ZPR-3. All elements in Kel-F (F, Cl, C, H), titanium oxide (Ti, O) and Teflon (F, C) are
included in the set of elements in the ADEN library.
Direct modification of the as-built models is also possible. If the coatings are not included in the
ADEN library, the coatings can be added manually to the as-built models. For example, if some
elements in the coating are not included in the ADEN library set of elements, the coatings can be
added to the relevant materials in the as-built model.

 171

It is likely that the primary or possibly only source for data regarding the coating mass per plate
and the coating composition is the set of available hot constants memos for ZPR-3, ZPR-6, ZPR-
9 and ZPPR.
The coating was the equivalent of a coat of paint. The average mass of coating per plate was
recorded for many types and sizes of coated plates, but the coating thickness was not recorded and
cannot be determined decades after the ZPR/ZPPR facilities shut down. When coatings have been
included in past models, the coatings were uniformly mixed into the plate material. In the hard
spectrum present in a ZPR/ZPPR assembly, the reactivity effect of homogenizing the coating into
plate material is negligible. In any case, attempting to represent the coating explicitly is likely to
cause roundoff problems in Monte Carlo calculations and other sorts of numerical problems in
deterministic models.
The most common coating used at the ZPR/ZPPR facilities was Kel-F. All bare uranium metal
plates (depleted uranium, natural uranium, HEU) used at ANL-E and ANL-W were coated with
Kel-F. Table 7.1 shows the composition of Kel-F.
 Table 7.1. Kel-F Composition.

 Element Weight Percent
 Hydrogen 0.5
                                           Carbon                 20.6
 Chlorine 30.5
 Fluorine 48.4
When the HEU plates in the ANL-E plate inventory were shipped to ZPPR after ZPR-6 and ZPR-
9 were shut down, the ZPPR staff removed the Kel-F from the HEU plates and sealed those plates
in cans. Only the HEU plates were canned at ZPPR. All depleted uranium plates in the ZPPR
inventory were coated with Kel-F.
A few other types of plates also were coated with Kel-F. Teflon and titanium oxide were used to
coat a few plate types such as some graphite plates in the ZPR-3 inventory. Coating of plate
materials other than uranium was not consistent. For example, some graphite plates were coated,
but the graphite plates used at ANL-E were not coated.
ADEN library entries do not include the coating for most coated plates, but there are a few
exceptions for plates coated with Kel-F. If the ADEN library entry for a coated plate includes H,
C, Cl and F, the ADEN library entry includes the Kel-F coating. The hot contants memos do
indicate which plates were coated and generally list the average coating mass per plate for coated
plates. Note that the average coating mass per plate depends on the size of the plate and increases
with increasing plate length.
Readers who consult the ADEN library or the hot constants memos will see references to colors
for some types of plates. These colors do not necessarily refer to the coatings. The ZPR/ZPPR
staff sometimes painted a small stripe or other marking on the end or top of a plate for identification
purposes. Dyes may have been added to coatings for the same reason.

 172

For example, a stainless steel plate and a clad plate of various types (Pu-U-Mo, Pu-Al, sodium,
sodium carbonate, etc.) look alike if they have the same external dimensions. In addition, size
ranges overlapped for many types of clad plates although plate weights could be used to distinguish
some plate types. The identification problem was even worse for DU plates and HEU plates
because the sizes and weights of those two types of plates were identical for practical purposes.
Using different colors and/or different patterns to mark different plate types made the different
types of plates visually distinguishable and minimized the likelihood of drawer loading errors. The
practice also minimized the likelihood of errors when drawers were unloaded, and plates were
returned to inventory.
7.1.3.2.1 Uncertainties Related to Plate Coatings
The uncertainty related to the average coating mass per coated plate is not known and probably
cannot be determined today. It is likely that this uncertainty is small, but it cannot be quantified.
In addition, a ZPR/ZPPR assembly typically contained many hundreds or many thousands of each
plate type/size, so random variations in the coating masses for individual plates have no significant
effect.
There is one uncertainty related to the coating mass per plate that can be quantified to some degree.
Some of the coating wore off during plate handling. This wear was more likely to be an issue to
for plates that were used frequently such as DU plates, HEU plates and depleted U 3O8 plates than
for plates that were rarely used. Other coated plates such as beryllium oxide plates may have been
used for only one or a few assembly programs, so there would be little coating loss on such plates.
Coated plates that were used frequently were recoated periodically. The hot constants memos list
the average coating mass per plate. In the absence of any additional information, the coating
masses in the hot constants memos are the only basis for modeling the coatings on plates.
ICSBEP/IRPhEP benchmarks of ZPR/ZPPR assemblies typically assume that the uncertainty in
coating mass due to normal handling is 10% [5,6]. In the absence of any additional information,
this 10% uncertainty is reasonable. Note that this mass uncertainty due to plate handling applies
regardless of whether a) the coating is included in the as-built model or b) is neglected in the as-
built model and treated as a bias for adjustment of the experimental k eff.
There are two options for treating the uncertainty in coating mass:
 1. If a high-fidelity Monte Carlo or deterministic model corresponding to the as-built Monte
 Carlo model with the coatings exists, the analyst can perturb that model by changing the
 concentration of the coating by the assumed uncertainty in coating mass. The reactivity
 worth between these models is the worth of the uncertainty in coating mass.
 2. If the original Monte Carlo or deterministic model does not include the coatings, the analyst
 can construct two versions of the original model. In Version A, the coatings are added at
 the nominal reference values. In Version B, Version A is perturbed by changing the
 concentration of the coating by the assumed uncertainty. The reactivity worth between the
 models is the worth of the uncertainty in coating mass.
The worth of the uncertainty in coating mass is small, so it would probably be better to double the
coating mass uncertainty in any perturbed Monte Carlo model and then to take half of the
calculated reactivity worth between the two Monte Carlo models as the worth of the coating mass

 173

uncertainty. Since the reactivity worth of the uncertainty in the coating mass is small, it may be
easier to compute this worth with a deterministic model if a deterministic model exists.
The reactivity worth of the uncertainty in coating mass is included in the total uncertainty for the
criticality measurement.
If the coatings are not included in the reference as-built model, neglecting the coatings is treated
as a bias (see Section 7.1.4).
7.1.3.3 Sodium Plates
The ADEN library contains entries for several different groups of sodium plates, and the hot
constants memos include entries for a few additional sodium plate types that are not included in
the ADEN library. The sodium plate types that are not in the ADEN library are probably sodium
plates that were used rarely and only for special purposes.
All sodium plates consist of sodium in stainless steel cans. The initial ZPR-3 inventory did not
contain any sodium plates. In early ZPR-3 assemblies, aluminum plates were used to simulate
sodium. Holes were drilled in those aluminum plates to approximate the density of sodium. After
a few years, sodium plates were fabricated for ZPR-3. Plates designated as NAHY (sodium cans
– heavy) in the ADEN library and hot constants memos were canned sodium plates manufactured
for ZPR-3.
Canned sodium plates were fabricated in the early 1960s or mid-1960s for use in ZPR-6 and ZPR-
9. These plates are designated as NALT (sodium cans – light) in the ADEN library and hot
constants memos.
Plates designated as NA in the ADEN library and hot constants memos were manufactured in the
late 1960s. Some of the NA plates were shipped to ZPPR; the remainder of the NA plates were
used in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 at ANL-E.
In addition to the standard sodium plates, the ADEN library and hot constants memos show sodium
plates designated as NAT (sodium cans – tunnel). NAT plates were similar to NA plates, but a
NAT plate had a lateral tunnel or hole through the center of the plate, which is why NAT plates
were called sodium tunnel plates. The hole in the NAT plate provided a way to perform various

For example, gamma doses were measured with thermoluminescent dosimeters (TLDs). Some
TLDs were circular disks that could be placed in the hole in a sodium tunnel plate for irradiation
purposes. However, it is likely that sodium tunnel plates were used primarily for small sample
worth measurements in ZPR-9. The matrix tubes in the center row in ZPR-9 had holes on both
sides. For small sample worth measurements, special drawers and plates were loaded into those
matrix tubes. The sides of the special drawers and plates also had holes. A sample tube was
inserted through those holes from the outside of the matrix tubes to the center of the core. A
sample connected to a mechanism was moved through the sample tube to obtain a radial worth
profile for the sample.
In addition to the sodium plates described above, the hot constants memos list sodium plates
designated as NADW. The NADW plates also consisted of sodium in stainless steel cans.
According to the ANL-E hot constants memo, the NADW plates were part of the ZPR-3 inventory.

 174

The NADW plates had nominal dimensions of ¼ x 1 x L inches where L was 2, 3, 4, 6, 7 or 8.
The reduced (1 inch) height of the NADW plates probably means they were used in drawers where
it was necessary to run cables from experimental equipment in the front of a drawer through the
length of the drawer and/or to construct partial drawers at the core/radial blanket boundary.
Although the NADW sodium plates are described in the hot constants memos, there are no entries
for NADW plates in the ADEN library. The NADW sodium plates were probably used
infrequently because they are not included in the ADEN library and have never been used in any
ICSBEP/IRPhEP benchmarks of ZPR/ZPPR assemblies.
7.1.3.3.1 Sodium Plate Uncertainties
There are two separate and independent sets of uncertainties for sodium plates. One set of
uncertainties relates to the sodium in the cans, and the second set of uncertainties relates to the
stainless steel cans. The 0.15% mass uncertainty applies to the sodium and the cans independently.
Separate composition uncertainties apply to the sodium and the cans.
The ZPPR hot constants memo lists the NA sodium plates as being 99.93% Na, 0.04% Ca, 0.005%
O, 0.02% C, and 0.005% Cl. The listings for the other types of sodium plates (NAHY, NALT,
NAT) in the ZPPR hot constants memo show similar distributions of Na, Ca, O, C and Cl. The
Ca, O, C and Cl impurities are included in the ADEN library compositions for the various types
of sodium plates.
ZPPR-15A is used here as an example of uncertainty analysis for sodium plates. For ZPPR-15A,
the assumed 0.15% uncertainty in the mass of the sodium in the NA plates was calculated to be
worth 1.55 pcm. An upper bound on the effect of the amounts of Ca, O, C and Cl in the Na plates
was calculated by doubling the existing impurities, thereby yielding an uncertainty in k eff of 0.12
pcm. The quadrature sum of the worths of the 1 mass and impurity uncertainties for the sodium
is 1.55 pcm.
The reactivity worth of the uncertainty in the sodium plate composition, i.e., the amount of
impurity present in the sodium, is small. It is sufficient for uncertainty analysis purposes to assume
the uncertainty in the Ca, O, C and Cl content of the sodium plates is 100%. Refining the treatment
of the sodium impurities is not warranted because any realistic assumption regarding sodium
impurities will not have a significant effect on the total uncertainty.
The small worth of the sodium impurities illustrates a relevant point about impurities in general.
If the total reactivity worth of the impurities in a material is small and would make a negligible
contribution to the total uncertainty for the criticality measurement, it is not necessary to expend
effort in refining the calculation of the impurity contribution. It is sufficient to assume that the
worth of the uncertainty in the impurities is 50% – 100% of the worth of the impurities.
The known exceptions to the statements in the preceding paragraph are discussed below.
For any clad or canned material, mass and composition uncertainties for the can are independent
of mass and composition uncertainties for the canned material. The importance of the mass and
composition uncertainties for the canned material depend upon the nature of the canned material.
It is necessary to compute the mass and composition uncertainties for the sodium cans in addition
to the uncertainties for the sodium because the reactivity worth for the can uncertainties can be

 175

larger than the reactivity worth for uncertainties in the sodium in the cans. This is a byproduct of
the facts that a) the reactivity worth of sodium per unit mass is much lower than the reactivity
worth of stainless steel per unit mass and b) the mass of the stainless steel can is comparable to or
greater than the mass of sodium in the can, depending on the plate size.
All cans and most other stainless steel components (drawers, matrix tubes, stainless steel plates)
in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies were made of Type 304 stainless steel. The discussion of uncertainties
for the sodium cans will be deferred to the general discussion of uncertainties in stainless steel
components in Section 7.1.3.6. Table 7.2 shows the computed worth of sodium can uncertainties
in ZPPR-15A. For comparison, the total worth of uncertainties in the sodium was 1.55 pcm.
 Table 7.2. Worth of Sodium Can Uncertainties in ZPPR-15A.

 Component Assumed Nominal Worth,
 Uncertainty Uncertainty wt.% pcm
                                Mass                  0.15                    1.05
                                Mn                     0.1             1.0    1.02
                                Cr                     0.2             19.0   0.11
                                Ni                     0.2             9.25   1.02
 Total 1.79
7.1.3.4 Sodium Carbonate Plates
The ZPR/ZPPR plate inventory also contained sodium carbonate (Na 2CO3) plates. The main
function of the sodium carbonate plates was to supply oxygen to the core. Most ZPR/ZPPR
assemblies simulated oxide fuel or carbide fuel, but the ZPR/ZPPR fuel plates were metal such as
HEU, DU, Pu-U-Mo alloy and Pu-Al alloy. Simulating carbide fuel just involved putting enough
graphite plates in the drawers to achieve the required average U:C ratio or Pu:C ratio in the core.
Since there are no oxygen plates, simulating oxide fuel required adding plate materials that
contained oxygen. The sodium carbonate plates supplied some of the required oxygen. The other
plate types that provided the necessary oxygen were iron oxide (Fe 2O3) plates and depleted U3O8
plates. The experimenters could create a good simulation of oxide fuel by carefully mixing the
metal fuel plates with iron oxide plates, depleted U3O8 plates and sodium carbonate plates. The
sodium in the sodium carbonate plates also provided some of the sodium required for the
simulation.
Sodium carbonate plates were very similar to standard sodium plates in design and size. A sodium
carbonate plate consisted of sodium carbonate in a Type 304 stainless steel can. The identifier for
a sodium carbonate plate is NACO. In addition to standard sodium carbonate plates, the
ZPR/ZPPR plate inventory also contained a small number of sodium carbonate tunnel plates
(identifier NACT). Sodium carbonate plates had the same dimensions as NA sodium plates. The
NACO and NACT sodium carbonate plates are included in the ADEN library and hot constants
memos.

 176

7.1.3.4.1 Sodium Carbonate Plate Uncertainties
One set of uncertainties applies to the the sodium carbonate in the cans, and a separate set of
uncertainties applies to the cans. The 0.15% mass uncertainty applies to the sodium carbonate and
separately to the cans. The composition uncertainties for the sodium carbonate cans are identical
to the composition uncertainties for all stainless steel cans, so the discussion of can uncertainties
will be deferred to the general discussion of stainless steel uncertainties in Section 7.1.3.6.
In addition to Na, C and O, the sodium carbonate contained ~0.088 wt.% Cl, ~0.008 wt.% H,
~0.004 wt.% S and ~0.152 wt.% other elements according to the ZPPR hot constants memo. The
ADEN library entries for sodium carbonate plates include Na, C, O, Cl, H and S, but those entries
do not include the other elements. The other elements are not specified in any available documents,
so it is necessary to make some assumption about them. Section 7.1.3.1 provided some suggestions
regarding potential sources of information. The other option is to make some reasonable
assumption regarding the unspecified elements. For example, an analyst could assume the missing
0.152 wt.% consists of equal amounts of Si, Ca and Fe.
The Cl, H, S and assumed other elements are the impurities. An upper bound for the reactivity
worth of the uncertainty in the sodium carbonate composition could be determined by calculating
a model with the impurity concentration doubled and assuming a uniform probability distribution
over that interval [8]. Unless the reactivity effect of doubling the assumed impurities is relatively
large, i.e., large enough to have a significant effect on the total uncertainty for the criticality
measurement, further refinement of the impurity treatment in the sodium carbonate plates does not
seem to be warranted.
7.1.3.5 Iron Oxide Plates
Iron oxide plates were used to provide some of the oxygen required to simulate oxide fuel. The
iron oxide plates were neither clad nor coated, so an iron oxide plate consisted of just iron oxide.
Most iron oxide plates had a thickness of 1/8 th inch or 7/64th inch.
The ADEN library has entries for 1/8th inch plates and 7/64th inch plates. The ADEN library entries
for the 1/8th inch plates apparently are for mixed ANL-E plates and ANL-W plates after the ANL-
E plates were shipped to ZPPR. The hot constants memos, particularly the ANL-E hot constants
memo, list separate entries for many iron oxide plates from ZPR-3, ANL-E and ZPPR that are not
included in the ADEN library, so it is possible to identify the iron oxide plates used at ZPR-3,
ZPPR and ANL-E. For ZPPR assemblies, the iron oxide plates used after ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were
shut down were probably a mixture of ANL-E plates and ANL-W plates. The identifier for iron
oxide plates in the ADEN library and hot constants memos is FEO.
7.1.3.5.1 Iron Oxide Plate Uncertainties
The assumed 0.15% mass uncertainty applies to the iron oxide plates. For the ICSBEP benchmark
of the high 240Pu ZPR-6/7 core, the computed worth of the 0.15% mass uncertainty for iron oxide
plates was 2.1 pcm (see ICSBEP benchmark MIX-COMP-FAST-002 [5]).
Uncertainty in the composition of the iron oxide exists due to the presence of Fe 2O3, FeO and Fe
in the iron plates. There is no additional information regarding the amounts of Fe 2O3, FeO and Fe

 177

in the iron plates, so it is necessary to make some assumption regarding the uncertainty in the
amounts of Fe and O in the iron oxide plates.
For the ICSBEP benchmark of the high 240Pu ZPR-6/7 core, it was assumed that a 0.5% uncertainty
exists in the Fe weight percent. The Fe concentration was increased by this amount and the mass
was preserved by decreasing the O concentration. The resulting uncertainty in k eff was 5.4 pcm.
The ADEN library entries for the iron oxide plates only list masses for iron and oxygen. These
plates are listed in the hot constants memos as having ~0.6 wt.% impurities in the standard 1/8 th
inch iron oxide plates and impurities of 0.04 – 0.06 wt.% for the 7/64 th inch iron oxide plates. The
ZPPR hot constants memo entry for iron oxide plates states that the impurities include Ta, As, P,
W and unspecified other elements. There is no available information regarding the actual
distribution of elements in the impurity component. The analysis for the MIX-COMP-FAST-002
benchmark assumed the impurities consisted of 0.3 wt.% Si and 0.3 wt.% C. The resulting
uncertainty in keff was 12 pcm.
In retrospect, it probably would have been better to assume the 0.6 wt.% impurities are equally
divided among Ta, As, P, W, C and Si. Such preferential approaches are recommended for new
analysis activities on ZPR/ZPPR assemblies, but re-evaluating all past assemblies that used iron
oxide plates is not warranted given the existing computed worth. An upper bound for the reactivity
worth of the uncertainty in the impurity concentration could be determined by calculating a model
with the impurity concentration doubled and assuming a uniform probability distribution over that
interval.
7.1.3.6 Stainless Steel Components
The average composition in a drawer or group of drawers in a ZPR/ZPPR assembly simulated the
homogeneous composition of a region such as the core, blanket or reflector of a fast reactor. That
simulation required matching the average concentrations of fuel components, coolant, cladding
and structural materials in each region of the target reactor as closely as possible given the
limitations of the finite ZPR/ZPPR material inventory.
The matrix tubes in ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPPR were Type 304 stainless steel. The initial set of
matrix tubes installed in ZPR-9 were an aluminum alloy. Those aluminum alloy matrix tubes were
used for the first nine ZPR-9 assemblies, i.e., ZPR-9/1 through ZPR-9/9. At the end of the ZPR-
9/9 program, the aluminum alloy matrix tubes were removed, and Type 304 stainless steel matrix
tubes were installed in ZPR-9. Those stainless steel matrix tubes remained in ZPR-9 until ZPR-9
was shut down in the early 1980s.
Most drawers used in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies were Type 304 stainless steel although ZPR-3 had
an inventory of aluminum alloy drawers that were used in early ZPR-3 assemblies. Aluminum
alloy drawers also were used in early ZPR-9 assemblies (ZPR-9/1 through ZPR-9/9).
Cladding and structural materials in the target reactor were simulated by stainless steel in the
ZPR/ZPPR assembly. The matrix tubes, drawers and cladding on clad plates provided some of
the necessary stainless steel. Stainless steel plates provided the remainder of the required stainless
steel. The iron in iron oxide plates also contributed to the total iron content of the assembly.

 178

Most or all stainless steel plates used in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies were Type 304 stainless steel. The
ZPR/ZPPR inventories contained stainless steel plates of many sizes ranging from 1/8 x 2 x 2 inch
to 2 x 2 x 12 inch. It is not known whether the plates were purchased in finished form from the
vendors or whether the vendors supplied the stainless steel stock that was machined to the finished
form at Argonne. In either case, the stainless steel was obtained at various times and from various
suppliers.
An initial set of stainless steel plates was obtained for ZPR-3. Separates sets of stainless steel
plates were obtained in the mid-1960s for ANL-E and in the late 1960s for ZPPR when those
facilities began operating. Additional stainless steel plates of various sizes were obtained as
needed for specific programs.
The preceding paragraph also applies to the stainless steel drawers. Initial sets of stainless steel
drawers were fabricated for ZPR-3, ZPR-6, ZPR-9, and ZPPR. Additional drawers were fabricated
as they were needed to construct larger assemblies. Assembly sizes increased radially and axially
over the operational lifetime of the ZPR/ZPPR facilities. Longer cores, axial blankets and axial
reflectors required longer drawers and/or back drawers. Increasing the core radius, radial blanket
thickness and radial reflector thickness required more drawers.
ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 shared a common plate inventory. Stainless steel plates were not routinely
shared between ANL-E and ANL-W although some of the stainless steel plates in the ANL-E
inventory may have been sent to ZPPR after ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were shut down. In any case, the
drawer master figures for ZPPR assemblies and for at least the later assemblies built in ZPR-6 and
ZPR-9 indicate the types or specific lots of stainless steel plates in the drawers because those
figures show the identifiers for the plates.
It is not necessarily possible to identify plate types for hand-drawn drawer master figures from
ZPR-3 assemblies and early assemblies built in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9. In many cases, particularly in
the ZPR-3 assemblies, the hand-drawn figures may indicate plate sizes and materials but not plate
types. In some cases, the plate sizes (lengths) are not clear on the hand-drawn drawer master
figures. The colors on the hand-drawn figures indicate the different materials such as HEU, DU,
sodium, graphite and stainless steel in the drawer, but the hand-drawn figures do not necessarily
allow the analyst to distinguish different lots of the same material such as stainless steel plates
from different suppliers.
In those cases, it may be necessary to study the relevant hot constants memo for the facility to
determine which plates were or could have been used in the assembly. It may also be necessary
to add those specific plates to the ADEN library, particularly for ZPR-3 assemblies.
The ZPPR hot constants memo has the most complete list of minor constituents and impurities in
stainless steel materials. For the stainless steel matrix tubes, stainless steel drawers and most of
the stainless steel plate types, the ADEN library entries and the ZPPR hot constants memo list
masses for C, Si, P, S, Cr, Mn, Fe, Ni, Cu and Mo. However, there are a few stainless steel plate
types for which there are no masses listed for Cu and Mo.
For stainless steel cans or cladding, all ADEN library entries and the ZPPR hot constants memos
list masses for Cr, Mn, Fe and Ni. However, the minor constituents and impurities listed for the
cans vary by plate type for clad plates. All cans of the same type, i.e., same ADEN identifier, such

 179

as NA (sodium) or NACO (sodium carbonate) have the same minor constituents and impurities,
but cans of different types such as NA and PUMD (Pu-U-Mo plates manufactured by Dow) do not
necessarily have the same set of minor constituents and impurities.
7.1.3.6.1 Stainless Steel Component Uncertainties
The 0.15% mass uncertainty discussed above applies to all stainless steel plates, cans and drawers
unless better information is found for a particular material or component. One exception to the
generic 0.15% mass uncertainty is that the mass uncertainty for the matrix tubes is assumed to be
2%. The 2% mass uncertainty for the matrix tubes was developed by R. W. Schaefer and R. D.
McKnight, former ZPPR and ZPR staff analysts, to provide a reasonable upper limit for the
uncertainty in the mass of the matrix tubes in ZPR-3, ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR (see Section 7.1.3).
The matrix tubes, drawers, individual lots of stainless steel plates, and stainless steel cans for
different types of clad plates were obtained at different times and possibly from different vendors
in most cases. Consequently, the matrix tubes, drawers, individual lots of stainless steel plates,
and stainless steel clad on clad plates can be regarded as independent and uncorrelated for purposes
of uncertainty analysis.
Individual uncertainty components are added in quadrature to determine the total uncertainty based
on the following equation:
                                       σtot = √(σ12 + σ22 + σ32 + . . . + σn2)
Because the uncertainty components are added in quadrature, correlation or lack of correlation
between different components is an important consideration in uncertainty analysis. For example,
suppose there are three independent and uncorrelated sets of stainless steel plates and that the
computed mass uncertainty for each set is 2 pcm. Then the total mass uncertainty contribution
from the three sets of stainess steel plates is √12, i.e., √ (2 2 + 22 +22), or 3.46 pcm. On the other
hand, if those three sets of plates are lumped together and treated as a single unit for uncertainty
analysis, there is an implicit assumption that they are completely correlated. The computed mass
uncertainty for the lumped set could be significantly larger than 3.46 pcm. The same consideration
applies to composition uncertainties. Assumptions about correlation between different materials
can affect total uncertainty.
Total uncertainty can be increased significantly if different groups of plates are grouped together
and treated as a single set for uncertainty analysis. For example, in the original Rev. 0 version of
the ICSBEP benchmark for ZPR-6/10, the different lots or types of stainless steel plates plus the
matrix tubes, drawers and cans were treated as one set. The resulting contribution of the mass and
composition uncertainties of stainless steel components to the total uncertainty was 115 pcm in the
Rev. 0 version. In the Rev. 1 version of the ZPR-6/10 benchmark, the different lots or types of
stainless steel plates, the matrix tubes, the drawers and the clad on clad plates were treated as
independent and uncorrelated. As a result of this change, the contribution of the mass and
composition uncertainties of the stainless steel components to the total uncertainty was 70 pcm in
the Rev. 1 version (see ICSBEP benchmark PU-MET-INTER-002 [5]).
Total uncertainty can be significantly underestimated if real correlations are ignored. Likewise,
total uncertainty can be significantly overestimated if one assumes strong correlations for items
that are either uncorrelated or weakly correlated.

 180

The estimated weight percent uncertainty data for the stainless steel components are presented in
Table 7.3. A representative value of the weight percent is shown in parentheses. The uncertainty
for each of the major elements is taken (conservatively) to be 0.2 wt.%. The uncertainty for Mn
in the stainless steel is taken to be 0.15 wt.% (or 10% of nominal value) based on the variation of
batch assays given in the hot constants memos. The uncertainties for the remaining minor elements
were assumed to be one half of the last significant figure provided in the hot constants memos, due
to round-off error. The uncertainty for the sum of trace elements was assumed to be 10% of the
typical wt.%. The uncertainties shown in Table 7.3 are the stainless steel composition uncertainties
assumed in ICSBEP/IRPhEP benchmarks of ZPR/ZPPR assemblies [5,6] and recommended for
ZPR/ZPPR analysis efforts.

7.1.3.7 Graphite Plates
Graphite plates were used for at least two different reasons in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies. The fuel
plates used in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies were metal (Pu-U-Mo alloy, Pu-Al alloy, HEU, depleted
uranium). The majority of ZPR/ZPPR assemblies simulated oxide fuel by using depleted U 3O8
plates, iron oxide (Fe2O3) plates and/or sodium carbonate (Na2CO3) plates to provide the required
oxygen to simulate oxide fuel. However, there was significant interest in carbide fuels when the
ZPR/ZPPR machines operated. Some ZPR/ZPPR assemblies, such as ZPR-9/31, simulated
carbide fuels by inserting graphite plates in the drawers to provide the necessary carbon to simulate
carbide fuel.
Graphite plates also were used in some ZPR/ZPPR assemblies to either soften the neutron
spectrum or to spread the neutron spectrum out. These assemblies typically were used for basic
physics measurements in a particular energy range rather than as simulations of sodium-cooled
fast reactors intended for power production. For example, ZPR-6/10 was referred to as the
plutonium-carbon-stainless steel benchmark because core drawers in that assembly only contained
Pu-Al plates, graphite plates and stainless steel plates. The graphite plates in ZPR-6/10 shifted the
spectrum down into the intermediate range.
Graphite plates used in ZPR-3 were coated with a mixture of titanium oxide and Teflon according
to the ZPR-3 hot constants memo. J. A. Morman, an experimenter at ZPR-6 and ZPR-9, confirmed
that the graphite plates in the ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 plate inventory were not coated [2].
The ZPPR hot constants memo shows 2 x 2 inch graphite blocks of several lengths and states that
the original ZPR-3 graphite plates were eliminated from the ZPPR inventory in 1983. Graphite
plates definitely were used in ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 assemblies. It is not clear whether graphite
plates were used in ZPPR assemblies. A cursory examination of ANL-NT-175 [7] does not show
any ZPPR assemblies containing graphite plates in the core drawers. The identifier for graphite
plates in the ADEN library and hot constants memos is C.

 182

7.1.3.7.1 Graphite Plate Uncertainties
The 0.15% mass uncertainty discussed above applies to all graphite plates.
The graphite plates are listed in the ZPPR hot constants memo as being 100% C. The ZPR hot
constants memo for ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 indicates that the graphite contained 0.001 – 0.02 wt.%
hydrogen and 0.01 – 0.05 wt.% other elements, i.e., impurities. There is no other specific
information regarding the composition of the graphite plates in the hot constants memos, and the
ADEN library entries for graphite plates only list carbon.
The ZPR/ZPPR graphite plates would have been nuclear grade graphite similar to CP-2 graphite.
J. D. Bess, a former staff member at Idaho National Laboratory, provided results of an analysis of
CP-2 graphite performed by Evans Analytical Group for Idaho National Laboratory in 2012. Table
7.5 shows the results of this analysis of CP-2 graphite. In the absence of any other information,
Table 7.5 provides the best available estimate of the likely impurities in the ZPR/ZPPR graphite
plates.
The worth of the impurities shown in Table 7.5 was calculated with the ZPR-6/10 as-built model
for the ZPR-6/10 ICSBEP benchmark (ICSBEP benchmark PU-MET-INTER-002 [5]). The
computed worth of these impurities was 9 ± 6 pcm. The uncertainty in the impurity content for
the graphite plates in ZPR-6/10 was assumed to be 50% of the values listed in Table 7.5. The total
uncertainty for the impurities in the graphite plates in ZPR-6/10 is the quadrature sum of the Monte
Carlo statistical uncertainty and 4.5 pcm (9/2) which is 7.5 pcm. The reactivity worth of the
uncertainty related to the graphite impurities is not a dominant component of the total uncertainty
for ZPR-6/10, so refinement of the treatment of graphite impurities did not seem to be warranted.
The ZPR-6/10 neutron spectrum was significantly softer than a typical ZPR/ZPPR neutron
spectrum because the graphite plates in ZPR-6/10 were intended to increase the importance of the
spectrum in the intermediate energy range. The large number of graphite plates in the ZPR-6/10
core and the softer spectrum in ZPR-6/10 compared to a typical ZPR/ZPPR assembly increased
the worth of the graphite plate impurities in ZPR-6/10 compared to the worth of graphite plate
impurities in a more typical ZPR/ZPPR assembly that simulated a carbide-fueled LMFR.

In a thermal reactor, a common practice is to replace all of the impurities by an equivalent B (or
