energy. The boron equivalent approach is not applicable in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies because there
is no characteristic energy in a ZPR/ZPPR assembly comparable to 0.0625 eV in a light water
reactor. In addition, the energy dependence of the cross sections for the various impurities over
the relevant energy range in a ZPR/ZPPR assembly is probably more complex than the energy
dependence of cross sections for impurities at thermal energies.
7.1.3.7.2 Water Absorption in Graphite Plates
Hydrogen is not an impurity in graphite in the sense that the elements in Table 7.5 are impurities,
but hydrogen is the most important contaminant that may be present in the graphite plates. The
graphite plates were porous and could either absorb water vapor from the atmosphere or release
trapped water vapor to the atmosphere, depending on humidity and temperature.
The coatings on some ZPR-3 graphite plates provided a barrier to absorption of water vapor from
the atmosphere and a barrier to release of any water vapor that was present in the plates at the time
of coating. For uncoated graphite plates, the amount of water vapor present in the plates depended
upon location, time of year and temperature. The atmospheric humidity at ANL-W in the Idaho
desert was lower than the humidity level at ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 in Illinois, and humidity varies by
season. Elevated temperature would reduce the moisture content in the graphite plates. The
elevated temperature could be seasonal, or it could result from reactor operating conditions. ZPR-
6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR were designed with cooling systems that kept the average reactor core
temperature close to room temperature in the reactor cell. The retrofitted cooling system installed
in ZPR-3 kept the average reactor core temperature in the 30 °C – 40 °C range in a plutonium-
fueled assembly.
The staff of ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 measured the moisture content of the graphite plates in the ZPR-6
and ZPR-9 inventory and included the measured hydrogen content of the graphite plates in the
ANL-E (ZPR-6 and ZPR-9) hot constants memo. The ANL-E hot constants memo states that the
graphite plates used in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 contained 0.001 – 0.02 wt.% hydrogen.

 185

Unlike the graphite impurities discussed in Section 7.1.3.7.1, uncertainty in the moisture content
of the graphite plates is a very important uncertainty in graphite plates. In fact, uncertainty in the
moisture content of the graphite plates is the dominant uncertainty for graphite plates and is one
of the dominant uncertainties for an assembly containing graphite plates.
Entries for graphite plates in the ADEN library only include the mass of carbon in the plates; it is
necessary to add the assumed hydrogen mass to the ADEN library graphite plate entry to compute
the reactivity effect of moisture in the graphite plates. Likewise, it is necessary to include an
assumed hydrogen mass in new ADEN library entries for graphite plates.
The hot constants memos list a range of 0.001% – 0.02 wt.% for the hydrogen content of the
graphite plates. That range is equivalent to a hydrogen content between 10 ppm and 200 ppm in
the graphite plates. This is equivalent to a total moisture (water) content of approximately 100
ppm – 2000 ppm.
Because the hot constants memos list a range of hydrogen values in the graphite plates, engineering
judgement is required to estimate the average hydrogen content in the graphite plates in a given

The following are two examples from ICSBEP benchmarks of ZPR/ZPPR assemblies. The first
example is for the ZPR-3/53 benchmark (see benchmark MIX-MET-INTER-004 [5]):
The graphite plates used in ZPR-3/53 were actually part of the ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 inventory. They
were shipped to ANL-W for use in ZPR-3/53. It was assumed that a realistic value of the moisture
content for graphite plates in the ZPR-3/53 critical configuration was 300 ppm with an uncertainty
of 200 ppm. This is based on the following reasoning. The 100 ppm – 2000 ppm range is for the
plates at ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 in Illinois. The plates were shipped to the ZPR-3 facility in
southeastern Idaho for this experiment. Southeastern Idaho is a desert, which means that the
graphite plates were in the dry desert environment for at least several weeks in the summer of 1968
prior to the date of the criticality measurement. In addition, the plates were loaded in the reactor
for some of this time. Because the retrofitted cooling system devised for ZPR-3 had limited
cooling capability, temperatures in the reactor core generally ranged from 30 °C to 40 °C. This is
the temperature range during reactor operation when the cooling system was turned on. It is likely
that temperatures in the matrix halves would have been higher when the reactor was not operating
because the matrix halves would have been separated and the cooling system would not have been
turned on. The reactor would have been shut down and the tables would have been separated for
most of any 24-hour period and for all of any weekend.
While there was some moisture in the graphite plates, it seems unlikely that it could have been
much higher than 500 ppm given the environmental conditions. It also seems unlikely that the
moisture content would have been much less than 100 ppm. The computed worth of 300 ppm of
hydrogen is ~60 pcm. The computed worth of the 200 ppm uncertainty in the moisture content is
~40 pcm.
The second example is from the ICSBEP benchmark for ZPR-3/59 (see benchmark PU-MET-
INTER-004 [5]):
ZPR-3/59 used coated graphite plates from the ZPR-3 inventory. The ZPR-3 hot constants memo
states that the coated graphite plates contained less than 70 ppm hydrogen. It is not known whether

 186

this value reflected a range of measured values or a detection limit. The coating would have
inhibited changes in the hydrogen content of the plates resulting from changes in environmental
conditions. It was assumed that the average hydrogen content in the graphite plates was 35 ppm
with a 35 ppm uncertainty which was treated as a bounding uncertainty with uniform probability
distribution. The computed worth of the 35 ppm hydrogen uncertainty is ~66 pcm.
The ICSBEP uncertainty guide [8] discusses assumed probability distributions for uncertainties
such as the uncertainty in the moisture content of the graphite plates.
The reactivity effects of the moisture content in graphite plates are not necessarily negligible. In
the ZPR-3/53 example, the assumed 300 ± 200 ppm hydrogen content had a computed reactivity
worth of 60 ± 40 pcm. In the ZPR-3/59 example, the assumed 35 ± 35 ppm hydrogen content had
a computed reactivity worth of 66 ± 66 pcm.
The options for treating the moisture content in the graphite are identical to the options for treating
the coatings on plates. Option 1 is to include the moisture content of the graphite plates in the
reference as-built model. If the moisture content of the graphite is included in the reference as-
built model, there is no bias, and the total uncertainty for the moisture content of the graphite is
included in the total uncertainty for the experimental k eff. If option 1 is adopted, the reactivity
worth of the uncertainty in the moisture content of the graphite is determined in the same way as
the uncertainty in the coating mass described in Section 7.1.3.2.1.
Option 2 is to neglect the moisture content of the graphite plates in the reference as-built model.
Neglecting the moisture content of the graphite plates introduces a bias that is corrected by
adjusting the experimental keff to compensate for this bias as discussed above and in Section 7.1.4.
Regardless of whether option 1 or option 2 is used, the worth of the uncertainty in the moisture
content of the graphite plates must be included in the total uncertainty for the criticality

7.1.3.8 Depleted Uranium Plates
The ZPR/ZPPR plate inventories contained large numbers of depleted uranium metal plates.
Those plates can be divided into two size categories. The first category consisted of small depleted
uranium (DU) plates with nominal dimensions of 1/8 x 2 x L inches where L ranged from 2 to 8
inches. There also were limited numbers of DU plates with a thickness of 1/16 th inch or heights
less than 2 inch. DU plates in the first size category were loaded into core drawers with HEU
plates to produce the desired average 235U enrichment in the core, and they were loaded into core
drawers with Pu-U-Mo plates or Pu-Al plates to produce the desired Pu:U ratio in the core. They
were also loaded into drawers with other plate types to produce the desired radial or axial blanket
composition.
The second size category consisted of large DU plates or blocks with nominal dimensions of 1 x
1 x L inches or 2 x 2 x L inches where L ranged from 1 to 5 inches. These blocks were loaded
behind the core to form the axial blanket or reflector and outside the core to form the radial blanket
or reflector. The ZPR/ZPPR staff constructed more realistic blankets and reflectors for later
assemblies, but the depleted uranium blocks were used for that purpose in many of the earlier

 187

The DU blocks also isolated the core from room return. Room return refers to reflection of
neutrons back into the assembly from external structures such as the tables, the side supports
constraining the matrix tubes and the reactor cell.
ZPR-3 received a shipment of DU plates prior to the start of operations in 1955. At least one
additional set of DU plates was delivered to ZPR-3 subsequently. An initial set of DU plates was
fabricated for ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 in the early 1960s, and additional DU plates may have been
fabricated for ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 at a later date. The first set of DU plates was fabricated for ZPPR
in the late 1960s, and it is likely that additional DU plates were required at ZPPR, especially after
the ZPPR matrix was expanded from 53 x 55 to 77 x 77 in the early 1970s. The procurement and
fabrication data for the DU plates used at ZPR-3, ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR are no longer available.
The individual lots of DU plates used at ZPR-3, ZPR-6, ZPR-9, and ZPPR were manufactured at
different times from different lots of source material. The same general uncertainties (plate mass,
235
 U content, impurities, etc.) apply to all DU plates at the four ZPR/ZPPR facilities.
The issue of separate plate inventories is relevant to constructing models of ZPR/ZPPR assemblies.
There were isolated instances in which DU plates were shared, but generally each facility used its
own DU plates. After ZPR-3 was shut down, the fuel plates and the more valuable non-fuel plates
in the ZPR-3 inventory were transferred to ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR. Likewise, after the ZPR-6
and ZPR-9 facilities were shut down, the fuel plates and the more valuable non-fuel plates in the
ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 inventory were shipped to ZPPR. If the loading records, drawer master figures
or other documents for an assembly indicate that DU plates from different facilities were used in
that assembly, the DU plates from the different assemblies can be treated as independent for
uncertainty analysis.
Note that depleted uranium plates were designated as UD (uranium depleted) in the ADEN library
and in the hot constants memos.
The ADEN library was initially developed when ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR were operating, and the
ZPPR staff continued making entries after ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were shut down in the early 1980s.
Since the ADEN library was developed to support ongoing operations at ZPPR, ZPR-6, and ZPR-
9, and was developed after ZPR-3 was shut down, the only ADEN library entries for ZPR-3 plates
are probably for the limited set of ZPR-3 plates (primarily HEU plates, Pu-Al plates, the Pu-U-Mo
SEFOR plates, sodium plates and some DU plates) that were used in the other facilities when ZPR-
3 was shut down. The ZPR-3 DU plates show up in the last ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR hot constants
memos, so those DU plates were in the inventories of those facilities after ZPR-3 shut down.
The hot constants memos list the ADEN library numbers for at least some of the DU plates that
are in the ADEN library. The most recent hot constants memo available is the ZPPR hot contants
memo from July 1983. DU plates may have been added to the ADEN library after July 1983, so
some DU plates listed without identification labels or numbers in the hot constants memos may
have ADEN library entries. It would be necessary to compare the depleted uranium masses in
ADEN library entries with the depleted uranium masses listed in the hot constants memos to
determine whether any DU plates were added to the ADEN library after the last ZPPR hot
constants memo was issued in 1983.

 188

The ADEN library only identifies the DU plate entries by ADEN number and the “UD” ADEN
identifier for depleted uranium, so it is impossible to determine the facility inventory to which a
given DU entry belonged from just the ADEN entry. The link between the facility plate inventory
to which a DU plate belonged and the ADEN library entry is provided by the ZPPR and ANL-E
hot constants memos. For each DU plate type/size, the ANL-E and ZPPR hot constants memos
list the lot which basically means the inventory to which the plate belonged. In the hot constants
memos and ADEN library descriptions, “APE” refers to “Applied Physics Division – East” or
ANL-E, and “APW” refers to “Applied Physics Division – West” or ANL-W. APE denotes the
plate inventory for ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 at ANL-E. APW1 denotes the ZPR-3 plate inventory, and
APW2 denotes the ZPPR plate inventory at ANL-W. For some DU plate sizes, e.g., the 1/8 x 2 x
3 inch DU plates, the hot constants memos show separate entries for APE, APW1 and APW2
because each facility had a separate set of those plates.
The ADEN library tends to be focused primarily on the plates used at ZPPR and in later assemblies
in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9. In most cases, ZPR-3 DU plates are not included in the ADEN library, so it
may be necessary to add specific ZPR-3 DU plate types to the ADEN library for analysis of a ZPR-
3 assembly. This may also be true to a lesser extent for some DU plates in the ANL-E inventory.
In general, it is necessary to compare the DU entries in the ADEN library with the relevant hot
constants memo for the facility and assembly of interest to determine whether the plates used in
that assembly are included in the ADEN library. In practice, the preceding sentence applies to all
plate types used in an assembly.
The ADEN library only lists 235U mass and 238U mass for DU plates. The ZPPR hot constants
memo lists 235U mass, 238U mass and average weight for a DU plate, but the average weight or
mass is just the sum of the 235U mass and 238U mass. The ANL-E hot constants memo lists 235U
mass and core weight. Any 234U mass present is assumed to be included with the 238U weight or
core weight of the plate. There is no way to determine the 234U content or impurity content of any
DU plate based upon the ADEN library and hot constants memos.
The DU plates were coated with Kel-F, a paintlike substance, to inhibit corrosion and material loss
during handing (see Section 7.1.3.27.1.3.2).
The ZPPR ADEN library entries do not include the Kel-F because ZPR/ZPPR analysts did not
include Kel-F in their models. However, the hot contants memos do list the average Kel-F mass
per plate for coated plates, so it is possible to add the Kel-F to the ADEN library entries.
Standards of practice evolve over time, and what were regarded as acceptable modeling
approximations decades ago are not regarded as acceptable today. The present practice is to
account for the Kel-F. The easiest way to account for the Kel-F is to add the Kel-F to the ADEN
library entries for coated plates and to include the Kel-F in the as-built model. The alternative is
to a) construct the as-built model without Kel-F and compute k eff without Kel-F and then b) add
the Kel-F to the coated plates in a copy of the as-built model and compute k eff with Kel-F. The
reactivity worth between these models is the bias in k eff associated with neglecting the Kel-F. From
experience, it is easier and faster to add Kel-F to the ADEN entries for coated plates and to include
the Kel-F in the base as-built model. The issue of bias associated with features that are neglected
in as-built models is discussed in more detail in Section 7.1.4.

 189

The original manufacturing and procurement documents for the DU plates may have listed the
impurities in the DU, but those documents are no longer available. The ADEN library and the hot
constants memos do not provide any information regarding impurities in the DU plates. In the
absence of any direct information, it is necessary to make some reasonable assumption regarding
impurities in the DU plates.
Impurities can be important in a thermal reactor because some impurities such as B and Cd have
large capture cross sections at thermal energies. Various other inpurities have smaller, but
nevertheless, significant capture cross sections for low energy neutrons. In the spectrum of a
typical ZPR/ZPPR assembly, neutron capture in impurities is small. Consequently, any reasonable
assumption regarding DU impurities is not likely to have a significant effect on k eff or on the total
uncertainty for the criticality measurement.
One reasonable assumption is that the reactivity worth of the DU impurities is approximately the
same as the reactivity worth of the mass uncertainty for the DU plates.
A second and better option is to examine a standard specification for natural or depleted uranium
such as an ASTM specification, specifications from American uranium suppliers, commercial
vendor documents or similar sources for natural or depleted uranium and to assume that the
impurities listed in those source documents are a reasonable approximation of the impurities in the
ANL depleted uranium. An ASTM specification is a reasonable generic composition for uranium.
Specifications from uranium suppliers may show a range of impurities and a range of impurity
values, so it is necessary to choose representative values. One relevant issue regarding
specifications from suppliers is that reducing impurity levels costs money. A supplier has no
motivation to reduce impurities below the levels that are acceptable for the intended use such as
manufacturing commercial reactor fuel.
A third option is to use an actual impurity measurement if such a measurement is available. A
chemical analysis was performed in 2018 of depleted uranium shipped from Y-12 to CERCA [9].
Table 7.6 shows the principal impurities from that analysis. It seems reasonable to assume that
the impurities listed in Table 7.6 are representative of depleted uranium impurities and that these
impurities apply to the DU plates. One could argue that Table 7.6 represents a single sample from
a single lot of DU, but Table 7.6 at least provides some actual measured data for depleted uranium.
Additional measured impurity data for DU would allow the analyst to refine the estimate of
impurities in the DU plates in the ANL-E and ANL-W inventories.
 Table 7.6. Recommended Impurity Composition for DU Plates.

                                              Ni           82          0.02839
                                              Fe          769          0.26627
                                              Cu           73          0.02528
                                              Si           30          0.01039

The options for treating DU impurities are the same as the options for treating the Kel-F coating
on DU plates. The impurities in DU can be included in the base as-built model. As an alternative,
the impurities in the DU can be neglected in the base as-built model, and the reactivity worth of
the impurities can be treated as a bias (see Section 7.1.4).
In principle, a first order approximation for the 234U content of the DU plates might be obtained
from the 234U content of depleted uranium produced in the United States today, but this would still
be only a reasonable approximation rather than an actual measured value for the DU plates in the
ZPR/ZPPR plate inventories.
7.1.3.8.1. Depleted Uranium Plate Uncertainties
The 0.15 % mass uncertainty discussed above applies to the DU metal plates.
According to the ANL-E hot constants memo, the average 235U enrichment of the APW1 (ZPR-3)
DU plates was 0.206 wt.%, the average 235U enrichment of the APW2 (ZPPR) DU plates was
0.220 wt.%, and the average 235U enrichment of the APE (ANL-E) DU plates was 0.211 wt.%.
The uncertainties in the 235U enrichments for APW1 DU plates, APW2 DU plates and APE DU
plates are not listed, so it is necessary to assign 235U enrichment uncertainty based on indirect
evidence.
The depleted U3O8 plates used in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies were manufactured by NUMEC. The
specification for production of these plates required a 235U enrichment of 0.22 ± 0.02 wt.% in the
uranium component. It appears that the 0.02 wt.% represented the two-sigma confidence interval,
so the corresponding one-sigma uncertainty for the 235U enrichment of the depleted U3O8 plates is
0.01 wt.%.
In general, the DU contribution of the DU metal plates to the core, blanket and/or reflector of a
ZPR/ZPPR assembly equaled or exceeded the corresponding contribution from the depleted U 3O8
plates. If the ZPR/ZPPR experimenters were concerned about tight specifications for 235U content
of the depleted U3O8 plates, it seems reasonable to assume they would have been equally concerned
about tight specifications for the 235U content of DU metal plates. In the absence of any other
information, a one-sigma uncertainty for the 235U enrichment of the DU metal plates of 0.01 wt.%
is recommended.
There is a tendency to dismiss uncertainties in the DU plates because “it is only depleted uranium.”
That tendency can result in an underestimate of the total uncertainty for two reasons. First, the
total mass of depleted uranium in the core, blanket and reflector of a ZPR/ZPPR assembly is large
in most cases, so the total mass of 235U in that depleted uranium is not negligible.
Second, the assumed 0.01 wt.% uncertainty in the 235U enrichment of the depleted uranium
corresponds to ~5% uncertainty in the mass of 235U in that depleted uranium. The 235U enrichment
uncertainty for HEU plates was very much smaller than 5%. Likewise, the uncertainty in the 239Pu
content of a Pu-U-Mo plate or Pu-Al plate was very much smaller than 5%. Consequently, the
reactivity worth of the uncertainty in the 235U enrichment in depleted uranium is not necessarily

 191

negligible relative to the reactivity worth of the uncertainty in the 235U enrichment of HEU plates
or the reactivity worth of the uncertainty in the 239Pu content of a Pu-U-Mo plate or Pu-Al plate.
One additional factor to consider is correlation. The 0.15% mass uncertainty is assumed to be a
systematic uncertainty because it reflects lack of knowledge regarding the equipment and
procedure for weighing plates. Consequently, the mass uncertainty for all DU plates from one lot
(APW1, APW2 or APE) is assumed to be fully correlated because all DU plates in one facility
inventory are assumed to be weighed with the same equipment, calibration standards and
procedure. However, the equipment and calibration standards used at ANL-E probably were not
the equipment and calibration standards used at ANL-W, so it is likely that the mass uncertainty
for DU plates in the ANL-E inventory is not correlated with the mass uncertainty for DU plates in
the inventories of ZPR-3 and ZPPR and that the mass uncertainties for ANL-E plates and ANL-W
plates are independent.
The correlation issue for the mass uncertainty is less clear for ZPR-3 and ZPPR plates because the
same equipment and calibration standards could have been used to weigh DU plates in the ZPR-3
inventory and DU plates in the ZPPR inventory. On the other hand, it is likely that relatively few
ZPR-3 DU plates (if any) were used in a ZPPR assembly or ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 assembly, so the
effect of assuming that the mass uncertainty is fully correlated for ZPR-3 DU plates and DU plates
in the ZPPR or ANL-E DU inventories is likely to be small.
Some or all of the ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 DU plates were shipped to ZPPR after ZPR-6 and ZPR-9
were shut down. The ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 plates were used in some ZPPR assemblies, e.g., ZPPR-
15, if there were not enough ZPPR DU plates of the required sizes. It seems reasonable to assume
that the mass uncertainties for the ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 DU plates and the ZPPR DU plates were
uncorrelated and independent if both ZPPR DU plates and ANL-E DU plates were used in the
same ZPPR assembly.
Available documents do not list the source(s) of the depleted uranium used in the various lots of
DU plates. The APW1 DU plates, APW2 DU plates and APE DU plates were acquired at different
times, so it seems reasonable to assume the 235U enrichment uncertainty is uncorrelated between
the APW1 DU plates, the APW2 DU plates and the APE DU plates. In practice, the correlation
issue for the mass uncertainty or the 235U enrichment uncertainty only matters when a significant
number of APE DU plates were used in a ZPPR assembly. Otherwise, the mass uncertainty can
be considered to be fully correlated for all DU plates used in an assembly, and the 235U enrichment
uncertainty can be considered to be fully correlated for all DU plates used in an assembly.
Some of the Kel-F coating on the DU plates wore off during plate handling. ICSBEP/IRPhEP
benchmarks of ZPR/ZPPR assemblies typically assume that the uncertainty in coating mass due to
normal handling is 10% [5,6]. In the absence of any additional information, this 10% uncertainty
is reasonable. Note that this mass uncertainty due to plate handling applies regardless of whether
a) the coating is included in the as-built model or b) the coating is neglected in the as-built model
and treated as a bias for adjustment of the experimental keff.
7.1.3.9 Natural Uranium Plates
The ZPR/ZPPR plate inventories included a few thousand natural uranium metal plates in each of
several sizes. There were not enough natural uranium plates to build a full ZPR/ZPPR core, but

 192

there were enough of these plates to build a central zone or to distribute them in some of the core
drawer masters throughout the core. In any case, the natural uranium plates were used
occasionally, but they were not used in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies on a regular basis.
The ZPPR and ANL-E hot constants memos and the ADEN library list only the 235U mass and the
238
 U mass in a natural uranium plate; any 234U present in natural uranium plates is lumped with the
238
 U mass or total plate core mass in the natural uranium plates. It seems reasonable to use any
standard nuclear data source such as Baum [10] to determine the 234U content of natural uranium
plates. The identifier for natural uranium plates in the ADEN library and hot constants memos is
UN.
The natural uranium plates were coated with Kel-F. The treatment of the Kel-F coating on natural
uranium plates should be consistent with the treatment of the Kel-F coating on depleted uranium
plates in any analysis that includes natural uranium plates and depleted uranium plates.
7.1.3.9.1 Natural Uranium Plate Uncertainties
The 0.15% mass uncertainty discussed above applies to the natural uranium plates. Likewise, the
10% uncertainty in the mass of the Kel-F coating discussed in Section 7.1.3.8 applies to the natural
uranium plates. There may be a small uncertainty in the isotopic distribution in natural uranium
plates, and there will be impurities in natural uranium plates. In principle, the approach to treating
impurities in natural uranium plates should be consistent with the corresponding treatment of
impurities in the DU metal plates. In practice, the uncertainties in the natural uranium plates are
generally negligible because the total number of natural uranium plates in a ZPR/ZPPR assembly
is likely to be small compared to the number of DU plates in that assembly.
To date, the experience with modeling natural uranium plates is limited to ZPPR-15. In ZPPR-15,
the worth of the 0.15% mass uncertainty for the natural uranium plates was computed to be 0.01
pcm and thus refining values for other natural uranium plate uncertainties was unwarranted.
7.1.3.10 Depleted U3O8 Plates
The plate inventories of the ZPR/ZPPR facilities contained large numbers of depleted U 3O8 plates.
Those plates served several purposes. The majority of ZPR/ZPPR assemblies simulated oxide
fuel, and the depleted U3O8 plates provided some of the oxygen required to simulate UO2 or PuO2.
For assemblies containing Pu-U-Mo plates, the depleted U3O8 plates also provided depleted
uranium to match the required uranium content and Pu:U ratio of the target reactor. For assemblies
containing HEU fuel plates, the depleted U3O8 plates provided depleted uranium to match the
required uranium content and 235U enrichment of the target reactor.
The depleted U3O8 plates were coated with Kel-F. Historically, ZPR/ZPPR analysts neglected
coatings such as Kel-F when they analyzed ZPR/ZPPR assemblies. The Kel-F coating on the
depleted U3O8 plates can be included in the base as-built model or it can be omitted from the base
as-built model and treated as a bias as described above and in Section 7.1.4. In either case, the
treatment of the Kel-F coating on depleted U3O8 plates should be consistent with the treatment of
Kel-F on depleted uranium metal plates.

 193

The ADEN library and hot constants memo entries for depleted U 3O8 plates only list 235U and 238U.
Any 234U that may have been present in the depleted uranium component of the U 3O8 is assumed
to be combined with the 238U.
The identifier for depleted U3O8 plates in the ADEN library and hot constants memos is UOD8.
7.1.3.10.1 Depleted U3O8 Plate Uncertainties
The ANL-E hot constants memo indicates that there were depleted U 3O8 plates in the ZPR-3
inventory (APW1 lot), ZPPR inventory (APW2 lot) and ANL-E (APE) inventory, but the only
ADEN library entries for depleted U3O8 plates (ADEN identifier UOD8) are for depleted U3O8
plates in the ZPPR inventory. The ZPPR and ANL-E hot constants memos shows slightly different
masses for the constituents of depleted U3O8 plates of the same sizes in the APW1 lot, APW2 lot
and APE lot. It seems likely that any depleted U3O8 plates in ZPR-3 assemblies came from lot
APW1 and that any depleted U3O8 plates in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 came from lot APE. The
conservative assumption is that any depleted U3O8 plates in a ZPPR assembly came from lot
APW2. Consequently, the conservative assumption is that any depleted U 3O8 plate uncertainty
for a ZPR/ZPPR assembly is fully correlated for all depleted U 3O8 plates in that assembly.
The 0.15% mass uncertainty discussed above applies to the depleted U 3O8 plates.
The depleted U3O8 plates were manufactured by NUMEC. The specification for production of
these plates required a 235U enrichment of 0.22 ± 0.02 wt.% in the uranium component. It appears
that the 0.02 wt.% represented a two sigma confidence interval, so the corresponding one sigma
uncertainty for the 235U enrichment of the depleted U3O8 plates is 0.01 wt.%.
There is no available information concerning impurities in the depleted U 3O8 plates. In ICSBEP
benchmarks of ZPR/ZPPR assemblies [5,6], a 0.042 wt.% contamination of iron was assumed in
the depleted U3O8 plates based on an impurity level of 0.042 wt.% listed in the hot constants
memos.
It would be more accurate to treat impurities in depleted U 3O8 plates by one of the methods listed
in Section 7.1.3.8 for the DU metal plates. It might be possible to find an ASTM specification,
commercial vendor document, materials handbook entry or other document as a source for a
representative set of impurities in U3O8. If no data can be found for U3O8, one reasonable
alternative is to assume that all impurities in the U3O8 are associated with the uranium component.
The options discussed in Section 7.1.3.8 for treating impurities in DU metal plates can then be
applied to the depleted U3O8 plates. In any case, it is unlikely that uncertainties related to
impurities in DU metal plates or depleted U3O8 plates will make significant contributions to the
total uncertainty for the criticality measurement.
The uncertainty for the Kel-F coating on the depleted U3O8 plates is dominated by the possibility
that some flaked off in handling the plates. It is assumed, that 10% of the coating could have been
lost for purposes of uncertainty analysis. Treatment of the Kel-F coating on the depleted U 3O8
plates and of the 10% uncertainty in Kel-F mass associated with handing the U 3O8 plates should
be consistent with the treatment of the Kel-F coating on DU plates discussed in Section 7.1.3.8.

 194

7.1.3.11          HEU Plates
The initial fuel plates in the ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 inventory were HEU metal plates and the
DU metal plates that were mixed with HEU plates in core drawers to obtain the desired average
235
 U enrichment in the core. ANL-W (ZPR-3) and ANL-E (ZPR-6 and ZPR-9) maintained
separate inventories of HEU plates until ZPR-3 was shut down.
The ANL-E hot constants memo clearly distinguishes ANL-W HEU plates from ANL-E HEU
plates. Most ANL-W HEU plates had dimensions of 1/8 x 2 x L inches and 1/16 x 2 x L inches
where L = 1, 2 or 3. Most ANL-E HEU plates had dimensions of 1/16 x 2 x L inches where L =
1, 2 or 3. ANL-E also had a limited number of HEU plates with thicknesses of 1/32 nd inch or
1/64th inch and a limited number of HEU plates with heights less than 2 inches.
ZPR-3 acquired Pu-Al plates in the early 1960s and Pu-U-Mo plates in the mid 1960s. Based on
examination of the assembly descriptions in ANL-NT-175 [7], plutonium fuel was not used in
ZPR-6 or ZPR-9 until approximately 1969. That time frame coincides with manufacture of Pu-U-
Mo plates by Dow and NUMEC for ANL-W and ANL-E.
It is not clear whether the ZPR-3 HEU plates were transferred to ZPPR or ANL-E after ZPR-3 was
shut down. ANL-NT-175 [7] indicates that all ZPPR assemblies were plutonium-fueled until
ZPPR-14 was built in 1985, which occurred after the HEU plates in the ANL-E inventory were
shipped to ZPPR. In any case, the ZPR-3 inventory of HEU plates would not have been sufficient
to build a uranium-fueled assembly at ZPPR.
Nearly all HEU plates consisted of HEU metal with a 235U enrichment of 93%. According to the
ANL-E hot constants memo, there were some HEU metal plates with 235U enrichments of 20%
and 31%. However, the numbers of HEU plates with 20% enrichment and 31% enrichment were
small, and it seems likely that such plates were only used to construct small zones in the center of
an assembly to perform special measurements.
The HEU plates used in ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were uranium metal plates coated with Kel-F.
All HEU plates in the ANL-E inventory were shipped to ZPPR after ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were shut
down in the early 1980s. The ZPPR staff cleaned the HEU plates, removed the Kel-F coating and
placed the bare metal plates in stainless steel cans. Various combinations of HEU plates were
placed in the cans to produce canned HEU plates with nominal dimensions of 1/16 x 2 x L inches
and 1/8 x 2 x L inches where L was 4, 6 or 8.
The word “nominal” is a relevant consideration for the canned HEU plates. The presence of the
can increased the external plate thickness to a value slightly greater than 0.0625 inches or 0.125
inches. Likewise, the can increased the external plate height to a value slightly larger than 2 inches
and the external plate length to a value slightly larger than 4, 6 or 8 inches.
Table 7.7 shows the nine sets of canned HEU plates used at ZPPR. It is important to note that
plates of the same nominal size in different series are not interchangeable for modeling purposes.
U93A and U93B are not identical, U93D and U93E are not identical, and U93G and U93H are not
identical. The bare metal plates had lengths of 1, 2 and 3 inches, and these different plate lengths
could be combined in different ways to produce the nominal lengths shown in Table 7.7. For
example, a 6 inch length could consist of two 3 inch plates, three 2 inch plates, or even a 1, 2, and
3 inch plate combination. An 8 inch length could be similarly broken into 1, 2, and 3 inch base

 195

parts. All canned plates in the same series contained the same combination of bare metal plates,
but plates in two different series such as A and B contained different combinations of bare metal
plates.

The ADEN library contains entries for all canned HEU plates (series A – I) used at ZPPR, but
there are limited ADEN library entries for the unclad HEU plates used at ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-
9. There are 599 entries in the original ADEN library. The ADEN numbers for the canned HEU
plates are 280 – 288, which indicates that the canned HEU plate entries were added while ZPPR
was operating. The ADEN numbers for the nine unclad HEU plates in the ADEN library range
from 521 to 588. This indicates that the ADEN library entries for unclad HEU plates were added
in the late 1990s or early 2000s as they were needed to prepare ICSBEP/IRPhEP benchmarks of
ZPR-3, ZPR-6 or ZPR-9 assemblies [5,6].
The ADEN library does not contain entries for all unclad HEU plates or DU plates used at ZPR-
3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9. If an analyst wants to create an as-built model for a uranium-fueled assembly
in ZPR-3, ZPR-6 or ZPR-9, it is necessary to compare the ADEN library entries for DU plates and
unclad HEU plates to the entries in the hot constants memos. The DU and HEU plate entries in
the ADEN library do not necessarily correspond to the DU and HEU plates in the assembly of
interest, so it may be necessary to add DU plates or unclad HEU plates to the ADEN library in
some cases. The new entries would be based on the data in the hot constants memos.
7.1.3.11.1 HEU Plate Uncertainties
The 0.15% mass uncertainty discussed above applies to the HEU plates (bare or canned). In the
case of canned HEU plates, this mass uncertainty applies separately to the HEU metal and the can.

 196

The stainless steel cans in the canned HEU plates used at ZPPR were made of Type 304 stainless
steel. Mass and composition uncertainties related to these stainless steel cans are treated in the
same way as uncertainties in mass and composition for other stainless steel components (see
Section 7.1.3.6).

7.1.3.11.1.1 HEU Enrichment
The original fabrication and procurement documents for the HEU plates are no longer available,
so it is necessary to use later measurements to determine the isotopic distribution and associated
uncertainties for the HEU metal. There are three sources of evidence currently available regarding
the uncertainties in the isotopic weight percents for the HEU metal in the coated or canned HEU
plates. One is a 1982 internal memorandum on the uncertainty in a measurement that used 1/16 x
2 x 3 inch plates. These values are shown (rounded to two decimal places) in the third column of
Table 7.8. That memo quotes an enrichment of 93.18 ± 0.02 wt.% observed in selected SPM
records. This quoted uncertainty appears reasonable. In fact, it is likely that the enrichment for
any single fuel fabrication batch would have been known even better. However, because of the
large inventory of 93% enriched uranium fuel, the enrichment was derived from many fuel batches.

The enrichment values quoted in the SPM records are consistent with the second source which is
a series of mass spectroscopy measurements performed on 1/16 inch plates in 1996. The quoted
uncertainties in measurement of the uranium weight fractions for a single sample were 1%, 0.25%,
2.5% and 0.5% for 234U, 235U, 236U and 238U, respectively. The observed consistency among 20
samples is much better than the quoted measurement uncertainties. The fourth column of Table
7.8 shows estimated uncertainties based upon the standard deviation of these measured values.
The review of a limited number of mass-spectroscopy measurements on 1/8 inch plates indicated
a similar consistency of the measured values and the mean enrichment values.
Finally, an estimate of the uncertainties in the weight fractions for the enriched uranium can be
inferred from the distribution of the enrichment values given in the ZPPR Hot Constants Memo.
The 235U weight percent values range from 93.05 to 93.30. These values appear to have a normal
distribution with ~70% of the values within ± 0.05% of their mean value. Estimated uncertainty

 197

values based on the distribution of these quoted enrichments, shown in the last column of Table
7.8, are consistent with the previous values and would appear to cover possible systematic
uncertainties without adding unnecessary conservatism. Because the sum of the uranium isotopic
fractions should be 100.0%, the uncertainty in the 238U weight fractions is also assumed to be ±0.05
wt.%.
In general, the 0.15% mass uncertainty for the HEU plates and the uncertainty in the 235U content
of the HEU metal make significant contributions to the total uncertainty in the criticality
measurement for a uranium-fueled assembly. The uncertainty contributions arising from the
uncertainties in the masses of 234U and 236U are small.
7.1.3.11.2 HEU Impurities
Impurity content in the enriched uranium is treated in two parts. The first impurity component is
the initial impurities that were present in the HEU metal when the original HEU plates were
manufactured in the 1950s and 1960s. The second impurity component is associated with corrosion
of the uranium after the uranium was weighed. This corrosion occurred after the HEU plates were
canned at ZPPR in 1982. The corrosion adds oxygen and hydrogen impurities, i.e., corrosion
impurities, without affecting the uranium mass inferred from the reported plate masses.
Initial Impurities in HEU Metal
These initial impurities were present in the uranium when the HEU plates were weighed, so the
impurity mass must be subtracted from the measured plate mass to determine the actual uranium
mass in the plates. The following is adapted from text prepared by R. W. Schaefer, a former
analyst at ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR, for an ICSBEP benchmark of a ZPR/ZPPR assembly.
The fundamental assumption in the Schaefer analysis is that the masses of 234U, 235U, 236U and
238
 U in the ADEN library and hot constants memos include the impurities in the HEU metal. Those
sources only list the average mass of 234U, 235U, 236U, 238U per HEU plate type, the sum of the
uranium isotope masses in that HEU plate type and the average mass of Kel-F coating per plate.
The ANL-E hot constants memo provides a more complete list of the unclad HEU plates used at
ZPR-3 and ZPPR.
The ZPPR hot constants memo lists the average mass of each Pu isotope, 241Am, 235U, 238U and
Mo in the plate core, i.e., the Pu-U-Mo fuel meat, as well as the average core mass for each Pu-U-
Mo plate type. The difference between the average core mass and the sum of the masses of U, Pu,
Am and Mo is assumed to be the impurities in the Pu-U-Mo alloy core of a Pu-U-Mo fuel plate
(see Section 7.1.3.12 below).
It is possible that the ADEN library and hot constants memos list only the actual measured masses
of the uranium isotopes but do not list the total measured mass of the plate including impurities.
Unfortunately, there is no available information to determine conclusively whether a) the
impurities are including in the listed uranium isotope masses or b) the listed uranium isotope
masses are the true average masses of those isotopes and do not include the mass of impurities in
the HEU plates. In the absence of any way to make that determination, the conservative approach
is to assume that the listed uranium masses also include the impurities in the uranium.

 198

The initial impurity levels in the enriched uranium were estimated from chemical analyses of the
plate material performed in the 1990s and 2000s. Information on the analyses associated with
procurement of the HEU plates is no longer available, and the hot constants memos do not list any
impurities. However, chemical analysis results are available from a process to recover the enriched
uranium from plates damaged by corrosion. Analysis reports were obtained for 20 samples, each
of which was analyzed for 18 impurities. The 18 impurities do not include the corrosion-related
impurities of oxygen and hydrogen. The analysis reports indicate that:
“Less-than values are limits of quantification, which are ten times the minimum detection limit.”
From an examination of the 20 reports, it was judged that large variations in the quantification
limit and a scarcity of values beyond the quantification limit preclude the determination of a
reliable weight ppm value for nine of the impurities. An example is cadmium for which the
quantification limit ranges from 10 ppm to 70 ppm over the 20 samples and there is no value
beyond the quantification limit. For each of the other nine measured impurities, there are at least
six values beyond the quantification limit and the other quantification limits are consistent. An
example of this is nickel for which there are 16 values, ranging from 120 ppm to 220 ppm, that are
beyond the quantification limit and for which there are four reports giving only quantification
limits which range from 180 ppm to 290 ppm. By averaging the values beyond the quantification
limit, the following nine impurity weight ppm estimates were obtained: C 340, Ni 174, Fe 125, Cu
65, Na 63, Ca 40, Si 35, Al 30, Mn 13.
This collection of nine impurity values, which total 885 ppm, was taken to be a reasonable
approximation to the initial impurity level in the enriched uranium. From one perspective, this
can be considered an underestimate of the impurity because it does not include any contribution
from the other nine impurities or from elements that were not analyzed. Alternatively, it tends to
be an overestimate because some of the measured carbon came from the recovery process. It is
assumed that these opposing effects approximately balance, and it is estimated that a one-sigma
uncertainty of 50% applies to this impurity model.
The reported impurity level for the Godiva critical assembly provides some evidence that at least
the estimated total impurity level in the enriched uranium is reasonable [11]. Godiva was
composed of “virgin material” whose estimated total impurity level is approximately 400 ppm,
comprised primarily of 160 ppm C, 110 ppm Si and 70 ppm Fe. It is further stated in LA-4208
that “recycled material” has impurity levels that are about twice as large. The presence of 236U
indicates that the ZPR/ZPPR HEU plates must have been made from recycled material. The
adopted 885 ppm impurity estimate for the ZPR/ZPPR HEU plates is consistent with the
approximate 800 ppm estimate for recycled material in LA-4208.
The analysis for ZPPR-15C is used here as an example. The ZPPR-15C reference as-built model
was modified by replacing 885 ppm of uranium with the nine impurities listed above. The
computed worth of the initial impurities was -26.00 ± 2.83 pcm. The assumed one-sigma
uncertainty in the impurities is 50%, so the total worth of the uncertainty in the impurity content
is √((26/2)2 + 2.832) or 13.3 pcm.
HEU Corrosion Products

 199

The following discussion only applies to the canned HEU plates used at ZPPR in the 1980s. it
does not apply to the coated HEU plates used at ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9.
When the HEU plates were used at ZPR-3, ZPR-6, and ZPR-9, the plates were coated with Kel-F
to prevent corrosion and material loss during handling, and the HEU plates were recoated as
needed. After the other facilities were shut down, the HEU plates were shipped to ZPPR where
the HEU plates were canned. At ZPPR, the HEU metal was cleaned, dried, and weighed just
before it was clad in 1982. Because the metal frit end plugs on the cans were porous, the HEU
metal began to corrode. Corrosion of the enriched uranium is discussed in a journal article [12].
Bulging of the thin cladding walls due to the presence of corrosion products was first noticed in a
few plates in 1985. Thereafter, attempts were made to halt the corrosion but a successful strategy
was not in place until 1995. By that time the periodic inspections, which had begun in 1985, had
rejected approximately 25% of the inventory. Shortly before the ZPPR-21 assemblies were built
in 1990, every clad plate was inspected, and only plates that passed inspection were used. A small
amount of uranium oxide and a much smaller amount of uranium hydride is believed to have been
present in the plates used in ZPPR-21. One of the material scientists who studied this corrosion
problem estimated the extent of corrosion in those plates [13]. The best estimate is that 1% of the
uranium corroded, 2.5% of that corrosion was in the form of uranium hydride (UH 3) and the
remaining 97.5% was in the form of uranium oxide when ZPPR-21 was built. The one-sigma
uncertainty on this estimate is 100%.
There is no other available information regarding corrosion in the HEU plates, so it is necessary
to make an assumption regarding the degree of corrosion and the amount of corrosion products
present in the cans for the configuration of interest. The degree of corrosion does not alter the
amount of HEU metal in the cans, but it does determine the amount of hydrogen and oxygen
present in the form of UH3 and uranium oxide. Since the corrosion progressed over time, it is clear
that initial formation of corrosion products on the surface of the HEU metal did not serve as a
barrier to further corrosion. In the absence of any additional information, it was assumed that the
progress of the corrosion was approximately linear over time between 1982 when the HEU plates
were canned and 1990 when ZPPR-21 was built. The amount of corrosion products present was
assumed to scale linearly over time between zero when the HEU plates were canned and the values
listed in the preceding paragraph when ZPPR-21 was built. The linearity assumption is arbitrary,
but there is no information to justify any other assumed model for the corrosion. In any case, the
contribution of the corrosion products to the total uncertainty appears to be small. The analysis
for ZPPR-15C is used here as an example.
ZPPR-15C was built in 1986 around the midpoint between the date when the HEU plates were
canned and the time when ZPPR-21 was built. In the absence of any other information regarding
corrosion of the HEU plates, it was assumed that a) 0.5% of the uranium had corroded when ZPPR-
15C was built, b) 2.5% of the corrosion was in the form of uranium hydride, c) 97.5% of the
corrosion was in the form of uranium oxide and d) the one-sigma uncertainty on the estimated
corrosion is 100%.
The reference as-built Monte Carlo model was modified by adding enough oxygen and hydrogen
to the HEU to match the assumed level of corrosion. The computed worth of the corrosion
impurities was 1 ± 3 pcm.
Treatment of Initial HEU Impurities and Corrosion Products

 200

The uncertainties related to the initial HEU impurities and the corrosion products in the canned
HEU plates used at ZPPR are included in the total uncertainty for the criticality measurement.
The initial HEU impurities and the HEU corrosion products in canned HEU plates are treated in
either of the following ways:
 1. The HEU impurities and any corrosion products can be included in the reference as-built
 model of the ZPR/ZPPR assembly.
 2. The HEU impurities and any corrosion products can be neglected in the reference as-built
 model. In that case, neglecting them is treated as a bias as discussed in Section 7.1.4.
7.1.3.12          Pu-U-Mo Plates
Dow and NUMEC manufactured Pu-U-Mo alloy fuel plates for ANL in the late 1960s. The
majority of those plates were shipped to ZPPR where they formed the initial fuel inventory for that
facility. The remainder of the Pu-U-Mo plates fabricated in the late 1960s were shipped to ANL-
E. Based upon the assembly descriptions in ANL-NT-175 [7], those Pu-U-Mo plates appear to be
the first plutonium fuel plates in the ANL-E inventory. The ADEN identifier for the standard Pu-
U-Mo plates manufactured by Dow is PUMD, and the corresponding identifier for the NUMEC
Pu-U-Mo plates is PUMN.
The fuel meat in a standard PUMD/PUMN Pu-U-Mo fuel plate consisted of ~28 wt.% Pu, ~69.5
wt.% depleted uranium and 2.5 wt.% Mo. It appears that the Mo was added for metallurgical
reasons because it does not seem to serve any specific reactor physics purpose. The fuel meat in
a Pu-U-Mo plate was enclosed in a stainless steel can.
The nominal outer dimensions of the stainless steel can in a standard PUMD/PUMN Pu-U-Mo
fuel plate were ¼ x 2 x L inches where L was 4, 5, 6, 7 or 8. In addition, there were a few Pu-U-
Mo fuel plates with other dimensions such as ¼ x 2 x 1 inches.
Can integrity was important to prevent contamination of adjacent plates, drawers and matrix tubes
and to minimize staff exposures. There was a small amount of free space between the can interior
and the fuel meat. This free space allowed for thermal expansion of the fuel meat during normal
operations and under accident conditions to minimize the probability of can failure.
The plutonium in a standard PUMD/PUMN Pu-U-Mo fuel plate contained ~11 wt.% 240Pu because
the plutonium in Pu-U-Mo plates was intended to simulate reactor grade plutonium; the remainder
of the plutonium in these plates consisted of 238Pu, 239Pu, 241Pu and 242Pu.
The ZPPR and ANL-E plate inventories also contained limited numbers of Pu-U-Mo plates in
which the plutonium contained ~27 wt.% 240Pu. The high 240Pu plates simulated high burnup
recycled plutonium fuel. There were not enough high 240Pu plates to build an entire assembly, but
there were enough high 240Pu plates to build a central zone of moderate size in an assembly. High
240
 Pu zones were built in the center of various assemblies including ZPR-6/7. The ADEN identifier
for the high 240Pu Pu-U-Mo plates is PUMH. It appears that the PUMH plates were manufactured
by NUMEC.
ZPR-3 obtained Pu-U-Mo plates in the mid-1960s for the SEFOR program. The internal design
of the Pu-U-Mo SEFOR plates (ADEN identifier PUMS) differed significantly from the internal
design of the PUMD/PUMN/PUMH plates. The nominal outer dimensions of the PUMS cans

 201

were 1/4 x 2 x L inches where L was 1, 3, 4, 5, 6 or 7. In addition, there were a few PUMS plates
with outer dimensions of 1/8 x 2 x 2 inches.
Both the Pu/U/Mo weight fractions and the Pu isotopics of the PUMS plates differed from the
corresponding values for the PUMD/PUMN plates. The average meat composition for a PUMS
plate consisted of ~19.5 wt.% Pu, 77.9 wt.% U and 2.6 wt.% Mo. The PUMS Pu contained ~8.7
wt.% 240Pu. The PUMS plates were used primarily at ZPR-3, although ZPR-3 borrowed some of
the ZPPR PUMD/PUMN plates for a few of the late ZPR-3 assemblies. In general, the ZPPR staff
and the ANL-E staff only used the PUMS plates if no other plutonium plates were available.
In addition to the standard Pu-U-Mo plates, the ZPR/ZPPR inventories contained small numbers
of special plates such as half-thickness plates (1/8 th inch), tunnel plates similar to the sodium tunnel
plates discussed above and plates designed to accommodate a thermocouple. These special Pu-U-
Mo plates are designated as PUMT in the ADEN library and hot constants memos.
There were relatively few PUMT plates of each type/size, and they were only used in a few drawers
in each half. For example, temperature measurements in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were made by loading
a few thermocouple drawers in each half of the core. The PUMT plates can be ignored for purposes
of uncertainty analysis because the number of PUMT plates in any core was very small compared
to the number of PUMD/PUMN/PUMS/PUMH plates in that core.
It is generally possible to determine which types of Pu-U-Mo plate (PUMD, PUMN, PUMH,
PUMS, PUMT or other special type) and sizes of Pu-U-Mo plates were used in each drawer master
from the drawer master records and from the type(s) of Pu-U-Mo plates in the facility inventory.
There is a minor exception to the preceding paragraph for ZPR-3. Some later ZPR-3 assemblies
used Pu-U-Mo plates borrowed from ZPPR. These ZPPR Pu-U-Mo plates will be distinguishable
from the PUMS plates on the drawer master figures. The ZPR-3 drawer master may list the ZPPR
Pu-U-Mo plates as “ZPPR Pu,” “Pu ALLOY (ZPPR)” or a similar designation that distinguishes
the ZPPR PUMD/PUMN plates from the ZPR-3 PUMS plates. It probably is not possible to
determine whether PUMD plates or PUMN plates were used in a ZPR-3 assembly because the
ZPR-3 drawer masters only distinguish ZPPR plates from the PUMS plates. The difference
between the ZPR-3 PUMS (SEFOR) plates and the ZPPR plates (PUMD and PUMN) is much
larger than the difference between the PUMD plates and PUMN plates.
7.1.3.12.1 Pu-U-Mo Plate Uncertainties
The stainless steel cans for the Pu-U-Mo plates were made of Type 304 stainless steel. The 0.15%
mass uncertainty and the composition uncertainties related to these stainless steel cans are treated
in the same way as uncertainties in mass and composition for other stainless steel components (see
Section 7.1.3.6).
The general 0.15% mass uncertainty does not apply to the Pu-U-Mo alloy because there are
existing records that allow better mass and composition uncertainty determinations for the Pu-U-
Mo alloy.
Pu-U-Mo Alloy Composition Uncertainties
The estimated uncertainty in the PUMD/PUMN Pu-U-Mo alloy composition is based upon some
knowledge of the fuel plate manufacturing process. Thousands of Pu-U-Mo plates, in sizes

 202

ranging from 1 inch to 8 inch were made from 1100 melts. Each melt yielded several 0.25 x 2 x 15
inch castings. One casting per melt was used for three assays to measure the composition of the
melt with samples taken from the top, middle, and bottom of the casting. The other castings were
cut and milled to precise plate dimensions, weighed, clad in stainless steel and then weighed again.
The casting process was similar for PUMS plates and PUMH plates although the numbers of melts
and castings were smaller for the PUMS plates and PUMH plates than for PUMD/PUMN plates.
A data file containing the recorded weight of each isotope in each individual plate of Pu-U-Mo
type is still available. The existence of this data file allows the estimates of the composition
uncertainties for Pu-U-Mo plates to be more precise than estimates of composition uncertainties
for most other types of plates in the ZPR/ZPPR inventories. In order to use this data file to compute
uncertainties, the user must know the number of Pu-U-Mo plates of each size and type (PUMD,
PUMN, PUMH, PUMS) present in the assembly of interest.
The number of Pu-U-Mo plates of each size and type in the assembly can be determined easily
from the files required to create an as-built model of the assembly. For example, the number of
Pu-U-Mo plates of each type and size can be determined for each drawer master in the
assembly/loading of interest, and the number of locations where each drawer master is present in
that assembly/loading can be determined from the matrix map for that assembly/loading.
The data file described in the previous paragraphs is used to generate mass and weight percent
statistics for the Pu-U-Mo fuel plate types in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies. As such, the following
expression (taken from historical ZPPR treatment) is used to estimate the variance in the plutonium
mass:
   
                                       N n                     
                                                             
 n N 1  ,
where
 1 is the plate-to-plate variation in Pu mass,
 2 is the error in using the cast-average Pu fraction for the plate-average Pu
 fraction,
 3 is the random error in the cast-average Pu fraction,
 4 is the systematic error in the chemical assay, 0.05%,
 5 is the systematic error in plate weighing, 0.05%,
 n is the number of plates of this type used in the assembly,
 N is the number of plates of this type in the inventory, and
 M is the number of melts used to produce the inventory.
This expression was developed by the ZPR/ZPPR staff to account for a phenomenon that can be
significant for Pu-U-Mo fuel. The phenomenon is that the plutonium component of the alloy
deposited preferentially at the location where the liquid metal entered the mold because the melting
points of Pu, U and Mo are 640 °C, 1135 °C and 2623 °C, respectively. Consequently, the element
fractions comprising the alloy varied somewhat, depending upon the location in the casting. A
small number of samples were extracted from various locations in castings produced from a given
melt. The average of chemical analysis results from the melt was used to assign a plutonium mass

 203

fraction to all of the plates from that melt. Thus, the declared plate-wise plutonium masses, which
were evaluated statistically to derive 1, have some associated error in them. The 2 and 3 terms
were introduced to account for this. With a nominal plutonium mass fraction of 0.28 for standard
Pu-U-Mo plates, these terms can impact the computed uncertainty. Systematic errors are accounted
for by the terms 4 and 5.
The values of N, 1, and plutonium mass per plate for the Pu-U-Mo plates were derived from the
available data file. They correspond to the dates of plate manufacture (i.e., before any decay of
241
 Pu to 241Am). For the fuel plates, 3 was estimated from variations in the assay data to be 1.1%.
The 2 was taken to be 1/4 of 3. The uncertainty in the plutonium contribution from each of the
plate types used in the assembly had to be combined when applying the expression above. This
was done by converting percent uncertainty to gram uncertainty and summing the mass
contributions.
The analysis for ZPPR-15A is used here as an example. In ZPPR-15A, the uncertainty in the total
plutonium mass was computed to be 0.0787 wt.%. Changing the plutonium (plus americium) mass
by this amount was worth 46.46 pcm.
The uncertainties in the plutonium isotopic weight fractions were determined using the same data
sources and a similar formula to those used for plutonium mass:
 2 2
                                              6 N n    7      2
   8
 n N 1 M ,
where
 6 is the plate-to-plate variation in the isotope weight percent,
 7 is the random uncertainty in an isotopic assay, and
 8 is the systematic error in the isotopic assay.
Like 1, 6 was derived from a statistical analysis of the plate-wise mass data. The 7 and 8 are
isotope dependent, and the values used by the Argonne-West Analytical Laboratory were used
here. For the major constituent, 239Pu, they are 0.25% and 0.0025%, respectively. Again, the
uncertainty contributions from the plate types were combined by converting percent uncertainty
to gram uncertainty and summing the mass contributions.
The data and formula were used to modify the Pu isotopic distribution in the ZPPR-15A
deterministic model. The relative uncertainty in the 239Pu weight percent was computed to be
0.0092%. In the deterministic model, the 239Pu concentration was increased by this amount and
mass was preserved by decreasing just the 240Pu concentration (a simplification justified by the
very small size of the other isotopic concentrations). The resulting change in k eff is 4.20 pcm.
The weight percent of 238Pu, 241Pu, and 242Pu in an assembly before decaying 241Pu was less than
2%. 240Pu is the only isotope besides 239Pu whose uncertainty would be expected to impact keff
appreciably. The relative uncertainty in the 240Pu weight percent is determined using values of
0.50% and 0.035% for 7 and 8, respectively. The relative uncertainty in the 240Pu weight percent
in ZPPR-15A is 0.0416%. Changing the 240Pu weight percent by 0.0416% led to a calculated
effect on keff of 2.58 pcm in ZPPR-15A.

 204

The combined uncertainty in keff due to the uncertainties in the original weight fractions of the
remaining three isotopes in ZPPR-15A was assumed to be no larger than the uncertainty in k eff
resulting from the uncertainty in 240Pu mass, i.e., 2.58 pcm. In principle, the total uncertainty in
the plutonium isotopic fractions could be reduced by using the constraint that the sum of these
fractions was unity. Because this uncertainty component does not make a significant contribution
to the total uncertainty in the system reactivity, further analysis was deemed unwarranted.
Some of the 241Pu decayed between the manufacture date and the date of the experiment. The Pu-
U-Mo NUMEC and Dow plates were manufactured in the late 1960s. The actual isotopic content
numbers in the ZPPR inventory database were decayed to a reference date of January 1, 1977 by
the ZPPR staff, so all plutonium compositions in the ADEN library correspond to January 1, 1977.
The estimated uncertainty in the 241Pu decay constant was assumed to be 1% in ICSBEP/IRPhEP
benchmarks of ZPR/ZPPR assemblies [5,6], and a nominal 241Pu half-life of 14.29 years was used
to decay the isotope. Increasing the decay constant increases the 241Am mass and decreases the
241
 Pu mass. For ZPPR-15A, increasing the 241Pu decay constant by 1% reduced keff by 3.03 pcm.
The specification for production of the NUMEC Pu-U-Mo plates required a 235U enrichment of
0.22 ± 0.02 wt.% in the uranium component. It appears that the 0.02 wt.% represented the two
sigma confidence interval, so the corresponding one sigma uncertainty is 0.01 wt.%. The 235U
mass was increased by 0.01% and the 238U mass was reduced correspondingly yielding an
uncertainty in keff of 26.78 pcm.
The uncertainty in the mass of molybdenum in the Pu-U-Mo fuel alloy was computed in the same
way as the plutonium mass uncertainty. The computed molybdenum mass uncertainty is 0.0835%.
Changing the core region molybdenum atom density yields an uncertainty in k eff of 0.17 pcm.
When the masses of plutonium and molybdenum were perturbed to compute mass uncertainties,
the depleted uranium mass in the Pu-U-Mo alloy was changed in the opposite direction to conserve
total alloy mass.
From experience, the dominant uncertainties for the Pu-U-Mo plate compositions are the
uncertainties in the total Pu mass and the uncertainty in the 235U enrichment in the DU component
of the Pu-U-Mo alloy.
Impurities in Pu-U-Mo Alloy
The trace impurities in the Pu-U-Mo alloy are not listed. The ZPPR hot constants memo lists the
average mass of each Pu isotope, 241Am, 235U, 238U and Mo in the plate core, i.e., the Pu-U-Mo
fuel meat, for each Pu-U-Mo plate type. The ZPPR and ANL-E hot constants memos also list the
average core mass for each Pu-U-Mo plate type. It is assumed here that the difference between
the average core mass and the sum of the average masses of the Pu, Am, U and Mo in each Pu-U-
Mo plate type is a reasonable estimate of the average impurity mass for that plate type. Table 7.9
lists the average impurity mass, average core mass and average impurity weight percent for each
standard Pu-U-Mo plate manufactured by Dow and NUMEC for ZPPR and ANL-E as well as the
SEFOR plates manufactured for ZPR-3. There does not seem to be any way to make a better
determination of the average impurity mass in the Pu-U-Mo alloy from the available records and
data. The impurity content of the Pu-U-Mo alloy in Dow plates is approximately an order of
magnitude higher than the impurity content of the Pu-U-Mo alloy in NUMEC plates.

 205

There appears to be some inconsistency in the hot constants memo listings for the average core
weight and average mass of each isotope or element in the Pu-U-Mo alloy for the high 240Pu plates
(PUMH) and the ¼ x 2 x 7 inch PUMS plates because the difference between the average core
mass and the sum of the individual constituent masses is negative for the PUMH plates and the ¼
x 2 x 7 inch PUMS plates. The ZPPR and ANL-E hot constants memos show consistent average
core masses for these plates. The source of the inconsistency has not been found, and it may not
be possible to resolve the inconsistency without additional information.

Treatment of Impurities in Pu-U-Mo Alloy
The uncertainty related to impurities in the Pu-U-Mo alloy is included in the total uncertainty for
the criticality measurement. The assumed Pu-U-Mo alloy impurities are treated in either of the
following ways:
 1. The Pu-U-Mo alloy impurities can be included in the reference as-built model of the
 ZPR/ZPPR assembly.
 2. The Pu-U-Mo alloy impurities can be neglected in the reference as-built model. In that
 case, neglecting them is treated as a bias as discussed in Section 7.1.4.
7.1.3.13          Pu-Al Plates
The first plutonium plates used in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies were Pu-Al alloy plates manufactured in
the early 1960s for ZPR-3. The fuel meat in these Pu-Al plates consisted of Pu alloyed with ~1.1
wt.% Al. Pure plutonium metal has multiple phases that have significantly different densities. For
example, the density of α-phase Pu is ~19.84 g/cm 3, and the density of δ-phase Pu is ~15.92 g/cm3.
These phase transitions are undesirable for operational and safety reasons. Addition of a small
amount of an alloying material such as gallium or aluminum stabilizes the Pu phase, which reduces
or eliminates phase transitions and the associated density changes.

 207

The standard Pu-Al plates contained ~4.5 wt.% 240Pu in the Pu component. There were two distinct
sets of standard Pu-Al plates. The Pu-Al alloy fuel meat in the first set of standard Pu-Al plates
was coated or clad with nickel. The Pu-Al plates with nickel-coated fuel meat are designated as
PANI (Pu-Al, NIckel) in the ADEN library and the hot constants memos.
The Pu-Al fuel meat in the second set of standard Pu-Al plates was not coated or clad with nickel.
The Pu-Al plates without the nickel coating on the fuel meat are designated as PANN (Pu-Al, No
Nickel) in the ADEN library and hot constants memos. The nominal compositions of the Pu-Al
fuel meat in PANI plates and PANN plates are the same; the only distinction between PANI plates
and PANN plates is the addition of a few mils of nickel coating to the fuel meat in a PANI plate.
In addition to the standard Pu-Al plates, there were high 240Pu Pu-Al plates that contained ~22.3
wt.% 240Pu in the Pu component. The fuel meat in the high 240Pu Pu-Al plates was not coated or
clad with nickel. The high 240Pu Pu-Al plates are designated as PAHN in the ADEN library and
hot constants memos. There were not enough high 240Pu plates to build an entire assembly, but
there were enough of these plates to build a central high 240Pu zone in an assembly.
Available documents do not explain why the fuel meat in the PANI plates was coated with nickel
while the fuel meat in the PANN plates and PAHN plates was not coated. The hot constants
memos and ADEN library list different vendor numbers for the PANI, PANN and PAHN plates,
so it is possible that the three sets of Pu-Al plates were obtained from different sources.
The drawer master figures for an assembly indicate which type of Pu-Al plate (PANI, PANN or
PAHN) was in each position in each drawer master, and the loading records indicate which drawer
master was in each matrix tube.
The Pu-Al alloy in all types of Pu-Al plates (PANI, PANN, PAHN) was enclosed in a stainless
steel can. The nominal outer dimensions of the stainless steel can in a Pu-Al plate were 1/8 x 2 x
L inches where L was 1, 2 or 3. In fact, the actual dimensions of the Pu-Al meat and the external
dimensions of the Pu-Al cans were slightly smaller than the nominal design dimensions.
Can integrity was important to prevent contamination of adjacent plates, drawers and matrix tubes
and to minimize staff exposures. There was a small amount of free space between the can interior
and the fuel meat to allow for thermal expansion of the fuel meat during normal operations and
under accident conditions to minimize the probability of can failure.
After ZPR-3 was shut down, the Pu-Al plates were shipped to ZPPR and/or ANL-E. The Pu-Al
plates were used in the later loadings of ZPR-6/7 and in ZPR-6/10. There were not enough Pu-Al
plates to build a ZPPR assembly, but the Pu-Al plates may have been used to supplement the Pu-
U-Mo plates in the largest ZPPR assemblies such as ZPPR-18 and ZPPR-19.
7.1.3.13.1 Pu-Al Plate Uncertainties
The stainless steel cans for the Pu-Al plates were made of Type 304 stainless steel. The 0.15%
mass uncertainty and the composition uncertainties related to these stainless steel cans are treated
in the same way as uncertainties in mass and composition for other stainless steel components (see
Section 7.1.3.6).
The general 0.15% mass uncertainty does not apply to the Pu-Al alloy because there are existing
records that allow better mass and composition uncertainty determinations for the Pu-Al alloy.

 208

Pu-Al Alloy Composition Uncertainties
Each Pu/Al fuel plate was weighed before and after cladding, and these masses were recorded in
a data file. Similarly, samples from each melt were analyzed when the fuel was cast, and the
results were recorded in this data file. This data file contains the recorded weight of each isotope
in each individual Pu-Al plate. This data file was used to derive the aluminum and plutonium
isotopic mass distributions for Pu-Al plates in the ADEN library and hot constants memos.
The data file for the Pu-Al plates is still available. The existence of this data file allows the
estimates of the composition uncertainties for Pu-Al plates to be more precise than estimates of
composition uncertainties for most other types of plates in the ZPR/ZPPR inventories. In order to
use this data file to compute uncertainties, the user must know the number of Pu-Al plates of each
size and type (PANI, PANN, PAHN) present in the assembly of interest. The number of Pu-Al
plates of each size and type in the assembly can be determined given knowledge of the drawer
master and the specific drawer loading information for a given assembly. Specifically, the
assembly matrix map and the file describing all drawer masters used in the assembly provide
sufficient information to determine the number of plates of every size and type as well as the
number of drawers present in the assembly.
The data file described in the previous paragraphs is used to generate mass and weight percent
statistics for the Pu-Al fuel plate types in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies. The Pu-Al fuel meat consists of
98.9 wt.% Pu and 1.1 wt.% Al, and standard Pu-U-Mo fuel meat consists of 28 wt.% Pu, 69.5 wt.%
U and 2.5 wt.% Mo. The melting points of Pu and Al are 640 °C and 660 °C, respectively. Because
the melting points of Pu and Al are similar and because Pu-Al alloy only contains 1.1 wt.% Al,
some of the discussion of uncertainties in the composition of Pu-U-Mo alloy in Section 7.1.3.12
does not apply to Pu-Al plates. In particular, issues related to preferential deposition of Pu at the
location where the liquid metal enters the mold that are important for a Pu-U-Mo alloy are not
important for a Pu-Al alloy.
All relative uncertainties in mass, composition and isotopics for the Pu-Al plates are determined
based on analysis of the data file of mass and composition information for the Pu-Al plates except
the 241Pu decay uncertainty.
The fuel for ZPR-6/10 consisted of Pu-Al plates, so ZPR-6/10 is used here as an example of
uncertainty analysis for Pu-Al plates. The uncertainty in the total plutonium mass in the Pu-Al
plates was computed to be 0.0720% based on analysis of the database of mass and composition
information for the Pu-Al plates. Increasing the plutonium (plus americium) mass in the Pu-Al
plates by this amount and decreasing the Al mass by the same amount to conserve Pu-Al mass
increased keff by 30.2 pcm.
The relative uncertainty in the 239Pu weight percent was computed to be 0.0256% for the Pu-Al
plates. The 239Pu concentration was increased by this amount and mass was preserved by
decreasing just the 240Pu concentration (a simplification justified by the very small size of the other
isotopic concentrations). The computed uncertainty in keff is 9.6 pcm for the Pu-Al plates.
The weight percent of 238Pu, 241Pu and 242Pu in the Pu-Al fuel, before decaying 241Pu, was less than
2%. The only isotope besides 239Pu whose uncertainty would be expected to impact keff
appreciably is 240Pu. The relative uncertainty in the 240Pu weight percent is 0.037% for the Pu-Al

 209

plates. Modification of the 240Pu weight percent led to a calculated effect on keff of 1.0 pcm for
the Pu-Al plates. The combined uncertainty in keff due to the uncertainties in the original weight
percents of the remaining three isotopes was assumed to be no larger than the 240Pu values, i.e.,
1.0 pcm. In principle, the total uncertainty in the Pu isotopic fractions could be reduced using the
constraint that the sum of these fractions was unity. Because this uncertainty component does not
make a significant contribution to the total uncertainty in the system reactivity, further analysis
appears unwarranted.
More than 70% of the 241Pu that was in the fuel plates when they were manufactured decayed by
the time ZPR-6/10 was built. The Pu/Al plates were made in 1960. ZPR-6/10 loading 24 was
made critical on September 30, 1981, and the half-life of 241Pu is 14.29 years. The numbers in the
inventory database are normalized to January 1, 1977. The estimated uncertainty in the decay
constant is 1%. Increasing the decay constant increases the 241Am mass and decreases the 241Pu
mass on the date of the experiment. Increasing the decay constant by 1% changes k eff by 2.9 pcm
for ZPR-6/10.
The uncertainty in the mass of aluminum in the Pu/Al fuel alloy was computed in the same way
as the plutonium mass uncertainty. The computed aluminum mass uncertainty is 0.10%. Changing
the core region aluminum atom density by this amount changes k eff by less than 0.1 pcm.
Impurities in Pu-Al Alloy
The trace impurities in the Pu-Al alloy are not listed. The ZPPR hot constants memo lists the
average mass of each Pu isotope, 241Am and Al in the plate core, i.e., the Pu-Al fuel meat, for each
Pu-Al plate type. The hot constants memos also list the average core mass for each Pu-Al plate
type. It is assumed here that the difference between the average core mass and the sum of the
average masses of the Pu, Am and Al in each Pu-Al plate type is a reasonable estimate of the
average impurity mass for that plate type. The same assumption was used in Section 7.1.3.12 to
estimate the impurities in Pu-U-Mo alloy.
There is one complication for the PANI (nickel-coated) plates. The ZPPR hot constants memo
combines the mass of the nickel coating with the mass of nickel in the stainless steel can for each
PANI plate. It appears that the average core weight for the Pu-Al core in a PANI plate also includes
the nickel coating because the difference between the listed core weight of a PANI plate and the
sum of the masses of Pu, Am and Al in that core is 3% of the core weight.
It is unrealistic to assume the impurity level in the Pu-Al meat of a PANI plate was 3 wt.%. The
nominal compositions of the Pu-Al cores in the PANI plates and PANN plates are the same, so it
seems reasonable to assume the impurities in the PANI plate cores were approximately the same
as the impurities in the PANN plate cores.
