The actual impurities are not listed in the hot constants memos. Plutonium is made by irradiating
uranium, so the likely sources of impurities in the plutonium are uranium impurities that are carried
over during the separation process, elements that migrate from the processing and separation
equipment into the plutonium and elements that migrate from the casting equipment into the Pu-
Al alloy. In the absence of any additional information, it seems reasonable to assume the impurity
distribution for depleted uranium discussed in Section 7.1.3.7is at least a first order approximation
of the impurity distribution in the Pu-Al alloy. Table 7.12 shows the assumed impurities in the

Impurities are important in a thermal spectrum because some impurities such as B and Cd have
large capture cross sections at thermal energies. In the hard spectrum of a ZPR/ZPPR assembly,
the capture cross sections of the impurities are small. Consequently, approximations made
regarding impurities in ZPR/ZPPR plates are much less important than approximations made
regarding impurities in a thermal spectrum. For example, the computed worth of the assumed
impurities in the Pu-U-Mo plates in ZPPR-15A was 2.00 ± 2.83 pcm. The computed worth of
impurities in Pu-Al plates also would be small and would probably be comparable to or smaller
than the statistical uncertainty in the Monte Carlo calculations used to compute the worth of the
Pu-Al impurities.
Treatment of Impurities in Pu-Al Alloy
The uncertainty related to impurities in the Pu-Al alloy is included in the total uncertainty for the
criticality measurement. The assumed Pu-Al alloy impurities are treated in either of the following
ways:
 1. The Pu-Al alloy impurities can be included in the reference as-built model of the
 ZPR/ZPPR assembly.
 2. The Pu-Al alloy impurities can be neglected in the reference as-built model. In that case,
 neglecting them is treated as a bias as discussed in Section 7.1.4.
7.1.3.14 Other Plate Types
The hot constants memos and the ADEN library list many other types of plates in the ZPR/ZPPR
inventories. It is not practical to provide a detailed description of every plate type used in some
assembly between ZPR-3/1 and ZPPR-21. The following is a brief discussion of a few other plate
types that were used occasionally.
7.1.3.14.1 Aluminum Plates
Aluminum plates (ADEN identifier AL) were used in ZPR-9 Assemblies 1 – 9 and in various ZPR-
3 assemblies. Holes were drilled in some aluminum plates to reduce the effective aluminum

 212

density. The drilled aluminum plates are designated AL45 (45% density with holes), AL56 (56%
density with holes) and AL63 (63% density with holes). Early ZPR-3 assemblies used the drilled
aluminum plates to simulate sodium because there were no sodium plates in the initial ZPR-3
inventory. Early ZPR-3 assemblies and ZPR-9 Assemblies 1 – 9 are probably the only assemblies
in which a significant number of aluminum plates were used. Other ZPR/ZPPR assemblies used
a limited number of aluminum plates primarily as spacers or to occupy free space in drawers, e.g.,
to eliminate free space at the back of a drawer.
The hot constants memos list the aluminum plate compositions as 100% aluminum because there
is no information regarding impurities in those plates. Aluminum has very low reactivity worth,
and it is likely that the reactivity worth of any impurities in the aluminum would be negligible. If
the worth of aluminum impurities is small or negligible, the reactivity worth of any uncertainty in
the impurity content of the aluminum would be negligible. From experience, it did not seem
worthwhile to devote effort to model the impurities in the aluminum plates.
In addition to aluminum plates, there were aluminum oxide plates in the ZPR/ZPPR inventories.
Aluminum and oxygen have very low reactivity worths. The preceding paragraph applies to the
aluminum oxide plates used in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies.
7.1.3.14.2 Zirconium Plates
Zirconium plates were used in ZPPR-15 and may have been used in a few other assemblies since
zirconium plates appear in the inventories at ANL-E and ANL-W. The hot constants memos list
the zirconium plate composition as zirconium and provide no additional information regarding
impurities in these plates. The 0.15% mass uncertainty for the zirconium plates was very small in
ZPPR-15, so the effects of impurities in the zirconium were assumed to be negligible in the hard
ZPR/ZPPR spectrum. It seems likely that the effects of zirconium impurities would be negligible
in any ZPR/ZPPR assembly.
7.1.3.14.3 Steel Blocks
In addition to stainless steel plates, the ZPR/ZPPR inventories contained large numbers of low
carbon steel blocks (ADEN identifier FE). These blocks were commonly used as axial and radial
reflectors in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies.
No specifications for these steel blocks have been found, but the composition listed in the inventory
records is consistent with low carbon steel such as SAE/AISI 1020 or SAE/AISI 1030. The Mn,
C and Cr weight percents are 0.71, 0.17 and 0.03, respectively, in these blocks. Because these
blocks are located in the axial and radial reflectors, i.e., low reactivity worth regions of the
assembly, the worth of any realistic perturbation in the weight percents of Mn, C and Cr was
negligible in as-built models that contained these blocks. The worth of any realistic impurities in
the steel blocks would also be negligible.
7.1.3.14.4 Calandria
A calandria was a 2 x 2 x 12 inch stainless steel can containing a 4 x 4 square array of stainless
steel tubes. PuO2 pins or UO2 pins were inserted into the 16 tubes in the calandria, and the
calandria was loaded into a standard drawer. The use of calandria is discussed in Section 7.2.1.
Figure 7.1 shows a photograph of the calandria and drawer from ZPR-6 that was used in the

 213

variable temperature rodded zone which is discussed later in this report. From the picture, one can
see the rough idea behind the calandria as one pin is only partially inserted and another pin not
inserted is lying beside the calandria. There is a normal loaded core drawer to the left of the
calandria in the figure. The small colored stripes stripes on the tops of the plates in the drawer
facilitated drawer loading, drawer checking, drawer unloading and plate inventory control. The
dark block at the back of the drawer is probably a 2 x 2 x 5 inch block of depleted uranium that
serves as an axial blanket or reflector. A spring was inserted behind the block to push the plates
to the front of the drawer.

 214

 215

 Figure 7.1. ZPR-6 Calandria Example.
There were two types of calandria. The free space inside a type 1 calandria was filled with sodium
to represent the reference configuration. The free space inside a type 2 calandria was empty, i.e.,
filled with air, to represent a sodium void configuration. The fuel pins and calandria provided a
way to estimate the effects of the geometry mismatch between the target reactor with fuel pins and
the plate representation in a ZPR/ZPPR assembly.
The hot constants memos provide information regarding the external dimensions of the calandria
and the compositions of the steel and sodium in the calandria. Drawer masters and reports
documenting measurements with pin/calandria zones may provide enough information to construct
a model of the pins and calandria. The mass and composition uncertainties for the stainless steel
calandria shell and tubes are identical to the mass and composition uncertainties for stainless steel
plates and other stainless steel components (see Section 7.1.3.6). The mass and composition
uncertainties for the sodium in the calandria shell are are identical to the mass and composition
uncertainties for sodium (see Section 7.1.3.3).
To date, no attempt has been made to model calandria, UO2 pins or PuO2 pins as no loadings
identified to be of interest used them. The hot constants memos provide detailed information
regarding the compositions of the oxide fuel and any clad surrounding the fuel, but they do not
provide any information regarding uncertainties for the UO2 and PuO2. The hot constants memos
also provide limited information regarding pin dimensions. Modeling the UO 2 and PuO2 pins
would require some assumptions regarding composition uncertainties for the UO 2 and PuO2 for a
criticality measurement. For a sodium void worth measurement with calandria, the UO 2 and PuO2
uncertainties would drop out because they would be correlated between the reference configuration
and the void configuration.
7.1.3.14.5 Boron Carbide Plates
Boron carbide plates in the ZPR/ZPPR inventories were used primarily to simulate fast reactor
control rods for control rod worth measurements (see Section 7.3). The boron in most boron
carbide plates in the ZPR/ZPPR inventory was natural boron, but there were some boron carbide
plates in which the 10B component was enriched. Likewise, most boron carbide plates were bare,
but there were some clad boron carbide plates.
Section 7.3.2.3 discusses the effects of material composition uncertainties for control rod worth
measurements. That discussion applies to any criticality measurement in which boron carbide
plates are present.
For a criticality measurement, the important boron carbide plate uncertainties are the 0.15% mass
uncertainty and the uncertainty in the 10B content of the plate. It appears that the values listed in
the ADEN library and hot constants memos for the average masses of 10B, 11B and C in a boron
carbide plate of a particular type and size are measured values, but there are no details regarding
the measurements, and there is no way to quantify the measurement uncertainty. Section 7.3.2.3

 216

discusses three potential approaches to assign an uncertainty to the 10B content of a boron carbide
plate.
The ZPPR hot constants memo lists impurities in the various types of boron carbide plates, so it is
possible to either a) include the boron carbide impurities in the reference model or b) omit the
boron carbide impurities from the reference model and treat the omission as a bias (see Section
7.1.4).
7.1.3.14.6 Tantalum
In addition to boron carbide, some ZPR/ZPPR experiments measured the worth of tantalum as a
potential LMFR control rod material. A fast reactor control rod was simulated by placing tantalum
plates and possibly sodium plates in one or more drawers. The tantalum was natural tantalum.
The 0.15% mass uncertainty applies to the tantalum plates.
The ANL-E hot constants memo lists the impurity content of the tantalum plates as 0.032 wt.%
“all else” for tantalum metal plates. The ZPPR hot constants memo lists the average impurity
content of the tantalum plates as 0.032 wt.% “other,” but the ZPPR hot constants memo also lists
impurity masses for two plate sizes. The hot constants memos do not indicate what elements are
included in the impurities.
Only one or a few drawers in an assembly contained tantalum plates for a standard control rod
worth measurement. The 0.032 wt.% impurities in tantalum can be neglected for practical
purposes unless tantalum was placed in many drawers in the assembly.
7.1.3.14.7 Polyethylene and Borated Polyethylene
Polyethylene foam was used to simulate steam in the ZPR-9/29 steam entry experiments.
Polyethylene plates were used to simulate water flooding in the ZPPR-20D space reactor accident
scenario. The 0.15% mass uncertainty applies to the polyethylene foam and polyethylene plates.
The hot constants memos list the polyethylene plates as consisting of just polyethylene, and
commercial polyethylene either has no listed impurities or a very low level of impurities. In the
hard ZPR/ZPPR spectrum, any impurities in the polyethylene plates can be neglected.
Borated polyethylene plates or blocks were occasionally placed outside the reflector of a very
small assembly to reduce room return. Due to their location outside the radial reflector, the borated
polyethylene plates can be neglected for purposes of uncertainty analysis.
7.1.4 Biases in As-Built Models
The as-built model of a ZPR/ZPPR assembly may not be an exact representation of the physical
configuration that was measured; some features of the actual ZPR/ZPPR reactor and environs may
be neglected in an as-built model. The experimental keff must be adjusted to account for these
neglected features to avoid introducing biases into calculations based upon the as-built model.
The most common feature that is neglected in the current analysis approach is room return. Room
return refers to reflection of neutrons back into the model by structures outside of the defined
model. In ZPR/ZPPR as-built models built to date, the model only considers the matrix tubes and
materials loaded in them. The bed and knees that support the matrix tubes would be an example
of non-trivial components that surround the matrix that might impact room return but are not in

 217

the present models. Consequently, bias related to neglecting room return applies to every

Most ZPR/ZPPR assembly configurations (loadings) have not been modeled or analyzed since the
assembly was initially built and analyzed by the ZPR/ZPPR staff during the assembly program, so
there may be future cases in which other approximations in modeling geometry require adjusting
the experimental keff to avoid introducing bias. Other potential sources of bias are neglecting
materials or material impurities for a specific assembly configuration. There are several legitimate
reasons for neglecting features of the measured physical configuration when constructing the
reference as-built model:
 1. It may be desirable to convert an as-built Monte Carlo model of a ZPR/ZPPR assembly to
 an equivalent deterministic model. For example, if deterministic codes are being used for
 reactor design purposes, a deterministic model of a ZPR/ZPPR assembly can be used as
 part of the validation for the deterministic codes. It may not be possible to represent some
 of the geometrical features of an as-built Monte Carlo model or of the actual physical
 configuration in the equivalent deterministic model. In that case, the reference as-built
 Monte Carlo model would omit geometry features that could not be represented in the
 deterministic code, and the omissions would be treated as a bias.
 2. Even if the geometry of the as-built Monte Carlo model can be represented adequately in
 an equivalent deterministic model, it may not be possible or practical to compute the
 resulting deterministic model. Including all structures between the outer boundary of the
 matrix tubes and the outer boundary of the reactor cell would result in a very large model
 with very large void regions outside the matrix tubes. In addition, obtaining meaningful
 deterministic cross sections for materials far outside the matrix tubes may be difficult or
 impossible.
 3. There may many trace elements in minor components of materials and impurities, and there
 are multiple isotopes in many elements. Including all of those isotopes in the reference
 model can increase the execution time for the as-built Monte Carlo model. This does not
 matter very much if the Monte Carlo model will only be computed once, but it does matter
 if the Monte Carlo model will be computed many times. For example, many people will
 compute an ICSBEP/IRPhEP benchmark of a ZPR/ZPPR assembly [5,6]. Increasing the
 number of isotopes in the benchmark model increases the probability of error on the part
 of the evaluator in the initial specification of the benchmark model, increases the
 probability of error when a user of that ICSBEP/IRPhEP benchmark makes a model of the
 benchmark and increases the execution time when the resulting model is computed. A
 common practice is to omit most or all impurities from an ICSBEP/IRPhEP benchmark
 model and to treat that omission as a bias.
7.1.4.1 General Treatment of Neglected Features and Bias
Suppose that the reference as-built model without the neglected feature is M 0, that the measured
experimental keff is kexp, and that the experimental keff adjusted for the neglected feature is kadj. A
neglected feature, F1, of the true physical configuration is generally treated in the following steps:
 1. Construct the reference as-built model, M0, that does not include the neglected feature and
 compute keff(M0) for model M0.
 2. Construct as-built model M1 that includes the neglected feature, F1, and compute keff(M1)

 218

 for model M1.
    3. Compute Δk10 = keff(M1) – keff(M0)                                              (1)
 4. The adjusted experimental keff is kadj = kexp – Δk10 (2)
The adjusted experimental keff, in step 4, kadj, accounts for feature F1 that is included in model M1
but is not included in model M0, the reference model. If the experimental keff is not adjusted as
shown in step 4, keff(M0) will be biased because model M0 does not include the neglected feature,
F1, that is included in model M1 and in the measured physical configuration.
Note that equation (2) in step 4 applies regardless of whether Δk 10 is positive or negative. If Δk10
is positive, then keff for the true physical configuration that included F1 is greater than keff for the
modeled configuration that did not include F1. In that case, the measured experimental keff must
be reduced to account for the fact that M0, the reference model, does not include F1. If Δk10 is
negative, then keff for the measured physical configuration that included F1 is less than keff for the
modeled configuration that did not include F1. In that case, the measured experimental keff must
be increased to account for the fact that M0, the reference model, does not include F1.
The kadj is the value that is used in comparisons with keff(M0) to determine the bias in the computed
keff of the reference model, M0, of the configuration of interest. This bias, i.e., the difference
between keff(M0) and kadj, results from uncertainties in the basic measured nuclear data,
approximations in the methods and codes used to process the basic nuclear data into an evaluated
format such as ENDF/B-VIII, approximations in the methods and codes used to process the
evaluated nuclear data into the final continuous energy or multigroup format required by the Monte
Carlo code or deterministic code used by the analyst, and any approximations in the Monte Carlo
or deterministic codes to compute keff. Even if model M0 is a perfect representation of the geometry
and materials in the physical configuration, there will be a difference between k eff(M0) and kadj
because the basic nuclear data and the codes used to process the basic nuclear data are not perfect.
Steps 1 – 4 apply to any neglected features or differences between the reference as-built model,
M0, and the true physical configuration that was measured. In general, the neglected features will
relate to a) geometry features that are neglected or approximated such as room return and b)
impurities in materials or other minor components of materials that are neglected in the reference
model.
If the bias is calculated with Monte Carlo models of M 0 and M1, the statistical uncertainty in Δk10
is included in the total uncertainty for the criticality measurement.
Suppose N features, F1, F2, . . . , FN, are neglected in the reference model. The analyst could repeat
steps 1 – 4 for each of the N features and compute N separate adjustments, Δk 10, Δk20, . . . , ΔkN0.
The kadj is determined as
                kadj = kexp – Δk10 – Δk20 – . . . – ΔkN0                              (3)
The process of treating each neglected feauture separately as described in the preceding paragraphs
and in equation (3) is a valid approach for determining the total bias associated with multiple
neglected features. Many people use this approach when there are multiple neglected features
because it shows the importance of each neglected feature. However, this approach has a few
drawbacks. First, it may require a lot of effort to construct all of the models and computer
resources to obtain a value for each of the N neglected features. Second, if Monte Carlo models

 219

are used to compute the biases, the statistical uncertainties in Δk10, Δk20, . . . , ΔkN0 contribute to
the total uncertainty. Some of the biases are small, so significant computing effort may be required
to provide accurate estimates of the biases.
There is a simpler method to determine the total bias and any associated uncertainty. The only
thing that really matters is the total bias and its uncertainty. The total bias incorporates all of the
differences between the reference model, M0, and the physical configuration that was measured,
i.e., the N features that were neglected in model M 0. Instead of constructing a separate model and
computing a separate bias for each of the N neglected features, it is recommended that the analyst
construct and compute a single model, M S, that includes all N neglected features. Then
            ΔkS0 = keff(MS) – keff(M0)                                                   (4)
is the total bias and σS0 is the associated uncertainty The σS0 is included in the total uncertainty
for the criticality measurement.
In addition to requiring less effort and time than computing a separate bias for each neglected
feature, constructing and computing model MS that includes all of the neglected features allows
more computer resources to be devoted to computing ΔkS0 and σS0, which results in better estimates
of both parameters. This approach does not suggest that investigation into large unexpected values
of ΔkS0 should not be carried out; instead, it simply states that it is equivalent in the end to the
desired goal and if ΔkS0 turns out to be small, it generally is justifiable to not expend considerable
effort on getting a breakdown of it into the N neglected features.
This discussion applies to any significant feature that is neglected or to any significant difference
between the actual physical configuration that was measured and the model of that configuration.
The difference may relate to approximations in material compositions or to approximations in the
representation of geometry.
The biases must be determined on a case-by-case basis. Examples of approximations in materials
are neglecting important impurities, Kel-F on coated plates and possibly the hydrogen (water)
content in graphite plates. The most common approximations with respect to geometry are
neglecting the interface gap as discussed earlier, neglecting room return, and neglecting important
features of experimental equipment for specific types of measurements.
7.1.4.2 Room Return
An adjustment and an uncertainty are needed for room return of neutrons to the assembly. The
assembly description in the as-built model created by software usually encompasses only the
matrix tubes and their contents because the relevant structures outside the matrix tubes will depend
upon the facility (ZPR-3, ZPR-6, ZPR-9, ZPPR) and possibly the experiment being modeled. In
reality, the matrix rests on a massive steel table with steel structures on the sides and top that
constrain the matrix tubes (see Figure 2.3 and Figure 2.7 through Figure 2.12). In addition, there
is a steel back plate behind the matrix tubes in each half to support the horizontal control rods and
experimental equipment. The matrix machine is located in a large reactor cell (room).
The steel table, structures on the sides and top, the back plate, control rod drives and reactor cell
(room in which the reactor is located) reflect neutrons back into the matrix tubes. The reflection
provided by these structures is known as room return.

 220

The reactivity worth of room return is the difference between keff for the reference as-built model
consisting of just the matrix tubes and drawers and k eff for an as-built model in which the external
structures (tables, side supports, top structures, back plate, reactor cell) have been added to the
reference model.
The reactivity worth of room return depends upon the size and composition of the axial and radial
blankets and reflectors. If the blanket and reflector are thick with no significant voids, the worth
of room return will be small. In most ZPR/ZPPR assemblies, the radial and axial blankets and
reflectors were thick enough that room return was small or negligible, and the experimenters
frequently made a special effort to minimize the effects of room return.
There were some cases in which room return was not necessarily small. Room return was found
to be significant in the Gas-Cooled Fast Reactor (GCFR) Program (ZPR-9/28, ZPR-9/29 and ZPR-
9/30) because the simulated gas coolant channels resulted in a void fraction of 40% – 50% in the
core and axial blanket of the GCFR assemblies and, consequently, in significant neutron leakage.
ZPR-9/32 simulated several severe hypothetical core disruption accidents with large void regions,
so there probably was high neutron leakage from some of the ZPR-9/32 configurations as well.
The reflector was relatively ineffective in a few assemblies. For example, the reflector consisted
of aluminum or aluminum oxide in some of the rocket reactor criticals (ZPR-9/1 through ZPR-
9/9). The point is that it is necessary to account for room return either by including the ex-core
structures in the reference as-built model or by adjusting the experimental k eff to account for the
bias introduced by neglecting room return.
In early ICSBEP benchmarks of ZPR/ZPPR assemblies, the benchmark model was an R-Z model
of the core, blanket and reflector with homogeneous compositions in the core, blanket and reflector
regions [5,6]. The effects of room return were estimated for those benchmarks by computing a
model with a close-fitting steel shell around the R-Z benchmark model. This close-fitting shell
probably overestimated the worth of room return in the R-Z models. One way to quickly assess
the importance of room return on the as-built model is to apply reflected boundary conditions to
the exterior of the modeled domain. This would generate an unrealistic room return component,
but if one finds it to be ~1 pcm, then it should be clear that adding more details to the existing
model to account for the real room return would not be worth the effort and thus only a bias needs
to be assessed. Contrarily, if one finds that applying reflected boundary conditions leads to a 300
pcm increase in keff, then that would indicate it might be worth investigating how expanding the
model to include more details might improve the model and its results.
In later ICSBEP/IRPhEP benchmarks of ZPR/ZPPR assemblies, the reference as-built model is
the benchmark model, and a better treatment of room return was devised which is that
recommended for assessing the bias due to room return.
Examination of Figure 2.3 and Figure 2.7 to Figure 2.12 shows that the structures surrounding the
matrix tubes are complex. In the absence of detailed drawings, it would not be practical to
construct highly detailed models of the tables, side supports (bed and knees), or other structures
surrounding the matrix tubes, but it is possible to construct reasonable approximations of those
structures that are adequate for analysis purposes.
For example, in the case of ZPPR-15A, the radial blanket thickness was ~15 cm, and the radial
reflector consisted of ~40 cm of stainless steel. The axial blanket and reflector dimensions were

 221

similar. The worth of room return in ZPPR-15A was computed as the difference between the
reference as-built model consisting only of the 77 x 77 array of matrix tubes and an expanded
model in which the steel table, steel structures on the sides and top of the matrix and the
surrounding room were added. The computed worth of room return was 5.01 ± 2.83 pcm for
ZPPR-15A; the computed worth of room return for ZPPR-15B, ZPPR-15C and ZPPR-15D was
smaller. For a ZPR/ZPPR assembly, a Monte Carlo calculation of an as-built model that runs one
billion (109) histories typically yields a statistical uncertainty of 1 – 2 pcm on ZPR/ZPPR models,
so the 2.83 pcm statistical uncertainty is the result of two calculations where each calculation ran
one billion histories. The 2.83 pcm Monte Carlo uncertainty is assumed to be the uncertainty in
the worth of room return.
Adding room return to an as-built model to account for the true physical configuration increases
reflection and increases reactivity; neglecting room return in the as-built reduces reactivity. The
computed worth of room return is subtracted from the experimental k eff to account for the reduction
in reactivity resulting from neglecting room return in the as-built model. If the effects of room
return are small, Monte Carlo calculations of room return may produce a negative worth. Any
computed negative room return worth is a statistical artifact of the Monte Carlo calculations
because actual room return cannot be negative.
7.1.4.2.1 Room Return Models for ZPR-6 and ZPR-9
ANL-7195 [4] discusses the design, construction and pre-operational testing of ZPR-6. ZPR-9
was constructed at approximately the same time as ZPR-6. Both machines were designed and
assembled by the same ANL-E staff, so ANL-7195 is assumed to apply to ZPR-9 as well. Figure
2.7 through Figure 2.9 in Section 2 and ANL-7195 were used to construct approximate models of
room return for ZPR-6 and ZPR-9. The bed and tables for ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were modeled as 20
cm of solid ASTM A36 carbon steel. For criticality safety purposes, a thickness of 20 cm is
generally treated as an infinite thickness for steel because a negligible fraction of the neutrons that
traverse 20 cm of steel will return to the core. An analyst could refine this treatment of the tables
by modeling the tables shown in Figure 2.8, Figure 2.9 and ANL-7195 more accurately, but it
seems unlikely that the improved model would have any discernible effect on the criticality

Figure 17 in ANL-7195 shows the best view of the table that the matrix tubes were loaded on.
Figure 24 and Figure 25 in ANL-7195 provide the best view of the side supports for the matrix
tubes in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9. It would be difficult to represent the vertical and horizontal
reinforcements for the side supports accurately without the design drawings, so the side support
on each side of the matrix tubes in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 was assumed to consist of 6 cm of steel to
account for the side support and reinforcements. There were neutron detectors on the top of the
core, but there are no other significant structures above the matrix tubes in the available
photographs thus nothing was assumed to be above the matrix tubes in room return models.
Based on Figure 33 of ANL-7195, there was probably ~36 in (91.44 cm) of space between the
back of the matrix tubes and the back plate that supported the control rod drives. Figure 33 of
ANL-7195 shows that the back plate only covered the central part of the matrix where the control
rods were located. There were penetrations in the back plate to allow positioning of control rod
drives and experimental equipment such as the Doppler sample drawer. It would be difficult to

 222

model the back plate and control rod drives accurately. For practical purposes, it seems reasonable
to assume
 a) A 91.44 cm separation exists between the back of the matrix tubes and the back plate
 b) The back plate extends to the full size of the matrix tubes
 c) The back plate consists of 2.5 cm of solid steel.
The increased area of the back plate in models and neglecting unused penetrations in the back plate
should compensate for the additional material in the control rod drives.
The reactor cell was 40 ft x 30 ft with a height of 30 ft, which corresponds to approximately 12 m
x 9 m x 9 m. The center of the machine was approximately 5.5 m from the south wall, 3.4 m from
the west wall and 2.1 m above the floor (see page 45 of ANL-6271 [3]). The 2.1 m height refers
to the height of the center matrix tube above the floor, and the center of the machine was offset
from the center of the reactor cell (see Figure 2.8 and Figure 2.9). The cell walls, floor and ceiling
consisted of reinforced concrete with a thickness of 1.2 m except for the side facing the control
room that had a thickness of 1.5 m.
The features described here can be added to an as-built model to provide a reasonable estimate of
the room return bias for an assembly built in ZPR-6 or ZPR-9.
7.1.4.2.2 Room Return Model for ZPPR
There is no equivalent of ANL-7195 [4] and ANL-6271 [3] for ZPPR. The ZPPR reactor cell was
cylindrical with an inner radius of ~25 ft (7.62 m). The height of the reactor cell was ~30 ft (9 m).
The walls, floor and roof can be modeled as 1.2 m of concrete. For criticality safety purposes, 61
cm of concrete is regarded as infinitely thick, so the exact thickness of the ZPPR cell walls mattered
for safety analysis and shielding analysis but not for present purposes.
The ZPPR tables were massive, and their design was probably very similar to the table design for
ZPR-6 and ZPR-9. Consequently, the tables were assumed to consist of 20 cm of solid ASTM
A36 steel in models.
The side supports for ZPPR constrained a much larger matrix than the matrix in ZPR-6 or ZPR-9,
so the side supports in ZPPR would have to be at least as massive as the side supports in ZPR-6 or
ZPR-9. Comparison of Figure 2.12 with Figure 2.7 through Figure 2.9 shows that the
reinforcements for the ZPPR side supports were significantly more massive than the
reinforcements for the ZPR-6 side supports. It is reasonable to assume ~7.5 cm of steel as a model
of the ZPPR side supports and reinforcements. Note that the ZPPR staff sometimes referred to the
side supports as the clamp.
Figure 2.11 and Figure 2.12 do not clearly show anything above the ZPPR matrix tubes, but it
seems reasonable to assume ~3 cm of steel above the matrix tubes to account for any structural
elements or detectors located above the matrix.
Figure 2.11 shows a mounting plate behind the matrix tubes. It is assumed that this mounting plate
is the back plate. Based on Figure 2.11, it appears that the back plate covered all of the matrix
tubes and that there were a significant number of penetrations in this back plate to allow flexibility
in locating control rods and other experimental equipment. For practical purposes, it seems
reasonable to assume a) 91.44 cm separation between the back of the matrix tubes and the back

 223

plate, b) the back plate is the size of the matrix and c) the back plate consists of 2.5 cm of solid
steel.
7.1.4.2.3 Room Return Model for ZPR-3
Design documents and safety analysis reports for ZPR-3 must have existed, but no such documents
have been located thus far. In the absence of such documents, any models of structures outside
the ZPR-3 matrix tubes are based on assumptions derived from Figure 2.1 through Figure 2.3.
These figures show the ZPR-3 machine and part of the reactor cell.
Figure 2.1 shows that the ZPR-3 table was not as massive as the ZPR-6 table, but Figure 2.1 shows
that there was a large amount of steel below the matrix tubes. It seems reasonable to model the
ZPR-3 table as 20 cm of solid steel since there is no information to provide a better model.
Unlike ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR, the side supports for ZPR-3 appeared to consist of three I-beams
in a framework. The approximate sizes and positions of these I-beams can be determined from
Figure 2.1. Based on Figure 2.1, it appears that I-beams or similar structures were also placed on
top of the matrix tubes. The other devices on top of the matrix tubes were probably detectors or
housing for electronics related to instruments of some type.
Figure 2.1 shows that the back plate was probably about 18 in (45.72 cm) from the back of the
matrix tubes. Figure 2.1 shows that the back plate was relatively thick and that there was
significant mass associated with the ZPR-3 control rod drives. This mass provided more reflection
near the center of the matrix tubes than the ZPR-6 control rods. It seems reasonable to assume a
solid plate thickness of ~3.5 – 4 cm to account for the back plates and control rod drives.
Figure 2.1 through Figure 2.3 show that the ZPR-3 machine was located near one corner of the
reactor cell. Based on these figures, the center of the matrix tubes was probably ~2.5 m from the
nearest wall (the wall behind the machine in Figure 2.1).
In Figure 2.3, the stationary table is on the left, and the movable table is on the right nearer the
sign and tool rack. The length of the matrix tubes is 33.5 in, and the separation between tables in
Figure 2.1 through Figure 2.3 appears to be ~60 in. Allowing for the back plate and control rod
drives behind the movable table and for reasonable work space behind the movable table, the back
of the matrix tubes on the movable table appears to be ~9 ft from the rear wall in Figure 2.3. Based
on these estimates, the center of the reactor was ~201 in or ~5.1 m from the rear wall in Figure 2.3
when the reactor was critical.
A reasonable assumption is that the ZPR-3 reactor cell had approximately the same dimensions as
the ZPR-6 cell, so the interior of the ZPR-3 reactor cell is assumed to be approximately 9 m x 12
m with a height of 9 m. The cell walls, floor and ceiling can be approximated as 1.2 m of concrete.
7.1.5 Modeling of Criticality Measurements
To date, many as-built Monte Carlo models have been constructed for ZPR/ZPPR assemblies. The
smallest ZPR-3 as-built Monte Carlo model input file had ~2000 lines. The largest ZPPR as-built
Monte Carlo model input file had ~50,000 lines. As-built models for ZPPR-18 and ZPPR-19
would be significantly larger than this.

 224

It is not practical to construct an as-built Monte Carlo model of a ZPR/ZPPR assembly manually
for several reasons. First, those models are complex and difficult to construct. Second, the time
required to construct an as-built Monte Carlo model of a ZPR/ZPPR assembly, especially one of
the larger, more complex ZPPR assemblies, would be excessive. Third, it would be difficult to
have high confidence that there were no typographical errors in the input file.
The fact that the Monte Carlo model runs successfully is only a confirmation that there are no
inconsistencies such as undefined or overlapping volumes in the geometry model. There could
still be errors in dimensions or compositions. Errors in material compositions would affect the
computed keff, but they would not affect whether the calculation completed without error messages.
Construction of an as-built Monte Carlo model of a ZPR/ZPPR assembly requires software to
automate production of the Monte Carlo model and requires conversion of the drawer master
figures and loading records to digital versions that are compatible with that software.
Unfortunately, there are two steps in the process that are difficult to automate. The available
loading records are PDF files that were scanned from the original paper documents. The first step
in constructing an as-built Monte Carlo model or deterministic model is converting the loading
records to a digital form that can be recognized by the software used to create the model. This
aspect has always involved a manual transcription of the PDF files to a digital form. This is a
tedious process, and the resulting digital file must be checked carefully against the original PDF
version of the loading records.
It has been suggested that optical character recognition software (OCR) could be used for this
purpose. Section 5 discusses the loading records and shows some typical examples from the four
facilities. It is possible that future OCR with possible assistance from artificial intelligence (AI)
may be able to produce an accurate digital version of the loading records. However, given the
variability in loading records shown in Section 5, it seems unlikely that the OCR available today
would produce an accurate transcription. In any case, it would still be necessary to check the
digital file produced by OCR against the original loading records.
Regardless of whether the original loading records are converted to digital form manually or by
OCR, the checking is necessary because an error in the digital version may be impossible to detect
in the final as-built model.
In the absence of OCR/AI to transcribe and convert the loading records to the required digital form,
the following manual procedure was used:
 1. Transcribe all loading records from loading 1 through the highest loading number of
 interest from the original PDF file(s) to a spreadsheet.
 2. Check the spreadsheet against the original PDF file(s) and make any necessary corrections
 in the spreadsheet.
 3. Convert the spreadsheet to a text file.
 4. Convert the resulting text file from (3) to the digital format required by the software used
 to produce the matrix map(s) for the loading(s) of interest.
 5. Process the file from (4) to create the matrix map(s) for the loading(s) of interest.
Step 4 assumes that software exists to convert the text file version of the spreadsheet to the format
required by the software used in step 5 to make the matrix map(s). It is easy to create software (or

 225

a script) to convert the format of the text file from step 3 to step 4. Likewise, it is not difficult to
create software (or a script) to process the file created in step 4 to create the matrix map(s) of
interest. Regardless, it is necessary use software for steps 4 and 5. For example, the length of the
transcribed ZPPR-15 loading records was ~15,600 lines. Transcribing those records manually,
checking the resulting spreadsheet, correcting any errors in that spreadsheet, and checking the
spreadsheet again required several weeks. It would not have been possible to go from step 3 to
the required matrix maps except by automating steps 4 and 5.
A specific plate-loading pattern in a drawer was called a drawer master. Physically, a drawer
master was a drawing or blueprint showing the location or position of each type of plate in a
drawer. The drawer masters were guides or templates used by the technicians to load the drawers.
The specification of which drawer master was in each matrix position in each half of the split-table
machine is known as a matrix loading map, matrix map or interface map. After the loading records
have been converted to a digital format, they must be processed to create the matrix map for the
assembly/loading of interest as described above. It is not practical to process the digitized loading
records manually, but again, software for this purpose can be created. The software that produces
the matrix map in step 5 can also create a list of all drawer masters present in each half of the
matrix as well as a count of the number of drawer masters of each type that were present in each
half of the matrix.
The available drawer master records also are PDF files that were scanned from the original paper
drawings (see Section 3). The second step in constructing an as-built Monte Carlo model of a
ZPR/ZPPR assembly/loading is to convert the drawer master figures to a digital form that can be
recognized by the software used to create the model. This also has always been a manual process,
and the resulting digital file must be checked carefully against the original drawer master figures.
Given the variability of the drawer master figures shown in Section 3, the prospect for using OCR
to convert the drawer master figures to a digital form does not seem to be better than the prospect
for using OCR to convert the loading records to a digital form.
After a digital matrix map file and digital file of drawer masters have been created, software can
use those files to create an as-built Monte Carlo model for the chosen assembly and loading. It is
also possible to use those files to create software that builds a deterministic model although multi-
group cross section library generation requires more detailed input and geometry handling than
that needed for an as-built Monte Carlo model.
7.2 Sodium Void Worth Measurements
Most of the reactors simulated in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies were sodium-cooled fast reactors.
ZPR/ZPPR assemblies used sodium plates to simulate the sodium coolant in a fast reactor. A
sodium plate or sodium can consisted of a sealed stainless steel can containing solid sodium.
Sodium density changes as the reactor inlet/outlet temperature changes, and that density change
affects the criticality of the system. Determining the relationship between operating temperature,
sodium density and its reactivity worth is an important part of safety analysis of sodium-cooled
fast reactors.
The ZPR/ZPPR staff measured the worths of sodium density changes and sodium voiding in many
assemblies. However, the nature of the ZPR/ZPPR materials inventories limited the types of

 226

measurements that could be performed and dictated the experimental techniques used to measure
the worth of sodium density changes and the worth of sodium voiding.
The most important limitation on measurements of the worth of sodium density changes or sodium
voiding in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies was the requirement to perform all measurements at low power
and at approximately room temperature (allowing for the increased core temperature due to
radioactive decay in plutonium-fueled cores). Loading drawers, unloading drawers, loading
matrix tubes, unloading matrix tubes and related drawer or plate handling activities were manual
operations. Operation of the reactor at high power for an extended period would have created too
much activation in non-fissionable materials and too many fission products in fissionable
materials, resulting in unacceptable radiation exposures for the staff who performed those manual
operations.
In addition, operating the reactor at high power and high temperature would have increased the
likelihood of clad failure in clad plates. Failure of a clad plate would have resulted in release of
plutonium from a clad plutonium fuel plate or potential exposure of hot sodium to air in a failed
sodium plate. Aside from the obvious direct safety issues, failure of a significant number of fuel
plates and/or sodium plates would have resulted in an extended shutdown for cleanup operations,
safety review and possibly an operational readiness review before operations could resume.
Sodium void worth measurements in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies consisted of complete sodium voiding
in a portion of the core. The reactivity worth of sodium per unit mass was measured with small
samples and intermediate samples. Reactivity worth measurements with small and intermediate
samples are discussed in a later section.
7.2.1 Sodium Void Worth Experimental Technique
The basic concept of sodium void worth measurements in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies was simple. The
experimenters replaced standard sodium cans with empty stainless steel cans in a portion of the
reactor and measured the resulting change in reactivity to determine the worth of sodium voiding.
Thus the sodium void worth experiments measured the difference in reactivity between a
configuration with solid sodium in the experimental zone and a configuration with no sodium in
the experimental zone, i.e., the reactivity worth of complete sodium voiding in the experimental
zone. It was not practice in the ZPR/ZPPR facilities to measure the reactivity changes associated
with small changes in sodium density except possibly in the context of small sample worth

Most ZPR/ZPPR sodium void worth measurements were based upon replacing sodium plates with
matching empty cans in the affected drawers. One basic problem with measurements in any of the
ZPR/ZPPR machines is that the plates used to simulate the reactor were small rectangular
parallelepipeds (RPPs) inside drawers in matrix tubes in a square lattice, whereas the reactor being
simulated consisted of a hexagonal array of hexagonal ducts containing clad fuel rods in a
hexagonal lattice surrounded by coolant. A carefully designed ZPR/ZPPR plate configuration
matched the average composition of the target reactor reasonably well, and the geometry mismatch
was not important for many types of measurements. That geometry mismatch is more relevant for
some types of measurements, particularly measurements such as sodium void worth in which
neutron streaming and axial leakage become important.

 227

The geometry mismatch between the target reactor and the representation of that reactor in the
critical experiment is not unique to ZPR/ZPPR assemblies. A similar mismatch occurs in other
critical experiment facilities that are or were used to simulate fast reactors. For example, the
materials inventory used at the BFS-1 and BFS-2 critical experiment facilities at IPPE in Obninsk,
Russia consists of circular disks that are loaded into tubes with circular cross sections. The tubes
are loaded into the BFS-1 machine or BFS-2 machine to create the critical configuration. The
tubes are vertical in the machine, and the disks are horizontal in the tubes.
As an alternative, one could use calandria. The ZPR/ZPPR inventories did contain some clad PuO 2
pins and clad UO2 pins. There were not enough of these pins to build an entire critical assembly,
but there were enough pins to build a pin zone in an assembly and to measure the effects of sodium
voiding and streaming in that pin zone. The pin diameter was 0.375 inches, and the standard pin
length was 6 inches although there were a few pins with a length of 3 inches.
The pins were inserted into calandria, and the calandria were loaded into standard drawers. A
calandria was a 2 x 2 x 12 inch stainless steel can containing a 4 x 4 square array of stainless steel
tubes. The PuO2 pins or UO2 pins were inserted into the 16 tubes in the calandria. There were two
types of calandria: 1) a type 1 calandria where the free space was filled with sodium to represent
the reference configuration and 2) a type 2 calandria where the free space was empty (i.e. filled
with air) to represent the void configuration. The fuel pins and calandria provided a way to estimate
the effects of the geometry mismatch between the target reactor and the plate representation in a
ZPR/ZPPR assembly.
Sodium void worth measurements with pins and calandria were conducted in the same way as
sodium void worth measurements with plates.
The most common place to establish a void zone in a ZPR/ZPPR assembly was in the radial and
axial center of the reactor, but the experimenters could and did create void zones elsewhere in the
reactor in some assemblies. The void zone could be asymmetric radially and/or axially and could
be located at the center of the core, near the outer boundary of the core or anywhere else in the
core. One common experiment was measurement of the worth of sodium voiding near a simulated
control rod or the effect of sodium voiding on the worth of a simulated control rod.
The dimensions of the sodium plates imposed one constraint on the axial size of a void zone. All
sodium plates had nominal external dimensions of 0.25 x 2 x L inches or 0.5 x 2 x L inches where
L is the plate length. There were limited numbers of sodium plates with lengths of 2 or 3 inches,
but most sodium plates in the facility inventories had lengths of 4, 5, 6, 7 or 8 inches. The
combinations of available plates imposed a constraint on the length of the void zone. The 2 x 2 x
12 inch dimensions of the calandria imposed a more severe constraint on the axial dimensions of
the void in a pin zone.
Another constraint on the axial extent of a void zone was that most plates with lengths of 4, 5, 6,
7 or 8 inches were made in the late 1960s for use at ZPPR and ANL-E. Those are the plates
designated by NA in the ADEN library. When the NA plates were manufactured, some of them
were shipped to ZPPR, and the remainder were shipped to ANL-E for use at ZPR-6 and ZPR-9.
Prior to manufacture of the NA plates, the numbers and sizes of sodium plates available for use in
ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were limited.

 228

In fact, the original ZPR-3 plate inventory had no sodium plates. Aluminum plates were used to
simulate sodium in early ZPR-3 assemblies. By drilling holes in aluminum plates, the ZPR-3 staff
made aluminum plates with approximately the correct average physical density to simulate
sodium. Ironically, the aluminum plates could have given ZPR-3 additional flexibility that was
not available with the canned sodium plates. By drilling additional holes in some aluminum plates,
the ZPR-3 staff could have studied the effects of reduced coolant density. This was not possible
with the canned sodium plates.
The size of the void zone varied from a single drawer or a 2 x 2 array of drawers in early assemblies
to the entire core in the case of ZPPR-12. Void zones frequently consisted of a 2 x 2, 2 x 3 or 3 x
3 array of drawers because these sizes corresponded approximately to voiding of a single fuel
subassembly, depending on subassembly design. It was possible to simulate the approximate area
or volume of one subassembly, but it was not possible to simulate the hexagonal boundary of one
subassembly accurately.
The technique used to measure the reactivity change associated with sodium voiding affected the
experimental procedure. The reactivity measurement techniques used at ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-
9 limited the size of the void zone because those techniques could not be used to measure large
void worths. ZPPR was limited for the same reason until the modified source multiplication
(MSM) technique was adopted at ZPPR. Adoption of the MSM technique allowed measurement
of negative reactivity worths up to -50$.
The experimental procedure and methods used to measure the reactivity change were identical in
ZPR-6 and ZPR-9. The experimental procedure and methods used to measure the sodium void
worth in ZPR-3 assemblies and in early ZPPR assemblies were similar to the experimental
procedures and methods used to measure sodium void worth at ANL-E. Adoption of the MSM
technique resulted in a significant change in the procedure for measuring sodium void worth at
ZPPR and expanded the range of possible void worth measurements that could be done.
7.2.1.1 Sodium Void Worth – Experimental Technique at ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9
A typical sodium void worth measurement at ZPR-3, ZPR-6 or ZPR-9 consisted of the following
steps:
 1. The excess reactivity of the core was measured for the reference configuration. In this
 context, “excess reactivity” means the excess reactivity that would be present if all DP
 control drawers, PSR blades and the autorod (if used) were moved to their most reactive
 positions and the reactor temperature was adjusted to a reference value. For a DP control
 drawer, the most reactive position is the position where the DP drawer is fully inserted.
 For a PSR blade, the most reactive position is the position where the PSR blade is fully
 withdrawn to its parked position, which is approximately 30 inches from the front of the
 matrix tube.
 2. The reactor was shut down, and sodium cans in the designated void zone were replaced by
 matched empty steel cans (void cans). A matched void can was an empty stainless steel
 can with the same external dimensions as the sodium can that was being replaced.
 3. The excess reactivity of the configuration with the sodium void zone was measured.
 4. The reactor was shut down, and the void cans were replaced by the original sodium cans.
 5. The excess reactivity of the reference core was measured again.

 229

Steps 1 – 5 refer to a single measurement. In a series of related measurements such as changing
the axial length or radial (X-Y) extent of the void region, steps 2 and 3 might be repeated until all
void configurations of interest were measured unless there was a need to adjust the reactivity of
the core for some of the measurements.
The power was held constant with the autorod during the measurement, the core temperature was
measured, the positions of all control rods were recorded, and the average autorod position was
determined. Reactivity was measured in inhours (Ih) or cents. A measured conversion factor was
used to convert inhours to %Δk/k. Inhour is rarely or never used as a unit for reactivity
measurement today, but it was in common use when ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 operated. At some
point, ANL-W switched to measuring reactivity in cents.
Measured excess reactivity consisted of the following components:
 1. The available reactivity contained in the control rods. These rods were calibrated using an
 inverse kinetics code.
 2. The available reactivity contained in the partially withdrawn autorod (if the autorod was
 present). The autorod was also calibrated using an inverse kinetics code.
 3. Corrections were made for 241Pu decay (if applicable) and for differences in the interface
 gap and core temperature between the different measurements. In most cases, the measured
 sodium void worths and the excess reactivity of the reconstructed reference configuration
 were corrected to the conditions (241Pu decay date, interface gap and average core
 temperature) of the original reference configuration.
The imprecision of the excess reactivity measurement is determined by (1) the precisions of the
control rod calibrations, the temperature coefficient, and the 241Pu decay coefficient and (2) the
scatter in the results due to non-reproducibility in the assembly table closure and control rod
positions between different reactor start-ups. Non-reproducibility refers to the fact that the
measured critical table closure and rod positions were not reproducible or repeatable to an arbitrary
degree of precision for different startups with the same core loading.
The experimental technique for sodium void worth measurements in early ZPPR assemblies, i.e.,
assemblies built prior to the use of the MSM technique, was similar to the experimental technique
used in ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9.
In critical configurations, reactivity was measured based on the steady-state positions of calibrated
control rods. For void configurations that were subcritical, several different techniques were used
to measure reactivity. These techniques included inverse kinetics analysis of rod drops, a polarity
coherence technique, reactor period measurements and subcritical source multiplication. This list
is not necessarily exhaustive; it is likely that other techniques also were used during the many
years that these facilities operated. Note that rod drop measurements only applied to the PSRs.
DP drawers were not used for rod drop measurements.
One problem with the procedure described above is that frequently the experimenters had to adjust
core boundaries or make other changes in the core loading to adjust reactivity prior to performing
the measurement. Sodium void worth can be positive or negative, depending upon the size of void
(length), size of the void zone (number of affected drawers), location of the void zone and the
specific assembly configuration. Likewise, the magnitude of the sodium void worth can be small

 230

or large for similar reasons. If the predicted void worth was positive, it might be necessary to
reduce excess reactivity. If the predicted void worth was sufficiently negative, it might be
necessary to increase excess reactivity.
There were two basic options for adjusting excess reactivity. The first option was to increase or
decrease the core size. The experimenters increased excess reactivity by substituting core drawers
for radial blanket drawers at the core-radial blanket boundary and decreased excess reactivity by
substituting radial blanket drawers for core drawers at the core-radial blanket boundary.
The second option for adjusting excess reactivity was changing the contents of some core drawers.
A core drawer containing one fuel column was referred to as a single fuel column (SCF) drawer,
and a core drawer containing two fuel columns was referred to as a double fuel column (DCF)
drawer. Replacing DCF drawers with SCF drawers at symmetric locations in the outer core
reduced the excess reactivity. Replacing SCF drawers with DCF drawers at symmetric locations
in the outer core increased the excess reactivity. The ZPR/ZPPR staff referred to increasing
reactivity by substituting DCF drawers for SCF drawers as a “spike” and to decreasing reactivity
by substituting SCF drawers for DCF drawers as a “despike.”
Any spike, despike or adjustment of the core boundary affected the flux distribution, power
distribution and measured worth of the void configuration. The positions of any partially inserted
control rods also had at least a small effect on these parameters.
The reactivity worth per kilogram for stainless steel is much larger than the reactivity worth per
kilogram for sodium, so any mismatch between the mass of stainless steel removed in the sodium
cans and the mass of steel added in the void cans during a sodium void worth measurement could
introduce a significant experimental uncertainty.
To minimize this experimental uncertainty, the experimenters attempted to match the amount of
steel in the sodium plate to be removed with the amount of steel in the void can to be inserted. In
practice, matching the stainless steel in the sodium plates to be removed with the stainless steel in
the void cans to be inserted generally meant that each sodium plate was replaced by a void can
with the same dimensions. For example, a ½ x 2 x 8 inch sodium plate was replaced by a ½ x 2 x
8 inch void can. This is clear from the drawer master figures or templates used by the technicians
as guides to load plates into drawers.
Note that only the sodium plates were replaced in core drawers in the voided zone. No other plates
in the affected drawers were changed in the measurement in order to minimize experimental
uncertainty.
Changing the core loading required shutting down the reactor, separating the matrix halves,
making the desired changes in the core loading, bringing the matrix halves together again and
moving the operational control rods to establish the desired configuration. There was some 241Pu
decay during the elapsed time, and the average reactor temperature could change slightly due to
the elapsed time required to establish the new configuration. In addition, there could be a small
difference in the interface gap between the reference configuration and the modified configuration.
Measuring the sodium void worth for multiple configurations could span several days and require
several modified configurations. In order to minimize experimental uncertainty and facilitate
analysis of the experiments, the experimenters adjusted the measured values for the sodium void

 231

worth to a common decay date, temperature and interface gap using a calculated 241Pu decay, and
measured temperature and interface gap coefficients in conjunction with measured temperatures
and interface gap separation parameters for each relevant loading. These coefficients were
measured during the operational measurements performed after the reference critical configuration
was established. The common decay date, temperature and interface gap for the sodium void
worth measurements were normally the values determined for the reference configuration for the
sodium void worth measurements.
7.2.1.2 Sodium Void Worth – Modified Source Multiplication Technique at ZPPR
Most of the discussion in Section 7.2.1.1 applies to later ZPPR measurements as well, but adoption
of the modified source multiplication (MSM) technique at ZPPR affected the experimental
procedure for sodium void worth measurements in significant ways.
A typical sodium void worth measurement sequence at ZPPR using the MSM technique consisted
of the following steps:
 1. The subcritical reference configuration was established. This was a reactor configuration
 that was slightly subcritical with all PSR blades fully withdrawn to their parked positions.
 2. The excess reactivity of the subcritical reference configuration was measured.
 3. The reactor was shut down, and sodium plates in the designated void zone were replaced
 with void cans to establish the desired sodium void configuration. The two tables were
 then brought together, and the PSR blades were fully withdrawn to their parked positions
 (subcritical configuration).
 4. The MSM measurements were made.
 5. Steps 3 and 4 were repeated for each sodium void configuration of interest.
 6. The reactor was shut down, and the subcritical reference configuration was rebuilt.
 7. The excess reactivity of the subcritical reference configuration was measured again.
There is one qualification regarding establishment of a subcritical reference for the MSM
technique. If it is certain that all reactivity measurements in the planned series will produce
negative worths, a single subcritical reference can be established for the entire series, and that
subcritical reference can be as close to critical as possible. One example in this category is a series
of measurements of configurations of simulated or mockup control rods. All configurations of
mockup control rods will have lower reactivity than the subcritical reference configuration that
has no mockup control rods, so a single subcritical reference configuration could be used for the
series of simulated control rod worth measurements.
If, on the other hand, the reactivity worth of some configurations in the series could be positive, it
may be necessary to establish a second subcritical reference configuration that is more subcritical
than the initial subcritical reference. Sodium void worth measurements provide an example where
it may be necessary to establish a second subcritical reference. Depending on the size of the void
region, the location of the void region, and the design of the reactor being similated in a ZPPR
assembly, a void configuration may have positive reactivity worth or negative reactivity worth. In
ZPPR-15A, for example, the initial subcritical reference for sodium void worth measurements was
established in loading 16. The reactivity worth of the first void configuration in loading 17 was
positive. To allow for the possibility that the second step in the void sequence might be positive,

 232

the experimenters established a second subcritical reference in loading 18 that was more subcritical
than the initial subcritical reference built in loading 16.
The MSM technique was a modification of earlier source multiplication techniques used at ZPPR,
and ZPPR was the only Argonne facility to use the MSM technique for reactivity measurements.
The MSM technique became the standard method used at ZPPR to measure sodium void worth
and various other reactivity effects. There is one qualification for this statement. The MSM
technique was used to measure reactivity effects in the range of cents to dollars. Other methods
such as the autorod or period measurements were used to measure reactivities that were small
fractions of one cent (or small fractions of one pcm) such as Doppler sample worths.
The MSM technique provided several advantages over previous reactivity measurement
techniques used at ZPPR. The MSM technique was applicable over a wider range of subcritical
states (up to -50$) than reactivity measurements based upon reactor period or calibrated B 4C shim
rod position, which had been used for excess reactivity measurements at ZPPR prior to adoption
of the MSM technique. The wider range of subcritical states available through the MSM
techniques made it practical to construct and measure experimental configurations at ZPPR that
could not be measured at ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9.
The MSM technique allowed measurements to be made with all operational rods and safety rods
fully withdrawn, which is a significant advantage because the presence of one or more partially
inserted control rods affected the flux distribution and the measured worths. Measurements at
ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 frequently required partial insertion of one or more shim rods.
Measurements based upon reactor period or calibrated control rods sometimes required adjusting
the reactivity by spiking, despiking or changing the core boundary between loadings as discussed
above. After the subcritical reference configuration was established, no further core changes were
required for the MSM technique unless it was necessary to establish a second subcritical reference.
Consequently, there were no shifts in the flux distribution with the MSM technique and no
additional delays to adjust excess reactivity after the subcritical reference was established.
The first step in the MSM technique is the establishment of a very slightly subcritical reference
configuration (typically -10¢ to -30¢) with all operational control rods fully withdrawn. The very
slightly subcritical state is important because a) the near critical state assures validity of the inverse
kinetics technique used to determine the excess reactivity of the reference state, b) the neutron flux
is low enough that detectors do not require significant dead-time corrections and c) the neutron
flux is in a fundamental mode spatial distribution which ensures that fundamental mode reactivity
is being determined.
Establishing the subcritical reference configuration required reducing the excess reactivity of the
reference critical configuration. This reduction could be accomplished by replacing core drawers
with radial blanket drawers or radial reflector drawers (if there was no radial blanket) at the outer
edge of the core.
The more common practice at ZPPR for adjusting excess reactivity was to change the contents of
some core drawers by spiking or despiking at symmetric locations in the outer core as described
above.

 233

For cores containing Pu-U-Mo fuel plates, there was a large spontaneous fission source due to the
240
 Pu in the Pu-U-Mo fuel plates (~11% of the total plutonium). This spontaneous fission neutron
source was widely distributed in the core fuel, so the flux distribution was predominantly
fundamental mode, even for configurations that were far subcritical.
It is not clear whether the MSM technique could be used in a configuration in which the only fuel
was uranium due to the lack of a distributed neutron source. However, adding a limited number
of Pu-U-Mo plates to the uranium-fueled core provided a workaround that allowed use of the MSM
technique. For example, there were four phases in ZPPR-15. ZPPR-15B simulated an end-of-life
core in which the fuel consisted of Pu-U-Mo plates. ZPPR-15C simulated a mid-life core in which
the fuel consisted of 50% Pu-U-Mo plates and 50% HEU plates plus DU plates. ZPPR-15D
simulated a beginning-of-life core in which the nominal fuel would consist entirely of HEU plates
and DU plates. In order to use the MSM technique, the actual ZPPR-15D core consisted of HEU
plates, DU plates plus a limited number of Pu-U-Mo plates in the outer core to provide the required
distributed neutron source.
If the reactivity of the reference subcritical configuration is known, then the reactivity of the
perturbed (sodium-voided) configuration can be determined from the following equation:
                                 ρ2 = ρ1 x (ε2/ε1) x (C1/C2) x (S2/S1) x (β1/β2)
where ρ is subcritical reactivity in units of dollars ($), ε is detector efficiency (ratio of detector
count rate to total production rate by fission), C is detector count rate, (S 1/S2) is the change in the
ratio of the adjoint-weighted inherent source to the adjoint-weighted fission source, and β is the
effective delayed neutron fraction. Subscript 1 refers to the reference subcritical reactor state or
configuration, and subscript 2 refers to the perturbed state, i.e., the sodium-voided configuration
in this case. S and ε were computed with XYZ nodal diffusion theory adjoints and XYZ nodal
transport theory by the ZPPR staff as part of the data reduction. Data reduction refers to processing
the raw measurements to produce the final published experimental data.
The best choice for the subcritical reference is the configuration that is closest to critical because
that configuration will be closest to the fundamental spatial mode, which will minimize
experimental uncertainty in the MSM technique. If all perturbed states are known to have negative
worth (as is the case when inserting simulated control rods), then the subcritical reference can be
established as close to the reference critical configuration as possible. On the other hand, if some
perturbed states may have positive worth (as is the case for sodium void worth), then the subcritical
reference state may require a greater degree of subcriticality to ensure that all perturbed
configurations are subcritical.
Occasionally, it was necessary to establish a second subcritical reference because the first
subcritical reference was not sufficiently subcritical to provide the reference configuration for all
planned perturbed configurations. For example, the initial subcritical reference for sodium void
worth measurements in ZPPR-15A was loading 16. The worth of an 8 inch void in 148 drawers
per half in loading 17 was larger than expected, so a second subcritical reference with a greater
degree of subcriticality was established in loading 18 for the remaining sodium void worth
measurements in ZPPR-15A.

 234

After the subcritical reference configuration was established, the detector data were recorded and
converted to count rates to form C1 in the MSM equation. After the detector data were recorded,
several operational control rods in symmetric positions were scrammed. The initial reactivity, ρ 1,
of the subcritical reference configuration was determined from inverse kinetics analysis of the
power history following this rod drop. The product ρ 1C1 calibrated the MSM technique.
The subcritical reference configuration was modified to create the experimental configuration of
interest. For the sodium void worth measurements, the modification consisted of replacing sodium
plates with empty cans in the designated void region. All operational control rods were fully
withdrawn in the subcritical reference configuration and in the experimental configurations of
interest, which eliminated any distortion of the flux or reactivity worth measurements due to
control rod effects.
After the experimental configuration of interest was established, several operational rods in
symmetric positions were scrammed to provide the data to determine C 2 and ρ2 for the perturbed
configuration.
After the subcritical reference configuration was established, a series of sodium void worth
configurations could be built and measured without any requirement to change the subcritical
reference configuration unless it was necessary to establish a second subcritical reference.
Likewise, there was no need to insert control rods except for the rod drops needed to provide data
for the MSM technique. After the last sodium void worth measurement was performed, the
subcritical reference configuration was rebuilt. Measuring the excess reactivity of the rebuilt
subcritical reference configuration provided an estimate of the reproducibility uncertainty.
In this context, reproducibility (or repeatability) uncertainty refers to the small difference in
measured results when the experimenter attempts to reconstruct a previous experimental
configuration as faithfully as possible. For example, a subcritical reference configuration was
constructed for the sodium void worth measurements. The various void configurations were
measured, and then the subcritical reference configuration was rebuilt. The small difference in
reactivity between the original subcritical reference configuration and the reconstructed subcritical
reference configuration is the reproducibility uncertainty. The reproducibility uncertainty arises
because it is not possible to recreate the original configuration exactly (plate positions, reactor
temperature distribution, interface gap, control rod positions, etc.).
Note that reproducibility uncertainty applies in some form to most or all types of measurements in
ZPR-3, ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR.
One could legitimately argue that these are only single estimates of the sodium void worths and
the reproducibility uncertainty and that the true sodium void worths and reproducibility uncertainty
might be different. In an ideal world with no cost or schedule constraints, the experimenters could
construct and measure the reference subcritical configuration, construct and measure and all of the
perturbed states such as the sodium void configurations, reconstruct and measure the reference
critical configuration, and then completely disassemble the reference subcritical configuration.
The sequence of building and measuring the reference configuration and the perturbed states could
be repeated many times. The experimenters could then perform a statistical analysis of the
accumulated data to determine the average sodium void worth for each configuration, the average
reproducibility uncertainty and the associated standard deviations. The outcome of the repeated

 235

series of measurements and statistical analysis would certainly be better estimates of the sodium
void worths and reproducibility uncertainty.
In the real world of budgets and schedules, this approach is not practical. Cost and schedule
constraints precluded repeated measurements. An experimental configuration such as a sodium
void configuration was measured once. The original subcritical reference configuration was rebuilt
once at the end of a series of experimental measurements. The difference between the reactivity
of the original subcritical reference configuration and the rebuilt subcritical reference
configuration was defined to be the reproducibility uncertainty. This reproducibility uncertainty
was assumed to apply to all experimental worth measurements in the series.
Note that this discussion of single measurements versus repeated measurements applies to ZPR-3,
ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR and applies to most or all types of measurements in these facilities. This
discussion also applies to most or all types of measurements at other critical experiment facilities.
Multiple detectors were widely distributed in the core, radial blanket and radial reflector in both
halves of the matrix to sample as much of the assembly as possible for the MSM technique. The
detectors were placed in asymmetric locations for the same reason.
Initially, 16 detectors were used for the MSM measurements, but the number of detectors used for
these measurements increased steadily. By the mid-1980s, the standard practice was to use 64
detectors, so there were 64 separate, but correlated, measurements. The experimenters performed
a statistical analysis of detector data as part of the data reduction and rejected any suspect detector
data. Each detector for MSM measurements occupied a 1/2x2x6 inch space at the front of the
core, blanket or reflector drawer. The detector cables extended from the back of the drawer, so it
was not possible to place a back drawer or a reflector block behind a detector drawer.
7.2.2 Sodium Void Worth – Uncertainty Analysis
The ZPR/ZPPR staff published measured sodium void worths and some associated uncertainties,
but the published uncertainties are generally not the total uncertainties for the ZPR/ZPPR sodium
void worths. Published uncertainties include the statistical uncertainty in the actual measurement
and small uncertainties related to adjustment to a common measurement configuration (common
241
 Pu decay date, temperature and interface gap).
For measurements based on the MSM technique, the published uncertainties may also include the
correlated uncertainty related to the reactivity measurement for the reference configuration,
reactivity scale calibration, and source ratio uncertainty.
For reactivity worth measurements based upon other techniques such as period measurements or
calibrated control rod positions, there is a similar correlated uncertainty related to measurement of
