the reference configuration if that configuration is used as the reference for a series of reactivity
worth measurements.
It is difficult to know which of the uncertainties discussed in the three preceding paragraphs are
included in the published uncertainty besides the statistical uncertainty in the measurement unless
this is explained in the report documenting the sodium void worth measurement. However, most
uncertainty components related to the experimental technique are likely to be small compared to

 236

the contribution from reactivity conversion with the possible exception of the statistical uncertainty
in the measurement.
For practical purposes, the published uncertainty is likely to be the best available estimate of the
measurement uncertainty for ZPR/ZPPR sodium void worth measurements. It seems unlikely that
any better estimate of the sodium void worth measurement uncertainty in any ZPR/ZPPR assembly
can be developed today.
Additional uncertainties contribute to the total uncertainty for the sodium void worth measurement
and are generally the dominant components of the total uncertainty.
7.2.2.1 Uncertainties Related to Experimental Technique for Sodium Void Worth
 Measurements
Sodium void worth measurements were straightforward in concept, but the experimental
uncertainties associated with those measurements depend strongly upon the details of experimental
procedures. Because measured sodium void worths were small in some cases, much care had to
be taken when building the reference and sodium void configurations to avoid introducing
unintended reactivity effects of comparable size.
One important part of this procedure was to minimize drawer handling and changes within
drawers. Only the sodium plates in the affected drawers were changed because the plate-to-plate
mass variations among plates of a given type, especially fuel, would introduce an additional
reactivity change. Consequently, each normal drawer in the voiding zone was removed from the
matrix, modified by replacing sodium-filled cans with empty void cans, and reloaded into the
matrix at its original location.
Handling only the drawers to be modified also minimized changes in the positions of plates in the
drawers, particularly axial changes near the drawer fronts. Eliminating all plate shifting, i.e.,
unintentional changes in the positions of plates in a drawer, during drawer handling was very
difficult. The interior width and length of a drawer had to be slightly greater than the width and
length of the nominal plate loading to avoid damaging plates or drawers during plate loading and
unloading operations, so very small lateral motions of some plates could occur during drawer
handling. Although a spring at the back of the drawer pushed the plates forward, very small axial
motions of some plates could also occur during drawer handling.
Unintentional changes in plate positions introduced additional experimental uncertainty because
the excess reactivity of the assembly changes slightly if the positions of the plates in the assembly
change. The change in excess reactivity may be very small, but it does occur. For this reason, the
procedures for drawer handling (including loading drawers into matrix tubes) attempted to
eliminate or at least minimize plate shifting.
Despite the procedures for drawer handling, some plate shifting did occur, and the effects of plate
shifting could be significant in some cases. Minimizing drawer handling minimized this source of
uncertainty.
Unfortunately, it was rarely possible to determine whether plate shifting had occurred or to
quantify the effects of plate shifting. There was no way to measure or determine plate positions
when the drawers were in the matrix, and the effects of any plate shifting that did occur were

 237

generally small. If plate shifting was significant enough to have a discernible effect on measured
reactivities, that effect was discovered after the fact based on some anomaly or inconsistency
observed during data processing. If such an anomaly was discovered and if no other likely cause
was sufficient to account for the anomaly, the anomaly might be ascribed to plate shifting.
ZPPR-12 provides an example of the effects of plate shifting. Analysis of the ZPPR-12 sodium
void worth measurements revealed inconsistencies that the ZPPR staff ascribed to plate shifting.
The ZPPR staff assigned an uncertainty to the effects of plate shifting in ZPPR-12, and this
uncertainty became the dominant uncertainty for some of the ZPPR-12 sodium void worth

In most cases, the effects of plate shifting are small and unquantifiable. In occasional cases such
as ZPPR-12 where plate shifting had a significant and recognized effect on measurements, the
report documenting the measurements may discuss the effects of plate shifting and any uncertainty
assigned to plate shifting by the ZPR/ZPPR staff.
Another significant experimental issue was the mismatch between the mass of steel in the sodium
cans removed from the assembly and the mass of steel in the void cans inserted into the assembly.
The difference in steel mass between individual cans of the same size is small, but the mismatch
can be significant in terms of reactivity because a) the total steel mass difference between all of
the sodium plates removed and all of the void cans inserted in a large void zone is not necessarily
small, b) the reactivity worth per kilogram for sodium is much lower than the reactivity worth per
kilogram for stainless steel and c) measured sodium void worth is small for some configurations.
ZPPR had a large inventory of stainless steel void cans that were identical in design to the sodium-
filled cans except that the void cans were empty. Each can had a unique serial number, and the
steel mass of each can was recorded in a database at the time of manufacture. The experimenters
could have used this database to select a set of void cans whose steel mass most closely matched
that of the sodium cans they were replacing. The inventory was large enough that this could be
done to a level where the steel mass difference was insignificant.
A similar argument could be made for sodium void worth measurements at ZPR-6 and ZPR-9
although the inventory of sodium plates and void cans at ANL-E was smaller than the inventory
of sodium plates and void cans at ZPPR.
R. W. Schaefer, a former analyst at ANL-E and at ZPPR, asserts that this matching did occur, at
least at ZPPR. However, there is no convincing evidence that this was a common practice for
several reasons. First, although the experimenters could have used the inventory database to select
the specific void can that most closely matched each sodium can to be replaced, no records have
been found to confirm this practice was followed. Second, J. A. Morman, an experimenter at ZPR-
6 and ZPR-9, confirmed that this was not the practice at Argonne’s ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 critical
experiment facilities [2]. Third, matching sodium plates and void cans at the individual plate level
would significantly increase the time, effort and cost required to perform each measurement
because it would be necessary to retrieve the exact void can that most closely matched each sodium
plate and to put that void can in the drawer in the exact position of the sodium plate that it matched.
This does not mean that sodium plate-void can matching at the individual plate level never
occurred, but it may not have been standard practice. In any event, if matching at the individual

 238

plate level did occur, the matching did not make the steel mass difference negligible. Published
sodium void worths from ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR include corrections for the steel mass
difference.
On the other hand, drawer master figures clearly show that sodium cans and sodium void cans
were matched at least at the level of external dimensions. For example, a ½ x 2 x 8 inch sodium
can was replaced by a ½ x 2 x 8 inch void can. This applies to all sodium cans replaced in the
sodium void worth experiments.
The masses of steel in the sodium cans removed and in the void cans inserted were known, so the
total steel mass difference resulting from replacing a set of sodium cans by a set of void cans could
be computed. The reactivity worth of the difference in steel masses could be determined from the
steel mass difference and the measured worth per unit mass for stainless steel. The worth per unit
mass for stainless steel was determined during the small sample worth measurements that were
performed in most ZPR/ZPPR assemblies (discussed in a later section). It was standard practice
at ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR to correct the measured sodium void worth for the difference between
the total stainless steel mass in the sodium cans removed and the total stainless steel mass in the
void cans inserted in a sodium void worth experiment. The steel mass correction was probably a
standard practice at ZPR-3 as well, but no documentation of this aspect is available. Both were
apparently done to simplify modeling efforts at the time and this correction is not included in the
present modeling methodology as will be discussed shortly.
Variation in how deeply drawers were inserted into the matrix tubes would introduce an additional
uncertainty in the axial positions of the plates. The experimenters would have made sure that the
fronts of all drawers in the voiding zones were exactly flush with the front edge of the matrix.
Tabs on the drawer fronts mated with notches in the sides of the matrix tubes to ensure consistent
positioning. Drawers were inserted into matrix tubes slowly to minimize plate shifting. The
procedure for loading drawers into matrix tubes minimized unintentional changes in the axial
position of the core material within each matrix half. Springs inserted in the backs of the drawers
to push the plates forward also minimized unintentional changes in axial plate positions in the
drawers.
The preceding paragraphs describe the general procedure for minimizing experimental
uncertainties, but there were some residual uncertainties related to the experimental technique.
The most obvious uncertainty in this category is the statistical uncertainty in the measurements.
There were statistical uncertainties in the detector count rates for each measurement and in the
process used to convert the measured count rates to a reactivity worth.
For sodium void worth measurements based on the MSM technique, there is also a correlated
uncertainty from the establishment of the reference subcritical configuration that includes the
reactivity scale calibration and source ratio. For reactivity worth measurements based upon other
techniques such as period measurements or calibrated control rod positions, there is a similar
correlated uncertainty related to measurement of the reference configuration if that configuration
is used as the reference for a series of reactivity worth measurements. These correlated uncertainty
components are likely to be included in the published uncertainties for the measured values.

 239

7.2.2.2 Reactivity Adjustments for Sodium Void Worth Measurements
Another experimental uncertainty is the reproducibility uncertainty discussed previously. The
reproducibility uncertainty arises because an experimental configuration cannot be recreated to an
arbitrary degree of precision. For any measurement involving multiple core loadings or multiple
reactor startups, it was not possible to reproduce the reactor temperature distribution, interface gap
or control rod positions to an arbitrary degree of precision.
The standard practice was to adjust each configuration to the 241Pu decay date, core average
temperature, and matrix interface gap of the reference (or subcritical reference) configuration.
There were small uncertainties related to the adjustment of measured reactivities to a common
date, temperature and interface gap, i.e., the corrections for 241Pu decay and for any differences in
the average core temperature or the interface gap between the reference configuration and the
sodium void configuration.
In general, the uncertainty in the measured 241Pu decay coefficient was approximately 10% of the
measured value if the 241Pu decay coefficient was measured. It is likely that a calculated 241Pu
decay coefficient was used in some assemblies, and a similar 10% uncertainty was probably
assumed for that calculated 241Pu decay coefficient. The measured temperature coefficient for a
ZPR/ZPPR assembly is small, and a typical uncertainty is 10% of the measured temperature
coefficient. The uncertainty in the measured interface gap coefficient was typically 10% – 20%
of the interface gap coefficient.
The uncertainties in the 241Pu decay coefficient, temperature coefficient and interface gap
coefficient are correlated for all loadings in a ZPR/ZPPR assembly unless there are significant
changes in the composition of the assembly during the assembly program. For configurations in
which uncertainties in these coefficients are correlated, these uncertainties are eliminated in
reactivity differences such as the step worths or the cumulative worths for sodium voiding because
uncertainties in the 241Pu decay coefficient, temperature coefficient and interface gap coefficient
are included in the adjustment of the measured reactivities to a common reference date, average
core temperature and interface gap and are included in the published uncertainties for the

In most cases, the average core composition did not change throughout an assembly program, but
there were exceptions. For example, the core composition changed between ZPPR-15B, ZPPR-
15C and ZPPR-15D as Pu-U-Mo plates were replaced by HEU plates and DU plates in ZPPR-15C
and ZPPR-15D. The 241Pu decay coefficient, temperature coefficient and interface gap coefficient
changed significantly between phases B, C and D of the ZPPR-15 program as the Pu-U-Mo plates
in the core were replaced by HEU plates and DU plates.
ZPR-6/7 provides another example of a significant change in core composition. The ANL-E plate
inventory contained a large number of standard Pu-U-Mo plates containing ~11 wt.% 240Pu in the
plutonium component and a smaller number of high 240Pu Pu-U-Mo plates containing ~27 wt.%
240
 Pu in the plutonium component. The number of high 240Pu Pu-U-Mo plates was not sufficient
to build an entire core, but it was sufficient to construct a high 240Pu zone in the center of an
assembly. After experiments were performed in the reference ZPR-6/7 core containing only
standard Pu-U-Mo plates, a high 240Pu zone was built in the center of the core. The 241Pu decay

 240

coefficient and related uncertainty would be at least slightly different for the reference ZPR-6/7
and the high 240Pu version.
In addition to the uncertainty in the measured temperature coefficient, there are two other
temperature-related uncertainties that are not included in published uncertainties for the measured
reactivities. In ICSBEP and IRPhEP benchmarks of ZPR/ZPPR assemblies, an estimated 0.5°C
temperature uncertainty from calibration of the in-core thermocouples and an estimated 1°C
temperature uncertainty in the average core temperature were assumed [5,6]. These are reasonable
values for the uncertainties in thermocouple calibration and average core temperature.
The effect of temperature uncertainty has two components. One component is the uncertainty in
thermocouple calibration. It seems likely that there was a single thermocouple calibration when
the operational measurements were performed, but verifying standard practice with respect to
thermocouple calibration would be difficult so long after the ZPR/ZPPR facilities were shut down.
The thermocouple calibration uncertainty is correlated in a series of measurements and is
eliminated in reactivity differences derived from a series of related measurements. In any case,
the effect of temperature uncertainty is dominated by the uncertainty in average core temperature.
The uncertainty in average core temperature is not necessarily correlated between different
loadings in the same assembly, so this uncertainty may contribute to the total uncertainty for the
sodium void worth measurement. In most cases, the contribution of the uncertainty in average
core temperature will be small and will not be a significant component of the total uncertainty.
However, for a very small measured sodium void worth, the contribution of the uncertainty in
average core temperature to the total uncertainty may not be negligible.
There are two contributions to the effect of the interface gap on the total uncertainty for sodium
void worth measurements. The first contribution arises from the uncertainty in the interface gap
coefficient. This uncertainty is typically 10% – 20% of the interface gap coefficient. The
uncertainty in the interface gap coefficient is correlated between different core loadings and is
eliminated in reactivity differences in a series of measurements.
The second contribution arises from the fact that the measured interface gap will not be uniform
or reproducible for a series of loadings such as a series of sodium void worth measurements. In
ZPPR-15, the largest gap difference for the series of sodium void worth measurements was ~1.5
mils, and the largest contribution of the uncertainty in the interface gap to the total uncertainty for
sodium void worth measurements was ~0.1 pcm. An uncertainty of 0.1 pcm is negligible. It seems
likely that any uncertainty related to variation in the interface gap width over a series of related
loadings in the same assembly would make a negligible contribution to the total uncertainty for a
sodium void worth measurement.
It should be noted that the interface gap uncertainty considered here is not the uncertainty in the
true interface gap discussed in Section 7.1. The uncertainty in the true interface gap results from
a) the fact that the matrix halves are neither perfectly flat nor perfectly parallel, b) the effects of
any deflection in the support plate due to the weight of the matrix tubes and loaded drawers and c)
the effects of any springing or rebound when the movable table touches the stationary table.
The interface gap uncertainty discussed here results from the fact that the separations measured by
the position indicators in the corners of the matrix varied slightly between reactor runs and were

 241

not perfectly reproducible. The difference in the interface gap between loadings may have resulted
from the springing/rebound effect or from other causes. The important point is that the average
measured corner separation varied slightly between reactor runs in a series of measurements.
Documents reporting measurements for a specific assembly may provide some clarification
regarding what is included in the reported uncertainties.
The uncertainties related to the reactivity adjustments are small compared to the uncertainty related
to reactivity conversion discussed below for measurements of sodium void worth in large zones.
However, for a very small void worth such as the worth of a very small zone, the reactivity related
to the 1° C uncertainty in core average temperature may not always be negligible.
7.2.2.3 Effects of Material Composition Uncertainties for Sodium Void Worth
 Measurements
For the sodium void worth measurements, the reference configuration or subcritical reference
configuration and the voided configurations were identical except for a) the replacement of sodium
plates by void cans in the successive void steps and b) any small drawer changes at the core
boundary to adjust excess reactivity (if necessary for specific cases). Consequently, for practical
purposes, the uncertainty contributions of any plates or steel components such as drawers and
matrix tubes to the uncertainties in the measured values are highly correlated between the reference
or subcritical reference configuration and the corresponding void configurations except for the
sodium plates removed and the void cans inserted. The uncertainty contributions of other plates,
drawers and matrix tubes will change slightly between the reference or subcritical reference
configuration and the void configuration due to the changes in neutron spectrum and leakage, but
these changes are small compared to the uncertainties discussed below.
The effect of uncertainties in the sodium plate compositions on the total sodium void worth
uncertainty was computed for ZPPR-15B. For the ZPPR-15B reference critical configuration, the
computed total uncertainty related to sodium mass and sodium impurities was 1.65 pcm. There
were approximately 896 core drawers per half including the normal core drawers, detectors
drawers in the core and the PSR control rod drawers. The void zone consisted of 52 drawers per
half, the maximum void region length was 18 inches, and the total length of the sodium columns
in the core drawers was 31 inches. To a first order approximation, the maximum worth of the
sodium mass and composition uncertainties for the ZPPR-15B sodium void worth measurements
is 1.65 x (52/896) x (18/31) = 0.055 pcm which is negligible.
The same calculation can be performed for the steel in the sodium cans and void cans. The total
uncertainty related to the steel in the sodium cans was 1.81 pcm in the ZPPR-15B reference critical
configuration. The steel mass change between the total stainless steel mass of the sodium cans
removed and the total stainless steel mass of the void cans inserted is only ~4% of the total stainless
steel mass of the sodium cans removed in the sodium void worth measurements. The maximum
worth of the steel mass change for the ZPPR-15B sodium void worth measurements is 0.04 x 1.81
x (52/896) x (18/31) = 0.0024 pcm.
These calculations could be refined, but the contributions of the uncertainties in the compositions
and masses of the sodium plates removed and void cans inserted to the total uncertainty in the
sodium void worth measurements would still be negligible in ZPPR-15B.

 242

A similar approach could be taken for sodium void worth measurements in other ZPR/ZPPR
assemblies. In general, the contribution of composition and mass uncertainties in the sodium plates
removed and void cans inserted to the total uncertainty for a sodium void worth measurement is
likely to be negligible unless the void zone is relatively large (many sodium plates) and the
measured worth is small (a few cents or a few inhours).
There is an indirect (and largely second-order) source of uncertainties related to the effect of
uncertainties in plate compositions and masses on the calculated void worth values. In this context,
plates refers to all plates (fuel, sodium, steel, depleted uranium, etc.) in the assembly rather than
to just the sodium plates in the voiding zone. This uncertainty is not related to the measured value.
Instead, it relates to the as-built model and calculations of the measured value. Calculations of the
measured sodium void worth are based upon the compositions and masses of the matrix tubes,
drawers and all of the plates present in the assembly during the measurement. All of these
compositions and masses are uncertain, and all of these uncertainties in the compositions and
masses of matrix tubes, drawers and different plate types introduce a small uncertainty into the
calculated worths. For practical purposes, the effects of the uncertainties in the compositions of
plates, drawers and matrix tubes on the calculated sodium void worth can be included in the total
uncertainty.
The effects of uncertainties in plate compositions and masses on k eff were computed for ZPPR-
15B loading 91, the subcritical reference case, and ZPPR-15B loading 94 (18 inch void zone in 52
drawers per half) for all of the uncertainties in plate compositions and masses in ZPPR-15B. The
difference in the total composition and mass uncertainty between loading 91 and loading 94 was
0.6 pcm. This is the contribution of the plate composition and mass uncertainties to the total
uncertainty for the sodium void worth measurement in loading 94.
A similar calculation was performed for the sodium void worth measurements in ZPR-6/7. In the
ZPR-6/7 case, the total contribution of the plate composition and mass uncertainties to the total
sodium void worth uncertainty was ~0.1 pcm.
Unless the measured sodium void worth is very small, it is likely that the contribution of
composition and mass uncertainties from all of the plates (fuel, sodium, steel, etc.) to the total
uncertainty for the sodium void worth measurement will be negligible.
7.2.2.4 Reactivity Conversion for Sodium Void Worth Measurements
The sodium void worth was measured in units of inhours or cents. Calculated worths and the
associated uncertainties are typically expressed in units of Δk, Δk/k 1k2 or pcm. Conversion from
the measurement units, inhours or cents, to the calculation units, e.g., pcm, or vice versa requires
βeff.
The estimated uncertainty in βeff is 5%, which is the value assumed for all ICSBEP/IRPhEP
benchmarks of ZPR and ZPPR assemblies [5,6]. The 5% β eff uncertainty also is consistent with
the limited number of measurements of βeff performed for ZPR and ZPPR assemblies and with
calculations of βeff for ZPR and ZPPR assemblies (see Section 7.1.2).
The 5% uncertainty in βeff contributes an additional uncertainty to the final sodium void worth.
The 5% uncertainty in βeff is generally the dominant uncertainty component for sodium void worth
measurements in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies. The one exception to that statement is the case where

 243

the measured worth is small and other uncertainty components (statistical uncertainty, contribution
from plate composition uncertainties, etc.) are not small relative to the measured worth. If the
measured worth is small, the 5% βeff uncertainty may be comparable to the other uncertainty
components.
All of the individual uncertainties for the sodium void worth measurement are added in quadrature
(square root of the sum of the squares of the individual uncertainties) to determine the total
uncertainty for the sodium void worth measurement.
7.2.2.5 Additional Non-Quantified Sources of Uncertainty in Sodium Void Worth
 Measurements
Calculated worths for large sodium void worths in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies usually agree reasonably
well with measured values, and the resulting values of (C/E – 1) are reasonably small. Note that
“C” refers to the calculated value, and “E” refers to the experimental value. For small sodium void
worths (a few cents or a few inhours) in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies, calculated worths frequently do
not agree well with measured values, and the resulting values of (C/E – 1) are not necessarily
small. Based on discussion with J. A. Morman, a former experimenter at ZPR-6 and ZPR-9, there
are several potential additional sources of uncertainties for the sodium void worth measurements.
Unfortunately, it does not seem likely that any of these sources of uncertainty can be quantified
accurately although all of them are small.
For a large measured worth, the contribution of these additional sources of uncertainty to the total
uncertainty is negligible because the other components such as the statistical uncertainty in the
measurement and the uncertainty in βeff will dominate when all of the uncertainties are added in
quadrature. For a very small measured worth, the contribution of these additional non-quantified
sources of uncertainty may account for the poorer values of (C/E – 1) in some cases.
7.2.2.5.1 Individual Plate Variations
The available information in the ADEN library defines the average plate of each type and size.
These average plates are used in all calculations with as-built Monte Carlo models or deterministic
models of any ZPR/ZPPR measurement. There are no available records to define the individual
plates and no available records to determine the specific plate at any location in an assembly.
Those records may have existed when the ZPR/ZPPR facilities operated, but it is unlikely that any
such records can be found today.
There were small variations in the masses, compositions and dimensions of the sodium plates and
void cans due to normal process deviations during fabrication. For a large sodium void region,
many sodium plates were replaced by void cans, so small variations between individual sodium
plates or void cans are likely to cancel each other out. For a large sodium void region, the average
sodium plates and void cans in the ADEN library are likely to be representative of the complete
set of sodium plates and void cans used in the experiment.
A relatively small number of sodium plates are replaced by void cans in creating a small void
region. Because only a relatively small number of plates or void cans are used, the individual
differences between the sodium plates or void cans used in the experiment and the average sodium
plates or void cans in the ADEN library may be more important. For a small void region, the
average sodium plate or void can values in the ADEN library and, consequently, the average

 244

sodium plate and void can values used in models may be less representative of the actual sodium
plates or void cans used in the specific experiment being analyzed.
7.2.2.5.2 7Plate Shifting
There was a spring in the back of each drawer to push the plates to the front of the drawer. In
addition, there were procedures for handling drawers to avoid introducing small gaps between the
drawer fronts and the plates in the drawers during drawer handling. Nevertheless, some plate
shifting could occur. For example, the assumed plate shifting was one of the largest uncertainties
for the sodium void worth measurements in ZPPR-12. The plate shifting problem in ZPPR-12 was
only recognized after the fact during the analysis of the measurement data.
Plate shifting introduced a small gap at the front of the drawer, so plate shifting is likely to be more
significant for a small void zone (4 – 8 inches) at the front of a drawer than for a large void zone
(18 – 24 inches) that extends over the full core length in the drawer. The small void zone generally
has a smaller worth than the large void zone, so plate shifting is likely to be more important for
the small void zone case.
Plate shifting is a likely explanation for the poor (C/E – 1) values for plate rotation experiments in
ZPPR-12. Rotating all plates in a drawer by 90° involved much more plate handling than just
replacing sodium plates with void cans, so there was a much larger potential for plate shifting to
occur in the ZPPR-12 plate rotation experiments.
It is possible that the effects of plate shifting were unrecognized or underestimated in some
measurements and that the springs and drawer handling procedures did not entirely eliminate plate
shifting in those measurements. In any case, it seems unlikely that the worth of any plate shifting
can be quantified accurately decades after the measurements were performed.
7.2.2.5.3 Uncertainty in Control Rod Calibration
There was an uncertainty in the control rod calibrations and in the control rod worth curves for any
ZPR/ZPPR assembly. All sodium void worth measurements depended on control rod calibration
to some degree. This is true for worth measurements based on calibrated control rods in ZPR-6
and ZPR-9 and for measurements based on the modified source multiplication method at ZPPR.
If the uncertainties in control rod calibrations and the control rod worth curves are known and if
the measurement data were available, it might be possible to quantify the effects of this uncertainty,
at least in principle. In practice, the effects of the uncertainty in control rod calibrations and the
control rod worth curves on measured reactivity values probably cannot be quantified because the
necessary data are not available today.
The uncertainty in the control rod calibration is more important for a small reactivity worth than
for a large reactivity worth, but the contribution of this uncertainty to the total uncertainty is likely
to be small.
7.2.2.5.4 Uncertainty in Control Rod Position
There was a small uncertainty in the exact control rod positions. The effect of that uncertainty is
more important for a small measured reactivity than for a large measured reactivity, but the effect
cannot be quantified today.

 245

7.2.2.5.5 Effects of the Table Separation Position Indicator Uncertainty
The effects of any uncertainty related to the table separation position indicators are more important
for a small measured reactivity worth than for a large measured reactivity worth. The uncertainty
discussed here relates to the fact that the table separations measured by the position indicators in
the corners of the the matrix halves varied slightly between reactor runs and were not perfectly
reproducible even if there were no changes in the reactor configuration between sequential reactor
runs. The contribution of table separation uncertainty to the to the total uncertainty for a measured
reactivity worth cannot be quantified accurately, but this contribution is likely to be small based
on calculations performed for ZPPR-15.
7.2.3 Steel Mismatch Correction in Sodium Void Worth Models
The reactivity correction for the mismatch between the steel in the sodium cans removed and the
steel in the void cans inserted was developed by the ZPR/ZPPR staff to facilitate modeling and
analysis of the sodium void worth measurements.
Ideally, when measured reactivities are corrected for the steel mismatch, the models can be
constructed such that the only difference between the reference configuration and the void
configuration is the concentrations of sodium in the void zone in the two models. Creating the
void configuration model is just a matter of removing sodium from the reference model in the void
region.
The as-built Monte Carlo models developed at present for sodium void experiments and any
deterministic models derived from those as-built Monte Carlo models explicitly represent the
sodium plates and the void cans. These models include the nominal masses and compositions for
the sodium cans and void cans based on the ADEN library. Any mismatch in the steel content of
the sodium cans and void cans is thus included in the as-built models, so it would be incorrect to
apply the reactivity correction for the steel mismatch. Consequently, any reported reactivity
correction for the steel mismatch is (should be) removed from the final reported experimental
void worths in order to provide a consistent set of measured worths for comparison with the worths
calculated using the as-built Monte Carlo models (or deterministic models derived from the as-
built Monte Carlo models).
7.2.4 Calculation of the Measured Sodium Void Worth
Section 7.1.5 discussed constructing high-fidelity as-built models of criticality measurements in
ZPR/ZPPR assemblies. That discussion applies to constructing models of sodium void worth
measurements as well. Loadings in any ZPR/ZPPR assembly were cumulative as discussed above,
so it is necessary to process the loading records for all previous loadings in addition to the loading
records for the sodium void worth configurations of interest.
The measured sodium void worths can be calculated by direct Monte Carlo using as-built Monte
Carlo models of the reference and voided configurations. The number of histories required to
produce an acceptable statistical uncertainty will depend on the measured sodium void worth and
associated total uncertainty. From experience, one billion (10 9) histories in a Monte Carlo
calculation of keff for an as-built ZPR/ZPPR model results in a one sigma statistical uncertainty in
the 1 – 2 pcm range.

 246

The principal uses of the as-built Monte Carlo model are a) nuclear data testing and b) validation
of codes and data for design calculations and analysis. For most reactor design and analysis work,
it seems likely that a deterministic code will be used. Consequently, it may be necessary to convert
the as-built Monte Carlo model to an equivalent deterministic model as part of the validation
process for the deterministic code. Assuming the cross section library processing for Monte Carlo
and the deterministic code are not equivalent, both should ideally be compared against the
experimental measurement as opposed to the deterministic code being compared against the Monte
Carlo model result.
In addition, it is advantageous to convert as-built Monte Carlo models to equivalent deterministic
models to perform the uncertainty analysis for ZPR/ZPPR experiments. Calculating the reactivity
effects of mass and composition uncertainties by Monte Carlo is difficult because these reactivity
effects are frequently small. Consequently, many histories and a large amount of computer time
are required to compute the reactivity effect of each mass or composition uncertainty. That
problem is compounded because frequently there are many mass and composition uncertainties to
be computed. It is much more practical to compute these reactivity effects with a deterministic
model. The means by which the deterministic model is generated were discussed at the beginning
of Section 7.
7.3 Control Rod Worth Measurements
Control rod worth is an important safety consideration in fast reactor design, so the ZPR/ZPPR
experimenters frequently measured the worth of simulated control rods as part of an assembly
program. It should be noted that the control rod worths measured in these experiments were not
the worths of the operational control rods used to control the ZPR/ZPPR reactors. The control rod
worth measurements discussed here are worth measurements for simulated or mockup control
rods.
The operational control rods used to control the ZPR/ZPPR reactors were the dual-purpose (DP)
drawers and the poison blades (PSRs) described above. All ZPR-3 assemblies, the early ZPR-6
assemblies, the early ZPR-9 assemblies and the first ZPPR assemblies used DP drawers for reactor
control. ZPPR introduced PSRs in ZPPR-2, and ZPPR-2 contained both DP drawers and PSRs.
ZPPR eventually eliminated all DP drawers in favor of PSRs. ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 introduced PSRs
shortly after ZPPR introduced them, but ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 continued to use both DP drawers and
PSRs together for reactor control until both facilities were shut down.
The DP drawers and PSRs were the safety rods and shim rods that provided operational reactor
control for the ZPR/ZPPR machines. The rod worths and worth curves were measured for the
operational control rods as part of the operational measurements that were performed after the
reference critical configuration was established for an assembly.
For experimental purposes, a simulated or mockup control rod consisted of one or more drawers
containing plates that simulated the composition of a fast reactor control rod. The size of the
mockup control rod varied. In ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9, a mockup control rod typically consisted
of one drawer in each half although larger versions may have been measured in some assemblies.
In early ZPPR assemblies, a mockup control rod might consist of a single drawer or a 2 x 2 array
of drawers in each half. In later ZPPR assemblies, a mockup control rod usually consisted of
several drawers, e.g., a 2 x 2 array or 2 x 3 array of drawers, in each half.

 247

A typical mockup control rod (CR) consisted of alternating columns of boron carbide plates and
sodium plates in one or more adjacent drawers. A control rod position (CRP) consisted of just
sodium plates in one or more adjacent drawers. A CRP was also called a sodium channel in some
cases. A CRP simulated a withdrawn control rod channel filled with sodium. A fully inserted
control rod was simulated by placing a CR in both matrix halves, and a fully withdrawn control
rod was simulated by placing a CRP in both matrix halves. A partially inserted control rod
generally was simulated by placing a CR in one half and a CRP in the other half. By carefully
arranging the boron carbide plates and sodium plates in the drawers, it also was possible to simulate
a configuration in which the CR was only partially inserted in one half with a CRP in the other
half or a configuration in which a CR was fully inserted in one half and partially inserted in the
other half to emulate a contiguous axial control rod that crosses the matrix interface.
The preceding paragraph describes a typical mockup control rod, but various alternate versions
were measured. For example, the mockup control rod might consist entirely of absorber plates
rather than alternating columns of absorber plates and sodium plates. In ZPPR-15D, experimenters
measured the worth of a segmented control rod. A segmented control rod consisted of short lengths
of control rod joined by short lengths of chain. The apparent intent is that the segmented control
rod could travel through a distorted control rod channel whereas a standard control rod could not
travel through a distorted control rod channel. Various non-standard control rod configurations
and designs were measured in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies.
The typical absorber plate used in a mockup control rod was natural boron carbide, but boron
carbide plates containing enriched 10B in the boron component were used on occasion. In addition
to boron carbide, the experimenters measured the worth of other materials such as tantalum for
control purposes.
The ZPR/ZPPR experimenters also examined methods to enhance control rod worth. For example,
the mockup control rod consisted of a single drawer in both halves for the ZPR-6/7 control rod
worth measurements. In one ZPR-6/7 experiment, the ZPR-6 staff placed 0.5 inch of BeO plates
on each side of the mockup control rod to determine the effect of softening the local neutron
spectrum on the control rod worth.
In a typical control rod worth measurement in ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9, there was only a single
mockup control rod in the center of the core. In some experiments, this mockup control rod was
moved to various locations in the core to measure control rod worth as a function of position.
Some of the early ZPPR assemblies also measured the worth of a single mockup control rod at one
or more core locations.
The larger size of the ZPPR matrix provided scope for more elaborate control rod worth
measurements. In control rod worth measurements in the 77 x 77 ZPPR matrix, there frequently
were multiple mockup control rods in the core. For example, there were 13 mockup control rods
in ZPPR-15.
7.3.1 Control Rod Worth Experimental Technique
The technique for measuring the worth of mockup control rods was very similar to the technique
for measuring sodium void worth discussed in Section 7.2.1, and the same methods for measuring
reactivities were used. Core drawers were replaced by drawers containing the CR(s), and the

 248

excess reactivity of the configuration containing the CR(s) was measured. This provided a
measurement of the CR worth relative to fuel in the same matrix positions. Replacing the CR(s)
with CRP(s) and measuring the excess reactivity of the configuration containing the CRP(s)
provided a measure of the worth of the inserted CR(s) relative to withdrawn CR(s).
7.3.1.1 Control Rod Worth – Experimental Technique at ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9
A typical control rod worth measurement at ZPR-3, ZPR-6 or ZPR-9 consisted of the following
steps:
 1. The excess reactivity of the core was measured for the reference configuration.
 2. The reactor was shut down, and core drawers were replaced by drawers containing the CR.
 3. The excess reactivity of the configuration with the CR was measured in a reactor startup.
 4. The reactor was shut down, and the mockup control rod was replaced with a CRP.
 5. The excess reactivity of the configuration with the CRP was measured in a reactor startup.
 6. The reactor was shut down and the reference core was restored.
 7. The excess reactivity of the reference core was measured again.
As is applicable, the power was held constant with the autorod during the measurement. Note that
the autorod was used to measure very small reactivities and to make fine adjustments in the reactor
power level, e.g., to compensate for temperature drift or power drift during an experiment, but the
autorod was not one of the operational control rods and was not part of the standard ZPR/ZPPR
reactor control system.
The core temperature was measured, the positions of all operational control rods were recorded,
and the average autorod position was determined. Corrections were made for differences in the
interface gap and average core temperature between the different measurements and for 241Pu
decay (if applicable). Because the reactivity worth of one or more mockup control rods could be
relatively large, it was sometimes necessary to adjust the excess reactivity of the core prior to
measuring the worth of the mockup control rod(s). This adjustment is discussed in the following
paragraphs.
The experimental technique for control rod worth measurements in early ZPPR assemblies, i.e.,
assemblies built prior to development of the MSM technique, likely was very similar to the
experimental technique used in ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9.
In critical configurations, reactivity was measured based on the steady-state positions of calibrated
control rods. For configurations that were subcritical, various techniques were used to measure
reactivity. These techniques included inverse kinetics analysis of rod drops, a polarity coherence
technique, reactor period measurements and subcritical source multiplication.
Steps 1 – 7 above outline the basic measurement procedure, but it was sometimes necessary to
adjust the core reactivity before measuring a planned control rod configuration.
The worth of a mockup control rod was generally much larger than the worth of sodium voiding
in a zone, and the mockup control rod worth was always negative. In addition, the mockup control
rod replaced normal core drawers, which made the negative reactivity change even larger. This
larger negative reactivity change required a larger adjustment in core reactivity and, consequently,
a larger shift in the flux and power distributions relative to the changes required for sodium void

 249

worth measurements. Because a CRP had a much smaller worth than a CR, measuring the worth
of a CRP might require a separate core reactivity adjustment relative to the adjustment for the CR
worth measurement.
Any reactivity adjustments required in control rod worth measurements in ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and
ZPR-9 were made either a) by interchanging core and radial blanket drawers at the core-radial
blanket boundary or b) by converting SCF drawers to DCF drawers or vice versa in the outer core.
These reactivity adjustments could cause significant shifts in the core power and flux distributions.
The reactivity range over which measurements based on reactor period, calibrated shim rod
position and other methods used at ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 was limited due to the techniques
used to measure the reactivity changes. This limited reactivity range constrained the number and
size of the mockup control rods that could be measured.
In principle, multiple mockup control rods could have been inserted. In practice, it seems likely
that only one mockup control rod was inserted in typical control rod worth measurements at ZPR-
3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 due to reactivity constraints related to measurement technique and the desire
to minimize core reactivity adjustments.
7.3.1.2 Control Rod Worth – Experimental Technique at ZPPR
Much of the discussion in Section 7.3.1.1 applies to control rod worth measurements at ZPPR as
well. In particular, the reactivity range constraint associated with the reactivity measurement
technique discussed in Section 7.3.1.1 applied to ZPPR experiments prior to adoption of the MSM
technique at ZPPR.
The MSM technique (see Section 7.2) was applicable to states that were up to -50$ subcritical, so
the constraint on the number of CRs present was eliminated for practical purposes. The worths of
CRs and CRPs were all negative relative to the subcritical reference configuration, so the need to
make further core reactivity adjustments after establishing the subcritical reference configuration
was eliminated. Because the worths of all CRs and CRPs were negative, the subcritical reference
configuration could be as close to the reference critical configuration as possible.
The MSM technique offered significant advantages over other techniques used to measure control
rod worth (and sodium void worth) at the ZPR/ZPPR facilities. First, the techniques discussed in
Section 7.3.1.1 required adjusting core reactivity for some experiments, particularly experiments
in which the expected reactivity change (positive or negative) was relatively large. Reactivity
adjustment could be accomplished by spiking or despiking at selected positions in the outer core.
Alternatively, the required reactivity adjustment could be accomplished by replacing blanket
drawers by core drawers or vice versa at the core-blanket interface. A separate reactivity
adjustment could be required for each experimental configuration. Each reactivity adjustment took
time, and each reactivity adjustment changed the flux and power distribution in the core. These
changes affected measured reactivity worths and other measurements such as foil measurements
of reaction rate distributions. The MSM technique eliminated the need for reactivity adjustments,
the associated shifts in power and flux distributions, and the effort required to make the core
changes.
Second, the MSM technique allowed a much wider range of experimental configurations to be
measured. For example, the techniques discussed in Section 7.3.1.1 might restrict a control rod

 250

worth measurement to one control rod. The MSM technique allowed measurement of multiple
control rods.
It should be noted that the rod drop used in the MSM technique was only possible with PSRs. A
rod drop was not feasible with the DP control rod drawers due to the potential for plate damage
during the rapid acceleration and deceleration in the rod drop. In addition, the mass of the DP
drawer would affect the speed of the rod drop and the reactor kinetics.
A typical control rod worth measurement at ZPPR using the MSM technique consisted of the
following steps:
 1. The subcritical reference configuration was established.
 2. The excess reactivity of the subcritical reference configuration was measured.
 3. The reactor was shut down, and the desired CR/CRP configuration was established.
 4. The MSM measurements were made.
 5. Steps 3 and 4 were repeated for each CR/CRP configuration of interest.
 6. The reactor was shut down, and the subcritical reference configuration was rebuilt.
 7. The excess reactivity of the subcritical reference configuration was measured again.
7.3.2 Control Rod Worth – Uncertainty Analysis
7.3.2.1 Control Rod Worth Uncertainties Related to Experimental Technique
Control rod worth measurements were simpler than sodium void worth measurements for several
reasons. First, in sodium void worth measurements, each core drawer in the void zone was
removed from the matrix, modified by replacing sodium plates with empty void cans, and reloaded
into the matrix in its original location. In the control rod worth experiments, configuration changes
were direct replacements of one set of drawers by another set of drawers. For example, a 2 x 2
array of normal core drawers in each half was replaced by another 2 x 2 array of drawers to create
a CR or CRP. This direct replacement reduced the problems associated with changes in plate
positions due to in-drawer plate substitution and drawer handling.
Second, changes for CR/CRP configurations in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies generally involved
significantly fewer drawers than changes for sodium void worth configurations in the same
assemblies. For example, changes for the sodium void worth measurements involved 148 drawers
per half in ZPPR-15A and 52 drawers per half in ZPPR-15B, ZPPR-15C and ZPPR-15D. Changes
for control rod worth measurements in ZPPR-15 involved 4 drawers per half for each CR/CRP, so
the total number of affected drawers for control rod worth measurements in ZPPR-15 ranged from
4 per half to 52 per half, depending on the number of mockup control rods present and on the
number of CRs and/or CRPs that were changed in each loading.
The difference in the number of affected drawers in sodium void worth measurements relative to
control rod worth measurements was more pronounced for ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 than for
ZPPR because the measurement technique limits that restricted the number of mockup control rods
in an assembly in ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were much less applicable to sodium void worth
measurements in those machines.
There was a small mismatch between the amount of stainless steel in the canned boron carbide
plates and sodium plates in a CR drawer and the amount of stainless steel in the sodium plates in

 251

a CRP drawer. Likewise, there was likely a small mismatch between the masses of stainless steel
in individual drawers. The mismatch for the drawer mass applies to all CR drawers, CRP drawers
and normal core drawers that were replaced by the CR and CRP drawers. This mismatch in drawer
masses does not apply to sodium void measurements because the same drawers were used in the
reference configuration and in the sodium void configurations.
The ZPR/ZPPR staff apparently did not regard any correction or uncertainty for the mismatch in
steel masses to be important for the control rod worth measurements. The steel mismatch and the
associated reactivity correction were reported for the sodium void worth measurements. Reports
for the ZPR/ZPPR control rod worth experiments do not mention any steel mass mismatch or any
correction for steel mass mismatch.
Mismatch in the steel mass is not likely to be important for the control rod worth measurements.
The reactivity worth of sodium is small, and the reactivity worth of stainless steel per kilogram is
much greater than the reactivity worth of sodium per kilogram. Consequently, correction for the
mismatch in steel masses could have a small but discernible effect for sodium void worth
measurements. For measurements of CR worth and CRP worth, the worth of replacing normal
core drawers with CR drawers and/or CRP drawers is large. Likewise, the worth of replacing a
CR by a CRP or vice versa is large. Any small correction or uncertainty related to the steel
mismatch in the control rod worth measurements should be negligible compared to the total
uncertainty for the measurement, which is generally dominated by the statistical uncertainty in the
measurement and the 5% uncertainty in the reactivity conversion from the measurement units,
inhours or cents, to the calculation units, Δk/k1k2 or pcm.
Standard drawer loading and drawer handling procedures applied to all ZPR/ZPPR experiments.
The experimenters would have made certain that all drawer fronts in front drawers were exactly
flush with the front edge of the matrix and that there were no gaps between front drawers and back
drawers (when back drawers were used in an assembly). Tabs on the drawer fronts mated with
notches in the sides of the matrix tubes to ensure consistent positioning of front drawers. Drawers
were inserted into matrix tubes slowly to minimize plate shifting. The procedure for loading
drawers into the matrix tubes minimized unintentional changes in the axial position of the core
material within each matrix half. Springs inserted in the the backs of drawers to push the plates
forward also minimized unintentional changes in the plate positions.
The preceding paragraphs cover general procedures for minimizing experimental uncertainties,
but there are residual uncertainties related to the experimental technique for control rod worth

For control rod worth measurements based on the MSM technique, there is also a correlated
uncertainty from the establishment of the reference subcritical configuration that includes the
reactivity scale calibration and source ratio. For reactivity worth measurements based upon other
techniques such as period measurements or calibrated control rod positions, there is a similar
correlated uncertainty related to measurement of the reference configuration if that configuration
is used as the reference for a series of reactivity worth measurements. These correlated uncertainty
components are likely to be included in the published uncertainties for the measured values.
Another uncertainty is the reproducibility uncertainty discussed above. It was more common to
report reproducibility uncertainty for sodium void worth measurements than for control rod worth

 252

measurements. In ZPPR-15, for example, the ZPPR staff reported the reproducibility uncertainty
for the sodium void worth measurements, but they did not report any reproducibility uncertainty
for the control rod worth measurements. This suggests that the ZPR/ZPPR staff did not regard
reproducibility uncertainty as a significant factor for control rod worth measurements.
It seems reasonable that reproducibility uncertainty would be neglected for control rod worth
measurements. Reproducibility uncertainty will not differ significantly for sodium void worth and
control rod worth measurements in the same assembly program. Measured CR/CRP worths are
much larger than measured sodium void worths in the same ZPR/ZPPR assembly. Reproducibility
uncertainty might make a small contribution to the total uncertainty for a sodium void worth
measurement because the measured sodium void worth and its associated total uncertainty are not
large. That same reproducibility uncertainty will make a negligible contribution to the total
uncertainty for the much larger control rod worth measurement in the same assembly.
The plate shifting component of reproducibility uncertainty is likely to be significantly larger for
sodium void worth measurements than for control rod worth measurements in the same assembly
because a) sodium void worth measurements involved more drawers than control rod worth
measurements and b) more drawer handling and plate handling were required for sodium void
worth measurements than for control rod worth measurements. The additional drawer and plate
handling required for sodium void worth measurements increased the likelihood of plate shifting
in sodium void worth measurements relative to control rod worth measurements. Other
components of reproducibility uncertainty such as the contributions from uncertainties in the table
separation (interface gap), average core temperature, control rod position and any 241Pu decay will
have similar magnitudes for sodium void worth and control rod worth measurements, but those
components will be less important for control rod worth measurements because the measured
control rod worths are much greater in magnitude than measured sodium void worths.
Consequently, the reproducibility uncertainty for control rod worth measurements is likely to be
be smaller than the reproducibility uncertainty for sodium void worth measurements in the same
assembly. In addition, the contribution of the reproducibility uncertainty to the total uncertainty
is likely to be much less important for control rod worth measurements than for sodium void worth
measurements in the same assembly because other uncertainty components, primarily the
component due to the βeff uncertainty and the statistical uncertainty in the measurement, are likely
to be much larger for control rod worth measurements than for sodium void worth measurements.
In the absence of any other information, the reproducibility uncertainty for a sodium void worth
measurement can be assumed to apply to a control rod worth measurement in the same assembly,
or reproducibility uncertainty can be ignored for control rod worth measurements. In either case,
the contribution of reproducibility uncertainty to the total uncertainty in a control rod worth
measurement is likely to be small or negligible compared to the contribution from the uncertainty
in βeff.
All uncertainty components related to the experimental technique are small compared to the
contribution from reactivity conversion.
7.3.2.2 Reactivity Adjustments for Control Rod Worth Measurements
The uncertainties associated with adjustment to a common decay date, temperature and interface
gap that were discussed in Section 7.2.2.2 also apply to control rod worth measurements in

 253

ZPR/ZPPR assemblies. The standard practice was to adjust each configuration to the 241Pu decay
date, core average temperature, and matrix interface gap of the reference (or subcritical reference)
configuration. This adjustment simplified analysis by providing a common basis for comparing
configurations and measured values.
These adjustments add small uncertainties because the measured temperature coefficient, interface
gap coefficient and 241Pu decay coefficient used for the adjustments had small associated
uncertainties. These uncertainties are included in the published uncertainties for the control rod
worth measurements.
Uncertainties in the 241Pu decay coefficient, temperature coefficient and interface gap coefficient
are correlated for all loadings in a ZPR/ZPPR assembly unless there are significant changes in the
assembly composition during the assembly program. For configurations in which uncertainties in
these coefficients are correlated, these uncertainties are eliminated in reactivity differences
between configurations because uncertainties in the 241Pu decay coefficient, temperature
coefficient and interface gap coefficient are included in the adjustment of the measured reactivities
to a common reference date, average core temperature and interface gap.
The thermocouple calibration uncertainty discussed in Section 7.2.2.2 is correlated for a series of
measurements and is eliminated in reactivity differences derived from a series of related
measurements such as the control rod worth measurements.
The uncertainty in average core temperature is not correlated between different loadings in the
same assembly, so this uncertainty may contribute to the total uncertainty for the control rod worth
measurement. In most cases, the contribution of the uncertainty in average core temperature will
be small and will not make a significant contribution to the total uncertainty, especially for control
rod worth measurements where the measured worth is large and the corresponding contributions
from statistical uncertainty and the uncertainty in β eff are large.
The measured table separation (related to the interface gap) will not be uniform for a series of
loadings such as a series of control rod worth measurements and will not be correlated for that
series. However, the table separation difference will be small, and the contribution of the
uncertainty in the table separation to the total uncertainty will be small. For the ZPPR-15 sodium
void worth measurements, the largest contribution of the uncertainty in the table separation to the
total uncertainty was ~0.1 pcm. The contribution of the uncertainty in the table separation to the
total control rod worth uncertainty would be similar. An uncertainty of 0.1 pcm is negligible. It
seems likely that any uncertainty related to variation in the table separation or interface gap width
over a series of loadings in the same assembly would make a negligible contribution to the total
uncertainty for a control rod worth measurement.
7.3.2.3 Effects of Material Composition Uncertainties for Control Rod Worth
 Measurements
For control rod worth measurements in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies, the reference configuration or
subcritical reference configuration and the CR/CRP insertion configurations were identical except
for replacement of core drawers by CR/CRP drawers in the mockup control rod positions.
Consequently, the uncertainty contributions of the plates, drawers, and matrix tubes to the
uncertainties in the measured values would be highly correlated between the reference or

 254

subcritical reference configuration and the corresponding CR/CRP configurations, excluding the
materials in the drawers that are changed. The uncertainty contributions of plates, drawers, and
matrix tubes will change slightly between the reference or subcritical reference configuration and
the CR/CRP configuration due to small changes in the neutron spectrum, but these changes are
negligible compared to other uncertainties discussed below.
There is a 0.15% uncertainty in the masses of the sodium plates, boron carbide plates, tantalum
plates or any other plates in the CR/CRP drawers (see Section 7.1). Uncertainty analysis for the
ZPPR-15 sodium void measurements showed that the worth of uncertainties in the sodium mass
and sodium impurities was ~0.05 pcm for the void worth measurements. The numbers of sodium
plates changed in sodium void worth measurements are comparable to or much larger than the
numbers of sodium plates in the CR/CRP drawers in a control rod worth measurement, especially
for measurements where there was only one CR/CRP. Consequently, the worth of uncertainties
in sodium mass or sodium impurities for sodium void worth measurements bound the worth of
uncertainties in the same parameters for control rod worth measurements in the same assembly.
In any case, the worth of uncertainties in sodium mass or sodium impurities in sodium plates in
CRs or CRPs is likely to make a negligible contribution to the total uncertainty for control rod
worth measurements.
The 0.15 wt.% uncertainty in the masses of absorber plates (boron carbide, tantalum, etc.) is not
necessarily negligible. For example, the worth of the 0.15% uncertainty in the mass of the boron
carbide plates was computed for ZPPR-15B loading 102 (L102). The computed worth of the
uncertainty in the mass of the boron carbide plates for ZPPR-15B L102 is 11.2 pcm, which is not
negligible for some measurements.
For most absorber materials such as tantalum, natural abundances can be assumed unless a
document states that the absorber material was enriched in one isotope. Boron is one exception to
this statement. The Chart of Nuclides [10] states that significant differences in observed
abundance values have been observed in some boron samples. Note, however, that it is not
appropriate to apply a generic uncertainty in the 10B content of natural boron listed in some data
sources to the ZPR/ZPPR boron carbide plates. This generic uncertainty is based on measurements
of boron from a variety of sources. The boron carbide plates of one size in the ZPR/ZPPR plate
inventories were produced by one manufacturer using one source of boron.
Boron in the ZPR/ZPPR boron carbide plates is typically natural boron although plate inventories
did contain a limited number of boron carbide plates enriched in 10B. The 10B and 11B masses in
boron carbide plates are probably measured values, but there are no details of the measurements
and no way to quantify the measurement uncertainty. Because it is unlikely that information
regarding uncertainties for the 10B content of the boron will be found, it is necessary to make an
assumption about the 10B/11B ratio or 10B content of the boron carbide plates. One reasonable
assumption is that the measurement uncertainty for modern measurements of 10B content or
10 11
  B/ B ratio are applicable to the ZPR/ZPPR boron carbide plates. Another reasonable but likely
conservative assumption is that the 10B uncertainty is in the 0.1% – 0.15% range, i.e., that the 10B
uncertainty in the 10B/11B ratio is about the same magnitude as the mass uncertainty.
A third standard approach is to assume that the uncertainty is the maximum rounding error of the
last significant figure. For example, if the listed 10B content is 18.32 wt.%, then the assumed

 255

uncertainty is 0.005 wt.%. A more conservative choice in that example would be to assume the
uncertainty is 0.01 wt.%, i.e., that the uncertainty is 1 in the last significant figure.
From experience, the total uncertainty for the control rod worth measurements is typically
dominated by the uncertainty in reactivity conversion from measured units to Δk/k 1k2 or pcm and
thus the effect of this assumption for the 10B/B uncertainty is generally small.
The indirect source of uncertainties related to the effect of uncertainties in plate compositions and
masses on the calculated sodium void worth values discussed in Section 7.2.2.3 applies to
calculated control rod worths as well. In this context, plates refers to all plates (fuel, sodium, steel,
depleted uranium, etc.) in the assembly rather than to just the plates in CRs and CRPs. This
uncertainty is not related to the measured value. All compositions and masses of plates, drawers
and matrix tubes in the materials database are uncertain, and these uncertainties in compositions
and masses of matrix tubes, drawers and different plate types introduce a small uncertainty into
calculated worths. For practical purposes, the effects of the uncertainties in the compositions and
masses of plates, drawers and matrix tubes on the calculated control rod worth can be included in
the total uncertainty.
The contribution of all plates, drawers and matrix tubes to the total uncertainty for the control rod
worth measurements was calculated for ZPPR-15 and ZPR-6/7. In both cases, the only
composition or mass uncertainty contributions that were not negligible were the contributions from
the 0.15% mass uncertainty for the boron carbide plates and the uncertainty in the 10B content of
the boron.
Unless the measured CR/CRP worth is very small, it is likely that the contribution of composition
and mass uncertainties from all of the plates (fuel, sodium, steel, etc.) to the total uncertainty for
the control rod worth measurement will be small except for the contributions from the mass
uncertainty for the absorber plates and the uncertainty in the isotopic composition of boron in
boron carbide plates (or the isotopic composition of some other absorber material in the CR).
7.3.2.4 Reactivity Conversion for Control Rod Worth Measurements
Control rod worths were measured in units of inhours or cents. Calculated worths and associated
uncertainties are expressed in units of Δk/k1k2 or pcm. Conversion from inhours or cents, to pcm
or from pcm to inhours or cents requires βeff which was generally calculated by the experimenters.
However, βeff is uncertain, and its estimated uncertainty is 5% (see Section 7.1.2). The 5%
uncertainty in βeff contributes an additional uncertainty to the final control rod worths.
In general, the 5% uncertainty in βeff and the statistical uncertainty in the measurement are the
dominant uncertainties for control rod worth measurements. All of the individual uncertainties for
the control rod worth measurement are added in quadrature to determine the total uncertainty for
the control rod worth measurement.
7.3.3 Calculation of the Measured Control Rod Worth
Section 7.1.5 discussed constructing high-fidelity as-built models of criticality measurements in
ZPR/ZPPR assemblies. That discussion applies to constructing models of control rod worth
measurements as well. Loadings in any ZPR/ZPPR assembly were cumulative, so it is necessary

 256

to process the loading records for all previous loadings in addition to the loading records for the
control rod worth configurations of interest.
The measured control worths can be calculated by direct Monte Carlo using as-built Monte Carlo
models of the reference and CR/CRP configurations. The number of histories required to produce
an acceptable statistical uncertainty will depend on the measured worth and associated total
uncertainty. From experience, one billion (109) histories in a direct Monte Carlo calculation of keff
for an as-built ZPR/ZPPR model results in a one sigma statistical uncertainty in the 1 – 2 pcm
range. Measured control rod worths are generally much larger than measured sodium void worths,
so direct Monte Carlo calculations using as-built Monte Carlo models of control rod worth
measurements are straightforward.
For routine reactor design and analysis work, a deterministic code is typically used. Consequently,
it may be necessary to convert the as-built Monte Carlo model to an equivalent deterministic model
as part of the validation process for the deterministic code, the details of which were given at the
beginning of Section 7.
7.4 Doppler Sample Worth Measurements
Doppler broadening of resonances is an important component of the temperature coefficient of a
fast reactor, so the Doppler reactivity worth of samples was measured in many ZPR/ZPPR
assemblies. The temperature coefficient of the ZPR/ZPPR reactor as a whole was determined as
part of the standard operational measurements for an assembly because this was an important
safety parameter for reactor operations. In addition, the temperature coefficient was used to adjust
measured reactivity from the average temperature of the reactor at the time of the measurement to
a standard temperature used for reporting purposes as discussed above. Unfortunately, it is not
possible to use the measured temperature coefficient of the ZPR/ZPPR reactor as a whole for
validation purposes.
Before plutonium fuel was introduced into ZPR-3 operations, there was only one thermocouple in
each half of the ZPR-3 matrix, and natural convection provided reactor cooling. After ZPR-3
began using plutonium fuel in assemblies, five additional thermocouples were added to each half
of the ZPR-3 matrix, and a rudimentary forced air cooling system was devised for ZPR-3.
In ZPR-6 and ZPR-9, reactor temperature was monitored by placing thermocouples on or adjacent
to fuel plates in several drawers in each matrix half. In ZPPR, multiple thermocouples were placed
in each matrix half to measure the reactor temperature during reactor operations. During normal
reactor operations in ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR, fans forced cooling air through the matrix tubes to
remove the power being generated and thus maintain a steady-state reactor operating temperature.
The following general procedure was used to measure the reactor temperature coefficient. After a
reference critical configuration was established, the steady-state temperatures measured by the
thermocouples were recorded. Then the fans that forced cooling air through the assembly were
turned off, and the reactor was allowed to heat up slowly due to radioactive decay of the plutonium
fuel. The reactivity change and reactor temperature change associated with this heating were
recorded as a function of time, and the recorded data were used to determine the reactor
temperature coefficient. It is not clear if or how temperature coefficients were determined for
uranium-fueled assemblies in which decay heating was small.

 257

It would not be possible to evaluate or model measurement of the ZPR/ZPPR reactor temperature
coefficient for several reasons. First, the number of thermocouples in each ZPR/ZPPR assembly
was limited. The average temperature measured by those thermocouples was regarded as a
representative temperature for the reactor as a whole, but that average temperature was not
necessarily the true temperature at any selected location within the reactor. There were not enough
thermocouples in any ZPR/ZPPR assembly to establish an accurate measured temperature
distribution within the reactor. In addition, the thermocouple locations generally are unknown
with the exception of thermocouple drawers in ZPR-6 assemblies and ZPR-9 assemblies. An
accurate temperature distribution in a ZPR/ZPPR assembly cannot be determined from the
measured temperatures even if the measured temperatures are available.
Second, the measured reactivity change in the temperature coefficient measurement included the
combined effects of Doppler feedback and thermal expansion of the materials in the reactor. There
was no measurement of the thermal expansion. It would not be possible to separate the two
reactivity effects or to compute an accurate thermal expansion with any realistic amount of effort.
Third, the data used to derive the reactor temperature coefficient cannot be found in any available
documents. Consequently, it is not practical to evaluate or model the measured reactor temperature
coefficient for a ZPR/ZPPR assembly.
It was possible to measure the Doppler worths of small samples in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies, and
Doppler sample worth measurements were common measurements in these assemblies.
7.4.1 Doppler Sample Worth Measurement Technique
The basic aspects of Doppler sample worth measurements were very similar in ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and
ZPPR. A similar procedure was probably used for any Doppler worth measurements conducted
in ZPR-3, but little information is available for such ZPR-3 measurements. Davey and Redman
[16] describe several experimental techniques for measuring Doppler worth that were in use when
the ZPR/ZPPR facilities operated. These techniques included the heated zone method, the heated
sample method and sample activation measurements.
The Variable Temperature Rodded Zone (VTRZ) designed for use in ZPR-6 was based on the
heated zone method in which a large zone in the center of the reactor is heated. The VTRZ had an
octagonal center zone that could be electrically heated to a maximum temperature of 550 °C. The
heated zone was designed to hold 2 x 2 x 12 inch calandrias. Each calandria contained 16 tubes
into which 0.375 inch diameter x 6 inch long stainless steel-clad UO 2 or mixed UO2-PuO2 fuel
rods could be inserted. The VTRZ was insulated and contained an air-cooled gap to protect the
drawers and plates outside the heated zone [16]. Program priorities changed, and the VTRZ was
never used.
Heated zone and heated sample methods measure the reactivity change associated with changing
the temperature of the heated zone or sample. In activation measurements, one foil is irradiated at
low temperature, and another foil of the same material is irradiated at an elevated temperature.
The difference in activation of the two foils is a measure of the Doppler effect on reaction rates.
Activation measurements are complementary to heated zone and heated sample methods. If
activation measurements were ever performed in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies, they would have been
uncommon measurements and probably would have been performed in ZPR-3 assemblies and

 258

early assemblies at ZPR-6 and ZPR-9. No documentation has been found to date on Doppler
activation measurements in any ZPR/ZPPR documents.
The heated sample method was the primary, or possibly only, technique used to measure Doppler
worth in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies.
The Doppler sample consisted of a cylindrical sample enclosed in a metal capsule. Sample
materials included depleted UO2, natural UO2, enriched UO2, depleted U metal and depleted U-
10Zr metal (90 wt.% U, 10 wt.% Zr). It is likely that the U-10Zr sample was fabricated specifically
for ZPPR-15 because ZPPR-15 simulated several phases of operations in the Integral Fast Reactor
(IFR) design that used either U-10Zr or U/Pu-10Zr fuel. There may have been other sample
materials including HEU metal, plutonium metal or compounds including HEU or plutonium
because the Doppler worths of various isotopes and materials were of interest for fast reactor safety
purposes. The document reporting a Doppler sample measurement is likely to describe the
sample(s) measured. The metal capsule enclosing the sample material generally consisted of
Inconel or a similar alloy.
A typical sample diameter was ~1 inch, and typical sample lengths were 10 – 12 inches long. In
at least some cases, e.g., oxides, the sample consisted of multiple pellets rather than a single solid
piece. It is not clear whether other samples such as the metal samples consisted of multiple pellets
or of a single piece. The fact that a sample consisted of multiple pellets explains the difference
