between the listed mass, density or atom density of the sample and the corresponding quantity
derived from the sample dimensions and physical density of the sample material. Figure 7.2 shows
a Doppler sample pellet, Doppler capsule and assembled Doppler sample rod. The coil visible in
the capsule and assembled rod is probably the heater coil. The wire projecting from the back may
be the electrical lead for the heater coil or for the thermocouple in the center of the sample material.

 259

 Figure 7.2 Doppler Sample, Doppler Capsule and Assembled Doppler Rod
Figure 7.3 is another view of the Doppler sample pellets and assembled components of the Doppler
sample mechanism. The small hole visible in the Doppler sample pellet provided space for the
thermocouple used to measure the sample temperature.

 260

 Figure 7.3. Doppler Sample Pellets and Components of the Doppler Mechanism.
The figures in this section are representative of the Doppler sample mechanisms used to measure
Doppler sample worths at the ZPR/ZPPR facilities, but there were minor differences between the
devices used at ANL-E and ANL-W. In addition, the designs of the Doppler sample devices likely
changed over time as better methods and equipment developed and possibly to meet the needs of
specific assembly programs.
There were two variations of the heated sample method. In one method, the Doppler sample and
mechanism were placed in a fixed location in the core, the temperature of the sample was
oscillated, and the resulting reactivity changes were measured. It is likely that some early Doppler
sample worth measurements in ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 used this method.
In the second method, the Doppler sample was oscillated into and out of the reactor at a sequence
of fixed temperatures. This second method was the standard technique used for most or possibly
all Doppler sample worth measurements in ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR. It was probably the standard
technique for later Doppler sample worth measurements in ZPR-3 as well. The second method is
described here.

 261

The Doppler sample was loaded into the Doppler mechanism which consisted of a heating element
surrounded by an outer tube or capsule. In most or possibly all cases, the sample temperature was
measured by a thermocouple inserted into a small cylindrical cavity or well in the center of the
sample. The most likely alternative would be to measure the temperature on the outer surface of
the sample.
The Doppler mechanism was placed in a tray which was placed in a matrix tube at the designated
core location. The tray containing the Doppler mechanism was typically placed in the center
matrix tube of the core, but Doppler sample worths were sometimes measured at other core
locations. The tray was long enough to extend through both halves of the matrix.
The worth of the sample was measured by measuring the reactivity change as the Doppler
mechanism and sample were oscillated into and out of the center of the core with the sample at a
fixed temperature. This reactivity change was determined from the change in critical rod position
of the calibrated, servo-controlled fine autorod that was used to measure very small reactivities
such as small sample worths and Doppler sample worths. In general, the autorod was located in
the radial blanket or reflector, but there were cases in which the autorod was placed in the outer
core region.
To reduce the experimental uncertainty, the sample was oscillated multiple times. After the
required number of oscillations was performed at one fixed temperature, the sample temperature
was increased to the next desired value, and the oscillation sequence was repeated.
Details of the actual experimental procedure have not been found. The heater was on the outside
of the sample, and the thermocouple was in a cavity in the center of the sample. In principle, there
could have been a temperature gradient between the outer surface of the sample and the
thermocouple in the center of the sample. It is believed that no significant temperature gradient
existed for two reasons. First, the experimenters would have been aware of the problem and would
have taken steps to ensure an equilibrium temperature in the sample with no significant
temperature gradient in the sample before making measurements. They were also aware that there
could be axial expansion of the sample during heating, and they corrected for that axial expansion.
Second, the sample was oscillated multiple times. If there was a significant temperature gradient
in the sample, the thermocouple would have recorded a temperature change as the number of
oscillations increased.
The worth of the heating element, capsule and other components of the mechanism was measured
by repeating the measurement sequence without the Doppler sample present in the mechanism.
The actual Doppler sample was enclosed in a metal capsule. In order to determine the worth of
just the sample, the encapsulated Doppler sample was replaced by an empty capsule during the
measurements without the sample present. The difference between the measured worths with and
without the Doppler sample determines the worth of just the Doppler sample. Sample and empty
capsule measurements were obtained at various temperatures between ~300 K and ~1100 K.
Because it was not always possible to match the measured temperatures of the heated sample and
the heated empty capsule exactly, there is no direct correspondence between the sample and empty
capsule measurements as a function of temperature. To establish a common basis for the two
measurements, the experimenters performed separate least squares fits of the heated sample and
empty capsule data to the equation

 262

                                     ρ(T) = [C1T0/(1-γ)][(T/T0)1-γ – 1] + C2
where C1, C2 and γ are fitting parameters, T0 is 300 K, and ρ(T) is reactivity as a function of
temperature in Kelvins. The fitting parameters were used to compute ρ(T) for the heated sample
and empty capsule data in increments between 300 K and 1100 K. The fitted data provided a
common basis for evaluating the Doppler effect between the reference temperature and the
elevated temperature over the experimental temperature range.
Two adjustments were commonly required to obtain completely consistent measurements. First,
the reference temperatures for the heated sample and empty capsule measurements might differ
slightly. Second, the mass of the capsule enclosing the Doppler sample and the mass of the empty
capsule used in the measurements without the Doppler sample might differ slightly.
For example, in ZPR-9/29, the reference temperatures for the heated sample (N-1) data and empty
capsule (MT-1) data were 298 K and 301 K, respectively, so the data were adjusted to 300 K by
subtracting the 300 K reactivity worth from the reactivity worth at all temperatures. A second
adjustment was required because the mass of the Inconel-600 capsule for the N-1 sample was
421.3 g while the mass of the Inconel-600 capsule for MT-1 was 388.5 g.
The reactivity change produced by heating the Doppler sample is very small relative to the
reactivity worth of the Doppler sample and the associated equipment, so a direct measurement as
described in the preceding paragraphs would be a small difference between two much larger
numbers and would have a relatively large experimental uncertainty. The experimental uncertainty
was reduced by using a balance tray. A balance tray consisted of a small tray which was placed
in the long Doppler tray at the opposite end from the Doppler samples and equipment. This small
tray contained a carefully selected group of plates (depleted uranium, stainless steel, enriched
uranium, plutonium, etc.) which approximately matched the mass, composition and worth of the
Doppler sample and related equipment. As the Doppler sample was oscillated into and out of the
core, the balance tray moved in the opposite direction. The reactivity worth of the balance tray
was measured when it was in the core, and the reactivity worth of the heated Doppler sample was
measured when it was in the center of the core. The difference in worth between the Doppler
sample plus equipment and the balance tray was small, so the small Doppler worth showed up
more clearly as the difference between two small worths.
Davey and Redman [16] indicated that a modification of the heated sample technique made the
reference sample unnecessary. The reference sample was likely the balance tray and any plates in
the tray. After this modification, the reference configuration became a void, i.e., the Doppler tray
without the Doppler sample, in the Doppler tray. Measuring the reactivity difference between the
void and the “sample in” position was accomplished with an autorod capable of reproducing
positions within ±0.001 inch.
Figure 7.4 shows a cross-sectional view of the Doppler sample equipment used in ZPR-9/29 with
the Doppler sample inside the heater coil. It is possible that other versions of the Doppler sample
equipment were used in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 between 1963 and 1982.

 263

 Figure 7.4. Doppler Sample Equipment Used in ZPR-9/29.
The heater tube or coil typically was made of nickel alloy and was ~0.050 inches thick. The heater
was suspended inside a stainless steel outer tube that was ~0.050 inches thick. The inner side of
the outer tube was silvered to reduce heat loss such that a constant temperature could be quickly
achieved for the sample. A vacuum was maintained in the ~0.095 inch space between the heater
tube and outer tube for the same reason.
The Doppler mechanism described in the preceding paragraph was used for measurements up to
1100 K. A second device existed that could be used for measurements up to 2000 K [16]. Graphite
was used for the heater, sample container and supporting pieces for the second device, and the
heater was supported by beryllia insulators.
ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 used the same Doppler equipment and samples. The Doppler equipment and
samples used at ANL-E were not necessarily identical to the Doppler samples and equipment used

 264

at ANL-W, and the Doppler samples and equipment used at ZPPR were not necessarily identical
to any Doppler samples or equipment used at ZPR-3.

worth measurements in ZPPR-15. Figure 7.5 shows a cross-sectional view of the Doppler sample,
equipment and tray. Figure 7.6 shows another view of the Doppler sample and equipment. Figure

One complication related to the Doppler sample worth measurements is that a Doppler sample is
subject to thermal expansion during measurement. The degree of expansion depends on the nature
of the sample. For example, oxide samples expand less than metal samples.
The primary effect of axial expansion of the sample is that the sample expands into a region of
lower worth. This effect is reduced by placing the sample in a location where the axial flux profile
is relatively flat. In general, that location is the axial center of the core. Thermal expansion also

 266

reduces the sample density and the collision probabilities in the sample, and these changes affect
neutron leakage from the sample.
Davey and Redman [16] describes various methods developed to reduce the effects of thermal
expansion. These methods included making special samples with reduced density and
mechanically constraining the samples to reduce expansion. The effects of thermal expansion
were studied systematically in ZPR-6.
In the ZPPR-15 Doppler sample worth measurements, the ZPPR staff calculated a correction for
thermal expansion in the two metal samples. The correction was based upon a calculated first
order axial worth profile for 238U. The calculated correction depended on the composition of the
sample (depleted U metal versus depleted U-10Zr alloy) and on the temperature of the sample.
The calculated correction to the reactivity worth ranged from ~0.8% at the lowest temperatures to
~1.7% at the highest temperatures.
No correction was calculated for the two UO2 samples measured in ZPPR-15. This indicates that
the ZPPR staff regarded the effect of thermal expansion in the UO 2 samples as negligible,
The ZPR/ZPPR experimenters were aware of the thermal expansion issue. It seems likely that any
relevant corrections for thermal expansion are included in published Doppler sample worths even
if the reports do not explicitly state that thermal expansion corrections were applied.
The correction for thermal expansion is small. Any uncertainty in the correction for thermal
expansion would make a negligible contribution to the total uncertainty for the Doppler sample
worth measurements.
7.4.2 Uncertainties for Doppler Sample Worth Measurements
In general, the uncertainties published by the experimenters for measurements of Doppler sample
worth are uncertainties that are directly associated with the Doppler reactivity worth measurement.
Those uncertainties include counting statistics, detector calibration, uncertainty in the measured
temperature of the Doppler sample or empty capsule and the uncertainty in the calibration of the
fine autorod. It is not known whether the uncertainty in the fitting of the data is included in the
published uncertainty, but any uncertainty in the data fitting is likely to be much smaller than the
5% uncertainty in βeff discussed below.
Because of the way in which Doppler sample worths were measured, all uncertainties related to
the overall reactor configuration, i.e., the uncertainties for the reference critical configuration, are
completely correlated between the cold Doppler sample measurement and the hot Doppler sample
measurement and, consequently, drop out of the uncertainty analysis of the Doppler sample
measurements. There are, however, several additional uncertainties related to the Doppler sample,
measurement technique and conversion of units that remain to be considered.
7.4.2.1 Reproducibility Uncertainty
The Doppler sample measurement technique eliminates nearly all components of reproducibility
uncertainty. Uncertainty related to control rod positions is eliminated except for a ±0.001 inch
uncertainty in the position of the fine autorod because only the autorod moves during the
measurement. According to Davey and Redman [16], the worth of the autorod position uncertainty
is approximately 3 x 10-8 Δk/k which is negligible compared to other uncertainties.

 267

The desired sample temperature was established, and the sample was oscillated multiple times
when the matrix halves were closed. This process could be repeated at each desired temperature
without any change in the position of the movable table, so uncertainty related to the interface gap
is eliminated.
There can be a small reactivity drift during reactor operation, but this is covered by the repeated
oscillations of the Doppler sample in the reactor.
There will be a small uncertainty in the precise position of the Doppler sample when the sample is
in the core. However, the “sample in” position is at the axial center of the core where the axial
power and flux distributions are relatively flat. In principle, the effect of a sample position
uncertainty of a few mils could be calculated. In practice, the small size of the Doppler sample
worth probably makes such a calculation very difficult or impossible. In any case, expending
much effort to quantify this uncertainty does not seem to be warranted because the total uncertainty
for the Doppler sample worth will be dominated by other uncertainty components.
7.4.2.2 Doppler Sample Mass Uncertainty
The actual mass of the Doppler sample is uncertain. All ICSBEP and IRPhEP benchmarks of ZPR
and ZPPR assemblies have assigned an uncertainty of 0.15% to the mass of any plate, drawer or
other component with the exception of the matrix tubes for which the mass uncertainty is
significantly larger [5,6]. This 0.15% uncertainty arises from lack of knowledge concerning the
specific procedure and equipment used for weight measurements plus an assumed uncertainty in
the weight calibration standards. There is no reason to believe that the Doppler sample weight was
known more accurately than those of other items used in ZPR or ZPPR experiments, so the 0.15%
weight uncertainty is assumed to apply to the Doppler sample.
The uncertainty in the mass of the sample does not affect the measured total worth of the sample,
but the 0.15% sample mass uncertainty does introduce a 0.15% uncertainty in the worth per unit
mass of the sample and in the calculated worth of the sample.
7.4.2.3 Doppler Sample Composition Uncertainty
The composition of the Doppler sample is uncertain. The uncertainty in the Doppler sample
composition has several possible components. For oxide samples such as UO 2, PuO2 or mixed
UO2-PuO2, the exact O:U or O:Pu ratio in the sample is unknown. This introduces a small
uncertainty in the amount of U and/or Pu in the sample. If available documents do not list any
uncertainty for the O:U ratio or O:Pu ratio, a range of 1.98 – 2.02 is probably a conservative but
reasonable estimate. Uncertainty in the O:U ratio or O:Pu ratio is unlikely to be a dominant
component of the total uncertainty.
Uranium samples or the uranium in UO2 samples may consist of natural uranium, depleted uranium
or enriched uranium. The uranium component of mixed U-Pu or mixed UO 2-PuO2 samples
probably consists of depleted uranium or natural uranium, but in principle there may have been
mixed U-Pu or mixed UO2-PuO2 samples in which enriched uranium was used.
The uncertainty in the uranium isotopic distribution in natural uranium is negligible. For depleted
uranium and enriched uranium, there will be a small uncertainty in the isotopic distribution.
Specifically, there is an uncertainty in the weight fraction of 235U in the depleted uranium and in

 268

the enriched uranium. For some samples, there could also be small uncertainties in the weight
percent of 234U and possibly in the weight percent of 236U. The contribution of the uncertainty in
the uranium isotopic distribution to the total uncertainty is likely to be small.
The Doppler sample worth measurements in ZPPR-15 will be used as an example. Four Doppler
samples were measured in ZPPR-15. Doppler sample N-3 was natural UO 2, sample N-11 was
depleted uranium metal, sample N-24 was depleted U-10Zr (depleted uranium metal alloyed with
10 wt.% Zr), and sample E-33-A was 33% enriched UO2.
The manufacturing specification for the depleted U 3O8 plates used in ZPPR required a two-sigma
uncertainty of 10% in the 235U content of the depleted uranium. No similar manufacturing
specification has been located for the depleted uranium metal plates or for the Doppler samples,
but it seems likely that the 235U content specification would have been similar or possibly much
tighter for the Doppler samples because similar considerations would apply with respect to the
effects of uncertainties.
The uncertainty in the 235U content of the Doppler samples is not important compared to the other
uncertainties for the Doppler worth measurements. Consider a depleted uranium sample
containing a nominal 0.2 wt.% 235U with a one-sigma uncertainty of 5% in the 235U content. At
the one-sigma level, the 235U range would be 0.19 wt.% – 0.21 wt.%, and the corresponding 238U
range would be 99.81 wt.% – 99.79 wt.% if one ignores the very small 234U component. This
uncertainty is much smaller than the assumed 0.15% uncertainty in the weight of the sample, so
the effect of uncertainty in the 235U content of the depleted uranium Doppler samples is considered
to be negligible.
Similar considerations apply to an enriched uranium or UO2 sample. The uncertainty in the 235U
content of the HEU plates used in the ZPR/ZPPR facilities was small (see Section 7.1). The
uncertainty in the 235U content of enriched uranium or UO2 Doppler samples would also be small
because significant 235U enrichment uncertainty would affect the quality of the measured Doppler
worths. If the uncertainty in 235U enrichment is small, the corresponding uncertainty in the 238U
content of a Doppler sample is small. The effect of uncertainty in the composition of an enriched
uranium sample is considered to be negligible compared to the 0.15% uncertainty in the sample
weight in the 5% uncertainty in the reactivity conversion factor, β eff.
For samples containing plutonium (PuO2, mixed UO2-PuO2, mixed U-Pu), the isotopic distribution
in the plutonium is uncertain. As in the case of uranium samples, it seems unlikely that the
plutonium isotopic distribution uncertainty in Doppler samples would be a dominant component
of the total uncertainty for Doppler sample worth measurements.
The N-24 sample used in ZPPR-15 consisted of U-10Zr (nominally 90 wt.% U alloyed with 10
wt.% Zr).
The present experience with analysis of Doppler sample worth measurements is limited to ZPR-
9/29 and ZPPR-15. ZPR-3, ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR may have had Doppler samples consisting
of other compounds besides U-10Zr, UO2, PuO2 and mixed UO2-PuO2.
In some cases, it may be possible to find information regarding uncertainties in Doppler sample
compositions (O:U, O:Pu, 235U enrichment, the weight percent of each constituent in compounds,
etc.) or to make reasonable assumptions regarding those uncertainties. If reasonable uncertainties

 269

in Doppler sample compositions can be determined, the effects of those uncertainties can be
computed in principle.
In practice, computing the effects of Doppler sample composition uncertainties would be very
difficult at the very least. The measured Doppler worth of a sample is typically ~0.1 pcm or less.
Computing the uncertainty components by Monte Carlo is not feasible, so a deterministic model
is preferred.
7.4.2.4 Temperature Uncertainty
In previous ICSBEP and IRPhEP benchmarks of ZPPR critical configurations [5,6], the estimated
uncertainty in the thermocouple calibration was 0.5 ºC or 0.5 K, and that uncertainty would also
apply to calibration of the thermocouple used to measure the temperature of the Doppler sample
or the temperature of the Doppler mechanism when no sample was present. However, the same
thermocouple was used for all Doppler sample measurements, so the effect of uncertainty in the
thermocouple calibration is correlated among all Doppler measurements.
In addition, the uncertainty in the sample temperature may be much larger than the uncertainty in
the thermocouple calibration. For example, the ZPPR experimenters stated that the published
uncertainties for the ZPPR-15 Doppler sample worth measurements included ±5 K temperature
uncertainty. Adding a 5 K uncertainty and a 0.5 K uncertainty in quadrature only increases the
total temperature uncertainty to 5.02 K. Consequently, the effect of the uncertainty in
thermocouple calibration is considered negligible.
7.4.2.5 Reactivity Conversion Uncertainty
Doppler reactivities were reported in the measurement units, cents or inhours. However, Doppler
reactivities are calculated in units of Δk/k1k2 or pcm. Conversion from the measurements units to
the calculation units or vice versa requires βeff. The uncertainty that is typically assigned to βeff in
ICSBEP and IRPhEP benchmarks of ZPR/ZPPR assemblies is 5% as discussed in previous
sections. The 5% value is assumed not only in ZPR/ZPPR benchmarks but also in many other
benchmarks in the ICSBEP and IRPhEP Handbooks [5,6]. The assumed 5% uncertainty is
consistent with the assigned uncertainty for the limited number of published β eff measurements in
ZPR/ZPPR assemblies and with calculations of those measured values. In fact, the experimenters
commonly used calculated βeff values when reporting the measurement results.
The uncertainty in βeff and the corresponding uncertainty in the Doppler reactivity worth when the
measured worth is converted from cents or inhours to pcm is 5%. For ZPPR-15, the uncertainty
in the mass of a Doppler sample is 0.15%. The 0.5 K uncertainty in thermocouple calibration is
equivalent to less than 0.5% uncertainty over the measurement temperature range. The uncertainty
in the composition of a sample is less than 0.1%. If all of these uncertainties are added in
quadrature, the resulting uncertainty in a Doppler worth is 5.03% when doing a comparison
between measured and calculated Doppler sample worths.
7.4.2.6 Total Uncertainty for the Doppler Sample Worth Measurement
In practice, uncertainty contributions related to the reproducibility of the Doppler sample position,
reproducibility of the autorod position, sample mass, sample composition and thermocouple
calibration discussed in Sections 7.4.2.1 through 7.4.2.4 are usually minor components of the total

 270

uncertainty compared to the contribution from the uncertainty in β eff. In a specific case the analyst
may have reason to believe that one of the uncertainties discussed in Sections 7.4.2.1 through
7.4.2.4 will make a significant contribution to the total uncertainty. In that case detailed analysis
of that uncertainty is warranted. Otherwise, it is unlikely that those uncertainties will make a
significant contribution to the total uncertainty, so any reasonable assumptions regarding those
uncertainties are adequate for determination of the total uncertainty.
Many of the uncertainty components for a Doppler sample worth measurement are likely to be
small although they should be included in the total uncertainty if they can be quantified. The
dominant component of the total Doppler sample worth uncertainty is likely to be the 5%
uncertainty in βeff discussed in Section 7.4.2.5. The other uncertainty that may be significant in
some cases is the uncertainty published by the experimenters.
The experimenters may state that the published uncertainty for the Doppler sample worth includes
the uncertainty in the temperature of Doppler samples as they did for ZPPR-15. The experimenters
were aware of the uncertainty in the temperature of the sample, so it is likely that this uncertainty
is included in the published uncertainty even if the source document does not make an explicit
statement in this regard. However, in the absence of an explicit statement regarding whether the
sample temperature uncertainty is included in the published uncertainty, the conservative approach
is to determine the effect of a 5 K sample temperature uncertainty and to include this value in the
total uncertainty.
The individual uncertainty components are independent and are added in quadrature to determine
the total uncertainty for the Doppler sample worth measurement.
7.4.3 As-Built Monte Carlo Models of Doppler Sample Worth Measurements
Creating an as-built Monte Carlo model of a Doppler sample worth measurement requires two
steps. First, the user constructs a base as-built Monte Carlo model of everything except the
Doppler sample, Doppler equipment and Doppler sample tray. This as-built Monte Carlo model
is constructed in the normal manner using any software and databases that are available to the user
for construction of an as-built Monte Carlo model of a ZPR/ZPPR assembly (see Section 7.1.5).
The Doppler sample, Doppler equipment and Doppler sample are not included in this base model
because the Doppler sample, Doppler equipment and Doppler sample tray are unique items that
are unlikely to be included in the software or databases used to construct the base model. The
resulting configuration will have an empty matrix tube at the location where the Doppler sample
is inserted.
In the second step, the Doppler sample, Doppler equipment and Doppler sample tray are added to
the empty matrix tube in the base model. For ZPR-9/29 models and ZPPR-15 models, this manual
process was used to add these items to the empty matrix tube in the as-built Monte Carlo model,
primarily because it is impractical to develop new software or to update existing software to
automate the infrequent task of modeling special experimental equipment, especially unique
experimental equipment. Assuming an MCNP input, the region where the Doppler equipment is
located is modified by adding the cells defining the Doppler sample and equipment to the empty
matrix tube. The surface cards and material cards required to define the added cells are inserted
in the appropriate locations in the input file. This report uses terms related to MCNP input, but
the same concept would apply to any other Monte Carlo code. Likewise, the same concept applies

 271

to any deterministic model, noting that cross section generation for the Doppler sample region is
expected to be rather complicated and would involve a similar manual approach.
The process of manually adding the Doppler sample and equipment to the base as-built Monte
Carlo model is straightforward. The most difficult part of the second step is finding enough
information to create a reasonable model of the Doppler sample and related items such as the
sample equipment. The ZPR/ZPPR staff published the measured Doppler worths and descriptions
of the samples, but they did not always publish detailed descriptions of the sample capsule, sample
equipment or sample tray. It may be necessary to use the available information and to make
reasonable estimates about missing information. For example, for the ZPR-9/29 model, some
dimensions were derived by assuming that Figure 7.4 was drawn approximately to scale,
measuring distances and dimensions on the figure with a ruler, and using known dimension
information to scale the distances and dimensions measured on Figure 7.4.
These two steps yield an as-built Monte Carlo model of the Doppler sample worth measurement.
If the assumed values are reasonable, the fact that they are assumed values will not have a
significant effect on calculated Doppler worths because any errors or uncertainties related to the
assumed values will be fully correlated between the heated and cold configurations and between
the configuration with the Doppler sample present and the configuration without the Doppler
sample present.
7.4.4 Calculations of Doppler Sample Worth
The measured Doppler worth of the sample is typically in the 0.01 pcm – 0.05 pcm range. As
stated earlier, experience is that one billion (10 9) histories are required in direct Monte Carlo
eigenvalue calculations of keff to obtain a statistical uncertainty of 1 – 2 pcm. Consequently,
computing the measured Doppler worths of the samples by direct Monte Carlo is not feasible today
with existing computing resources (at least 100 times more histories would be required). It is
possible that some of the recent perturbation theory based techniques in Monte Carlo codes, or
better computing resources, would yield statistically meaningful Doppler sample worths. To date,
the Doppler sample worths have only been computed using deterministic models.
7.5 Axial Expansion Worth Measurements
It was not possible to perform a whole core axial expansion worth measurement on the ZPR/ZPPR
machines because it was not permissible to operate at a high temperature nor to measure such
temperatures on these machines. Neither the cooling system, plates, or facility were designed for
high power level applications, noting that higher burnup on the plates would lead to radiological
problems related to manual loading and unloading of drawers and matrix tubes.
There were two additional practical limitations on any attempt to perform a true axial expansion
worth measurement on the ZPR/ZPPR machines. First, there was no practical way to measure
axial expansion in many or all drawers in an assembly. Even if there were no other constraints,
the backplate and control rods might interfere with any such measurement. Second, there was no
practical way to measure or infer an accurate temperature distribution throughout the reactor.
The plates and drawers were rigid, and the ZPR/ZPPR machines were constrained to operating at
relatively low power. Those facts limited options for estimating the worth of axial expansion. One
approach was to measure the axial worth profiles of samples of reactor materials such as fuel,

 272

sodium, cladding and structural materials. The measured worth profiles were used to estimate the
effects of axial expansion. This is another application of the small sample measurement technique
discussed in Section 7.7. The uncertainties that apply to measurement of axial worth profiles of
samples are discussed in Section 7.7.
In principle, similar to the Dopper sample measurements, the experimenters could design special
equipment to a) heat materials in one or more matrix tubes, b) measure the resulting axial
expansion of those materials and c) measure the associated reactivity change. Existing
documentation does not indicate if this approach was ever used in any ZPR/ZPPR assembly, but
the technique would be difficult for several reasons. First, it would be necessary to measure the
axial expansion in the test materials accurately. Second, it would be necessary to measure the
temperature distribution in the test materials accurately. Third, it might be necessary to separate
the reactivity component due to axial expansion from the Doppler reactivity contribution.
Another option was to simulate axial expansion by mechanically introducing gaps between groups
of plates. Axial expansion worth measurements performed using this technique in ZPPR-15 are
described in the next section. Axial expansion worth measurements may have been performed in
other ZPR/ZPPR assemblies, but such measurements were likely to be at least broadly similar to
the ZPPR-15 axial expansion measurements because the constraints related to low power and rigid
plates of fixed sizes apply to all four ZPR/ZPPR machines. In any case, a special mechanism
would be required to simulate the effects of axial expansion in any ZPR/ZPPR assembly.
7.5.1 ZPPR-15 Axial Expansion Measurements
Axial expansion worth experiments were performed in ZPPR-15A loading 61 (ZPPR-15A L061),
ZPPR-15B loading 117 (ZPPR-15B L117) and ZPPR-15D loading 206 (ZPPR-15D L206). A
special segmented drawer was constructed for each measurement. The back of the segmented
drawer was connected to a spring-loaded cable that could be pulled away from the front of the
drawer and front of the matrix tube to introduce gaps between drawer segments. Releasing the
cable eliminated the gaps between drawer segments, so the segmented drawer was essentially
identical to any other core drawer when the cable was released. The small gaps introduced between
drawer segments simulated core axial expansion as closely as possible given the constraint that the
core materials consisted of rigid plates of fixed sizes.
The segmented drawer design allowed experimenters to measure the reactivity worths of the
reference and expanded configurations in one reactor run. Performing all required measurements
in one reactor run minimized experimental uncertainty by minimizing reproducibility uncertainty,
eliminating any plate shifting effects that might result from drawer and plate handling, and
ensuring that the only difference between the reference state and the expansion configuration was
the introduction of small gaps between segments in the special drawer.
7.5.1.1 ZPPR-15A L061 Axial Expansion Experiment
The first axial expansion experiment was performed in ZPPR-15A L061. A standard ZPPR-15
core drawer contained 18 inches of core plates, 13 inches of axial blanket plates and 5 inches of
axial reflector plates. The segmented drawer consisted of four segments with the first three
segments ~6 inches in length and the last 18 inches. The three 6 inch segments contained core
plates while the 18 inch segment contained the axial blanket and axial reflector plates. The lengths

 273

listed here are approximate because they ignore the 0.030 inch stainless steel plates attached to the
front and back of each drawer segment to prevent plates from moving axially within the segments.
Gaps of 0.25 inches were introduced between segments at the ~6, 12 and 18 inch segment
positions.
After analysis of the ZPPR-15A axial expansion experiment was completed, the ZPPR staff
concluded that the axial expansion experiment in ZPPR-15A was not representative of axial
expansion in an LMFR for two reasons. First, the drawer used for the ZPPR-15A axial expansion
experiment had only one column of Pu-U-Mo fuel plates and, consequently, had an average
composition with much lower fissile content and reactivity worth than one would find in a typical
LMFR. Second, the gap at 18 inches was a gap between the core and the axial blanket. The ZPPR
staff concluded that this core-axial blanket gap was neither realistic nor representative of an actual
LMFR case.
These two issues illustrate two of the problems associated with providing a realistic simulation of
axial expansion by introducing small gaps between drawer segments. A realistic axial expansion
measurement requires a drawer composition that is representative of the LMFR being simulated
and an expansion configuration that is representative of the real expansion geometry.
7.5.1.2 ZPPR-15B L117 Axial Expansion Experiment
Analysis of the ZPPR-15A axial expansion experiment caused the ZPPR staff to modify the
experimental technique for subsequent axial expansion experiments in ZPPR-15B L117 and
ZPPR-15D L206 to a) eliminate the unrealistic gap at the core-axial blanket interface and b) use
an expansion drawer loading with two fuel columns. Using an expansion drawer with two fuel
columns resulted in an average drawer composition that was more representative of a typical
LMFR fuel assembly.
With the exception of the segmented expansion drawer, all drawer masters used in ZPPR-15B
L117 and ZPPR-15D L206 were standard drawers for which descriptions were available in the
ZPPR-15 drawer master library. The axial expansion drawers, 15-1-207 and 15-1-879, were not
available in the ZPPR-15 drawer master library. ZPPR reports and the collected notes of R. W.
Schaefer, a former ZPPR staff analyst, were reviewed to determine how the segmented expansion
drawers were constructed. Those sources were sufficient to allow modeling of the expansion
drawers for the ZPPR-15B and ZPPR-15D axial expansion experiments. The limited information
available regarding the axial expansion drawers illustrates the difficulty the user may encounter
in creating models of less common measurements.
The segmented drawer for ZPPR-15B L117 was divided into three parts. The first part consisted
the first 6 inches of the core (0 – 6 inches), and the second part consisted of the second 6 inches of
the core (6 – 12 inches). The third segment consisted of the remainder of core (12 – 18 inches)
plus the axial blanket (18 – 31 inches) and axial reflector (31 – 36 inches). All plates used for the
core in the segmented drawer were 6 inches long. The plates used for the axial blanket and axial
reflector in the segmented drawer were identical in size and type to the plates used for the axial
blanket and reflector in the remainder of the core. All plates in the segmented drawer were part of
the standard ZPPR plate inventory.

 274

A 0.030 inch steel plate was fixed to the open end(s) of each segment to prevent axial motion of
the plates in that segment. No explicit details regarding construction of the segmented drawer
have been found, but it is likely that a normal 36 inch drawer was cut into segments of the required
length to make the segmented drawer. That would have been the easiest way to make a segmented
drawer and would have provided the best match for the other drawers in the core. The drawer
segments were connected by mylar tape.
The reported axial expansion consisted of introducing 6.4 mm gaps in the core at 152 mm and 305
mm from the front of the segmented drawer according to the ZPPR report. Note that these reported
values are rounded metric values and that the gaps were introduced 6 inches and 12 inches from
the front of the drawer, and it is likely that the actual gap width was 0.25 inches or 6.35 mm.
7.5.1.3 ZPPR-15D L206 Axial Expansion Experiments
The axial expansion drawer was divided into nine segments for the ZPPR-15D L206 axial
expansion measurements. The nominal segment length was 2 inches for each of the first eight core
segments. The remaining 2 inches of the core, the 13 inch axial blanket and the 5 inch axial
reflector made up the ninth segment which had a total length of 20 inches. There was a 0.020 inch
steel plate fixed to the open end(s) of each segment to prevent axial motion of the plates in that
segment. Figure 7.8 shows the segmented drawers used in the ZPPR-15D axial expansion

All plates used for the core in the segmented drawer were 2 inches long. Plates used for the axial
blanket and axial reflector in the segmented drawer were identical in size and type to the plates
used for the axial blanket and reflector in the remainder of the core.

 Figure 7.8. Axial Expansion Configurations for ZPPR-15D Measurements.
The fuel used in ZPPR-15B consisted entirely of Pu-U-Mo plates. There were 6 inch Pu-U-Mo
plates and 6 inch sodium plates in the ZPPR plate inventory. In ZPPR-15D, ~10% of the core
drawers contained Pu-U-Mo plates. The remainder of the ZPPR-15D core drawers contained HEU
plates. The fuel in the ZPPR-15D expansion drawer consisted of HEU plates.
When ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were shut down, the HEU plates in their inventory were shipped to ZPPR.
Those plates consisted of HEU metal coated with Kel-F, a paint-like coating used to inhibit
corrosion and material loss during handling. The ZPPR staff removed the Kel-F coating and sealed
these HEU plates in stainless steel cans with nominal lengths of 4 – 8 inches. Those canned HEU
plates were much too long to fit into the 2 inch long segments in the expansion drawer.

 275

Consequently, eighteen 1/16x2x2 inch HEU metal plates were removed from the cans, cleaned
and coated with Kel-F for use in the axial expansion experiments. Eighteen HEU plates were
required to load nine drawer segments with two HEU fuel columns per segment.
The total width of the core plates in each segment was slightly less than the nominal 2 inch interior
width of the drawer segment. The existence of a small amount of free space would allow plate
motion in the X-direction (lateral direction) when the expansion drawer was loaded into the matrix
and when the segments were moved during the experiment. Any plate shifting in the X-direction
would introduce an additional experimental uncertainty. To eliminate free space and plate motion
in the expansion drawer, the experimenters placed small, curved shims on each side of the core
plates in the segments. The curved shims acted like springs to make any plate motion in the X-
direction negligible.
In ZPPR-15D L206, six expansion measurements were made in five reactor runs. Table 7.13
shows the measurement configurations for the ZPPR-15D measurements. In the measurements
with two gaps, approximately 2 grams of mylar tape held the segments together. The gap spacing
was determined by small staples that connected adjacent segments for the cases with no mylar
tape.

Note that the six measurements in Table 7.13 do not represent six separate cases for modeling
purposes. The ZPPR staff believed that there was an unidentified problem with the measurement
in data file 54 (reactor run 352) and that the measurement in data file 54 should be rejected.
Data files 50 and 51 for reactor run 350 were two measurements of the same quantity performed
in tandem during the same reactor run.
The file 56 measurement is a repetition of the file 47 measurement to determine the random error
associated with reproducibility.
Experimenters varied the number and size of the gaps in ZPPR-15D L206 to determine whether
discrete gaps of the sizes used in the ZPPR-15 experiments were an adequate approximation of the

 276

uniform expansion that would actually occur in an LMFR. The ZPPR staff concluded that the
ZPPR-15B and ZPPR-15D axial expansion experiments were an adequate representation of axial
expansion in an LMFR.
7.5.2 ZPPR-15 Axial Expansion Measurement Uncertainties
The published uncertainty for the axial expansion reactivity in ZPPR-15B L117 was 0.4% of the
measured axial expansion worth. The largest published uncertainty for the axial expansion
measurements in ZPPR-15D L206 is 1.1% of the measured axial expansion worth.
The uncertainties discussed in the preceding paragraph are primarily statistical uncertainties in the
measurements, but they are not the total uncertainties for the measured axial expansion worths.
Almost all uncertainties that are applicable to analysis of the reference critical configurations (see
Section 7.1) are fully correlated between the reference critical configurations and expansion
configurations in ZPPR-15B L117 and ZPPR-15D L206 due to the experimental procedure used
for the axial expansion measurements. Consequently, those uncertainties drop out of the reactivity
difference measurements. However, there are a few uncertainties that remain to be considered.
Conversion from the natural measurement units, cents, to the calculation units of Δk/k 1k2 or pcm
requires knowledge of the delayed neutron kinetics parameters, particularly β eff. However, βeff is
uncertain, and that uncertainty should be included in the total uncertainty for the axial expansion
worth expressed in %Δk/k or pcm. The estimated uncertainty in β eff is 5%, which is the value
assumed for ICSBEP/IRPhEP benchmarks of ZPR and ZPPR assemblies [5,6] as discussed in
Sections 7.1 and 7.2. The 5% uncertainty in βeff applies to all measured axial expansion worths
and is the dominant uncertainty for these measurements.
Reactor run 353 (data file 56) was a reconstruction of reactor run 349 (data file 47) to determine
the random error associated with reproducibility of the experimental configurations. If it were
possible to reproduce the earlier configuration and measurement conditions exactly, the measured
worths in data file 56 and data file 47 would be identical within the statistical uncertainty of the
measurements. In fact, there is ~3% difference between the measured values in reactor run 349
and reactor run 353. This 3% difference is much larger than the statistical uncertainty in the
measurements. Consequently, the reproducibility uncertainty for the ZPPR-15 axial expansion
experiments is assumed to be 3%. Although the reproducibility uncertainty was measured for only
one configuration, this uncertainty should apply to all ZPPR-15 axial expansion measurements.
For common measurements of large or relatively large reactivity worths such as control rod worth
measurements and most sodium void worth measurements, reproducibility uncertainty is likely to
be small or negligible. For uncommon measurements of very small reactivities involving complex
equipment such as the axial expansion equipment, reproducibility uncertainty can contribute
significantly to the total uncertainty.
The exact amount of mylar tape used in the experiments is not listed although it was estimated to
be ~2 grams. The ZPPR staff computed the expansion worth for data file 52 with and without
mylar tape present in their model. The expansion worth was only 0.5% larger with the mylar tape
present. The total worth of the mylar tape is much less than the 5% uncertainty in β eff or the 3%
reproducibility uncertainty, so the mylar tape will be neglected and the associated uncertainty will
be 0.5% for any configuration where mylar tape was present.

 277

The statistical uncertainty, the βeff uncertainty, the reproducibility uncertainty and the mylar tape
uncertainty are independent, so they are added in quadrature to give the total uncertainty for the
axial expansion measurements. Table 7.14 shows the individual uncertainty components and the
total uncertainties for the axial expansion measurements in ZPPR-15B and ZPPR-15D. The 5%
βeff uncertainty and the 3% reproducibility uncertainty are the dominant contributors to the total
axial expansion worth uncertainty when the individual uncertainties are added in quadrature.

 Table 7.14. Uncertainty Components and Total Uncertainties For ZPPR-15 Axial

                           βeff, %                  5            5       5     5     5      5

                      Mylar Tape, %                0.5           0      0.5   0.5   0.5     0
                          Total, %                5.87         5.83 5.96 5.88 5.90 5.85
 a) All uncertainties are percent of the measured value.
The mylar tape uncertainty is specific to the ZPPR-15 measurement technique and equipment. The
uncertainties that apply to similar axial expansion measurements in other assemblies may depend
on how the measurements were performed, but there will be some uncertainties such as statistical
uncertainty that are common to axial expansion measurements using techniques similar to the
technique used in ZPPR-15.
The reactivity is measured in cents or possibly in inhours for some older experiments. The units
for calculations are Δk/k1k2 or pcm. Conversion between the natural measurement units and the
calculation units requires βeff. Measuring βeff was difficult, so the ZPR/ZPPR staff rarely measured
βeff. In general, the ZPR/ZPPR staff calculated the βeff required for conversion of experimental
measurements. The uncertainty in βeff that is assumed in ICSBEP and IRPhEP benchmarks of
ZPR/ZPPR experiments is 5%. This uncertainty seems reasonable, and there does not seem to be
any valid reason for assuming a lower value. In the limited number of measurements of β eff for
ZPR/ZPPR assemblies that have been reviewed, the smallest experimental uncertainty was ~3%,
and that value did not necessarily include all of the applicable uncertainties. The 5% uncertainty
in βeff will apply to any reactivity measured in cents or inhours.
There is a reproducibility uncertainty associated with any experimental measurement. If an
experiment is performed, the experimental configuration is disassembled, the experimental
configuration is reassembled, and the experiment is repeated, the second measurement will not
agree with the first measurement to an arbitrary degree of precision. There will be small
differences in positions, temperatures and other parameters that will result in a small difference
between the first measured value and the second measured value. The ZPR/ZPPR experimenters

 278

determined the reproducibility uncertainty in some cases, so that value is applicable to the
uncertainty analysis. In other cases, it was not practical or possible to determine the reproducibility
uncertainty due to cost, schedule and other considerations. If no reproducibility uncertainty was
determined by the ZPR/ZPPR staff, any assumed reproducibility uncertainty must be based on
engineering judgement.
7.5.3 Calculation of Axial Expansion Worth
The measured axial expansion worths in ZPPR-15 were in the range from 0 pcm to -1 pcm. It is
probable that any similar measurements in other ZPR/ZPPR assemblies would be of similar
magnitude. The magnitude of the measured axial expansion worth is small because the
measurement was limited to one experimental drawer. It is not clear why there was only one axial
expansion drawer. Perhaps there were operational constraints that limited the number of axial
expansion drawers. Perhaps the measurements obtained were adequate for their intended
purposes. In any case, the measurements were performed many years ago, so it seems unlikely
that additional information will be found today.
In principle, the worth of axial expansion can be computed by Monte Carlo as the difference
between keff for the reference configuration prior to expansion and keff for the configuration after
axial expansion. As stated earlier, experience is that one billion (10 9) histories are required in
direct Monte Carlo eigenvalue calculations of keff to obtain a statistical uncertainty of 1 – 2 pcm.
Consequently, computing the measured axial expansion worths by direct Monte Carlo is not
feasible today with existing computating resources (at least 100 times more histories would be
required). It is possible that some of the recent perturbation theory based techniques in Monte
Carlo codes, or better computing resources, would yield statistically meaningful axial expansion
worths. To date, the axial expansion worths have only been computed using deterministic models
whether that by by the original ZPPR analysts or more recent efforts.
7.6 Radial Bowing Worth Measurements
Performing a true radial bowing worth measurement on the ZPR/ZPPR machines would have been
impossible. In addition to the requirement to operate at low power that was discussed in Section
7.5, a separate problem relates to the plate inventories. All of the plates were small and rigid. The
lengths of Pu-U-Mo plates and clad HEU plates were 4 – 8 inches. The lengths of Pu-Al plates
and bare HEU plates were 1 – 3 inches. The lengths of diluent plates such as sodium plates and
stainless steel plates were 2– 8 inches. There were no long plates for which the effects of bowing
could be measured. In addition, the drawers and matrix tubes were rigid.
Radial and axial worth profiles were routinely measured in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies for samples of
reactor materials (see Section 7.7), so in principle the measured radial worth profiles could be used
to estimate the effects of radial bowing. In practice, interpretation of a radial worth profile is more
complex than interpretation of an axial worth profile. The plate loading in a core drawer has a
very high degree of heterogeneity, and this heterogeneity is reflected in the intra-drawer flux
distribution in the X-direction.
A radial sample worth traverse typically started with the sample in the approximate center of the
core. The sample was moved in steps from the center of the core to the outer edge of the core,
radial blanket or radial reflector in the X-direction. Consequently, the sample passed by or through

 279

many drawers during the traverse. At each step, a sample worth was measured. The measured
sample worth at each step depends on exactly where the sample was relative to the various types
of plates in the drawer. In principle, the sample would be at or near the same types of plates at
each step. For example, the sample might be next to a column of fuel plates at each step.
Positioning the sample at the same relative position within a drawer at each measurement step
reduced the effects of the non-uniform intra-drawer flux resulting from the heterogeneous nature
of the plate columns in the drawer.
The presence of single column fuel (SCF) drawers and double column fuel (DCF) drawers in the
core would complicate measurement of radial sample worth profiles because there would be
differences in the distribution of fuel and non-fuel plate columns between SCF drawers and DCF
drawers.
In an axial sample worth traverse, the sample was located in one specific drawer and was moved
axially from the front of the drawer to the back of the drawer in steps. A sample worth was
measured at each axial step. Because the sample was moved axially within one drawer, it was
always next to the same plate columns in the core. The fact that the sample occupied the same
position in the X-direction during the axial traverse reduced the effect of the intra-drawer flux
structure.
In addition to sample worth traverses, there were at least two techniques for measuring the effect
of radial bowing. In the first technique, the plates in a group of drawers were rearranged to
simulate radial bowing. In the second technique, a special oscillator mechanism was used to move
a group of plates in a single drawer. The bowing oscillator could only move the plates a small
distance because the range of motion was limited to the small distance between the tops of the
plates in the drawer before motion and the inner surface of the matrix tube containing the drawer
and oscillator mechanism. Both techniques were used in ZPPR-17A. The ZPPR-17A radial
bowing measurements are described here as examples of these two techniques.
The first bowing measurement in ZPPR-17A was based upon rearranging the plates in 96 core
drawers near the outer boundary of the core to move fuel and structural material outward toward
the core-radial blanket interface. The second ZPPR-17A bowing measurement used a new
oscillator device to lift the core plates in one drawer a small distance toward the core-radial blanket
interface.
7.6.1 Plate Rearrangement Measurement of Bowing Worth in ZPPR-17A
This experiment simulated bowing of core fuel assemblies. The simulation included outward
radial motion of the duct and its contents, which resulted in a corresponding inward movement of
the inter-subassembly sodium due to the change in the gap width between subassemblies.
Bowing in ZPPR-17A was simulated by rearranging the columns of plates in 4 x 6 arrays of
drawers on the left and right sides of each matrix half near the core-radial blanket interface. This
rearrangement moved fuel and structural material outward and moved sodium inward to occupy
the vacated space.
Plate rearrangment may have been used to simulate radial bowing in various ZPR/ZPPR
assemblies. Rearranging plates to simulate radial bowing was a simple experimental technique
that did not require any special equipment or technique. The advantage of plate rearrangement

 280

was its simplicity, but there are two potential disadvantages associated with plate rearrangement.
The first disadvantage is that the plate motions in the ZPR/ZPPR experiment may be significantly
larger than the motions of materials during realistic radial bowing in the reactor being simulated.
The second disadvantage is that the measured bowing worth may be significantly larger than a
realistic radial bowing worth in the reactor being simulated.
7.6.1.1 Plate Rearrangement Configurations
The plate rearrangement experiment was performed in ZPPR-17A loadings 71 – 74. Loading 71
was the initial subcritical reference configuration. The plate rearrangements were performed in
loadings 72 and 73. Loading 74 was a reconstruction of loading 71. The reactivity difference
between loadings 71 and 74 is a measure of the reproducibility uncertainty for the experiment. In
this context, reproducibility uncertainty results from several factors.
The surfaces of the two matrix halves are neither perfectly flat nor perfectly parallel, so there were
small gaps at some points on the surfaces of the matrix interface, even at the nominal full closure
position. It was not possible to reproduce this interface gap between matrix halves to an arbitrary
degree of precision. Likewise, it was not possible to reproduce control rod positions or reactor
temperature distribution to an arbitrary degree of precision. The drawer handling and motion
required to change drawer contents and matrix loadings could introduce small lateral or axial shifts
in plate positions within the affected drawers. The combination of the uncertainty in the interface
gap, uncertainties in control rod positions, uncertainty in reactor temperature distribution and the
effects of plate shifting combine to form a reproducibility uncertainty for the experiment.
Figure 7.9 through Figure 7.14 show the matrix maps for half 1 and half 2, respectively, of ZPPR-
17A loadings 72, 73 and 74. Loadings 71 and 74 have identical matrix maps, so separate maps
were not created for loading 71. The plates were rearranged in 4 x 6 arrays of core drawers on the
left and right sides of the core in both matrix halves to simulate bowing, so plates were rearranged
in a total of 96 drawers. The drawers where plates were rearranged are clearly visible in Figure
7.9 through Figure 7.12 because of the coloring in the figures.

 Figure 7.14. ZPPR-17A Loading 74 – Half 2.
ZPPR-17A was divided into an inner core zone and an outer core zone. In the outer core zone, the
Pu-U-Mo fuel extended over the full height of the core, 20 inches in each matrix half. In the inner
core zone, there was a 6 inch internal blanket region followed by 14 inches of fuel plates in each
matrix half.
The ZPPR-17A core contained single column fuel (SCF) drawers and double column fuel (DCF)
drawers. Each SCF drawer contained a single fuel column in the center of the drawer, and each
DCF drawer contained two fuel columns separated by a 0.5 inch column of sodium carbonate
plates. Figure 7.15 shows the 17-0-107 drawer master, the most common SCF drawer master in
the inner core zone. Figure 7.16 shows the 17-0-205 drawer master, the most common DCF drawer
master in the inner core zone. The central axial blanket zone of depleted uranium plates (UD) is

 287

clearly visible on the left hand side in Figure 7.15 and Figure 7.16. The Pu-U-Mo fuel plates are
the “PUMN” columns in all of the drawer master figures.

 Figure 7.15. Drawer Master 17-0-107 – Inner Core SCF Drawer.

 288

 Figure 7.16. Drawer Master 17-0-205 – Inner Core DCF Drawer.
In the reference SCF configuration in loadings 71 and 74, there was a 0.125 inch iron oxide (FEO)
column, a 0.5 inch sodium (NA) column and a 0.25 inch depleted U 3O8 (UOD8) column on either
side of the fuel (PUMN) column in the SCF drawer; the contents of the SCF drawer were
symmetric about the central fuel column.
Each DCF drawer contained two fuel columns separated by a 0.5 inch column of sodium carbonate
plates. In the reference DCF configuration in loadings 71 and 74, there was a 0.25 inch fuel
(PUMN) column, a 0.25 inch sodium (NA) column and a 0.25 inch depleted U 3O8 (UOD8) column
on either side of the central 0.5 inch sodium carbonate (NACO) column; the contents of the DCF
drawer were symmetric about the central sodium carbonate column.
Figure 7.17 shows drawer master 17-0-103, a reference SCF drawer in the outer core zone in
loadings 71 and 74. Figure 7.18 shows drawer master 17-0-203, a reference DCF drawer in the
outer core zone in loadings 71 and 74.

 Figure 7.18. Drawer Master 17-0-203 – Outer Core DCF Reference Configuration.
