The standard SCF drawers in the outer core only contained 0.5 inch sodium plates (Figure 7.17),
so it was necessary to change the drawer configurations in the plate shifting zones as a preliminary
step prior to the plate shifting experiment. In loading 72, each 0.5 inch sodium plate column in
the outer core region of the SCF drawers in the plate shifting zone was replaced by two 0.25 inch
sodium plate columns, and the 0.25 inch depleted U3O8 column and the sodium columns were
rearranged to place the depleted U3O8 column between the two 0.25 inch sodium columns. This
change placed 0.25 inch sodium columns along the left and right edges of the drawer.
The standard DCF drawers in the outer core (Figure 7.18) where the plate-shifting zone was located
were also rearranged in loading 72. The rearrangement for the DCF drawers consisted of
interchanging the columns of 0.25 inch sodium plates and 0.25 inch depleted U 3O8 in the core
region to place 0.25 inch sodium columns along the left and right edges of the drawer. These
rearrangements for the SCF and DCF drawers in the plate-shifting zone in loading 72 produced
the initial configuration for the plate-shifting experiment in loading 73.
Loading 73 was the simulated bowing configuration. In loading 73, the 0.25 inch sodium column
closest to the radial blanket in each drawer in the plate shifting zone was moved inward to the
inner side of the drawer, i.e., the side closest to the core center, and all other plate columns in the
drawer were shifted 0.25 inch outward toward the radial blanket to simulate bowing. Figure 7.19
shows drawer master 17-0-144, a rearranged SCF drawer master in loading 73. Figure 7.20 shows
drawer master 17-0-222, a rearranged DCF drawer master in loading 73.

 Figure 7.19. Drawer Master 17-0-144 – SCF Rearranged Configuration – Loading 73.

 291

 Figure 7.20. Drawer Master 17-0-222 – DCF Rearranged Configuration – Loading 73.
The plate rearrangement reactivity worth was measured with the modified source multiplication
(MSM) technique discussed in Section 7.2. Loading 71 provided the subcritical reference for the
plate rearrangement worth measurement. The initial measurements required to calibrate the MSM
technique were obtained in loading 71. Loading 72 was built by modifying 96 drawers near the
core-radial blanket boundary, and a rod drop was performed to provide the data required by the
MSM technique for loading 72. Then the 96 drawers inserted in loading 72 were modified by
rearranging the plate columns to create loading 73. A rod drop was performed to provide the data
required by the MSM technique for loading 73. Finally, the initial loading 71 configuration was
reconstructed in loading 74 to measure the reproducibility uncertainty for the plate rearrangement
experiment.
When ZPPR-17A was built, the standard practice at ZPPR was to use 64 detectors for the MSM
technique, so there would be 64 separate, but correlated, measurements. Each detector for MSM
measurements in ZPPR-17A occupied a 1/2x2x6 inch space at the front of the core, blanket or
reflector drawer. The detector cables extended from the back of the drawer, so it was not possible
to place a back drawer behind a detector drawer.
7.6.1.2 Plate Rearrangement Reactivity Uncertainty
The reported uncertainty for the subcritical source multiplication analysis was 1.2%, and the
reported configuration reproducibility uncertainty for the plate rearrangement experiment was
2.8%. These two uncertainty components are independent, so the total experimental uncertainty

 292

is obtained by adding the 1.2% and 2.8% uncertainties in quadrature to get the total experimental
uncertainty of 3.1%.
Any uncertainties related to the compositions or dimensions of the drawers and matrix tubes are
fully correlated for loadings 71 – 74 because the drawers and matrix tubes were present for all
loadings in this series. The only plate changes between loadings 71 and 72 relate to replacement
of 1.27 cm sodium plates by 0.635 cm sodium plates in the SCF drawers in the rearrangement zone
in loading 72. Consequently, all uncertainties related to dimensions or compositions of matrix
tubes, drawers and plates in loadings 71 – 73 cancel except for those related to the sodium plate
replacement in the rearrangement zone. Analyses of many reference critical configurations of ZPR
and ZPPR assemblies have shown that the reactivity effects of sodium plate uncertainties are small
or negligible when all of the sodium plates in the entire assembly are included in the analysis. The
effects of uncertainties for sodium plates in the SCF drawers in the 96-drawer rearrangement zone
in ZPPR-17A are negligible compared to the other uncertainties considered here.
For the actual rearrangement measurement in loadings 72 and 73, all plate uncertainties are fully
correlated because the same plates were present in loadings 72 and 73.
The plate rearrangement technique is simple and does not require any special equipment. The
applicable uncertainties for the plate rearrangement technique depend on how the reactivity worth
was measured. In most cases, the uncertainties in the dimensions and compositions of matrix
tubes, drawers and plates will be fully correlated between the reference configuration and the
rearranged configuration.
A measurement uncertainty is associated with any ZPR/ZPPR measurement. The actual reactivity
may be measured with the modified source multiplication technique, calibrated control rods or
some other method. The specific uncertainty for the reactivity measurement method will depend
on the method.
Reproducibility uncertainty applies to most measurements.
The natural measurement unit of reactivity is cents (or inhours for some early measurements), but
the natural reactivity unit for calculations is pcm. Conversion between cents and pcm requires β eff.
The experimental uncertainty is 3.1%, but βeff is also uncertain. The standard assumed uncertainty
in βeff for ICSBEP/IRPhEP benchmarks of ZPR/ZPPR experiments is 5% [5,6] as discussed in
Sections 7.1 and 7.2. This uncertainty in βeff and the experimental uncertainty apply to any plate
rearrangement measurement. If the 3.1% experimental uncertainty and 5% uncertainty in β eff are
added in quadrature, the resulting total uncertainty for the measured plate rearrangement worth
expressed in pcm is 5.9%.
The worth of the ZPPR-17A plate rearrangement experiment was approximately -20 pcm. This
value can be calculated by direct Monte Carlo calculations.
The discussion in Section 7.6.1 focused on the plate rearrangement experiment in ZPPR-17A, but
a plate rearrangement experiment in another ZPR/ZPPR assembly was probably performed in a
similar manner. In general, the types of uncertainties discussed here for the ZPPR-17A plate
rearrangement experiment are applicable to any similar plate rearrangement experiment in another
ZPR/ZPPR assembly although specific numbers such as the measured reactivity worth and the
experimental uncertainty will be specific to the assembly and configuration of interest.

 293

7.6.2 Bowing Oscillator Measurement of Bowing Worth in ZPPR-17A
An oscillator mechanism provided an alternative to plate rearrangement as a means to measure the
reactivity worth of bowing. An oscillator mechanism moved a group of plates in a drawer to
simulate radial bowing. An oscillator mechanism was used to measure the worth of radial bowing
in ZPPR-15, but the bowing measurement in ZPPR-15 seems to have been unsatisfactory because
it was never published.
The ZPPR-15 oscillator mechanism tilted one end of a group of plates in the oscillator drawer to
simulate bowing. A new bowing oscillator mechanism was developed for ZPPR-17A. This
mechanism simulated bowing in a special drawer divided into two parts. The oscillator mechanism
raised the core plates and the front part of the special drawer vertically within the matrix tube
containing the bowing oscillator. The distance available for vertical motion was limited to the
small space between the tops of the plates and the inner surface of the top of the matrix tube.
For clarification purposes, the convention for ZPPR is that the axial direction is along the axis of
the drawer and matrix tube. Consider a ¼ x 2 x 8 inch PUMD Pu-U-Mo plate in Figure 7.21
below. The 8 inch length of the plate is oriented along the Z-axis which runs from left to right in
Figure 7.21. The ¼ inch thickness of the plate is oriented along the X-axis which runs from top to
bottom in Figure 7.21. The 2 inch height of the plate is oriented along the Y-axis which is normal
to the surface in Figure 7.21. The bowing oscillator raised the core plates and the front part of the
special drawer a small distance along the Y-axis, i.e., toward the top of the matrix tube containing
the bowing oscillator.
7.6.2.1 Bowing Oscillator Configuration in ZPPR-17A
The bowing oscillator measurement was made in loading 69 and was repeated in loading 75 to
measure the reproducibility uncertainty.
The bowing oscillator was drawer master 17-0-841 which was located at row 26, column 49 of
matrix half 1 (ZPPR shorthand notation 126-49). The bowing oscillator was located near the peak
of the radial core worth gradient at a position corresponding to the outermost fuel assembly
adjacent to the radial blanket.
There were actually four oscillator mechanisms in half 1 of ZPPR-17A loading 75. In addition to
the bowing oscillator located in 126-49, an axial expansion oscillator was installed in 166-55, a
plate column oscillator was installed in 148-31, and another plate column oscillator was installed
in 148-68.
Figure 7.21 shows drawer master 17-0-841 for the bowing oscillator. The front 21 inches or 53.34
cm of the bowing oscillator was the section that moved vertically in the matrix tube. This section
was made from a standard drawer that was cut to 53.34 cm length. The standard 0.031 inch-thick
drawer bottom was replaced with a 0.010 inch-thick bottom. The reason for the replacement is
not listed in available documents, but the most likely explanation is that the reduced bottom
thickness creates an additional 0.021 inches of space for the vertical motion of the bowing device.
The clearance between the tops of the plates in the drawer and the top of the matrix tube was small,
so reducing the thickness of the drawer bottom is an obvious way to gain more space for vertical
motion of the oscillator. In the experiment, the front portion of the oscillator was reported to have

 294

been raised 0.133 cm or 0.0524 inches, so the 0.021 inch gained by reducing the drawer bottom
thickness represents 40% of the total vertical motion of the oscillator.

 Figure 7.21. Drawer Master 17-0-841 – Bowing Oscillator.
The nominal length of the core plates in the front part of the bowing oscillator was 19 inches.
There were several gaps in the front section of the oscillator to accommodate structures related to
the oscillator. The drawer master shows a 0.46 cm gap at the front of the plates (B in Figure 7.21)
that contained approximately 8 g of stainless steel and 1.7 g of plastic from the potentiometer.
There was a 0.41 cm axial gap between the plate boundaries at 5 inches, 10 inches and 15 inches
(nominal positions) in the front part of the bowing oscillator (C in Figure 7.21). Each of these
gaps contained about 4 g of low carbon steel in the form of screws.
The first 2.54 cm (axially) of the 0.635 cm-wide depleted U 3O8 column on the right side of the
core region in the bowing oscillator (VOID in bottom left corner of Figure 7.21) was absent
because some of this space was occupied by the front potentiometer. The resulting gap (0.25 x 2
x 1 inch) was filled with approximately 1 g of crushed aluminum foil to prevent shifting of adjacent
plates.

 295

The gap at the back of the front section of the oscillator (D in Figure 7.21) had a length of ~1.34
inches or 3.4036 cm (1.875 x 2 x 1.34 inches). This gap contained approximately 36 g of
aluminum, 9 g of stainless steel, 40 g of low carbon steel and 5 g of plastic.
The depleted U3O8 column on the left side of the core region in the front part of the oscillator
(upper side of Figure 7.21) was 0.125 inches thick. This allowed a 0.125 inch gap on the left side
of the core region that accommodated cables and a clamping bar to restrain the motion of the plates
in the core region (A in Figure 7.21). This gap extended over the entire length of the front section
(0.125 x 2 x 21 in.). This gap contained approximately 477 g of stainless steel, 3 g of copper wire
and 2 g of Teflon.
The figure for drawer master 17-0-841 and the available reports do not provide any additional
information regarding the geometry or composition of the front portion of the bowing oscillator
drawer or of the oscillator components. The compositions of the front plate, bottom and sides of
the modified drawer were assumed to be identical to the compositions of the corresponding
components of standard drawers since the modified drawer was created from a standard drawer.
The stainless steel components inside the modified drawer were assumed to be Type 304 stainless
steel because this type of stainless steel was commonly used at ZPPR. The matrix tubes, drawers
and stainless steel plates used at ZPPR were made of Type 304 stainless steel. The low carbon
steel in the modified drawer was assumed to be generic carbon steel containing 0.5 wt.% carbon
and 99.5 wt.% iron (see LA-UR-09-00380, Criticality Calculations with MCNP: A Primer). The
type of plastic in the plastic components was not specified in any available records. It is unlikely
that this plastic was Teflon because Teflon was listed specifically for the 0.125 x 2 x 21 inch gap
on the left side of the front section. In the absence of any other evidence, the plastic was assumed
to be nylon because nylon was a very common plastic at that time. It is sometimes necessary to
make assumptions about minor materials because available documents do not always list specific
compositions for non-standard materials used as minor components in experiments.
The axial blanket in the stationary part of the oscillator was the standard axial blanket for ZPPR-
17A except for the replacement of one column of standard 0.25 inch wide depleted U 3O8 plates by
two columns of stainless steel plates on the left side of the drawer. The replacement stainless steel
plates had a height of 1.0 inch rather than the normal 2.0 inch to leave space for cables from the
oscillator mechanism.
The normal steel axial reflector had a length of 5.0 inches and height of 2.0 inches in ZPPR-17A.
The stainless steel reflector plates in drawer master 17-0-841 had a total length of 4.75 inches, and
the stainless steel plates in the leftmost 0.25 inches of the reflector were 1.0 inch high to make
space for the cables.
Drawer master 17-0-841(see Figure 7.21) provided sufficient detail to model the bowing oscillator.
7.6.2.2 Bowing Oscillator Reactivity Measurement Technique
The modified source multiplication technique was not used for the bowing oscillator measurement.
Instead, the operational control rods were used to establish a critical configuration with all four
oscillators in their reference positions.

 296

For the bowing oscillator measurement, the reference configuration for the bowing oscillator
consisted of the oscillator drawer in the lower position in the matrix tube. The measurement
consisted of raising the front part of the oscillator mechanism containing the core plates 0.133 cm
or 0.0524 inches vertically in the matrix tube and measuring the associated change in reactivity.
The measured reactivity was derived from inverse kinetics processing of the measured data.
The bowing oscillator measurement was performed in loading 69 and repeated in loading 75 to
determine the experimental reproducibility. Because only the oscillator position changed during
the measurement and because the measurement was performed during a single reactor run, many
of the standard components of reproducibility uncertainty, such as plate shifting during drawer
loading and handling, interface gap uncertainty and control rod position uncertainty, are not
relevant for the bowing oscillator measurement. The reproducibility uncertainty for the bowing
oscillator measurement is determined by the reproducibility of plate positions in the oscillator
mechanism and reproducibility of the vertical motion of the oscillator.
The oscillator mechanism was removed from the reactor, and the plate loading was loosened and
clamped again between the two oscillator measurements to assess the reproducibility of plate
positions. The movement indicator at the oscillator front failed before it could be calibrated for
the measurement in loading 69, so the vertical motion during the measurement in loading 69 could
not be determined precisely. The ZPPR staff concluded that the reproducibility uncertainty is not
more than 5%, but they could not refine it any further.
Table 7.15 shows the motion for the bowing oscillator measurement in loading 75 as recorded at
four measuring points on the oscillator drawer mechanism. The moving section of the oscillator
mechanism cannot be assumed to act like a rigid body. The plates in the oscillator mechanism
were rigid, but the drawer itself could flex slightly when it was lifted. Consequently, the recorded
motions at the four measuring points are slightly different as shown in Table 7.15. Vertical Motion
of the Bowing Oscillator in Loading 75.. The ZPPR staff concluded that it is legitimate to average
the left and right measurements because there was no significant worth gradient across the width
of the drawer. They also concluded that the axial worth gradient is sufficiently linear to justify
averaging the front and back motions. The averaging yields an average motion of 0.132 cm
whereas the ZPPR staff regarded 0.133 cm as the effective motion for the bowing oscillator

 Table 7.15. Vertical Motion of the Bowing Oscillator in Loading 75.

 Axial Location Motion (cm)
 Left Right Average
                                  Front (0.33 cm)        0.147 0.133      0.140
                                  Back (51.03 cm) 0.122 0.127             0.125
7.6.2.3 Bowing Oscillator Reactivity Uncertainty
There were no changes in drawers, plates or other materials during the bowing oscillator
measurement. Any uncertainties related to compositions or dimensions of matrix tubes, drawers,
plates or other materials are fully correlated for the bowing oscillator measurement and,
consequently, cancel. There were no changes in the positions of the matrix halves or of the

 297

operational rods, so uncertainties related to the interface gap or control rod positions are not
relevant. The time required for the measurement was short, so uncertainty related to temperature
is not relevant. The only motion during the measurement was the motion of the oscillator
mechanism. The plates in the front part of the oscillator were clamped, so there is no uncertainty
related to plates shifting in the drawer.
Inverse kinetics was used to process the data for the bowing oscillator measurement. The reported
statistical uncertainty for the inverse kinetics data processing is 1.9%. In addition, there is an
uncertainty in the calibration of the oscillator motion. The reported calibration uncertainty is
approximately 2.9%. The combined uncertainty for the data processing and calibration
uncertainties is 3.5%.
The repeated bowing oscillator measurements in loadings 69 and 75 were intended to quantify the
reproducibility uncertainty for the experiment. The vertical motion in loading 69 could not be
determined precisely because the movement indicator at the oscillator front failed before it could
be calibrated for the measurement in loading 69. Consequently, the ZPPR staff concluded that the
reproducibility uncertainty is not more than 5%, but the reproducibility uncertainty could not be
refined further.
A reproducibility uncertainty range of 0 – 5% for the bowing oscillator measurement is appropriate
but any value chosen in that range is arbitrary. Table 7.16. Experimental Uncertainty Range for
the ZPPR-17A Bowing Oscillator Measurement. shows the experimental uncertainty range based

Other oscillator mechanisms may have been developed for measurements of bowing in other

7.6.3 Modeling Radial Bowing Experiments
An as-built Monte Carlo model of a plate rearrangement experiment can be constructed in the same
way as any other as-built model of a ZPR/ZPPR experiment. All of the drawer masters for a plate
rearrangement experiment are standard drawer masters that can be modeled in the same way as
any other drawer master. The software that creates an as-built Monte Carlo model of the reference
critical configuration can be used to create as-built Monte Carlo models of a plate rearrangement
experiment (see Section 7.1.5). No subsequent modification of as-built Monte Carlo models of a
plate rearrangement experiment is needed.
It is likely that the measured worth of a plate rearrangement experiment is large enough to be
calculated by direct Monte Carlo. As an alternative, a deterministic model of a plate rearrangement
experiment can be constructed for computational purposes.
It was possible to construct as-built Monte Carlo models of the ZPPR-17A bowing oscillator in
the lowered and raised positions. It may also be possible to construct as-built Monte Carlo models
of bowing measurements in other assemblies if enough details can be located to model the
experimental equipment.
The measured worth for the bowing oscillator simulation in ZPPR-17A was -0.047 pcm. From
experience, about one billion (109) histories are required to obtain a one sigma of 1 pcm – 2 pcm
for keff in the reference critical configuration. In the absence of a significant advance in Monte
Carlo code capabilities or in computer hardware capabilities, it is not practical to compute this
value by direct Monte Carlo calculations. It is thus necessary to create a deterministic model to
calculate the ZPPR-17A bowing oscillator measurement. Deterministic calculations have been
performed in the past for this bowing oscillator measurement yielding -0.044 pcm for the exact
geometry defined by Table 7.15 and -0.048 pcm for the approximate geometry where the average
position was used. Both of these are well within the uncertainty on the measurement.

 299

7.7 Sample Worth Measurements
Because the reactivity worths of different materials were of significant interest for fast reactor
design purposes, the worths of small and intermediate samples of various materials were frequently
measured at the ZPR/ZPPR facilities. Similar sample worth measurements were performed at fast
critical experiment facilities in other countries such as the U.K. and Germany in that time period.
The sample materials that were routinely measured encompassed fuel ( 235U, 239Pu, 240Pu, 241Pu),
fertile materials (238U, 232Th), potential control rod materials (10B, Ta), coolant (Na) and various
structural materials (stainless steel, Fe, Cr, Ni, Mo). Samples of other materials were measured
occasionally for special programs. For example, the experimenters measured the worth of
polyethylene foam during the GCFR program because this foam was used to simulate steam entry
under accident conditions in ZPR-9/29.
In principle, these measured sample worths served multiple purposes. One obvious purpose is to
determine the reactivity worths of potential materials for reactor design or safety analysis purposes.
Measuring the worth of sodium samples as a function of position provided data regarding the worth
of changes in sodium density and the worth of sodium voiding in accident scenarios, particularly
in the period before the ZPR facilities had adequate inventories of sodium plates and void cans to
perform sodium void worth measurements in zones of intermediate and large sizes. Measuring
the worths of various materials as a function of radial or axial position provided data regarding the
worth of material motions such as radial bowing or axial expansion under upset conditions.
Historically, one basic problem with the small sample worth measurements was that the ratio of
the calculated worth to the experimental worth, i.e., C/E, was significantly worse for small sample
worth measurements than for any other common type of experimental measurement performed at
the ZPR/ZPPR facilities. For samples of fuel materials, this was known as the central worth
discrepancy.
The central worth discrepancy was not restricted to ZPR/ZPPR measurements. The central worth
discrepancy applied to small sample worth measurements in simulated LMFRs in various fast
critical experiment facilities overseas as well. Central worth discrepancy was the term used to
refer to the large C/E discrepancies for fuel samples, but the C/E issue applied to many types of
samples in many facilities and tended to be worse for non-fuel samples.
This discrepancy did not arise in the very small, very hard spectrum assemblies constructed at Los
Alamos National Laboratory (LANL). C/Es for small sample worth measurements in the classical
LANL critical assemblies such as JEZEBEL (bare plutonium metal sphere), GODIVA (bare HEU
sphere) and BIGTEN (10% enriched uranium metal) were generally good, but each of these LANL
assemblies had a simple, uniform composition and a very hard spectrum. In contrast to the
classical LANL critical assemblies, a ZPR/ZPPR assembly simulating an LMFR contained many
different materials in a complex geometry and had a softer, much broader neutron spectrum
characteristic of an LMFR. Consequently, small sample worth measurements in assemblies
simulating LMFRs at Argonne and elsewhere exhibited much larger C/E differences than small
sample worth measurements in the small, clean LANL assemblies.

 300

C/Es for all ZPR/ZPPR small sample worth measurements were significantly worse than C/Es for
other measurements in these facilities. In addition, C/Es of most samples of non-fuel materials
tended to be significantly worse than C/Es of samples of fissile materials in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies.
The ZPR/ZPPR staff devoted much effort to investigating the sources of the central worth
discrepancy and reducing C/Es for small sample worth measurements. This effort included study
of the analytical methods used to compute sample worth and experiments specifically designed to
examine experimental uncertainties associated with small sample worth measurements.
7.7.1 Small Sample Worth Experimental Techniques
In the ideal small sample worth measurement, introduction of the sample would cause negligible
distortion or depression of the local flux at the measurement location. The sample would have
negligible self-shielding and negligible internal flux distortion and depression. The sample would
be small enough that a neutron would not have multiple reactions in the sample. If these conditions
are met, the measurement can be analyzed with first order perturbation theory.
In reality, introduction of the sample must cause a modification of the local geometry because the
sample and related equipment displace the materials that would otherwise be present at the sample
location. The method used to introduce the sample affects the modeling of the sample worth
measurement. In principle, differences in methods used to infer the sample worth from the reactor
response to introduction of the sample might also affect the measured sample worth and C/E.
To date, no effort has been made to model or analyze any small sample worth measurements in
ZPR/ZPPR assemblies and the following discussion is based primarily on ZPR/ZPPR documents,
loading records for ZPR/ZPPR assemblies, and Refs. 16 – 19.
7.7.1.1 Radial and Axial Tube Oscillator Measurements
Four general experimental techniques were developed to introduce the sample into the reactor.
The oldest and most convenient sample insertion method was the radial or axial tube oscillator.
For the axial tube oscillator, a small stainless steel tube replaced one or more columns of plates
such as sodium plates in a special drawer. A sample was placed in the tube and oscillated between
a position in the core or axial blanket and a position far outside the core. The sample position far
outside the core was assumed or defined to have zero worth, so the reactivity change between the
sample in the core and the sample in the withdrawn position was the worth of the sample.
The axial tube oscillator allowed the experimenters to measure the sample worth as a function of
axial position in the drawer. Placing the axial tube oscillator in different matrix positions allowed
the experimenters to measure axial worth profiles as a function of radius if desired.
The methods for installing and using the axial tube oscillator at ANL-W and ANL-E probably
were very similar.
The general concept of the radial tube oscillator was similar in all ZPR/ZPPR facilities, but the
details of use varied between facilities, particularly between ANL-E and ANL-W. Based on
examination of loading records for some ZPR-3 assemblies, the radial tube oscillator was installed
at the interface between matrix halves along the center row in ZPR-3. The matrix tubes had notches
on the sides that mated with tabs on the drawers to ensure consistent drawer positioning. ZPR-3
loading records for sample worth measurements indicate that drawers were pushed back into the

 301

matrix tubes along the center row to make space for the radial sample tube oscillator. It is possible
that these notches were sufficient to provide the required space for the radial tube oscillator. It is
also possible that the front ends of matrix tubes in the center row of the matrix differed from the
front ends of the other matrix tubes in ZPR-3, which is somewhat visible in Figure 2.1. It seems
unlikely that any question regarding the matrix tubes in the center row can be resolved definitively
at this point in time. The radial tube oscillator was installed in the resulting/designed gap in the
center row in half 1 and in the center row in half 2. Apparently, ZPPR used the same approach as
ZPR-3 regarding installation of the radial tube oscillator but there is no clear indication of any
modifications. In any event, the report documenting small sample measurements with the radial
tube oscillator and the loading records for the assembly of interest are likely to indicate where the
oscillator tube was installed.
This indicates that ZPR-3 and ZPPR had a small inventory of drawers without tabs that could be
recessed in the matrix tubes if desired. In fact, according to the ZPPR-15 loading records, one
ZPPR-15 drawer master used drawers without tabs.
Note that ANL-E and ANL-W used different methods to install and use the radial tube oscillator.
The ANL-E use of radial tube oscillators is discussed in detail later in this section.
Changing samples manually would require shutting the reactor down, entering the cell, changing
samples, exiting the cell, and restarting the reactor because it was not possible to enter the reactor
cell when the reactor was operating. That process would require significant time and would impact
reactor operations and scheduling, particularly with respect to sample worth measurements. In
addition, that process would introduce additional measurement uncertainties related to the
interface gap, control rod positions and reactor temperature distribution. Based on available
documents, there were automated, remotely-operated sample changer mechanisms to change
samples and to oscillate the samples during sample worth measurements. ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and
ZPPR had automated sample changer mechanisms. It seems likely that ZPR-3 had a similar device
for the reasons outlined in this paragraph.
The radial tube oscillators used in ZPR-3 and ZPPR apparently consisted of a stainless steel tube
through which the sample traveled. The sample was connected to a hollow stainless steel push rod
or tube that moved the sample to the desired position in the oscillator tube.
In principle, the sample could be positioned at any radial location. In practice, it appears that the
center of the sample typically was placed at the center of the drawer when the sample was in the
inserted at an in-core position. As in the case of the axial tube oscillator, the sample was oscillated
between a position in the core or radial blanket and a withdrawn position far removed from the
center of the assembly. The sample position far outside the core was assumed or defined to have
zero worth, so the reactivity change between the inserted sample and the sample in the withdrawn
position was the worth of the sample.
The reports that document small sample worth measurements in ZPR-3 and ZPPR assemblies
frequently describe the samples in detail. This includes the sample itself and any clad or housing
enclosing the sample. Note that the samples used in the axial and radial tube oscillators were
cylindrical or annular.

 302

To date, no information regarding the radial or axial oscillator tubes used in ZPR-3 and ZPPR has
been found although this information may be contained in one or more of the many ZPR-3/ZPPR
documents that are available but have not been examined due to time constraints. The same
statement applies to the hollow stainless steel push rod or tube that connected the sample to the
mechanism that oscillated the sample during operation of the oscillator. In any event, the oscillator
tube inner diameter had to be just slightly larger than than the outer diameter of the samples, and
the oscillator tube had a very thin wall. The ANL-W oscillator tube thickness was probably in the
0.01 – 0.02 inch range because this is similar to the thickness of the oscillator tubes used at ANL-
E. The same samples were used in the radial and axial tube oscillators, so the oscillator tubes and
push rods for the radial and axial oscillators used at ANL-W were probably identical in design.
No description of the axial sample tube oscillator used at ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 has been identified,
but it also seems likely that any axial sample tube oscillator used at ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 was similar
to the radial tube oscillator used at ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 because the same samples would have been
used in the radial and axial tube oscillators.
The methods for installing and using a radial sample tube oscillator differed significantly between
ANL-W and ANL-E. Furthermore, the method for installing a radial tube oscillator differed
significantly between ZPR-6 and ZPR-9. The reason for the different methods used in ZPR-6 and
ZPR-9 is not clear because ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were built at approximately the same time in
Building 315 at ANL-E and were operated by the same staff.
The following is a description of the radial tube oscillator used in ZPR-6/7 around 1970. It is
possible that there was a different approach to radial sample worth measurements in very early
ZPR-6 assemblies, but such records before ZPR-6/6A have not been inspected due to time
constraints. For practical purposes, it does not matter how radial sample worth measurements were
made in early ZPR-6 assemblies because the first ZPR-6 assembly for which scanned records exist
is ZPR-6/5.
The radial tube oscillator used in ZPR-6 consisted of a double-walled thin stainless steel tube
connected to a remotely-operated device that could a) insert a sample into the oscillator tube from
a cylindrical magazine, b) oscillate the sample within the sample tube and c) transfer the sample
from the oscillator tube back to the magazine. One significant difference between ZPR-6 and
ANL-W is the manner in which the samples were oscillated. At ANL-W a sample was connected
to a long hollow rod or tube that moved the sample between inserted and withdrawn positions
within the oscillator tube. At ZPR-6, a sample was oscillated pneumatically between the magazine
and the end of the sample tube.
In ZPR-6 the cavity for the radial tube oscillator was created by pushing all drawers back one inch,
i.e., into the matrix tube, in the central row in the stationary half (half 1). This created a cavity
that was one inch wide and approximately two inches high. The fact that a 1 x 2 inch cavity could
be created in the center row of the stationary half of ZPR-6 suggests that the front ends of some
matrix tubes in the center row of the stationary half of ZPR-6 must have been significantly different
from the front ends of the other matrix tubes in ZPR-6. Note that ZPR-6 assemblies were generally
symmetric about the center column, so any accommodation required to install the radial tube
oscillator probably involved center row matrix tubes on one side of the reactor rather than all
matrix tubes in the center row.

 303

The thickness of each wall of the double-walled radial oscillator tube used at ZPR-6 was 0.01
inches, and the outer diameter of the outer tube was 1.0 inch. Samples used in the axial and radial
tube oscillators were cylindrical or annular and were typically enclosed in a sample holder or
capsule. A typical sample had an outer diameter of ~0.87 inches and was enclosed in a stainless
steel sample holder or capsule with a wall thickness of ~0.032 inches although there were
significant differences between some individual samples. The radial oscillator tube sat on a
support that had a height of ~1 inch and width of ~1 inch. This support was essentially an inverted
tray. The wall thickness of the support (vertical sides and horizontal top) was ~0.032 inches. The
space enclosed by the sidewalls and top of the support was empty.
The method for installing the radial tube oscillator in ZPR-9 differed significantly from the method
for installing the radial tube oscillator in ZPR-6.
To date, no records of small sample worth measurements (if there were any) in ZPR-9 Assemblies
1 – 9 have been examined. Further, the procedure for making sample worth measurements in ZPR-
9 Assemblies 1 – 9 has not been found although it may be documented in reports related to those
assemblies if small sample worth measurements were made in those assemblies.
The first ZPR-9 matrix tubes were made of aluminum. The aluminum matrix tubes were replaced
by stainless steel matrix tubes at the end of the ZPR-9/9 program, and those stainless steel matrix
tubes were present for all subsequent ZPR-9 assemblies. The records for ZPR-9 Assemblies 10 –
27 were not scanned, so no records exist for those assemblies. The following description of radial
tube oscillator measurements in ZPR-9 is based on reported measurements in ZPR-9/30 and ZPR-
9/31. Since the same matrix tubes were used for ZPR-9 Assemblies 10 – 36, it is likely that the
same method was used to install the radial tube oscillator in ZPR-9 Assemblies 10 – 36.
There were holes in the sides of some of the matrix tubes in row 23, the center row, in the stationary
half (half 1) of the ZPR-9 matrix. The holes extended from column 21 to column 43 according to
the ZPR-9/30 report. The center column and outermost column on one side in ZPR-9 were column
23 and column 45, respectively, so it is not clear whether the range of columns in which the matrix
tubes had holes was 21 – 43, as the report indicates, or 21 – 45 or 23 - 45. Undated pictures of the
ZPR-9 indicate the holes extended through column 45. The radial tube oscillator had to pass though
all matrix tubes between the outer edge of the matrix and the central column(s) of row 23, so it
seems likely that the matrix columns in columns 44 and 45 of row 23 in the stationary half of ZPR-
9 also had holes.
The centers of the holes in the sides of the ZPR-9 matrix tubes were 1.75 inch from the fronts of
the matrix tubes in the stationary half. The holes were vertically centered in the matrix tubes, and
the diameter of each hole was1.25 in (3.175 cm).
Special drawers were placed in these matrix tubes for radial sample worth measurements. Each of
these special drawers had holes in the sides that matched the sizes and positions of the
corresponding holes in the matrix tubes. These special drawers and matrix tubes allowed the radial
oscillator tube to extend from the center of ZPR-9 to the outer edge of ZPR-9.
The loading of these special drawers differed from the loading of standard drawers in the ZPR-9
assembly. For some standard plate types such as iron oxide plates and depleted uranium oxide
plates, the ANL-E plate inventory contained special versions with holes drilled in them to

 304

accommodate the radial oscillator tube. There were no drilled Pu-U-Mo plates, so Pu-U-Mo plates
were replaced by empty stainless steel void frames at the locations where the radial oscillator tube
passed through the special drawers.
The radial oscillator tube used in ZPR-9 is not described, but it seems likely that the radial
oscillator tube used in ZPR-9 was similar to the radial oscillator tube used in ZPR-6 as well because
ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 had the same staff, used the same experimental equipment and shared a common
inventory of plates, drawers, etc. The samples used in ZPR-9 were part of the common ANL-E
inventory.
Reports documenting small sample worth measurements in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 frequently describe
the samples and sample capsules or clad in detail. Note that samples used at ANL-E were not
necessarily identical to samples used at ZPPR, and samples used at ZPR-3 were not necessarily
identical to samples used at ZPPR or at ANL-E. Available records do not indicate whether the
ZPR-3 samples were transferred to another facility or discarded when ZPR-3 was shut down.
Although ANL-E and ANL-W had separate sets of samples, it is possible that ANL-E and ANL-
W did share samples occasionally.
Radial and axial sample tube oscillators offered several advantages for small sample worth
measurements. These oscillators were relatively convenient and easy to use experimentally. They
provided a way to measure worth profiles at many radial or axial locations relatively quickly in
one reactor startup or run. Automated sample changers allowed measurements to be obtained for
multiple samples without the need to shut the reactor down to change samples manually.
However, the radial and axial tube oscillators also had several significant disadvantages. First,
they introduced a cavity. For the axial tube oscillator, the oscillator tube replaced one or more
columns of normal plate materials, generally sodium plates, in the oscillator drawer. For the radial
tube oscillator, it was necessary to displace or remove normal core and radial blanket materials in
drawers located in the center row to provide space for the oscillator tube. Second, the sample
housing or clad, the oscillator tube and any push rod or tube connecting the sample to the oscillator
mechanism introduced a small amount of stainless steel that would not otherwise be present in the
assembly. Third, the empty space inside the oscillator tube and the empty space in the cavity
surrounding the oscillator tube introduce streaming paths for neutrons. The importance of the
streaming paths depends upon the size of the ZPR/ZPPR assembly. Streaming was more important
for a small assembly than for a large assembly. The net effect of the material displacement,
additional stainless stainless steel and neutron streaming associated with introduction of the radial
and axial sample tube oscillators was a small distortion of local conditions, e.g., local flux, at the
measurement location. From the analysis standpoint, the radial and axial tube oscillators
introduced geometrical complications that were difficult to accommodate in computational models
based on the analytical tools available when the ZPR/ZPPR facilities operated.
7.7.1.2 Drawer Oscillator Measurements
The radial and axial sample tube oscillators were experimentally convenient, but they had the
disadvantages described in the preceding section. The second experimental technique for small
sample measurements in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies, the drawer oscillator, eliminated many of the
disadvantages associated with the radial and axial tube oscillators. The drawer oscillator was used
in ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR. It may have been used in ZPR-3 as well.

 305

The drawer oscillator was a specially-fitted drawer that was much longer than a normal drawer.
This special drawer was connected to remotely-operated equipment that could a) oscillate the
drawer in the matrix tube, b) insert a sample into the drawer from a set of samples in a multi-
sample magazine and c) transfer a sample from the drawer to the sample magazine. Karam et al
provide a more thorough description of the drawer oscillator [19].
The samples were inserted in a special box in the oscillator drawer; the remainder of the drawer
was filled with normal plate materials for the core and axial blanket. Because the remainder of the
drawer oscillator was filled with normal plate materials, the environment near the sample in the
drawer oscillator was less perturbed than the environment near the sample in the radial or axial
tube oscillator. The dimensions of the sample box were 2 x 2 x Z inches where Z ranged from
0.125 inches to 2 inches.
A small sample box such as a sample box where Z = 0.125 inches or Z = 0.25 inches was generally
loaded transverse to the normal plates in the oscillator drawer. A report documenting small sample
worth measurements with the drawer oscillator may describe the positioning of the sample box in
the oscillator drawer. The drawer master for an oscillator drawer is likely to show the position and
orientation of the sample box.
The drawer oscillator provided an axial sample worth profile. Obtaining a radial sample worth
distribution would require shutting the reactor down, moving the drawer oscillator to another
location and restarting the reactor for each desired radial position. This sort of relocation may
have been performed occasionally, but it probably was not standard practice in any of the
ZPR/ZPPR facilities.
The drawer oscillator provided significant experimental flexibility relative to the radial and axial
tube oscillators. Experimenters could insert a special sample in the sample box. Depending upon
the size of the sample and the size of the sample box, the sample might fill the sample box. This
provided flexibility with respect to sample size, which might be advantageous for samples of very
low worth per unit mass. By oscillating the drawer, experimenters could measure the worth of the
special sample relative to normal core materials at corresponding axial locations.
Another option was to fill the 2 x 2 x 2 inch sample box with regular plates that matched the normal
plate columns outside the sample box. The experimenters could then measure the worth of
removing a plate from the sample box or the worth of replacing one plate type in the sample box
by another plate type or sample. There were additional options involving special foils that could
be inserted into a sample box without removing any of the normal plates in the sample box. For
example, a thin foil could be inserted between plate columns to measure the sample worth of the
foil with minimal perturbation of the local environment. In the limit of an infinitely thin foil, there
would be no perturbation of the local environment. It is likely that some or all of these special
foils were different from and much larger than the standard foils used to measure reaction rate
distributions in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies. Other options for use of the drawer oscillator existed, but
the primary options for use of the drawer oscillator are the options described here.
The drawer oscillator offered the large advantage of providing measurements in a normal cell
environment whereas the radial and axial tube oscillators necessarily introduced perturbations in
the local environment where the measurement was obtained. The drawer oscillator did, however,
have one drawback in plutonium-fueled assemblies. There was little decay heating and no

 306

significant temperature-related issues in uranium-fuel assemblies. There was significant decay
heating in a plutonium-fueled assembly. For example, the Pu-U-Mo alloy in a standard Pu-U-Mo
plate consisted of 28 wt.% Pu/69.5 wt.% depleted U/2.5 wt.% Mo, and the Pu component contained
11 wt.% 240Pu. Movement of the drawer oscillator in a plutonium-fueled assembly slightly altered
the local temperature distribution in the oscillator drawer and introduced a temperature-related
precision problem in the plutonium-fueled core. Any change in the local temperature distribution
introduced a small Doppler reactivity. This Doppler reactivity was very small, but the measured
worth of the sample also was small in many cases. In addition to the Doppler reactivity
contribution, there was a small uncertainty contribution from axial expansion effects due to
changes in the local temperature distribution. Reported sample worths were commonly expressed
in Ih/kg or ¢/kg, but many samples only weighed a few grams. Consequently, actual measured
sample worths were of the order of one Ih, one cent or a small fraction of an Ih or cent. Relative
to the actual measured sample worth, the temperature-related precision limit in a drawer oscillator
measurement in a plutonium-fueled assembly can be a relevant uncertainty.
Another minor issue in drawer oscillator measurements is that introduction of a sample,
replacement of one sample by another sample, replacement of a fuel plate in a sample box by a
non-fuel plate, etc. necessarily introduced a small perturbation in the sample box relative to the
reference configuration in the sample box. This perturbation is unavoidable and is akin to the
perturbation resulting from inserting the actual sample in the radial or axial sample tube oscillator.
The sample is small, and the resulting perturbation is small. Nevertheless, the perturbation
introduced by inserting, removing or changing a sample is not zero to an arbitrary degree of
precision.
The relevant issues for the two preceding paragraphs are that a) the sample, sample box and drawer
oscillator introduced a small perturbation in the local environment relative to the reference
configuration with a standard drawer in the matrix tube, and b) movement of the drawer oscillator
in a plutonium-fueled assembly introduced a small perturbation in the local temperature
distribution. The effects of these perturbations were small, but they were not zero and could affect
the measured sample worth. Whether those effects were small depended on the sample or sample
configuration being measured.
7.7.1.3 Shim Oscillator Measurements
The third experimental technique for small sample measurements was the shim oscillator. The
radial oscillator tube, axial oscillator tube and drawer oscillator were developed relatively early in
history of ZPR/ZPPR small sample worth measurements. It is not clear when the shim oscillator
was developed. The shim oscillator technique was based on using a thin stainless steel blade to
oscillate thin foil samples into an out of a drawer in the ~1.5 mm air gap between the tops of the
plates in a drawer and the lower surface of the top of the matrix tube. The foil samples the flux at
the top of the plates across the width of the plates in the drawer.
The drawer does not move, so the temperature changes associated with the drawer oscillator in a
plutonium-fueled core are eliminated. There is no significant amount of resonance material in the
oscillator mechanism, so the nonuniform temperature distribution along the drawer does not
introduce any temperature issues such as Doppler reactivity related to the drawer oscillator
mechanism. Very small sample reactivities were measured accurately with the shim oscillator.

 307

The principal limitation of the shim oscillator is that this technique is limited to thin foil samples
that sample the flux across the top of the drawer.
7.7.1.4 Fuel-Thickened Zone Measurements
The fourth experimental technique for sample worth measurements is establishment of a “fuel-
thickened” zone in which thin foils of fuel material are inserted next to fuel plates in a zone in the
assembly. The foils are inserted into many stationary drawers, and there is no oscillation. The
fuel-thickened zone is not small. The reactivity worth of the added foils is the difference in
reactivity between the reference configuration without the added foils and the corresponding
configuration with foils added in the fuel-thickned zone. While this technique is not exactly a
small sample worth measurement, its relationship to small sample worth measurements is
sufficiently close that it provided another way to investigate the central worth discrepancy.
Whereas the three previous techniques required significant approximations in analytical models,
the fuel-thickened zone technique was amenable to the standard analysis techniques used for
ZPR/ZPPR assemblies. The drawback of fuel-thickened zone measurements is that the foils must
be loaded into many drawers and removed from those drawers after the reactivity measurement
has been made. Loading and unloading the foils could take significant time, depending on the size
of the fuel-thickened zone. In addition, loading the foils, unloading the foils and the associated
drawer handling increase the potential for plate shifting effects that could affect reactivity

Apparently, this technique was used occasionally in uranium-fueled assemblies. There is no
indication that this technique was used in a plutonium-fueled assembly. In at least some cases, the
foils used in the fuel-thickened zone were much larger than the standard irradiation foils used for
reaction rate distribution measurements. For example, in ZPR-6/9, the HEU foils used for the fuel-
thickened zone measurement were 152.4 x 50.8 x 0.25 mm. Reports documenting measurements
in fuel-thickened zones may describe the specific foils used for the measurements.
Fuel-thickened zone measurements have one disadvantage compared to measurements using radial
tube oscillators, axial tube oscillators, drawer oscillators and shim oscillators. For sample worth
measurements with oscillators, all measurements with all samples at all radial or axial positions
could be performed in one reactor startup or run, at least in principle. Performing all measurements
in one reactor startup eliminated the reproducibility uncertainty related to the interface gap, the
reproducibility uncertainty related to control rod position and the reproducibility uncertainty
related to the reactor temperature distribution except possibly for the temperature issue discussed
above for the drawer oscillator. The fuel-thickened zone measurements required a separate reactor
startup, so the reproducibility uncertainties related to the interface gap, control rod positions and
reactor temperature distribution are relevant to fuel-thickened zone measurements.
7.7.1.5 Conversion of Reactor Response to Sample Worth
The following discussion of the reactivity measurement techniques for small sample worths is
taken from Ref. 17. Three basic methods were used to derive the sample worth from the measured
reactor response. First, the sample reactivity worth could be derived from a positive reactor period
measurement. This is a special case of inverse kinetics. The reactor is made critical, and then the
sample is introduced. The resulting positive period is measured, and the inhour equation is used

 308

to compute the reactivity change. The positive period method was not useful in plutonium-fueled
assemblies due to the large spontaneous fission source from 240Pu decay and to the difficulty in
separating the sample reactivity from reactivity changes associated with temperature changes
during the measurement.
Second, a calibrated autorod was used to maintain constant reactor power after introduction of the
sample. The change in autorod position after the sample was introduced was a measure of the
sample worth. The autorod was calibrated by inverse kinetics. In plutonium-fueled cores,
temperature drift due to decay heating during the sample oscillations introduced a reactivity drift.
The reactivity drift associated with temperature drift could be removed by assuming a low order
polynomial and solving for the coefficients that remove the temperature drift based on a least
squares approach. The sample reactivity is then derived from the mean change in autorod position
when the sample is oscillated between the inserted and fully withdrawn positions.
Third, the autorod was used to hold the reactor at constant power. If the reactor power is allowed
to change during the oscillation, direct inverse kinetics methods can be used to determine the
sample worth. As in the autorod method, temperature drift during the oscillation can be addressed
by assuming a low order polynomial for the reactivity and using the least squares approach to solve
for coefficients that remove the reactivity effect of temperature drift. For a plutonium-fueled
assembly, it is necessary to know the spontaneous fission source, but this can be measured by a
rod drop.
According to Ref. 17, positive period measurement, a calibrated autorod and direct inverse kinetics
methods have been used to determine small sample worths at Argonne, and all three methods result
in the “same” sample worth. ANL-E commonly used the autorod method. ZPPR generally used
inverse kinetics methods.
7.7.2 Uncertainties for Small Sample Worth Measurements
For any ZPR/ZPPR reactivity measurement, there was a statistical uncertainty in the measured
data. For the radial tube oscillator, axial tube oscillator, drawer oscillator and shim oscillator, this
uncertainty could be reduced by oscillating the sample multiple times between the inserted and
withdrawn positions and then performing a statistical analysis of the multiple reactivity
measurements after correcting for the reactivity associated with any temperature drift during the
measurements. The time required to perform an individual fuel-thickened zone measurement
precluded repetitions. In addition, plate shifting could be relevant consideration for repeated fuel-
thickened zone measurements. The statistical uncertainty in the reactivity measurement is
included in the published uncertainty for the sample worth.
For sample worths derived from changes in the position of an autorod, the uncertainty in the
autorod calibration was a significant contributor to the total experimental uncertainty in some
cases. For sample worths derived from inverse kinetics analysis, the corresponding uncertainty
contribution was the uncertainty in the kinetics parameters used for the inverse kinetics analysis.
In principle, for oscillator measurements there may be a very small reproducibility uncertainty
related to the position of the sample during the oscillation because the position of the sample when
it is inserted is not necessarily reproducible to an arbitrary degree of precision. Although there
may be a small reproducibility uncertainty related to the position of the sample during the

 309

oscillation, this uncertainty is negligible compared the statistical uncertainty in the measurement
and the reactivity conversion uncertainty discussed below.
There can also be a small uncertainty related to plate shifting during drawer handling and similar
activities for the drawer oscillator. Plate shifting refers to changes in the positions of plates in a
drawer relative to the nominal reference position in which all plates are pushed forward as far as
possible with no gaps between the plate columns and the front plate of the drawer (see Section
7.2). In principle, drawer loading procedures, drawer handling procedures and the springs inserted
in the backs of drawers to push to plates forward ensured that there were no gaps between the plate
columns and the fronts of normal drawers. The same practices applied to the drawer oscillator.
In addition, rigid spacers, shims and springs were used to fix the position of a sample in a sample
drawer such as the drawer oscillator. Despite these precautions, plate shifting did occur
occasionally. For example, assumed plate shifting was the dominant uncertainty in some of the
sodium void worth measurements performed in ZPPR-12.
In ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPPR, there could be a small amount of plate shifting when the drawers are
pushed back into the matrix tubes to make space for the radial tube oscillator, at least in principle.
However, that plate shifting would not have any significant effect on sample worths measured with
the radial tube oscillator. In the drawer oscillator, loading plates in the drawer and changing
samples could result in plate shifting and a small uncertainty related to plate positions.
Unfortunately, it was rarely possible to determine whether plate shifting had occurred or to
quantify the effects of plate shifting. There was no way to measure or determine plate positions
when the drawers were in the matrix, and the effects of any plate shifting that did occur were
generally small. If plate shifting was significant enough to have a discernible effect on measured
reactivities, that effect was discovered after the fact based on some anomaly or inconsistency in
the measurements. If such an anomaly was discovered and if no other likely cause was sufficient
to account for the anomaly, the anomaly might be ascribed to plate shifting.
In one sense, plate shifting is an after-the-fact explanation for a minor anomaly in the measurement
that cannot be explained by obvious things such as equipment failure. In another sense, plate
shifting is an unquantifiable uncertainty for many types of measurements because it is not possible
to know the true positions of the plates in the reactor. In any case, any uncertainty contribution
from plate shifting is likely to be small compared to the reactivity conversion uncertainty discussed
below.
One relevant factor for small sample worth measurements is that sample size matters, and it matters
more for some materials than for other materials. In the ideal case, the sample is so small that a)
the sample has no effect on the local environment and b) multiple reactions do not occur in the
sample. A very thin foil approaches the ideal case because as the foil thickness goes to zero the
potential for a single neutron to be involved in multiple collisions within the foil goes to zero. In
the real case, a sample of finite size causes a small perturbation in the local environment, and
multiple collisions could occur in a sample if the sample was sufficiently large.
In some cases, the sample inventory contained multiple samples of the same material with different
masses or sizes. If multiple samples of the same material existed, the experimenters could measure
the worths of these samples and extrapolate the results to the worth of an infinitely small sample.
Apparently, this extrapolation was done for sample worth measurements in some ZPR/ZPPR

 310

assemblies. Based upon reports from the GCFR critical experiments program, the sample size
effect was small for heavy metal samples but very large (±50%) for some heavy absorbers and
light scattering materials. Reports of small sample worth measurements may indicate whether the
sample size effect has been considered. The sample size effect may affect C/Es in some cases,
particularly for heavy absorbers and light scattering materials and for sample worths expressed in
Ih/kg or ȼ/kg.
Ref. 17 discusses two sources of systematic uncertainties for the four sample worth experimental
techniques discussed in Section 7.7.1. First, plates of the same type (material) and size were not
identical to an arbitrary degree of precision. There could be very small differences in composition,
mass or dimensions between different plates of the same type and size due to normal
manufacturing tolerances and variations in material compositions. The sample worth was
measured at a location in the presence of a specific group of plates (types and sizes). If that group
of plates was replaced by a different group of plates of the same types and sizes and the sample
worth was measured again, there would be a very small effect on the measured sample worth
because the local environment near the sample differed slightly in the two cases.
Second, the samples were enclosed in capsules or cladding. The worth of the capsule was assumed
to be separable from the worth of the sample. The mass of the capsule generally was small, and
the worth of the capsule was only a few percent of the worth of a fuel sample. Nevertheless, this
assumed separability probably introduces a small systematic error because the presence of the
capsule must introduce a very small perturbation in the sample. The measured worth of the sample
plus capsule is likely to be slightly different from the sum of the measured worths of the bare
sample and capsule if it were possible to measure those worths separately.
The worth of the capsule was only a few percent of the sample worth for samples of high worth
such as fuel isotopes or 10B. The situation is less clear for samples of low worth, e.g., sodium, that
were encapsulated. For an encapsulated sample of low worth material, the worth of the capsule
may be larger than a few percent of the worth of the sample material. In that case, the capsule may
introduce a larger perturbation in the sample, and the separability assumption discussed in the
preceding paragraph may introduce a larger systematic error.
Published uncertainties do not account for the variation between plates or for any uncertainty
introduced by the assumed separability of the sample and capsule. It was assumed that the
magnitude of these two systematic errors is small.
The report documenting a small sample measurement may discuss additional uncertainties for that

In general, it is necessary to assume that the published uncertainty for a small sample worth
measurement reflects everything that the experimenters knew and could quantify regarding
measurement uncertainties for the published sample worth. It also is necessary to assume that any
experimental uncertainties that are not included in the published measurement uncertainty are
small. For practical purposes, it is unrealistic to assume that a better estimate of the measurement
uncertainty for a published small sample worth measurement can be determined unless the
documents for a specific assembly provide sufficient additional information.

 311

Sample worths were measured in inhours or cents, the natural units for reactivity measurements.
However, the natural units for reactivity calculations are Δk/k 1k2 or pcm. When ZPR/ZPPR
analysts calculated sample worths, they calculated the sample worths in Δk/k 1k2 or pcm. For
purposes of comparing measured and calculated sample worths, they either converted the
calculated worths to the measurement units (inhours or cents) or else they converted the measured
reactivity worths to Δk/k1k2 or pcm. In either case, it was not the standard practice to consider any
uncertainty in the conversion factor between the reactivity measurement units and the reactivity
calculation units in ZPR/ZPPR reports. At present, the standard practice is to include the
uncertainty in the reactivity conversion factor in the total uncertainty for the measurement.
Conversion from the natural reactivity measurement units to the calculation units or vice versa
requires knowledge of the delayed neutron kinetics parameters, particularly β eff. However, βeff is
uncertain, and that uncertainty contributes to the total uncertainty when the sample worths are
converted from the measurement units to the calculation units or vice versa. The estimated
uncertainty in βeff is 5%, which is the value assumed for all ICSBEP/IRPhEP benchmarks of ZPR
and ZPPR assemblies [5,6]. The 5% βeff uncertainty also is consistent with the limited number of
measurements of βeff performed for ZPR and ZPPR assemblies and with calculations of β eff for
ZPR and ZPPR assemblies.
The 5% βeff uncertainty applies to the conversion factor between the reactivity measurement units
and the reactivity calculation units. This 5% uncertainty is independent of the measurement
uncertainty published by the experimenters.
The 0.15% mass uncertainty discussed in Section 7.1 applies to sample masses unless the
description of the sample provides a better estimate of the sample mass uncertainty. The document
reporting sample worth measurements for an assembly may indicate any uncertainty in the sample
compositions. The mass uncertainty and any composition uncertainty contribute to the total
uncertainty, but the dominant components of the total uncertainty are likely to be the published
measurement uncertainty and the 5% βeff uncertainty.
The quadrature sum of the published measurement uncertainty, the 5% uncertainty in the reactivity
conversion factor and any contributions from sample mass uncertainty and sample composition
uncertainty is the total uncertainty for comparison of calculated and measured small sample
worths.
7.7.3 Modeling Small Sample Worth Measurements
One significant contributor to the high C/Es for small sample worth measurements is that it was
and still is difficult to construct an accurate model of a small sample worth measurement. When
the small sample worth measurements were performed, the ZPR/ZPPR staff had all of the required
information regarding the reactor configuration, experimental techniques, measured data, samples,
radial and axial tube oscillators, drawer oscillators, etc. However, they were limited by the
modeling capabilities of the time. It was not possible to construct a high-fidelity as-built Monte
Carlo model of the reactor and sample equipment with the available software and limited budget.
The same can be stated for deterministic models of the time. All sample worth calculations were
based upon deterministic models which were limited to R-Z, X-Y and X-Y-Z models with
multigroup cross sections processed with MC 2-II and SDX. (SDX was a one-dimensional cell

 312

code that accounted for the plate heterogeneity in the reactor unit cell, and MC 2-II was a fast reactor
multigroup library generation code).
In principle, it is possible to construct much better models today because modern computer
software and hardware are much better than the computer software and hardware that were
available to the ZPR/ZPPR staff. The limiting factor today is that there may be limited information
available regarding the sample equipment such as the radial and axial tube oscillators or regarding
special foils that were used for some measurements.
If enough information regarding the sample equipment and samples can be found, it may be
possible to incorporate a model of the sample worth measurement into a high fidelity as-built
Monte Carlo model. The combinatorial geometry package in any of the major Monte Carlo codes
allows the user to describe the geometry of the ZPR/ZPPR plates, drawers, matrix tubes, samples,
sample equipment, etc. in as much detail as the available information allows and modern
computing capabilities allow for much larger models than those in the 1980s. The continuous
energy cross section option in modern Monte Carlo codes provides the most accurate available
treatment of the nuclear data. The accuracy that can be obtained on the sample worth will still be
limited by the magnitudes of the measured sample worths (e.g. 0.01 to 0.5 pcm) which are still
beyond the present Monte Carlo capabilities.
Creating a geometrically true deterministic model of a small sample worth measurement is either
equally or more difficult than creating a high fidelity as-built Monte Carlo model of those
measurements. Creating a “drawer homogenized” model would likely introduce or require
additional approximations that may preclude the approach getting an accurate solution.
While it is possible that future software and computer developments may undermine these
conclusions, at present, modeling the oscillator configurations, particularly the radial and axial
tube oscillators, and samples accurately will require considerable effort. As stated, the ZPR/ZPPR
analysts devoted effort to constructing deterministic models of small sample worth measurements
and did calculate small sample worths with limited success.
According to two former ZPR/ZPPR analysts, calculations for high worth samples such as 239Pu
and 10B produced reasonable results, but calculated results for low worth samples resulted from
indifferent to poor. In fact, sometimes the calculated worth for sodium did not even have the right
sign. For high worth samples, the high sample worth dominated over modeling limitations (or
assumptions) and the perturbation in the local environment introduced by the sample and sample
equipment. Calculated sample worths improved after the importance of the sample equipment and
sample environment were recognized [17,18].
Although it may be possible to construct an as-built Monte Carlo model of a sample worth
measurement, it may not be feasible to compute a sample worth using that as-built Monte Carlo
model. Experimenters frequently published sample worths in units of Ih/kg or ¢/kg, but these are
normalized values. Many reports do list the actual measured sample worths. The mass of a typical
sample was a few grams, and the measured worth of a sample ranged between a fraction of an
inhour and a few inhours or between a fraction of a cent and one cent. In units of pcm, the
measured worth of a sample ranged between a fraction of a pcm and a few pcm. From experience,
running one billion (109) histories on a direct Monte Carlo eigenvalue calculation of an as-built
model of a ZPR/ZPPR assembly will yield a one sigma uncertainty of 1-2 pcm for k eff. It may be

 313

possible to use some of the more advanced techniques available in modern Monte Carlo codes to
compute small sample worths, but it can be considered impractical to compute small sample worths
using direct Monte Carlo eigenvalue calculations of as-built ZPR/ZPPR models.
Another consideration is that experimenters measured sample worths at many radial and axial
positions using the radial tube oscillator, axial tube oscillator, drawer oscillator and shim oscillator.
In addition, the worths of many different samples were measured in some assemblies.
Consequently, the sample worth measurements for an assembly may include many samples
measured at many radial and/or axial positions.
With the caveat in the preceding paragraphs, it may be possible to model some of the sample worth
measurements in a ZPR/ZPPR assembly if sufficient material describing the samples and sample
equipment can be located.
The following are possible ways to model the various types of small sample worth measurements
performed at the ZPR/ZPPR facilities. The discussion in the remainder of Section 7.7.3 should be
viewed as initial concepts for modeling small sample worth measurements; there may be better
methods available. In addition, what is feasible in terms of modeling and calculations changes as
computer hardware and software evolve.
In the following discussion of Monte Carlo models, specific terms and concepts associated with
MCNP such as cell, surface, universe and material cards are used. Most other Monte Carlo codes
have similar concepts that can be used to construct as-built Monte Carlo models of ZPR/ZPPR

7.7.3.1 Fuel-Thickened Zone Experiments
The model for a fuel-thickened zone experiment does not differ in any significant way from the
model for many other types of ZPR/ZPPR experiments. The limiting factor for modeling a fuel-
thickened zone experiment is finding enough information regarding a) the special foils used in the
experiment, b) the positions of those foils in the experimental drawers and c) the locations of the
experimental drawers in the assembly. The loading records for the assembly should provide the
locations of the experimental drawers in the assembly, and the report documenting the fuel-
thickened zone experiment plus the drawer master figures for the assembly may provide
information regarding the positions of the special foils in the experimental drawers.
It is necessary to find an adequate description of the special foils inserted in the fuel-thickened
zone. A description of those foils may be included in the report documenting the fuel-thickened
zone experiment. Those foils need to be added to the ADEN library. Once the special foils have
been added to the ADEN library, those foils can be treated just like standard plates in modeling
the drawer masters in the fuel-thickened zone. The software used to create a standard as-built
Monte Carlo model of a ZPR/ZPPR assembly can then be used to create a model of a fuel thickened
zone experiment. The worth of the fuel-thickened zone may be large enough to calculate by Monte
Carlo.
Because a fuel-thickened zone experiment does not differ significantly from a standard assembly
loading such as the reference critical configuration in terms of basic geometry, a deterministic
model that is equivalent to the as-built Monte Carlo model can be created using the software that
would be used to create a deterministic model of a criticality measurement (see Section 7.1).

 314

7.7.3.2 Shim Oscillator Experiments
If an adequate description of the shim oscillator and the sample foils used with the shim oscillator
can be found, modeling a shim oscillator experiment is not difficult although it does require two
additional steps compared to creating a standard as-built model of a ZPR/ZPPR assembly.
First, the shim oscillator was inserted in the space between the top of a drawer and the bottom
surface of the top of the matrix tube in one matrix location. Each unique drawer master/matrix
tube combination is represented as a universe in the as-built MCNP model (or by the equivalent
of a universe in another Monte Carlo code). The drawer master in the matrix tube where the shim
oscillator was placed was probably present in several or many matrix tubes. Suppose the shim
oscillator is inserted in drawer master D in matrix tube location L, that drawer master D is present
in many matrix tubes and that the drawer master D/matrix tube combination is universe U in the
model. Because drawer master D is present in many matrix tubes, universe U is present in many
locations in the lattice. Inserting the shim oscillator in drawer master D/universe U in the model
effectively puts the shim oscillator in every matrix tube where drawer master D is located or,
equivalently, in every lattice position containing universe U.
To put the shim oscillator in only one matrix location, it is necessary to create a drawer master D’
that is identical to drawer master D except that drawer master D’ has a different identification
number or label than drawer master D. Drawer master D’ is placed only in location L where the
shim oscillator is inserted. Drawer master D’ will correspond to a separate, unique universe, U’.
Universe U’ will be present only in the lattice position corresponding to matrix location L.
Modifying drawer master D’/universe U’ to include the shim oscillator will place the shim
oscillator at the correct location in the as-built model.
After drawer master D’ has been created, the second step is to place the shim oscillator in the
correct position in drawer master D’. There are two ways to place the shim oscillator in drawer
master D’/universe U’. The first way to place the shim oscillator in the correct position in drawer
master D’ is to include the shim oscillator and foil in the initial definition of drawer master D’.
The stainless steel shim and the sample foil are added to the ADEN library as standard plates. The
shim and sample foil are then placed in the correct positions in drawer master D’ when drawer
master D’ is defined for whatever software is used to to create the as-built model. The software
will then create the as-built Monte Carlo model with the shim oscillator in the correct position.
