This approach treats the shim and foil as standard plates for the model of drawer master D’.
This approach has been used to model experimental equipment in as-built models including the
axial expansion experiments in ZPPR-15 and the radial bowing experiment in ZPPR-17A. One
advantage of this approach is that in principle software can be used to create an equivalent
deterministic model of the shim oscillator experiment.
The second way to place the shim oscillator in the correct position is to create the as-built Monte
Carlo model including drawer master D’/universe U’ at location L but without the shim oscillator.
The shim oscillator and foil are then added to universe U’ manually. The cell cards required to
define the shim oscillator at the correct position are added to universe U’, and the existing cells in
universe U’ are modified to accommodate the shim oscillator cells. The corresponding surface
cards and material cards are inserted at the appropriate locations in the as-built Monte Carlo input

 315

file. To date a shim oscillator has not been modeled, but a similar approach was used to place
Doppler sample equipment and proton recoil spectrometers in as-built Monte Carlo models. This
approach can be used with at least some Monte Carlo codes.
7.7.3.3 Drawer Oscillator Experiments
Modeling a drawer oscillator experiment is similar to modeling a shim oscillator experiment in
many ways, but there is no need to create a clone drawer master D’ for a drawer oscillator
experiment. There is only one drawer oscillator and it is placed at only one location in the matrix,
so the drawer master defining the drawer oscillator is unique. The loading records for the drawer
oscillator measurement will show where the drawer oscillator was located in the matrix.
The first difficulty in modeling a drawer oscillator experiment is finding an adequate description
of the drawer oscillator. The drawer oscillator was a special long drawer. It may be difficult to
find a description of the drawer oscillator that provides enough information about the special
drawer, sample box and any related hardware to construct an adequate model of the drawer, sample
box and hardware. For practical purposes, the special drawer could be modeled as a drawer with
no front plate or back plate in both matrix halves.
The second difficulty in modeling a drawer oscillator experiment is that the drawer master figures
for the assembly and/or the report documenting the drawer oscillator experiment in the assembly
may not provide any description of the contents of the drawer oscillator. In principle, the drawer
master figures for an assembly include all drawer masters used in all loadings in the assembly
program. In practice, the set of available drawer master figures for an assembly is not necessarily
complete. A drawer master that was used for one measurement in a single loading may not be
included in the file of drawer master figures. It is not possible to know whether a drawer master
figure is missing because it was overlooked during scanning or because it was not retained by the
ZPR/ZPPR staff after completion of the assembly program.
If there is no drawer master figure for the drawer oscillator, it is possible that the report
documenting the drawer oscillator may provide a figure or an adequate text description of the
sample box, contents of the sample box and drawer oscillator for modeling purposes.
In any case, if there is sufficient information to model the long drawer, sample box, any related
hardware and the contents of the drawer oscillator, i.e., the sample and the plates in the drawer
oscillator, it is possible to construct an as-built model Monte Carlo model of a drawer oscillator
experiment.
The long drawer, sample box, any related hardware and most samples are not included in the
standard ADEN library, so it will be necessary to add them to the ADEN library. The drawer is
deconstructed into plates (rectangular parallelepipeds or RPPs) defining the front, back, bottom,
sides and any internal partitions, and these individual plates are added to the ADEN library. This
also applies to the sample box and to many samples placed in a sample box. Most plates in the
drawer oscillator will be in the standard ADEN library. However, the sample box was 2 x 2 x Z
inches in where Z ranged from 0.125 to 2. The plates in the sample box were shorter than most
plates used in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies, so it may be necessary to add some of the plates in the
sample box to the ADEN library.

 316

After the plates required to define the long drawer, sample box, any related hardware, the samples
and possibly some plates in the sample box have been added to the ADEN library, the drawer
master representing the drawer oscillator and sample can be defined for the software used to create
the as-built Monte Carlo model. The drawer oscillator and its contents consist entirely of RPPs,
so the drawer master representing the drawer oscillator can be modeled in the same way as any
other drawer master in the assembly. After all drawer masters have been modeled, an as-built
Monte Carlo model of the drawer oscillator experiment can be constructed in the usual manner.
In principle, the software used to create a deterministic model of a criticality measurement can be
used to create an equivalent deterministic model of the drawer oscillator experiment (see Section
7.1).
7.7.3.4 Axial Tube Oscillator Experiments
Constructing an as-built Monte Carlo model of a tube oscillator experiment requires information
about the tube oscillator and samples. Some reports documenting tube oscillator experiments
describe the samples in sufficient detail for modeling purposes, but it may be difficult to find
enough information to model the oscillator tubes accurately.
To date, description of the tube oscillators used at ZPR-3 and ZPPR have not been found, but such
descriptions may exist in some reports documenting sample worth measurements at those facilities.
The oscillator tube inner diameter had to be just slightly larger than than the outer diameter of the
samples to allow the samples to pass through without binding, and the oscillator tube wall had to
be very thin to minimize the perturbation introduced by the stainless steel in the tube. The ANL-
W oscillator tube thickness was probably in the 0.01 – 0.02 inch range because this is similar to
the thickness of the oscillator tubes used at ANL-E.
It is not clear how the tube oscillators used in ZPPR differed from the tube oscillators used in ZPR-
3 although the ZPPR tube oscillators must have been much longer than the tube oscillators used at
ZPR-3 or ANL-E. Aside from length, the tube oscillators and samples used at ZPPR were not
necessarily identical to the tube oscillators and samples used at ZPR-3. Likewise, the tube
oscillators and samples used at ANL-E were not necessarily identical to the tube oscillators and
samples used at ANL-W.
ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 generally used the same experimental equipment and materials (including
samples), so it is likely that ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 used the same tube oscillators or that they used
similar tube oscillators. Section 7.7.1 described the radial tube oscillator used ZPR-6/7. It is likely
that the radial tube oscillator used in ZPR-9 was similar or identical to the radial tube oscillator
used in ZPR-6. Note that the description of the ZPR-6 radial tube oscillator in Section 7.7.1 is the
only radial tube oscillator description that has been found. It is possible that other documents may
provide better descriptions of the radial and axial tube oscillators used at ANL-E.
Since the same samples were used in radial and axial tube oscillator measurements and the same
methods were used to position the samples in the oscillator tubes, it seems likely that the tubes
used in radial and axial tube oscillator measurements were similar or identical. This applies to
ANL-E and ANL-W.
If there is sufficient information to model the axial tube oscillator and samples, it is possible to
construct an as-built Monte Carlo model of an axial tube oscillator measurement with reasonable

 317

effort. There was only one axial tube oscillator, so the drawer master, D osc, defining the axial tube
oscillator drawer is unique. If the drawer master figures for the assembly include a figure for the
drawer containing the axial oscillator tube, there is no need to create a clone drawer master, D osc’,
for the axial tube oscillator drawer like the clone drawer master that is required for a model of a
shim oscillator measurement. The axial tube oscillator drawer master will provide sufficient
information to model the axial tube oscillator drawer and its contents except for the oscillator tube.
The as-built Monte Carlo model of the assembly can be constructed in the normal manner although
it will be necessary to leave empty space where the oscillator tube would be located. The oscillator
tube and sample are added manually to the as-built Monte Carlo model as described below.
If the drawer master figures do not include a figure for the axial oscillator drawer, it is necessary
to make two assumptions. Suppose the axial tube oscillator is installed in matrix location L, that
drawer master D was present in location L in the loading immediately prior to installation of the
axial oscillator, and that the combination of drawer master D and the surrounding matrix tube is
MCNP universe U (or equivalent structure in another Monte Carlo code). First, it necessary to
assume that the contents of the axial tube oscillator drawer are identical to the contents of drawer
master D except for that fact that the axial oscillator tube replaces one or more columns of the
plates that were present in drawer master D. This assumption seems reasonable because one
requirement of any small sample worth measurement was to minimize perturbation of the sample
environment.
Second, it is necessary to make assumptions regarding a) which column or columns of plates were
removed to make space for the axial tube oscillator and b) how the remaining plate columns may
have been moved to make space for the oscillator tube. In most cases, the axial tube oscillator
would replace one or more columns of sodium plates. In the case of the GCFR program, the axial
tube oscillator probably replaced one or more columns of the void cans used to represent coolant
channels in the GCFR. The diameter of the oscillator tube may require removal of multiple
columns of plates and an assumption regarding whether and how the remaining plate columns are
shifted laterally to make space for the tube. For example, the radial oscillator tube used in ZPR-6
had an outer diameter of one inch. It is likely that the same radial tube oscillator was used in ZPR-
9 and that the axial tube(s) in the ANL-E axial tube oscillator(s) also had an outer diameter of one
inch. The largest sodium plate thickness or void can thickness in the ZPR/ZPPR plate inventories
was 0.5 inches, so the axial tube oscillator displaced multiple plate columns in any assembly in
ZPR-6 or ZPR-9. This may have been true for ZPR-3 and ZPPR as well, but no description of the
axial tube oscillators used at ZPR-3 and ZPPR has been found. However, the inner diameter of
any axial tube oscillator used in any ZPR/ZPPR assembly would be just large enough to allow
samples to pass through without binding, and the wall of the tube would be thin to minimize the
effect of the tube on the surrounding environment.
In general, the ocillator tube would be placed in the lateral center (X-direction) of the drawer. The
plate columns removed to make space for the tube would be sodium plates (or void cans for sodium
void worth measurements) and, if necessary, other plate columns of low reactivity worth. The
remaining plate columns would be moved outward toward the sides of the drawer to make space
for the tube in the center.
The assumptions regarding the plate columns removed and any shifting of the remaining plate
columns in the oscillator drawer are not necessarily trivial and may introduce a significant

 318

uncertainty that cannot be easily quantified. If there is no drawer master figure for the axial
oscillator tube drawer, the user must carefully consider whether the assumptions required to define
a drawer master for the axial oscillator drawer introduce an unquantifiable uncertainty that reduces
the value of the axial tube oscillator measurements to an unacceptable degree and whether it is
worthwhile to proceed to modeling of the axial tube oscillator measurement.
Construction of a model for an axial oscillator tube measurement is similar to the procedure
described in Section 7.7.3.2 for a shim oscillator measurement. Suppose it is necessary to assume
that drawer master D, the drawer master present in matrix location L in the previous loading, is
representative of the axial oscillator drawer except for the presence of the oscillator tube and the
effect that insertion of the oscillator tube had on the plate loading in the drawer. Drawer master D
may be present in many matrix tubes, so universe U may be present at many locations in the lattice.
To put the axial tube oscillator in only one matrix location, it is necessary to create a clone drawer
master D’ for drawer master D. D’ has a different identification number or label than drawer
master D. Drawer master D’ is placed only in location L where the axial tube oscillator is inserted.
Drawer master D’ will correspond to a separate, unique universe, U’. Universe U’ will be present
only in the lattice position corresponding to matrix location L. Modifying drawer master D’
universe U’ to include the axial tube oscillator will place the axial tube oscillator at the correct
location in the as-built model.
Construction of the drawer master model for the axial oscillator tube drawer proceeds in the same
way whether a) there is a drawer master figure to use as a guide in constructing the model of the
axial oscillator tube drawer or b) there is no figure and the analyst constructs drawer master D’
and universe U’ to model the axial tube oscillator drawer based on the assumptions outlined above.
In either case, the drawer master model for the axial tube oscillator drawer is constructed with the
plate columns in the designated locations and with empty space where the oscillator tube is located.
The resulting as-built Monte Carlo model will have an empty space where the oscillator tube is
located.
The axial oscillator tube, sample and any push rod are added by manually modifying the as-built
Monte Carlo model. The universe defining the axial tube oscillator drawer is modified by adding
the cells defining the axial oscillator tube, sample and any push rod (for ZPR-3 or ZPPR models).
The surfaces defining these cells are added to the surface cards, and the compositions in the added
cells are added to the material cards. This description was expressed in the terms that are relevant
to MCNP (universe, cells, surface cards, material cards), but the same concept applies to any other
Monte Carlo code.
It may be possible to produce a deterministic model of an axial tube oscillator experiment using
the software used to create a deterministic model of a criticality measurement (Section 7.1), but it
may be necessary to make compromises regarding the geometry of the oscillator tube, sample and
push rod (if any). The oscillator tube, sample and any push rod were circular or annular. The
circular or annular geometry can be represented explicitly in the as-built Monte Carlo model. It
may not be possible to represent circular or annular objects exactly in a deterministic model.
Instead, it may be necessary to convert circular and annular bodies to equivalent rectangular
objects in the deterministic model. This approach was used to create models of the ZPPR-15
Doppler worth measurements. The actual Doppler samples and equipment are circular or annular,

 319

but the Doppler samples and equipment were converted to equivalent rectangular objects in the
deterministic models of the ZPPR-15 Doppler worth measurements.
7.7.3.5 Radial Tube Oscillator Experiments
If sufficient information regarding the axial tube oscillator, samples and axial tube oscillator
drawer master can be located or reconstructed with reasonable assumptions, a model of an axial
tube oscillator experiment can be constructed with modest additional effort compared to
constructing a model of the reference critical configuration. The preceding sentence does not apply
to modeling radial tube oscillator experiments. Creating a model of any radial tube oscillator
experiment involves very much additional work due to the way in which the radial tube oscillator
was installed.
For present purposes, assume there is enough information to model the radial oscillator tube,
sample and any push rod. For ZPR-6 models, assume there is enough information to model the
support under the radial oscillator tube.
In ZPR-3 and ZPPR, it appears that drawers in the center row on one side of the reactor were
pushed back slightly into the matrix tubes to make space for the radial oscillator tube. In the
present context, one side refers to the center column and to all columns on one side of the center
column, i.e., to the Y-axis of the assembly, so the affected locations were the matrix tubes in the
center row in both halves on one side of the Y-axis (vertical axis) of the assembly. The drawers
were pushed into the matrix tubes in both halves, creating space to install the oscillator tube in the
notches in the fronts of the matrix tubes in the center row.
The first issue is that the drawer masters in matrix tubes in the center row were probably present
in many other matrix tubes in the assembly. Terms from MCNP input are used to describe these
details, but the same concept should apply to any other Monte Carlo code. Suppose that drawer
masters D1, D2, D3, . . . , Dn are the drawer masters in the center row that are pushed back to make
space for the radial oscillator tube and that universes U1, U2, U3, . . . , Un are the universes that
correspond to drawer masters D1, D2, D3, . . ., Dn, respectively. It is likely that drawer masters D1,
D2, D3, . . . , Dn are present in many matrix tubes in the assembly, so universes U 1, U2, U3, . . . , Un
are present in many lattice positions.
It is necessary to create drawer masters D1’, D2’, D3’, . . . , Dn’ as clones of drawer masters D1, D2,
D3, . . . , Dn, respectively. Universes U1’, U2’, U3’, . . . , Un’ correspond to drawer masters D1’,
D2’, D3’, . . . , Dn’, respectively. Drawer masters D1’, D2’, D3’, . . . , Dn’ replace drawer masters
D1, D2, D3, . . . , Dn, respectively, in the center row positions where drawers are pushed into the
matrix tubes, and universes U1’, U2’, U3’, . . . , Un’ replace universes U1, U2, U3, . . . , Un,
respectively, in the lattice positions where the radial tube oscillator is installed. In MCNP, it may
be possible to use the tr cards or trcl cards to translate these universes such that they appear at the
offset coordinates. Other Monte Carlo codes may have equivalent capabilities.
Creating drawer masters D1’, D2’, D3’, . . . , Dn’ is step 1. Step 1 is not difficult because there is
no difference between drawer masters D1, D2, D3, . . . , Dn and drawer masters D1’, D2’, D3’, . . . ,
Dn’, respectively, except for their positioning in the matrix tubes.
Step 2 is recessing drawer masters D1’, D2’, D3’, . . . , Dn’ in the matrix tubes. As stated, it may
be possible to use the tr cards and trcl cards in MCNP (or their equivalents in other Monte Carlo

 320

codes) to reposition the drawer universes in the lattice to enable the offset. As an alternative, the
software used to create the drawer master models and the as-built Monte Carlo model may allow
the drawer to be recessed in the matrix tube when the drawer masters are created. In that case,
drawer masters D1’, D2’, D3’, . . . , Dn’ will be positioned correctly, and step 2 will be complete.
In some Monte Carlo codes it may be necessary to make the adjustment in the drawer positions
manually. While it is possible in principle to make the necessary adjustments manually, that
process is likely to be tedious, difficult and prone to errors because there may be many axial planes
or surfaces that require adjustment. One complication for step 2 is that the Monte Carlo code may
use the same surfaces to define the axial positions of of plates and drawer components in many
different drawer masters including D1, D2, D3, . . ., Dn and many other drawer masters that are not
recessed in the matrix tubes.
Step 2 is not trivial if it is necessary to write an auxiliary code to perform the modification or to
make adjustments manually, especially if there are many drawer masters D 1’, D2’, D3’, . . . , Dn’.
On the other hand, after the auxiliary code is written, it can be used for all subsequent models of
radial oscillator tube measurements.
If steps 1 and 2 can be accomplished, step 3 is to manually modify universes U 1’, U2’, U3’, . . . ,
Un’ to add the radial oscillator tube, sample and any push rod with the sample at the correct radial
position in the center row. Note that the first inch of the matrix tube is typically treated
homogeneously to avoid specifying the notches, so this effort will involve introducing space and
adjusting the mass densities of those affected regions. In general, step 3 requires a) adding the
appropriate cell cards to universes U1’, U2’, U3’, . . . , Un’ for the radial oscillator tube, sample and
any push rod, b) inserting the surface cards needed to define those structures, and c) inserting the
corresponding material cards required to specify compositions for the radial oscillator tube, sample
and any push rod.
The process for modeling a radial oscillator tube experiment described above applies to ZPR-6
with two minor differences. First, the radial tube oscillator was installed in the stationary half of
ZPR-6, so it is not necessary to clone any drawers in the movable half of ZPR-6. Second, the
radial oscillator tube in ZPR-6 sat on a support, so it is necessary to add the support manually when
the radial oscillator tube and sample are added to the ZPR-6 radial oscillator tube experiment.
In ZPR-9, the radial tube oscillator was installed through 1.25 inch holes in the sides of the matrix
tubes on one side of row 23, the center row of the ZPR-9 matrix tubes, in the stationary half. The
centers of the matrix tube holes were 1.75 inches from the fronts of the matrix tubes and were
vertically centered in the matrix tubes.
Because the radial tube oscillator had to pass through all matrix tubes, drawers and plates between
the center of the reactor and the outer edge of the ZPR-9 matrix, special drawers were used in the
matrix tubes through which the radial oscillator tube passed. These drawers had 1.25 inch holes
in their sides that aligned with the corresponding holes in the matrix tubes. These special drawers
and matrix tubes allowed the radial oscillator tube to extend from the center of ZPR-9 to the outer
edge of ZPR-9.
The loading of these special drawers differed from the loading of standard drawers in the ZPR-9
assembly. For some standard plate types such as iron oxide plates and depleted uranium oxide
plates, the ANL-E plate inventory contained special versions with holes drilled to accommodate

 321

the radial oscillator tube. There were no drilled Pu-U-Mo plates, so Pu-U-Mo plates were replaced
by empty stainless steel void frames at the locations where the radial oscillator tube passed through
the special drawers.
It is possible that the drawer master figures for a ZPR-9 assembly will include drawer master
figures for all of the special drawers that were present during the radial tube oscillator experiment.
In that case, the analyst can construct drawer master models in the normal manner for all drawer
masters including the drawer masters for the special drawers. The as-built Monte Carlo model can
be constructed in the normal manner but the introduction of circular holes might complicate the
construction of this model depending upon the assumptions made about plate geometries in the
code that builds the Monte Carlo model. The as-built model will likely not include the radial
oscillator tube or samples. The as-built Monte Carlo model must be modified manually to add the
cells defining the radial oscillator tube and samples to the universes that define the special drawers,
to add the surfaces that define the radial oscillator tube and sample to the surface cards and to add
any compositions required for the radial oscillator tube and sample to the material cards.
If the drawer master figures for the assembly do not include figures for the special drawers, then
it is necessary to create a set of cloned drawer masters as described above. This raises a question
regarding how much additional uncertainty is associated with the assumptions required to define
the drawer masters through which the oscillator tube passes. The most significant assumption is
the assumption regarding the plate loading in the first few inches at the front of the drawer because
that is where the oscillator tube is located.
Suppose that drawer masters D1, D2, D3, . . . , Dn are the drawer masters in the center row through
which the radial oscillator tube passes and that universes U 1, U2, U3, . . . , Un are the universes that
correspond to drawer masters D1, D2, D3, . . ., Dn, respectively. It is likely that drawer masters D1,
D2, D3, . . . , Dn are present in many matrix tubes in the assembly, so universes U 1, U2, U3, . . . , Un
are present in many Monte Carlo lattice positions. Note that drawer masters D 1, D2, D3, . . . , Dn
will be the drawer masters that were present in the matrix tubes in the previous loading, i.e., the
loading immediately preceding the loading in which the radial tube oscillator measurement is
made.
It is necessary to create drawer masters D1’, D2’, D3’, . . . , Dn’ as clones of drawer masters D1, D2,
D3, . . . , Dn, respectively as described above. Creating drawer masters D1’, D2’, D3’, . . . , Dn’ is
step 1.
Step 2 is modifying drawer masters D1’, D2’, D3’, . . . , Dn’ to account for the effect of the radial
oscillator tube on the plate loadings in these drawer masters. For some standard plate types such
as iron oxide plates and depleted uranium oxide plates, the ANL-E plate inventory contained
special versions with holes drilled to accommodate the radial oscillator tube. There were no drilled
Pu-U-Mo plates, so Pu-U-Mo plates were replaced by empty stainless steel void frames at the
locations where the radial oscillator tube passed through the special drawers.
The hole through which the tube passed was 1.75 inches from the front of the matrix tube and had
a diameter of 1.25 inches, so this hole extended from 1.125 inches to 2.375 inches. Plates generally
had standard lengths that were integer multiples of one inch, so it is likely that any drilled plate or
void frame had a length of at least three inches.

 322

The alternate possibility is that the front of the drawer contained one inch plates, which would
allow two inch plates to be placed where the oscillator tube was positioned. This is possible, but
it seems unlikely because one inch plates were available for only a few plate types.
In the few cases where the standard ADEN library includes a plate with a hole such as a sodium
tunnel plate, the hole is homogenized with the rest of the plate material to conserve mass. Putting
the oscillator tube through such a plate would have the effect of double counting the hole in the
plate. Consequently, any plates in the standard ADEN library with holes should be ignored.
For modeling purposes, some reasonable assumptions may be required regarding the the
modifications required in drawer masters D1’, D2’, D3’, . . . , Dn’ to account for the oscillator tube.
For example, the plates in drawer masters D1’, D2’, D3’, . . . , Dn’ will not be identical to the plates
in D1, D2, D3, . . . , Dn because the plates in D1’, D2’, D3’, . . . , Dn’ must account for the hole
required to install the oscillator tube. Note that drawer masters D1, D2, D3, . . . , Dn may offer some
guidance regarding what constitutes reasonable assumptions, particularly with respect to the likely
plates in drawer masters D1’, D2’, D3’, . . . , Dn’.
It is recommended that the analyst should place standard plates or void frames with a length of at
least three inches in the fronts of drawer masters D 1’, D2’, D3’, . . . , Dn’. Subsequent modification
of universes U1’, U2’, U3’, . . . , Un’ will account for the oscillator tube and for the holes in the
plates, drawers and matrix tubes.
After the required modifications have been made in the models for drawer masters D 1’, D2’, D3’, .
. . , Dn’, the as-built Monte Carlo model can be constructed in the normal manner. Universes U 1’,
U2’, U3’, . . . , Un’ will correspond to drawer masters D1’, D2’, D3’, . . . , Dn’, respectively. Drawer
masters D1’, D2’, D3’, . . . , Dn’ replace drawer masters D1, D2, D3, . . . , Dn, respectively, in the
center row positions where the oscillator tube is installed, and universes U 1’, U2’, U3’, . . . , Un’
replace universes U1, U2, U3, . . . , Un, respectively, in the lattice positions where the radial tube
oscillator is installed.
The as-built Monte Carlo model described in the preceding paragraph does not contain the
oscillator tube or sample. This as-built Monte Carlo model must be modified to add the cells
defining the radial oscillator tube and samples to the universes (U 1’, U2’, U3’, . . . , Un’) that define
the special drawers, to add the surfaces that define the radial oscillator tube and sample to the
surface cards and to add any compositions required for the radial oscillator tube and sample to the
material cards. This modification can be performed manually or by writing an auxialiary code to
automate the process.
The drawers in ZPR-9 were not recessed to make space for the radial tube oscillator, so it is not
necessary to adjust the as-built Monte Carlo model of a ZPR-9 radial tube oscillator experiment to
account for any recessed drawers in the center row of the matrix.
At present it is not clear whether it is possible to create a deterministic model of a radial tube
oscillator experiment because it is not clear how the radial oscillator tube would be included in the
deterministic model. Creation of a deterministic model of a radial tube oscillator experiment
would require much more work than creation of a deterministic model of a fuel-thickened zone
experiment, shim oscillator experiment, drawer oscillator experiment or axial tube oscillator
experiment.

 323

In addition, a deterministic model of a radial tube oscillator experiment would require more
compromises with respect to geometry than a deterministic model of a fuel-thickened zone
experiment, shim oscillator experiment, drawer oscillator experiment or axial tube oscillator
experiment. The geometric compromises are most significant for ZPR-9 due to the method in
which the radial tube oscillator was installed in ZPR-9.
Clearly, creating an as-built Monte Carlo model of a radial tube oscillator experiment requires a
lot of extra work compared to creating an as-built Monte Carlo model of most other experiments.
The analyst must decide whether the value of the radial sample worth measurements is consistent
with the amount of effort required to create as-built Monte Carlo models and/or equivalent
deterministic models and with the difficulty of the calculations.
With regard to modeling small sample worth experiments, it is noted that some of the ZPR/ZPPR
small sample data is unique and that the U.S. does not currently have the capability to obtain that
data in an assembly similar to a ZPR/ZPPR assembly and probably will not have such a capability
at any time in the foreseeable future. Sample worths can probably be measured at the National
Critical Experiment Research Center (NCERC) in Nevada, but the available facilities at NCERC
cannot model a fast reactor at the level of detail provided by ZPR/ZPPR assemblies.
7.7.4 Modeling and Analysis of Small Sample Worth Measurements
When the ZPR/ZPPR facilities operated, all analyses of small sample worth measurements were
based on calculations with deterministic models. Those deterministic models improved over the
years between 1955 and 1990 as computer software and hardware improved, and C/Es improved.
The ZPR/ZPPR staff invested much time and effort in analyzing small sample worth measurements
and investigating the central worth discrepancy; experiments were performed to examine possible
sources of the central worth discrepancy. Much of the investigation of the central worth
discrepancy was focused on four heavy absorbers: 235U, 238U, 239Pu and 10B.
The ZPR/ZPPR staff investigated the effect of delayed neutron parameters on the central worth
discrepancy and concluded that the central worth discrepancy is sensitive to the delayed neutron
parameters, particularly delayed neutron yields. Differences in the delayed neutron parameters
likely affect calculated reactivity worth due to their effect on nuclear data processing and cross
section generation. Use of modern delayed neutron data, modern evaluated nuclear data and
modern nuclear data and cross section processing codes might improve the accuracy of modern
sample worth calculations relative to the accuracy achievable when the ZPR/ZPPR facilities
operated.
The delayed neutron parameters also affect the conversion of the measured reactor response to
reactivity worth. The measured reactor response data are no longer available, so it is impossible
to improve measured sample worths by applying modern delayed neutron parameters to the
conversion of measured reactor responses to sample reactivity worths. The published small sample
worths are the best available values.
There are several separate areas that relate to understanding the central worth discrepancy. First,
reactivity measurement techniques and reactor response unfolding (derivation of reactivity worth
from the measured reactor response to the sample insertion) could affect measured sample worths.
A fundamental component of the reactivity measurement technique is the method used to introduce

 324

the sample into the reactor and the resulting perturbation of the environment at the sample location.
In ZPR/ZPPR sample worth measurements, fuel-thickened zone experiments and the shim
oscillator introduced minimal perturbations in the location where the sample was placed. The
drawer oscillator closely resembled a standard drawer, so the drawer oscillator introduced only a
small perturbation in the sample environment. The radial and axial tube oscillators introduced
much larger perturbations in the local geometry where the sample was measured due to the changes
in local geometry required to install the oscillator tubes. In addition, the radial and axial tube
oscillators introduced extra steel in the form of the oscillator tubes and any push rod used to
position the samples. The effects of the radial and axial tube oscillators on the sample environment
are not small. Ref. 17 stated that the use of radial and axial tube oscillators is limited to samples
and assemblies in which these perturbations can be ignored and in which calculations can be
performed with an unperturbed flux.
Second, C/Es may be sensitive to the characteristics of individual assemblies. The composition
and degree of heterogeneity in plate loading could be very different between two assemblies, and
these differences produce corresponding differences in the neutron spectra of the two assemblies.
The C/E for a sample measured in one assembly could be significantly different from the C/E for
the same sample measured in another assembly due to differences between the two assemblies.
Third, calculational models and reactor physics codes evolved over the years. The initial
calculations of ZPR-3 small sample worth measurements were performed with one-dimensional
spherical geometry or possibly cylindrical geometry because these were the only options available.
Over the years, these one-dimensional models were supplanted by R-Z models, X-Y models and
X-Y-Z models as the capabilities of the reactor physics codes and computer hardware evolved.
However, computer hardware in the ZPR/ZPPR era still limited the sizes of mesh intervals in larger
models, particularly X-Y-Z models.
Fourth, any uncertainties or errors in the basic nuclear data or in the broad group cross sections
used for the calculations will affect C/Es. The quality of the nuclear data improved significantly
over the period when the ZPR/ZPPR facilities operated. The early ZPR-3 small sample worth
measurements were probably analyzed with multigroup cross sections based upon ENDF/B-I data.
The later ZPPR small sample worth measurements were likely analyzed with multigroup cross
sections based upon ENDF/B-V data. Much later nuclear data evaluations are available today.
The approximations required to convert the basic nuclear data to the broad group cross sections
used in deterministic calculations can have a significant impact on C/Es. One significant
approximation is that required to model some sample worth measurement techniques in the cross
section processing codes. No approximation was required for fuel-thickened experiments because
the fuel-thickened zone drawer masters were completely compatible with MC 2-II and SDX, the
codes used to generate multigroup cross sections when the ZPR/ZPPR machines operated. The
foil used in the shim oscillator was thin and spanned the tops of the plates in the drawer. The
orientation and position of the shim oscillator would have complicated generation of accurate
multigroup cross sections.
Whether the drawer oscillator required significant approximations for MC2-II/SDX purposes
depends upon the sample box and the contents of the sample box. If the 2 x 2 x 2 inch sample box
was used with regular plates, the drawer oscillator configuration was compatible with MC 2-
II/SDX, and any modeling approximation was minor. Alternatively, if the 2 x 2 x 2 inch sample

 325

box was filled with a single large sample, the resulting configuration might require significant
approximations for cross section generation purposes. Likewise, a smaller sample box that was
positioned transverse to the regular plate columns in the drawer oscillator could require significant
approximations for cross section generation purposes.
Radial and axial tube oscillators introduced significant perturbations in the sample environment.
These perturbations were difficult to model for cross section generation purposes. That is why
Ref. 17 stated that the use of the tube oscillators is limited to cases in which the perturbations can
ignored and in which calculations can be performed with an unperturbed flux. That probably
meant cases in which the sample worth was sufficiently large that the local perturbations in the
sample environment introduced by the sample and sample equipment had only a minor effect on
calculated sample worths. Radial and axial tube oscillator measurements required significant
assumptions or approximations for cross section generation purposes. In any case, Refs. 17 and
18 showed that it is important to model the sample environment including the sample and the
sample equipment as accurately as possible to minimize the perturbation introduced by the sample
and sample equipment on the calculated sample worth and C/E.
7.8 Neutron Spectrum Measurements
Several different techniques existed for measuring the neutron spectrum in a critical assembly
[16,21] when the ZPR/ZPPR machines operated, but the requirement that the experimental
equipment must fit into a drawer eliminated some of those options. The two primary methods
used to measure neutron spectra in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies were measurements of spectral indices,
i.e., reaction rate ratios, and spectrum measurements with proton recoil spectrometers.
Spectral indices are discussed below as a type of foil irradiation measurement. Spectral index
measurements have two advantages. The first advantage is that spectral index measurements can
be made at many locations simultaneously. Foils can be placed in many drawers in the core, radial
blanket and radial reflector in the same core loading. Likewise, foils can be placed in many
positions on the X-axis, Y-axis, Z-axis and diagonal in the same core loading. All of the foils are
irradiated simultaneously in the same reactor startup/run. The only limitations are the number of
foils of each type in the inventory, the effort required to load the foils into the drawers, the effort
required to remove the foils from the drawers and the effort required to count the foils.
The second advantage of spectral index measurements is that in a sense they are free. Reaction
rate distributions were standard measurements, so the data for 235U(n,f), 238U(n,f), 238U(n,γ) and
239
 Pu(n,f) were available because these were the standard reaction rate distributions that were
measured in most assemblies. Determining the spectral indices generally involved using foil data
that would exist in any case when reaction rate distributions were measured. Normally, the
denominator for a spectral index was either 235U(n,f) or 239Pu(n,f).
The disadvantage of a spectral index is that a spectral index is a relatively crude measure of the
neutron spectrum at any given location. The distribution of spectral index values as a function of
position provided a coarse indicator of the change in spectrum as a function of position, but a
spectral index value does not provide a detailed neutron spectrum at any location.
Proton recoil spectrometers were used for detailed neutron spectrum measurements in ZPR/ZPPR
assemblies. The advantages of a proton recoil spectrometer measurement for a ZPR/ZPPR

 326

assembly are that a) the basic measurement provided very detailed spectrum data over the
applicable energy range of the spectrometer and b) the measured spectrum data could be collapsed
into the energy group structures that the ANL staff used for fast reactor analysis. This allowed for
a direct comparison of measured and calculated neutron spectra. The disadvantages of the proton
recoil spectrometer method are that a) the spectrometer was located in one drawer at a single
location in the assembly and b) the spectrometer measurement and analysis of the resulting data
were difficult, tedious processes.
The proton recoil spectrometer required a slightly subcritical reactor to avoid saturating the
electronics and the need for dead-time corrections. According to Ref. 16, early spectrometer
measurements in plutonium-fueled assemblies required a highly subcritical reactor (as much as
10% subcritical). By 1970 when Ref. 16 was published, the required subcritical margin had been
reduced to ~1%.
7.8.1 Proton Recoil Spectrometer Measurement Technique
The proton recoil spectrometers used for spectrum measurements in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies were
gas-filled proportional counters. The basic operating principle of those gas-filled proportional
counters is that neutron scattering in the gas creates recoil nuclei in the gas. The recoil nuclei
create ionization that the proportional counter detects.
The actual counter consisted of a small, thin-walled stainless steel cylinder or tube filled with gas.
The outer tube functioned as the cathode; a thin wire in the center of the tube functioned as the
anode. The counter was connected to a preamplifier and associated equipment.
The choice of fill gas in the counter is an important determinant of counter performance. The fill
gases used for the ZPR/ZPPR proportional counters were hydrogen and methane. Hydrogen was
an obvious choice because the scattering cross section of hydrogen is well known and large. The
hydrogen-filled counter worked well down to energies around 1 keV, but the useful upper limit for
the hydrogen-filled counter was several hundred keV. For energies above a few hundred keV, it
was necessary to use a fill gas with higher stopping power such as methane. A methane-filled
counter had an effective lower energy limit of 100 keV and an effective upper energy limit in the
MeV range.
The proportional counter had to discriminate between ionization pulses produced by neutron
scattering in the fill gas and ionization pulses produced by gamma ray interactions. The neutron-
induced ionization pulses resulted from neutron scattering in the fill gas. There was relatively little
gamma scattering in the low-density fill gas; gamma-induced ionization pulses resulted primarily
from electrons created by gamma interactions with the stainless steel counter tube.
Some gammas reaching the counter were produced during the reactor run in which the
spectrometer measurement was being made. However, a significant fraction of the gammas
reaching the counter were decay gammas from previous irradiations, i.e., previous reactor runs.
Improvements in electronics and development of reliable multichannel analysis facilitated
discrimination between neutron-induced pulses and gamma-induced pulses based on pulse shape
and size. The recoil nucleus from neutron scattering produced ionization over a relatively short
track, resulting in a large, narrow pulse. The electron resulting from gamma scattering produced

 327

much less ionization over a longer track and could even escape from the gas. As a result, the
gamma-induced pulse was significantly smaller and broader than a neutron-induced pulse.
The gamma problem could be reduced in several ways. One option was to place the counter tube
in a thin lead sleeve to reduce the gamma flux reaching the counter. Section C and Table II of Ref.
22 show how effectively even a very thin lead sleeve can reduce the electron background produced
by gamma scattering in a proton recoil spectrometer.
In addition to placing the counter tube in a lead sleeve, a second way to minimize the gamma flux
was to perform the spectrum measurement during the initial approach-to-critical before significant
fission products could accumulate in the assembly. Another way to minimize the gamma flux was
to perform the spectrum measurement after the reactor had been shut down for a few days, e.g., on
a Monday, because the shutdown period allowed some of the fission products in the assembly to
decay.
Placing the counter tube in a lead sleeve and carefully choosing the date for the spectrum
measurement significantly reduced the problem of false counts produced by gamma scattering.
Two gas-filled proportional counters were used for neutron spectrum measurements in ZPR/ZPPR
assemblies. One counter consisted of a stainless steel cylinder filled with hydrogen gas, and the
other counter consisted of a stainless steel cylinder filled predominantly with methane gas. A
small amount of nitrogen gas was added to the hydrogen or methane in the counters. Thermal
neutrons created monoenergetic 585 keV protons via the 14N(n,p)14C reaction. These protons were
used to establish an absolute relationship between pulse height and proton energy for the counters.
For neutron spectrum measurements at ZPR-6 and ZPR-9, the proportional counters were
calibrated in a thermal spectrum in the Argonne Thermal Source Reactor (ATSR) at ANL-E. For
neutron spectrum measurements in ZPPR assemblies, the proportional counters were calibrated in
a thermal spectrum in the thermal column of the Argonne Fast Source Reactor (AFSR) at ANL-
W. The AFSR began operations in October 1959, so any spectrometers used in ZPR-3 after the
AFSR startup could have been calibrated in AFSR.
Davey and Redman [16] lists typical design information for the proton recoil spectrometers used
at Argonne in the 1960s. The counter tube consisted of stainless steel with a wall thickness of ~0.8
mm. The hydrogen-filled counter had a diameter of ~16 mm and an effective length of ~32 mm.
The hydrogen gas pressure in the tube was ~5 atm, and the hydrogen-filled tube also contained a
small amount of methane. The methane-filled counter had a diameter of ~25 mm and an effective
length of ~61 mm. The methane gas pressure in the tube was ~5 atm. Both counter tubes contained
a small amount of nitrogen. A 6 mm lead sleeve surrounded the counter tube.
In fact, there were various Argonne spectrometer designs. E. F. Bennett and T. J. Yule were the
primary developers of the proton recoil spectrometer technique as it was used in ZPR/ZPPR
neutron spectrum measurements [22]. Figure 2 of ANL-7763 shows hydrogen-filled and methane-
filled counters with dimensions that are slightly different from the values listed in the preceding
paragraph. The counters shown in ANL-7763 would be typical of counters used in ZPR-6 and
ZPR-9 in the early 1970s. Figure 7.22 is a reproduction of Figure 2 in ANL-7763. However, the
counter and spectrometer designs evolved over time, and sometimes a new design was developed
for a specific assembly program.

 328

 Figure 7.22. Hydrogen and Methane Counters Shown in ANL-7763.
ANL-7763 states that the hydrogen gas pressure was ~10 atm and the methane gas pressure was
~8 atm. Bennett and Yule [22] note that these are approximately the upper limits for gas pressure
because resolution worsens at higher gas pressures due to electron capture in contaminants in the
gas. Note that these gas pressures are significantly higher than the values listed by Davey and
Redman [16].
Bennett and Yule also noted that the counter tube sizes had to be limited in plutonium-fueled
assemblies. The Pu-U-Mo fuel plates used in the ZPR/ZPPR assemblies contained 28 wt.%
plutonium, and the plutonium in the Pu-U-Mo plates contained 11 wt.% 240Pu. Spontaneous fission
in 240Pu produced a high neutron flux even in configurations that were far subcritical. In order to
perform spectrum measurements in plutonium-fueled configurations that were only slightly
subcritical (1% – 2% subcritical), counter tubes had to be small to avoid saturating the electronics.
Spectrometer designs evolved over the years, so different facilities probably used different
spectrometer designs. In ZPPR-2, for example, one counter consisted of a 9.53 mm diameter
cylinder filled with hydrogen gas at 10 atmospheres total pressure, and the other counter consisted

 329

of a 15.9 mm diameter cylinder filled predominantly with methane gas at 8.2 atmospheres pressure.
The active length of each counter was approximately 25 mm. A 12.7 mm lead sleeve was placed
around each counter to reduce the gamma background. The counter and associated hardware
occupied a 50.8 x 50.8 x 254 mm volume at the front of the drawer for these measurements.
The point is that there was not a standardized spectrometer that was used at all times in all facilities.
In some cases, a spectrometer might be designed for a specific program. The counter tubes used
in the GCFR Program (ZPR-9/28, ZPR-9/29 and ZPR-9/30) were designed for that program and
were larger than the standard counter tubes used in earlier assemblies. It is necessary to consult
available documents to find any available information regarding the spectrometer used in a given

The proton recoil spectrometer and some of the associated electronics such as the preamplifier
were loaded in the front of a drawer. Some or all of the remaining space in the drawer was filled
with normal plates for the core, blanket or reflector, depending on the location of the drawer in the
matrix. Typically, the spectrometer was placed in the center of the core, but there were exceptions
in which spectra were desired in other locations.
Several computer codes were used in sequence to process the raw data from the spectrum
measurement. Collectively, these codes were referred to as the Proton Spectrum to Neutron
Spectrum (PSNS) codes. In addition to processing the data, the PSNS codes corrected for
systematic measurement errors that are inherent in this form of neutron spectroscopy.
Initially, there were five PSNS codes. The following discussion of their functions is taken from
Ref. 22.
PSNS-1 performed a survey of the measured data and identified any problems in the measured
data.
The first systematic error in the measured data was the nonlinear relationship between energy and
ionization at low energies, which introduced errors into the measurement for lower energy
neutrons. The PSNS-2 code corrected the measured data for this effect.
The internal electric field lines were distorted near the ends of the counter, creating a transition
region where multiplication decreased gradually relative to multiplication in the main part of the
chamber. This effect introduced the second systematic error into the measured data because events
near the ends of the counter did not produce the same response as events in the main part of the
chamber. The PSNS-2 code applied an electric field response function to correct the spectrum for
the internal electric field distortion. The designs of the counters used for some spectrum
measurements eliminated the need for this correction.
The third systematic error in the measured data was a result of the finite size of the spectrometer.
Some proton-recoil tracks hit the walls of the chamber and were truncated. Other tracks entered
the end regions of the chamber where there was no multiplication. In either case, collection of
ionization in the sensitive region of the counter was incomplete, so the relationship of proton
energy to collected ionization was biased. The PSNS-3 code corrected for the wall-and-end
distortion created by the finite size of the detector in the methane counter. The PSNS-4 code
applied the corresponding wall-and-end response correction to data obtained with the hydrogen
counter.

 330

The fourth correction related to carbon scattering in the methane counter. The ionization spectrum
in the methane-filled spectrometer contained proton recoils, electrons from gamma interactions
and carbon recoils from elastic scattering of neutrons by carbon. Carbon recoils produce about
25% less ionization than proton recoils for the same incident neutron energy, and the elastic
scattering cross sections of carbon and hydrogen are different. Both of these factors introduce
errors into the measured spectra. The PSNS-3 code included a correction for carbon recoils in the
methane counter.
PSNS-5 derived the final neutron spectrum from the corrected proton recoil data produced by the
first four codes in the series.
The PSNS codes, measurement equipment and data processing procedures evolved between 1971
when ANL-7763 was issued and the dates of later ZPPR spectrum measurements. The original
five PSNS codes were merged into a single code and simplified at ZPPR. Many of the corrections
applied by the original PSNS codes were either rendered unnecessary by improvements in
equipment and procedures or were shown to have little effect on improving the data. The need for
electric field corrections was eliminated by changes in the proportional counter design. The
correction for variations in the energy release (W) per ion pair formed as a function of energy (E)
was eliminated because there were large uncertainties in the energy release. The uncertainties in
the corrections for wall-and-end effects in the counter chamber, i.e., for the finite size of the
counter chamber, have uncertainties whose magnitudes are comparable to the resulting corrections.
Corrections for carbon recoils were retained in the revised code. The code that subtracts the
gamma contribution was rewritten at ZPPR, and codes that produced graphic displays of the
spectrum data were written.
7.8.2 Uncertainty Analysis for Neutron Spectrum Measurements
It is difficult to perform an accurate uncertainty analysis for the neutron spectrum measurements
because much of the required information was either never published or was published in an
incomplete form by the experimenters. Again, the problem is that the information published by
the ZPR/ZPPR experimenters was adequate to meet the needs of the sponsors and ANL analysts
when the experiments were performed. The desire to fully quantify and document all significant
uncertainties that exists today was much less prevalent in the period when the ZPR/ZPPR machines
operated.
The radial position of the counter in the drawer was fixed by supports. The axial position of the
counter in the drawer was fixed by the preamplifier and by various support plates in the counter
drawer. The internal components of the counter drawer eliminate any significant uncertainty
regarding the position of the counter.
There are small uncertainties in the dimensions and compositions of the components of the proton
recoil spectrometer just as there are uncertainties in the dimensions and compositions of the plates,
drawers and matrix tubes in the assembly. These uncertainties do not affect the actual measured
values, but they could have a small effect on calculated spectra.
n principle, the uncertainties in dimensions and compositions of the plates, drawers, matrix tubes
and components of the spectrometer make a small contribution to the total uncertainty for the
measured spectrum because the dimension and composition uncertainties affect the accuracy of

 331

the model used for calculations of the spectrum. In practice, the contribution of any uncertainties
in component dimensions and compositions to the total uncertainty is likely to be negligible
compared to the uncertainties associated with the measurement and the measured spectrum.
Performing proton recoil spectrometer measurements, analyzing the resulting measured data and
converting the measured data to a neutron spectrum were difficult, tedious tasks. E. F. Bennett
and T. J. Yule probably performed all of the neutron spectrum measurements at ANL-E. It seems
likely that neutron spectrum measurements at ANL-W also were performed by one or two people
who specialized in those measurements. ZPPR loading records and logbooks, for example,
sometimes specify that a particular individual will install and remove experimental equipment.
One problem with the published neutron spectra is that much of the published data is graphical.
In particular, this is true for comparisons between measured and calculated spectra. It seems likely
that the only way to use the graphical data at present is to use optical character recognition (OCR)
software to convert graphical data to digital data. That approach was used for at least one
ICSBEP/IRPhEP benchmark for another reactor, but it introduces an additional uncertainty related
to the conversion. Quantifying the uncertainty associated with the OCR conversion process
requires the user to make assumptions regarding the accuracy of the original graphical data and
the accuracy of the subsequent OCR conversion from graphical data back to digital data. In
addition, the graphical spectrum data generally do not include the uncertainties assigned by the
experimenters to the measured spectrum data, which makes it difficult or impossible to quantify
any uncertainties for the measured spectra unless additional information is provided in available
documents.
Unless the reader has experience with performing neutron spectrum measurements, it is generally
necessary to rely on the information published by the experimenters to quantify the uncertainties
associated with the published spectra. For tabular data, the published uncertainties include the
uncertainties in the measured count rates after the raw data were processed as described here, but
it may not be clear whether the published uncertainties include more than just the statistical
uncertainties in the count rates. Known systematic measurement errors were corrected with the
PSNS codes or the equivalent ZPPR software, but there are uncertainties associated with some of
those corrections. To date, published reports for the spectrum measurements in ZPPR-2, ZPR-
9/29 and ZPPR-15 have been reviewed and, none of those reports makes any explicit statements
regarding the uncertainties in the PSNS corrections.
In the published report for the ZPPR-2 spectrum measurement, the experimenters stated that the
measured spectra should be “relatively free of systematic errors” and that the uncertainties listed
with the processed data should be representative of the uncertainties associated with the
measurement. There is no further information.
In the ZPR-9/29 report on the neutron spectrum measurement, the tabular data listed the measured
flux, the error and the resolution. No additional information was provided. The ZPR-9/29
spectrum measurements were performed by E. F. Bennett and T. J. Yule, the ZPR staff members
who developed the proton recoil spectroscopy technique as it was used at ANL. It is reasonable to
assume that Bennett and Yule would have accounted for all known uncertainties in the data
processing.

 332

The ZPR-9/29 report listed the resolution or full width at half-maximum (FWHM) for the
measurements. The resolution clearly deteriorates at lower neutron energies. The FWHM is 2.35σ
for the assumed Gaussian distribution (Ref. 21, pages 113 – 116). The total uncertainty for the
ZPR-9/29 spectrum measurement was assumed to be the quadrature sum of the statistical
uncertainty and the uncertainty related to the resolution or FWHM because no additional
information was provided.
The report on the ZPPR-15 neutron spectrum measurements listed uncertainties. However, the
experimenters stated that additional uncertainties of 5% to 10% are applicable below 10 keV and
above 1 MeV, but they do not specify the source of these additional uncertainties. The
experimenters also stated that uncertainties in the energy calibration for both counters have
correlated components estimated to be 1% increasing to about 15% for the range below 2 keV in
the hydrogen counter. The experimenters did not provide any additional information on this issue.
For the work done recently, assumptions were made about the distribution of these additional
uncertainties.
The point of this discussion concerning the uncertainties in the spectrum measurements, like those
which have been reviewed thus far (ZPPR-2, ZPR-9/29 and ZPPR-15), is that the information
provided by the experimenters is likely to be incomplete. Unless the reader has practical
experience regarding neutron spectrum measurements, it seems necessary for the reader using the
ZPR/ZPPR spectrum data either to accept the published uncertainties as the best values available
today or to make reasonable assumptions about the total uncertainties for the spectrum

7.8.3 Modeling Neutron Spectrum Measurements
The difficult part of constructing as-built Monte Carlo models for neutron spectrum measurements
is modeling the proton recoil spectrometer. Modeling the remainder of the core follows the
standard process described in Section 7.1.5. The loading records are processed to create the matrix
map for the relevant loading, and the drawer master records are processed to define the drawer
masters.
From experience, the drawer master describing the spectrometer drawer will show the plates in the
drawer, but the spaces occupied by the counter tube, supports, preamplifier, etc. will be blank.
Pictures of the device further help to understand the layout of components. To date, an as-built
Monte Carlo model has been constructed with empty volumes where the spectrometer equipment
is located and then later was modified to add the spectrometer.
The report for the spectrum measurement will probably describe the counter tube and its position.
The supports for the counter tube may be described. If the supports are not described, it may be
possible to make reasonable assumptions about the supports or to ignore them. The supports are
small, and they would have been designed to have little or no impact on the measurement.
The report for the spectrum measurement may describe a lead sleeve surrounding the counter tube.
The need to reduce the gamma flux around the counter tube was recognized in the 1960s. It is
likely that a lead sleeve would have been used for a spectrometer measurement even if the report
does not mention the sleeve unless the report explicitly states that there was no lead sleeve. Ref.
16 lists a 6 mm sleeve. Ref. 16 was published in 1970, so the 6 mm sleeve probably applies to

 333

measurements in the 1960s. For ZPPR-2, the lead sleeve thickness was 12.7 mm, and later
spectrometer measurements in ZPPR probably used a similar thickness. For ZPR-6 and ZPR-9, a
sleeve thickness of 6 mm – 10 mm seems reasonable. The 6 mm thickness would apply to
spectrum measurements in the 1960s; the 10 mm thickness would apply to spectrum measurements
after 1970.
It is unlikely that reports will contain any description of the preamplifier, so it will be necessary
either to make a reasonable assumption about the preamplifier or to ignore it. The preamplifier
was not close to the counter tube, so it is unlikely to have any significant effect on the measured
values. In addition, the experimenters would have placed the preamplifier as far from the counter
tube as they could to minimize the influence of the preamplifier on the measurement.
The neutron spectrum was measured in the gas inside the counter tube, so the appropriate tally for
a Monte Carlo calculation of the spectrum is the volume inside the counter tube. A methane-filled
counter tube and a hydrogen-filled counter tube were required for spectrum measurements because
the useful upper limit for the hydrogen-filled counter was several hundred keV. If the designs are
available, it would be possible to compute the neutron spectrum with both counters, but it is not
clear that it is necessary to do so. The difference between the two calculated spectra is likely to
be smaller than the uncertainty in the measured spectrum and is likely to be significantly smaller
than C/E for the spectrum measurement. The methane counter tube is larger than the hydrogen
counter tube, so it is easier to obtain acceptable Monte Carlo statistical uncertainty for the methane
counter tube. The gas pressure in early spectrometers was ~5 atm although it was higher in later
spectrometers as discussed above.
If the spectrometer is located in or near the center of the core, it is possible to compute the neutron
spectrum by direct Monte Carlo. The Monte Carlo calculation for the ZPR-9/29 neutron spectrum
required one billion (109) histories, but the statistical uncertainties for the fluxes in the chosen
energy bins were acceptable.
It may be difficult to compute the spectrum by direct Monte Carlo if the spectrometer is located
far from the center of the core. The flux falls significantly between the core center, the radial
blanket and the radial reflector. Consequently, the number of histories required to obtain
acceptable statistics in the energy bins may be very large if the spectrometer is located near the
outer edge of the core, in the radial blanket or in the radial reflector.
It is possible to convert the as-built Monte Carlo model to a deterministic model for the spectrum
calculations. Use of a deterministic model circumvents the low flux problem in locations far from
the center of the core, but obtaining good cross sections for the deterministic model of the
spectrometer may be difficult.
7.9 Gamma Dose Distributions – Thermoluminescent Dosimeter Measurements
The ZPR/ZPPR fast reactor simulations included the core, blanket, reflector and, in some cases,
ex-core structures such as a shield or reactor vessel. Gamma dose measurements are used to
validate calculations of gamma heating in important reactor components including those ex-core
components. Consequently, gamma doses were measured in some ZPR-9 and ZPPR assemblies
and probably in some ZPR-6 assemblies as well. There may have been gamma dose measurements

 334

in later ZPR-3 assemblies, but to date only criticality measurements have been studied in ZPR-3

7.9.1 Thermoluminescent Dosimeters
Various techniques exist for measuring gamma doses [16, 21, 23]. The principal technique used
to measure gamma doses in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies was irradiation of thermoluminescent
dosimeters in the core, blanket, reflector and, in some cases, other ex-core structures of a critical
assembly. A thermoluminescent dosimeter (TLD) consists of a thermoluminescent material in a
capsule. The thermoluminescent material contains a number of electron or hole traps which are
stable at room temperature [16, 21, 23, 24]. Some of these traps are filled when ionizing radiation
creates electrons or holes in thermoluminescent material. When the irradiated thermoluminescent
material is subsequently heated, the electrons or holes are released from the trapping centers by
thermal ionization. Ionized carriers move through the thermoluminescent material until electron-
hole annihilation occurs. This annihilation is accompanied by emission of a photon. Measurement
of the number and intensity of photons emitted as a result of electron-hole annihilation provides
an estimate of the radiation dose received by the thermoluminescent material during irradiation.
There are several thermoluminescent materials and potential capsule materials. The choices of
thermoluminescent material, capsule material and capsule thickness are important considerations
for TLD measurements. Various combinations of thermoluminescent materials, capsule materials
and capsule thicknesses were investigated and used for gamma dose measurements in the assorted
reactors operated at Argonne over the years.
The standard TLD used for gamma dose measurements in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies consisted of LiF
encapsulated in stainless steel. Neutron reactions with 6Li obscure the gamma contribution to the
measured dose, so the Li in the LiF used for the ZPR/ZPPR TLDs was enriched to approximately
99.993% 7Li. For convenience, “TLD” will refer either to the LiF thermoluminescent material
inside the capsule or to the LiF material plus the stainless steel capsule in this report.
One standard TLD used in ZPR/ZPPR gamma dose measurements consisted of a LiF rod in a
cylindrical stainless steel capsule. The LiF rod had a 1 mm square cross section and a height of 6
mm. A typical stainless steel capsule had an outer diameter of 3.175 mm (0.125 in) and height of
12.7 mm (0.5 in).
The capsule wall thickness was a very important parameter for TLD measurements because the
thickness of the capsule wall determines whether electron equilibrium is established in the TLD.
It is likely that the ZPR/ZPPR experimenters tested various wall thicknesses and adopted a
standard wall thickness based on those tests. A steel capsule with a 0.035 inch wall thickness was
used for TLD measurements at ZPPR and ZPR-9 in the 1970s and thereafter, so it is probable that
the standard capsule wall thickness for the LiF rods was 0.035 inches.
The capsule material was probably Type 304 stainless steel because Type 304 stainless steel was
widely used for experimental equipment by the ZPR/ZPPR staff. In addition, the matrix tubes,
drawers and stainless steel plates used at the ZPR/ZPPR facilities were Type 304 stainless steel.
A second type of TLD used in later ZPR/ZPPR measurements consisted of a cylindrical stainless
steel capsule containing one or more LiF disks. The capsule used in the ZPPR-15 measurements,
for example, had an outer diameter of 0.5 inches and height of 0.25 inches. This capsule could

 335

contain up to five LiF disks. If multiple disks were placed in the capsule, the recorded measured
dose was typically the average of the measured doses for the disks in the capsule. The dimensions
of the LiF disks are not listed in reports consulted thus far. It seems likely that each LiF disk was
a circular disk or chip with a diameter of ~0.39 inches and a thickness of approximately 0.019 –
0.039 inches because a) there was a constraint on capsule wall thickness and b) the disks had to be
inserted into and removed from the capsule without damaging the disks. The probable capsule
wall thickness was 0.035 inches, and the probable capsule wall material was Type 304 stainless
steel.
There may have been other types of TLDs used in the ZPR/ZPPR measurements during the many
years that ZPR-3, ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR operated.
7.9.2 TLD Experimental Procedure
LiF rod TLDs could be used at many locations in the core, blanket and reflector of an assembly
because the rods could be inserted almost anywhere in the assembly. Rod TLDs could be placed
between the ends of adjacent plates in a plate column or into grooves cut into some of the larger
stainless steel plates. In addition, the designs of some clad plates included a small recessed area
in one end cap into which a rod TLD could be inserted. LiF rod TLDs were used in many
ZPR/ZPPR gamma dose measurements, and the rod TLDs may have been the first LiF TLDs used
in ZPR/ZPPR gamma dose measurements.
Capsules containing LiF disks required special plates with holes into which the capsules could be
inserted. In ZPPR-15, for example, the capsules containing the LiF disks were placed in cavities
in special sodium tunnel plates, i.e., sodium plates with a 0.5 inch cavity, which replaced normal
sodium plates at selected locations in the assembly. TLDs containing LiF disks were used in the
core and blanket of ZPPR-15. A TLD drawer was created by replacing one sodium plate in the
standard drawer at the desired location by a sodium tunnel plate containing a TLD. TLDs
containing LiF rods were used outside the core and blanket in ZPPR-15.
TLDs were placed at many locations in the core, radial blanket and radial reflector to measure the
gamma dose as a function of position. TLDs might also be placed in any special regions outside
the radial reflector. For example, ZPPR-15B had a simulated shield on one side, and TLDs were
placed in that shield zone. TLDs were typically placed in drawers along the center row on the X-
axis, but TLDs might also be placed in drawers along the center column on the Y-axis.
TLDs were usually placed near the front plates of front drawers, i.e., near the interface between
matrix halves, to maximize the measured doses. Most or all of the TLDs were generally placed in
one half of the split table machine. Likewise, most drawers containing TLDs contained a single
TLD.
The heterogeneous plate distributions within the drawers, particularly core drawers, resulted in
non-uniform intra-drawer neutron and gamma flux distributions. In drawers containing one TLD,
that TLD was generally placed at the same relative position in all drawers of the same type (core,
radial blanket or radial reflector). In the present context, the same relative position means the TLD
was located in the same column of plates or between the same columns of plates, at the same
distance from the drawer sidewalls, and at the same distance from the front plate of the drawer in

 336

all drawers of the same type. That approach reduced the effect of intra-drawer heterogeneity on
the relative gamma dose distribution in the assembly.
Section 7.10 discusses placing multiple foils in selected drawers to measure intra-drawer neutron
reaction rate distributions for various drawer types and drawer environments. The ZPR/ZPPR staff
used a similar procedure for TLD measurements. Multiple TLDs were placed in a few drawers at
select locations to measure intra-drawer gamma dose distributions for characteristic drawer types
and environments. Measuring the intra-drawer gamma dose distributions in characteristic drawer
types and environments provided a means to relate the dose measured at a single point in a drawer
by a single TLD to the average gamma dose in the drawer in the same way that cell factors related
reaction rates measured by individual mapping foils to cell-averaged reaction rates in drawers (see
Section 7.10).
After all TLD drawers were loaded into the matrix, the reactor was made critical, and the TLDs
were irradiated at the desired power for the desired time. At the end of the irradiation, the reactor
was shut down. The TLDs remained in the reactor for some time after reactor shutdown to correct
for the non-equilibrium irradiation conditions. The TLDs were then removed from the reactor.
The thermoluminescent material, i.e., the LiF rod or disk, was removed from each capsule and
heated under carefully controlled conditions. Thermal ionization induced by heating the
thermoluminescent material releases the trapped electrons and holes from the trapping centers in
the material. Subsequent electron-hole annihilation in the heated material releases photons that
are counted. The intensity of the light emitted from the heated thermoluminescent material is a
measure of the gamma dose absorbed by the TLD.
There were strong intra-drawer heterogeneity effects in many ZPR/ZPPR assemblies, and these
heterogeneity effects resulted in very non-uniform gamma flux distributions in the drawers. Figure
7.23 shows the intra-drawer dose measurement in ZPPR-15B. Figure 7.24 shows the intra-drawer
dose measurements in the double fuel column (DCF) drawers in ZPPR-15D; Figure 7.25 shows
the intra-drawer dose measurements in the single fuel column (SCF) drawers in ZPPR-15D.

 337

 Figure 7.23. Intra-Drawer Gamma Dose Measurement in ZPPR-15B.

 338

  Figure 7.24. Intra-Drawer Gamma Dose Distribution in ZPPR-15D – Double and Single
 Fuel Column Cells.

 339
