7.9.3 TLD Uncertainties
The published uncertainty for a ZPR/ZPPR TLD measurement is generally just the measurement
uncertainty, and that measurement uncertainty is only a small component of the total uncertainty
for the measured gamma dose. For example, the published uncertainty for ZPPR-15 TLD
measurements was 2%. Additional uncertainties and corrections are relevant to determining the
final measured dose rates and total uncertainties for the TLD measurements. The ZPPR-15 TLD
measurements are used here as an example, but the uncertainties discussed in this section apply to
any TLD measurement in any ZPR/ZPPR assembly.

 340

7.9.3.1 Correction for Non-Equilibrium Irradiation Conditions
In a real reactor application, the reactor is running at steady state for a prolonged period, and the
relevant quantity is the gamma dose at selected locations under steady state irradiation conditions.
In the ideal TLD experimental measurement in ZPR/ZPPR, TLDs would be inserted and
withdrawn while the reactor was operating at the desired power level under steady state conditions.
Inserting or withdrawing TLDs during steady state reactor operation, similar to the concept of how
sample oscillators worked as discussed in Section 7.7, was not possible for any of the ZPR/ZPPR
machines.
TLD irradiations in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies were necessarily performed under non-equilibrium
conditions. The TLDs were inserted while the reactor was shut down. The reactor was brought to
the desired power, and the TLDs were irradiated for the desired time. In the ZPPR-15 TLD
measurements, for example, the integrated reactor power was approximately 300 watt-hours. The
reactor was then shut down, and the TLDs were removed approximately 20 hours later.
If the TLDs were removed from the reactor immediately after shutdown, they would miss the
contribution from gammas produced by decay of longer-lived fission products. The importance
of leaving irradiated TLDs in the reactor for some time after shutdown was measured in ZPPR and
in ZPR-9.
If it were possible to insert TLDs, irradiate them for long enough to establish equilibium and
remove them while the reactor was operating at steady state power for a long period, the TLD
measurement would reflect the steady state gamma flux in the reactor. That gamma flux would
include prompt gammas from the irradiation period plus gammas produced by decay of long-lived
fission products from reactions that occurred before the TLDs were inserted. When the TLDs were
removed, they would miss some gammas from fissions during the irradiation period, but the
missing gammas from the irradiation period fissions would be balanced by the gammas recorded
from decay of long-lived fission products from fissions that occurred before the irradiation period.
This approach would effectively record the steady gamma flux in the reactor.
This approach was not possible in a ZPR/ZPPR assembly for two reasons. First, it was not
physically possible to insert and remove TLDs while the reactor was operating. It was necessary
to shut the reactor down to insert and remove the TLDs, and both of those operations required
significant time. Second, many other experiments and measurements were conducted in any
ZPR/ZPPR assembly. The realities of schedule and budget limited the amount of time that could
be spent on any given measurement. Consequently, it was not possible to establish true
equilibrium for the irradiation period or to record every gamma produced by decay of long-lived
fission products created during the irradiation period. It is recommended as part of any analysis
effort to reproduce the TLD measurements to use calculations with and without delay gammas as
bounding limits on the comparison.
In ZPPR-2, the E1 and E2 experiments were performed to measure the non-equilibrium effect. In
the E1 experiment, the TLDs were removed 44 hours after shutdown. In the E2 experiment, the
TLDs were removed 30 minutes after irradiation. The E1/E2 ratio was in the 1.05 – 1.10 range,
depending upon the radial and axial position of the TLD in the assembly (Ref. 26, pp. 181 – 183).

 341

The non-equilibrium effect was also measured in ZPR-9/27, the Fast Test Reactor – Engineering
Mockup Critical (FTR-EMC) program in ZPR-9. TLDs were removed from the reactor in three
batches at approximately 2.5 hours, 6.5 hours and 18 hours after irradiation. During the reactor
run, an ionization chamber that was sensitive to gammas was located in the back drawer at matrix
position S-17/18 [27]. The ionization chamber current was recorded on a strip chart recorder for
the period before the run, during the run and for 16 hours after shutdown. The rate of gamma
decay at the ionization chamber location was assumed to be representative of the remainder of the
reactor. The strip chart recording was used to derive fractional corrections for the TLDs. The
corrections for the three retrieval times were approximately 1.6% ± 0.3% for 2.5 h – 18 h, 1.0% ±
0.3% for 6.5 h – 18 h, and 0.5% ± 0.3% for 18 h – ∞ (Ref. 27, pages 130 – 131).
The TLDs were removed from ZPPR-15 after 20 hours of post-irradiation decay in the reactor, so
the uncertainty in the non-equilibrium correction for the ZPPR-15 TLD measurements is ~0.3%.
One conclusion from the FTR-EMC experiments in ZPR-9 was that the background radiation
contribution to the measured TLD dose prior to reactor startup was negligible. It is assumed that
this conclusion is applicable to ZPR/ZPPR TLD irradiations in general unless a document indicates
otherwise for a specific assembly. Likewise, the corrections and uncertainties measured in the
ZPR-9 FTR-EMC measurements of non-equilibrium effects are assumed to be applicable to
ZPR/ZPPR TLD irradiations in general unless a document indicates otherwise for a specific

7.9.3.2 Correction for Shine
In general, all drawers containing a single TLD were located in the same half of the assembly. If
some drawers contained multiple TLDs to map intra-drawer gamma dose distributions resulting
from intra-drawer heterogeneities, those drawers might be located in the other half of the assembly.
For example, each ZPPR-15 drawer containing one TLD was located in half 1. Four ZPPR-15
drawers containing multiple TLDs were located in half 2.
At the end of the TLD irradiation, the reactor was shut down, and the two halves of the reactor
were separated. The TLDs remained in the reactor for approximately 20 hours prior to removal to
correct for the non-equilibrium irradiation conditions discussed in Section 7.9.3.1. In principle,
this shutdown configuration also allowed TLDs in the low-flux regions in one half to be affected
by shine from the high-flux region at the center of the core in the other half since the TLDs were
relatively close to the fronts of the drawers.
The shine effect was mitigated by the presence of the personnel shields. The personnel shields
were mounted on tracks and were placed between matrix halves after the halves were separated to
reduce the dose received by personnel working on the machine (e.g. inserting or removing drawers
when the reactor was shut down). The shield for each half in ZPR-9 was a 8 inch sandwich of
steel, benelex, boral and lead that attenuated post-irradiation gammas by a factor of approximately
15 – 20. ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were constructed at the same time in Building 315 at ANL-E, so the
ZPR-6 personnel shields would have been similar to the ZPR-9 personnel shields. The ZPPR
personnel shields would have been at least as thick as the ZPR-9 shields because the larger cores
in ZPPR would have resulted in larger doses than the doses received by personnel working between
matrix halves of ZPR-6 or ZPR-9. Initially, ZPR-3 did not have personnel shields (see Figure 2.1

 342

and Figure 2.2). Personnel shields were added to ZPR-3 sometime between 1955 and 1968 (see
Figure 2.3), but there are no details available regarding the ZPR-3 shields or when they were added.
The contribution of shine to the gamma dose was measured in the ZPR-9 FTR-EMC experiments.
Background dosimeters were taped to the personnel shields and to various locations on the
platform and matrix tubes to measure the effects of shine during the post-irradiation period before
the TLDs were removed from the reactor. No consistent shine effect was measured in the FTR-
EMC experiments [27]. The personnel shields mitigated the shine effect in ZPPR-15 in the same
way that the ZPR-9 shields mitigated the shine effect in the FTR-EMC experiments, so there was
no correction for shine and no associated uncertainty for the TLD measurements in ZPPR-15.
The personnel shields would have similar effects in all of the ZPR/ZPPR machines, so it is assumed
that there is no correction for shine and no associated uncertainty for TLD measurements in any
of the ZPR/ZPPR assemblies unless a specific document states otherwise for a particular assembly.
7.9.3.3 Correction for Electron Equilibrium Effects
The operation of a TLD is based on cavity ionization theory [24,25]. For gamma dose
measurements with TLDs, one assumption of cavity ionization theory is that electron equilibrium
is established. For electron equilibrium to be established, the amount of energy entering the cavity
equals the amount of energy removed from the cavity. This means that each electron entering the
cavity is balanced by another electron of approximately the same energy leaving the cavity.
The thickness of the capsule walls or sleeve surrounding the LiF is important. If the sleeve is too
thick, scattering of the gamma flux introduces an unnecessary error. If the sleeve is too thin, the
measured dose in the cavity will be lower than it would be if electron equilibrium existed.
Theoretical and experimental studies were performed at Argonne to determine the preferred cavity
wall material and corresponding wall thickness to establish electron equilibrium for use with the
LiF thermoluminescent material. For LiF with a stainless steel sleeve, analysis of the FTR-EMC
configuration in ZPR-9 led to the conclusion that the capsule sleeve thickness was sufficient to
establish electron equilibrium and, consequently, that the measured dose in the TLD corresponds
to the gamma ray energy deposited in a small stainless steel sample at the TLD location subject to
gamma spectrum effects and fast neutron sensitivity to be discussed below. It is reasonable to
assume that the capsule and TLD designs were standardized for ZPR/ZPPR assemblies.
The assumption of electron equilibrium is applicable to TLD measurements at ZPPR and to TLD
measurements performed at ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 after the late 1960s. It is less clear how the electron
equilibrium assumption applies to any TLD measurements performed on the ZPR/ZPPR machines
in the 1960s. A lot of developmental work concerning TLD measurements occurred in the 1960s,
so the capsule wall thickness may not have met the requirements for electron equilibrium in some
early ZPR TLD measurements. It would be necessary to consult reports and other available
documents for early ZPR TLD measurements to determine what information those sources can
provide regarding capsule wall thickness and electron equilibrium.
7.9.3.4 Variation in Individual TLDs
The thermoluminescent materials were purchased from standard commercial suppliers. The initial
thermoluminescent materials purchased for ZPR/ZPPR operations were 1 x 1 x 6 mm LiF rods,
which had a one-sigma variation of ~5.8% in sensitivity to gamma irradiation due to normal

 343

variations in the manufacturing process. Testing of subsequent batches of rods showed intra-batch
variations in sensitivity of 3.5% – 8% due to manufacturing variations.
In the early 1970s, ANL experimenters developed an intra-batch sensitivity selection method that
significantly reduced the statistical variation in batches of TLDs used for experiments at ZPPR,
ZPR-6 and ZPR-9. In this method, a purchase lot of TLD rods was divided into a number of
individual batches. The second step was to inspect the TLD rods and to remove any over-sized or
under-sized rods and any rods with visible chips or cracks. The remaining rods in each batch were
then exposed to a given gamma dose, measured and sorted according to sensitivity. The final set
for each batch was obtained by removing any rods with sensitivities falling outside of a ±5%
tolerance band about the average measured sensitivity for the batch.
At the end of the selection process, the intra-batch variation in sensitivity for a batch of TLD rods
was reduced to ~2.5%. It would have been possible to repeat the process to reduce the variation
further, but available documents state that this was not done.
For TLD measurements prior to the early 1970s, i.e., prior to development of the intra-batch
sensitivity selection method, a reasonable one-sigma variation in sensitivity for a batch of TLDs
is approximately 6%. For TLD measurements after development of the intra-batch sensitivity
selection method in the early 1970s, a reasonable one-sigma variation in sensitivity for a batch of
TLDs is approximately 2.5%.
7.9.3.5 Calibration Uncertainty
For absolute gamma dose measurements, it was necessary to calibrate the TLDs by exposing at
least a subset of them to a known gamma field. In a typical calibration procedure, a gamma source
was suspended a fixed distance above a group of TLDs in a large high-bay building. The TLDs
were suspended above ground level to reduce the problem of backscattered gammas. The TLDs
were exposed to a fixed gamma dose, stored for 24 hours, and then read. This provided the
calibration required for absolute gamma dose measurements. Relative or normalized gamma dose
measurements would not require the calibration procedure.
The distance between the TLDs and the gamma source, the irradiation time, post-irradiation
storage time and the readout procedure could be carefully controlled and generally made minor
contributions to the calibration uncertainty. Note that readout procedure refers to heating the
stored TLDs under carefully controlled conditions and measuring the photons emitted during
electron-hole annihilation as the TLD is heated.
One uncertainty for the calibration measurements was the uncertainty in the gamma source
strength. According to the available documents, the gamma source used at ZPPR was a 0.804
Curie 60Co source. The uncertainty in the source strength for this source was listed as ±2% in
available documents, so a calibration source uncertainty of 2% was assumed for analysis of the
ZPPR TLD measurements. The uncertainty in the source strength for other gamma sources would
be specific to the gamma source and would probably differ from the ±2% source strength
uncertainty for the ZPPR 60Co source.
There are additional calibration uncertainties related to sample uniformity and to the readout
procedure. The ZPPR staff assigned a 5% uncertainty to the ZPPR-2 TLD calibration data but did
not quantify the individual components. The ZPR-9 staff also included a 5% uncertainty attributed

 344

to the sample uniformity and readout procedure without further quantifying those individual
components [27]. The ZPPR staff later developed a method to reduce the variation in intra-batch
sensitivity for a batch of TLD rods to approximately 2.5%, which would likely reduce the 5%
uncertainty attributed to the sample uniformity and readout procedure.
Aside from any contribution due to counting statistics, the uniformity of the calibration samples
and the uncertainty related to the readout procedure are the principal components of the calibration
data uncertainty. It is assumed here that the 5% uncertainty assigned to the ZPPR-2 TLD
calibration data by the ZPPR staff refers to the same calibration uncertainty as the 5% uncertainty
assigned to sample uniformity and readout procedure by the ZPR-9 staff.
If one assumes a 5% uncertainty for the sample uniformity and readout procedure (calibration data)
and a 2% uncertainty in the 60Co source strength, the combined uncertainty is ~5.39% for the ZPPR
TLD measurements. Reducing the variation in intra-batch sensitivity would reduce the total
uncertainty below 5.39%, but the reduction cannot be quantified accurately since the contributions
from the individual components are not known accurately.
A total calibration uncertainty of ~5.4% was assumed for ZPPR analysis to allow for the reduction
in the variation in intra-batch sensitivity in the calibration samples.
The 5% uncertainty for calibration data seems reasonable for TLD calibrations performed after
development of the intra-batch sensitivity selection method in the early 1970s. For TLD
calibrations performed before development of this method, a reasonable estimate for the
uncertainty in the calibration data is probably in the 6% – 7% range in the absence of any additional
information. The uncertainty in the source strength of the gamma source used for the calibration
will be specific to the source used for the calibration. ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 probably used the same
gamma source. ZPPR had its own gamma source. To date, no documentation has been found on
ZPR-3 measurements that identifies whether TLD measurements were performed in ZPR-3.
7.9.3.6 Variations in Gamma Ray Spectrum
A TLD consists of a stainless steel capsule or sleeve (Z ≈ 26) surrounding LiF (Z ≈ 8.2). This
configuration does not represent a matched cavity dosimeter. Gamma ray energy absorption
coefficients and mass stopping powers are different for the stainless steel sleeve and the LiF cavity
material. Both of these energy-dependent parameters can induce systematic errors whose
magnitude depends upon the difference between the gamma source spectrum used for calibration
and the ZPR/ZPPR assembly gamma ray spectrum. The ZPR/ZPPR gamma ray spectrum depends
strongly on the TLD location in the assembly.
Based upon theoretical and experimental work performed at ANL in the early 1970s, the maximum
error due to the mismatch between the calibration spectrum and the local spectrum in the assembly
was estimated to be ±10% in the fueled core region(s) where the gamma spectrum is relatively
hard.
Most ZPR/ZPPR assemblies consisted of a core, blanket and reflector, and occasionally there was
a shield zone outside the radial reflector. The gamma spectrum change significantly between the
core, blanket, reflector and any structure outside the radial reflector. In the reflector region where
the local gamma spectrum is much softer than the calibration spectrum, the measured dose was

 345

estimated to be less than the true dose by up to 30% ± 15%. The uncertainty in this value arises
from the uncertainty in the calculated gamma spectrum in the reflector.
It is likely that the error in the blanket was intermediate between the error in the core and the error
in the reflector because the gamma spectrum softens gradually between the core, blanket, reflector
and any external shield.
These values were derived for the ZPR-9 FTR-EMC experiments [27], but the ZPR-9 FTR-EMC
configurations are sufficiently similar to most ZPPR experiments that these values should apply to
ZPPR TLD measurements as well.
In the absence of any additional information or experimental evidence, the ZPR-9 FTR-EMC
experiments should apply reasonably well to most ZPR/ZPPR assemblies, but there are some
exceptions.
First, ZPPR-14, ZPPR-16 and ZPPR-20 simulated space power reactors with BeO reflectors. ZPR-
9/1 through ZPR-9/9 simulated nuclear rocket engines with aluminum or Al/BeO reflectors. If
TLD measurements were performed for any of these assemblies, additional analysis would be
required at least for the reflectors because the ZPR-9 FTR-EMC results would not apply to a BeO
reflector, solid aluminum reflector or Al/BeO reflector. Additional analysis might also be required
for the core regions because the reflector would influence at least the outer core in these small

Second, ZPPR-20D simulated a launch accident with water immersion, and ZPPR-20E simulated
a launch accident with earth burial. The ZPR-9 FTR-EMC results would not apply to the core
regions of ZPPR-20D or ZPPR-20E. It is unlikely that TLD measurements were performed in
these two configurations because the focus of these two configurations was criticality safety in
launch accident scenarios.
Third, experimenters constructed special regions outside the radial blanket or radial reflector of
some assemblies to study features of ex-core regions in specific reactor designs. The applicability
of the ZPR-9 FTR-EMC results to such special regions would have to be determined on a case-by-
case basis. Additional analysis might be required for any special ex-core regions.
7.9.3.7 Dose-Response Curve and Dose Dependence
In the ideal case, the dose-response curve is linear up to the saturation point at which all traps are
filled. The response curve for LiF is linear up to 1000 rads; the LiF response curve is supralinear
beyond 1000 rads. The dose rate dependence at doses up to 1010 rad/sec is negligible according to
observations (see Ref. 25, p. 174).
7.9.3.8 Reproducibility
Assessment by ANL experimenters in the early 1970s was that it is possible to obtain 2% – 3%
reproducibility for a given dosimeter and from dosimeter to dosimeter within the same batch (see
Ref. 25, pp. 174 – 175). No later assessments have been found, so a 3% reproducibility uncertainty
is assumed to be applicable to TLD measurements in any ZPR/ZPPR assembly.

 346

7.9.3.9 Stability, Past History and Electronic Drift
LiF shows some evidence of fading over time; the amount of fading is less than 10% per month.
It is possible to correct for this effect if the TLD readout always occurs at a fixed time after
irradiation. Note that “read” and “readout” refer to measuring the photons emitted when the TLD
is heated under controlled conditions after irradiation.
LiF response shows sensitivity to past irradiation history, particularly pre- and post-irradiation
parameters. The LiF response decreases if the LiF has been exposed previously to irradiation
greater than about 104 rads.
There could also be some drift in the electronics for long readout periods, but it was possible to
correct for this drift. If reference TLDs are read out with the initial calibration data, interspersing
readouts of the reference TLDs that were given comparable calibration doses on the day of the run
with readouts from the TLDs irradiated in the subsequent experiment provides a correction for any
electronics drift.
These effects were recognized by ANL experimenters in the early 1970s. Experimenters would
have corrected for effects associated with stability, irradiation history and electronic drift for TLD
measurements performed after the early 1970s. This would include all of the ZPPR assemblies
plus later ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 assemblies. It would not necessarily apply to ZPR-3 or to TLD
measurements in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 that were performed before the early 1970s.
7.9.3.10 Response to Fast Neutrons
TLDs are sensitive to both gammas and fast neutrons, so the dose measured by a TLD includes a
contribution from fast neutrons [24, 25, 27]. Elastic scattering of fast neutrons in the TLD
produces recoil nuclei, and slowing down of these recoil nuclei creates electron-hole pairs similar
to those created by gamma interactions in the TLD. The net effect is that elastic scattering of fast
neutrons contributes to the total number of filled electron or hole traps in LiF and, consequently,
to the number and intensity of photons detected when the TLD is read.
Any experimental determination of the magnitude of the neutron contribution is complicated for
two reasons. First, the neutrons are always accompanied by gammas, and the gammas may make
the dominant contribution to the TLD response. Second, the magnitude of the neutron contribution
depends upon the neutron spectrum. The importance of the neutron contribution decreases as the
neutron spectrum softens from the core to the reflector.
Limited experimental and analytical studies of the fast neutron effect were performed at ANL and
elsewhere in the 1960s and early 1970s. The general conclusion of the reports produced at ANL
at that time is that more work was needed, but there is no evidence that the fast neutron issue was
studied in any detail at ANL after the early 1970s.
In a comparison of measured and calculated neutron contributions [28] to the measured dose, the
calculated and measured curves had similar shapes, but the measured values were lower than the
calculated values by an order of magnitude. The likely explanations of the reduced neutron
contributions were a) reduced ability of low-energy recoil ions (nuclei) to produce ionization and
b) the higher probability of recombination as the ionization density increases. Recombination is a
greater issue for the recoil ion produced by neutron scattering than for an electron produced by a

 347

gamma interaction. For the same doses produced by gammas and fast neutrons, the
thermoluminescent output will be significantly greater for the gammas than for the neutrons.
The contribution of fast neutrons to the measured dose in TLDs was assessed for the FTR-EMC
critical experiments in ZPR-9. Calculations indicated that the fast neutron contribution ranged
from 10% ± 5% of the observed dose at the center of the core to 0.5% ± 0.5% in the shield for the
FTR-EMC experiments [27].
The ZPPR staff reported that the neutron contribution for the ZPPR-15 TLD measurements was
~20% and was a function of position, but they did not correct the measured values for the fast
neutron contribution. The report listing the measured TLD values for ZPPR-15 explicitly states
that the reported values include the fast neutron contribution.
This illustrates a common problem with some types of ZPR/ZPPR measurements. The ZPR/ZPPR
staff state that the measured values include contributions from some other factor, but they do not
correct for that factor. Correcting for the other factor is left up to the analyst who is using the data.
It is not known why the experimenters made some corrections but chose not to correct for others
of which they were aware.
In the absence of any additional information, the fast neutron contribution assessed in the ZPR-9
FTR-EMC experiments is at least a first order approximation for the fast neutron contribution in
most other ZPR/ZPPR TLD measurements. The exceptions to this statement are the same
exceptions discussed with respect to variations in gamma spectrum in Section 7.9.3.6 for the same
reasons.
A realistic uncertainty for the fast neutron contribution in the core is either one-half of the quoted
fast neutron contribution or 5% of the measured dose. A legitimate case could be made for either
of those values. In the reflector, 0.5% of the measured dose seems like a reasonable value for the
uncertainty in the fast neutron contribution. In the blanket, assuming the uncertainty in the fast
neutron contribution is one-half of the uncertainty assumed for the core seems reasonable.
It is possible to calculate the contribution of fast neutrons to the measured dose, but Ref. 28
indicates that the measured contribution was lower than the calculated contribution by an order of
magnitude in a comparison of measured and calculated contributions. It does not appear that
anyone on the ZPR/ZPPR staff studied the fast neutron contribution problem in any detail after the
early 1970s. It is possible that this is discrepancy is simply an artifact of the limited accuracy of
the modeling being done at the time. It is possible that the fast neutron issue was studied and
possibly even resolved elsewhere after the early 1970s, but resolving the fast neutron contribution
problem is beyond the scope of this document.

The published gamma doses in ZPPR-15 include the fast neutron contribution. This is probably

been corrected for the fast neutron contribution. Determining a precise value for the fast neutron
correction as a function of position is possible in principle but difficult in practice. Whether the
effort to determine the fast neutron sensitivity correction more accurately is worthwhile depends

 349

upon the accuracy of shielding calculations in general. If shielding calculations are accurate to
10% – 20%, it might be worthwhile to attempt to determine the fast neutron correction more
accurately. If the inherent accuracy of shielding calculations is in the 50% – 100% range, refining
the fast neutron sensitivity correction slightly is likely not worth the effort.
The uncertainties for individual TLD measurements must be combined correctly if the gamma
doses are normalized to a specific measured value such as the largest value in a table. It is not
valid to divide all of the measured values and uncertainties in a table by a selected reference value
from that table without further correction because that selected reference value is itself uncertain.
The correct procedure for determining the uncertainty for a normalized ratio is the following (see
Ref. 29, Section V.E):
 1. Consider x with uncertainty σx, y with uncertainty σy, and the desired ratio R = x/y.
 2. Define Sx = σx/x, Sy = σy/y, and SR = σR/R.
    3. Then SR = √((Sx)2 + (Sy)2)
SR is the correct relative uncertainty for any ratio such as normalization in which S x and Sy are
independent.
7.9.4 Gamma Dose Calculations
As-built Monte Carlo models can be created for the gamma dose measurements in a ZPR/ZPPR
assembly. However, it would be very difficult to calculate the gamma doses measured in any
ZPR/ZPPR assembly by direct Monte Carlo calculation of an as-built model for the same reasons
that direct Monte Carlo calculations of foil measurements are very difficult (see Section 7.10).
The actual TLDs are either 1 x 1 x 6 mm square rods or disks with ~10 mm diameter and ~0.5 mm
thickness. Each individual TLD occupies a negligible fraction of the assembly volume, so very
few neutrons or photons will encounter any given TLD during normal particle tracking.
Consequently, the statistical uncertainties in TLDs will be very large for direct Monte Carlo
calculations.
There are likely to be many TLDs distributed in the core, radial blanket and radial reflector of a
ZPR/ZPPR assembly. In principle, it might be possible to use splitting/Russian roulette, weight
windows and other variance reduction techniques to improve the Monte Carlo statistics for TLDs
at one or two locations, but those variance reduction techniques will also make the Monte Carlo
statistics worse at all other TLD locations.
Another problem with any direct Monte Carlo calculation of the TLD measurements is that the
neutron and gamma fluxes fall significantly between the core center, the radial blanket and the
radial reflector, which exacerbates the problem of obtaining meaningful statistics for the TLD

The combination of the negligible volumes of individual TLDs, the large number of TLDs in the
assembly, and the large reduction in flux between the inner core, radial blanket and radial reflector
makes any direct Monte Carlo calculation of the fluxes or reaction rates in the TLDs very difficult.
Future developments in Monte Carlo methods or computer hardware capabilities may make direct
Monte Carlo calculations of TLD measurements feasible, but it does not seem to be practical to
calculate TLD measurements by direct Monte Carlo as this is being written.

 350

Monte Carlo calculations with point detectors and other next event estimators would also be very
difficult for ZPR/ZPPR as-built models. Next event estimators can work well in models with large,
homogeneous regions because it is relatively straightforward to compute the contribution to a next
event estimator under those circumstances. However, as-built models of ZPR/ZPPR assemblies
do not contain any large, homogeneous regions. Instead, each matrix tube in an as-built model
contains many individual cells with thicknesses ranging from ~0.1 mm to ~10 mm, and there may
be many matrix tubes between the location of the particle and the location of the next event
estimator.
Consider a scattering event at point (x1,y1,z1) and a point detector at point (x2,y2,z2). The point
detector estimator assumes that after the collision at (x1,y1,z1) the scattered particle travels directly
to the point detector at (x2,y2,z2) and makes a contribution to the point detector estimator score.
This means it is necessary to compute the distance through every cell (region) between (x 1,y1,z1)
and (x2,y2,z2), to compute the appropriate cross section in each of those cells and then to compute
the optical path length through each of those cells. This process is repeated for each point detector
at each collision. For a few detectors in a model with large, homogeneous regions, next event
estimators can work very well. For an as-built ZPR/ZPPR model with many thousands of very
small cells and many locations of interest, e.g., TLD locations, computing the TLD doses with
next event estimators such as point detectors would require very large computer resources.
It is likely that the most practical way to perform meaningful calculations of TLD measurements
in any as-built Monte Carlo ZPR/ZPPR model is to convert the as-built Monte Carlo model of the
TLD configuration to a deterministic model for the calculations. This of course comes with it own
set of approximations but one cannot argue that it is computationally unrealistic to obtain an
answer by direct Monte Carlo.
7.10 Reaction Rate Distributions – Foil Irradiation Measurements
Davey and Redman [16] discusses various techniques used to measure reaction rates in ZPR-3,
ZPR-6 and ZPR-9. One of the principal methods used to measure reaction rate distributions in
ZPR/ZPPR assemblies was irradiation of small metallic foils. These foil irradiation measurements
provided experimental data to validate calculations of flux and power distributions in fast reactor
designs.
Reactivity measurements provided integral data regarding the effects of changes in reactor
configuration such as sodium voiding or insertion of simulated control rods on reactivity for the
system as a whole. In addition to measuring reaction rate distributions in the reference critical
configuration, the experimenters irradiated foils in some of the perturbed configurations to provide
data regarding the effects of the configuration change on reaction rate distributions throughout the
reactor.
One limitation of foil irradiations in perturbed configurations is that foil irradiations required a
critical configuration. It was sometimes necessary to adjust the reactivity of the perturbed
configuration to achieve a critical configuration, which affected flux and power distributions to
some degree. Another consequence of the criticality requirement is that it generally was not
practical to perform foil irradiations for perturbed configurations that were far subcritical, e.g.,
ZPPR configurations with multiple inserted mockup control rods, because the required reactivity

 351

adjusts to reach a critical configuration would have too much effect on power and flux
distributions.
Foil irradiations also provided an estimate of the neutron spectrum throughout the reactor. The
experimenters used proton recoil spectrometers to make detailed neutron spectrum measurements,
but a proton recoil spectrometer only measured the spectrum within one drawer at one location.
Making a detailed spectrum measurement at another location required shutting the reactor down,
relocating the spectrometer and restarting the reactor. Foils could be placed at many locations in
the core, blanket and reflector to measure radial and/or axial reaction rate distributions throughout
the assembly in one reactor run. In addition, proton recoil spectrometer measurements required a
subcritical reactor to avoid saturating the spectrometer electronics. Foil irradiations were
performed in critical configurations, so foils could be irradiated during some other types of
experiments.
7.10.1 Foil Irradiation Experimental Technique
The technique used for foil irradiations was similar at all of the ZPR/ZPPR facilities, but some
details of pre- and post-irradiation operations differed between ANL-E and ANL-W. One example
of such a difference is the foil calibration procedure. Some aspects of post-irradiation data
processing may also have differed between ANL-E and ANL-W. Note that the description for
ANL-W is focused on ZPPR. To date no foil irradiations that may have been taken at ZPR-3 have
been analyzed.
The basic experimental technique for foil irradiations consisted of the following steps:
 1. The reactor was shut down.
 2. Drawers at selected locations were removed from the matrix, modified by inserting foils
 between columns of plates and reloaded into the matrix.
 3. The reactor was made critical, and the foils were irradiated at the desired power level for
 the desired time.
 4. The reactor was shut down and allowed to return to a safe radiological state.
 5. Drawers containing foils were removed from the matrix, the foils were removed, and the
 drawers were reloaded into the matrix.
 6. The irradiated foils were counted.
The number of foils inserted, and the exact locations of those foils, depended on the ZPR/ZPPR
assembly and configuration in which the measurements were made. Foils were typically placed
in drawers in the center row and/or center column in the core, radial blanket and radial reflector.
In some cases, foils were placed in drawers at an angle to the center row, e.g., 45°. Axial reaction
rate distributions were measured by placing foils at multiple axial locations in one or more drawers.
Because assemblies were usually symmetric about the center row(s), the center column(s) and the
interface between matrix halves, foils were typically placed in one octant, i.e., in one quarter in
one half of the assembly. Foils might be placed in a row or column of drawers across the entire
assembly in special situations such as configurations that were not symmetric about the center
row(s) or center column(s). For example, a simulated shield zone was constructed on one side in
some ZPPR-15B loadings, creating an asymmetry about the center columns in the core. Foil
measurements for the shield zone also included foils in the core, radial blanket and radial reflector
on the opposite side from the shield zone. In the uncommon case where an assembly was not

 352

axially symmetric about the interface between matrix halves, foils might be placed in both halves,
especially for axial reaction rate profiles.
There were several types of foils, and the number of foils in the inventories varied by foil type.
For example, there were many more 235U foils than 239Pu foils. The most common reaction rate
measurements were 239Pu(n,f), 235U(n,f), 238U(n,f) and 238U(n,γ) although the ZPR/ZPPR material
inventories included small numbers of foils of other types for special measurements.
In a typical ZPPR foil irradiation, foils of two or more distinct types were placed in the same radial
and axial location. ZPPR had thin foil holders made of stainless steel or aluminum. Each of these
foil holders had holes to accommodate several different foils, so multiple foils, i.e., foils of
different types, could be irradiated at each location simultaneously. Note that the holes in the foil
holders were slightly separated, so there was a small separation between individual foils in the
same foil holder. The foil holders provided positive positioning for the foils and protected the foils
from damage during drawer loading and handling.
ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 also irradiated foils of two or more distinct types at each location in most cases.
ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 had foil holders similar to the ZPPR foil holders, but a common practice in early
assemblies at ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 was to use ordinary aluminum foil as a foil holder. The aluminum
foil was folded around the foils and suspended from the top of the plates in the drawer to position
the foils in the drawer. Another practice at ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 was to attach the foils to the sides
of plates.
The foils were typically placed between columns of plates in the drawers. However, occasionally
the experimenters laid the foils horizontally across the tops of the plates in the drawers.
The measured foil data were presented in two forms in ZPR/ZPPR reports. It was not practical to
place foils between every column of plates in every drawer in a row and/or column of a ZPR/ZPPR
assembly because the supply of foils was limited and because it would not be economically feasible
to load, unload and count that many foils. A second consideration is that it was not possible to
calculate accurate reaction rates for many individual foils at their exact locations in the assembly
during the period when the ZPR/ZPPR facilities operated due to computer hardware and software
limitations of that time.
The standard ZPR/ZPPR practice was to place one foil of each type between two specific columns
of plates in many drawers in a row, column or diagonal of an assembly. These foils were referred
to as mapping foils.
The experimenters attempted to maintain consistent foil positioning for mapping foils in each
drawer type, but it was not always possible to maintain consistent foil positions in different drawer
types. Core drawers, blanket drawers and radial reflector drawers all had different plate loadings
and might contain plates of different thicknesses and types, so the intra-drawer position of a
mapping foil frequently differed between core drawers, blanket drawers and reflector drawers. For
example, the mapping foils might be placed between a fuel plate column and a sodium plate
column in all core drawers. In blanket drawers, the mapping foils might be placed between a
column of depleted uranium plates and a column of sodium plates. In reflector drawers, mapping
foils would be placed between columns of stainless steel plates. Because the plate loadings and
plate thicknesses differed for core, blanket and reflector drawers, the intra-drawer X-coordinate of

 353

the mapping foil might also differ between drawer types. The presence of single and double
column fuel drawers in a loading also affected mapping foil positioning in some cases.
The mapping foils provided detailed reaction rate distributions throughout an assembly. Because
reaction rates in individual foils could not be computed accurately when the ZPR/ZPPR facilities
operated, the experimenters converted the mapping foil data to cell-averaged reaction rates that
could be computed accurately with the available computing resources.
Although it was not practical to place many foils in every drawer location of interest, it was
possible to place multiple foils of the same type between different plate columns in drawers at a
few select locations in the assembly. The experimenters used the reaction rates determined from
these more detailed measurements to compute average reaction rates in representative drawer
environments for reaction types of interest. These average reaction rates were called cell factors.
The cell factors were used to relate the reaction rate measured by an individual mapping foil to the
average reaction rate in the unit cell, i.e., drawer, containing that mapping foil.
Muliplying the reaction rate measured by each mapping foil by the appropriate cell factor, i.e., the
cell factor that most closely corresponded to the drawer environment at the mapping foil location,
produced cell-averaged reaction rates for the drawers that contained the mapping foils.
Cell factors were measured for various representative drawer environments in the assembly
including environments at the boundaries between different regions such as the core-blanket
interface and environments where single and double column fuel drawers were mixed. When the
ZPR/ZPPR facilities operated, cell factors were measured in the cell environments of interest. The
general consensus today is that modern computers, software and nuclear data evaluations make it
possible to compute cell factors that will be more accurate than the cell factors measured in the
ZPR/ZPPR assemblies.
The following is a description of typical foils used in ZPPR foil irradiations. 235U(n,f) reactions
were measured with 235U foils. The 235U foils were 12.7 mm (0.5 inches) in diameter and 0.112
mm (~0.0044 inches) thick. 238U(n,f) and 238U(n,γ) reactions were measured with 238U foils. The
diameter and thickness of the 238U foils were 12.7 mm and 0.140 mm (~0.0055 inches),
respectively. 235U foils and 238U foils were coated with Kel-F and then were covered on the top
and bottom with 0.0025 mm aluminum disks. The aluminum disks protected the foils during
handling and use.
239
  Pu foils were used to measure 239Pu(n,f) reactions. The diameter and thickness of the 239Pu foils
were 10.8 mm (~0.43 inches) and 0.127 mm (0.005 inches), respectively, and the nominal
plutonium mass in a foil was ~150 mg. The 239Pu foils were clad in 0.025 mm aluminum but were
not coated.
These foils are representative of the 239Pu, 235U and 238U foils used for foil irradiations at ZPPR
although the ZPPR foil inventory may have had similar foils with slightly different characteristics
such as different sizes. The ZPPR inventory also contained limited numbers of foils of other types.
Any material that could be cut into a shape that would fit the sample holders could be made into
an irradiation foil.
ANL-E and ANL-W maintained separate foil inventories. The dimensions and compositions of
the 235U, 238U and 239Pu foils in the ANL-E inventory were similar to the corresponding ZPPR

 354

foils, but ANL-E foils were not necessarily identical to the ZPPR foils. In addition, ANL-E may
have had multiple sets of 235U, 238U and 239Pu foils with different dimensions and compositions.
The report that documents foil irradiation results for an assembly is likely to describe the foils used
for those irradiations.
The 239Pu foils were not pure 239Pu. Likewise, 235U foils were not pure 235U, and 238U foils were
not pure 238U. The isotopic compositions of the different types of foils were known, and the
experimenters corrected for other isotopes in the foils when deriving the foil reaction rates from
the raw measurement data.
7.10.2 ZPPR Foil Irradiation Measurement Uncertainties
In addition to basic counting statistics, there are a number of other uncertainty components that
determine the total uncertainty for foil measurements in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies, and the relevant
uncertainties depend upon whether the quantity of interest is a relative reaction rate, an absolute
reaction rate, a cell-averaged reaction rate or a spectral index (reaction rate ratio for foils of
different types).
Pre- and post-irradiation techniques for foil measurements may have differed between ANL-E and
ANL-W, so some of the uncertainties differ for foil irradiations at ANL-E and ANL-W. The
uncertainties for ZPPR foil measurements will be discussed here. Uncertainties for foil
measurements at ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 will be discussed in Section 7.10.3.
To date no foil irradiation measurements in ZPR-3 have been reviewed. If foil irradiation
measurements were performed in ZPR-3, it is likely that uncertainties for ZPR-3 foil
measurements would be similar to the uncertainties for ZPPR foil measurements because a) some
of the ZPPR staff originally worked at ZPR-3 and b) both facilities would have used the Argonne
Fast Source Reactor (AFSR) at ANL-W for foil calibration, at least after the AFSR began
operations.
7.10.2.1 ZPPR Mapping Foil Reaction Rate Uncertainties
Mapping foils were placed at many locations in a ZPR/ZPPR assembly. These foils provide the
basic data for relative or normalized reaction rate distributions, absolute reaction rate distributions
relative to a specific power and irradiation time, cell-averaged reaction rate distributions and
reaction rate ratio or spectral index distributions. Section 7.10.2.1 discusses the uncertainties for
the basic ZPPR mapping foil data and for reaction rate distributions normalized to some value such
as the maximum measured foil value. Uncertainties related to the absolute reaction rates for ZPPR
foil irradiations are discussed in Section 7.10.2.2.
The published uncertainties for the mapping foils include several uncertainties in addition to the
actual counting statistics for the foil. These additional uncertainties are a) a 0.3% reproducibility
uncertainty related to foil positioning in the counting system, b) uncertainties related to corrections
for other isotopes in the foils, c) uncertainty related to correction for decay during the irradiation
period, d) uncertainty related to correction for decay during the elapsed time between the end of
irradiation and the foil counting and e) uncertainty related to any dead time corrections for the
counting system.

 355

The 0.3% reproducibility uncertainty refers to the fact that it was not possible to place every foil
at exactly the same position in the counting system to an arbitrary degree of precision. Tests in
which the operation of placing a foil in the counting system and counting it was repeated multiple
times showed that the effect of non-reproducibility in foil positioning on the measured count rate
was 0.3%.
In addition to the published uncertainties for the mapping foils, there is a 0.1% uncertainty in the
foil mass and an approximately 0.8% uncertainty related to the discrete channel boundaries for
integration of the peak in the ZPPR counting system (see IRPhEP benchmark ZPPR-LMFR-EXP-
002, Section 2.7.1.1 in Ref. 6). The uncertainty regarding discrete channel boundaries arises from
the fact that other fission product gamma peaks overlap the gamma peaks of 239Np, 133I, 97Nb, 132I
and 97mNb that were measured in the counting system.
There are also small uncertainties related to half-lives, fission yields, etc., but those uncertainties
are negligible compared to the counting statistics, 0.3% reproducibility uncertainty and 0.8%
channel boundary uncertainty.
Standard foils were irradiated, and the fission product gammas were counted to measure reaction
rates. An alternate technique based on solid state track recorders (SSTRs) was used occasionally
to address the problem of spectral softening in the radial blanket and radial reflector. A standard
238
 U foil had a 235U weight fraction of approximately 0.0022, corresponding to normal depleted
uranium. At locations far from the center of the core, fissions in the 235U component could make
a significant contribution to the measured 238U(n,f) reaction in a standard 238U foil. SSTRs were
sometimes used to minimize or eliminate the 235U contribution to the measured 238U(n,f) reaction
rate. The following is a description of the use of SSTRs in ZPPR-15.
The 238U fission rate was measured with SSTRs rather than 238U foils in locations outside of the
core and radial blanket in ZPPR-15B loading 134. Special 238U foils were used in the SSTR
measurements. These foils had a thickness of 0.25 mm, a diameter of 9.5 mm and a 235U fraction
of 3.0 ± 0.1 x 10-6 whereas standard 238U foils had a 235U fraction of approximately 0.0022. The
very low 235U fraction in the SSTR foils eliminated the 235U fission contribution in 238U(n,f)
measurements in regions with a relatively soft neutron spectrum. Packets of 238U foils and mica
were wrapped in aluminum foil, placed in drawers and irradiated. After irradiation, the fission
fragment tracks were counted to determine the number of fission tracks per unit area. Although
the reports are not clear regarding the function of the mica, it seems likely that the mica served as
the recording medium for the fission tracks. The tracks in the mica were probably counted visually
to determine the fission rate although the counting process may have been automated at some
point.
Power was reduced for the SSTR irradiation. The SSTR data were converted to units of
fissions/atom-watt-second using the integral power measured by the ex-core detectors.
Comparison of activation foils and SSTR data in a previous core indicated that SSTRs measure a
10% lower fission rate than foils. The SSTR data were adjusted to match the foil data by the
experimenters before the data were published.
For the SSTR data, there are the standard statistical uncertainties in counting tracks plus three
additional uncertainties. The first of these is a 3% random uncertainty for reproducibility in
counting tracks. The second is a 2.5% systematic uncertainty for adjustment of SSTR data to

 356

match the foil data. The third is a 2% uncertainty for the foil calibration. All of these uncertainties
are one-sigma values.
Foil irradiation was the standard technique for measuring reaction rate distributions in ZPR/ZPPR
assemblies. Any non-standard or alternate reaction rate measurement technique such as use of
SSTRs has a separate, unique set of associated uncertainties. In principle, the primary uncertainty
components for an alternate measurement technique are described in the document reporting the
reaction rate measurement results. In practice, the experimenters were not consistent about
documenting uncertainties beyond the reported measurement uncertainties (generally counting
statistics and minor adjustments).
The total uncertainty for an individual mapping foil is determined by adding the published
uncertainty, the 0.1% uncertainty in foil mass and the 0.8% uncertainty related to the discrete
channel boundaries for integration of the peak in the ZPPR counting system in quadrature (square
root of the sum of the squares).
The total uncertainty for any non-standard or alternate reaction rate measurement technique must
be determined by what the analyst can learn from the report documenting the reaction rate
measurement and from any supplementary research regarding the technique used for the reaction
rate measurement.
The 0.8% uncertainty related to discrete channel boundaries for integration of photopeaks applies
to the overlap of other fission product gamma peaks with the set of fission product peaks measured
in the counting system. In many cases, the non-standard foils discussed above were not fissionable
materials, so there were no fission product peaks to count. In such cases, it was necessary to count
other gammas, and the set of gammas counted likely differed for each type of non-fissionable foil
material. Details of counting of non-standard or non-fissionable foils are generally not available
today.
For non-standard foils that were not fissionable, the 0.8% uncertainty arising from overlapping
gamma peaks may not apply.
The uncertainties discussed above must be combined correctly if the reaction rates are normalized
to a specific measured value such as the largest value in a table. It is not valid to divide all of the
measured values and uncertainties in the table by a selected reference value from that table because
that selected reference value is itself uncertain. The correct procedure for determining the
uncertainty for a normalized ratio is the following (see Ref. 29, Section V.E):
 1. Consider x with uncertainty σx, y with uncertainty σy, and the desired ratio R = x/y.
 2. Define Sx = σx/x, Sy = σy/y, and SR = σR/R.
    3. Then SR = √((Sx)2 + (Sy)2)
SR is the correct relative uncertainty for any ratio such as normalization in which S x and Sy are
independent. In the present case, SR is an approximation because there are correlations for some
of the corrections. However, the uncertainties for those corrections are small compared to the
counting statistics, 0.3% reproducibility uncertainty and 0.8% uncertainty for the discrete channel
boundaries discussed above, so accounting for these correlations would not significantly affect S R.

 357

7.10.2.2 ZPPR Absolute Foil Reaction Rate Uncertainties
The uncertainty analysis in Section 7.10.2.1 applies to relative or normalized reaction rate
distributions and ratios such as the ratio of the measured foil reaction rate at each location to the
maximum measured foil reaction rate. For calculations of relative or normalized distributions and
ratios, the units in which the measured reaction rates are reported do not matter because they cancel
out in ratios. Likewise, uncertainties in calibration of the counting system do not matter for relative
distributions or ratios of foils of the same type. Relative or normalized mapping foil data do not
depend upon the power level or duration of irradiation in the reactor.
The ZPPR experimenters also used the foils to measure absolute reaction rates. Absolute reaction
rates do depend upon the power level and duration of irradiation. Absolute reaction rates were
expressed in units of reactions per atom-watt-second. Conversion of the basic mapping foil data
to absolute reaction rates requires relating the measured mapping foil reaction rates to a specific
reactor power and irradiation time.
Determining absolute foil reaction rates required calibration of the detector system used to count
the foils. The ZPPR staff measured a calibration factor to relate the number of counts recorded in
the gamma counting system to the number of reactions required to produce those counts. If C γ is
the number of counts recorded in the detector system for a reaction and N is the number of reactions
that occurred to produce Cγ counts in the detector system, then the calibration factor, ε γ, was
defined as
 εγ = (Cγ)calib/(N)calib
according to Ref. 30.
For calculations of absolute reaction rates, uncertainties related to detector calibration and the
calibration factor must be added to the uncertainties listed in Section 7.10.2.1 for the basic mapping
foil data. The following is a summary of a description of reaction rate calibration techniques at
ZPPR by S. B. Brumbach and D. W. Maddison of the ZPPR staff [30].
Foil masses were measured, and the uncertainty in the measured masses was less than 0.1%. The
foil mass uncertainty was neglected for calibration purposes because it is small compared to other
sources of uncertainty for detector calibration. Uncertainties in the foil material isotopics were
neglected for the same reason.
Back-to-back (BTB) fission chambers were used for the calibration measurements. The BTB
chambers were a fundamental component of the detector calibration process. Fissionable and
fissile materials were electroplated onto small stainless steel substrate disks (15.88 mm diameter,
0.08 mm thick) which were placed in the BTB chambers. Deposit masses were ~100 μg for 235U
and 239Pu and ~250 μg for 238U.
The primary deposit standards were 235U deposits. A weighed amount of 235U was dissolved, and
a known amount of the resulting solution was used for the electroplating process. After
electroplating, the mass of 235U remaining in the solution was measured to establish the mass of
235
 U deposited on the substrate. Mass values could also be verified by irradiating pairs of deposits
in a BTB chamber and comparing count rate ratios to mass ratios to verify mass values. Dissolving

 358

one of the deposits and determining its mass by isotope dilution mass spectrometry provided
additional mass verification. The uncertainty in the mass of the reference 235U deposit was 1.2%.
After the mass standard for the reference 235U deposit was established, masses of other fissile
deposits were determined relative to the reference 235U deposit in the BTB fission chamber
measurements in the Argonne Fast Source Reactor (AFSR) thermal column. Use of the AFSR
thermal column for establishing the mass values required knowledge of thermal cross sections and
g-factors for 235U and 239Pu. A 1% correction with a 0.4% uncertainty was applied to observed
BTB count rates for fission fragment pulses lost below a predetermined bias level.
The mass of the 239Pu deposit used in the reaction rate calibration was determined by the AFSR
thermal column BTB chamber method. The components of the uncertainty in the 239Pu deposit
mass are: 1) 0.1% for counting statistics in the BTB chamber, 2) 0.42% for the 239Pu cross section,
3) 0.28% for the 239Pu g-factor, 4) 0.31% for the 235U cross section, 5) 0.16% for the 235U g-factor,
6) 1.2% for the 235U reference deposit mass and 7) 0.4% for the BTB fission chamber correction.
The total uncertainty for the 239Pu deposit mass was 1.4%.
The masses of other 235U deposits were also determined by irradiation in the thermal column with
the reference 235U deposit. The uncertainty components for one of these 235U deposits are: 1)
0.05% for counting statistics in the BTB chamber, 2) 1.2% for the reference 235U deposit mass, 3)
0.4% for the BTB fission chamber correction. The total uncertainty for any 235U deposit mass
except the reference deposit was 1.3%.
Deposits used to calibrate the 238U fission rate were made of natural uranium. The natural uranium
deposit was irradiated in the AFSR thermal column with a reference 235U deposit. This irradiation
allowed the 235U mass and, consequently, the 238U mass in the natural uranium deposit to be
determined. The components of the uncertainty in the 238U mass in the natural uranium deposit
are: 1) 0.3% for counting statistics in the BTB chamber, 2) 0.8% for the isotopic composition of
the deposit, 3) 1.2% for the mass of the reference 235U deposit and 4) 0.4% for the BTB fission
chamber correction. The total uncertainty in the 238U deposit mass in the natural uranium deposit
was 1.5%.
A BTB fission chamber was a thin-walled aluminum hemisphere with a diameter of approximately
3.56 cm. The fissile deposit substrate disks were mounted back-to-back on a lip in the center of
the chamber. One or two irradiation foils could be centered between the backs of the deposits for
a given measurement.
A fundamental assumption in the BTB chamber irradiations was that both deposits experience the
same neutron flux and spectrum, but the chambers were irradiated in reactor environments where
flux gradients existed. Ideally, the deposits were perpendicular to the direction of the flux gradient
during irradiation, but that was not possible in some cases because orientation of the chamber was
restricted by cables and gas tubes protruding from the back of the chamber. In addition, neutron
fission and capture in foils placed between the substrate disks could in principle introduce a
gradient. Effects of flux gradients could be determined by measuring count rates, rotating the BTB
chamber 180° about the axis defined by the projecting tubes and cables to face the opposite
direction and obtaining another count rate. If the count rate ratios from the two orientations were
different, an average value could be used. The wires and gas tubes projecting from the back of the
BTB chamber were symmetric about the axial centerline of the chamber (see Ref. 30, Figure 1),

 359

so rotating the BTB chamber 180° did not introduce any asymmetry related to the wires and gas
tubes.
Effects of flux gradients and self-shielding in a BTB chamber with a 239Pu foil between the
substrate disks were measured in several ZPPR environments. No statistically significant
variations in the calibration constants were found, so no self-shielding corrections were applied to
BTB chamber measurements during ZPPR irradiations when 239Pu foils or 235U foils were placed
in the chambers. The situation with respect to 238U foils was less clear, but no corrections were
applied to BTB chamber data for the effects of any of the foils on any of the deposits.
The deposits in the BTB chambers provided reference values for calibrating foils that were placed
in the chambers. The BTB chamber contained a 235U foil, 235U deposit, 239Pu foil and 239Pu deposit
for the irradiation.
The largest single uncertainty for the calibration foils resulted from counting statistics. This
uncertainty was approximately 0.5% for 239Pu fission, 0.4% for 235U fission, 1% for 238U fission
and 0.5% for 238U capture. The other significant uncertainty for the calibration foils was the 0.3%
reproducibility uncertainty when the calibration foils were placed in the detector and counted.
Several minor corrections were made to the count rates in the calibration foils. Uncertainties
related to these corrections were not propagated because either the uncertainties were negligible
or else the uncertainties appeared in a ratio and, consequently, cancelled out.
The components of the uncertainty for the absolute 239Pu fission rate foil calibration are: 1) 0.5%
uncertainty for counting statistics, 2) 0.3% reproducibility uncertainty and 3) 1.4% 239Pu deposit
mass uncertainty. The total uncertainty in the absolute 239Pu fission rate foil calibration was 1.5%.
The components of the uncertainty for the absolute 235U fission rate foil calibration are: 1) 0.4%
uncertainty for counting statistics, 2) 0.3% reproducibility uncertainty and 3) 1.3% 235U deposit
mass uncertainty. The total uncertainty in the 235U fission rate foil calibration factor was 1.4%.
Absolute 238U fission rate calibration required simultaneous irradiation of a depleted uranium foil,
natural uranium deposit and 235U deposit in a BTB chamber. The components of the uncertainty
for the absolute 238U fission rate foil calibration are: 1) 1.5% for the 238U deposit mass uncertainty,
2) 0.3% for the reproducibility uncertainty, 3) 1% for gamma counting statistics for the foil and 4)
0.7% uncertainty for fission chamber counts due to 238U fission. The total uncertainty in the 238U
fission rate foil calibration factor was 2.0%.
Absolute 238U capture rate calibration involved simultaneous irradiation of a 239Pu deposit and 238U
foil in a BTB chamber in the AFSR thermal column. The components of the uncertainty for the
absolute 238U capture rate foil calibration are: 1) 1.4% for the 239Pu deposit mass, 2) 0.5%
uncertainty for counting statistics for 238U capture, 3) 0.3% reproducibility uncertainty, 4) 0.6%
for the 238U capture cross section and 5) 0.2% for the 238U g-factor. The total uncertainty in the
238
 U capture rate foil calibration factor was 1.6%. Table 7.19 provides the total uncertainties for
the 239Pu, 235U and 238U calibration factors.

 360

 Table 7.19. Total Uncertainties for the 239Pu, 235U and 238U Calibration Factors.

The total uncertainty for an absolute foil reaction rate measurement is the sum of the total mapping
foil uncertainty and the total calibration factor uncertainty added in quadrature.
There were no reference deposits or reference foils for some of the uncommon or non-standard
foils in the ZPPR foil inventory. Consequently, it was not possible to determine absolute reaction
rates for such foils. If no reference deposits or reference foils were available for calibration, the
experimenters applied an arbitrary normalization to the measured values.
7.10.2.3 ZPPR Cell-Averaged Reaction Rate Uncertainties
A mapping foil was placed between two specific columns of plates in a drawer, so the reaction rate
measured in that foil was affected by the adjacent plates. For example, the reaction rate measured
in a 235U foil placed between a fuel plate and a sodium plate differed from the reaction rate
measured by a 235U foil placed between a sodium plate and a depleted uranium plate in the same
drawer.
It was not practical to compute accurate reaction rates for individual mapping foils at their exact
locations in any ZPR/ZPPR assembly when the ZPR/ZPPR machines operated. Monte Carlo
calculations of foils in their exact locations in detailed as-built models were not possible then and
continue to be an issue today. Calculations of foil reaction rates by the ZPPR staff were based on
deterministic models in R-Z, X-Y or X-Y-Z geometry. Due to the computer hardware limitations
of that era, there was either one mesh point or four mesh points (2 x 2) in the X-Y plane of the unit
cell defined by a drawer and matrix tube.
The standard practice at ZPPR was to convert the mapping foil data to cell-averaged reaction rates
that could be computed with the computers and software available at that time. In this context, a
cell consisted of the drawer, plates and surrounding matrix tube at the desired location.
Although it was not practical to place multiple foils in every drawer of interest, it was possible to
place multiple foils in selected drawers to measure intra-drawer reaction rate distributions in a
limited number of drawer types in representative cell environments. A cell factor was measured
by placing foils between various columns of plates in a drawer to determine an average reaction
rate for the unit cell represented by that drawer and its neighbors. The ratio of the average reaction
rate in the unit cell to the measured reaction rate for the mapping foil at the specific location of
interest in the cell was the cell factor. For example, for the 239Pu(n,f) reaction, 239Pu mapping foils
were placed adjacent to Pu-U-Mo fuel plates in drawers at many core locations. At selected core
locations representing typical unit cells, 239Pu foils were placed between many of the plate columns
in the drawer. The average 239Pu(n,f) reaction rate measured in the unit cell divided by the

 361

239
  Pu(n,f) reaction rate for the 239Pu mapping foil adjacent to the Pu-U-Mo plate in that unit cell
was the 239Pu(n,f) cell factor for that cell.
The measured cell factor was applicable to any drawer master in the same unit cell configuration,
i.e., a drawer master with similar plate columns (ignoring differences in the plate lengths resulting
from the finite plate inventory) and with similar neighboring drawers. Cell factors were measured
for various combinations of drawer types in the core, radial blanket, axial blanket and at the
boundary between different regions such as the core-radial blanket interface.
Multiplying the reaction rate in the mapping foil at location L by the appropriate cell factor for
that mapping foil location converted the mapping foil reaction rate at location L to an average
reaction rate for the cell, i.e., to a cell-averaged reaction rate, that could be computed with the
computing resources available in the 1970s and 1980s when ZPPR operated. In this context, cell
refers to the drawer and matrix tube at location L. Cell-averaged reaction rates were determined
for the relevant reactions of interest such as 239Pu(n,f), 235U(n,f), 238U(n,f) and 238U(n,γ).
The total uncertainty for a cell-averaged reaction rate includes a component from the mapping foil
data and a component from the determination of the relevant cell factor. The following discussion
is a summary of an analysis of uncertainties in cell-averaged reaction rates by S. B. Brumbach and
J. M. Gasidlo of the ZPPR staff [31].
There are three uncertainty components for the determination of cell factors for absolute fission
and capture rates. First, determining cell factors required measuring and/or calculating reaction
rates inside Pu-U-Mo fuel plates and depleted uranium (DU) metal plates (see Ref. 31, Section
IV). The plates used at ZPPR were solid, so special procedures were required to determine in-
plate reaction rates. There are systematic uncertainties related to determining these in-plate
reaction rates. Table 7.20 shows the systematic uncertainties for determination of in-plate reaction
rates for the Pu-U-Mo and depleted uranium metal plates.
 Table 7.20. Uncertainties in Determination of In-Plate Reaction Rates.

 Reaction Pu-U-Mo DU metal
 σ, % σ, %
 239
                                              Pu(n,f)     0.5
 235
                                              U(n,f)      0.5          0.5
 238
                                              U(n,f)      1.5          0.2
 238
                                              U(n,γ)      1.0          0.0
The uncertainties for the depleted uranium plates in Table 7.20 are due to uncertainties in isotopic
composition and loss of fission products. Pu-U-Mo plates and ZPPR HEU plates were canned, so
it was not possible to measure in-plate reaction rates for these materials directly. The uncertainties
for Pu-U-Mo plates in Table 7.20 arise from applying the results of the Stanford-Robinson
experiment and measurements with half-thickness fuel plates.
The Stanford-Robinson experiment was performed by G. Stanford and W. Robinson of the ANL-
E staff. They interleaved 235U foils and 238U foils, placed the resulting stack of foils in a hole in a

 362

special plate and irradiated the stack to obtain an approximate intra-plate fission distribution. The
experiment was performed only once, so it represents a single cell environment. It is not clear why
235
 U foils were used rather than 239Pu foils in an attempt to measure the intra-plate fission
distribution in a Pu-U-Mo plate.
Measurements with half-thickness fuel plates provided data that approximated the reaction rate at
the center and outer surfaces of a standard fuel plate.
The consensus today is that current computers, software and nuclear data can provide more
accurate intra-plate reaction rates than the measurements that were possible when the ZPR/ZPPR
machines operated.
In practice, the approximations involved in determining in-plate reaction rates do not have a large
effect on the total uncertainty for cell-averaged reaction rates because the total uncertainty for the
cell-averaged reaction rates is dominated by the mapping foil uncertainty and the calibration factor
uncertainty.
The second cell factor uncertainty component results from the counting statistics and foil
positioning uncertainty in the cell factor measurement. Counting statistics and foil positioning
uncertainty vary for different cell factors and measurement configurations. The exact nature of
the contents of neighboring drawers affects the measured reaction rates in foils in the cell of
interest. For example, let SC denote a single column fuel drawer, DC denote a double fuel column
drawer and RB denote a radial blanket drawer. If the middle drawer is the cell for which a cell
factor is being measured, then SC-SC-SC, DC-SC-DC, SC-SC-RB, and DC-SC-RB are four
different environments for the center SC drawer. Each of these environments produces different
reaction rates in the center SC drawer. It is noteworthy to point out that the importance of local
gradients can depend upon changes well beyond just the adjacent drawers. Regardless, it was
necessary to measure cell factors for various environments and configurations in ZPPR. In the
present context, environment refers to the unit cell for which the cell factor is being measured and
the adjacent drawers on both sides of the unit cell of interest.
For example, Table 7.21 to Table 7.24 give the measured cell factors for ZPPR-15B. Column 1
in each of these tables gives the measured cell factor, column 2 gives the reported uncertainty for
the cell factor and column 3 gives the relative uncertainty for the cell factor.
Column 4 in Table 7.21 to Table 7.24 gives the applicable cell environment. The entries in column
4 correspond to the following:
 a) SC – single fuel column drawer,
 b) DC – double fuel column drawer,
 c) Sym Zr – drawer with symmetric Zr column(s),
 d) Asym Zr – drawer with asymmetric Zr column(s),
 e) RB – radial blanket,
 f) AB – axial blanket,
 g) RR – radial reflector.
Finally, column 5 cites the axial region over which the cell factor is applicable. In some cases, the
entry in column 5 refers to an actual range to which the cell factor applies such as 0.0 mm – 381.8

 363

mm. “All” indicates that the cell factor applies over the entire axial range. If there is a single
number in column 5, then the cell factor applies to that axial position.
