The third uncertainty component for the cell factor determination is the appropriate uncertainty for
detector calibration for absolute reaction rate measurements.
The uncertainty in the determination of in-plate reaction rates, counting statistics for the relevant
cell factor in Table 7.21 to Table 7.24 and the relevant detector calibration uncertainty must be
added in quadrature with the mapping foil uncertainty to determine the total uncertainty for the
cell-averaged reaction rate that corresponds to the selected mapping foil.
The general consensus today is that current computers, software and nuclear data can provide more
accurate cell factors than the measured cell factors obtained when the ZPR/ZPPR machines
operated.
The mapping foil measurements are the primary reaction rate data. Cell-averaged reaction rates
are derived from the mapping foil data by application of measured or computed cell factors. When
the ZPR/ZPPR facilities operated, available computer hardware and software restricted calculation

 368

of reaction rates to cell-averaged reaction rates in most cases. While it may be difficult or
impossible to compute mapping foil reaction rates by Monte Carlo today, it is possible to compute
mapping foil reaction rate distributions with deterministic models. Given that the primary
disadvantage of computing foil reaction rates in deterministic codes today is obtaining the cross
sections for the foil itself, having a cell (drawer) averaged measured value to compare against
could be of significant value. However, from experience with ZPR/ZPPR foil calculations, it is
sufficiently accurate to directly calculate the measured foil reaction rate distributions with a
deterministic code. Thus if it is possible to compute mapping foil reaction rates with acceptable
accuracy, it is recommended that analysts calculate mapping foil reaction rates rather than cell-
averaged reaction rates because the uncertainties associated with in-plate reaction rates, detector
calibration and the cell factor measurement can be eliminated.
Consequently, the mapping foil data are likely to be of more interest than the cell-averaged reaction
rates for future applications.
7.10.2.4 ZPPR Spectral Index/Reaction Rate Ratio Uncertainties
In addition to the reaction rate distributions based on mapping foil data, the absolute reaction rate
distributions and the cell-averaged reaction rate distributions, it was common practice at ZPPR to
determine and report reaction rate ratios. A reaction rate ratio, also known as a spectral index, was
determined by dividing one cell-averaged reaction rate by another cell-averaged reaction rate at
the same location. The denominator was typically either the 239Pu(n,f) reaction rate or the 235U(n,f)
reaction rate. The reaction rates were commonly abbreviated as F9 for 239Pu(n,f), F5 for 235U(n,f),
F8 for 238U(n,f) and C8 for 238U(n,γ). Note that F9, F5, F8 and C8 are sometimes written as f9, f5,
f8 and c8, respectively.
The following is a summary of the uncertainty discussion for spectral indices in Refs. 30 and 31.
Some uncertainty components are common to all absolute reaction rate calibrations, so these
common components do not contribute to the total uncertainties for the spectral indices. The total
uncertainty for a reaction rate ratio or spectral index combines a) the uncertainty for the mapping
foil in the numerator, b) the uncertainty for the mapping foil in the denominator, c) the uncertainty
for the cell factor for the numerator reaction, d) the uncertainty in the cell factor for the
denominator reaction, e) the systematic uncertainties in determination of in-plate reaction rates
and f) the uncertainty in the calibration factor for the reaction rate ratio. These six uncertainties
are added in quadrature to determine the total uncertainty for the reaction rate ratio or spectral
index.
The uncertainties for the mapping foil in the numerator, the uncertainty for the mapping foil in the
denominator, the uncertainty for the cell factor for the numerator reaction, the uncertainty for the
cell factor for the denominator reaction and the systematic uncertainties in determination of in-
plate reaction rates were discussed in previous sections.
Ref. 30 provides a detailed description of procedures for determining absolute reaction rate
calibrations and calibration factors.
The following is an example of the uncertainty determination for the calibration factors for the
spectral indices in ZPPR-15.

 369

The 1.5% uncertainty in the calibration factor for the F8/F5 ratio combines 1) a 1% uncertainty for
the fission count rate for 238U, 2) a 0.4% uncertainty for the fission count rate for 235U, 3) a 0.7%
uncertainty in 238U counts for the natural uranium deposit irradiated at ZPPR as part of the
calibration, 4) a 0.3% uncertainty in the fission chamber counts from the natural uranium deposit
irradiated in the Argonne Fast Source Reactor (AFSR) and 5) a 0.8% uncertainty in the mass
fraction ratio for the natural uranium deposit.
The 0.9% uncertainty in the calibration factor for the F5/F9 ratio consists of 1) a 0.42% uncertainty
in the 239Pu thermal cross section used in the calibration, 2) a 0.28% uncertainty in the 239Pu g-
factor used in the calibration, 3) a 0.31% uncertainty in the 235U thermal cross section used in the
calibration, 4) a 0.16% uncertainty in the 235U g-factor used in the calibration, 5) a 0.4% uncertainty
in the 235U fission count rate and 6) a 0.5% uncertainty in the 239Pu fission count rate.
The 1.2% uncertainty in the calibration factor for the C8/F9 ratio consists of 1) a 0.6% uncertainty
in the 238U thermal cross section used in the calibration, 2) a 0.2% uncertainty in the 238U g-factor
used in the calibration, 3) a 0.42% uncertainty in the 239Pu thermal cross section used in the
calibration, 4) a 0.28% uncertainty in the 239Pu g-factor used in the calibration, 5) a 0.5%
uncertainty in counting statistics and a 0.3% positioning uncertainty for the 238U measurement and
6) a 0.5% uncertainty in counting statistics and a 0.3% positioning uncertainty for the 239Pu

The 1.7% uncertainty in the calibration factor for the F8/F9 ratio combines 1) a 1% uncertainty for
the fission count rate for 238U, 2) a 0.5% uncertainty for the fission count rate for 239Pu, 3) a 0.7%
uncertainty in 238U counts for the natural uranium deposit irradiated at ZPPR as part of the
calibration, 4) a 0.3% uncertainty in the fission chamber counts from the natural uranium deposit
irradiated in the Argonne Fast Source Reactor (AFSR), 5) a 0.8% uncertainty in the mass fraction
ratio of the natural uranium deposit and 6) a 0.6% uncertainty from the 235U and 239Pu thermal
cross sections and g-factors used in the calibration.
The spectral indices published when ZPPR operated are based on cell-averaged reaction rates
because it was not possible to compute accurate reaction rates for individual mapping foils at that
time. However, in addition to the uncertainty in the mapping foil in the numerator and the
uncertainty in the mapping foil in the denominator, a spectral index based on cell-averaged reaction
rates includes additional uncertainties related to the cell factors, determination of in-plate reaction
rates and the calibration factor for the reaction rate ratio.
Today it is possible to compute reaction rates for individual mapping foils using deterministic
methods. A new reaction rate ratio or spectral index can be determined based on just the mapping
foil data for the reactions of interest at the location of interest. The uncertainties for this new
reaction rate ratio, R, based on mapping foil data are the uncertainties for the two mapping foils
and the uncertainty for the ratio, SR, described at the end of Section 7.10.2.1. If it is possible to
compute mapping foil reaction rates with acceptable accuracy, it is recommended that analysts
calculate spectral indices directly from the mapping foil reaction rates rather than using spectral
indices based on cell-averaged reaction rates because the uncertainties associated with cell factors,
determination of in-plate reaction rates and the calibration factor for the reaction rate ratio can be
eliminated.

 370

7.10.3 ANL-E Foil Irradiation Measurement Uncertainties
The following discussion applies to both ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 because ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 were built
at the same time, shared the same material inventory, and were operated by the same experimental
staff. The discussion of experimental techniques for foil irradiations in Section 7.10.1 also applies
to ANL-E facilities. There were some differences in foil calibration techniques between ANL-E
and ANL-W, and there may have been some minor differences in post-irradiation processing as
well.
The foils used at ANL-E were similar to the foils used at ANL-W, but they were not identical to
ANL-W foils. For example, Table 7.25 shows the foils used in ZPR-6/7. Uranium foils were
coated with Kel-F, and then a 0.001-in thick disk of aluminum foil was glued to each side of each
uranium foil to prevent fission fragment loss and to protect the foil. Plutonium foils were clad.
The foils described in Table 7.25 are representative examples of the uranium and plutonium foils
in the ANL-E foil inventory, but there were other sizes of the standard 235U, 238U and 239Pu foils
as well as foils of other materials.
Any material that could be shaped to fit the sample holders used for foil counting could be made
into a foil, and the foil inventory contained foils of other materials in addition to standard 235U,
238
 U and 239Pu foils. A relevant distinction between the standard 235U, 238U and 239Pu foils and
foils made of other materials relates to calibration for absolute reaction rate measurements. Much
effort was devoted to calibrating standard 235U, 238U and 239Pu foils for absolute reaction rate
measurements. That may not have been the case for foils of other materials. Consequently,
uncertainties discussed for relative or normalized reaction rates in mapping foils generally apply
to standard and non-standard foils, but uncertainties discussed for absolute reaction rate
measurements with standard foils do not necessarily apply to absolute reaction rate measurements
(if any) with non-standard foils.
The report that documents the foil measurement will probably include a description of the foils
used in the experiment.

ANL-E had foil holders similar to the foil holders used at ZPPR, but at least some early ANL-E
assemblies either used aluminum foil to position the irradiation foils in the drawers or used a very
small amount of silicone grease (< 1 mg) to affix foils to plates in the drawers.
In the initial detector system used at ANL-E, gamma activity of irradiated foils was counted with
NaI(Tl) scintillation detectors in an automated foil counting system. Fission rates were determined
by counting fission product gammas above 550 keV. The capture rate in 238U foils (depleted
uranium foils) was determined by counting 239Np gamma activity at 106 keV using a coincidence
technique. Fission product counting was performed first and was followed by coincidence
counting of depleted uranium foils.
The ANL-E foil counting system was later expanded by addition of two 200-sample automatic
sample changers and one 300-sample automatic sample changer. Each of these new sample
changers had a Ge(Li) detector, and all three of the new detectors were connected to a common

 372

computer-based data acquisition system. Addition of the Ge(Li) detectors made the ANL-E and
ANL-W counting systems nearly equivalent.
One minor consequence of using the Ge(Li) detectors was increased counting time to achieve the
same statistical uncertainty as the NaI(Tl) system. The NaI(Tl) detector was based on integral
counting of fission product gammas. The Ge(Li) detectors counted several individual fission
product photopeaks and integrated the result.
The gamma counting data were then processed with several computer codes to fit an analytical
function to the selected photopeak(s) and to correct for decay rates, counting system dead time,
background radiation and, in the case of 239Np coincidence counting, accidental coincidences and
gamma ray self-absorption. Relative reaction rates per unit mass of foil material were obtained
from these codes. These relative reaction rates were then corrected for contaminating isotopes in
the foils to yield relative reaction rates per unit mass of the principal isotope ( 239Pu, 235U, 238U) for
each foil.
7.10.3.1 ANL-E Mapping Foil Reaction Rate Uncertainties
Uncertainties in the basic mapping foil data at ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 are similar to the uncertainties in
basic ZPPR mapping foil data (see Section 7.10.2.1). In addition to counting statistics, the
published uncertainty associated with ANL-E mapping foil data includes uncertainties related to
a) reproducibility uncertainty related to foil positioning, b) correction for decay during the
irradiation period, c) correction for decay during the time between the end of irradiation and foil
counting, d) dead time corrections for the counting system, and e) corrections for other isotopes in
the foils.
The uncertainty in the foil mass is approximately 0.1%.
In principle, there is one distinction between the total uncertainty for ZPPR mapping foil data and
ANL-E mapping foil data. Section 7.10.2.1 discussed a 0.8% uncertainty related to the discrete
channel boundaries for integration of the peak in the ZPPR counting system that arises because
other fission product gamma peaks overlap the gamma peaks of 239Np, 133I, 97Nb, 132I and 97mNb
that were measured in the counting system.
The NaI(Tl) scintillation detectors counted all fission product gammas above 550 keV, so the
overlap issue does not arise for the NaI(Tl) system. Because the Ge(Li) detectors counted several
individual photopeaks, the overlap issue does apply to mapping foils that were counted with the
Ge(Li) detectors.
Available documents do not show when ANL-E acquired the Ge(Li) detectors, but that probably
happened sometime after ZPPR began operations, i.e., sometime after 1969. In addition, unless a
report states which counting system was used to count the foils from a particular experiment, it is
not possible to determine whether a set of foils was counted with a NaI(Tl) detector or a Ge(Li)
detector. The conservative position is to assume the 0.8% uncertainty related to discrete channel
boundaries for integration of the photopeaks applies to all ANL-E mapping foil data.
The total uncertainty for an individual mapping foil is determined by adding the published
uncertainty, the 0.1% uncertainty in foil mass and the assumed 0.8% uncertainty related to the

 373

discrete channel boundaries for integration of the photopeaks in the counting system in quadrature
(square root of the sum of the squares).
For non-standard foils that were not fissionable, the 0.8% uncertainty arising from overlapping
gamma peaks may not apply.
The total uncertainty for any non-standard or alternate reaction rate measurement technique such
as use of the solid state track recorders discussed in Section 7.10.2.1 must be determined by what
the analyst can learn from the report documenting the reaction rate measurement and from any
supplementary research regarding the technique used for the reaction rate measurement.
If a ratio of mapping foil reaction rates is computed, the correct procedure for determining the
uncertainty for a normalized ratio is the procedure listed in Section 7.10.2.1 based on Section V.E
of Ref. 29:
 1. Consider x with uncertainty σx, y with uncertainty σy, and the desired ratio R = x/y.
 2. Define Sx = σx/x, Sy = σy/y, and SR = σR/R.
    3. Then SR = √((Sx)2 + (Sy)2)
SR is the correct relative uncertainty for any ratio such as normalization in which S x and Sy are
independent. SR is an approximation for mapping foil ratios because there are correlations for
some of the corrections. However, the uncertainties for those corrections are small compared to
the counting statistics, reproducibility uncertainty and assumed 0.8% uncertainty for the discrete
channel boundaries discussed above, so accounting for these correlations would not significantly
affect SR.
7.10.3.2 ANL-E Absolute Foil Reaction Rate Uncertainties
The uncertainty analysis in Section 7.10.3.1 applies to relative or normalized reaction rate
distributions and ratios such as the ratio of the measured foil reaction rate at each location to the
maximum measured foil reaction rate. The units in which the measured reaction rates are reported
do not matter for normalized distributions and ratios because the units cancel out in ratios.
Likewise, the power level, irradiation time and uncertainties in calibration of the counting system
do not matter for relative distributions in foils of the same type.
Absolute reaction rates were expressed in units of reactions per atom-watt-second, so absolute
reaction rates do depend on the power level and duration of irradiation. Conversion of the basic
mapping foil data to absolute reaction rates required relating the measured mapping foil reaction
rates to a specific reactor power and irradiation time.
Determining absolute foil reaction rates also requires calibration of the detector system used to
count the foils. To compute the total uncertainty for absolute foil reaction rates, uncertainties
related to detector calibration and the calibration factor must be added to the uncertainties listed in
Section 7.10.3.1 for the basic mapping foil data.
Detector calibrations at ANL-E were based on a) irradiations in a reference thermal spectrum
provided by the thermal column of the Argonne Thermal Source Reactor (ATSR), b) simultaneous
irradiations at the faces of absolute fission counters located in the ZPR-6 or ZPR-9 assembly and
c) radiochemical analysis of irradiated foils. The following material is a summary of information
in the IRPhEP benchmark of ZPR-6/7 (see benchmark ZPR-LMFR-EXP-001 in Ref. 6).

 374

on his experience and research while performing identical types of measurements in the same
facility several years after the ZPR-6/7 measurements were performed. Note that uncertainties in
the foil mass and composition are included in the principal components in each of these tables.
Specifically, they are included in the chamber mass component in Table 7.26, in the self shielding
component in Table 7.27, and in the 99Mo yield component in Table 7.28.

 foils and measurement foils, efficiency changes of detector with thickness, foil positioning
 uncertainty and other random errors.
Although the uncertainties listed in Table 7.26 through Table 7.28 were derived for ZPR-6/7, they
are applicable to ANL-E assemblies in general in the absence of more detailed information for a
specific assembly. Fission chamber calibration, thermal column calibration and radiochemistry
calibration were all used for ZPR-6/7, but foil reaction rates in other assemblies may be based on
one or two of these methods. The total uncertainty for detector calibration will depend on which
methods were used for the calibration.
The total uncertainty for an absolute foil reaction rate measurement is the sum of the total mapping
foil uncertainty and the total calibration factor uncertainty added in quadrature.
Absolute reaction rates were determined for 238U(n,γ), 238U(n,f), 235U(n,f) and 239Pu(n,f). Foils of
various other materials were fabricated and used in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9, but there were no
corresponding detector calibrations for these other foil materials in most cases. In such cases, the
experimenters applied an arbitrary normalization to the measured foil reaction rates.

 377

7.10.3.3 ANL-E Cell-Averaged Reaction Rate Uncertainties
The constraints discussed in Section 7.10.2 regarding foil measurements and calculation of foil
reaction rates at ZPPR also apply to foil measurements at ZPR-6 and ZPR-9. Cost considerations,
schedule constraints and the finite foil inventory made it impractical to place foils next to every
column of plates in every drawer in the row(s) and column(s) of interest in an assembly. Likewise,
calculations of foil reaction rates were based on deterministic models in R-Z, X-Y or X-Y-Z
geometry due to computer hardware and software limitations when the ZPR/ZPPR facilities
operated. In general, there was either one mesh point or four mesh points (2 x 2) in the X-Y plane
of the unit cell consisting of a drawer and matrix tube.
Multiplying the reaction rate in the mapping foil at location L by the appropriate cell factor for
that mapping foil location converted the mapping foil reaction rate at location L to an average
reaction rate for the cell, i.e., to a cell-averaged reaction rate, that could be computed with the
computing resources available when the ZPR/ZPPR machines operated. In this context, cell refers
to the drawer and matrix tube at location L. Cell-averaged reaction rates were determined for the
relevant reactions of interest such as 239Pu(n,f), 235U(n,f), 238U(n,f) and 238U(n,γ).
The procedure for determining the cell factors required to compute cell-averaged reaction rates at
ANL-E was similar to the procedure used to determine cell factors at ZPPR. A cell factor was
measured by placing foils between various columns of plates in a drawer to determine an average
reaction rate for the unit cell represented by that drawer and its neighbors. The ratio of the average
reaction rate in the unit cell to the measured reaction rate for the mapping foil at the specific
location of interest in the cell was the cell factor. Cell factors were measured in representative
environments in the assembly as discussed in Section 7.10.2.3.
The available ZPPR documents do not discuss the actual mechanics of measuring cell factors. A
common practice at ANL-E was to make intra-cell foil measurements in sample boxes. In ZPR-
6/7, for example, intra-cell measurements were made in 2 inch cubic stainless steel sample boxes
with 10-mil (0.25 mm) walls. The foils described above were placed between plates of a unit cell
loading in a sample box. A small amount of high-vacuum silicone grease (< 1 mg) was used to
stick the foils to the plates to fix their positions in the unit cell. A 1 mil (0.025 mm) thick aluminum
sheet was placed between a foil and an adjacent U3O8 plate to prevent fission product transfer. A
similar process was likely used to measure cell factors in other ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 assemblies.
ZPPR may also have used a similar process.
Data from the sample boxes were used to determine cell-averaged reaction rates. The cell average
reaction rate, rca, is defined by
 rca = (ΣriAi)/(ΣAi)
where the subscript i refers to a region of the cell such as a fuel plate or U 3O8 plate, Ai is the atom
density in region i of the isotope in question, and ri is the per atom reaction rate in region i. The
values of ri were determined from “point values” of the reaction rates (reaction rates in the foils)
plus auxiliary information about the spatial distribution of the reaction in the plate of U 3O8 or fuel.
Such auxiliary information was derived from subsidiary experiments of several types:
 a) irradiation of depleted uranium foils inside a simulated fuel plate consisting of alternating
 layers of enriched and depleted uranium bounded by 15 mils of stainless steel

 378

 b) irradiation of stacks of depleted uranium foils in holes in depleted uranium plates and
 stacks of enriched uranium foils in holes in enriched uranium plates in selected assemblies
 c) investigation of the perturbations to the reaction rates at the top and bottom of the drawer
 due to the gap and the matrix tube steel
The accuracy of the derived correction factors was believed by the experimenters to be ±1% or
better.
The foils used for measurements of absolute reaction rates and cell factors were calibrated by the
following independent methods:
 a) comparison with absolute fission counters
 b) comparison with radiochemical analysis
 c) comparison with observed counting rate ratios for foils simultaneously irradiated on a
 rotating wheel in the ATSR thermal column
Bulk samples from U3O8 plates and some of the clad plutonium foils were analyzed
radiochemically to give absolute determination of 238U(n,γ), 238U(n,f) and 239Pu(n,f) reaction rates.
For fission rates, separated 99Mo activity was counted; for 238U(n,γ), separated 239Np activity was
counted.
The fission chambers were placed in 2 inch cubic voids several drawers away from the core center.
Foils adjacent to the faces of the fission chambers were included in the irradiations.
Total uncertainty for a cell-averaged reaction rate includes a component from the mapping foil
data and a component from the determination of the relevant cell factor. The discussion in Section
7.10.2.3 is generally applicable ANL-E foil measurements because ANL-E and ZPPR used similar
foils, similar plates and similar equipment. In fact, the Pu-U-Mo fuel plates and the majority of
the sodium plates used at ANL-E and ZPPR were identical.
Determining cell factors required measuring and/or calculating reaction rates inside Pu-U-Mo fuel
plates and depleted uranium (DU) metal plates. The plates used at ZPPR and ANL-E were solid,
so special procedures were required to determine in-plate reaction rates. There are systematic
uncertainties related to determining these in-plate reaction rates. Table 7.20 in Section 7.10.2.3
shows the systematic uncertainties for determination of in-plate reaction rates for the Pu-U-Mo
and depleted uranium metal plates.
The uncertainties for the depleted uranium plates in Table 7.20 are due to uncertainties in isotopic
composition and loss of fission products. Pu-U-Mo plates were canned, so it was not possible to
measure in-plate reaction rates for these materials directly. Uncertainties for Pu-U-Mo plates in
Table 7.20 arise from applying the results of the Stanford-Robinson experiment and measurements
with half-thickness fuel plates as discussed in Section 7.10.2.3.
Measurements with half-thickness fuel plates provided data that approximated the reaction rate at
the center and outer surfaces of a standard fuel plate.
Current computers, software and nuclear data can provide more accurate intra-plate reaction rates
than the intra-cell measurements that were possible when the ZPR/ZPPR machines operated.

 379

Approximations involved in determining in-plate reaction rates make a minor contribution to the
total uncertainty for cell-averaged reaction rates because the total uncertainty for the cell-averaged
reaction rates is dominated by the mapping foil uncertainty and the calibration factor uncertainty.
The second cell factor uncertainty component results from the counting statistics and foil
positioning uncertainty in the cell factor measurement. Counting statistics and foil positioning
uncertainty vary for different cell factors and measurement configurations. The exact nature of
the contents of neighboring drawers (SCF core, DCF core, radial blanket, etc.) affects the measured
reaction rates in foils in the cell of interest, so it was necessary to measure cell factors for various
environments and configurations in any ZPR/ZPPR assembly. In the present context, environment
refers to the unit cell for which the cell factor is being measured and the adjacent drawers on both
sides of the unit cell of interest.
The third uncertainty component for the cell factor determination is the appropriate uncertainty for
detector calibration for absolute reaction rate measurements.
The general consensus today is that current computers, software and nuclear data can provide more
accurate cell factors than the measured cell factors that were possible when the ZPR/ZPPR
machines operated.
The uncertainty in the determination of in-plate reaction rates from Table 7.20, counting statistics
for the relevant cell factor and the relevant detector calibration uncertainty must be added in
quadrature with the mapping foil uncertainty to determine the total uncertainty for the cell-
averaged reaction rate that corresponds to the selected mapping foil.
The mapping foil measurements are the primary reaction rate data. When the ZPR/ZPPR facilities
operated, it was necessary to convert the mapping foil data to cell-averaged reaction rates due to
computer hardware and software limitations. It may be difficult or impossible to compute mapping
foil reaction rates by Monte Carlo today, but it is possible to compute mapping foil reaction rate
distributions with high-fidelity deterministic models. The uncertainties associated with in-plate
reaction rates, detector calibration and the cell factor measurement can be eliminated if mapping
foil reaction rates can be computed with acceptable accuracy.
The recommendation made at the end of Section 7.10.2.3 for ZPPR foil measurements applies to
foil measurements in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 as well. If it is possible to compute mapping foil reaction
rates with acceptable accuracy, it is recommended that analysts calculate mapping foil reaction
rates rather than cell-averaged reaction rates because the uncertainties associated with in-plate
reaction rates, detector calibration and the cell factor measurement can be eliminated.
7.10.3.4 ANL-E Spectral Index/Reaction Rate Ratio Uncertainties
A reaction rate ratio or spectral index was determined by dividing one cell-averaged reaction rate
by another cell-averaged reaction rate at the same location. Spectral indices determined from
reaction rate measurements provide useful data for comparison with benchmark calculations.
Uncertainties in published spectral indices arise from foil mass and composition data, counting
statistics, physical characteristics of the foil counting systems, absolute calibration of the foil data
and conversion of point (mapping foil) reaction rate data to cell-averaged values. As noted in
Section 7.10.3.2, three calibration methods were used at ZPR-6 and ZPR-9. Table 7.26, Table
7.27 and Table 7.28 list the uncertainties for these calibration methods.

 380

The discussion of spectral index uncertainties in ZPPR measurements in Section 7.10.2.4 also
applies to ANL-E spectral index uncertainties because similar foils were used to make similar
measurements in similar configurations. The contributors to spectral index uncertainty listed in
Section 7.10.2.4 are a) the uncertainty for the mapping foil in the numerator, b) the uncertainty for
the mapping foil in the denominator, c) the uncertainty for the cell factor for the numerator
reaction, d) the uncertainty in the cell factor for the denominator reaction, e) the systematic
uncertainties in determination of in-plate reaction rates and f) the uncertainty in the calibration
factor for the reaction rate ratio. These six uncertainties are added in quadrature to determine the
total uncertainty for the reaction rate ratio or spectral index.
The uncertainties for the mapping foils were discussed in Section 7.10.3.1; the uncertainties for
the cell factors and in-plate reaction rates were discussed in Section 7.10.3.3.
The uncertainty for the calibration factor for the reaction rate ratio will depend on the method used
for detector calibration. No documents similar to Refs. 30 and 31 have been found for foil
measurements at ZPR-6 and ZPR-9. If a fission chamber was used for the calibration, the
uncertainties for the calibration factor will be similar to the uncertainties listed in Section 7.10.2.4
for ZPPR. If the calibration factor was determined by another method, the uncertainties for the
calibration factor will be different from and likely larger than the uncertainties listed in Section
7.10.2.4. Unless the report documenting the spectral indices for the assembly of interest lists the
method used to determine the calibration factor and the associated uncertainties, it may be difficult
to quantify accurate uncertainties for the published spectral indices for an assembly built on ZPR-
6 or ZPR-9.
Spectral indices published when ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 operated are based on cell-averaged reaction
rates because that was the standard practice at that time. Spectral indices based on cell-averaged
reaction rates includes uncertainties related to the cell factors, determination of in-plate reaction
rates and the calibration factor for the reaction rate ratio in addition to the uncertainties for the
mapping foil in the numerator and the mapping foil in the denominator.
Today it is possible to compute reaction rates for individual mapping foils using deterministic
methods. A new reaction rate ratio or spectral index can be determined based on just the mapping
foil data for the reactions of interest at the location of interest. The uncertainties for this new
reaction rate ratio, R, based on mapping foil data are the uncertainties for the two mapping foils
and the uncertainty for the ratio, SR, described at the end of Section 7.10.2.1.
The recommendation made at the end of Section 7.10.2.4 for ZPPR foil measurements applies to
foil measurements in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 as well. If it is possible to compute mapping foil reaction
rates with acceptable accuracy, it is recommended that users calculate spectral indices directly
from the mapping foil reaction rates rather than using spectral indices based on cell-averaged
reaction rates because the uncertainties associated with cell factors, determination of in-plate
reaction rates and the calibration factor for the reaction rate ratio can be eliminated for spectral
indices based directly on mapping foil data.
7.10.4 Material-Related Uncertainties
The direct experimental uncertainties for foil measurements and for the data derived from foil
measurements, i.e., spectral indices, are discussed in Section 7.10.2 and Section 7.10.3. However,

 381

there is an indirect (and largely second-order) source of uncertainties related to the effect of
uncertainties in material compositions on the measured values and on data derived from the
measured foil data such as spectral indices. Section 7.1 divided uncertainties in criticality
measurements into uncertainties related to the measurement, uncertainties related to geometry and
uncertainties related to materials, i.e., uncertainties related to the compositions of the plates,
drawers and matrix tubes. Section 7.10.2 and Section 7.10.3 addressed uncertainties related to the
foil measurements. The effects of geometry uncertainties are not significant for foil measurements.
The effects of composition-related uncertainties can be significant in a limited number of cases.
ICSBEP benchmark MIX-COMP-FAST-001 [5] contains an extensive analysis of the effect of
material composition uncertainties on the total uncertainty assigned to the benchmark k eff for the
ZPR-6/7 uniform core configuration. The effects of a subset of the material composition
uncertainties on calculated spectral indices were examined in the IRPhEP benchmark for ZPR-6/7
(see benchmark ZPR-LMFR-EXP-001 in Ref. 6).
The selected composition uncertainties were:
    1.   Plutonium mass (0.0805 wt.%)
 235
 2. U enrichment in depleted uranium in Pu-U-Mo plates (0.01%)
 3. Matrix steel mass (2 wt.%)
    4.   Sodium mass (0.15 wt.%)
 5. Iron mass in iron oxide plates (0.5 wt.%)
    6.   U3O8 mass (0.15 wt.%)
 235
 7. U enrichment in U3O8 plates (0.02%)
 235
 8. U enrichment in depleted uranium reflector (0.02%)
This particular subset was chosen to examine sensitivity to a wide range of plate types and
materials and because these uncertainties made the largest contributions to the total material
composition uncertainty in MIX-COMP-FAST-001. Other material composition uncertainties
made much smaller contributions to the overall uncertainty in MIX-COMP-FAST-001.
Deterministic calculations with the benchmark model for loading 41 were used to examine the
sensitivity of the calculated spectral indices to these composition uncertainties. Table 2.3.7 of
IRPhEP benchmark ZPR-LMFR-EXP-001 [6] shows calculated effects of the material
composition uncertainties on measured spectral indices for the ZPR-6/7 core region. Total
material composition uncertainties in that table ranged from 0.019% to 0.373%. None of the
uncertainties in material compositions were significant for the spectral indices in the ZPR-6/7 core.
Table 2.3.8 of IRPhEP benchmark ZPR-LMFR-EXP-001 shows calculated effects of the material
composition uncertainties on measured spectral indices for the ZPR-6/7 blanket region. Total
material composition uncertainties in that table ranged from 0.100% to 2.237%.
The significant uncertainties in Table 2.3.8 of ZPR-LMFR-EXP-001 were uncertainties for
spectral indices involving the threshold fission rate for 238U, i.e., spectral indices for F8. For cell-
averaged spectral indices in the core, total composition-related uncertainties were negligible for
non-threshold reactions (F5, C8, F9) and small for threshold reactions (F8). For cell-averaged
spectral indices in the blanket, total composition-related uncertainties were small for non-threshold
reactions but significant for the threshold F8.

 382

In general, the effects of composition uncertainties on foil measurements or spectral indices will
be negligible or small for non-theshold reactions and small for threshold reactions such as F8 (or
238
 U fission) in the core of a ZPR/ZPPR assembly, but there are a few obvious exceptions:
 1. ZPPR-20 included two launch accident configurations for a space reactor. The core
 spectrum was significantly softer in these launch accident configurations than in standard
 ZPR/ZPPR assemblies, so the effects of material composition uncertainties may not be
 small or negligible for the ZPPR-20 launch accident configurations.
 2. A few assemblies built in ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 simulated carbide fuel, e.g., ZPR-9/31. ZPR-
 6/10 and a few other assemblies included graphite plates in the core to shift the core
 spectrum down into the intermediate range to measure basic physics data in that range.
 3. There may be a few other ZPR-9 assemblies before ZPR-9/26 and some early ZPR-3
 assemblies that had softer core spectra than standard ZPR/ZPPR assemblies that simulated
 LMFRs.
In the radial or axial blanket of most ZPR/ZPPR assemblies except for the three groups listed in
the previous paragraph, the effects of material composition uncertainties on non-threshold
reactions for foil measurements and spectral indices will be small. The effects of some material
composition uncertainties on threshold reactions may be significant in the radial or axial blanket
of any ZPR/ZPPR assembly.
The importance of material composition uncertainties for foil measurements increases in the radial
or axial reflector because the neutron spectrum becomes progressivily softer as the distance of the
foil from the center of the core increases. Any significant material composition uncertainties for
foil measurements are added in quadrature with the other uncertainties for the foil measurements.
7.10.5 As-Built Models and Calculations
In principle, the foil reaction rates measured in a ZPR/ZPPR assembly could be computed by
Monte Carlo for an as-built model that included the foils. In practice, very large computer
resources would be required to calculate foil reaction rates measured in ZPR/ZPPR experiments
by direct Monte Carlo. An individual foil occupies a volume less than 0.001 in3 which is a
negligible fraction of the ZPR/ZPPR assembly volume or even a single drawer volume. In a
simulation, very few neutrons will enter any given foil, so the statistical uncertainty of the
calculated reaction rate for that foil will be very large. It might be possible to use weight windows,
splitting/Russian roulette and other forms of biasing to force more tracks through a given foil to
lower the variance for that foil. In fact, a single foil at the center of ZPPR-9 was calculated once,
but that calculation required a lot of human effort and computer time.
In most ZPR/ZPPR assemblies, there were foils distributed at 30 to 50 matrix locations in the core,
radial blanket, axial blanket and reflector to measure reaction rate distributions, so any technique
that lowers the variance for one foil or group of foils near the same location will make the variance
worse for foils at other locations.
Another problem with any direct Monte Carlo calculation of the foil measurements is that the flux
falls by several orders of magnitude between the core and the reflector, which exacerbates the
problem of obtaining meaningful statistics for calculations of foil measurements, particularly in
regions that are not near the center of the core.

 383

The combination of the negligible volumes of individual foils, the large number of foils in the core,
blanket and reflector, and the large reduction in flux between the core and reflector makes any
direct Monte Carlo calculation of foil measurements impractical for any realistic amount of effort
except possibly for one foil or a few foils near the center of the core.
Monte Carlo calculations with point detectors and other next event estimators are also impractical
for ZPR/ZPPR as-built models. A point detector or similar next event estimator would create a
score in each foil after each neutron interaction, but the complexity of the ZPR/ZPPR as-built
geometry makes this approach infeasible. Next event estimators can work well in models with
large, homogeneous regions because it is relatively straightforward to compute the contribution to
a next event estimator under those circumstances. However, as-built models of ZPR/ZPPR
assemblies do not contain any large, homogeneous regions. Instead, each individual matrix tube
in an as-built model contains many distinct cells (regions) with thicknesses ranging from ~0.1 mm
to ~10 mm.
Consider a neutron scattering event at point (x1,y1,z1) and a point detector at point (x2,y2,z2). The
point detector estimator assumes that the neutron travels directly from the collision point at
(x1,y1,z1) to the point detector at (x2,y2,z2) and scores the contribution to the point detector
estimator. This means that it is necessary to compute the distance through every cell (or distinct
region) between (x1,y1,z1) and (x2,y2,z2), to compute the appropriate cross section in each of those
cells and then to compute the optical path length through each of those cells. This process is
repeated for every point detector at every collision. For a few detectors in a model with large,
homogeneous regions, next event estimators can work very well. For an as-built ZPR/ZPPR model
with many thousands of very small cells and many foil locations of interest, next event estimators
such as point detectors do not seem to be computationally practical. This has been confirmed in
previous calculations of as-built ZPR/ZPPR models.
Note that the preceding paragraphs were written in 2024. It is possible that future developments
in Monte Carlo methods and computer hardware may make Monte Carlo calculations of foils in
as-built models practical, but at present it is not feasible to calculate statistically meaningful foil
reaction rates using Monte Carlo methods for a distribution of foils in a ZPR/ZPPR assembly.
Consequently, it is necessary to convert the as-built Monte Carlo models of foil measurement
loadings to deterministic models in order to perform meaningful calculations of the foil reaction
rate measurements. This comes with its own approximations but experience indicates that
sufficiently accurate results can be achieved.
There was a small amount of self-shielding in the foils. The agreement between calculated and
measured foil reaction rates will be improved slightly by accounting for this self-shielding. In
some cases, the reports state whether the published reaction rates have been corrected for self-
shielding in the foils. Itmay be possible for the analyst to account explicitly for self-shielding in
the foils in calculations if desired or necessary.
In a Monte Carlo calculation, the foils can be included explicitly in the as-built model although
the fundamental problem of the feasibility of Monte Carlo calculations of foil reaction rates in as-
built models remains.

 384

In a deterministic calculation, the analyst accounts for self-shielding during cross section
processing. The foil is placed at the correct location in the model of the drawer used for cross
section processing. It may be necessary to approximate the foil for cross section processing
because it may be difficult or impossible to represent the true foil geometry in a cross section
processing code. For example, in the case of a one-dimensional cross section processing code, the
foil is represented as a thin slab at the correct location. Past experience with generating foil cross
sections has also utilized Monte Carlo explicit geometry “lattice” representations of a ZPR/ZPPR
to obtain foil cross sections (order 1000 cm3 region of interest).
7.11 Measurement of βeff
Measurement of βeff was a difficult, complicated process. Consequently, the value of β eff used to
convert measured reactivities between the natural measurement units, inhours or cents, and the
computational reactivity units, Δk/k1k2 or pcm, was generally calculated by the ZPR/ZPPR staff.
E. F. Bennett used noise and static techniques to determine β eff in five ZPR-9 assemblies [32].
Yarlagadda, Bennett and Wade analyzed the measurements and calculated β eff for those five
assemblies [35]. Four methods were used to interpret the experimental data, propagate errors and
determine βeff from the experimental data.
The experimental uncertainty for the detemination of β eff was 2.27% for the noise technique, 10.6%
for the static technique, 10.7% for a mixed noise/static technique, and 3.5% for the ratio technique
[35]. The value of (C/E – 1) was small for the noise technique and the ratio technique, but the
value of (C/E – 1) was relatively large for the static technique.
For the five ZPR-9 measurements of βeff, the experimental uncertainty and the agreement between
the experimental measurement and the corresponding calculated value depend strongly on the
experimental technique. The noise technique produces the smallest experimental uncertainty and
smallest (C/E – 1).
For reactivity measurements discussed in previous sections, a 5% uncertainty in β eff was assumed.
Based on the spread of measured values of βeff, the associated experimental uncertainties and
values of (C/E – 1) in Refs. 32 and 35, the 5% uncertainty in β eff assumed above is consistent with
the best measurement technique, i.e., the noise technique, and the corresponding calculated β eff for
ZPR/ZPPR assemblies.
7.12 Other Experimental Measurements
Sections 7.1 – 7.10 discussed various types of experimental measurements that were commonly
performed in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies, but many other types of measurements were made between
the first loading of ZPR-3/1 in 1955 and the last loading of ZPPR-21 in 1990. In some cases,
especially early ZPR-3 measurements, the data are no longer relevant to fast reactor design. In
other cases, the available data may not be sufficient to model and analyze the experiment with
acceptable accuracy. It is not possible to discuss every type of experiment that was conducted at
the ZPR/ZPPR facilities between 1955 and 1990, but some measurements that were conducted
occasionally will be described briefly. It is noted that there are a substantial amount of documents
available that detail many experiments done or proposed at the ZPR/ZPPR facilities.

 385

The effects of the difference between the plate geometry in standard ZPR/ZPPR assemblies and
the pin geometry that would be present in the fast reactors being simulated was investigated by
using calandria and the limited supply of fuel pins in the inventory to construct pin zones. The
pins and calandria can be modeled, and the resulting configurations can be analyzed in the same
way as other reactivity measurements described above.
The alignment of columns of sodium plates (or of void cans in the case of voiding measurements)
created natural neutron streaming paths in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies. The reactivity worth of this
streaming was sometimes measured by creating a zone in which the plates were rotated 90° in
alternating drawers in a checkerboard pattern to block the streaming paths. The plate rotation
experiments can be modeled in the same was as standard configurations. However, calculating
accurate reactivity effects with good C/Es for the plate rotation experiments may be difficult
because the worth of neutron streaming in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies is relatively small. One such
checkerboard plate rotation was analyzed for ZPPR-12, but the resulting C/Es were poor. Rotation
configurations require a lot of drawer and plate handling, so it is likely that the plate shifting
discussed in Section 7.2 could be a significant additional and possibly unquantifiable source of
uncertainty for the plate rotation experiments.
Room return was generally very small in ZPR/ZPPR assemblies because the core was surrounded
by a thick blanket and/or reflector containing large amounts of depleted uranium and steel.
However, there were exceptions in which room return could be significant. In the GCFR Program
(ZPR-9/28, ZPR-9/29 and ZPR-9/30), the 40 – 50% void fraction in the core and blanket increased
the importance of room return. In some cases, room return became more important because the
reflector was relatively leaky, e.g., the aluminum reflector in ZPR-9 Assemblies 1 – 9. The effects
of room return were measured occasionally by introducing significant modifications in the radial
reflector and measuring the resulting effect on reactivity. Room return measurements can be
analyzed in the same way as other reactivity measurements.
Bennett [32] used reactor noise to measure βeff with low uncertainty (see Section 7.11). Noise
coherence measurements were used to estimate spatial decoupling in several ZPPR assemblies.
The ZPR/ZPPR staff used reactor noise techniques for various other purposes as well. To date, no
attempt has been made to model or analyze any of the ZPR/ZPPR noise measurements. One
potential difficulty regarding analysis of the noise measurements is finding the measurement data
in a form that is amenable to analysis. For example, in the ZPPR-15 spatial decoupling
measurements, the measurement data are presented graphically. It might be possible to use OCR
to convert the graphical data to a digital form, but that conversion would introduce an additional
uncertainty. The original reactor noise data are no longer available, so it is necessary to use the
available published data and to determine how to calculate results that can be compared to the
measured data.
Many other types of measurements were made on ZPR/ZPPR assemblies, but it may be difficult
to construct high-fidelity models of those experiments based on available data. Likewise, the
original measurement data are no longer available in many cases, and it may be difficult to compute
quantities that can be compared to the available data in a straightforward manner.

 386

8 SOURCES OF EXPERIMENTAL DATA AND RELATED INFORMATION
The reactor logbooks discussed earlier contain information about the reactor operating conditions,
e.g., control rod positions, temperatures and table corner separations, but they generally do not
contain any information regarding experimental measurements.
Any laboratory notebooks used to record measurements were discarded long ago. Likewise, any
tapes, disks or other electronic media used to store digital data from the data acquisition systems
have been discarded. Even if any of the electronic media still existed, the combination of physical
degradation and technological obsolescence would likely render them unreliable or useless at this
time.
The surviving information regarding the ZPR/ZPPR experimental programs consists of published
reports and related documents. Unfortunately, there is no single comprehensive listing of all
reports and documents related to the ZPR/ZPPR programs.
Much of the final documentation for programs at ZPR-3, ZPR-6 and ZPR-9 consisted of formal
Argonne National Laboratory (ANL) reports. The numbering convention for ANL reports
changed over time, but reports in this category would generally be designated as ANL-NNN or
ANL-XX-YY where NNN consists of two or more digits corresponding to the sequence number
in the series of ANL reports, XX probably consists of two digits designating the publication year,
and YY consists of two or more digits corresponding to the sequence number in the publication
year. In addition to documenting experimental measurements, the formal ANL reports also
covered experimental methods, analysis of experiments and related topics. These reports were not
limited to experiments done on ZPR/ZPPR, but included experiments done across the entire active
ANL fast reactor program.
Another related category of reports is the series of Reactor Development Program Progress
Reports. That series is designated ANL-RDP-NN where NN consists of two or more digits. The
ANL-RDP reports were monthly or quarterly progress reports sent to the sponsoring agency. Note
that ANL-RDP reports covered all aspects of reactor development programs at Argonne, so most
of any particular ANL-RDP report may cover topics unrelated to ZPR/ZPPR programs.
ANL-NT-175 [7] provides an overview of the critical experiment programs at ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and
ZPPR. Appendix C of ANL-NT-175 is a compilation of references for all assembly programs at
ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR. In addition, Appendix C of ANL-NT-175 also contains some general
references to critical experiment programs and their relationship to fast reactor development.
There may be additional references for critical experiments programs at ZPR-6, ZPR-9 and ZPPR,
but ANL-NT-175 is a starting point for information regarding critical experiment programs at these
three facilities.
There is no corresponding overview of assembly programs at ZPR-3 or compilation of references
for ZPR-3 assembly programs.
While some ZPPR programs may have published experimental measurements and related material
in formal ANL reports, most of the ZPPR experimental results and related materials were
published in a series of technical memoranda that were designated as ZPR Technical Memoranda.
These documents were initially numbered as ZPR-TM-NNN, but this designation was later
changed to ANL-ZPR-NNN where NNN ranges from 1 to 500. The entire series is frequently

 387

referred to as the ZPR-TM series. Some reports in this series were monthly or quarterly progress
reports, but many reports in the ZPR-TM series were devoted to a specific topic such as an
experimental method, analytical method or analysis of a specific experiment at ZPPR. Note that
occasionally a report number was assigned, but the report to which that number was assigned was
never issued. Consequently, there are a few gaps in the ZPR-TM series for unpublished reports.
ZPR-TM-500 is an index of the contents of all of the ZPR-TMs.
Many of the earlier reports in the ZPR-TM series cover critical experiment programs and related
materials at ZPR-6 and ZPR-9. Some of the late ZPR-3 programs are documented in the early
ZPR-TM reports. In addition, some of the earlier ZPR-TM reports covered experimental methods
and equipment used at ZPR-6 and ZPR-9.
It should be noted that the monthly and quarterly reports in the ZPR-TM series frequently contain
experimental data from multiple assembly programs, e.g., ZPPR-17, ZPPR-18 and ZPPR-19, in
the same report. In many cases, there was a significant time lag between measuring the data and
processing the raw data to produce the final measured values. In addition, occasionally published
data were revised, and the revised data were published in a later report. Consequently, to obtain
all of the measured data from a ZPR/ZPPR assembly program, it is necessary to examine the ZPR-
TMs for the time period when the assembly program was running and for a period of approximately
two years after the assembly program ended.
Although the ZPR-TM series became the primary vehicle for reporting experimental results,
analytical results and methods development in 1969, more formal ANL reports were sometimes
issued to document ZPR/ZPPR programs such as the GCFR Program (ZPR-9/28, ZPR-9/29 and
ZPR-9/30) and development of experimental or analytical methods of broader interest for the fast
reactor community.
The ZPR/ZPPR facilities were part of Argonne’s Applied Physics Division and its predecessors.
An important source of information is the Applied Physics Division annual reports that were issued
in the 1960s and early 1970s. In the 1960s and early 1970s, the Applied Physics Division issued
a formal annual ANL report documenting all analytical and experimental work performed during
the reporting period. Ref. 33 is one report in that series.
Another source of information is three sets of internal documents issued by the ZPR/ZPPR
facilities. These documents cover a wide range of topics including assembly planning, equipment
development, experimental methods development, operational methods, facility operations and
experimental results.
The available ZPR-3 documents include internal memos #60 – #90 and a series of progress letters.
The progress letters report experimental details and results from a variety of ZPR-3 assemblies.
ZPR-C referred to ZPR-C(hicago) or ANL-E, and ZPR-I referred to ZPR-I(daho) or ANL-W. The
ZPR-C memos are 198 internal memos concerning operations at ZPR-6 and ZPR-9. The ZPR-C
memos cover the time period from June 1969 through January 1981.
The ZPR-I memos are approximately 550 memos covering operations at ANL-W between June
1969 and the end of the ZPPR-21 program in 1990. The ZPR-I memos include some of the late
ZPR-3 assemblies and all ZPPR assemblies.
